<language>English</language>
<page-type>preface</page-type>
<sig>v</sig>

## PREFACE

"Florence, the most beautiful and most famous daughter of Rome" <note>original: "FIRENZE, la Bellissima e Famosissima Figlia di Roma"</note>—was no mere metaphor of Dante, but a very true title for the first of the modern states.

The accumulated energies of the Florentines were focused on the collective life of the trade associations, and in no other community was the guild system as thoroughly developed as it was in Florence.

A complete and connected history of the guilds has never been compiled. This present work is put forth—perhaps more tentatively than exhaustively—to supply that omission.

The subject is a large one, and the sources of information are many and various. I have tasted at many springs and drunk from many wells—and my subject matter has been drawn from the following sources: (1) Manuscripts from the twelfth to sixteenth centuries; (2) Printed matter, including books and periodicals; (3) Letters from authorities and friends; (4) Personal knowledge of Florence and the Florentines.

In the study of manuscripts, I have relied heavily on the labors of such experts as Emily Baxter, Guido Biagi, R. Davidssohn, Lewis Einstein, F. T. Perrens, J. A. Symonds, and Pasquale Villari, and I have freely used their readings.

This I have done because of initial difficulties regarding the time and funding required for original research. The early constitutions and statutes of many of the guilds were written in a nearly unsolvable mixture of abbreviated Latin and vernacular Tuscan—the deciphering of which would easily consume any person's natural lifetime. When I sought for some student to undertake even a superficial survey, I was met with the crushing but practical reply—"the result is not worth the effort!" <note>original: "the game is not worth the candle!"</note>

<summary>In this preface, Staley explains that his book aims to fill a historical gap by providing a comprehensive history of the Florentine guilds. He acknowledges the significant research challenges, including the difficult linguistic nature of original guild manuscripts, and credits several prominent scholars for their foundational work.</summary>
<keywords>Florence, Guilds, Trade Associations, Dante, historical research, manuscripts, Tuscan dialect, economic history, Emily Baxter, Guido Biagi, Pasquale Villari</keywords>

<header>PREFACE</header>

In the catalog of printed books in my bibliography, I wish to highlight the following as the most helpful: Biagi’s *Private Life of the Renaissance Florentines*; Cantini’s *Tuscan Legislation* <note>original: “Legislazione Toscana”</note>; Cibrario’s *On the Political Economy of the Middle Ages* <note>original: “Della Economia Politica del Medio Evo”</note>; Davidsson’s two works; Einstein’s *Italian Renaissance in England*; Hyett’s *Florence: her History and her Art*; Ildefonso’s *Delights of the Tuscan Scholars* <note>original: “Delizie degli Erudite Toscani”</note>; Perrens’ *History of Florence* <note>original: “Histoire de Florence”</note>; Peruzzi’s *History of Commerce and the Bankers of Florence* <note>original: “Storia del Commercio e dei Banchieri di Firenze”</note>; the works of “Leader Scott” <note>pseudonym of Lucy Emily Baxter</note>, Symonds, the Villanis (Giovanni, Filippo, and Matteo), and Villari.

The *Collections of Tuscan Laws*, *The Consultations* <note>original: “Le Consulte”</note>, *The Florentine Observer* <note>original: “L’Osservatore Fiorentino”</note>, *The Florence Gazette*, and the *Statutes of the People and Commune of Florence, 1415* <note>original: “Statuta Populi et Communis Florentiæ”</note>—published in Fribourg in 1778—have been quite invaluable. Indeed, I have used the last of these authorities extensively as a representative guide for the middle period of the Renaissance.

Through my correspondence, I have received very useful assistance from the late Rev. S. T. Baxter and Mrs. Baxter (“Leader Scott”), Dr. Biagi and Dr. Villari of Florence, Signore Lisini of Siena, and Mr. Langton Douglas of London. I beg to offer my heartiest acknowledgments to all of them.

In the same regard, I offer sincere thanks to Mr. G. F. Barwick and the staff of the Reading Room at the British Museum for their helpful and always courteous service; to Miss A. R. Evans—a devoted student of Florentine lore—for her helpful research; to Miss E. De Alberti for her excellent translations of Italian works; and to my publishers for their politeness and kind consideration.

***

Omissions are unavoidable in a work of this nature and scope. Furthermore, I readily admit that I have not updated all my information to the very end of the period I cover—for example, regarding “The Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers” and “The Guild of Silk.” This in no way affects my overall purpose or diminishes the usefulness of my work.

<summary>The author lists the key historical texts and archival records used to research the Florentine guilds and acknowledges the scholars and librarians who assisted in the project. He also notes that while some guild histories are not updated to the very end of the Renaissance, the work remains comprehensive for its stated purpose.</summary>
<keywords>bibliography, historiography, Florence, Tuscany, Renaissance, Guild of Bankers, Guild of Silk, British Museum, archival sources, statutes</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of "The Guilds of Florence" by Edgcumbe Staley. It follows the author's acknowledgments and discussion of his primary sources and reference works.</meta>

->PREFACE vii<-

Where dates are disputed, I have selected those that best fit my overall framework. The British equivalents I have assigned to the various coins used in Florence represent the average of their constant fluctuations in value. For example, I have valued the gold florin of 1252 at roughly ten shillings throughout this entire work.

In many instances, particularly in the final four chapters, I have followed my own judgment regarding artistic attribution and criticism, setting aside conventional theories. My arguments regarding Giotto and his Bell Tower <note>original: "Campanile"</note>, the Comacine Guild <note>An influential medieval guild of stonemasons and architects</note>, and the religious life of the Florentines are based solely on their own merits. I believe I am justified in my optimistic view of the superiority of Florence and its people over all rivals; by its very nature, Florence was not only the leader of the Tuscan League but the center of modern civilization.

I have intentionally avoided focusing on individuals—with the exception of the Medici family—and I have refrained from providing critical evaluations of individual Renaissance artists and writers. My goal has been to demonstrate that these figures were generally the protégés of the Guilds, acting as corporate bodies, or of powerful merchants.

Regarding the many Italian words necessarily used throughout this book, I must explain my approach. First, I have chosen to use archaic spellings because they better reflect the historical period than modern versions—for example: *Chronicle* <note>original: "Cronica", modern: "Cronaca"</note>, *Calimala* <note>the guild of cloth merchants; original: "Calimala", modern: "Calimara"</note>, *stretching-shed* <note>original: "Tiratolo", modern: "Tiratoio" or "Tiratorio"</note>, *Notary* <note>original: "Notaio", modern: "Notaro"</note>, and so on. Secondly, the definitions I have provided for Tuscan words in the text are those I find most appropriate for the subject. Where dictionaries failed to provide a suitable definition, I have provided my own, ensuring they remain entirely consistent with the context.

The illustrations come from many sources. I have utilized illuminated manuscripts from the British Museum and the Laurentian Library in Florence. Although these reproductions unfortunately cannot capture the exquisite coloring of those jewel-like miniatures

<summary>The author explains his methodology for currency conversion and dating, defends his focus on the corporate power of the Guilds over individual artists, and explains his preference for archaic Italian terminology.</summary>
<keywords>Florence, gold florin, Giotto, Comacine Guild, Medici, Renaissance, Guilds, historical linguistics, illuminated manuscripts</keywords>

->PREFACE viii<-

These have been reproduced both in their original sizes and as enlargements, though the latter has undoubtedly made their delicate penmanship appear coarser.

One very interesting feature of these beautiful pictures should be noted: while the skillful Florentine artists who drew them depicted figures in the Florentine costumes of the period, they added architectural details, furniture, foliage, and other background elements based on the local environment. In both Paris and Flanders, the superior craftsmanship of Florentine illustrators <note>original: "illuminators"</note> was fully recognized, and these artists received warm welcomes and generous pay.

I am indebted to many kind people for the inclusion of several magnificent Florentine woodcuts from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries in their original sizes. Among them, I thank Messrs. Kegan Paul & Co. for numbers 2, 15, 37, 41, 48, 54, 56, 59, 60, and 61, taken from Kristeller's *Early Florentine Woodcuts*; Bernard Quaritch, Esq., for numbers 68 and 69—and also for the reproduction of number 28 from a manuscript miniature.

I also wish to acknowledge the kindness of Messrs. Sampson, Low & Co. for permission to reproduce woodcut number 52; J. M. Dent, Esq., for number 7; the State Archives of Siena <note>original: "Archivio di Stato Sienese"</note> (Signore A. Lisini) for Plate XXIX; and Dr. <note>original: "Dottore"</note> G. Biagi for three plates from his *Private Life of the Renaissance Florentines*.

The small heraldic shields <note>original: "shields of arms"</note> appearing at the end of certain chapters are reproduced from drawings I made for this purpose. They are copied from sculptural and pictorial decorations on the facades of the Guild Shrine of Or San Michele and the Palace of the Merchants <note>original: "Palazzo della Mercanzia"</note>, as well as from the carvings above the doors <note>original: "overdoors"</note> of Guild residences, the Mint <note>original: "Zecca"</note>, and other buildings—some of which were actually removed during the last century.

Indexing such a comprehensive work has been no easy task. I have tried to prioritize trades, traders, trade customs, and trade processes rather than simply listing...

My enthusiastic love for the "City of the Lily" <note>Florence, so named for the red lily on its coat of arms.</note> has grown a hundred times over as I have worked through my story of *The Guilds of Florence*.

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE
## *THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE* <note>original: "LE ARTI DI FIRENZE"</note>

### CHAPTER I

### FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY

I. **FORMATIVE FORCES.** Geographical position. Climate of Tuscany. "A favored Race." Origin of Florence. Roman influences. Barbarian inroads. Charlemagne. "Florence the Beautiful" <note>original: "Firenze la Bella"</note>. The Popes. Guild <note>original: "Collegium"</note>. The Commune.

Early records missing. The Humble Ones <note>original: "Umiliati"</note> <note>A religious order influential in the wool trade.</note>. Feuds and warfare. "Change the State!" <note>original: "Mutar lo Stato!"</note>. Guelphs and Ghibellines. Battle of Campaldino. Machiavelli's views.
III. **EDUCATION AND CULTURE.** The Bell Tower—"Gospel of Labor." Boastings—"The Spirit of the Bell Tower" <note>original: "Il Spirito del Campanile"</note>. Shopkeeper-gentlemen. English travelers in Tuscany. Thomas's Diary.
IV. **TRADE ROUTES AND SEA POWER.** Roman roads. Commercial agents. Buonaccorso Pitti. Innkeepers <note>original: "Ostellieri"</note>. Commercial Treaties. Vastness of Florentine commerce. Foreign Consuls. Six maritime Consuls. The "Guild of the Sea!" <note>original: "Arte del Mare!"</note>. Florentine navy. International law. Reprisals. Florence as the head of the Tuscan League.

At the end of the Dark Ages, the classic Valley of the Arno served as a healthy nursery. There, gentle Florence nurtured three young sisters: Art, Science, and Literature.

No envious Paris <note>A reference to the mythological Judgment of Paris.</note> came that way to throw apples of discord among the enchanting Graces of the Renaissance. There was never any question about which sister possessed the most subtle magic; instead, each developed her own distinct and rare charms without competing with the others. With their voices harmonized and their heavenly hair intertwined, the three sisters linked their graceful arms. They danced gaily, their shapely feet moving the flowing, gold-threaded garments that softly veiled the perfect curves of their beautiful bodies. Their enchanting rhythm was the music of the new

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Civilization—we know it and them—but what of their origin? From where did they come? And who were their ancestors?

Commerce and Industry—that well-matched and well-mated pair—very early made their busy home by the Arno’s healthy banks. Sheltered by the gracious cliffs of Fiesole and the shady woods of San Miniato, they stretched their vigorous limbs along the virgin fields and fertile uplands, occasionally dipping themselves and their belongings in the invigorating stream. Strengthened by the crisp Tuscan breezes and cheered by the sunlit, sky-blue skies, they set about raising their sturdy family.

Industry—the loving Mother—stayed by the domestic hearth, tirelessly nourishing and encouraging her children (some of whom are depicted in the carvings on Giotto’s famous Bell Tower <note>The Campanile of Florence Cathedral, featuring reliefs of various trades and arts.</note>), while Commerce—the energetic Father—traveled the wide world over seeking markets for his wares, returning time and again with hands well filled with gold and other rare treasures.

Together, this hardworking pair produced from Nature’s generous bounty the woolly fabric, the silky strand, and brilliant dyes. These, wisely combined by skillful hands, provided their growing offspring with health, wealth, and wisdom too.

<margin>A hand-drawn bracket marks this paragraph.</margin>
To the intelligent student of Florentine history, it comes as no surprise that her people—so violent in political quarrels, so refined in culture, and so magnificent in their lifestyle—were all the while a nation of shrewd businesspeople: enterprising merchants, skillful artisans, and diligent workers.

From the twelfth to the end of the sixteenth century, Florence easily held the first place in the life and work of the known world; she was, in fact, Athens and Rome combined! The reason for this preeminence must be attributed to three factors: the circumstances of climate, geographical position, and the unique characteristics of the race.

The climate of Tuscany—a highland country of hills and plains—shared neither the draining temperature of the sluggish south nor the severity of the frozen north. Men...

# FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY

...thrived greatly under stable weather conditions which aided healthful labor and inspired enterprise.

Geographically, Florence was the mistress of the world's commerce. In her hands, she held all the northern roads to Rome, while like a Colossus, her feet were placed upon the waterways of Venice and Genoa—the great trading centers of the south. From Pisa, she ruled the seas.

The Tuscan race was a fusion of many vigorous lineages: Etruscan, Greek, Latin, and Teuton. Each element played a specific role in forming a people who were, physically and mentally, equal to any and every task they chose to set for themselves. Dino Compagni <note>A 14th-century Florentine chronicler and politician.</note> describes the Florentines of the fourteenth century as "built with a beautiful stature beyond other Tuscans" <note>original: "formati di bella statura oltra le Toscani"</note>, and calls them "the favored race."

Vitality of mind and body, and the free exercise of industrial instincts, were the seeds from which grew all the splendid characteristics of the Florentines of the Renaissance.

Shelley's muse sings this:

> ->“ Florence, beneath the Sun,<-
> ->Of cities, fairest one! ”<-

The origin of Florence is shrouded in mystery and shadow. Fiesole <note>An ancient hilltop town overlooking Florence.</note> is said to have been one of her maternal ancestors, and Dante calls her:

> ->“ Etruscan Fiesole—the hilly cradle of a noble race. ” ¹<-

In any case, at a very remote period, the warlike people of the hills used to descend to the riverbanks to trade with those brave lowlanders who ventured that far.

At the meeting point of the Fiesole stream—the *Mugnone*—and the *Arno*, a small settlement of peaceful men and women gradually appeared, and there the primitive markets of the countryside were centered. This settlement quickly became a town of considerable size and importance and was known to the Romans, officially, as *Fluentia* <note>Latin for "flowing," the name from which "Firenze" or "Florence" eventually derived.</note>.

<meta>This page continues from page 2, continuing the discussion of the legendary and historical origins of Florence, moving from its relationship with Fiesole to the Roman era and the subsequent barbarian invasions.</meta>

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

When Julius Caesar came to Fiesole to avenge a Roman defeat—where the Consul Fiorinus had been killed—he changed its name. It had been marked on his military chart as *Campus Martis* <note>Field of Mars</note>, but he renamed it Fiorentia in honor of his relative's memory.

Florus <note>A Roman historian of the 2nd century.</note> ranks Florence with Spoletium, Interamnium, and Præneste as "those splendid *municipalities* <note>original: "municipia"</note> of Italy"; and Pliny includes the "*Fluentini* or Florence" in his list of Romano-Etruscan colonies.

While dates are all uncertain, we know that the Romans rebuilt the town on the usual *Castrum* <term>a Roman military camp or fortified town layout</term> plan of intersecting streets, and lived there among all the typical buildings of a Roman commercial city. Her growth and trade received a great boost from the construction of the magnificent Flaminian Way, which crossed the Arno at the point where the Ponte Vecchio <note>Old Bridge</note> still connects the two parts of the modern city.

The civilization and prosperity of the Roman *Castra* <term>fortified towns</term> were swept away by the wild invasions of the barbarians from the North. Wave after wave of savagery rolled over the entire land. Goths, Vandals, Lombards, and Saxons had their way with the pleasant fields and lovely gardens of the Arno. Finally, Totila—known as the "Scourge of God"—arrived and butchered the remaining inhabitants, leaving fair Florence as nothing but a wasteland and a rubbish heap.

Roman farms, villas, baths, and theaters were leveled to the ground. Where busy gates, docks, and markets once gathered crowds of skilled workers—coming from productive fields and herds, from the sea and riverside, and from busy looms and noisy smithies—there were now only ruined walls and battered gates. Behind the scattered stones lurked the cowardly sons of industrious ancestors. Their hands, lacking honest skills, sought only the stolen goods of their neighbors.

Along with the conquering Lombards came many German families, who were granted tracts of Italian land for living and farming. Drawn by its fertile promise, many bearded and fur-clad barbarians settled on Tuscan soil. Their chieftains built castles there, employing...

# FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY

...the forced labor of the wretched people of the land. From these strongholds, they exercised lordship over simple laborers and rough workmen, while every one of them paid due homage to their feudal lord.

Barbarians came and barbarians went, and hundreds of years rolled by. Nothing but the ancient Christian shrine of San Giovanni <note>The Florence Baptistery</note> remained to show where Florence had once been. There, under its sheltering eaves, the good Baptist—their second patron saint of their well-being, established after warlike Mars was deposed—rallied the frightened survivors of the city and the refugees driven by misfortune.

Fragile huts—the homes of simple fishing folk—clustered by the riverbank, contributing to a new township. Boats began once more to travel down the stream in search of food and profit. People breathed again, their hopes revived, and they dreamed once more of life, peace, health, and work. The old fire in their blood awakened their lion-like energy, and another Florence rose from the ashes of the dead like a phoenix.

Under the strong rule of the good Queen Theodolinda <note>Queen of the Lombards</note>, who held her court at Ravenna between the years 556 and 625, busy hands unearthed the blocks of Roman masonry. Around the budding city, they built the *Primo Cerchio* <note>First Circle</note>—the first medieval wall. The tide of misfortune had turned, and beautiful Florence proudly raised her head to greet the Monarch of the West <note>Charlemagne</note>.

In 786, Charlemagne entered her gates with an imposing retinue. He found her people rebuilding the Romano-Lombardic town and busying themselves with many useful industries.

The wise king noted the vigor and intelligence of the townspeople, and he recognized especially their skill in processing skins and wool. He greatly encouraged these worthy crafts and granted new privileges. By decree¹ he extended the *Comitatus* <term>the territory under a count's jurisdiction</term> or *Contado* <term>the rural area surrounding and controlled by a city</term> to a three-mile radius from the Baptistery. The tears he is said to have shed at Leghorn <note>Livorno</note> at the sight of invading...

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Viking ships, which were draining the resources of Tuscany, must have been brushed aside as he approvingly bestowed upon the new city the title: "Beautiful Florence!" <note>original: "Firenze la Bella!"</note>—and beautiful she was, like a flower basket. In the words of Faccio degli Uberti: "For there a great basket of flowers has been placed!" <note>original: "Che li ra posta una gran cest dei fiori!"</note>

Two wise Popes—Adrian I and Leo III—did much in the eighth and ninth centuries to encourage the arts and crafts. Because no Italian at that time was capable of foundry work, Greek artisans in gold and bronze, in particular, were invited to settle in Rome. Rich silken hangings, which could not be manufactured in Europe, were imported from the East, and men were put to work to imitate them.

Paschal I, Gregory IV, and Sergius II took up the mantle of their predecessors and encouraged industrial arts of all kinds. Metal bas-reliefs and sanctuary lamps, glass vessels for the Mass and ornamental glassware, pottery mosaics, stone objects encrusted with gems, enamel painting, fresco decorations, and many other ornamental and useful crafts were fostered. These were promoted not only in the Eternal City <note>Rome</note> but also by craftsmen who traveled all over Italy and established settlements in Florence and other places.

The laborers continued to toil and the city continued to grow until, in 825, a *Collegium* <term>a commercial university for the Arts and Crafts</term> was established—as it was in other centers of population—under the auspices of the Emperor Lothair. This was the "Coronation of Florence." Every head of a family and every captain of a trade became a ruling councillor in a popular government conducted by public meetings.

As a fief of the Romano-German Empire in the tenth century, Florence governed its own commerce, collected its own taxes, and defended itself. Its influence and example spread in every direction. Its markets attracted dealers and adventurers from every land; its industries drew in workmen and apprentices. By liberating the peasants of the soil from the control of feudal lords, the city became the mistress of her own destiny as well as theirs.

Through all these means, Florence laid the foundations of the only...

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of the early development of Florence's trade councils and the coronation of the city under Emperor Lothair, transitioning into the emergence of the Commune and the influential reign of Countess Matilda.</meta>

->FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 7<-

free government possible in the Middle Ages—that of the Commune.

Determining exactly when the Middle Ages ended and the Renaissance began is an exceptionally difficult task. Italians, and Florentines in particular, never fell to the same dismal depths as other peoples; their intellects and energies were always much sharper and more active than those of most people living in the surrounding states. In short, Florence was a precious lantern that burned with an inextinguishable brilliance, lighting up all the cities of Europe.

Bonifacio III, Marquis of Tuscany, died in 1076 and left his formal sovereignty to his daughter, Countess Matilda. Popularly known as “the Great Countess,” she lived at Lucca but frequently held court in Florence whenever she was not fighting on the battlefield. Her fame was so great that many children born in Florence and the *Contado* <term>the rural territory surrounding the city</term> were named “Tessa” or “Contessa” in her honor.

Matilda was famous for her strict administration of justice. During the early years of her reign, she personally presided over the Court of Pleas, assisted by advisors whom she chose from the *Grandi* <term>the nobility or leading citizens</term>. She strongly encouraged the industries and trade of the Commune and readily approved the military expeditions of the *Popolani* <term>the merchant class or common people</term> against the aggressive nobles of the Empire. Nevertheless, the Countess had ambitions beyond the narrow borders of the *Contado* and allowed the city leaders to govern its affairs largely as they pleased.

In 1078, Florence was enclosed within its Second Wall, and at the same time, it was divided into six *Sestieri* <term>wards or "sixths"</term>. Each was presided over by a *Buonuomo* <term>literally "good man," a magistrate</term> chosen by Matilda from the families of the *Grandi*. This magistrate administered justice, governed the population, and commanded the militia of his ward.

In 1101, the Countess made an extended stay in Florence, and

...called together a Council of the *Anziani* <term>Elders or Ancients</term>—the heads of the *Grandi* <term>noble</term> families—and also the *Capitudini* <term>heads</term> of the *Popolani* <term>commoner</term> trades, to draft a constitution for the government of the Commune. In this document, the *Buonuomini* <term>Magistrates or "Good Men"</term> adopted a new title that showed their personal authority and independence: Consul—a title that, until then, had been held only by the supreme rulers of states.

After the death of Matilda in 1115, no one took her place as the ruler of Florence. Instead, the city's government was managed by the Six Consuls, who thus became the rulers of the Commune. At the same time, Florence renounced its loyalty to the Emperor and declared itself in control of its own destiny.

The preserved yearly records of the city begin only in the twelfth century. Eighteen of these—written on the back of Sheet 71 of Codex 772 in the Vatican Palatine Library—cover the years 1110 to 1173. A longer series of records, running from 1107 to 1247, is preserved in Codex 776 in the Magliabecchian Library in Florence. These documents include entries of the names of Consuls and other state officials, along with notes on contemporary events connected to the political and commercial progress of the inhabitants of Florence. It has been truly said: “Merchants made her history, and merchants have chronicled it.”¹

Meanwhile, another influence was at work during the Middle Ages that kept skilled labor and enterprising trade alive: the monasteries. In these institutions, manual labor was required to prevent idleness. Indeed, some communities were founded primarily on cooperative principles—for example, the *Umiliati* <term>The Humble Ones</term>, or the Humble Fathers of St. Michael of Alexandria.²

The Order began when many Italians, mostly Lombards, were banished to Germany by Emperor Henry I in 1014. These exiles united through religion and labor by working at various trades, particularly wool processing. Returning to their homes in 1019, they retained their...

Until 1140, the *Humble Fathers* <note>original: "Umiliati"</note> were laymen, but in that year the Order was changed into one composed solely of men in Holy Orders. It is true that they no longer performed the manual labor themselves, but they gathered around their monasteries and cells everywhere great numbers of lay workers of all ages and every class, whose labors they directed and whose morals they protected. The head of this early labor bureau was called the "*Market Master*" <note>original: "Mercato"</note>.

In no other city or republic did the Humble Fathers achieve anything like the success that marked their work in Florence. Indeed, in some places, the industry failed entirely to attract workers; for example, in Pisa—where they had begun operations about the same time as in Florence—they were forced, in 1302, to beg for alms to maintain their factory. A few years later, they were obliged to give up operations and leave the place entirely. In Florence, it was very different; their arrival in 1238 was warmly welcomed, and its importance was recognized by the shrewd manufacturers and workers.

<margin>Ink marks resembling closing brackets appear at the ends of the first three lines of this paragraph.</margin>
Three conditions appear to have been constant in the political and commercial history of Florence which, when viewed in connection with their possible effect upon one another, were absolutely contradictory. First: the incessant warfare—feuds, banditry, and retaliations—which kept the population in a constant turmoil. Florence herself stirred up some of these as she gradually acquired rural districts and went on to conquer and annex more distant towns and lands. Second: the extraordinary frequency with which the form of government was changed; "*Changing the State*" <note>original: "Mutar lo Stato"</note> became a household proverb. Magistrates who were acclaimed and trusted one day were disgraced, dismissed, and even killed the next. Third: the amazing prosperity of the city and the rapid increase of trade associations or Guilds, under fixed rules and duly elected officers. In truth, on one and the same day, a man might be called upon to fight to the death in

The struggle between the <term>Guelphs</term> <note>a political faction supporting the Pope</note> and the <term>Ghibellines</term> <note>a political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor</note>, which actually began shortly after the death of the <term>Countess Matilda</term>, was a struggle for supremacy between, on one hand, a democracy of merchants and traders—aided by their workers—and, on the other, an aristocracy of nobles and soldiers of fortune—supported by their retainers. These names were first used in Florence in 1215, but were originally given by <term>Emperor Frederick II</term>—the former to designate the supporters of the Pope, and the latter to distinguish the followers of the Empire.

The <term>Battle of Campaldino</term> on June 11, 1285, proved, through the victory won for Florence, the progress made in commercial enterprise and prosperity. In spite of many lengthy wars with all her neighbors, Florence was in a good and happy condition. Her population was increasing rapidly in number and in wealth. Every man was making money in his trade, and everything went as happily as a marriage bell. Festivals and feasts multiplied; children went about dressed in new garments of fine cloth and silk; and women, wearing garlands of fresh flowers and crowns of silver and gold—the work of skillful craftsmen—sang and danced the livelong day.²

->FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 11<-

Among her artisans and her peasants, class hatred still rankled, having always threatened her internal peace.

The constant feuds and factions that distracted Florence—from the first day in 1177 when the <term>Uberti</term> <note>a powerful Ghibelline noble family</note> tried to seize the Lordship until the very end of the Republic—did nothing more or less than refine political parties and test out policies. The substantial result was a level of solidarity that had no equal in Europe. Her rulers were men of exceptional grit, and her laws—forced by the urgency of circumstances—were notable for their commitment to liberty, broad-mindedness, and justice.

For example, the merchants of the <term>Calimala</term> <note>the guild responsible for the finishing and refocusing of foreign woolen cloth</note>—the finishers of imported woven cloth—carried on their business undaunted by domestic troubles. Its members belonged to every political party in the State. When the feud between the <term>Donati</term> and <term>Cerchi</term> <note>rival families whose conflict led to the Black and White Guelph factions</note> was at its peak, thirty-eight merchant families sided with the former—the <term>Neri</term> or “Blacks”—and thirty-two with the latter—the <term>Bianchi</term> or “Whites”—while just as many others remained neutral.1

In his *History of Florence*, Machiavelli provided an excellent and insightful view of the fluctuations to which governments are subject. He says:

> “The general course of changes in States moves from a condition of order to one of disorder, and from disorder, they pass back again to order. Since it is not the fate of worldly affairs to remain stationary, when they have reached their highest state of perfection—beyond which they cannot go—they must necessarily decline. Similarly, when they have descended to the lowest point and reached the very depth of debasement through their disorders, they must necessarily rise again, as they cannot go any lower.”2

> “Cities that govern themselves as Republics—especially those that are not well-structured—are exposed to frequent revolutions in their government.”3

> “The causes of nearly all the evils that afflict Republics are found in the great and natural enmities that exist between...”

Perhaps the most perfect, and certainly the most beautiful, building in Florence is the famous <term>Campanile</term> <note>the bell tower of the Florence Cathedral</note>. <term>Vasari</term> <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), an Italian painter and architect famous for his biographies of artists</note> says: "Giotto not only created the design for this bell tower, but also sculpted part of these 'stories' in marble, in which the beginnings of all the arts are represented." These stories are told in hexagonal panels, not in the formal and religious style common in that age, but freely from the perspective of everyday life. <term>Giotto</term> <note>Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267–1337), the pioneering Florentine artist</note> took great pride in his Florence and in her progress; therefore, he decorated his Campanile with records of her industries and her commerce.

His first subjects are "The Creation of Adam" and "The Creation of Eve." Next, he presents "The Labors of Adam and Eve"—the man working patiently with his spade, the woman with her weighted distaff. Then follows "Jabal—the father of those who have cattle," setting forth man's pastoral work. After Jabal comes his brother, "Jubal—the father of all who play the harp and organ." Tubal Cain is next in order—the teacher of the art of working in metals. Labor in the vineyard, personified by Noah, follows; and here the so-called Scriptural subjects end. The Seven Arts and Sciences follow in turn—Astronomy, Arithmetic, Geometry, Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric, and Music—each portrayed in a separate panel.

A dignified group comes next, probably illustrating the judicial function, and then three subjects showing man’s mastery over land, air, and sea: a horseman, an aeronaut (<term>Daedalus</term> <note>a mythical Greek inventor who designed wings of wax and feathers to fly</note>), and a ship with its crew of navigators.

Pastoral industries follow: ploughing and transport, along with painting represented by <term>Apelles</term> <note>the most renowned painter of ancient Greece</note>, and sculpture represented by <term>Phidias</term> <note>a famous Greek sculptor and architect of the 5th century BC</note>. These chiseled pictures of life and human activity have turned Giotto's Campanile into a pulpit, from which the "Gospel of Intelligent Labor" is preached for all time.

The Florentines of old looked down with obvious contempt on the citizens of other states, especially on the inhabitants of cities they had conquered. These cities, in turn, had petty rivalries among themselves—Siena, Pisa, Volterra, Montepulciano, San Gimignano, and the rest. Nothing pleased the citizens of Florence more than to boast of their victory in 1260 at <term>Montaperti</term> <note>The author likely refers to the long-standing rivalry involving this battle, though historically, Florence suffered a devastating defeat by the Sienese at Montaperti in 1260; the Florentines later avenged this at the Battle of Colle in 1269</note> and other successes whenever they met people from the defeated cities.

This characteristically Tuscan trait led every city to boast of its own importance and the superiority of its public institutions and buildings. The "<term>Spirito del Campanile</term> <note>original: "Spirito del Campanile" — "Spirit of the Bell Tower," a term for "campanilismo," or fierce local loyalty and pride in one’s own town</note>," as it was called, was nowhere more rampant than in Florence. There, everyone seemed only too ready to disparage their neighbors while boasting of their own prominence, the excellence of their craft, or the superiority of their city.

The Florentines were essentially a nation of shopkeepers, but at the same time, they were a republic of independent gentlemen. While they were more industrious than any of their contemporaries and more frugal than most people, their leisure was marked by creations in art, science, and literature, and their tables were distinguished by mirth, learning, and hospitality.

Each political party in the state sought in turn to outdo the other in the advancement and adornment of their beloved city. Fine work started by one party was refined and completed by another. Wealth, honor, and life itself were always at the service...

...of the State. Every man was, first and foremost, a citizen, and only then a private individual. The glory of "Florence the Beautiful" <note>original: "Firenze la Bella"</note> was the true mark of a family's social standing.

The Commune thrived remarkably despite the stimulating effects of constant political unrest, becoming the center of an intellectual culture so sophisticated and broad that it has no equal in world history. This culture was a democratic quality, not the exclusive possession of the elite. As a defining trait of the Florentines from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries, it is displayed in the architecture of <term>Arnolfo</term> <note>Arnolfo di Cambio (c. 1240–1302), the architect of the Florence Cathedral and Palazzo Vecchio</note>, the painting of <term>Cimabue</term> <note>Cenni di Pepo (c. 1240–1302), a pioneer of Italian painting who moved toward naturalism</note>, the sculpture of Giotto, and the poetry of Dante.

When discussing the acts, statutes, and laws of Florence, Dante describes the people as superior to all others in Italy for their civic virtues, unwavering faith, religious sincerity, and noble charity. He believed that all these excellent qualities formed the foundation upon which the city’s commercial dominance rested.

Florence was a Republic of merchants and artisans. Her citizens, though distinguished as *Nobility* <note>original: "Nobili"</note> and *Commoners* <note>original: "Popolani"</note>, were united under the general title "The People of Florence" <note>original: "Le Genti di Firenze"</note>.

A very important factor in the extraordinary drive and success of the merchants and craftsmen of Florence was the influence of education and literature on all classes of the population. Even the most ordinary people were <term>casuists</term> <note>those who resolve moral problems by applying general principles, often through clever reasoning</note>, philosophers, and diplomats; they were keen observers of human nature and instinctive judges of character.

During the Middle Ages, learning was regarded almost exclusively as the servant of religion, but in the era of the Renaissance, it was looked upon as a companion to everyday life.

One of the social phenomena of the era of the Republic of Florence—and one very difficult to understand from our modern perspective of education and economics—was the combination in the same person of a merchant or artisan with refined literary taste, scholarly culture, rare qualifications for political office, and sharp instincts for commercial business.

<header>FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY</header>

<margin>General character</margin>
Industry, which usually aims to supply necessities and luxuries, was from the beginning a means of power or at least improvement in all regions of human civilization. It provided the Florentines with a direct path to the highest achievements in art, science, literature, and discovery. Whether they were nobles, merchants, craftsmen, or laborers, they have been remembered as philosophers, public speakers, astronomers, writers, poets, painters, sculptors, architects, and more.

Interest was so intense among all classes in everything that increased knowledge and skill in the practice of their various trades that teachers of every level always found attentive audiences. In a letter from Petrarch to Boccaccio, he calls the Florentine intellect quick and subtle rather than serious and mature: <note>original: "O ingenia magis æria quam matura!" — "Oh, minds more flighty than mature!"</note>

Historians such as Ricordano Malespini, Dino Compagni, and Giovanni Villani tell many interesting stories about how widespread education was in Florence during their times. Tailors left their workbenches to attend lectures on Greek; blacksmiths set aside their hammers to take up the historian’s pen; wool carders found time to study law; barbers sought the professor's chair of poetry; and butchers engaged in literary research, and so on. "There was no one," says Dino Compagni, "in Florence who could not read," and "even the boys driving the donkeys sang verses from Dante!"

---

The establishment of the University of Florence was achieved in the same way the Guilds were brought into existence. It resulted from the great movement toward organization that began to sweep over Europe in the early eleventh century.

<margin>Association</margin>
By the middle of the thirteenth century, the partnership between learning and industry was fully recognized as a necessity for successful commercial pursuits. Classes were established from time to time for higher technical training, and at length, in 1349, the <term>Studio Fiorentino</term> <note>The historical University of Florence, established by the city government</note> was founded with an annual endowment of two...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the establishment of the University of Florence, detailing its rapid growth, its pioneering academic chairs, and its administrative similarities to the city's Guilds.</meta>

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

...one thousand five hundred gold florins—about £1,200 sterling—with Clement VI granting the Papal Bull for the recognition of the faculties. <note>Rashdall, "Universities of Europe," vol. ii. pp. 46-50.</note>

The development of the University was rapid. In 1348, there were only six faculties <term>original: scholæ</term> under as many teachers. By 1421, there were forty-two professors, and by 1472, a great number of branch academies and technical schools were thriving amazingly. The University of Florence holds the distinction of establishing the first chairs of Greek and Poetry in Italy—the former in 1360 and the latter in 1373.

Among the earliest professors was Master <term>original: Messere</term> Filelfo, who, in the latter part of the fourteenth century, had as many as four hundred pupils belonging to leading families. In 1360, Giovanni Boccaccio—the first Professor of Poetry—introduced Leontius Pilatus to the City Council <term>original: Signoria</term>, by whom he was appointed the first Professor of Greek. His appointment proved to be a great incentive for the Florentines to enter enthusiastically into the study of ancient monuments, which resulted in their superiority in the subtleties of the plastic arts.

The statutes of the "University of Scholars" <note>original: "Universitas Scholarum"</note>—as the legal title was known—were submitted to the "Revisers of Guild Statutes for the Commonwealth of Florence" <note>original: "Approbatores Statutarum Artium Communis Florentiæ"</note>. They were drafted in the same spirit and order as the statutes of the Guilds, with corresponding offices, bylaws, and other regulations.

Quite young boys were admitted to enroll, just as they were in the Guilds, and it was possible for an ambitious youth to attain his doctorate or degree by the age of seventeen.

Every student was required to be of legitimate birth and a registered native of Florence. There was no age limit and no class qualification. Each was allowed a stipend of one gold florin per month—a meager amount indeed—but medical students, who lived under very strict rules regarding dissections and other matters, were privileged to receive an allowance of red wine and spices—"just to keep up their spirits!" <note>Statuta Populo Florentiæ, p. 74.</note>

<meta>This page continues the description of the University of Florence's administration, moving from its organizational similarities to the Guilds to the specific regulations governing students and professors, as well as listing notable historical figures associated with the institution.</meta>

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Four licensed merchants were appointed as moneylenders, or pawnbrokers, specifically for students, who were forbidden from borrowing from anyone else. These officials were called *feneratori*—<term>Latin: usurers</term>. Additionally, no student was allowed to carry weapons of any kind.

The Rector was elected annually by a vote of all students who had reached the age of eighteen, and he was granted discretionary power over the entire University.

Theology students looked to Rome for professional advancement and financial support. In a University roll from 1404, some students are recorded as having requested and received two, three, or even more benefices <term>church appointments providing an income</term> from the Pope—with total gross revenues amounting to an annual value of roughly three hundred gold florins each!¹

Strict sumptuary laws <term>laws regulating personal expenditure on luxury items</term> were enacted. Students were forbidden from wearing garments made of "noble cloth"—as the high-quality, finished Florentine cloth was known—whereas professors were permitted to wear this rich material. Black was required for everyday use, but on state occasions, scarlet robes decorated with fur and gold embroidery were worn.

Only a few of the distinguished men connected with the University of Florence can be mentioned here:

*   **Leonardo Bruni Aretino** (1369–1441)—the man who revived the study of Greek.
*   **Leon Battista Alberti** (1405–1472)—architect and scientist.
*   **Angelo Poliziano** (1414–1494)—philosopher and writer.
*   **Antonio Minucci** (1431–1487)—lecturer in law and history.
*   **Pico della Mirandola** (1461–1494)—theologian and moralist.
*   **Leonardo da Vinci** (1452–1519)—engineer and humanist.

Many English travelers visited Tuscany—particularly during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries—and naturally found much to astonish them. Two of these, Sir Richard Guylforde and Sir Richard Torkington, were the first to write down their impressions. Their "Diaries"—written in 1506 and 1516, respectively—were shaped by a medieval spirit.

The civilization of the Renaissance, which they encountered, seems to have been quite beyond their comprehension. The things that struck them most strongly were the manufacture of glass at Murano and the use, by the Venetians, of basins and ewers <term>large jugs used to carry water for washing</term> in their daily washing!¹

In the middle of the fifteenth century, two other English travelers went on their separate ways through Italy. They were much more intelligent and more in touch with the movements of the age than the pair who had preceded them. As great admirers of the Florentines, they praised both their characteristics and their customs.

Hoby’s "Diary" is full of personal experiences. Everyone with whom he had social dealings charmed him with their gentlemanly manners. He was, later on, prompted solely by this experience to write his famous translation of "*Il Cortigiano*" <note>Italian: "The Book of the Courtier," a courtesy book by Baldassare Castiglione</note>. The richness of domestic decoration also impressed him. He slept, he says:
> "in a chamber hung with cloth of gold and velvet," while on the bed was "silver work, and the bolsters <term>long, thick pillows</term> were of rich silk."²

Thomas’s account³ is of a more ambitious character; he contrasts the universities of Italy, where the students were mostly gentlemen, with similar English centers of education, where, as he writes,
> "there, children of men of low status are sent to school in the hope of living upon hired learning <note>original: "live upon hired learning," meaning to earn a living through professional education rather than inherited wealth</note>."

The Italians, he says:
> "are modest in dress, neat at the table, and restrained in speech."

Regarding the division of classes, he was impressed by the fact that the leading merchants were, for the most part, gentlemen.
> "If there are," he writes, "three or four brothers, one or two of them go into a trade; and, in case there is no division of their father’s inheritance, then the merchants work for their brothers’ benefit, as well as for their own. And because their reputation does not suffer by reason of their trade, it follows that there are more wealthy men in Italy than in any other country."

With respect to Florence, all classes struck him by their talkativeness and their obvious desire to appear eloquent. “He is not,” he writes, “considered a man among them who cannot play the orator in his speech, as much in gesture as in word.” The Academy was one of the most interesting sights he saw during his visit. He describes how the learned Florentines, from various ranks of society, met there—the Duke among them. One person, chosen beforehand, would ascend the pulpit and deliver an oration lasting more than an hour. “Never have I heard,” writes the narrator, “a teacher <term>reader</term> in a school, nor a preacher in a church, conduct <note>original: "handle"</note> themselves better.”

After the fall of the Roman Empire, the trade routes, with their inns <term>hostelries</term> and relay stations <term>posts</term> for horses, were restored by Charlemagne and maintained by successive Emperors and their feudal lords <term>feudatories</term>. Three kinds of establishments were provided by the Imperial Government for its couriers and for foreign expeditions:
1. *Civitates* <note>Latin: "Cities"</note>, in the towns—where numbers of horses were kept for dispatch anywhere throughout the State. 2. *Mutationes* <note>Latin: "Changes" or relay stations</note>, in the villages—where relays of animals were stabled for immediate use. And 3. *Mansiones* <note>Latin: "Stayings" or lodging houses</note>, in the country—where men and horses, engaged in long and wearisome journeys, might rest for a while.

Generally, commercial travelers from Florence were men traveling in groups, but frequently enough, all the members of a family went abroad with a father or son who had been appointed as a resident agent in a foreign city for some wealthy business house.

# FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 21

A natural sense of self-interest was linked to these expeditions, which were always filled with adventure and romance.

A notable soldier, merchant, diplomat, and man of letters named Buonaccorso Pitti relates in his *Chronicle* <note>original: "Cronica"</note> how he completed his journeys through France and Germany in the year 1395. 

> "Being required," he writes, "to travel to Paris on behalf of the Florentine Republic, I set out on the 28th of January of that same year. I took the road through Friuli and spent thirty-five days in the snow with workers clearing the glacier before I was able to pass with ten oxen. I stopped in turn at Constance, Basel, and Langres... I returned by way of Burgundy and Germany. After arriving at Treviso, I sent my loaded pack horses on to Padua while I went to Venice. I left Venice on the 22nd of March, rested at Mestre, and reached Padua that night. On the morning of the 23rd, I set out with two good riding horses belonging to the Lord of Padua; without stopping to eat or drink, I reached Ferrara at eight o’clock that evening. There, I hired some of the Marquis’s horses and continued to San Giorgio, within ten miles of Bologna. In the morning, before sunrise, I arrived in Bologna, and taking two fresh horses, I reached Scarperia late at night. I arrived in Rome early in the morning of March 25th."

This distinguished Florentine—who had already been sent as an Ambassador to Paris in 1374—was also something of a financial gambler. He made risky investments, gave and accepted loans at high interest rates, and was prone to "short-selling" <note>original: "selling for a fall"</note>—as we say today. One day he was wealthy and the honored guest of princes and rich merchants; the next, he was ragged and broke, unable to raise even a few small coins <term>soldi</term> for a shave at Burchiello’s barber shop!

Many of the agents of Florentine commercial houses became as famous in the history of their city as they were in the wider world of Europe. # FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 23

They established themselves in Paris, Caen, Arles, Perpignan, Saint-Gilles, and other places in France, as well as throughout Flanders and Germany.

Trade routes crossed and re-crossed one another, but all converged upon Florence. Along these routes, her merchants entered into arrangements with various local rulers. In the early days, however, it was common practice for hill tribes to swoop down upon the pack trains that carried consignments of merchandise back and forth. To safeguard her commercial interests, Florence entered into many treaties with her neighbors: Pisa in 1171; Lucca in 1184; the <term>Lords of the Mugello</term> <note>original: "Signori del Mugello"</note>—who were robber chieftains—in 1200 for safe passage; Bologna in 1203 against trade reprisals; Faenza in 1204 regarding legal jurisdiction; Perugia in 1218 concerning the wool and silk trades; and the <term>Maremma</term> <note>The coastal region of Tuscany.</note> chieftains in 1251 for the security of cattle drives and other matters. Several treaties were made with Siena and Pisa that dealt with territorial as well as commercial policy.

Regarding sea-borne merchandise, the chief ports for Florentine trade were Ancona, Rimini, and Venice on the east, and Pisa, Leghorn <note>Modern Livorno.</note>, and Genoa on the west.

The commercial relations of Florence grew rapidly. Goro Dati celebrated the fact that—as he puts it—"The Florentines were well acquainted with all the holes and corners of the known world." In the fourteenth century, more than three hundred agents were dispatched every year on commercial journeys.

Resident Florentines were first appointed as Consuls at foreign ports in 1329. The qualification for this important office was simply citizenship, but only men who were expected to extend the fame and influence of Florence through their personal strength of character and business aptitude were chosen.

These officers were established in Eastern ports, where each was assisted by a secretary—with a monthly salary of four gold <term>florins</term> <note>The standard gold coin of Florence.</note>—two assistants, and a native <term>interpreter</term> <note>original: "dragoman"</note>. Each Consul had three horses at his disposal. He was forbidden to engage in trade himself or to act in any way for other states. His salary was paid by fees levied upon merchandise entering and leaving the port.

<note>Goro Dati, "History of Florence" [original: "Istoria di Firenze"], Book 4, p. 56.</note>

## THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE 24

In London, the Florentine Consul’s income was derived from percentages on Bills of Exchange <note>original: "Lettere di Cambio"</note> and on the value of cargoes bought and sold. Similar rates were in force at Constantinople, Lyons, Bruges, and other major trading centers. Florentine merchants and bankers were numerous everywhere: there were fifty-one business houses in Turkey, twenty-four in France, thirty-seven in Naples, and so forth.

The first significant benefit for the Republic was the granting of land at various foreign ports to build residences for the consuls, offices, warehouses, hospitals, and churches. Between 1423 and the end of the century, resident Florentine Maritime Consuls were appointed in Alexandria, Naples, Majorca, Constantinople, and Cyprus, as well as on the shores of the distant Black Sea, and in Persia, India, and China.

Attached to each of these high officials were chancellors, purveyors, interpreters, various inspectors, clerks, and a sizable bodyguard of soldiers. In short, "miniature Florences" sprang up everywhere; they claimed and obtained the same rights, privileges, and honors granted to the mother city. The costs of these establishments were covered by freight dues on cargoes entering and leaving the ports. Pisa was the most accessible port in Tuscany, and she was well worth the sacrifices that the wars with her brave and industrious inhabitants cost the people of Florence. Pisa had her own dedicated Consul, who ranked as the chief magistrate of a great maritime <term>Guild or University</term> <note>A "university" in this context refers to a formal association or corporation of people with a common purpose, rather than an educational institution.</note> associated with the <term>Cloth Merchant Guild</term> <note>original: "Calimala"</note> of the capital city. The majority of the raw wool imported by the woolen manufacturers and the foreign cloth consigned to the "Calimala" was unloaded on her docks. From there, it was sent to Florence or to various depots established in Prato, Empoli, Volterra, and Poggibonsi.

It is impossible to say exactly when Florentine merchants and <term>adventurers</term> <note>original: "venturers"; merchants who risked capital in overseas trade.</note> first focused on acquiring maritime facilities. The success of the Pisans, the

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Florence's maritime expansion, shifting focus from the establishment of foreign consulates to the city's strategic efforts to secure its own access to the sea through treaties and the acquisition of ports like Pisa and Talamone.</meta>

# FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY

The Genoese and the Venetians recognized the possibilities before them. Naturally, these two cities did everything they could to hinder the competition of their inland sister city, and had their own internal conflicts not played such a significant role in their commercial prosperity, they likely would have succeeded in blocking her ambitions.

Apparently, the first concrete step Florence took to obtain maritime rights was in 1254, when Pisa granted free import and export for Florentine merchandise. The treaty signed that year became the basis for the many disputes between the rival cities, which eventually led to the ultimate downfall of Pisa. For many years, however, Florentine merchants were content to hire the ships of established maritime states.

In 1279, Rosso Bazzaccari, a Pisan shipmaster, lent his fine new vessel, the *San Pietro*, to Nasico Nassi—a Florentine merchant—to transport two hundred mule-loads of goods from Porto Pisano to Palermo.¹

By 1285, the power of Florence was so great that the people of Pisa, wishing to maintain good relations, sent an embassy to the Florentine government. The ambassadors brought large, opaque glass bottles of what was claimed to be rich white Vernaccia <note>original: "Vernacera"</note> wine as gifts; however, they were found to be full of gold florins <term>gold florins</term> <note>The primary currency of Florence, containing approximately 3.5 grams of gold, which became the dominant trade currency of Western Europe.</note>!²

Many treaties were made with Pisa for the benefit of the Florentine shipping trade. These were all more or less favorable, although the Pisans did not hesitate to tax Florentine goods whenever and however it suited them. In 1329, Florence was placed on the same commercial footing as Pisa, and her merchandise was freed from all restrictions. In 1356, the port of Talamone was acquired from the Sienese because Pisa had returned to taxing goods, and the Florentine merchants hired fourteen war galleys to protect their trade from the Genoese and Pisans. The capture of Pisa in 1406 finally gave Florence possession of the entire Tuscan coastline.

In 1421, *I Sei Consoli del Mare*—**the Six Maritime Consuls**—were elected in addition to the trade consuls already established at Pisa. All six resided at Pisa until 1426, when three were stationed in Florence. Their duties were mostly similar to those of the Consuls of the Guilds. In fact, the sea and its navigation were annexed to the Republic of Florence and were enrolled among her *Arti* <term>Arti</term> <note>The professional and trade guilds that governed Florentine economic and political life.</note>!

The three Consuls at Pisa were occupied mainly as follows: 
1. To oversee all the commerce of the port. 
2. To encourage traders and navigators to use that port. 
3. To prevent contraband and to protect Florentine merchandise. 
4. To prepare the way for commercial treaties with other cities and states. 
5. To examine all bills of lading and ship's business papers. 
6. To inspect the crews and supervise the wages paid out. 
7. To inspect the vessels and undertake repairs. 
8. To keep accurate ledger accounts, and so on.

The three Consuls resident in Florence were required: 
1. To receive and file reports from Pisa. 
2. To furnish every sort of shipping information, which they were required to post in the loggia of the *Mercato Nuovo* <note>The "New Market" in Florence, a central hub for banking and the silk and gold trades.</note> and in other public places. 
3. To approve or reject the appointment of all men named for foreign consulates. 
4. To receive complaints and lawsuits regarding marine matters and to adjudicate them. 
5. To make representations to the Council of State in cases requiring official interference, and so forth.

The Sea Consuls settled the number of the crew for each vessel and its armament, and they appointed the officers; however, relatives of the Consuls could not be enrolled. Vessels taking the Eastern route usually sailed in September, and those to the West in February. Fifteen days before their departure, a public notice was posted. Merchants, skippers, and crew were permitted to reside at Pisa

Contracts with sailors were drawn up by the Maritime Consuls. Sometimes they leased galleys for a monthly or yearly rent, while reserving certain rights and imposing specific conditions. For example, in 1429, a galleon was assigned to Domenico Dolfini for five years, on the condition that he made five voyages annually, loaded his vessel with gold, silver, wax, and some thousand pieces of Florentine-made cloth, and unloaded his cargoes only at Porto Pisano <note>The primary port of Pisa.</note>.

Both at Pisa and in Florence, the Maritime Consuls were charged with countless responsibilities beyond their technical authority. For example, at Pisa, the three Consuls performed the functions of the old city magistrates. They supervised the forests, fisheries, and other resources in the city's vicinity, and managed the export of native-grown grain, along with the duties of land drainage and cultivation.

The *Arte del Mare* <term>Arte del Mare</term> <note>The Guild of the Sea.</note> was an immediate and immense success. In the year it was established, six guardships were completed in the Port of Livorno—which had been declared a free port for Florentine merchandise. Through her Maritime Consuls, Florence encouraged foreign shipbuilders who were master craftsmen to settle at Pisa, Livorno, and her smaller ports. To each man was granted one gold florin a month for a period of two years, along with free housing for ten years. Shipwrights and caulkers were exempt from all taxes for twenty years.

Four broad-beamed galleons—*Galee di Mercato* <note>Merchant galleys.</note>—and six shallow-bottomed vessels—*Fuste* <note>Light, fast galleys.</note>—were immediately placed under construction, and one of each was launched every month. The timber came from the Forests of Cerbaie in Tuscany, which were declared State property in 1427, and the Mugnone sawmills were built at public expense.

FLORENTINE COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY

...commerce. The earliest maritime trade routes were: eastward to Tunis, Alexandria, Cyprus, Jaffa, and Constantinople; and westward to Sicily, Majorca, Barcelona, Marseilles, and Algiers. Certain vessels traded directly with British and Flemish ports. The voyages were precisely timed and regulated so that an effective connection was maintained among all ships at sea. The Port of Pisa <note>Porto Pisano</note> was the final gathering place for all freight vessels.

The first private merchant ships were built in 1480, and their owners were granted the rights previously held by the six Maritime Consuls. They were permitted to sail when and how they pleased and to load whatever cargo their owners or captains desired; however, all parties involved in the venture were subject to the same regulations that had existed previously. Beyond this, owners paid fees for the use of the piers, harbors, and warehouses.

By the end of the fifteenth century, the merchant navy of Florence included eleven large and fifteen small galleons—all in active service. Her special "galleon-florin"—minted in 1422 at the request of Taddeo Cenni, a Florentine merchant in Venice—was in wide circulation at a high exchange rate. In short, the <term>Arte del Mare</term> ("the Guild of the Sea") was the ancestor of the modern Lloyd’s of London insurance syndicate!

The invention of the compass did much to simplify maritime trade routes; voyages were shortened, coastal pirates were avoided, and ports of call became unnecessary.

The overseas commerce of the Renaissance and its development led to Florence’s global supremacy in material wealth and social progress. Goro Dati, writing about this dominance, valued the fixed capital of the Republic in his time—the middle of the fourteenth century—at twenty million gold florins.¹

What is now called International Law was completely unknown in old Florence and her territories. To those busy traders, nothing appeared more reasonable than to shut the door against neighbors...

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

...who would not submit to their terms, and to impose taxes upon all foreign products. Consequently, the treaties with Siena, Volterra, Pisa, Genoa, Lucca, Arezzo, and other communes and cities were dictated by commercial rather than political motives.

Insurance contracts were usually drawn up for all shipments, whether of goods or bullion. These were intended to protect against three chief contingencies: accidents on land, risks at sea, and the thefts of "light-fingered" criminals in general. The premiums paid by Florentine merchants ranged from six to fifteen percent of the declared value of the goods.¹

The issue of reprisals or retaliation was always a very important part of the policy of Florentine merchants. The origin of the system dates back to the days of Frederick II. In 1239, the <term>Podesta</term> <note>The chief magistrate of a medieval Italian city</note> of Pisa failed to forward to the Vicar of the Empire, Gebhard d'Arnstein, the sum of nearly five thousand pounds due to Count Ridolfo di Capraja. As a result, the Count received the authority and license to "seize the goods and persons of the Pisans" to settle that debt. This custom grew rapidly until, by 1298, the merchants of Florence enforced reprisals against Perugia for the sum of six hundred *lire*, Fano for two thousand, Spoleto for two hundred and fifty, Pisa for fifty-five, and Forli for fourteen hundred. Each of these towns had either borrowed money from Florentines or had seized merchandise on its way to or from Florence. Viterbo, Venice, and Padua received similar treatment.²

Against Sinola—where, in 1297, a pack-mule <term>sumpter-mule</term> <note>A mule used for carrying heavy loads or baggage</note> laden with fine Florentine cloth had been stolen—the Podesta, acting on the advice of the Consuls of the Seven Greater Guilds, awarded a sum of two hundred and forty gold florins for the value of the goods, two hundred for damages, and forty for the legal expenses attached to the suit. That same year, the Pisans were ordered to pay a fine of eight hundred *lire* for the plundering of a ship laden with corn.

Questions of retaliation were constantly arising between Florence and her great rivals, Genoa and Venice; as a rule, they were settled to the advantage of the tactful and resourceful men who guided the city's destiny. ### CHAPTER II

## GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS

I. **Origin.**—*Colleges of Workers and Artisans.* <note>original: "Collegia Opificum et Artificium"</note> Community of interest. Mutual protection. Lothair. First Florentine Consuls. *The Powerful, the Wealthy, and the Commoners.* <note>original: "Potente, Grasso, Minuto"</note> Ancient families. Clan associations <note>original: "Consorterie"</note>, or "Society of Towers." Companies <note>original: "Compagnie"</note>, or "Trade Corporations." Early mentions of trades.

II. **Development.**—*Good Men* <note>original: "Buonomini"</note>, or Trade Consuls of Guilds. The council of the "Heads" or "Priors" of the Seven Greater Guilds. First List of Guilds—seven Greater—fourteen Lesser. <term>Podestà</term> <note>The chief magistrate of the city</note>—Guido Novelli. <term>Gonfalonieri</term>—Standard Bearers. Military element. Charles of Anjou. Five Intermediate Guilds. Struggles between Capital and Labor. Giano della Bella. Second List of Guilds—twelve Greater, nine Lesser. "Defender of the Guilds." Freedom of industry. The "Ordinances of Justice." <note>original: "Ordinamenti della Giustizia"</note> A Code of Guild Statutes. Financial Position of the Guilds. Duke of Athens. "The Powers." <note>original: "Le Potenze"</note> The <term>Guelph Party</term> <note>original: "Parte Guelfa"; the political faction supporting the Pope</note>. The "Ciompi" Rising <note>A 1378 revolt by unrepresented wool carders and lower-class workers</note>. Michele Lando. Three Workmen's Guilds—*Artisans and laborers.* <note>original: "Artieri e operai"</note> Countless minor trade associations. Third List of Guilds. Four Universities of Trades under the Medici. Shrinkage and decay.

III. **Constitution.**—Compulsory Guild membership. *The Unaffiliated!* <note>original: "Scioperati!"</note> Conditions and Rules. Apprenticeship. Women eligible. Officers. Differences and disputes. Emigration of Artisans. Pains and Penalties. Various Prohibitions. Hours of work. Public clocks.

The origin of the Florentine Guilds has been accurately traced back to the corporations of merchants and artisans that existed in Rome under Numa Pompilius. They were called "Colleges" or "Bodies of Workers and Artisans." <note>original: "Collegia or Corpora Opificum et Artificium"</note>

These "Colleges," which by their rules could be mobilized for military purposes, also went by the name of "Schools"—meaning "Schools" or "Professions." <note>original: "Scholæ"</note> In times of peace they were known as "Schools of Arts," <note>original: "Scholæ Artium"</note> but in war they were enrolled as "Schools of Soldiers." <note>original: "Scholæ Militum"</note> <sup>1</sup>

Men of similar age, instincts, tastes, and occupations gathered in these various "Schools," which protected their common interests and supervised their morals and general well-being. Each

# GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS 35

The "*Schola*" <note>original: "Schola" — Latin for school or guild association</note> was provided with a staff of properly qualified and legally appointed teachers, who instructed young men and boys in the duties and responsibilities of craftsmanship. Under the supreme authority of the State, each "*Schola*" or "*Collegium*" <note>original: "Collegium" — Latin for an association, society, or guild</note> was governed by its own officers. These officials were chosen from among and by the admitted members, and the leaders were called "Consuls."

For a long time, the "*Scholæ*" flourished greatly and provided immense benefits to all classes of people. However, from the fall of the Roman Empire until well into the ninth century, the "*Scholæ*" appear to have suspended their charitable activities; at any rate, very little is recorded about them or their members during this time. Continuous feuds and devastating wars scattered both merchants and artisans far and wide. The light of industry and the torch of commerce were put out. The land was stripped bare, and cities and towns were either destroyed or turned into camps for mercenary soldiers.

Nevertheless, some of the industries and enterprises that the "*Scholæ*" had encouraged continued fitfully and uncertainly within families or through individuals working alone without a formal organization. As the pressures of hardship eased and the security of life and property became more certain, traditions that had been passed down in secret from father to son once again became established rules.

Shared interests—the need for mutual defense and the advantages of cooperation—asserted themselves once again. In various places, the economic structures of the old Roman "*Collegia*" began to revive. This was the state of affairs in Italy when, in 825 AD, the Emperor Lothair issued his "*Constitutiones Olonenses*" <note>original: "Constitutiones Olonenses" — The Ordinances of Olona, a legislative act regulating education and associations</note>. In this decree, eight cities and towns in northern Italy were named as suitable population centers for the establishment of new "*Collegia*" or "*Scholæ*."

These cities were Bologna, Cremona, Florence, Ivrea, Milan, Padua, Turin, and Venice. The "*Scholæ*" in each location had a different name, reflecting the specific industrial character of each city. For example: in Bologna, they were called "*Compagnie*" <note>Companies</note>; in Florence, "*Capitudini*" <note>Leagues or leaderships</note> or "*Arti*" <note>Arts or Guilds</note>; in Padua, "*Fragili*" <note>Fraternities or Guilds</note>; and in Venice, "*Consorti*" <note>Partnerships</note> or "*Matricole*" <note>Registers or membership rolls</note>; while Rome retained the original...

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

the style of a "guild" <note>original: "Collegium"</note> or "corporation" <note>original: "Universitas"</note>. It is quite interesting to note that in the case of Florence, the title "Heads of Families" <note>original: "Capitudini"</note> exactly expresses its political constitution, while the designation "Guilds" <note>original: "Arti"</note> indicates its industrial characteristics.

Apparently, the Florentines were somewhat slow to take advantage of the provisions in Lothair's "Constitutions" <note>original: "Constitutiones"</note>. Rome had Consuls leading its industries by 901, and Ravenna followed in 990—where the corporations of butchers, fishermen, merchants, and others were regularly organized. Ferrara did the same in 1015. However, Florence showed no distinct progress until the first year of the twelfth century. For nearly three hundred years, the city had endured an almost endless series of petty conflicts and class jealousies. Eventually, the people split into two camps: the "Nobles" <note>original: "Grandi"</note> and the "Traders" <note>original: "Popolani"</note>.

These nobles were the direct descendants of the old Teuton lords. After acting as robber-captains, they made peace offerings to the traders. The traders, in turn, accepted them as leaders for punitive and aggressive expeditions against raiders and their fortresses. As early as 1081, a joint expedition against robber bands—who infested the territory around Florence and looted the pack-mule trains traveling back and forth—proved that united action between noble and trader was wise.^1

Some of these nobles <note>original: "Grandi"</note>—such as the Uberti, the Donati, the Alberti, the Caponsacchi, the Gherardi, the Lamberti, and the Ughi families—combined the life of landed property owners with the role of city magnates.^2

Many noble families were also allowed a governing influence in the affairs of the trade associations, and quite a few descendants of the nobility sought admission as active participants in commercial businesses.^3 These nobles laid aside their titles and even changed their names so that their integration into the industrial life of the City-State <note>original: "Commune"</note> might be—

The Tornaquinci, Popoleschi, Tornabuoni, Giachiotti, Cavalcanti, Malatesta, and Ciampoli were among the Nobles <note>original: "Grandi"</note> who thus joined their fortunes with the Commoners <note>original: "Popolani"</note>.
