> “Caponsacco had already descended
> To the market from Fiesole: and Guida
> And Infangato were good citizens.” ¹

In this way, the division of the population into two parts was modified, and we find Florence arranged into three classes: 1. The Powerful <note>original: "Potente"</note>—the ruling class; 2. The Wealthy <note>original: "Grasso," literally "Fat"</note>—the middle class; and 3. The Little People <note>original: "Minuto"</note>—the working class.

The population of Florence, her trade, and her fame increased rapidly; but along with her prosperity, a dangerous rivalry developed between the noble families and their retainers, and the merchants and their workpeople. The latter, while readily admitting nobles into their trading and industrial societies, resented the claims of the Nobles <note>original: "Grandi"</note> to superiority in the control of public affairs.

The seizure of power on one hand was met by the encroaching on privileges on the other. A spirit of resentment was born which embittered the conditions of Florentine life for many generations. The breach between the two extreme parties in the local government <note>term: Commune; the self-governing urban political entity</note> widened gradually, and the influence of the middle class was unable to bridge the gap.

The nobles formed themselves into defensive organizations known as Clans <note>original: "Consorterie"</note>—or the Society of the Towers <note>original: "Societa delle Torre"</note>. Each clan consisted of a noble family—or a union of noble families—their households, and their dependents. They built fortified palaces which served as residences in times of peace and as fortresses during popular riots: “Families of the Tower and Loggia” <note>original: "Famiglie di Torre e Loggie"; a loggia is an open-sided gallery or room</note> became a common expression for families of distinction.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the noble families in Florence and their integration into the social and political structure of the city, transitioning into the architectural and organizational defenses used by both the nobility and the emerging merchant class.</meta>

<page-num>39</page-num>
<header>GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS 39</header>

"Towers" were common, and twenty of them featured "loggias" <note>original: "Loggie"</note>, or arcades, for festivities and public displays. Some of these towers rose to a height of 270 feet, but in 1250 they were all reduced to a height of fifty feet to comply with the demands of the *Popolani* <note>The common people or middle-class citizens</note>. It is a great shame that no pictorial representation of Florence and her towers has been preserved; she likely presented a far more imposing appearance than even San Gimignano does today.

Of the noble families who had towers within the city boundaries as early as 1186 were the Uberti, Malespini, Amidei, Buondelmonti, Donati, Adimari, Pazzi, Tosinghi, Ubaldini, Caponsacchi, Amieri, Nerli, Vecchietti, Tornaquinci, Soldanieri, Abati, and Infangati.

To counteract the power of the nobles, the traders organized themselves into *Compagnie* <note>Companies or Corporations</note>. Each one was made up of merchant families engaged in similar industries, along with their workpeople. These *Compagnie* were not only associations with fixed rules and regulations for conducting their trades, but they were also bands of men trained in self-defense, fully capable of holding their own during times of conflict.

Research into the Archives of Florence¹ reveals the existence of the following traders and trades during the eleventh and twelfth centuries:

Scipione Ammirato <note>A 16th-century historian of Florence</note> provides an account of how the city was governed in 1204,¹ as well as the order of seniority for the magistrates. At the head were two Consuls, known as the Military Consuls, who were the predecessors of the *Podestà* <note>The chief magistrate of a city-state</note> and the *Capitano del Popolo* <note>Captain of the People, a high-ranking official representing the middle class</note>. Following them were three Priors from the three principal Guilds: the "*Calimala*" <note>Cloth Finishers</note>, the "Wool" workers, and the "Bankers." Next were six Senators of the City, one Officer of Justice, and twelve "*Buonuomini*" ("Good Men")—with two representing the people of each <term>sestiere</term> <note>One of the six administrative districts of Florence</note>. Finally, there were Special and General Councils of influential citizens; the General Council included all the officials mentioned above, except for the members of the Special Council. Additionally, the three Priors appointed six Syndics or Inspectors—one for each <term>sestiere</term>—who reported to them daily on all public and private events occurring in their respective quarters.

This administrative structure demonstrates the immense power of control over public business—both commercial and political—exercised by the representatives of the Guilds. Indeed, the six Senators of the city were appointed by the six Greater Trades (one from each); in effect, they served as the Consuls of the Guilds.

The year 1204 is also memorable for a treaty between Florence and Siena. While this treaty protected the liberties of the Sienese, it also vastly increased the prestige and the wealth of the Florentines.

<meta>This page documents the formalization of the Florentine guild hierarchy in 1236, distinguishing between the Greater and Lesser Guilds, and begins to describe the political shifts of 1266 under Count Guido Novelli.</meta>

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>
<page-num>42</page-num>

This document is the first to bear the signatures of the Priors of the Trades or Guilds.

Several sub-councils played a part in the government of Florence. One of these—the third in rank and authority—was the “Council of the Heads of the Seven Greater Guilds” <note>original: "Consiglio delle Capitudini delle Sette Arti Maggiori"</note>. This council was summoned whenever new taxes had to be levied and for all matters concerning the trade and progress of the city.

In 1236, thirty-six "Good Men" <note>original: "Buonuomini," a group of respected citizens acting as advisors</note> assembled in a council at the residence of the Consuls of the “Calimala” merchants. By special decree, they met to determine the formal titles and order of precedence for the principal trade corporations operating in Florence. They divided them into two categories, which they called the “Greater” and “Lesser Guilds,” respectively—thereby emphasizing the distinction between the wealthy classes <note>original: "popolo grasso," literally "fat people"</note> and the common people <note>original: "popolo minuto," literally "small people"</note>. In the first category, they arranged the guilds in the following order: 

1. Judges and Notaries <note>original: "Giudici e Notai"</note>; 
2. Merchants of the “Calimala” <note>original: "Mercatanti o Arte di Calimala," the cloth-finishers and international merchants</note>; 
3. Money Changers <note>original: "Cambio"</note>; 
4. Woolen Manufacturers <note>original: "Lana"</note>; 
5. Silk Manufacturers <note>original: "Seta"</note>; 
6. Doctors and Apothecaries <note>original: "Medici e Speziali"</note>; 
7. Skinners and Furriers <note>original: "Pellicciai e Vaiai"</note>.

In the second category, the following crafts were placed: 

1. Butchers <note>original: "Beccai"</note>; 
2. Shoemakers <note>original: "Calzolai"</note>; 
3. Blacksmiths <note>original: "Fabbri"</note>; 
4. Leather-dressers and Tanners <note>original: "Cuoiai e Caligai"</note>; 
5. Builders and Stonemasons <note>original: "Muratori e Scarpellini"</note>; 
6. Wine Merchants <note>original: "Vinattieri"</note>; 
7. Bakers <note>original: "Fornai"</note>; 
8. Olive-oil Merchants and Provision Dealers <note>original: "Oliandoli e Pizzicagnoli"</note>; 
9. Linen Manufacturers <note>original: "Linaiuoli"</note>; 
10. Locksmiths <note>original: "Chiavaiuoli"</note>; 
11. Armorers and Sword-makers <note>original: "Corazzai e Spadai"</note>; 
12. Harness-makers and Saddlers <note>original: "Coreggiai"</note>; 
13. Carpenters <note>original: "Legnaiuoli"</note>; and 
14. Innkeepers <note>original: "Albergatori"</note>.

The year 1266 was a most important one in the history of the Guilds. Count Guido Novelli, who had been *Podesta* <note>The chief magistrate of the city-state</note> for two consecutive years and was virtually the absolute master of Florence, invited two members of a semi-religious Order in Bologna to follow

The Order, or Club—for that is what it truly was—was called the "Brothers of the Holy Virgin Mary" <note>original: "Fratelli della Santa Maria Vergine"</note>; but, in jest, it was known as the "Crowing Cocks" <note>original: "Capponi di Cinto"</note>! Its members were young men of noble families holding the rank of knight. Because of their extravagant and luxurious lifestyles, they were popularly known as the Jolly Fellows <note>original: "Frati Gaudenti"</note>!

<margin>¹ Villani, Book vii, chapter 13.</margin>
The two "Friars" <note>original: "Frati"</note> in question were Roderigo degli Andalò and Catalano de’ Malavolti—the former a Ghibelline and the latter a Guelph.¹

The new **Podestàs** <note>original: "Podestas," the chief magistrates of the city</note> were formally installed in the Badia <note>original: "Badia," the Abbey, which served as the official residence of the Head of the State</note>. To assist them, a Council of Thirty-six **Good Men** <note>original: "Buonuomini"</note> was chosen by Novelli. This council was composed of an equal number of merchants and artisans, and was split evenly between Ghibellines and Guelphs.

This Council met daily in the offices of the **Calimala** <note>original: "Calimala," the guild of international cloth merchants</note> to advise the Podestàs, deliberate on matters of public interest, and arrange for the Republic's government expenses. The first business to occupy their attention was the reorganization of the Guilds. They had two primary goals: first, to increase the efficiency of industrial and commercial ventures; and second, to adapt the guilds to the military needs of the time.

The Council compiled a list of the six most important corporations, placing the professional "Guild of Judges and Notaries" at the top, just as it had been in 1236. After a thorough and detailed review of all existing regulations and provisions—which had developed out of long-standing traditions and customs—the Council drafted a preliminary constitution that was generally suitable for all the various Guilds.

In each Guild, three primary officers were appointed:

1.  The **Consul** <note>original: "Consul"</note>, who served as the Guild's representative in the supreme government of the Republic.
2.  The **Head** <note>original: "Capitudo," likely referring to the "Capitudine"</note> or Master, who controlled the internal affairs of each Guild.
3.  The **Standard-bearer** <note>original: "Gonfaloniere"</note> or Leader, who directed civil functions and military matters.

--- Page 86 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the 1266 political reforms in Florence, specifically the military organization of the Guilds under Standard-bearers and the subsequent power struggles between the democratic Guild factions and the Ghibelline nobility, eventually leading to the intervention of King Charles of Anjou.</meta>

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The last appointment was a complete novelty, and it indicated an important development in the political character of the Guilds, as well as a new direction in the Government of the Republic. To each **Standard-bearer** <note>original: "Gonfaloniere"</note> was entrusted a Standard, or Banner, decorated with the coats of arms assigned at that time to each Guild. The craftsmen were allowed free use of these banners, thus becoming organized groups of armed citizens who could be called to their Standards whenever necessary. "These Standards, Banners, and Flags," says G. Villani, "were established so that if anyone in the city staged an armed rebellion, the members and associates of each armed company could stand under their banner <term>Gonfalon</term> to defend the people and the Republic."¹

These groups were called "Companies of Militia," which numbered twenty within the city and ten to twenty in the **surrounding countryside** <term>Contado</term>. According to the same authority, in the year 1338, there were twenty-five thousand men between the ages of sixteen and seventy capable of bearing arms.

Documents² from the year 1266 prove conclusively that the policy which dictated and successfully implemented the reorganization of the Guilds that year was strongly opposed by the Ghibelline **Chief Magistrate** <term>Podesta</term>, who was acting in sympathy with the **Nobles** <term>Grandi</term>. However, the popular movement was too strong for him; he not only had to yield but also had to pave the way for an alliance with the Pope.

The new constitution of the Guilds was distinctly democratic in character. It provoked violent opposition from the aristocratic party in the State, who eventually succeeded in abolishing the **Thirty-six Good Men** <term>Buonuomini</term> and restoring the dominance of the Ghibelline nobles.

King Charles of Anjou, who seized the office of Chief Magistrate in 1268, restored the Guelph influence. He brought back the "Thirty-six" but also appointed a private advisory board of twelve **aristocrats** <term>Grandi</term>. To calm public resentment against reactionary government, Charles accepted a Council of One Hundred, chosen—

<meta>This page continues the history of the Florentine Guilds following the 1266 reforms, specifically focusing on the exclusion of the lower classes from political power and the eventual rise of the Lesser Guilds.</meta>

...exclusively from the **Commoners** <note>original: "Popolani"</note> to assist his Privy Council. At the same time, the Consuls of the Seven Greater Guilds were established as a Court of Final Appeal in all legal cases, whether political or commercial.

The **Small People** <note>original: "Popolo Minuto"</note>—the members of the Lesser Guilds—were entirely ignored. Consequently, a vast political and social hostility was created, which later erupted in a destructive revolution.

Below the **Small People**—which actually consisted only of those members of the Lesser Guilds who had been granted the right to vote <term>Franchise</term>—was the great mass of the population: the *Ciompi*, or working classes. They were derisively called "Wooden Shoes" and possessed no civic rights of any kind. They were denied the privilege of free association in companies, corporations, or craft guilds. Their labor conditions were nearly as harsh as those of the early inhabitants of Florence under the rule of the old Lombard lords.

Times, however, were changing. There was a growing ambition among the lowest classes to achieve, at the very least, the right to vote and the power of trade association, even if they could not yet win the right to a share in the government of the Republic. Dormant forces were gathering that needed very little to be roused, and that awakening was not far off.

. . . . . . . .

Gradually but surely, the Lesser Guilds were rising in importance. This was due not only to their increasing membership and the social status gained through their growing wealth, but also because members of the Greater Guilds were investing money in the various minor crafts.

A leveling-up of social classes was achieved in 1280, when five of the Lesser Guilds reached such influential positions that they were publicly recognized as a group separate from the other nine. 1. **Butchers** <note>original: "Beccai"</note>—wholesale and retail.
2. **Shoemakers** <note>original: "Calzolai"</note> and leather workers.
3. **Smiths** <note>original: "Fabbri"</note> and workers in metals.

The Five Intermediate Guilds—whose chief officers had not yet been granted the prestigious title of Consul—were often invited to join the discussions of the Consuls of the Seven Greater Guilds on equal terms. Such instances occurred in April 1285, September 1287, July 1293, and January 1297.¹

During the election of Priors <term>high-ranking city magistrates</term> in 1293—which included Giano della Bella—Lapo Salterelli (a judge) and Dino Pecora (a butcher) spoke alongside well-known members of the Albizzi, Gualterotti, and Peruzzi families. These joint consultations were usually held in the Baptistery of San Giovanni and were presided over by the <term>Podestà</term> <note>the chief magistrate of the city</note> and the <term>Captain of the People</term> <note>the political leader representing the middle class and the guilds</note>.

These Five Intermediate Guilds do not seem to have attempted to officially enroll among the Seven Greater Guilds. The reason may have been that their backgrounds and social connections were quite different. There is always a social divide between the upper professional classes and the ranks of tradesmen and artisans.

However, we should probably examine this unexpected situation more closely. For the shopkeepers and superior workmen of Florence, gaining freedom from an inferior social and political status—and being accepted into a higher circle of prestige and influence—must have been very attractive. On the other hand, there was a clear danger of being completely absorbed into a complex system of city life where the ruling powers held absolute rank, wealth, and authority.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Florentine guild system's reorganization and the establishment of the Priors as the city's executive body following the 1282 list of guilds.</meta>

-># THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

In 1415, the Guilds were reorganized into Seven Greater and Fourteen Lesser Guilds, a structure that continued until 1534.

In 1282, Bartolo de' Bardi of the "Calimala" <note>refiners of imported cloth</note> merchants, representing the district <term>sestiere</term> of Oltrarno; Rosso Bacherelli of the "Bankers," representing San Piero Scheraggio; and Salvi del Chiaro Girolamo of the "Wool Merchants," representing San Pancrazio, were elected Priors <note>the chief magistrates of Florence</note>. They held office for two months and assumed the right of residence with the Captain of the People in the Badia <note>the Abbey of Florence</note>. Through their aristocratic behavior, they "created an aristocracy among the Traders."¹

During their term of office, a new position was created with the title of "Defender of the Guilds and Crafts, and Captain and Preserver of the Peace" <note>original: "*Difensore dell' Arti e degli Artefici, e Capitano e Conservatore della Pace*"</note>. The first person to hold this high office was Bernardino della Porta, a renowned wool merchant. Consequently, there were three supreme magistrates: the *Podesta* (the President of the Republic, who was always a foreigner); the Captain of the People (a nobleman); and the Defender of the Guilds (a merchant).

Two councils, composed exclusively of members from the three Senior Guilds, were assigned to the "Defender." The following year, due to constant lobbying by their Consuls, three more Priors were added: Ghanus Detaineti for the Silk Guild <note>original: "*Arte della Seta*"</note>; Viezus Vecosii for the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries <note>original: "*Arte de' Medici e Speziali*"</note>; and Toginus Aurifex for the Guild of Furriers and Skinners <note>original: "*Arte de' Pellicciai e Vaiai*"</note>. At the same time, the title of "Defender of the Guilds" was changed to "Captain of the Guilds." He took precedence over the "Captain of the People," ranking second only to the *Podesta*.

The steadily increasing wealth of the Merchant Guilds and the strongly aristocratic leanings of their members sparked feelings of resentment and jealousy among the craftsmen of the Lesser Guilds.

While in theory every citizen worked for the common good, in practice, disagreements arose periodically. Under various excuses, these conflicts became more or less intense between the members of the different Guilds regarding customs duties, manufacturing processes, legal privileges, and monopolies.

***

¹ "The Consultations" <note>original: "*Le Consulte*"</note>, pp. 116-140 (Dr. Hartwig).

--- Page 91 ---
<meta>This page continues the history of the Florentine guild system's economic regulations and the legal measures taken by the Priors between 1290 and 1292 to prevent monopolies, ensure trade liberty, and punish fraud.</meta>

->### GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS<-

Both merchants and artisans did not hesitate to abandon long-established methods. Questions regarding prices, samples, and business agreements—which had governed industries for years—were openly ignored. Every man sought to take advantage of his neighbor; in short, a kind of internal toll system was established between different trades and between individual men.

To such a point did these disturbances reach that on June 30, 1290, the Priors <note>the chief magistrates of Florence</note> issued a decree which re-established free trade and prohibited all types of customs duties and private settlements <term>compositions</term> <note>financial arrangements made to bypass standard taxes or legal penalties</note> within the limits of Florentine territory. Secret inspectors were appointed to ensure that no craftsman, whether belonging to the Greater or the Lesser Guilds, attempted to violate the freedom of labor and sale.¹

On July 3 of the same year, two decrees were passed by the Priors which prohibited members of the Merchant Guilds, under heavy penalties, from creating monopolies, secret compacts, or agreements for fake <term>spurious</term> sales. Every type of business procedure designed to impose arbitrary prices on goods was also strictly prohibited.²

Any merchant or trader guilty of neglecting these provisions was subject to legal proceedings and was liable to a fine of one hundred pounds. Moreover, the Guild to which such a person belonged was fined five hundred *lire* for failing to enforce the decrees, and the Consuls, Rectors, or Priors were each fined two hundred *lire*.

Other decrees were passed in 1291 and 1292. In the latter year, the Consuls and heads of all the Guilds met in a conference and added one more severe regulation to the Code of Prohibitions—specifically, the removal from the <term>Matriculation Registers</term> <note>the official membership rolls of the guilds</note> of the names of any offenders convicted of fraud or falsification of any kind.

Appeals to the Pope, to the Emperor, or to any foreign power or prince were severely punished; and the Notaries who assisted—

<meta>This page continues the history of the Florentine guild system's economic regulations, specifically detailing the strict legal measures taken to protect the rights of artisans and the common people against the Florentine nobility through the landmark "Ordinances of Justice" enacted in 1293.</meta>

->THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

Those involved in drawing up such appeals were punished by being suspended from their offices. These measures—which were almost Draconian in their severity—served as effective safeguards against the merchant aristocracy's attempts to seize the rights and liberties of the artisan democracy.

Freedom of industry was always a prominent feature of the Republic’s political structure. In 1475, the <term>Signoria</term> <note>the supreme governing body of Florence</note> actually passed a law stating that every man was free to earn a living as he chose. This could be done without needing approval from legal judges or medical doctors regarding his competence, and without obstruction or interference from unethical citizens.

A significant and historic turning point for the Republic’s liberties and commerce was the passing of the <term>Ordinamenti della Giustizia</term> <note>Ordinances of Justice</note>, which became law on January 18, 1293. These have been called the Magna Charter of Florence. Their primary supporter, if not their actual author, was the famous Giano della Bella, who sided with the common people despite belonging to the noble house of Pazzi.

This famous edict, which consisted of twenty-four provisions, was issued to protect the public from the increasing power grabs of the nobility. Its three main rules were:

1. The exclusion of the <term>Grandi</term> <note>the noble class</note> from the government.
2. The punishment of the *Grandi* for crimes committed against the <term>Popolani</term> <note>the common people</note>.
3. The expansion of the powers of the Craft Guilds.

Before this time, the office of Prior had always been open to any member of the nobility who also belonged to a guild. From this point forward, a noble could only hold this office if he publicly renounced his rank with the official approval of the Council of State.

Among the penalties was a death sentence for any noble who, either personally or through a hired assassin, killed a member of the common people. The law also ordered that his property be seized and his house completely demolished.^1

***

^1 P. E. Giudici, "History of the Italian Communes," <note>original: "Storia dei Comuni Italiani"</note> Book 6.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the legal and structural reforms in late 13th-century Florence, specifically following the enactment of the Ordinances of Justice which empowered the trade guilds and restructured the city's governance.</meta>

# GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS

The <term>Ordini</term> <note>the "Orders" or "Ordinances"</note>—as they were also called—confirmed the number and ranking of the Guilds. At the same time, they decreed that every member and apprentice must take a solemn oath upon joining to maintain peace and harmony.

The creation of trading companies that operated outside the Guilds' Constitutions, as well as the forming of agreements and contracts not authorized by established commercial law and custom, were made capital offenses. Any Guild that engaged in such transactions or permitted them was subject to a fine of one thousand *lire*, and its Consuls were fined five hundred *lire* each.

The passage of the "Orders" naturally provoked fierce and powerful opposition from the nobility and the merchant aristocracy. Their resentment was, in a sense, shared by many craftsmen and shopkeepers who relied on the patronage of these wealthier citizens.

By the end of the thirteenth century, a vast number of trade customs and business practices had become established. While these helped protect the Guilds' interests to some degree, they also caused some confusion and uncertainty in commercial affairs.

In 1300, the Heads of the Guilds, in consultation with the Chief Magistrates, decided to revise these statutes, regulations, and bylaws. On April 4, a "Commission of Seven Merchants" was appointed and given the authority to choose seven additional members. Neri Berri was named President, and consequently, the commission is known by his name. The fourteen commissioners were secluded in the monastery of the Servite Brothers for many days; each commissioner was provided with food, stationery, and an allowance of thirty-two *lire*. Their deliberations were unanimous, and they recorded their resolutions as statutes. In 1301, these received the approval of the Guild Consuls and the Chief Magistrates of the Republic. They were titled "The Statutes of the University of Commerce of Florence." <note>The term "University" (Università) here refers to a corporate body or guild of merchants.</note>

***

¹ <note>original: "Provvisione x. 216-226." These refer to the *Provvisioni*, which were the official records of the legislative acts and decrees of the Florentine Republic.</note>

The Statutes were made generally applicable to all the Guilds. Their incorporation into a formal charter provided each Guild—whether composed of merchants or craftsmen—with the core of its corporate constitution. The *Calimala* Guild, as the city’s leading trade organization, led the way by adopting the new Code.

The signatures ^1 attached to the report of these deliberations are interesting. They show not only the order of precedence among the Seven Greater Guilds at that time, but also the various ranks and titles of the signatories. The names of the "Judges and Notaries" appear first. There are six of them—one for each <term>sestiere</term> <note>one of the six districts or wards of the city</note>. Of these, three are judges styled *Dominus* <note>Lord or Sir</note>, and three are notaries. One of these is styled *Dominus*, while the other two are addressed simply as *Ser* or *Messere* <note>Master</note>. Next in order come the signatures of the four Consuls of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries." Two are styled *Magister medicus* <note>Master of Medicine</note>, while the others have no title.

Next follow the names of the three Consuls of the "Guild of Bankers and Money-changers." They have no titles, but one is distinguished as "Piero Borgi, who has his office in the old market," and so on. Four Consuls of the "Merchants of *Calimala*" come next, without any distinguishing titles. They are followed by the six Consuls of the "Guild of Wool," who are also untitled, except for the first, who is styled *Ser Notarius* <note>Master Notary</note>—a lawyer serving as a wool merchant!

The "Por San Maria Merchants" <note>The Guild of Silk Manufacturers and Retailers</note> are represented by four Consuls. Three are untitled, and the fourth is styled *Dominus*. Finally, there are the four Consuls of the "Skinners" <note>Furriers</note>, each of whom has the name of his specific constituency added: 
1. *de populo Sancti Stephani a Ponte* <note>from the parish of St. Stephen at the Bridge</note>
2. *de populo Sancte Cicilie* <note>from the parish of St. Cecilia</note>
3. *de populo Sancte Marie Ughi* <note>from the parish of St. Mary Ughi</note>
4. *de populo Sancte Liberale* <note>from the parish of St. Liberale</note>

The Duke of Athens <note>Walter VI of Brienne, who was granted temporary dictatorial powers in Florence</note> began his term of office as <term>Podesta</term> <note>the chief magistrate or governor of the city</note> in 1342 by yielding to the requests of the nobles and more prominent merchants. However, when he realized that his advances were met with distrust and that there was a movement to limit his authority, he sought another source of support. To gain favor with the common people, he appointed a butcher to lead the <term>Priors</term> <note>the executive council of the city government</note> whom he had nominated, placing three merchants and three artisans alongside him. This course of action met with violent opposition, but the Duke persisted in his populist policy.

His own position was largely due to the support of the populace, and consequently, he was obliged to show them some favor in return. He always spoke of the lower classes as "*Le bene Popolo*" <note>original: "Le bene Popolo" — The good people</note>. Among his smaller but quite significant measures, he permitted the "Association of Wool-Carders"—who had previously been entirely subordinate to the Guild of Wool Merchants—to have and display their own banner, which featured a Lamb. To the "Association of Wool-Dyers," who claimed they were being oppressed by the two great guilds of "Calimala" and "Wool," he—

conceded the privilege of being ruled by <term>Capitudini</term> <note>Heads or leaders of the guilds</note> of their own free choice.

For the benefit of the lowest orders of the population, the Duke formed six <term>Brigate</term> <note>Brigades or companies</note> or Societies—one for each <term>sestiere</term> <note>one of the six districts or wards of Florence</note>, with the title of "<term>La Potenza</term>" <note>original: "La Potenza" — The Power</note> or Local Authority. The duties of these Societies, which were comprised of the more prominent men or leaders of the lower classes in each quarter, were to elevate the tastes and pursuits of the people, and to encourage them to emulate the fashions of the wealthier citizens.¹

These measures proved to be encouragements and incentives for the people to seek, by fair means or by foul, a general betterment of their social and political condition. The way was thus made clear for the terrible "Revolt of the <term>Ciompi</term>" <note>The lowest class of laborers, specifically wool carders, who were not represented by a guild</note> in 1378, which marked the high-water mark of democratic power. Several causes contributed to the accomplishment of this <term>coup d'état</term> <note>original: "coup d'état" — a sudden, decisive exercise of force in politics</note>.

Jealousies and feuds between the nobles and the aristocratic merchants of the Greater Guilds were incentives for imitation on the part of the workers. The <term>Parte Guelfa</term> <note>The Guelph Party, a powerful political faction supporting the Pope</note>, through its immense wealth and power, had become an instrument of oppression. The promise of liberty and equality made by the defeat of the Ghibellines <note>The political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor</note> was not fulfilled. Espionage and tyranny were widespread. Every man's hand seemed raised to oppress those beneath him in position or in wealth. Such were the embers of a smoldering fire, which only needed the torch of revolution to kindle into a significant conflagration.

Piero degli Albizzi in 1370 made no secret of his family's intention to convert the Republic into an oligarchy. The Ricci, the Strozzi, and other influential families sided with the Albizzi. The <term>Popolo Minuto</term> <note>original: "Popolo Minuto" — The "little people" or the lower working classes</note> saw the danger which threatened the liberty of the tradespeople and artisans; but in Salvestro de' Medici—whose family ranked among the first of the <term>Popolo Grasso</term> <note>original: "Popolo Grasso" — The "fat people" or the wealthy, elite merchant class</note>—the popular cause found a true champion.

Salvestro was appointed to the office of <term>Gonfaloniere di Giustizia</term> <note>Standard-bearer of Justice, the highest judicial and executive post in the Florentine Republic</note>.

In 1370, Salvestro <note>Salvestro de’ Medici</note> was elected, and he immediately called an assembly of the people in the <term>Palazzo Vecchio</term> <note>The Old Palace, Florence's town hall</note>. A massive crowd filled not only the Palace but also the <term>Piazza della Signoria</term> <note>The main public square of Florence</note>. When Salvestro threatened to resign his office due to opposition from the aristocratic party, total chaos broke out. At the height of the excitement, Benedetto degli Alberti looked out of a window and shouted:— "Long live the people!" <note>original: "Viva il Popolo!"</note>

This was the spark that fell upon highly flammable material. The cry echoed throughout the city. Shops were closed, and the entire populace took up arms. The <term>Parte Guelfa</term> <note>The powerful political faction supporting the Pope</note> also armed themselves, but they did not dare to provoke a confrontation with the masses, who surged up from every quarter of the city.

The Consuls of the Greater Guilds intervened, but to no effect, and the armed companies of the Guilds marched into the Piazza under their banners. The <term>Ciompi</term> <note>The lowest class of laborers, specifically wool carders</note> assumed these bands were deployed against them, and the spark immediately erupted into a flame. This violence destroyed the palaces of the Albizzi, Pazzi, Strozzi, Soderini, Castiglionchi, Caviccioli, Buondelmonti, Serragli, and other noble families. Fire was set to the residences of the Guild Consuls, and some of them were completely destroyed, while the archives, documents, and membership rolls of many Guilds were ruthlessly burned.

A reign of terror followed, and the city was abandoned to looting and violence. Finally, an attack was made upon the Supreme Magistracy sitting at the <term>Palazzo Vecchio</term>. The magistrates fled, and the mob—headed by a wool-carder called Michele Lando, who carried the Standard of Justice which had been seized from the office of the <term>Gonfaloniere</term> <note>The high official responsible for justice and order</note>—rushed into the Council Chamber.

Lando turned around and, facing his followers, cried out, "Look, the Palace is yours, and the city is entirely in your hands. What will you do now?"

"Make you the Standard-bearer of Justice!" <note>original: "Gonfaloniere di Giustizia!"</note> was the thunderous reply.

A new government was installed on July 23rd, consisting of nine <term>Priors</term> <note>The chief magistrates of Florence</note>—three from the Seven Greater Guilds, three from the...

The first of these Subordinate Guilds was made up of nine or ten thousand wool-washers, wool-sorters, wool-beaters, wool-combers, and wool-carders, who had until then been attached to the Great Wool Guild <note>The Arte della Lana</note>. This Corporation was granted a banner bearing a figure of the Angel of Judgment with a sword and a cross.

The Second Guild was composed of dyers, fullers, carding-comb-makers, loom-makers, and weavers of wool, silk, and flax: their banner displayed a white arm upon a crimson field, the hand holding a sword upon which was inscribed "*Giustizia*" <note>original: "Giustizia"</note>—"Justice."

The Third Guild united together sheep-shearers, butchers, menders of skins, hosiers, knitters, tailors, makers of doublets, of banners, of church ornaments, of sandals, etc. Their banner bore the Divine Arm with a red sleeve, reaching out of a cloud and holding an olive branch.

There is much uncertainty regarding how the Statutes of 1301 were adapted to the unique circumstances of the new corporations. Nevertheless, there are entries in the records of the six <term>sestieri</term> <note>The six administrative districts of Florence</note>, and in those of the councils of the <term>Capitudini</term> <note>Guild leaders or captains</note> or Priors of the three new guilds, which show that their officers ranked as equals with those of the other guilds in holding public office. For example: in the district of <term>Santo Spirito</term>, Giovanni dei Capponi, a wool manufacturer of the "Guild of Wool Merchants," and Leoncino de Francino, a carder of the "Guild of Wool Workers," are named. In <term>San Giovanni</term>, the records mention Giovanni di Bartolo, a spicer and apothecary of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries," and Benedetto da Carlova, a sandal-maker of the "Guild of Workmen and Artificers.²"

The incorporation of these three guilds gave much satisfaction to the humbler and coarser citizens. The laboring class, though viewing the more comfortable lives of their wealthier fellow citizens with natural envy, were truly inspired by the grand old Florentine spirit. This natural ambition, which was a constant force for the improvement and advancement of every class, was based upon a universal sense and appreciation of high ideals.

However, prospects of contentment were quickly dimmed, and the newly enfranchised craftsmen became restless once more. They began to adopt the manners and even the clothing of the wealthier citizens, and developed a desire for military exercise.

The old spirit of insubordination was not dead, and men refused to work under the current labor conditions. <term>Giostre</term> <note>Jousts or tournaments</note>, or tournaments and feasting in the markets, held undeniable charms. Workshops were closed, and the streets were filled with idlers and merry-makers. Disorder and rioting soon became common. The principle "if a man wishes to eat, he must work" was ignored, and famine threatened the city.

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The three new guilds made a further demand: that a <term>staio</term> <note>A bushel</note> of corn should be given free to every man who asked for help. They also proposed a redistribution of public money. The entire body of the "Ciompi" assembled in the Piazza Santa Maria Novella and prepared to enforce these demands by force of arms.

Michele Lando again proved his resolve. He ordered the great bell to be tolled, and when the militia companies of the Guilds had assembled, he led them in person against his former associates, crying: "Long live the Trade Guilds and the People!" The undisciplined mob gave way, and the wool-comber <term>Gonfaloniere</term> <note>The "Standard-bearer of Justice," the supreme magistrate of Florence</note> surrendered his <term>gonfalon</term> <note>A processional banner or flag</note> as a pledge that peace was assured. This marked the end of the "Ciompi" Revolt.

The dominance of democratic power was, nevertheless, short-lived, for the year 1382 was marked by the intense efforts of the nobles and aristocratic merchants to reduce the influence of the <term>Popolo Minuto</term> <note>The "little people" or lower working classes</note>. Reforms were introduced into the election of high officials: the office of <term>Gonfaloniere di Giustizia</term> was again restricted to members of the seven Greater Guilds, while the office of Prior was shared equally by the seven Greater and the fourteen Lesser Guilds. The three new guilds were suppressed, and the number of recognized guilds was reduced to the original twenty-one.¹

In 1387, however, a concession was made to the claims of the working members of the community, whereby two new Priors were appointed to specifically represent the working population. Thus, the eight Priors who formed the new <term>Signoria</term> <note>The governing council of the Florentine Republic</note> consisted of two representatives for each of the four quarters of the city; this arrangement was confirmed by the Council of State in 1393.²

The subject of the precedence of the guilds, and their various ranks on the official Roll of the Guilds, is one that can never be satisfactorily explained. Some of the guilds that appear low in the hierarchy were composed of men of the highest distinction—for instance, the great architects and sculptors of the—

# GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS

The Renaissance belonged to the <term>Lesser Guild</term> of the “<term>Masters of Stone and Wood</term>!” Again, why should the “<term>Butchers</term>” be thirteen ranks higher than the “<term>Bakers</term>”? This inconsistent arrangement likely could not have been clearly explained even in old <term>Florence</term> itself. Ultimately, it was not so much a comparison of industries as it was a relative scale of workers that fixed each trade and its representatives in a traditional position within <term>Florentine Society</term>.

Below the fourteen <term>Lesser Guilds</term> there were, from time to time, groups of workers who organized themselves into trade associations. These were never recognized as <term>Guilds</term> in the generally accepted sense of the term. Under the date 1285, there is a paragraph in a <term>Codex</term> <note>An ancient manuscript text</note> titled *Various Manuscripts* <note>original: "Manoscritti varii"</note>, referring to the “<term>Guild of Bridle and Bit-makers</term>” <note>original: "Arte de' Frenai"</note> and the payment made to the Guild for some land between the <term>Porta Balli</term> and the <term>Porta Via Nuova</term>.

The Records¹ of 1309–1316 name many such associations under the general term <term>Arte</term> (Guild): “Coopers” <note>original: "Bottariai"</note>, “Bow and Arrow-makers” <note>original: "Arcariai"</note>, “Trough-makers” <note>original: "Madiariai"</note>, “Basket-makers” <note>original: "Cerchiariai"</note>, “Dealers in cloth remnants and cuttings” <note>original: "Baldrigariai panni"</note>, “Retailers of Sundries” <note>original: "Ritagliai"</note>, “Scrap-iron dealers” <note>original: "Ferravecchiai"</note>, “Poulterers” <note>original: "Pollaiuoli"</note>, and “Mattress-stuffers” <note>original: "Materassai"</note>.

The Archives contain a curious entry dated February 6th, 1321, in the form of a list of <term>Guilds</term> which had paid their share of the <term>Gabella</term> <note>An excise tax or, in this case, a forced war loan</note> levied the previous year. The loan in question amounted to the sum of 300,000 gold <term>florins</term>—roughly £150,000—and was undertaken not only by all the <term>Merchant and Craft Guilds</term> of the time, but also with the cooperation of the all-powerful <term>Parte Guelfa</term> <note>The dominant political faction in Florence supporting the Papacy</note>.

The number of <term>Guilds</term> or <term>Corporations</term> listed rises to forty-four! They include “Ironfounders” <note>original: "Fornaciariai"</note>, paying ninety-two <term>lire</term>; “Dice-makers” <note>original: "Dadaiuoli"</note>, paying two and two-thirds gold <term>florins</term>; and “Horse-jobbers” <note>original: "Prestatori Ronzoni"; those who traded or hired out horses</note>, paying sixty-seven <term>lire</term>.

In 1426, the aristocratic party in the State attempted to reduce the number of the fourteen Lesser Guilds to seven. The leaders of this movement were the Albizzi—who were always opponents of the popular cause—under the leadership of Niccolo da Uzzano. However, they were stopped in their efforts by the gallant opposition of members of the rising Medici family, who consistently presented themselves as friends of the people.

Early in the fifteenth century—due to the increased importance of the working classes and improved conditions for labor and wages—two new <term>Guilds</term> <note>original: "Arti"</note> were enrolled, though they were not formally incorporated. One of these, called the Guild of Haberdashers <note>original: "L'Arte de' Merciai"</note>, was an association of small shopkeepers and traders. The other, the Guild of Laborers <note>original: "L' Arte de' Lavori"</note>, comprised the lower class of workers and unskilled laborers.

By the year 1530, the Guild system had reached the peak of its splendor and power. After that, new economic forces came into play which led to the decline of many characteristics of Florentine industry and commerce. These forces perhaps had little effect on the Greater Guilds, but they produced many reforms and reorganizations within the Lesser Guilds and among their members.

A final grouping of the Lesser Guilds was completed in 1534. By a <term>Decree</term> <note>original: "Provvisione"</note> dated July 17 of that year, the "fourteen Lesser Guilds" were divided into four Universities. Each University was ruled by one Consul, one Chancellor, two Overseers <note>original: "Provveditori"</note>, three Treasurers, three Syndics or Inspectors, and four Messengers <note>original: "Donzelle"</note>—

This system of consolidation was necessary for several reasons. First and foremost was the decline in Florentine industries due to foreign competition. Second were the changing fashions and customs, along with the invention of new trades. Third was the absorption of the wealthier members of the Craft Guilds into the more aristocratic social circles of the nobles and merchants.

The fifteenth century ended with Florence so prosperous, beautiful, and healthy that she had no rival in Europe.

The closing of factories and shops, which was notable in the sixteenth century, did not, however, indicate a decline in wealth and influence. Rather, it simply showed that fewer men found it necessary to engage in humble occupations. The ranks of the wealthy and leisured classes were being steadily replenished by "new money" <note>self-made men</note>, while at the other end of the social ladder, there was a marked decrease in poverty and begging. In fact, by the middle of the sixteenth century—the chronological limit of this volume—Florence presented the rare spectacle of a State whose citizens were either all wealthy or, at the very least, comfortably well-off. Only then did the spirit of idle ease begin to weaken the mental and physical vigor of her enterprising people.

On the other hand, the hard-working life of good Florentines in the pursuit of their many industries is very strikingly shown in a will from the year 1395.<gloss>1</gloss> A certain Lapaccino del Toso de' Lapaccini, who died during that year, left instructions that a penalty of one thousand gold florins should be paid by each and every one of his sons who, between the ages of sixteen and thirty-five, spent a whole year without working at some trade or undertaking some commercial enterprise.

To enter a Guild, five conditions <note>The original text lists six conditions despite mentioning "five."</note> had to be fulfilled:
1. To be a native-born Florentine.
2. To have two sponsors to vouch for family and personal character.
3. To have never appeared before magistrates for any crime.
4. To meet a property qualification—either through his own holdings or those inherited upon the death of his father.
5. To pay a silver tax to the State as security.
6. To pay an entrance fee to the specific Guild.

The silver tax varied—it was adjusted from time to time by the *Signoria* <note>The governing council of the Florentine Republic</note>—and was considered a poll tax or head tax. The payment of this tax granted immediate political rights to the payer. The entrance fee—generally a substantial sum—varied according to the circumstances of the individual or his family. Its payment entitled the payer to full membership in his Guild.

A significant difference was made in the amount of each of these payments depending on whether one was a member of the Merchant Guilds or a member of the Craft Guilds. The members of the former were of two classes: (1) *Masters* <note>original: "Maestri"</note>—full members—and (2) *Disciples* <note>original: "Discipuli"</note>—probationers or apprentices. In Latin manuscripts and early printed books of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, "dis-"

The term *apprentice* <note>original: "discipulo"</note> is used in a general sense. The members of the latter group—the Craft Guilds—consisted of three classes: (1) *Masters* <note>original: "Maestri"</note>, (2) *Workmen* <note>original: "Lavoranti"</note>, and (3) *Apprentices* <note>original: "Garzoni"</note>.

The *apprenticeship* <note>original: "Tirocinio"</note> lasted from five to seven years, but sons of Masters were entitled to easier and shorter terms—generally four or five years.

At the end of his time, the apprentice was still required to work for his master for three years for a small annual payment. At the end of that period, the workman was entitled to call himself a *Master-workman* <note>original: "Capo lavoro"</note>. The sons of Masters were also permitted to serve a shorter workman's probation of only two years; they also paid reduced taxes and lower fees.

In his tenth year, each individual paid his Master's Recognition fee, or *Entrance Fee* <note>original: "Buona Entrata"</note>, and became a full Master of his Craft.<note>1</note>

A few extracts from the records of apprenticeships will be interesting, as they show the variety of employments and the details of mutual arrangements between master and apprentice at certain dates:

1272. A father from Ema <note>original: "Æma"; a river and valley south of Florence</note> binds his boy to a Tanner for eight years. The lad is to receive "clothes and board as befits a merchant and artisan of that trade."

1274. A man binds his son for two years as an *apprentice* <note>original: "discipulo"</note> to a retail cloth dealer to learn the trade—the father paying down three lire.

1291. A man "of the parish of San Giovanni di Chuota, in the territory of Count Guido Novelli, gives his son as an *apprentice* <note>original: "discipulo"</note> for three years to Messere Cambizzino, a shoemaker of the Uberti family in the parish of Santa Felicita <note>original: "Santa Felicia"</note> in Piazza. The master is to give yearly a tunic, a vest, stockings, and a pair of good shoes."

1293. Another binds his nephew for one year to his master—an innkeeper—the latter to give the apprentice "wine, food, and a bed, all of good quality and worthy of the trade."

1295. A young man "from Castelnuovo is apprenticed as an apprentice <note>original: "discipulo"</note> to a locksmith for one year, with the master being bound to pay him forty soldi <note>soldi: small silver coins used in Florence</note>."

1300. A man "binds his orphan brother for five and a half years to Ricchio Bonsignori and Venturi Ammanti, merchants—who live in a house on the new bridge of Rubaconte. The apprentice <note>original: "discipulo"</note> is to receive food and clothing—of good and decent quality—as well as shoes; he is also to be cared for, whether healthy or sick, for any period of time less than a month."

1306. A certain man from San Savino in Monte Carelli apprentices <note>original: "engages himself as discipulo"</note> himself to a baker in the parish of San Pancrazio for seven years—to receive clothing, board, and lodging," and so on.¹

Many entries in the registration records <note>original: "articles of matriculation"</note> and the records of association prove that women were not disqualified by their sex from enjoying the rights of membership in the guilds. For example, in 1294, before the Council of Guild Heads <note>original: "Capitudini"</note>, Donna Santa—wife of Palmerio of the parish <note>original: "popolo"</note> of San Ambrogio—wished to be admitted as a worker into the "Guild and Association of Belt and Girdle-makers" <note>original: "Arte e Universita Zonariorum"</note>. She stated that she had paid three pounds as an entrance fee to the treasurer of the guild. Thereupon, with the approval of the Council, she swore to observe all the statutes and regulations of the guild, and Messer Lapo Benci, the Rector, admitted her to full membership. A witness's signature is appended to the document of enrollment: "Corso Guglielmo, Rector of the Guild of Strap-makers" <note>original: "Corsus Guellilme,—Rector artis Coregiariorum"</note>.

In the earliest records of the trades, we find that the heads of each craft bore the title of "Consul," which was the same title given to the rulers of the city-state <note>original: "Commune"</note>. This led to considerable confusion. For example, in the negotiations entered into with the people of the community <note>original: "Commune"</note> of Pogna in 1184 for their protection, the "Consuls of Florence" <note>the city leaders</note> attached their signatures above those of the "Consuls of the Trades" <note>the guild leaders</note>.

<page-num>69</page-num>
# GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS

A document¹ dated 1193 contains an account of the agreement <note>original: "Convention"</note> between the City-State <note>original: "Commune"</note> of Florence and the Lords of the Castle of Trebbio. In this document, the confusion over titles is resolved by using the designation Rector <note>original: "Rettore"</note> for the heads of the trades.

The title of Rector was changed again in 1204, when Prior <note>original: "Priore"</note> was adopted; however, this was abandoned very shortly after because it conflicted with the title of the three Priors of the Three Great Guilds. "Consul" was once again used as the title for the heads of the guilds when that title was no longer used by the Head of State.²

No citizen could hold the office of Consul unless he was actively practicing his trade <note>original: "calling"</note> and lived at his shop or place of business. All those elected were required to be natives of Florence, except in the guilds of "Judges and Notaries" and "Masters of Stone and Wood"—both of which were open to foreigners.

Every citizen appointed to the supreme office of the guild was required to serve his term or pay a fine of one hundred gold florins.³

As might have been expected, conflicting opinions frequently disrupted the unity of the Council of Consuls of all the guilds. Something of this nature occurred regarding the peace negotiations started in 1280 by Cardinal Latino dei Frangipani, who was acting as a Papal Legate.⁴

These negotiations were attempts to reconcile the followers of the two major political parties in the state—the Guelphs <note>The pro-Papal political faction</note> and the Ghibellines <note>The pro-Imperial political faction</note>—to allow the latter to return to the city. The commissioners included Lapo del Prato, Orlando Baldovini, and Cervo del Foro, representing the Intermediate Guilds of Butchers, Blacksmiths, and Shoemakers, respectively. They, along with the Consuls of the Judges and Notaries, the Silk Merchants, and the Doctors and—

<page-num>70</page-num>
->THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

The Apothecaries promised, on behalf of their Guilds, to do everything in their power to carry out the proposed conditions and to vigorously oppose any attempts to ignore the peace settlement.

The names of the Consuls for the Calimala <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants of Foreign Cloth</note>, the Wool Merchants, the Bankers and Money-changers, the Skinners and Furriers, and the Retail Cloth Dealers were not added to the document. Therefore, we may conclude that they did not support the Cardinal's terms. Regardless, the settlement failed, and the *Parte Guelfa* <note>The Guelph Party; the pro-Papal political faction</note> grew even stronger.

The frequent and unpredictable changes in the status and authority of the Guilds and their Consuls are nowhere better described than in a thirteenth-century manuscript <term>Codex</term>.<gloss>1</gloss> In the list of Consuls from October 1295 to May 1296, two representatives from each of the Twelve Greater Guilds were appointed to sit on the General Council of the Guilds. The only exception was the guild of "Judges and Notaries," whose representatives held an established right to preside over the meetings without needing a special election.

The same manuscript goes on to state that the number of Consuls elected for these and other purposes was variable and unequal. For example: the "Calimala" had only three; the "Bankers" had four to six; the "Wool Merchants" and "Shoemakers" had five to six; the "Silk Merchants," "Doctors," and "Butchers" had four; the "Smiths" had three to five; the "Retail Cloth Dealers" had two to seven; the "Furriers" had one to six; and the "Masters of Stone and Wood" <note>The Guild of Masons and Carpenters</note> had three. Undoubtedly, these variations were caused by the nature of the business occupying the General Council’s attention or by specific trade circumstances.

From time to time, disputes and jealousies arose concerning the election of Consuls for the various Guilds, causing resentment and even feuds among the members of the different corporations. The Priors made many efforts to end these quarrels. In 1329, they summoned a general representative Council to discuss the best measures to address the widespread dissatisfaction with the current state of affairs.

<page-num>71</page-num>
<header>GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS</header>

From each properly formed Guild, they chose two members along with the *Gonfaloniere* <note>Standard-bearer</note> of each. The result of their deliberations was that no man should be elected to the office of Consul in any Guild if he failed to receive at least fifty votes from fully qualified members. The candidates elected were authorized to hold office for four months.

The voters’ list for each Guild in the election of Consuls was enclosed in a small box, the keys to which were held by the current Consuls. All these boxes were packed into a large chest for which only the Captain of the People, the Priors of the Guilds, and the Standard-bearer of Justice had keys. Such precautions were numerous and were necessary to preserve the integrity and fair practice of the members and the Constitution of each Guild.

Disputes between the Guilds—whether in their capacity as corporations or in relation to individual members—which could not be settled in the courts of the Consuls, nor ended by the Consuls of all the Guilds in a united session, were referred first of all to the "Tribunal of the Mercanzia" <note>The Merchant Court of Florence, which handled commercial law</note> and finally laid before the *Podesta* <note>The city’s chief magistrate and administrator</note>, the Captain of the People, and the Defender of the Guilds, acting as a Supreme Court of Appeal. The ruling of these three dignitaries was accepted as final.

Once every year, in January, each of the Guilds appointed a Syndic <note>A legal representative or administrative official</note> to assist the Consuls in carrying out their orders. They were required to swear an oath before the Captain of the People, in the presence of the two Councils and the Heads of the Greater Guilds, to provide honest and worthy service to the State and to ensure that the members of their trade obeyed the Magistrates. They were required to examine the credentials of all companies, leagues, conventions, undertakings, obligations, and contracts which they found existing among the people. All such agreements that were contrary to, or deviated from, the strict letter of their Constitutions were annulled and forbidden.

They were also required to enter, in the Registries of their trades and districts, the names and dates of baptism of all men

...from eighteen to seventy years of age, including their trades or occupations and dwellings, and to add notes regarding their health, character, ability, and diligence.

Companies consisting of families or traders usually included many people. For example, in the State Archives, there is a notice dated October 28, 1304, regarding a declaration of bankruptcy before the Court of the <term>Podesta</term> <note>The city’s chief magistrate</note> by the Ranieri Ardinghelli Society (or Company). It had eighteen partners—fourteen from the latter family and five from the former—who were merchants of the "<term>Calimala</term>" <note>The Guild responsible for finishing and dyeing foreign cloth</note>. The total liabilities were one hundred and twenty-three thousand <term>lire</term>^1.

The emigration of skilled artisans and craftsmen was strictly forbidden by several <term>Provvisioni</term> <note>Legislative decrees or provisions</note> issued at various times. The classes of workmen most frequently targeted by these laws were those of the "<term>Calimala</term>" Guild (finishers of foreign cloth), the "Wool Guild" (dyers and fullers), and the "Silk Guild" (weavers of gold and silver cloth). With intense earnestness and constant vigilance, the merchants and manufacturers strove to keep the production of all merchandise within Florence, especially those goods in which Florentine workers excelled over all others. The sharp spirit of monopoly was never more clearly displayed than in these efforts.^2

Offenses of every kind—whether against the Guild Statutes or against individual Guilds—were heavily punished, as were crimes committed against people who were not members of the Guild in question. In the "Council of the Hundred," a petition was presented in 1292 by the <term>Priors</term> <note>The executive leaders of the city and guilds</note> of the "<term>Calimala</term>" merchants. They requested that felonies or other misdemeanors committed by Guild members should be punishable only through the courts of each Guild’s <term>Consuls</term> <note>The elected officials who managed the Guild's internal affairs and justice</note>. The petitioners pledged: 
(1) to be held responsible for such persons, subject to a fine for any breach of this promise; and 
(2) to expel offenders from their Guilds and prohibit them from working in the various industries connected with them.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of urban regulations and the daily lives of workers in Florence, following the previous section on Guild legal jurisdictions and the prohibition of emigrating skilled labor.</meta>

<page-num>73</page-num>
<header>GENERAL HISTORY OF THE GUILDS 73</header>

Among a number of prohibitions established by the <term>Signoria</term> <note>The governing body of Florence</note> and put into effect by the Consuls of the Guilds were the following:

1. No animal suffering from a disease shall be allowed to drink at the public fountains.
2. Swallows shall not be disturbed, and frogs shall not be carried through the city.
3. No one shall be allowed to spin tops in the streets, and boys shall be whipped for throwing stones at fish in the river.

Work hours naturally varied over time and differed across various industries. As was the rule elsewhere, work generally lasted from dawn to dusk, with breaks for food and rest. There were no more than two hundred and seventy-five working days in the year, as Church festivals and other holidays took up the remaining time.

Clocks were not common in old Florence, and only wealthy people carried watches. Consequently, the time of day was regulated by the striking of bells. Perhaps the earliest record of a public clock is dated March 15, 1352. On that day, the large clock of the <term>Palazzo Vecchio</term> <note>The city’s town hall; original: "Old Palace"</note> struck the hours for the first time.

The first bell used to mark the passing of busy hours was hung in the <term>campanile</term> <note>bell tower</note> of the ancient Church of <term>Santa Maria Ughi</term>. This church was located in the <term>Piazza delle Cipolle</term> <note>original: "Piazza delle Cipolli"; literally "Onion Square"</note>, just behind the <term>Palazzo Strozzi</term>. Every afternoon at three o'clock, several strikes told workmen to stop their labor. This early hour was chosen because the city gates were closed to both exit and entry at dusk during the winter, and many laborers lived in the <term>Contado</term> <note>The rural territory surrounding the city</note> outside the city walls.

There is a legend of a charming flower and herb-seller named Berta, who left a sum of money to the Church of <term>Santa Maria Maggiore</term>. She requested that an additional bell be rung at four o'clock, in both winter and summer, to signal the end of the day's paid labor. This bell was called "*La Trecca*" <note>original: "the Fruiterer’s bell"</note> and, due to its shape, "*La Cavolaia*" <note>literally "the cabbage-seller," though the author translates it as "the gentle cabbage"</note>. The first Grand Duke, Cosimo I, transferred the duties of the workmen’s bell to the great bell of the <term>Duomo</term> <note>The Cathedral</note> and ordered it to be rung at half-past three daily throughout the year.

<page-type>text</page-type>

The bell of the <term>Bargello</term> <note>A fortified palace used as a prison and the headquarters of the Captain of the People; now a national museum</note> was known as “The Mountaineer” <note>original: “*La Montanara*”</note>, named after the town from which it was captured by the Florentines in 1302. This bell tolled every evening to warn loyal citizens to set aside their weapons and return indoors. Because of this custom, it was also called “The Bell of Arms” <note>original: “*La Campana delle Armi*”</note>. Cosimo I ordered that any servant found idling in the streets, or loitering for lack of work, when this bell tolled in the evening, should have his right hand amputated! At all public executions, “The Mountaineer” tolled as the condemned were led to the gallows.

Upon the succession of Alessandro de’ Medici to the position of his ancestors on May 1, 1532, Florence became the capital of a Duchy. By his order, “The Bell” <note>original: “*La Campana*”</note> was taken down and smashed into pieces, “lest its sound should awaken echoes of lost freedom!” The last knell tolled on October 1st, 1532, and it marked the end of an eventful and vigorous era. The liberties of a free people and of a free parliament were buried in the grave of the Republic of Florence!

At first glance, it seems somewhat anachronistic to include a guild of legal and professional people among the trade corporations of the Republic of Florence.

Although the members of the Guild of Judges and Notaries were in no sense businessmen, strictly speaking, their functions were absolutely necessary for the advancement of the industries and commerce of the artisans and merchants around them. On the other hand, the judicial system of Florence was built up primarily upon the requirements of trade, the interests of which—

were paramount in the political constitutions of the city and its territory.

Extraordinary characteristics of the Florentines of the Middle Ages were their love of fairness and reverence for justice, and their administration by individuals and councils without bias or partiality. Throughout the entire history of Florence, nothing is more remarkable than the frequency and regularity with which they called upon the help of individuals and powers completely external to the matters at hand. The most notable example of this is seen in the selection of foreigners to fill the highest office in the State—that of the <term>Podestà</term> <note>The chief magistrate and administrative officer of the city, intentionally chosen from another city to ensure neutrality</note>. It was considered—quite rightly—that a stranger would likely bring an impartial mind, free from any local favoritism, to all questions submitted for judgment.

The pioneers of Florence's industrial and commercial activities expected this principle to be applied in settling all matters relating to trade and merchants. While family ties and class distinctions were restrictive and forbidden when assigning judicial roles to men raised and educated within the bounds of the <term>Commune</term> <note>The self-governing city-state of Florence</note>, no such limitations existed for men trained in other centers of learning.

Bologna, the mother of universities, was the early source to which the people of Florence looked for legal advisers. Its fame for teaching jurisprudence was unrivaled, and its faculty of law attracted students from every city and country in Europe. In 1262, there were more than twenty thousand men engaged in the study of <term>canon law</term> <note>The system of laws and legal principles made and enforced by the Church hierarchy</note> and <term>civil law</term> <note>The body of law based on Roman codes dealing with private relations between members of a community</note> within its borders. Many clever young Florentines traveled there, and after making their names as legal experts, they were welcomed home again as valuable assistants to their fathers or their fathers' business partners.

The city's prosperity, and the prospect of honor and payment from wealthy citizens, also attracted legally qualified men from other states. Upon all such

Graduates of the university were conferred the degree of <term>Doctor of Law</term> <note>original: "Doctor-juris"</note>.

The constant and increasingly numerous questions, disputes, and settlements—which are inseparable from all interactions between people and between different trades—created the necessity for a publicly recognized body of men learned in law and equity.

A College of Judges existed in Florence during the twelfth century, though the actual date of its establishment is based on guesswork. In any case, membership rolls and records of their acts still exist from the year 1187.

The first mention of a Tribunal of Judges is in a document from the year 1197. This probably led to the formal incorporation of a Guild of Judges during the same period that the early <term>Companies</term> <note>original: "Compagnie"</note>, or organizations of merchants and artisans, were developed into the more ambitious <term>Guilds</term> <note>original: "Arti"</note>. <note>L. Cantini, "Legislation," i. 105-107 and iii. 62.</note>

A document <note>Archives of the Reformations, Book xxvi.</note> from the year 1193, preserved in the Archives of Florence, contains an account of a convention made between the <term>Commune</term> <note>The self-governing city-state</note> of Florence and the Lords of the Castle of Trebbio, in which the seven <term>Rectors</term> <note>original: "Rettori"</note>—the leaders of the Guilds—are named. This is especially interesting as the legal document in question was drafted for signature by certain Judges and Notaries of the city.

In the Treaty of 1204 between Florence and Siena, the signatures of the Consuls of five Guilds are attached, namely: Judges and Notaries, the <term>Calimala</term> <note>The Guild of cloth finishers and merchants of foreign cloth</note>, Wool Merchants, Bankers and Money-changers, and Silk Merchants. Again, in 1229, the Treaty with Orvieto is signed in a similar way, and it is noteworthy that the Consuls of the "Guild of Judges and Notaries" come first in each case. Such records prove that the Guild had been in active and honorable existence for many years.

At a State Council held on April 15th, 1279—summoned to discuss matters relating to the <term>Papal Court</term> <note>original: "Court of Rome"</note>, where all the Guilds were represented by their Consuls—the signatures of <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "Dominus"</note> Ugo Altoviti, <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "Dominus"</note> Jacobus Gerardi, <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "Dominus"</note> Alberti...

<meta>This page continues the history of the Guild of Judges and Notaries, focusing on the specific roles of its officials and the guild's unique status regarding the use of Latin versus the vernacular in its records.</meta>

<page-num>78</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The names Ristori, Ser Benzi Dandi: <term>Notary</term> <note>original: "Notarius"</note>, Lord Gerardus Maneti: <term>Notary</term> <note>original: "Notarius"</note>, and Ser Cioe, son of Giacomo Buere—“Consuls of the Judges and Notaries” <note>original: "Consules Judicum et Notariorum"</note>, are listed first.

The precise meaning of the title “Consul” is clearly distinguished from that of “Judge.” The former’s office was “for the maintenance of Justice” <note>original: "pro manutendum Justitiæ"</note>, while the latter’s was “for the searching and determining of causes” <note>original: "ad causas cognoscendum et terminatum"</note>. This distinction is strikingly highlighted by the use of the two terms in documents from 1197, 1225, 1227, and 1235.

These documents, and the Statutes of the Guild, were always written in Latin and never displayed in the vernacular. However, all such authorities and laws were required to be copied out in the ordinary language of the time. The scholarship of the notaries employed was demonstrated by their use of the “della Crusca” <note>The refined literary standard established by the Accademia della Crusca</note> or polished style. The exemption of the “Guild of Judges and Notaries” from this custom was a mark of the superior learning of its members, who were accustomed to the study and use of the classical tongue.

In the Archives and other historical sources, the infrequency of references to the “Guild of Judges and Notaries” is quite remarkable. While the various industries were gradually being formed into corporations, the legal profession appeared to have no united existence. This may have been because judicial and notarial functions were originally called into play as secondary and supportive to the interests of various commercial operations. Goro Dati, however, in speaking of the Guild, says:
> “It has a Proconsul at the head of its Consuls; it wields great authority and may be considered the parent branch of the entire notarial profession throughout Christendom, since the great masters of that profession have been leaders and members of this Guild. Bologna is the fountain of doctors of the Law—Florence, of doctors of the Notariate.” ¹

<note>¹ "History of Florence," ed. 1775, p. 133. <note>original: "Storia di Firenze"</note></note>

### THE GUILD OF JUDGES AND NOTARIES

The leadership of the Guild was composed of the Proconsul and eight Judges, who were called Consuls, just as in the Merchant Guilds. The Proconsul was the head of the Consuls, chosen from among their members. It was required that he had practiced the legal profession for at least twenty years without any stain on his reputation. This high-ranking official took precedence in all public functions immediately after the <term>Podestà</term> <note>The chief magistrate of the city-state</note> and the <term>Captain of the People</term> <note>A high official appointed to protect the interests of the common citizens</note>. He was the highest-ranking of all the Consuls of all the Guilds, and he was granted supreme authority in their legal matters. He was also provided a Palace for his residence on the street later called the <note>original: "Via del Proconsolo"</note> Street of the Proconsul.¹

The Proconsul and Consuls could summon a meeting of all the members—both judges and notaries—at any time. They could also bring in any number of judges to serve as legal assistants whenever necessary. They presided over all civil and criminal cases involving members of the Guild. Their advice was sought whenever any group of citizens proposed new laws to the State.

Regarding the Guild itself, the Proconsul and Consuls presided over the admission and enrollment of new members. These same high officials also conducted the required examinations for candidates.

Membership in the Guild was sought by the sons of noble families and influential merchant citizens. They desired it as much for the social status it provided as for its professional benefits.

Enrollment was mandatory for everyone seeking legal appointments. However, no one was eligible for enrollment if they had lived away from Florence for ten years or more, or if their father, brothers, or uncles had failed to pay all taxes and fees owed to the State in full. Every candidate was required to demonstrate legal competence and skill in notarial work, and they had to pass a rigorous public examination conducted by the Consuls.
