was an early necessity of commercial convenience and legal jurisprudence. The delivery of judgments and their registration involved two distinct but inseparable functions.

While all members were equal in brotherhood within the internal economy of the Guild, precedence was granted to the Judges in all public business. The Notaries were constantly jealous of their seemingly lower status. Occasionally, this rivalry grew serious; in 1287, it resulted in a partial separation of the Guild's two branches.

That year, each division elected its own separate Consuls to manage its affairs independently. Any Guild business requiring the agreement or disagreement of both divisions—the Judges and the Notaries—had to be voted on first in separate sessions. Afterward, they adjourned to the Church of San Piero Scheraggio, where a final decision was reached through a joint vote.

By the end of the century, the dispute was settled, and both sections loyally shared the Guild's work and honors. From then on, the distinguished conduct of the Judges and Notaries elevated the Guild’s reputation to the highest place in the hierarchy of corporate life.

The residence of the Consuls of the "Guild of Judges and Notaries" was located at the corner of the <note>original: "Via de' Pandolfini"</note> Pandolfini Street—a modest building that did not rival the grand palaces of the Consuls of the Merchant Guilds. Above its main entrance was the ***Stemma*** <term>Stemma</term> <note>A coat of arms or escutcheon</note> of the Guild: a gold star on a blue field. These armorial bearings were changed in later times, and four blue stars on a golden field were substituted instead.

The ***Podestà*** <note>The chief magistrate of Florence</note> was the supreme judge in all criminal cases, but he delegated his authority to the three senior Judges of the Guild who were not serving as Consuls. He rarely, if ever, presided over the court personally, except in special cases involving the honor of the State. The first ***Podestà***—appointed in 1207—was Gualfredotto.

<meta>This page continues the description of the high magistrates of Florence, transitioning from the household of the Captain of the People to the judicial oversight provided by the Guild of Judges and Notaries.</meta>

<page-num>82</page-num>

His functions were commonly discharged by a Court of three Senior Judges. Uberto da Lucca was appointed the first Captain of the People in 1251.

These two Chief Magistrates <note>The Podestà and the Captain of the People</note> always signed the oath of allegiance to the Commune before the Proconsul and the Consuls of the "Guild of Judges and Notaries." The former <note>The Podestà</note> was bound to defend the Republic and to lead her forces in time of war, while the latter <note>The Captain of the People</note> was charged with the protection of the Guilds and the maintenance of the city's peace.

In each *sestiere* <note>one of the six districts</note> of the city, as it was originally divided under the rule of the good Countess Matilda, there was a Tribunal presided over by the *Buonuomo* <note>literally "Good Man"</note>, whose title was recognized early on as Consul. From the year 1242, he was assisted in the discharge of his duties by two Judges, two Notaries, and two *Provveditori* <note>superintendents</note> of the Court.

The two Judges handled civil and criminal cases respectively, under the titles of *Giudice Civile dei Quatieri* <note>Civil Judge of the Quarter</note> and *Giudice dei Malafizi* <note>Judge of Crimes or Misdemeanors</note>. Each Tribunal displayed a sign or banner with armorial bearings, which were also worn by the officials attached to each court in addition to the emblem of the Guild.

By the middle of the thirteenth century, however, all cases and trials were moved to the Central Tribunal established at Or San Michele. This was first held in the church or oratory, and then in the granary, but the inconvenience of the overcrowding became so great that buildings were erected in the *Orto* <note>garden</note> attached to the Sanctuary. Over the entrance, they displayed the emblem of the Guild—a large golden star upon a light blue field.

To the Judges—who presided here in rotation—were assigned the investigation of claims and dues, the interpretation of rules of precedent and procedure, the meaning of enactments, and the determination of all matters affecting custom and ancient tradition which arose in any and all of the Guilds. Criminal suits were also heard and decided in this Central Court of Justice.

<page-num>83</page-num>

In the fourteenth century, the city returned to the earlier system of the District Courts <note>original: *Sestieri*</note>—a step made necessary by the increase in population and the inability of the Central Tribunal at Or San Michele to handle the volume of business brought before it.

Tribunals were established at: 
* Santa Maria Novella—for the district of San Pancrazio and Borgo SS. Apostoli; 
* Santa Croce—for the districts of San Piero Maggiore (or Porta San Piero) and San Piero Scheraggio; 
* San Giovanni—for the districts of Santa Maria Maggiore and Porta del Duomo; 
* and at San Spirito—for the districts in Oltrarno <note>the area "beyond the Arno" river</note>.

In 1343, equal portions of the surrounding countryside <term>Contado</term> were assigned to these four Courts, as population and construction there had increased in a wonderful manner. The old Central Tribunal was kept for special cases, and consequently, the duties of the Judges and Notaries were greatly increased.

Another improvement for those seeking justice was made in connection with the extension of municipal jurisdiction to the countryside: the creation of a traveling court of "Doctors and Experts of Law" <note>original: *Doctores et Sapientes Juris*</note>, men skilled in legal technicalities. This court was under the presidency of the Priors of the Greater Guilds, who attended by rotation and signed their names to the court's decisions. This council of experts—practically a Court of Assize <note>a court which sits at intervals in each county to administer civil and criminal law</note> as we understand the term—was served by six Judges appointed by the Proconsul and Consuls of the Guild. They were well paid, considering the inconveniences and difficulties involved in exercising their authority; however, they were required to deposit security money of two hundred *lire* each as a guarantee of just and fair conduct when they were outside the city boundaries, where they were, in a way, a law unto themselves.

The "Council of Justice" <note>original: *Consiglio di Giustizia*</note>, or "Judges of the Rotation" <note>original: *Giudici alla Rota*</note>, was appointed in 1502. Five Judges—all Doctors of Law—were elected for a term of three years. They sat twice a week in the lower and inner chamber of the Palace of the Chief Magistrate <term>Podestà</term>. This hall had a floor made of circular blocks of red and green

Their decisions were presented to the <term>Proconsul</term> <note>the head of the Guild of Judges and Notaries</note>, who was responsible for delivering the final sentence.

This arrangement lasted until the end of the century and proved much more effective for the rapid dispatch of legal business than the previous disorganized systems. During this time, religious lawsuits were entirely removed from the court’s jurisdiction, and church officials were no longer appointed as legal advisors, as had previously been the custom.

The "Judges of the Wheel" moved in the sixteenth century to the Piazza dei Castellani—which was renamed Piazza de' Giudici and now serves as the location for the National Library.

The most important legal tribunal in Florence was the "Court of Merchandise" <note>original: *La Corte della Mercanzia*</note>. Founded around the year 1296, it combined the powers of a court of justice with the functions of a chamber of commerce. It was composed of six senior judges—all members of the Guild of Judges and Notaries—presided over by a foreign <term>legal consultant</term> <note>original: *juris consult*</note> or doctor of laws, who was usually a graduate of the University of Bologna. This president held the title of "Foreign Official" <note>original: *Ufficiale Forestiere*</note>. This title reflects the characteristic desire of the ancient Florentines for completely unbiased and impartial judgment in matters affecting the general well-being of the Commonwealth.

As a formality, the president of the court was required to be enrolled as a member of the Guild of Judges and Notaries. He had the power to summon any citizens who, either personally or through their business partners, had incurred debts or liabilities abroad. He could also summon any person believed to possess information or evidence related to a lawsuit. In agreement with the six judges, he could seize the account books of all merchants and tradesmen and could compel those in debt to pay whatever restitution the court ordered at the request of any foreign plaintiff.

The laws it was called upon to administer went by the name of "The Statute of 1296" <note>original: "*Il Statuto di ’96*"</note>. Its objects, which were threefold, were:
1. To ensure that Florentine merchants and their merchandise could travel with all possible security and freedom throughout the entire world.
2. To ensure that the credit of the State was maintained under all circumstances and at all hazards.
3. To provide that foreigners should have no just cause for grievance.

The jurisdiction of the Court was at first confined to the interests of the six Greater Guilds; but as the inferior crafts grew in influence, it was extended over the members of the fourteen Lesser Guilds, and later on, over all sorts and conditions of people.

The greatest difficulties with which the Court of Merchandise <note>original: *Mercanzia*</note> had to contend were in connection with international questions. These arose from the fact that every Florentine trader in a foreign land was regarded as a surety for his fellow-citizens at home. It was to this Tribunal that all questions affecting the interests of Florentine commerce beyond Tuscany were submitted for judgment.¹

It is interesting to note in the records of Florentine history how strikingly the high-mindedness and judicial integrity of her merchants and craftsmen were exhibited in the favorable view taken by the Court of Merchandise <note>original: *Mercanzia*</note> of appeals addressed to it by foreigners. The most elaborate precautions were taken so that the subjects of other states should have no excuse for complaining of partial or unfair treatment.

The Court of Merchandise <note>original: *Mercanzia*</note> was also the final Court of Appeal in counter-lawsuits between members of the various Guilds.² One of the many customary disputes that arose daily between traders in the market and their customers came before the Tribunal of the Court of Merchandise <note>original: *Mercanzia*</note> on March 31, 1315. Among its many other functions, which are almost too numerous to mention, the Court took charge of the goods and property of deceased members of the Guilds. It also appointed trustees to manage these estates for the benefit of the lawful heirs.¹

In 1327, the seven magistrates of the *Mercanzia* <note>Court of Merchandise</note> were appointed as collectors of the Assay, or Masters of the Mint. This was done for the "preservation of the good reputation of the city, which is spread throughout the whole world because of the integrity and value of the good coins and the golden florins made there." A later decree in 1394 gave the *Mercanzia* the right to prosecute forgers and those who devalued the coinage, as well as those who created "corners" <note>Monopolies or market manipulations</note> to tighten the money market.

The seven magistrates also exercised the power to reopen closed accounts, to investigate the misappropriation of funds, to evaluate debtors' financial statements, and to sit as a Court of Bankruptcy. The *Mercanzia* acted in this latter capacity during the severe banking disasters that followed the war between England and France in 1340 <note>This refers to the financial crisis caused when King Edward III of England defaulted on massive debts to Florentine banking houses</note>.

In 1347, through a further extension of its powers, the Court’s jurisdiction came to include legal questions and offenses involving maritime affairs.

Indeed, the "University of the *Mercanzia*," as it was officially titled, was for all intents and purposes the prototype of our modern Courts of Arbitration.

The Tribunal of the *Mercanzia* was held at the residence of the *Ufficiale Forestieri* <note>Officer of Foreigners</note>, a massive building in the *Piazza della Signoria* located between the *Palazzo Vecchio* and the *Palazzo Uguccione*. The six assistant judges also resided there during their term of office. Within the Hall of Audience, immediately over the seats—

In the hall of the Judges were frescoes of the Seven Virtues, designed by Antonio Pollaiuolo. On the facade, Taddeo Gaddi painted his celebrated fresco—"The Six Virtues and the Six Judges." Although this, unfortunately, disappeared long ago, the stone-cut shields bearing the coats of arms of the Greater Guilds still remain over the principal entrance. Above everything runs the legend: "All wisdom comes from the Lord God" <note>original: "Omnis sapientia a Domino Deo est."</note>.

The greatest period of the *Mercanzia* <term>Court of Merchandise</term> was from 1391 to 1470. In the latter year, Lorenzo the Magnificent claimed for himself much, if not all, of the functions of the *Ufficiale Forestiere* <term>Foreign Official</term>, and greatly reduced the authority of the Tribunal.

Lorenzo’s successors as Rulers of Florence were, many of them, not very scrupulous in their administration of public affairs; law and order frequently yielded to circumstances and political convenience. In 1532, the *Signoria* <term>Governing Council</term> was abolished, and Alessandro de' Medici was proclaimed *Gonfaloniere di Giustizia* <term>Standard-bearer of Justice</term> for life. From then on, Florence became the victim of exactly what she had striven for centuries to avoid—one-man rule <note>original: "il governo d'un solo"</note>.

Certainly, at times, glimpses of freedom and good government appeared as the years rolled on. For example, in 1568, Cosimo I, the first Grand Duke of Tuscany, gave a new constitution to and bestowed many privileges upon the Tribunal of the *Mercanzia*.

Regarding the sessions of the various courts in old Florence, little is known about the hours or the procedure. Business was, however, greatly interrupted by frequent public holidays and ecclesiastical festivals. No judges sat on Sundays or on Saints' days, of which there were more than thirty in the year. Many vacation days were observed at Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, Pentecost, Corpus Christi, and the feasts of Saint Mary and Saint John the Baptist.

In addition to the public courts, the councils of the various Guilds required the assistance of judges. These judges not only acted as legal advisors but were also the ones who actually announced the decisions reached by the councils.

The laws against debtors were very severe. Not only was it...

->THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

It was not permissible for creditors to subject unfortunate debtors to personal physical abuse, but they were liable to imprisonment at the request of the Magistracy, where they were kept "with meager provisions, crowded and packed together in a filthy place."

At a council of the Twelve Greater Guilds held on December 7, 1304, Guilio, Vanno, and Chelo—silk manufacturers and merchants of the "*Por Santa Maria*" <term>The Silk Guild district</term>—were declared bankrupt, and the Syndics <term>legal representatives of the commune</term> were instructed to sell their goods. The same procedure was followed in February 1305, when the Society or Company of Lamberteschi Lamberti failed.<sup>1</sup>

A law of 1398 <sup>2</sup> forced debtors to serve as executioners. On the other hand, it was provided that whenever the great bell sounded to summon the citizens to a general meeting, no one could be arrested for debt.

Judicial sentences often erred on the side of severity. Consequently, it was a common practice for appeals to be addressed to higher courts for a reduction of penalties. Reducing a sentence in no way lowered the standing or prestige of a judge. If they were considered rigorous, they were always acting in accordance with the directions of the Statutes and the moral code of the time. In that era, moral laxity was often met with equal harshness.

As an example of the methods used against those who committed capital crimes, there is an interesting record <sup>3</sup> of the case of a man named Lorenzo Pieri Chorus, of the *Popoli* <term>parish or district</term> of Santa Felicita. On February 18, 1318, he was ordered by the Council of One Hundred to pay three thousand *lire* for the fatal wounding of an unnamed person from the *Popoli* <term>parish</term> of SS. Apostoli, with whom he was at peace <note>This "at peace" status indicates there was no formal feud or "vendetta" to legally mitigate the violence</note>. # THE GUILD OF JUDGES AND NOTARIES

...banished and an outlaw, having reached a settlement of friendship and marriage with the family of the deceased, his petition for the restoration of his civic rights is granted. He is ordered to be brought into the city and conducted to San Giovanni <note>The Baptistery of Florence</note> without having to submit to the shame of wearing a fool's cap or a mock bishop's hat <term>mitre</term>."

> "In Florence," to quote the words of Francesco Guicciardini, the famous historian (1483–1540), "it commonly happens that when a man has committed a violent offense, no attempt is made to punish him with severity; instead, efforts are made to help him escape on the condition that he disarms and does not repeat his evil conduct." ¹

Capital punishment and physical torture were used only in extreme cases or during times of popular riots. Fines and imprisonment were the typical punishments handed out by the judges to offenders. Suspension from practicing one's craft was also the standard punishment for an artisan <term>artizan</term> found guilty of a misdemeanor.

The archives are naturally full of references to the rulings of all the courts. Generally, these lawsuits were trivial in nature; however, in those days, as now, when a man was determined not to be fined <term>mulcted</term> for court costs, he did not hesitate to take his case to the Court of Appeal. For instance, a tavern-keeper <term>tavernaio</term> in 1279 appealed to the Superior Court against a sentence of twenty *soldi* <term>shillings or silver coins</term> imposed by the four consuls of the "Guild of Butchers." The man appears to have lost his appeal because, according to the evidence of one of the consuls, he had sold drinks in violation of trade regulations.

The state prison, called the *Stinche*, was built in 1307. The name was derived from the Castle of Stinche <term>Castello di Stinche</term> in the Val di Geve, which belonged to the Cavalcanti family. A popular uprising against the growing power of this ancient family led to the capture of the castle. Its garrison were taken prisoner and sent to the dungeons beneath the prison, which thereby acquired its name.

<page-num>90</page-num>

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

It happened quite often that prisoners were left to die miserably and alone in the *Stinche* <note>a famous Florentine prison named after the castle of the same name</note> and the other prisons of Florence. Condemned criminals were imprisoned—either sentenced to life imprisonment or while awaiting execution—in the dungeons of the *Bargello* <note>the palace of the Captain of the People</note>, which also contained an *oubliette* <term>a secret dungeon with an opening only at the top</term>. Human skulls and bones have frequently been discovered under this building.

The release of a prisoner was a somewhat rare occurrence; it was usually carried out on a Sunday or a Saint's day. Through a touching religious ceremony, the prisoner was led to the Church of San Giovanni <note>The Baptistery of Florence</note> and offered at the altar, from which he emerged a free man.

Women—judging by a great number of legal enactments—gave the authorities much trouble. They were absolutely forbidden to enter a Court of Justice, and Judges were warned not to listen to their complaints. A Statute of 1294 gives this strangely ambiguous warning: "Women are a sex to be looked upon as most dangerous in disturbing the course of justice!"

Many sumptuary laws <term>laws intended to regulate personal expenditure and restrain luxury</term> were directed against the excess of feminine adornment during the fourteenth century, and Judges were called upon to enforce these strictly. Many judges very cunningly evaded this duty by enlisting the help of Notaries, upon whom fell the burden of investigation and the unpopularity of issuing punishments.

A story is told by Sacchetti <note>Franco Sacchetti (c. 1335–1400), an Italian writer and government official</note> ¹ about Messere Amerigo Amerighi of Pesaro—a Judge during Sacchetti's term as Prior—who was ordered to enforce certain regulations regarding the fashions of the time. He instructed a Notary well-versed in such matters to prepare a report. The Notary reported that one woman, whose headdress was too high, refused to lower it, saying, "Why, no, don't you see it is a wreath?" Another, wearing many buttons on her dress, defended herself with the remark, "Yes, I can wear these; they are not buttons. You see, they have no shanks <term>loops or stems used to attach a button to fabric</term>." A third woman, accused of wearing ermine, replied, "This is not ermine; it is the fur of a suckling <note>an unweaned animal, implying it was a common fur rather than the restricted luxury fur of a stoat</note>." When the unhappy Notary asked:

"What is this suckling?" she replied: "Oh, it is only an animal!"

"A good woman and a bad one equally require the stick!" was an old and familiar saying among the Florentines. It was perhaps somewhat harsh and ungentlemanly, but it was never more applicable than to women who wished to engage in lawsuits!

The statutes regarding gambling, card playing, and similar activities were frequent and threatening, and their application gave the Judges endless trouble and resulted in many inconsistencies. The *Archivio della Grascia* <note>The "Archives of the Grascia," the office responsible for provisions and the enforcement of sumptuary laws</note> preserves many such acts; they also show how greatly worried judicial dignitaries in Florence were regarding the enforcement of such decrees. A friend of Messere Amerighi actually scribbled in the margin of one of the excellent Judge’s summaries of sumptuary laws <term>laws intended to regulate personal expenditure and restrain luxury</term>:

<margin>¹ See Guido Biagi, "The Private Life of the Renaissance Florentine," p. 46.</margin>
> "If there is a person you do hate,
> Send him to Florence as a magistrate!"¹

The ability, integrity, and sophistication of the Florentine Judges soon gained approval all over Europe. This recognition had a reciprocal influence upon the individuals, encouraging them to live up to their reputation. The esteem in which the office of Judge was held in Florence is evidenced by the honorable title of "*Messere*" <term>an honorific title meaning "Sir" or "Master"</term>, which was generally granted to the judicial members of the Guild.

Judges were granted equal precedence with Knights and Doctors of Medicine in all ceremonies, whether public or private. They were always invited to marriage feasts as guests of the highest distinction. In common with those of equal rank, Judges wore long red cloaks lined with miniver <term>a white fur used for lining garments, often from the bellies of squirrels</term>, and an inner, tighter-fitting garment of the same color. Degrees in official rank were displayed by variations in the length and fullness of their robes, and in the quality and quantity of fur decorations. The head covering—a close-fitting cap with a falling curtain or sash—was also red.

<page-num>92</page-num>

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Some advice on ideal behavior, written almost whimsically, can be found by anyone with the time to search the Archives of Florence for matters relating to the "Guild of Judges and Notaries" and its individual members.

One learned and moralizing scribe says: "Keep well in mind that when you pronounce a sentence, you should proceed straightforwardly, loyally, and justly. Do not allow yourself to be swayed from this by bribes, love, or fear; by family relations or friendship; or for the sake of a companion. For the person against whom you give your sentence will become your enemy, and the person you intended to serve will consider you neither honest, nor loyal, nor straightforward, and will instead always distrust and despise you."

The payment of Judges depended as much upon the individual as upon the circumstances. Each was required to possess a certain private income as an essential qualification for office. This income might come from inheritance or from practicing as an advocate in the Supreme and Foreign Courts. The amounts paid by the State to Judges for judicial services were not so much regular salaries as they were commissions based on the business transacted. For example, in 1290, two legal experts <term>jurisprudents</term> appointed to assist the Treasurer of the Commune received only one gold florin a month each!¹

Civil cases of the first instance <term>the first level of a legal case</term> were heard before the Judge of the Court of each *Sestiere* <term>one of the six administrative districts of Florence</term>. He was required to have earned the degree of Doctor of Law at Bologna or another legal university and to be a registered citizen of Florence. His term of office was six months, and he might be re-elected—or not—as the Council of State decided. The salary was hardly proportional to the dignity of the office—a paltry sum of twenty-five *lire*! In 1291, the Judge of a certain district received as much as twenty-five *lire* a month, while another only received twenty-four for a four-month period.²

The Judges who sat as assessors <term>legal advisors or assistants to a judge</term> or delegates of the Chief Magistrate were well compensated. In 1292, the judicial assistants—

...assistants of the Captain of the People were paid forty-five *lire* each for presiding at the drawing of the “*Taglia*.” <note>The *Taglia* refers to a tax or military levy, often associated with the league of Guelph cities.</note>¹

Judges of Appeal, however, were regarded as superior dignitaries and were paid on an even more liberal scale. In 1286, one such official received five hundred *lire* for himself and his two Notaries.² In 1358, a Judge of Appeal received as much as fifteen hundred *lire* per year <note>original: "per annum"</note>.

Judges were forbidden to perform their duties privately, as well as publicly, on all Festivals and Fasts. Their *sportelli* <term>small windows or wickets used for business</term> might indeed be open on these days of religious obligation, but only for the delivery of messages and for brief replies to inquiries.

The dignity of their position, and the high esteem with which they were generally regarded by people of all classes, did not, nonetheless, prevent the miscarriage of justice, nor the degradation of their office at times by both Judges and Notaries. The common experience of noble ideals failing to uphold themselves at all times and under all circumstances was, unfortunately, confirmed often enough in busy, turbulent Florence.

Boccaccio, Sacchetti, and other popular writers and critics of various periods provide many instances where right and justice were forced to yield to corruption and fraud. Bribes were freely offered, and often enough just as freely taken. One litigant having offered the Judge a fat ox to obtain a favorable verdict, his opponent promptly sent in a fine pregnant cow; the shrewd magistrate accepted both and dismissed the case! “I would rather see my son,” said Sacchetti, “become a sportsman than a Judge.”³

While these mockeries of justice were treated as occasions for ridicule, they had an effect on public opinion. Boccaccio’s severe criticisms <term>strictures</term> of unrighteous Judges are very harsh. “They,” he says, “pretend that they are ministers of justice and of God, but they are indeed the executors of injustice and the friends of the devil.”⁴

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The inclusion of merchants in such honors might seem like an anachronism; nevertheless, knighthood was not only generally recognized but also greatly sought after by men of high position.

The creation of knights in Florence depended upon three circumstances: the visit of a foreign monarch; the assumption of the office of *Podestà* <term>the chief magistrate of a medieval Italian city-state</term> by a foreign sovereign—both Charlemagne and Charles of Anjou bestowed this honor—and the will of the people, either expressed by the rulers of the state in a public meeting or vehemently demanded by a tumultuous assembly. In the latter category were Michele Lando and sixty-four other citizens, who were made knights by the popular voice during the Ciompi Rising <note>A rebellion of unrepresented wool workers in 1378.</note> in 1378.

New knights were invested publicly. In the name of the Republic, they were entrusted with a banner, a lance, a sword, and a shield—the latter bearing the arms of the state. Regarding the symbols of knighthood, Dante wrote:

> “. . . . Galigaio showed
> The gilded hilt and pommel.” <note>original: "Paradiso," Canto xvi.</note>

Their ennoblement also required the formal certification of the Superior Court of Judges. Candidates were required to present their credentials to this court after they had been prepared by notaries.

After 1323, the investiture was held at the *Ringhiera* <term>a raised stone platform or balcony</term>, a platform built along the front of the Palazzo Vecchio. This was where the supreme magistrates were solemnly sworn in, state decrees were publicly announced, and military commanders received their insignia of office. It served as the Florentine *Agora* or *Forum* <note>Greek and Latin terms respectively for a public square or marketplace used for judicial and political business.</note>.

No one desired the distinction of an order of chivalry more earnestly than judges and notaries. The former sought it to qualify for the highest offices in the state and for diplomatic appointments to foreign nations. The latter sought it to attain, in a single leap, the status that allowed them to exchange their humble writing tools for the gold-sheathed dagger of knighthood.

<page-num>95</page-num>

<header>THE GUILD OF JUDGES AND NOTARIES</header>

Turning now to the other section of the Guild—the “body of honorable Notaries,” as they were called—we must remember that, unlike their distinguished colleagues on the judicial bench, these were men who had been born, educated, and trained in Florence. As boys attending monastery schools, or later the elementary schools of the *Studio* <term>the University of Florence, or *Studium Generale*</term>, or Academy, they learned the basics of notarial law from one of the many legal teachers found throughout northern and central Italy in the twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth centuries. These teachers were mostly law graduates from Bologna who were seeking positions as judges in the civil and criminal courts.

All Notaries, before pleading in Court, were required to appear before the Proconsul and the eight Consuls of the “Guild of Judges and Notaries.” They had to provide a financial guarantee of two hundred *lire* <term>the local currency of Florence</term> as a pledge that they would “practice their profession faithfully and legally, and would never be guilty of even the slightest overcharging or extortion.” Each was also required to register his unique signature, or mark, upon being admitted to practice.

<image-desc>An ornate calligraphic monogram or mark serving as a legal signature. It features stylized, interlocking characters including what appears to be an "N", "S", and "L", adorned with decorative flourishes and four small circular dots.</image-desc>

->REGISTERED MARK OR SIGNATURE OF THE<-
->NOTARY NICCOLO DA FERENTERINO, 1236.<-

One of the Guild’s statutes decreed that no Notary was qualified to plead or practice within the judicial jurisdiction of the Republic unless he had lived in Florence for the last ten consecutive years. A Notary was also required to come from a respectable family whose members had duly paid all their taxes and rates for at least twenty years. Regularly admitted Notaries were titled “Experts in the Law” <note>original: "Sapientes juris"</note> in official documents. They were attached to every court and to all the primary offices of the State.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the roles played by notaries in the government of the Florentine Republic, detailing specific official positions like the Notary of the Reformation and the Chancellor.</meta>

<page-num>96</page-num>

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

One of the most important officers of the Republic was the Notary of the Reformation <note>original: "Notaio della Riformagione"</note>. His duties were those of Secretary to the Priors, and his responsibility was to keep a register of their decisions. He was always a foreigner—generally a Lombard <note>a person from the region of Lombardy in northern Italy</note>—and his salary ranged from one hundred *lire* in 1358 to four hundred and fifty.<sup>1</sup> Three days before leaving office, he had to hand a copy of all acts issued by the Supreme Council of State to the Standard-bearer of Justice <note>original: "Gonfaloniere di Giustizia"</note>. For serious neglect of duty, he was liable not only to heavy fines but even to imprisonment.

A special Notary was appointed annually to assist the State Treasurer in keeping the public accounts and preparing the annual Treasury balance sheet. To serve as auditors for this government department, two senior Notaries or advocates, who were doctors of law, were named. Their duty was to examine, check, and either pass or refuse all statements regarding the receipt and spending of public money.

Two Notaries were attached to the personal staff of the Standard-bearer of Justice. One acted as a personal secretary and retired from office along with his chief. The other was the permanent secretary of the office; he was in charge of the law books, business registers, lists of reforms carried out or proposed, and all other documents relating to the department. His salary was only one hundred *lire* a year. Another officer of this State department was the Chancellor <note>original: "Cancelliere"</note>, who was also a Notary. He managed the Standard-bearer’s private expenditure account and conducted his correspondence.

These three offices, though quite subordinate, were highly sought after by young men possessing literary tastes or who were ambitious to rise in the service of the State. Coluccio de’ Salutati, Leonardo Bruni, Carlo Marsuppini, Poggio Bracciolini, Marcello Vergilio, and Niccolo Machiavelli were among those who, in turn, held the Chancellorship.

Four Notaries, “duly registered and of good reputation and intelligence,” were appointed annually to serve in the Supreme Council of State. While holding these appointments, they were—

These officials were forbidden to undertake any other professional duties. They maintained the State Records and kept all documents and materials on hand that were likely to be needed during government deliberations. They were paid for the copies they produced, with rates ranging from seven *lire* <term>lira</term> <note>a unit of currency</note> for complete lists of citizens subject to the <term>Catasto</term> <note>income tax</note>, to seven *soldi* <term>soldo</term> <note>a smaller unit of currency; 20 soldi equaled one lira</note> for drafts of motions presented before the Council.<sup>1</sup>

The State often paid lucrative fees to Notaries for copying Statutes and other documentary records. In 1291, two Notaries received forty-two *lire* for copying, decorating with illustrations, and binding two new Statutes. Another Notary, who compiled an alphabetical register of the names of exiles from the time of the <term>Podesta</term> <note>the chief magistrate or city administrator</note> Pietro dei Stefaneschi until the year 1291, was granted a sum of forty gold florins. In 1246, six Notaries were ordered to copy out the Register of Citizens for the <term>Estimo</term> <note>a tax based on the valuation of property</note>, for which they were paid thirty *lire*.<sup>2</sup>

Each Guild had its own designated Notaries, whose nominations and appointments were generally made at a joint meeting of the Guild Consuls. On December 31, 1326,<sup>3</sup> the following Guilds were provided with notaries for a six-month term: Bakers, Armorers and Swordmakers, Oil, Cheese, and Provision Merchants, Woolen Merchants, Tanners, Doctors and Apothecaries, Judges and Notaries, Butchers, Skinners and Furriers, Retail Cloth Dealers and Linen Merchants, Wine Merchants, Carpenters, Innkeepers, Locksmiths and Metal Workers, Silk Merchants, and Blacksmiths.

These legal officials were engaged daily, either in the Superior Courts or in the Consular Courts of the various Guilds. In these latter tribunals, they acted as confidential advisors to those involved in lawsuits and also served as pleaders in court. They were permitted to collect fees from the people seeking their help, and they also received fixed payments every two years from the Guilds for which they worked.

This dual occupation led gradually to the creation of a new order of legal officials—an intermediate rank, so to speak, within the membership of the Guild. Senior or more ambitious Notaries obtained general recognition as Leaders, Advocates of Appeal, and so forth; they were entrusted with the higher duties of the profession and, at times, were admitted as Assessors <note>legal advisors who sit with a judge</note> in certain lawsuits to the Judges on the bench. This is an interesting development in legal procedure and was undoubtedly the precursor to the British system of barristers and solicitors.

Much of the Notaries' time was occupied with drafting charters—both commercial and political—drawing up business agreements, contracts, and legal judgments; preparing balance sheets and other auditing matters; conducting foreign correspondence for merchants; and dealing generally with the thousand and one clerical details of Florence’s immense trade.

Every business house and bank had its own specialized Notary, as did the wealthier nobles and the more prominent private citizens. In addition to this, Notaries were dispatched for longer or shorter periods to the many foreign cities and districts where Florentine merchants had branch houses and agencies. One man, Lamberto Velluti—a member of the wealthy silk-manufacturing family—was employed as a Notary on one of the ships of the Peruzzi Company. It is recorded of him that after he had gained sufficient capital through fees and charges, he set up in business on his own account as a shipper of merchandise.

All embassies to foreign courts and all special missions for signing treaties and other international engagements required the services of Notaries. They were required to give notice at the <term>Monte Comune</term> <note>The public debt office or state treasury; literally "Common Mountain"</note>—the public loan office—of all legal documents drawn up by them for the payment of taxes and to deposit copies at the Offices of State within a month of their execution.

Notaries were also employed in drafting wills, copies of which they were required to file within thirty days after the testator's death. They were forbidden to draft legal documents

Notaries were appointed from time to time to inquire into and report upon disorders among the Republic's hired soldiers. These mercenaries were originally members of military companies first enrolled under *Condottieri* <term>Foreign Captains</term> in 1250, when the faction fights between the *Grandi* <term>the old aristocracy</term> and the *Popolani* <term>the merchant and working classes</term> were at their height. Their duties, in the first instance, were the defense of the *Contado* <term>the surrounding rural territory or countryside</term>, but their services were retained later for the safeguarding of the city as well. Four hundred men were required each night to patrol the following streets: Porta Rossa, Calimala, Baccano, Por Santa Maria, and the Corso degli Adimari, along with other streets and squares where most of the residences and offices of the Guilds, the principal banks, and the great mercantile companies were located, together with the shops of the more prominent tradespeople.

If women troubled worthy judges with their fashions and their charms, impoverished notaries harassed the fair sex in their search for legal citations regarding breaches of the sumptuary laws <term>laws intended to restrain luxury and extravagance</term>. The protocols concerning dress were written out by these "gentlemen of the long robe," who, not content with their faultless penmanship, busied themselves with the enforcement of these prohibitions.

The officials of the *Grascia* <term>a municipal office overseeing the food supply and public decency</term> were quick-witted notaries. It was their amusement and their profit to interrogate all the women they met. When they saw one wearing, for example, two rings ornamented with fine pearls, or a little cap or wreath embroidered and embellished with gold, they noted down her name. A summons was probably issued against her and her husband, and the latter, to avoid a public spectacle, paid the fine and the notaries’ costs to boot!¹

It may be truthfully said that every walk in life in old—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the roles and social standing of notaries in Florentine society, moving from their interactions with the law and public officials to their appearance, professional regulations, and their symbolic representation in contemporary literature and games.</meta>

<page-num>100</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Florence was filled with the busy services of these ubiquitous clerks and legal pleaders. Indeed, the functions of the notaries were so integrated into the private lives of the citizens that, while on one hand everyone was only too happy to sue their neighbor, on the other hand, the "curse of the law" became a common saying. Those who had experienced the miseries of litigation were known to greet their more fortunate neighbors with the trite saying: "May sorrow, evil, and lawyers stay far from you!"

The position of the notaries in court was directly below the judges’ seats. They were provided with raised desks, over which they would lean to consult with their clients.

Their clothing was more somber than that of the judges. Originally, they wore black or dark gray cloaks without fur, but at a later date, they gained the right to add that decoration. Attached to the belts of their long tunics, they carried pouches or bags—much like the merchants’ *<term>scarselle</term>* <term>purses or pouches worn at the waist</term>—containing writing materials, which were the distinctive marks of their profession. These pouches were usually worn quite plain and unadorned, in contrast to the elaborate coats of arms emblazoned upon the money bags of the nobles and merchants.

Strict regulations were enforced against rebellious or delinquent notaries. For example, if any notary was ten days late in paying taxes, dues, or contributions of any kind, he was disbarred and not permitted to practice until he had fully paid his debts.

In *The Game of Chess* <note>original: "Il Giuoccho delle Scacchi"</note>, Antonio Miscomini includes a woodcut of the Bishop’s Pawn, as we call the piece on the King’s right; this pawn is described by William Caxton in his *Play of Chess* in 1481 as follows:

For as much as among the common people of..."

The honesty of industrial methods was always under the supervision of legal officials. Besides this, Notaries were permitted to deal wholesale in textiles and other goods. In several documents, they sign their names with a dual title—for example, Notary-Wool Merchant <note>original: "Ser Notaio-Lanaiuolo"</note>, or Lord Wool Dealer-Notary <note>original: "Dominus Lanarius-Notarius"</note>.

While the senior Notaries adopted the dignified and arrogant manners of their higher-ranking colleagues in the Guild—the Judges—the younger ones were denied the title of *Messere* <term>Messere: a formal title of address, similar to "Lord" or "Sir," reserved for judges and high officials</term> until they had officially achieved a seat on the judicial bench. Regardless of their skills or influence, they were simply classified as Notaries. In 1495, the Notaries were established as a separate class and were forbidden from entering any commercial firm or accepting any trading agency. They were also prohibited from engaging in any kind of retail business.

-> . . . <-

It is difficult to determine the exact number of Judges and Notaries who practiced within the State's borders over time. The latter were, as might be expected, always in a significant majority. In the year 1358, Villani <note>Giovanni Villani (c. 1276–1348), a Florentine chronicler</note> says, “there were nearly one hundred Judges and upwards of five hundred Notaries.” This is a high number for a population that had been devastated by famine in 1346 and by the plague in 1348. Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), author of the "Decameron"</note> records that this latter plague killed as many as 96,000 out of a total of 160,000 inhabitants between March and September!$^1$

No writer has provided posterity with a more vivid and honest account of the legal profession in old Florence than Ser Lapo Mazzei, the virtuous Notary of Prato, described as a wise man of “rough soul and frozen heart.” As a man of self-denying spirit, with deep religious sympathies and extensive knowledge of morality, his letters are highly interesting.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the professional and social roles of Florentine notaries, transitioning from their dual commercial roles to the social scrutiny they faced and the eventual restructuring of their Guild into a "College" in 1597.</meta>

# THE GUILD OF JUDGES AND NOTARIES

If a member of the "Guild of Judges and Notaries" did anything at all that violated standard decorum and social norms, he immediately became a target for satire, and no one hesitated to mock him. Violations of proper manners often led to some prankster placing a thistle under the tail of the legal official’s horse. As the poor animal bolted back to its stable at a frantic gallop, the air was filled with the mocking shouts of passers-by!

The Guild continued to prosper throughout the "reigns" of the early Medici princes, even though many of the Judges' privileges were significantly reduced and the financial misconduct of the Notaries was secretly tolerated.

Nearly the last record in the archives regarding the "Guild of Judges and Notaries" dates to December 28, 1597. On that day, a decree was signed by Grand Duke Ferdinand I <note>Ferdinand I de' Medici (1549–1609), the Grand Duke of Tuscany who expanded the power of the Medici dynasty</note> which abolished the Guild's ancient title and replaced it with the "College of Judges and Notaries." Membership was divided into three ranks:
1. Judges
2. Advocates
3. Notaries
This structure officially recognized the intermediate rank established in the previous century.

Eight consuls were elected: two from the rank of Judge, two from the rank of Advocate, and four from the rank of Notary. The Council of the "College" consisted of eight members—four Judges and four Notaries. A Matriculation Board <term>Matriculation Board: a regulatory body responsible for the formal licensing and enrollment of professional members</term> was also established, composed of two Judges, two Advocates, and four Notaries. It was ordered that every year, two Advocates should be appointed as legal counsel for poor citizens in criminal cases. These advocates were required to plead for their clients without receiving any fee or payment, as the Guild itself undertook the responsibility of paying them.

The great reputation of the Judges and Notaries has been passed down to modern times, despite many serious scandals and flaws. Today, the legal profession remains the most important and popular career in Italy. It is the ambition of even small shopkeepers, prosperous farmers, and skilled artisans to see their sons graduate in law and become advocates in the courts.

## CHAPTER IV

# THE "CALIMALA" GUILD

### THE GUILD AND CORPORATE BODY OF THE MERCHANTS OF CALIMALA <note>original: "L'ARTE E UNIVERSITA DE' MERCANTI DI CALIMALA"</note>

I. ORIGIN.—Meaning of the name. “French Cloths” <note>original: "Panni Franceschi"</note>. The finishing of foreign cloth. Merchants of the Calimala, 1190. Cavalcanti. The Chiefs of the Mugello. Early predominant influence of the Guild.
II. CONSTITUTION.—Statutes—Code, 1201-1209. Charitable purposes. Usury. Legal procedure. Trade restrictions. Enrollment. Associated trades. Games. Working hours. III. DEVELOPMENT.—Superiority of Florentine methods. Mercantile companies. Friction between the guilds. Guido del’ Antella and his “Memoirs” <note>original: "Ricordanze"</note>. Dangers of commercial travel. Fame of Florentine cloth. Leading “Calimala” families. Foreign competition. The record of five hundred years.

Various names and titles are given in documents and by authorities for the master merchant guild of Florence: “The Guild of Merchants,” “The Guild of Merchants in Foreign Cloth,” “The Guild of Calimala,” “The Guild of the French Calimala,” etc., etc.

The spelling of the distinctive name “*Calimala*” also varies: “*Kallismale*,” “*Calimara*,” etc. Its most probable derivation comes from the fact that the residence and offices of the guild were situated in the Via di Calimala, a narrow street which led into the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note>—where the chief business of the merchants of the guild was also conducted.

Above the entrance of the Residence, a shield was mounted displaying the Guild's coat of arms: a golden eagle perched on a white wool bale against a red background. This same design was also displayed on the *Gonfalon* <term>a heraldic banner or ensign</term>.

<margin>{ <unclear>Pw</unclear></margin>
Machiavelli, writing about the commercial activities of the "*Calimala*," states:
> "The production of wool fabrics was so successful that the workers only needed to dye and finish them before they were ready for immediate export. The merchants involved in this industry established an important Guild named the '*Calimala*,' after the street where they were located."¹

Regarding the term "*Francesca*" or "*Franceschi*" <note>original: "French"</note> as used by the Guild, it is worth noting what Fernando Arrivabene says about religious orders:
> "In 1182, the famous Saint Francis, founder of the great religious order, was born in Assisi, Umbria, to Pietro Bernadones, a man of humble origin. At his baptism, he was named Giovanni, but as a young man, he was called 'Francesco' because of the fluency with which he spoke French—a language that was then essential for Italians in the trade for which his father intended him."²

This suggests that active trade between Italy and France existed before 1182. Undoubtedly, the terms "*Francesca*" and "*Franceschi*" originally referred specifically to France and its markets in Florence, but their meaning eventually expanded to include goods from other nations. Consequently, "*Panni Franceschi*" <note>original: "French Cloths"</note> came to refer to cloth manufactured in England, Flanders, and Spain, as well as France.

From early times, wool was the primary industry of the Florentines. They worked it with such remarkable diligence and skill that the production from their looms soon exceeded what was needed locally. They began to seek markets beyond the borders of the growing town, and traders, traveling in groups—

Commercial relations with England existed during the reign of Henry II. In any case, that monarch established a twice-yearly Cloth Fair within the grounds of the Priory of Saint Bartholomew in the city of London. He also encouraged the formation of a Weavers' Guild, modeling it after similar associations in Florence and Flanders.

<margin>red bracket and handwritten note: trade.</margin>
With rare insight, the Florentine traders bartered their fabrics for rich fleeces and fine woolen yarns. As they traded, the eyes of both parties were opened: the Florentines recognized the superiority of the native raw material, while the local people saw the superior quality of the Florentine craftsmanship.

<margin>two red check marks in right margin</margin>
In addition to their skill in weaving, Florentine workers excelled as cutters and folders, and they were unrivaled as dyers. The Guild’s business was exclusively the re-dressing and finishing of foreign-woven woolen cloth. When foreign cloth was processed using the methods of the Florentine merchants, it became a material without equal, which commanded the highest prices when placed on the European markets.

While it is impossible to set an exact date for the first formal incorporation of the "*Calimala Francesca Mercanti*" <note>original: "French Merchant Calimala"</note>, it can be safely stated that the first steps in that direction were taken at the end of the eleventh century. During that period, under the supportive rule of Countess Matilda, the industrial progress of Florence was already remarkable.

Perhaps the earliest documentary evidence of the "*Calimala*" as a corporate body dates to the year 1190, when the "Merchants of the Calimala" are named. Under the same date, it is recorded that the Florentine Cavalcanti family played a leading role in the foreign cloth trade and that they gave up their house on the Via di Calimala to serve as offices for the merchants.¹ It may also be interesting to note that the very first names entered in the earliest surviving Roll of...

The matriculations <note>official enrollments or registrations</note> of the Guild of the “*French Calimala*” <note>original: “Calimala Francesca”</note> included those of the two sons of the donor of this property.¹

From 1190 onward, mentions of the “*Calimala*” and its operations appear frequently in the Archives of Florence. For example, a document dated October 21, 1190, describes the Guild as being in active operation.² This document is a deed of gift for land and buildings intended for the benefit of the Guild. In it, Giambone di Ceffuli and his son, Diede, with the consent of their wives, irrevocably transfer certain property to Giovanni di Buoninsegna and Ugone d’Angiolotti, identified as the “Consuls of the Old Merchants of the Calimala.”

The earliest entry in the List of Consuls is dated 1192, recording that Giano Cavalcanti, Ranerio di Ugone della Bella, and Ugo d’Angiolotti served in that office.

The importance of the “*Calimala*” Guild was formally recognized in 1199 in a document stating that the <term>Consuls of the Merchants</term> <note>original: “Consules Mercatorum”</note> sat in the Superior Council of the Commune. They served alongside the three representative Priors of the Guilds and the ten <term>Good Men</term> <note>original: “Buonuomini,” a council of respected citizens</note> under the presidency of the <term>Podesta</term> <note>the chief magistrate of the city</note>, Pagano de’ Porcari.³ At that time, there were six “*Calimala*” Consuls, led by Stoldo da Musetto. The business before the Council was the drafting of a treaty of peace and friendship with the robber chieftains of the Mugello and other districts belonging to Lombardy, Venice, and Bologna, through which vital trade routes passed.

Stoldo da Musetto and Raniero della Bella—two of the “*Calimala*” Consuls—were appointed to sign the treaty, in which the Chieftains promised:

1. To protect Florentine merchants and their merchandise throughout their feudal territories.
2. To treat the requirements of the merchants as their own.

The official designation of the "*Calimala*," during the first twenty years of the thirteenth century, was: "The Guild and University of the Merchants of Calimala" <note>original: "L'Arte e Universita de' Mercanti di Calimala"</note>.

The statutes of the "*Calimala*" Guild are found in Latin in many manuscripts preserved in the Florentine libraries. The earliest volume <note>original: Codex</note> dates from 1301–1309. It is held in the Magliabecchian Library and is written in the hand of Matteo Beliotti and Giovanni Ser Lapi—both notaries of Florence—and their assistants.¹

It opens with a dedication to God which states that the constitution of "the Craft and University of the Merchants of the Calimala <note>original: Kallismale</note> of Florence" is established in reverence of Saint Mary, Saint John the Baptist, Saints Peter, Paul, Philip, James, and Miniato, and all the saints. It is also created in honor of the Holy Roman Church and the Pope <note>original: Sovereign Pontiff</note>; the Lord <term>Podestà</term> <note>the chief magistrate of the city-state</note>, the Lord <term>Capitano</term> <note>the Captain of the People, a high-ranking military and political official</note>, and the Commonwealth of Florence; and, finally, with all due respect for all worthy merchants and companies belonging to the "*Calimala*."²

The first part consists of thirty-two sections which address—as the charming <note>original: quaint</note> heading says—"all things pertaining to God and to the soul." It discusses religious observances, good works, honest conduct, obedience to magistrates, and everything else that contributes to making a virtuous, hardworking, and respectable citizen.

<margin>
<image-desc>A hand-drawn symbol of a circle with a cross through it, resembling a crossed-out O or a wheel.</image-desc>
aly
</margin>
The religious profession of faith discussed in the first section is noteworthy. It indicates the close relationship that existed during the Middle Ages and early Renaissance between daily religious life and industrial and commercial activities. <note>The preceding lines are underlined in red ink in the original.</note> Every morning, monks chanted Mass in the ancient church of San Giovanni on behalf of the members of the Guild and for the success of their business ventures.

Guild members were required <note>original: constrained</note> to observe the annual church festivals, which numbered forty, not counting Sundays. <note>The phrase "Guildsmen were constrained" is underlined in red ink in the original.</note>

On the Eve of St. John the Baptist—the patron saint of Florence—every member of the Guild was required to visit the church and deposit a wax candle weighing nearly half a pound as an offering to the patron saint.

The "Merchants of the Calimala" bound themselves never to use blasphemous language. <term>Usury</term> <note>the practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates</note> was forbidden "because it is a sin especially displeasing to God."

<margin>Almsgiving</margin>
Among the religious duties of the Guild were numerous annual contributions of money and goods to monasteries for the relief of the city's poor and <insert>sick.</insert> Several hospitals were also maintained at the expense of the "Calimala."

Regarding food and drink, moderation and abstinence were encouraged for everyone connected to the Guild. Forty pounds per year was the very modest sum set aside for the table of the Consuls, who were provided with board during their six months of office at the Guild’s expense at the Residence in the Via di Calimala <note>Calimala Street</note>.

The workmen employed by the "Calimala" for the repair and decoration of the churches of San Giovanni <note>St. John</note> and San Miniato al Monte <note>St. Minias on the Mountain</note> were subject to <insert>strict rules of conduct.</insert> They, and indeed all members of the Guild, were warned under threat of heavy penalties—including expulsion—to lead irreproachable lives and to treat women, children, and domestic servants with respect and kindness.

The second part of the Statutes contains forty-five sections. These deal with legal questions, financial matters, disputes affecting members of the Guild, rules for membership and apprenticeship, and regulations for trading companies and associations of workers.

The first section deals with the powers of the Consuls, who are decreed to be the supreme authority over all persons and legal cases within the Guild. Legal procedures, the employment of legal assistance, and the requirement to obey the rulings of the Court of Consuls are all fully explained.

The rights of the creditor are emphasized, and provisions are made for liquidating estates in bankruptcy. The sale of a bankrupt person's assets could only be conducted at the request of the Consuls in Council. Earnest money—ranging from ten to fifty percent—was due at the start of all transactions, and payments were required to be made in installments. All receipts required the seal of a cashier, were signed in their presence, and were verified by the representative <term>Syndic</term> of the Treasurer. Merchants or agents who defaulted on their debts were publicly posted at the Guild Office in the Via di Calimala <note>Calimala Street</note>; however, a ten-day grace period was allowed before the Guild resorted to extreme measures.

All disputes—whether regarding the interpretation of the Guild's Statutes and Bylaws or those of the associated companies, or matters affecting the interests or customs of the Guild—were submitted to the Consuls in Court. The Consuls appointed a Special Commission of merchants, at their discretion, to investigate all such matters.

Merchants were not permitted to sell any type of cloth except for those specifically named in the Statutes, nor were they allowed to export fine wool or any of the ingredients necessary for the industry.

Sales were restricted to the interior of shops, and pieces of cloth for sale were not permitted to be displayed outside. The exchange of goods directly between the warehouses of merchants was also forbidden. No one was authorized to deal in foreign cloth unless they were granted formal permission from the Consuls. People seeking such authorization were required to provide a sworn statement <note>original: "affidavit"</note> before the Guild Notary regarding the respectability of their family connections, their own personal integrity, and their financial honesty.

Laborers' societies, or companies, were affiliated with the *Calimala* specifically to avoid confusion with similar organizations under the Wool Guild <term>Arte della Lana</term>. Their privileges and the scope of their work were strictly limited. No worker or group of workers was permitted to work for both guilds. The *Calimala* laborers were exclusively engaged in handling foreign-made woolen cloth. As <insert>red circle: a</insert> rule, the <insert>red underline: Calimala</insert> employed entire families rather than groups of unrelated individuals. The statutes and bylaws of the *Calimala* are full of records of names and occupations where these restrictions are clearly visible.

On the other hand, *Calimala* merchants welcomed the sons of merchants from other guilds, especially from the guilds of "Judges and Notaries" and "Doctors and Apothecaries." The only condition for apprenticeship in such cases was that the apprentice must not follow his parents' profession. Sometimes fees were paid for entry into the leading merchant houses, but generally, a mutual arrangement was made, which often had a marriage alliance in mind.

Instead, they were required to receive and deliver their pieces of cloth and make all complaints to the syndics <term>legal representatives or administrative officials</term> and overseers of the Guild in their respective neighborhoods.

Certain sections of the second part of the Statutes deal with the deaths of members and the management of their affairs. Whenever a full member, an associate, an apprentice, or the son of a member who was at least eighteen years old (even if not yet enrolled) died, the Consuls did not sit in court that day. All workshops and Guild offices were closed until after the funeral; only *il sportello* <note>the wicket; a small door or gate</note> remained open, just as it was when looms were idle during a festival.

# THE “CALIMALA” GUILD

## THE “CALIMALA” GUILD

The third part of the statutes contains fifty-six sections dealing with <note>original: "le buone usanze di Kalimala"</note> "the good customs of the Calimala"—the traditions, practices, and regulations of the guild.

The first section established the value of the *denario* <note>a standard silver coin</note>, the standard currency of the market. It decreed that any change in its value could only be authorized by the Consuls in Council.

Several sections address methods for paying accounts, credit terms, and similar matters. In modern terms, these were "bills of exchange" with terms of three months, two months, eight days, or "at sight." These were issued upon notice that cloth was being shipped, whether it was being imported from foreign sources for finishing by "Calimala" agents or delivered to foreign buyers after the refinement process in Florence was complete.

The statutes clearly state that only whole pieces of cloth imported from "beyond the mountains" <note>referring to Northern Europe, such as France and Flanders</note> and from England could be sold at retail by "Calimala" merchants in Florence, and only at a fixed rate. However, they were permitted to sell remnants of any type of cloth to retail dealers.

All pieces of foreign cloth finished in Florence by "Calimala" workers were required to be placed on the market within eight days of receiving the guild's official stamp. The reason for this rule is explained in the statutes: it was intended to prevent merchants from hoarding stock to artificially drive up prices.

At the time these statutes were drafted—between 1301 and 1309—the price for high-quality finished cloth was one silver florin per *canna* <note>a traditional Italian unit of length, roughly equal to two yards</note>; lower-quality pieces were less expensive. The *canna* served as the official standard of measurement.

Sales were restricted to the interior of shops; merchants were not allowed to display fabric pieces or samples in doorways or windows. This rule was likely established out of respect for the concerns of the Consuls of the Wool Guild <note>the *Arte della Lana*, which focused on local production</note>, whose interests might have been harmed by the competing sale of imported woolen cloth. Furthermore, garments made from foreign cloth finished by the "Calimala" were forbidden from being sold as merchandise in the Florentine markets.

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Upon every piece or length of finished cloth, of every kind and color, an official ticket or card was attached in plain view. This card bore the fixed price, the name of the *villa* <note>workshop or factory</note>, and the name of the *maestro* <note>master maker</note>.

An officer was commanded to travel through all the streets and visit every house where the industry was practiced to ensure that every detail of the work fully met the standards or models kept in the central hall of the *Calimala* <note>the guild of cloth finishers and merchants of foreign cloth</note> offices. All such matters were handled with the utmost accuracy; even the smallest deviation—including the size of the tickets or the handwriting on them—was punished with fines and dismissal.

Sometimes a manufacturer was stubborn, but he paid for his folly with double fines. If he continued to be negligent, he lost his *Bollo* <note>the guild's official seal of guarantee</note>, and his name was removed from the guild roll.

As early as 1292, the Consuls of the *Calimala* received authorization from the Greater and Special Councils of the Craft to punish offenders with fines and by striking all members who broke the guild's rules and customs from the membership registers, along with their accomplices and anyone who received illegal materials.<sup>1</sup>

<margin>// Two diagonal red marks</margin>
Many statutes in this third part are directed against fraud and irregularities in business. The aim of the *Calimala* was to conduct guild business in a strictly honorable and almost religious manner. Every contract began with an invocation to the Trinity and a prayer for the benevolent aid of Saint Mary and all the saints.

A well-known form of profanity—whereby a dishonest or greedy salesman would move his *canna* <note>a measuring rod</note> along the cloth while reciting the names of the Trinity or the names of the saints to count out a certain number of *braccia* <note>forearm lengths or cubits</note>—was constantly practiced. Selling by guesswork on the part of the buyer, where a bid exceeding the actual legal value was accepted, was another scheme used to defraud.

### THE "CALIMALA" GUILD

<margin>Fraud — cheating in the measurement of cloth</margin>
Cutting cloth shorter than its standard length and then selling it as if it were the full measurement was a common trick in the lower-class shops. In one of his charming *Novelle* <note>short stories</note>, Sacchetti describes what happened to a certain Soccebonelli of Friuli, who went to buy some cloth. The merchant measured out four yards but managed to stealthily pull some back; to cover the fraud, he said to Soccebonelli: "If you want this cloth to turn out well, leave it to soak in water all night, and you will see how excellent it becomes." Soccebonelli did as he was told, and then he took the cloth to a cutter <note>a professional tailor who cuts fabric</note> and asked him to measure it. "It seems to me," said the tailor, "to be five *braccia* <term>a Florentine unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches</term>." Soccebonelli explained how he had been cheated, but he received little sympathy. Indeed, one man he met told him about a person "who bought one *braccio* of Florentine cloth, kept it in water all night, and by the next morning it had shrunk so much that nothing was left!"¹

It was believed that many pieces of cloth that came from Milan and other places, which were sold before the bales were even opened, had been dyed there. Andrea del Castagno—a naturalist painter and cynical diarist who lived from 1390 to 1457—writes as follows: "I heard that a certain agent named Giovanni del Volpe, seeing that this sort of cloth sold well, thought of saving money for his firm by dyeing it in a cheaper and inferior way."

The Consuls constantly issued denunciations and penalties against all these and other sorts of fraud. A first offense resulted in a fine of three gold florins, and the sale was pronounced null and void. Repeated acts of dishonesty or questionable dealings were met with even heavier fines, and could even lead to suspension or expulsion from the Guild.

The Fourth Part of the Statutes contains fifty-eight sections, which deal exclusively with the election of the Guild’s officers and their functions.

At the head were four Consuls and a Treasurer, who were elected every six months by the votes of the general Master-merchants and confirmed by the Masters of the various companies incorporated into or affiliated with the "Calimala" Guild, such as:

Candidates had to be "adherents of the *Parte Guelfa* <note>the political faction supporting the Papacy</note>, lovers of the Holy Roman Church, and of untarnished reputation, both within the Guild and the Commune <note>the city-state of Florence</note>."

The method of election was as follows: the names of eligible candidates were first written upon paper and placed in an urn. From there, under the direction of three merchants chosen as scrutineers <term>officials who oversee the counting of votes</term> for that purpose, the oldest merchant present drew five slips. These five selected candidates could not be partners in the same business house or company, nor could they be associated with any of the five retiring officials.

Electors—who were fully registered and active members of the Guild residing within the *Contado* <term>the rural territory surrounding Florence governed by the city</term>—were granted one vote for each retail shop owned by an individual. However, the possession of a wholesale factory gave a company two votes. The voting was conducted by casting black and white beans. If any chosen candidate was "white beaned" <note>rejected or vetoed by the vote</note>, the three scrutineers ordered another selection of names to be drawn from the urn. This process continued until the election was completed. Any merchants who failed to attend or vote were punishable by fines. Furthermore, those who were finally elected were required to serve their terms of office or forfeit twenty-five *lire*. Each Consul received a salary of about forty *lire*, and the Treasurer received ten *lire* for their terms of office.

The four Consuls were bound by strict rules. They were not allowed to go beyond the boundaries of the *Contado*, except for religious purposes, on behalf of the Guild’s interests, or when nominated as ambassadors of the Republic to foreign states.

1. To grant registration to those they considered worthy;

3. To protect the factories, shops, and agencies of Guild members, whether at home or abroad; 
4. To assist merchants in recovering debts; 
5. To distribute charities and oversee the religious works of the Guild; 
6. To represent the Guild on all official and ceremonial occasions; and

The Consuls were also responsible for nominating representatives of the Guild in all foreign countries with which there were commercial relations. Lastly, they had the authority to appoint, when necessary, a Court of Arbitration to settle all trade disputes, whether they occurred within or outside the jurisdiction of the "*Calimala*." This court was composed of six influential merchants who were entrusted with interpreting the Statutes and Ordinances of the Guild.

<margin><unclear>pu</unclear></margin>
Every month, the Consuls of the "*Calimala*" met with the Consuls or heads of the city's other guilds for consultation on general commercial matters. This was done in preparation for presenting measures and provisions to the Council of State. These meetings carried a political character and were extremely powerful in the government of the Republic.

The Consuls were assisted in the exercise of their duties by two Councils. The first—called the "General Council"—was composed of twelve members who were merchants belonging to separate business houses or companies within the Guild. All matters of general interest were submitted to this Council for three successive days for their approval or rejection. The second Council—styled the "Special Council"—had eighteen members chosen from among the master merchants who had expert knowledge of specific departments within the operations of the Guild and its affiliated crafts. The General Council submitted all matters requiring expert advice to them, and their sessions also lasted over three days. They handed their report to the General Council, who, after arriving at a final decision, placed the matter before the Consuls. To avoid "packing" the Councils <note>the practice of filling a committee with biased supporters to ensure a specific outcome</note>, no companies or affiliated trades connected with the "*Calimala*" were permitted to have more than two representatives. All votes were taken by means of beans <note>a traditional method of secret balloting where different colored beans represented "yes" or "no" votes</note>.

He was directed to submit his report every month to a special panel of merchants chosen by lot. In cases where matters required investigation and correction, the report with notes was submitted to a second panel consisting of twelve master-merchants. His term of office lasted for one year, at the end of which his acts and general conduct were reviewed by three experienced examiners. They imposed fines upon the unfortunate fellow in proportion to the severity <note>original: "heinousness"</note> of his neglect of duty. So far as we can discover, Notaries never escaped without a penalty, nor—it goes without saying—were they ever rewarded for faithfulness and perfect conduct!

-># THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

transactions of the merchants, and to hand over the balance, or to receive the same, upon the completion of all contracts and orders. The <term>Chiavari</term> <note>literally: "Key-bearers"</note> were registrars of population, membership, deaths, and wills, as well as auditors of the cash accounts of the affiliated operative companies. They kept the keys of all the minor offices and acted as cashiers for deposits made by workers and small dealers into the Guild Treasury. Their number varied according to circumstances.

Besides these officials, there were small committees of merchants appointed from time to time who scheduled the wage tables of workers employed by the <term>Calimala</term> <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth</note>. They supervised the numbering and labeling of foreign cloth before and after it had been finished in Florence. Once a year, in July, two merchants were appointed to fix the price of dyeing, to which all dyers were bound to adhere, unless, of course, they chose to accept lower prices on their own initiative.

The testing of weights and measures was the responsibility of another sub-committee, along with the examination of cloth lengths to prevent short measures, deficient weight, and inferior quality.

The watching, cleaning, and lighting of the area around the Residence of the Consuls was managed by a Watch Committee of three or four members, who employed twenty or more <term>sbirri</term> <note>armed watchmen or guards</note> for the purpose, each armed with a stout staff and a lantern.
