Members of the Guild and their workers were subject to severe disciplinary measures regarding their behavior in the streets, particularly in the *Via di Calimala* and in the *Mercato Nuovo* <note>New Market</note>. The entertainment of friends and social interaction were subject to restrictions. The Consuls had full authority for dealing with all unruly citizens. Fines and imprisonment in the <term>Stinche</term> <note>the city prison</note> were served out impartially to friend and foe alike.

The fifth part of the Statutes treats, in twenty sections, of the <term>Sensali</term> (brokers or agents), the <term>Tintori</term> (dyers), and the <term>Racconciatori</term> <note>cloth repairers or restorers</note>...

# THE "CALIMALA" GUILD

The workers employed by the merchants of the "<term>Calimala</term>" <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth</note> included Patchers, the <term>*Tagliatori*</term> (Cutters), the <term>*Piegatori*</term> (Folders), and the <term>*Compitori*</term> (Finishers).

The duties of the <term>*Sensali*</term> <note>brokers or inspectors</note> were to inspect all imports of foreign cloth upon arrival and to distribute the fabric to the various associations of laborers. Within twenty-four hours of the cloth's delivery to the Guild Offices in Florence, the <term>*Periti dell' Arte di Calimala*</term>—the guild's experts—conducted a careful examination of every piece of foreign cloth. They inspected the quality of the wool, the method of manufacture, and the length and weight. Satisfactory pieces were immediately sent to the workshops, while those that failed to meet the trade's requirements were set aside for further consideration.

Any citizen could be admitted to the position of <term>Sensale</term> if they possessed a good reputation for religious piety and integrity in their business dealings. Before being enrolled in the records of the "<term>Calimala</term>," they were required to provide personal financial security and obtain bail from their friends as a guarantee.

Once a month, they had to submit a detailed report to the Consuls sitting at the Guild Residence. This report documented their operations, the origin and condition of all cloth received, and the specific processes to which it had been subjected. Their report also served as the medium for complaints made by the workers and for reporting any misconduct by those with whom the <term>Sensali</term> had dealings.

The first step in treating foreign cloth was not the actual dyeing, but rather the preparation of the fabric for that process. When first unrolled, the pieces were generally found to be covered with knots and blemishes that coarsened the surface. Eradicating and smoothing over these flaws required the greatest possible care. This process was carried out by both women and men, who used very fine pliers, needles, and hot irons. Sometimes even darning was necessary, but this had to be done with extreme delicacy using foreign wool of exactly the same quality as the original piece.

***

<term>Note:</term> Three old <term>*Tiratoli*</term> (fulling mills) <note>Fulling mills were used to cleanse and thicken cloth</note> belonging to members of the Guild were still standing in 1898. Located in the Via de' Servi, Via del Castelluccio, and Via degli Alfani, each bore the name <term>*dell' Aquila*</term> (of the Eagle), referring to the eagle that served as the arms, or trademark, of the Guild.

## THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

The Dyers of the <term>*Calimala*</term> <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth</note> were required to weigh and measure all pieces of foreign cloth immediately upon receiving them from the <term>*Sensali*</term> <note>brokers or inspectors</note>.

No piece of cloth was handed over to the dyeing cauldrons until it had been inspected in detail by the foreman of that group of workers.

->EXPERIMENTING WITH DYES.<-
->SIXTEENTH CENTURY.<-

Most foreign cloth, because of its finer texture—which greatly surpassed local manufacturing—was also much more receptive to absorbing dyes and producing far more beautiful tints. After being dipped many times and stirred with smooth wooden poles in the dye bath, the pieces were hung up to dry, stretched on frames. The opinions of expert dyers were sought at this stage, and careful attention was paid to the requirements of fashion. Every faulty piece was immediately returned to the cauldron for further soaking. 

Upon a successful result in the dyeing process, the pieces of cloth were again weighed and measured by the *Sensali*. Any losses in weight and dimensions were charged to the dyers, who had the right to recover these costs through a fixed allowance set against shrinkage.

The importation of dyes and dyeing materials, and the rules concerning their use, were under the direct administration of the merchants of the *Calimala*. Only vegetable dyes were

## THE "CALIMALA" GUILD

Agents were employed and sought in every accessible land. The time and talents of the most prominent citizens were given freely to the discovery of new dye plants and to their export to Florence. The acquisition of a new dye was as much a matter of state policy as was the procurement of <term>mordants</term> <note>substances used to fix dyes to fabrics</note> and other additives for the dyeing industry. The war with Volterra, for instance, was fought solely to gain possession of the district's famous <term>alum</term> pits <note>Alum was an essential mineral used to ensure dyes adhered to cloth</note>, as the use of that material was vital.

The primary plants used for dyeing were <term>*Guado*</term> (woad) for blue, <term>*Robbia*</term> (madder) for red, and <term>*Oricello*</term> (white moss) for scarlet.

Woad grew in abundance all around Florence, but careful cultivation produced such a bountiful crop and ensured such a high-quality product that growing it became a profitable occupation throughout the countryside.

Madder was also common enough in Tuscany, but the finest variety was found near Rome, where it had been a specialty since the time of Pliny.<sup>1</sup> In the fifteenth century, the region around Chiana and the Tiber Valley produced madder worth many thousands of <term>florins</term> <note>the gold currency of Florence</note>, nearly all of which was purchased by the <term>Calimala</term> merchants.<sup>2</sup> A great deal of madder was also imported from the Rhone Valley.

The introduction of "white moss" <note>also known as orchil, a lichen-based dye</note> was due to a Florentine <term>Calimala</term> merchant named Bernardo (or Nardo) Alamanno. His discovery of its properties as a dye was entirely accidental. While on a commercial expedition in the <term>Levant</term> <note>the region of the eastern Mediterranean</note> in 1261, he observed that a small plant turned into a crimson-violet liquid when moistened with uric acid. By experimenting with this dye, he soon noticed its value for creating distinct colors and long-lasting stains. Consequently, Bernardo packed a large bale of the moss and brought it back with him to Florence.

Once home, he sought the help of members of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries," and soon the eyes...

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

The eyes of the inspectors of the *Calimala* opened wide at the brilliance of the new dye. Nothing so splendid had ever been seen in a Florentine dye shop. Bernardo's fortune was made, and he took the family name of *Rucellai*, which his descendants still keep today while continuing their ancestral industry in Florence. One of his most famous descendants, Giovanni Rucellai, was a perfect example of the noble merchant who valued the dignity of his position. He not only knew the secret of making money, but he also understood how to spend it well. "I think," he wrote in his *Zibaldone*—or *Stray Thoughts*—"that it has brought me more honor to have spent money well than to have earned it well."

The method of extracting the superb scarlet-purple dye was very simple. Bunches of *oricello* <term>orchil lichen</term> were cut after flowering and hung in the sun to dry. The dried moss was then ground into a very fine powder in a mortar and mixed in a wooden vessel with a splash of sour wine. While stirring, uric acid <note>Historically derived from fermented urine</note> was added gradually, and the mixture was shaken thoroughly once a day. Soda ash was added to this liquid in a ratio of twelve parts to one part of powder, and the entire mixture was filtered through chalk or lime.

<margin>////</margin>
Strict regulations were enforced on dyers to ensure the colors were perfect. Only the purest and most expensive materials were permitted for treating the finest cloths. Woad <term>a plant used for blue dye</term> was guarded as carefully as the white moss. No one was allowed to sell it outside the Guild membership, under penalty of a fine of five hundred pounds (approximately £20). Every dye had its own fixed sale price and official market quotation.

The exclusive right to sell coloring ingredients for dyeing woolen cloth belonged to certain members of the Guild, and all other persons were forbidden from offering them for sale. A note in the Florentine Archives records that in 1347, a company of *Calimala* merchants sold forty-four thousand pounds of woad to two merchants from Valencia for eight hundred gold florins (roughly £400).<sup>1</sup>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the strict regulations governing the Florentine dyeing industry, specifically focusing on the use of madder and the prestigious orchil scarlet dye used by the Calimala Guild.</meta>

# THE "CALIMALA" GUILD

The export of *robbia* <term>madder</term> outside the borders of the State—especially the variety known as <note>original: "di Romandiola"</note> "from Romagna"—was strictly prohibited by a section in the Statutes of 1415, with fines imposed in increments of one hundred *lire*.

Furthermore, it was forbidden to pass off one color for another or to imitate recognized tints by blending various shades to deceive the dyer or the buyer. Cochineal, Brazil-wood, and various other dyeing ingredients were used for cloths other than those classified as "the finest." Blending colors was perfectly acceptable when special names were given to the cloth dyed that way; however, all such names had to be written on large white labels and fastened to every length or roll of fabric. Madder could be used freely in dyeing cloths other than the fine white or grey foreign-made fabrics, which were classified as *Scarlattini*.

The favorite color in the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries was *Scarlatto d'oricello* <term>orchil scarlet</term>, a rich purple-red produced from orchil dye with a small amount of madder added. This shade was required for all state robes and for ceremonial tapestries and hangings. It was also used for the *berretta* <term>cap</term> worn by everyone who had the right to enter the Superior Courts. This scarlet color was most carefully protected. Any dyer who dared to produce *Scarlatto di Colpo* <term>imitation scarlet</term> was expelled from the trade, and all pieces of cloth dyed in that manner were seized and burned. Tuscan painters have preserved this rich color for us in the backgrounds of their paintings and in the clothing of the figures they portrayed.

As early as 1279, the superiority of Florentine dyers was confirmed by correspondence between the Papal Court and the Consuls of the "Calimala" Guild. The Guild maintained the exclusive right of Florentine dyers to dye and finish the cloth used for the red robes of the Cardinals, and for other church purposes where that specific type of cloth and color were required.

The dyers of Florence rapidly became famous throughout the world.

<margin>¹ G. Venturi Rosetti, <note>original: "L’Arte del Tingere"</note> “The Art of Dyeing.”</margin>

Rosetti says: “The Venetians must admit that they learned their craft from the Florentines.” ¹ Their skill and care are still evident today in the excellent condition and vibrant colors of the hangings, tapestries, banners, and costumes preserved in many public museums and private collections. These items rival, and perhaps even surpass, the best craftsmanship of the present day.

Once dry, the cloth that was considered sufficiently and satisfactorily dyed was passed to the cutters, patchers, and piecers, who prepared the fabric for the final stage of its production. These workers were often less skilled, and since their tasks were relatively simple and minor, they were poorly paid. Nevertheless, their work was strictly inspected by the foremen of the folders and finishers to ensure they did not make mistakes when cutting the fabric to the required lengths or accidentally join pieces of cloth of different qualities or shades of color. Strict oversight was also maintained regarding remnants and scraps, which could be sold as profitable goods by the *Rigattieri* <term>retail cloth-dealers</term> and other market peddlers. Patching was only used for second-quality foreign cloth. The goal of this process was to provide the folders and finishers with a fabric of perfectly consistent texture.

The folders and finishers, along with the dyers, were the most important and highly trained among the working classes in Florence. Their first task was to identify and correct the mistakes and careless work of the previous handlers. Constant friction existed between these two groups of workers; the intermediate workers teased the finishers for being too picky, while the finishers scolded the intermediate workers for their negligence.

The folders were required to re-verify the weights and measurements of the pieces of cloth and to categorize the different qualities according to their various destinations. When the cloth was being prepared for shipping, the rolls and pieces had to be folded in a specific manner, which...

...should do nothing to disturb the "nap" <term>the raised surface of the fabric</term> of the cloth or cause friction.

The <term>Finishers</term> had to smooth the cloth and correct its surface by applying heat, using either weighted rollers or heated flat-irons. The specific methods they used have never been recorded in detail, but it is clear they were laborious and quite technical, as every yard of finished cloth was subjected to a rigorous examination.

<columns>2</columns>
A special Committee of Experts, called the <term>Inspectors of Spots and Blemishes</term> <note>original: "Ufficiali delle Macchie e Magagne"</note>, was employed by the "<term>Calimala</term>" Guild to visit the cloth finishers' workrooms and test the cloth in hand under every condition.

<columns>1</columns>

All work—whether cutting, piecing, patching, finishing, or folding—was subjected to the most detailed examination. Poor workmanship, the presence of blemishes, and roughness of the surface were all heavily penalized. Fines were imposed, and if they were not paid, the offender's entire security deposit or bail, or a portion of it, could be seized. The names of those who failed to meet these standards were posted at the "<term>Calimala</term>" offices, and in serious cases, they were stripped of the right to practice their trade within the city boundaries.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Calimala Guild’s regulations and history, transitioning from the specific penalties for poor workmanship to the broader development of its statutes and its relationship with prominent Florentine mercantile families and religious institutions.</meta>

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The statutes established in the first decade of the fourteenth century—which were revised and expanded many times in the following centuries—became the foundation for the constitutions of all the other guilds.

Very interesting records concerning the members, their duties, their charities, and the general progress of the guild can be found in documents preserved in the libraries of Florence and the archives of many noble families. Among these are many instructions dating from the mid-twelfth century regarding the maintenance and decoration of the Baptistery of San Giovanni. There are also records of land purchases and sales in 1192, 1193, and 1216 made on behalf of the Hospital of Sant’ Eusebio. In 1228 and 1237, many <term>*Provvisioni*</term> <note>legislative ordinances</note>, or agreements, were made concerning the ancient Church of San Miniato al Monte, which was placed under the protection of the “*Calimala*.” In the latter year, all members of the guild were required to take an official oath. This oath, which was registered before the Consuls, bound each member to follow the guild's regulations, bylaws, customs, and privileges for the entire year.

The first Florentine mercantile company was established in connection with and under the sponsorship of the “*Calimala*.” The <term>*Provvisione*</term> <note>ordinance</note> that created it is dated 1234. It was registered for the sale of foreign cloth after it had been refined and finished by workers associated with the guild. One of the earliest companies was that of the Scali, which went bankrupt in 1326 after being in business for nearly one hundred years.

A fourteenth-century <term>Codex</term> <note>a manuscript book</note> provides the following list of mercantile companies working in partnership with the “*Calimala*” Guild <gloss>1</gloss>: the Canigiani, the Spini, the Migliori, the Guadagni, Lapo Bounagrazia, Buonaccorso Soldini, Marino Soldani, Diotifici Filippi, Lapo Marini, Lapo Soldini, Simone Giamini, and Diotisalvi Artimisi. A parchment from the year 1300 contains twenty-one other names, including the Cenchi, Bardi, Pazzi, Frescobaldi, Peruzzi, Scali, and Nerli families.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Calimala Guild’s regulations and history, specifically focusing on its strict prohibition against dealing in locally produced cloth and its efforts to manage labor relations and jurisdictional boundaries with other guilds, such as the Silk Guild.</meta>

# THE "CALIMALA" GUILD

<margin>Merchants</margin>
It should be remembered that the "Calimala" merchants dealt only with foreign-made cloth. They were expressly prohibited from finishing, preparing, keeping, or selling cloth manufactured in Florence. This regulation was established not only to avoid damaging the local wool-weaving industry—which was governed by the Guild of Woolen Merchants—but also as a necessary precaution to avoid labor disputes with the workers.

As might be expected, there was a constant risk of confusion and friction between the agents and the workers employed by the guilds. Many regulations <note>original: "Provvisioni," legislative ordinances</note> were passed to minimize and remove all conflicts of interest. Separate associations for dyers, piecers, patchers, cutters, folders, and finishers were established for the "Calimala" merchants to prevent workers from being employed by two different guilds at once. Under no circumstances would a "Calimala" merchant employ a worker who did not belong to a "Calimala" organization.

<margin>Conflicts</margin>
From time to time, friction also occurred between the merchants and workers attached to the Por Santa Maria <note>original: "Por Santa Maria," the Guild of Silk Manufacturers</note>. This guild also employed dyers, carders, and other workers, as well as agents and salesmen. In 1324, mutual arrangements were made whereby certain labor associations, workshops, and stalls for the sale of each guild’s merchandise were set apart to avoid conflicts of interest. That same year also saw the creation of the first official register of "Calimala" merchants operating in foreign lands.

<margin>✓ /</margin>
Regarding the foreign relations of the "Calimala" merchants, the regulations were just as precise and detailed as those governing the domestic industry.

<margin>/</margin>
By the end of the thirteenth century, there was not a country in Europe where Florentines were not the primary controllers of trade. The "Calimala" Consuls obtained authorization from the government of the Republic to establish agencies in all the major wool-producing and cloth-manufacturing centers.

->THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

One of the agents of the "Calimala" Guild who traveled far and wide was Guido di Filippo di Ghidone dell’ Antella. He was born in Florence in 1254 and left behind his *Ricordanze*,¹ or diary, of his journeys and experiences. In 1267, he says he went to Genoa on business connected with the company of Lamberto dell’ Antella and lived there for eighteen months. In 1270, the company of Rinuccio Cittadini sent him to Venice, where he remained for two years. He visited Ravenna in 1273 with his father on business regarding a loan. His next employment was at home—five years in the office of Lamberto dell’ Antella and twelve years in the accounting office of the Scali Company. During this latter period, he was sent as a representative of his firm at various times to Pisa, Naples, St. Jean d’Acre, France, and the Papal Court. After leaving the Scali—where he had been made a partner in 1290—he lived in France for three years, working with the Franzesi family. In 1296, with two partners, Neri Filippi and Lapo Ciederni, he rented a *tavola*—a banker’s table <note>original: "tavola," a money-changer's bench or banking counter</note>—in the Mercato Nuovo <note>the New Market in Florence</note> from the Baccherelli banking house. Two years later, he joined Giovanni de’ Cerchi and his company, but he left them in 1301 when the conflict between the Cerchi (*Bianchi* <note>the "Whites" faction</note>) and the Donati (*Neri* <note>the "Blacks" faction</note>) began.

In every part of France—which had now become a second homeland to the Florentines—the "Calimala" merchants had agencies: in l’Île de France—Paris and St. Denis; in Champagne—Provins, Lagny, and Troyes; in Berry—Bourges; in Provence—Marseilles, Toulon, Arles, Saint Gilles, and Avignon; and in Languedoc—Nîmes, Montpellier, Narbonne, Béziers, Perpignan, Carcassonne, and Toulouse.

In all these places, Florentine agents and traders were numerous, receiving and fulfilling orders. While they obeyed the laws of the land where they lived, they also worked under the same regulations that governed their countrymen at home. The agency at Nîmes was established in 1296, and that—

->THE "CALIMALA" GUILD<-

...established in Paris in 1325—the same year that Montpellier became a residential and commercial center for Florentines.

The French agencies were managed by a resident Consul, or multiple Consuls—as there were eventually two or three such magistrates—who were elected by the votes of the resident "Calimala" <note>The *Arte di Calimala* was the Florentine guild responsible for the finishing and trade of foreign cloth.</note> merchants and traders. These officials were received at the King's Court and treated with the honors due to an ambassador from a foreign power. Their duties and powers were exactly like those of the Consuls in Florence. They had authority over postal services, couriers, and all forms of communication. They verified dates, routes, and payments for all commercial travelers and received reports regarding the transportation of goods. They also supervised all transactions between Guild merchants and local traders at the regional wool sales and cloth fairs, which were very numerous throughout France, especially in the Champagne region.

In these and many other duties, the Consuls were assisted—just as they were in Florence—by councils and officials of various ranks. Appeals were permitted to be taken to the Court of the Consuls in Florence, and the rulings of those magistrates were accepted as final.

were employed from time to time. Among the more famous were Brunetto Latini, Cino da Pistoia, Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio, and Giovanni Villani.

Pieces of cloth sent to Florence were carefully measured and weighed before dispatch. Each bore the seal of the agency making the shipment in two places and, in addition, a label indicating the length, the width, the price in gold florins, the name of the manufacturer, and the name of the town of origin.

From ten to twelve pieces made a *torsello* <term>a large bale of cloth</term>, which was wrapped in felt and covered with two layers of canvas sacking. The bales were generally sent directly to one or another of the General Depots at Narbonne, Montpellier, or Marseilles. From there, after inspection by "Surveyors of Cloth-in-Transit" stationed at each center, they were dispatched to Florence.

The twofold trade of the "*Calimala*" <note>The *Arte di Calimala* was the Florentine guild responsible for the finishing and trade of foreign cloth.</note> merchants—involving the purchase of raw native cloth, its transport to Florence for refinishing, and the sale of finished pieces received from the workshops of the Guild—was, of course, not confined to France alone. Agencies and offices were opened in Italy, Spain, Portugal, Flanders, England, and Germany.

This bale consequently contained thirteen pieces of cloth, as well as a garment and a hood for a special customer. Francesco Balducci states ^1 that typically only ten pieces were packed into a single bale.

The Guild of "*Calimala*" prohibited its members from extending credit for more than three months, imposing severe penalties for failure to comply. Later, this period was extended to six months for shipments of foreign cloth sent to or from Florence, and to eight months for bales of wool arriving from overseas.

Under the date of 1338, Giovanni Villani ^2 records that:
> "The '*Calimala*' merchants receive more than ten thousand pieces of cloth annually from across the Alps and from France to be refined in Florence. Their value exceeds three hundred thousand gold florins. All of these are sold in Florence, not including the pieces sent out of the city and sold in the East, along the Mediterranean, and in all the major cities of Europe."

<margin>✓</margin>
The demand for the finished cloths of Florence became enormous. Consequently, there was a tendency to maintain high prices not only for the goods themselves but also for shipping freight. This state of affairs reached its peak in the middle of the fifteenth century, when communication methods expanded and the business relationships of the "*Calimala*" merchants grew immensely.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Calimala Guild's trade regulations, specifically focusing on tariffs, the role of Visiting Inspectors, and the challenges and social aspects of international merchant travel.</meta>

<page-num>136</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

<margin>sp. {</margin>
Rates were charged upon cloth manufactured in, and finished for, countries which established tariffs against Florence; the tax was as much as five gold florins for pieces thirty-four <term>braccia</term> <note>an Italian unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches</note> in length.¹ “The objects of this policy," as Pagnini rightly says,² "was to create reciprocity, to prevent competition, to control production, and to limit trade.”

The *Calimala* Consuls and Council in their corporate capacity, and also the individual companies of merchants, were accustomed to send Visiting Inspectors from time to time on tour to look after the interests of the Guild and of the trade. Matters concerning private interest and enterprise were investigated just as thoroughly as questions of international importance.

The dangers to which merchants and agents were exposed at the hands of hostile and oppressive rulers of foreign states, or controllers of foreign manufacturing, were plainly shown by the seizure, in 1271, by order of King <term>Philippe le Bel</term> <note>Philip the Fair</note>,³ of all Florentine traders in France. He and his greedy counselors extorted heavy ransoms, making no distinction between honest and fraudulent merchants.⁴

The Visiting Inspectors had no light work to do, but they entered upon their adventurous undertakings bravely. They generally started on the journey in groups and were joined by others desiring to visit France and other European states for business or for pleasure.

The sole means of travel was by horseback. Dressed in fine attire and accompanied by their wives and other lady friends, many servants, and much baggage, the processions assumed impressive dimensions and became occasions of much celebration and many adventures. When time hung heavy, or when darkness set in, a common occupation was to count their prayer beads and to recite <term>Pater-Nosters</term> <note>Latin: "Our Fathers"</note> in fulfillment of vows taken before they started.

<margin>noble merchants</margin>
The fame of Florentine cloth was vastly increased by the high reputation of the "Calimala" merchants. While eagerly seizing every opportunity for self-enrichment, for the advancement of their beloved city, and for the honor of their Guild, they were simultaneously remarkable for their self-restraint and nobility of character.

<margin>list of family wealth</margin>
Between the years 1401 and 1548, we find in the public records that the following families contributed the most members to the Guild: Altoviti, 108; Strozzi, 107; Marbegli, 75; Guidetti, 72; Acciaiuoli, 71; Capponi, 61; Nasi, 59; and Soderini, 55. The names of the following also appear many times: Alberti, Albizzi, Adimari, Amidei, Buondelmonti, Cerchi, Frescobaldi, Guicciardini, Lamberti, Medici, Pazzi, Peruzzi, Ridolfi, Ricci, Spini, Tornabuoni, Vettori, and Villani. Still earlier families were the Cavalcanti, Donati, Bardi, Corsini, Rinucci, Pucci, Ardinghetti, Rinuccini, Chermonisti, Bandinelli, Buonaccorsi, and Dell' Antella.

All Europe looked on amazed at the enterprise, the wealth, and the power of the city on the Arno <note>Florence</note>, and for a very long time, no merchants or manufacturers but hers ruled the international commerce of the world.

<margin>keen interest shown</margin>
The "Calimala" merchants had safely guarded the methods and the secrets of their craft, but a spirit similar to their own was springing up in England and in Flanders. There was no reason why other men should not do what the Florentines had done, and many a student, statesman, and trader set their minds to work to find out the reasons for the ascendancy of Florence.

<margin>drafted bill/law</margin>
England was the first to step into the arena; under Henry VII, a law was passed by the British Parliament to prohibit the export of unshorn <note>unfinished</note> cloth. Other countries followed suit. This

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the decline of the Calimala Guild, detailing how international competition and misguided protectionist policies led to the eventual, unrecorded dissolution of the institution after centuries of dominance.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

This was a blow to Florence from which she never recovered; because, along with the prohibition of exports, native workmen appeared on the scene who had learned something of the Florentines' methods.

Before the city had recovered from the effects of hostile legislation and treatment by its former customers, Grand Duke Cosimo I, following a traditional Florentine protectionist instinct, issued a government decree in 1561. This decree forbade the importation of serges and light woolen cloths from England and Flanders! This action was a case of "cutting off one’s nose to spite one’s face!" It was a final and deadly blow, and the entire grand structure of the "Guild and University of the Calimala Merchants" <note>original: "Arte e Università de' Mercanti di Calimala"</note> tottered toward its collapse!

In 1359, the State granted the "Calimala" Guild a site to build a residence for the Consuls and their courts, replacing their cramped quarters in the old Cavalcanti Palace. The doors of this "Temple of Commerce" were opened during prosperous times, but they were closed during the days of declining power. No historian has recorded who closed them, or when they were shut—never to be opened again. After the Republic was abolished in the year 1532, the grand old Guild declined slowly but surely. Its death and burial went unnoted, and no notary <term>scrivano</term> left even a single word describing its final moments.

<margin>Calimala</margin>
The "Calimala" Guild had held a dominant position—industrially, commercially, socially, and politically—in the history of Florence for more than five hundred years!

The manufacture of woolen cloth is undoubtedly one of the most ancient industries of the human race. In an old volume entitled “A Treatise on Painting, Sculpture, and Architecture” <note>original: "Trattato della Pittura, Scultura, ed Architettura"</note>, written by Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo—a painter from Milan—there is a pithy proverb from Ecclesiastes: “In the hands of the skillful shall the work be approved.” In this book, he gives the following quaint reason for the existence of the wool industry¹:

> “Because our bodies, being born naked by Nature, were troubled in various ways by the harshness of the air, it most cleverly invented the Arts of Weaving and Tailoring; not so much for the defense and safeguarding of our bodies from the injury of the weather, as for decoration and decency; and to this same end, it has also discovered (in a word) all the other Mechanical Arts.”

The historical records of every civilized nation give an early and prominent position to the production of, and the trade in, wool. The Persians, the Egyptians, the Greeks, and the Romans—the great civilizing and commercial races of the world—used and improved the manufacture of woolen cloth. Under the universal dominion of the latter power, the expansion of the woolen industry synchronized with that of military and civil jurisdiction; the trade, then as now, followed the flag.

<margin>✓ ✓ ✓</margin> The first reliable records of the woolen industry in Tuscany show it to us as already in a thriving condition, providing employment to the majority of the inhabitants of the towns and villages. From a document¹ dated May 10, 846, it appears that the weaving of wool was carried on in Lucca under the terms of a trade association and with a code of regulations.

We may fairly assume that Florence was not far behind its neighbor chronologically. As the capital of an enlightened line of Marquises and Dukes of Tuscany, we may be sure that the most important industry of the age was not without encouragement and cooperation within the limits of her influence and jurisdiction during the ninth, tenth, and eleventh centuries.

Under the beneficial rule of the Countess Matilda <note>Matilda of Tuscany (1046–1115), a powerful medieval ruler and supporter of the Papacy who greatly aided Florentine development</note>, the prosperity of Florence grew significantly. The workmen at her looms and the merchants in her markets spread her fame far and wide. The Commune became a Republic of Industry and Commerce, and her wool merchants and manufacturers were listed among the very first of the Consuls <note>The highest-ranking magistrates of the Florentine Republic</note>.

Among the many trades that were actively pursued in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, the following are noted in the surviving portions of the State Archives:

> “1062. *Fulling-mill*—a mill for cleaning and thickening cloth. <note>original: "Gualchiera"</note>”
> “1096. Peter—dyer—wool dyer. <note>original: "Petrus—tentore"</note>”
> “1136. Scartone—comb maker—woolen-comb maker. <note>original: "pettinario"</note>”
> “1148. Peter, son of Peter—furrier—cloth-presser. <note>original: "Petrus fil. Petri—pelliparius"</note>”
> “1193. Guerius—shearer—sheep-shearer. <note>original: "tonditor"</note>”

The locations of these early industries were well within the *Second Circle*—the city walls of 1074 <note>original: "Secondo Cerchio"</note>—as the safety of life and property was not guaranteed in the surrounding countryside <note>original: "Contado"</note> beyond. In the Prato district—which, along with Monte Orlando, was enclosed within the city's boundaries in 1107—a great number of wool workers were settled. The processing of wool was also carried out in Via Alfani, Via dei Servi, Via Ginori, Borgo Pinti, Via della Pergola, and in the Piazza delle Travi during the twelfth century.

In a state paper from the year 1197, there is a law concerning the cities and lands of Tuscany in which the people of Florence are described as: “wool-workers from Olivero.” ¹

<margin>limited data</margin>
The precise date of the first incorporation of the “Wool Guild” in Florence is quite uncertain. Much of what we know about its founding is based on conjecture, for during the memorable riots of the *Ciompi* <note>A rebellion of unrepresented wool carders and lower-class workers in 1378.</note> in 1378, most of the Guild's documents were destroyed by fire. This fact, combined with the scarcity of the remaining State Records, leaves us very much in the dark regarding the initial organization and early development of the Guild. Perhaps the earliest preserved record is a list of the names of the Consuls up to the year 1138.²

<margin>First Survey</margin>
The “Wool Guild” was almost certainly the first corporate society or trade corporation in Florence, and it existed before her wool and cloth merchants began to travel through—

This development led to the division of the wool-workers of Florence and the establishment of a separate Corporation of dealers and finishers of foreign-made cloth—the “*Calimala*.” In a very true sense, the “*Arte della Lana*” <note>The Wool Guild</note> was the mother of the “*Arte di Calimala*” <note>The Guild of Foreign Cloth Finishers and Merchants</note>, but as time went on, the greater profits

Notices of the Guild are frequent during the first thirty years of the thirteenth century, and the Consuls signed their names to treaties with other states along with the Consuls of the Guilds of “Judges and Notaries,” “*Calimala*,” “Silk Merchants,” and “Bankers.”

The organization of the Wool Guild followed that of the “*Calimala*” merchants. Before the promulgation of the Statutes—drafted between 1301 and 1309—the “Guild of Wool” was ruled by Priors, who were later called Consuls, and whose number in that year was eight. They had the power to make regulations and laws for the direction and benefit of the Guild, and they held full jurisdiction in all civil and criminal cases over all enrolled members. They were chosen by lot from among the most skillful masters of the craft.

<margin>[</margin>
Matriculation <term>The formal process of being admitted into a guild as a registered member.</term> followed the rule observed by the “*Calimala*” Guild; qualifications of birth, education, and parental income were necessary. The relations between the matriculated members of the Guild and the operatives, who were engaged in all the various processes of the wool industry, were exactly the same for both Guilds.

<margin>Both Guilds</margin>
At first sight, it seems probable that difficulties and confusion would arise between the "Calimala" Guild and the Wool Guild. Certainly, there were some inconveniences in the early period due to the similarity of the merchandise in which each was interested. However, it was soon recognized that the business of the former was exclusively concerned with the finishing of foreign-made woolen cloth, and had nothing in common with the processing of raw wool and the manufacture of cloth.

<margin>Regulated and protected each other</margin>
The Consuls and Councils of each of the two Guilds passed regulations and rules which made it practically impossible for one to harm the other. No member of the Wool Guild was allowed to keep or sell foreign-woven cloth. The weaving of expensive cloth was restricted—perhaps with a view to avoid competition with the "Calimala" Guild's trade in finishing fine foreign-made materials. On the other hand, cloth made of inferior cardings was condemned to be burned—a wise precaution against any temptation to force <term>shoddy</term> <note>inferior quality wool made from shredded rags</note> pieces onto the market.²

<margin>Guild members must not interfere with other Guild members</margin>
A special <term>rubric</term> <note>a titled section or heading within a legal code</note> affirmed the right of the "Guild of Wool," and its Consuls and duly elected officers, to control the business and the workpeople of the Guild. At the same time, the members were bound not to interfere in any way with members of other Guilds. Persons not enrolled <note>original: "matriculated"</note> in the Wool Guild were forbidden to make and sell woolen pieces, and further were restrained from mixing dyes or doing other things connected with the wool industry.³

The *Stimatori* <note>original: "Stimatori"</note> and *Sensali* <note>original: "Sensali"</note>—the official measurers and brokers—

Officers of the Guild—acting under the express orders of the Consuls—made a scrupulous examination of the cloth pieces before they were placed upon the market. Each piece had to meet the exact standard for length and weight; the latter varied considerably after the processes of fulling <term>fulling</term> <note>a step in wool manufacturing involving cleansing and thickening the cloth</note> and dyeing.¹

Falsifications, adulterations, and irregularities of all kinds were severely punished by fines, the destruction of the cloth, and the posting of the names of all offending manufacturers and merchants at the Guild offices. The mixing of linen thread with wool was condemned, unless its quality and description were plainly marked upon the woven cloth. This industry, however, was fairly prosperous, especially for export; cloth manufactured this way bore the name of *Moscolato* <note>original: "Moscolato" — mixture</note> and *Tintilano* <note>original: "Tintilano" — dyed in the grain</note>.²

A piece of woolen cloth usually measured from thirty to thirty-two *ulne* <note>original: "ulne" — an old measurement unit similar to an ell</note>. The yard-measure used in the workshops was a little longer than the *canna* <note>original: "canna" — a measuring rod</note> of the "Calimala," which was the standard yard-measure of commerce. The *canna* used by the Wool Guild measured one and a half *braccio* <note>original: "braccio" — a "forearm" or cubit</note>, each *braccio* being 22.97 English inches.

The average weights for a bundle of woolen yarn were as follows: *Garbo* <note>wool imported from the Algarve</note> serges weighed one pound; fine qualities, whether white or colored, weighed one pound four ounces; and for *San Martino* <note>the finest quality of cloth</note>—finest qualities only—one pound five ounces. Each weight was determined by the scales of the *Battitori* <note>original: "Battitori" — wool-beaters</note>.

It was permissible to buy and sell pieces of cloth, *boldroni* <note>original: "boldroni" — whole fleeces of lambs' wool without the skin</note>, woolen yarn, and all-woolen sundries in packs or bundles. However, in each transaction, absolute honesty was required in the deduction of the weight and value of the tare <term>tare</term> <note>the weight of the packaging or impurities to be subtracted from the gross weight</note> from the purchase price, whether that included sacks, leaking moisture, pieces of fat or skin, dust, or any other foreign matter.

Disputed weight allowances <term>tares</term> <note>deductions made for the weight of packaging or impurities</note> were to be taken immediately before the Consuls for their decision. Anyone attempting to pass off rubbish of any kind as high-quality, sound wool was punished by a fine of one hundred *lire*. The use of dishonest weights or applying undue pressure by hand upon the scales resulted in a penalty of two hundred *lire*.

The office of the *Sensale* <note>original: "Sensale" — broker or agent</note> was just as important to the Wool Guild as it was to the "Guild of *Calimala*." Many of these "middlemen" earned enormous profits and became influential merchants. However, a curious entry in the archives from the year 1326 states that a certain wool broker declared he had earned no more than fifty *lire* that year!

The Guild Consuls required that all payments for yarn, cloth, raw wool, and industry supplies be made in advance for sales conducted within a hundred miles of the city. Furthermore, they prohibited discounts of any kind. Payments involving customers or agents beyond that distance were managed through "Letters of Credit" with specific interest rates, agreed upon with the cooperation of the "Guild of Bankers and Money Changers."

The Guild's statutes were revised in 1317, 1331, 1333, 1338, 1362, 1415, and 1428; additions were made in 1319, 1333, 1337, 1361, 1427, and many times during the sixteenth century. In all these proceedings, the Wool Guild bears its full title of "*Arte e Università della Lana*" <note>original: "Arte e Università della Lana" — The Guild and University of Wool</note>.¹

This bridge also served another useful purpose: it provided the residents of the three *Borghi*, or suburbs—collectively known as Oltrarno across the river—with a ready means of access to the new wool factories. These poor people were thus able to find work, and the entire district was quickly transformed. Later in the history of Florence, Oltrarno became known by the name of Via de’ Bardi, after one of the rich banking families who built their palace there.

The methods used by the various groups of workers in the manufacture of cloth were largely the same as those still found today in countries where modern machinery has not yet been introduced.

After the fleeces were sheared from the sheep—ideally in one whole piece—they were washed. Hard water was avoided because it was found to make the wool feel harsh to the touch. Ammonia, in one form or another, was usually mixed into the water. This also had the benefit of making the processed wool take dye more evenly. Scouring the wool in vats of hot soap-suds required two men per vat; they used strong poles to toss the bundles of wool back and forth to each other, thereby separating the dirt and dissolving the grease.

The next step involved lifting the scoured and cleaned fleeces out of their bath and letting them drain. Meanwhile, they were rinsed with fresh water from the river Arno <note>The Arno River in Florence provided the necessary water for the city's extensive textile and tanning industries.</note> to remove the suds. Drying slowly was

<keywords>Wool Guild, textile manufacturing, labor roles, wool scouring, Arno River, Florentine industry, wool processing</keywords>

--- Page 218 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical description of the Florentine wool manufacturing process, moving from the washing and drying of the wool to the specific stages of combing, oiling, blending, and carding, as well as the administrative roles of the Master-spinners.</meta>

<page-num>150</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The wool was found to dry best in breezy, warm air, but the goal was to ensure it did not become too dry, for fear of it cracking and splitting.

Combing the wool followed. At first, large brushes or rakes were used; their teeth were set into sturdy leather backs, which provided a more flexible base than wood. Later, cylindrical combing machines made of iron and leather were introduced.

Oiling was a crucial step to prevent stiffness and excessive curling. The oil was applied to the combed wool using sprinklers with perforated "rose" heads. This process was found to be useful in helping the fibers stick together when they reached the spinning stage.

Blending the wool was a distinct science in itself. It was practiced by the most experienced workers and was essential both for economic reasons and for the production of new types of fabrics.

Carding, the first step in the process of making yarn, was a very important matter that required the skill of well-trained craftsmen. The carding comb for weaving *rascia*—<term>white serge</term>—was usually about sixteen inches wide, with enough wire teeth to allow one hundred and ten threads to be set upon the loom. For sky-blue serges, the comb was seventeen inches wide, with wires for one hundred threads; for pale and faded blue serges, the comb was the same size, but one hundred and five wires were set upon the loom. There were no restrictions on the size of the comb or the number of thread wires for other kinds of colored cloth.

Spinning and winding followed closely on the heels of one another. These tasks were usually performed by women and girls, but all apprentices were expected to understand both these processes through hands-on experience and to be skilled in them.

It was the duty of the *Stamaiuolo* <note>Master wool-spinner or yarn manager</note> to distribute wool yarn to the *Filatrice* <note>Spinner or female winder</note> in knots or bundles, and to record the name of each woman, along with the number and quality of the knots. At the same time, he had to agree with her on the price for winding each particular job. The winders were forbidden to transfer their

The actual production of cloth required many processes, of course, between the delivery of the wound yarn and the output of the finished woollen cloth pieces. Weavers, fullers, and dyers each in turn handled the lengths of cloth before they reached the presses of the finishers and folders.

The dyers of Florence made up a large and significant part of the population. They seem to have been divided into three classes: 1. Dyers of foreign cloth for the "Calimala Guild"; 2. Dyers of native cloth for the "Wool Guild"; and 3. Dyers of silk for the "Silk Guild." All were dependent on the "Calimala" for the supply of dyes, mordants, and all other ingredients of their trade. Each dyer paid the sum of three hundred and ten gold florins to the treasurer of the guild as a guarantee or bail to show he intended to practice his trade in good faith; in return, he received official permission to carry on the industry. Every dye-house and its contents, along with samples of dyed goods, had to be prepared annually for a thorough inspection by the guild officials.

<margin>Confirmed</margin>
While the dyers were not permitted to incorporate themselves into a separate <term>Arte</term>—guild—they were allowed to associate themselves in families and groups to pursue any specialized operations of their craft. All such companies were subordinate to the "Wool Guild" regarding their political and social status. The only exception was made for certain foreign dyers employed by the "Silk Guild," who did not fall under the authority of the "Wool Guild."

Dyers were required to show diligence in their work and provide prompt and faithful service to their employers. They were obligated to record in a book, within twenty-four hours, all the cloth they received for dyeing. They were not allowed to travel through the city or the <term>Contado</term>—the surrounding territory—seeking work, but were required to remain in their workshops until they received pieces of cloth from the <term>Sensali</term>—brokers.

The cost of dyeing one hundred pieces of woolen cloth in Florence during the fifteenth century may be estimated by the following list¹: 

Sky-blue <note>original: "Sbiadato"</note>, emerald <note>original: "Smeraldino"</note>, and light blue <note>original: "Azzuro"</note> cost three florins. Tan <note>original: "Pelo di Leone"</note> and bright green <note>original: "Verde chiaro"</note> cost four florins. Middle gray <note>original: "Bigio di mezzo"</note> and shaded white <note>original: "Cupo di bianco"</note> cost five florins. Dried red <note>original: "Rosa secca"</note>, pale carmine <note>original: "Sanguigno di sbiadato"</note>, and pink <note>original: "Gherofanato"</note> cost six florins. Celestial blue <note>original: "Celestino"</note>, pale purple <note>original: "Violetto"</note>, and coffee-brown <note>original: "Bruschino"</note> cost eight florins. Dark green <note>original: "Verde-Bruno"</note>, woad-red <note>original: "Berrettino di guado"</note>, and mulberry-black <note>original: "Morello di grana"</note> cost ten florins. Monk’s gray <note>original: "Monachino"</note> cost twelve florins. Deep rose <note>original: "Rosato"</note> cost twenty-five florins. Lucca scarlet <note>original: "Lucchesino"</note> cost twenty-eight florins, and vermilion <note>original: "Scarlatto"</note> cost thirty-five florins.

These prices were fixed by the Consuls and Council of the "Wool Guild," with the expert advice of officers appointed to investigate the matter. It was mandatory that the colors used in dyeing be permanent, not liable to fade. Any cloth that was poorly dyed was either re-processed, cut up and sold to street vendors <term>hucksters</term>, or burned. Dyers were permitted to use inferior dyes if they wished, but they were required to declare this and attach labels stating the fact to the dyed pieces.

Alum—which was essential as a fixing agent <term>mordant</term> for the colors—was brought from mines in the Maremma, where the remains of early excavations had been ground into powder by the weather.

The Duke of Athens, upon taking over the government of Florence, showed favor to the dyers—who, incidentally, did much to support his authority—by granting a petition they presented to him in 1342.² In this document, after offering the Duke several flattering compliments, the petitioners continue: "Grant us our own Consuls, chosen from our own Guild of Dyers and Washers, and free us from the control <term>yoke</term> of the 'Wool Guild,' so that we may carry on our industry without interference or delay <term>let or hindrance</term> in your Highness's

service." Three Consuls were appointed, but they were not recognized by the "Guild of Wool."

No worker could be employed by any merchant who had not first proved his ability and obtained a formal written testimony of it. Employers were required to provide their workers with all the tools of their trade. For mutual convenience, workers engaged in the same process were employed in groups and worked in the same rooms. The manufacturing of woolen cloth was forbidden in private homes.¹

Each manufacturer was required to pay his workers sufficient daily or weekly wages; the amount of these had to be submitted to the Consuls of the Guild for their approval. The standard wages paid to *Filatori* <note>spinners</note> and *Lanini* <note>wool carders or laborers</note> were, for each bundle of serge yarn, one <term>soldo</term>, and either ten <term>denari</term> or *piccioli* <note>small copper coins</note>. A *Filatrice* <note>female spinner</note> generally received one soldo and five *piccioli* for the same quantity. The average daily wage of an adult worker was one soldo and six denari, worth about one shilling and sixpence <note>at the time of the author's writing</note>. In times of trade depression, wages naturally declined, and a day's wage amounted to no more than thirty *piccioli*—perhaps about eight pence.

<margin><insert><unclear>Unc</unclear></insert></margin>
Every worker had security of tenure in his home. A *Provvisione* <note>an ordinance or decree</note> prevented manufacturers from evicting their employees—either from their jobs or their houses—except for grave reasons, which had to be stated before the Council of the Consuls and approved by a vote. House owners were also forbidden from raising the rents of dwellings except by the express permission of the Consuls.

All citizens were strongly cautioned not to take any instrument or tool used in the trade as a pledge <note>collateral for a loan</note> from woolen workers. The sale of wool, woolen yarn, or woolen cloth by workers was strictly prohibited. No money-changer or market lender was allowed to lend money on the security of whole pieces of woolen cloth, cloth remnants, woolen yarn, or raw wool. Despite the prohibition, every such transaction was punished with a fine of fifty <term>lire</term>.

<margin>Hours of work were controlled; overtime was forbidden.</margin>
Wool sorting and beating were forbidden within the walls of the city, as was also the <term>scutching</term> <note>the process of cleaning cotton or flax by beating it</note> of cotton and all other noisy employments, from the tolling of the three o'clock bell to the striking of the bell at <term>Matins</term> <note>the first prayer service of the day, held in the very early morning</note>. Overtime—as we call it—was forbidden, and no worker was permitted to carry on his trade, even secretly, after <term>Compline</term> <note>the final church service of the day, held before bedtime</note>.¹

<margin>State care for workers; hours of work and rest.</margin>
The care which the State extended to the well-being of the wool operatives is evidenced in a number of <term>Provvisioni</term> <note>legislative decrees or ordinances</note> regulating the hours of work and rest. It was strictly prohibited for any noise to be made in the streets during the night.

In all the workshops of the Guild, games of chance were strictly forbidden; indeed, the only indoor game allowed was chess, which—as a quaint old chronicler puts it—"has in it the element of patience and quietness."²

<margin>No merchant or agent allowed to emigrate.</margin>
Certain *Provvisioni* dealt with the questions of the emigration of operatives and the location of foreign agencies. No merchant, agent, workman, or apprentice was permitted to leave Florence and establish himself in any foreign land except by the express permission of the Consuls of the Guild. Later on—in the fifteenth century—the emigration of workpeople was wholly forbidden. These measures were doubtless necessary for the safeguarding of the secrets of the trade and for the protection of the Florentine monopoly of foreign markets. In the same way, the export of raw native wool and woolen yarn, as well as of madder, woad, and other dyeing materials, was forbidden.

It is a great pity that all the old looms, implements, and accessories of the industry have disappeared. As late as 1858, an ancient <term>telaio</term> <note>wool-cloth loom</note> was still in working order in an old house from the time of Arnolfo di Cambio <note>a famous 13th-century Florentine architect and sculptor</note> in the Piazza delle Travi on the Lung’ Arno degli Alberti.

Neither Tuscany, nor the whole of Italy, could supply anything like the quantity, much less the quality, of wool needed to meet the requirements of the Florentine looms. The rearing

->THE GUILD OF WOOL<-

Raising sheep was not a profitable business in Tuscany in early times. The breed was certainly hardy, but because the better land was used for farming, the flocks grazed on the meager vegetation of barren hillsides. This did not produce the heavy fleeces found in better-fed sheep. In the fifteenth century, the number of sheep in Tuscany exceeded one million; but while some sheep in good condition only yielded three or four pounds of coarse wool, a Spanish, English, or Flemish sheep produced a fleece that averaged eight or nine pounds of excellent quality wool.¹

The determination and thoroughness that the shepherds and their masters—most of whom were wealthy members of the Wool Guild—brought to the raising of sheep produced good results. Tuscan raw wool eventually replaced the famous products of Puglia, Taranto, and Modena, and it fetched profitable prices in all markets for the manufacture of strong and durable cloth.

The wool industry of Florence had active and enterprising rivals in Pisa, Genoa, Venice, Bologna, Ferrara, and in Lombardy and France. At the same time, in each of these manufacturing centers, there were statutes and regulations that absolutely forbade the importation of foreign wool and the processing of foreign-made cloth. Florence, on the other hand, followed an entirely different policy, with results that were as beneficial to the home industry as they were successful in achieving dominance in all foreign markets.

<margin>wealth <unclear>perhaps</unclear></margin>
The wealth that poured into the coffers of her merchants enabled them to purchase the finest wool offered at all foreign fairs. England, France, Spain, and Portugal readily sold their rich fleeces to the agents of the "Wool Guild." Prices ranged from sixteen *soldi* <note>a former Italian silver coin and unit of currency</note> per hundred pounds of raw Tuscan wool to sixteen hundred *soldi* for the same weight of the best French, Narbonne, and Portuguese raw wool.

From the Algarve <note>the southernmost region of Portugal</note> came the best wool of all—adapted into the Tuscan name—

"*Garbo*." <note>The term "Garbo" (meaning grace or elegance) originally referred to wool imported from the Maghreb or Algarve regions, but it eventually came to signify the highest grade of Florentine woolens.</note> Consequently, "*Panne di Garbo*" <note>original: "Panne di Garbo"; Garbo cloth</note> was the finest cloth woven in Florence, and the street where it was primarily manufactured was called *Via di Garbo* (Garbo Street). Spanish wool was also of exceptional quality. The merino sheep, introduced into the country by the Romans centuries earlier and crossed with the native breed, had established a high reputation for purity of color and a silky texture. No wool was as useful as this pure white variety for fine manufacturing; it was also known by the name "*Lana di Garbo*" (Garbo wool).

<margin>English wool from British monasteries</margin>
Henry II was the first English king to grant trading privileges to Florentine merchants for the purchase of British-grown wool. As early as 1284, the quantity of raw wool bought by Florentine merchants from English monasteries was considerable. Several wool-trading companies were established in London and elsewhere. Among them was the firm of *Messer Tommaso Spigliati and Lapo Ugo Spini*.¹ Letters still exist written by one of their agents, *Simone Gherardi*, who, in an account of his commercial journey in 1285, speaks of the excellence of the wool offered for sale by the British monasteries. Other companies included those of *Messrs. Bindo Isquarta, Jacopo, Riccomanno, de' Mozzi, Peruzzi*, and *Pulchi*, along with representatives of the *Bardi* family.

By the year 1315, more than two hundred monasteries in England, France, Spain, Portugal, and Flanders were supplying the Florentine Wool Guild. The names of these locations look very strange in their Italian versions; for example:

# THE GUILD OF WOOL

They called Melrose *Merusotte*, Galloway *Gonellasso*, and Kelso *Chilosola*, and so on.<sup>1</sup>

The best British wool came from the Cotswolds and from Chichester—Tuscanized into *Codignaldo* and *Scrisestri*.

> “The wool of Britain,” wrote an old historian, “is often spun so fine that it is, in some sense, comparable to a spider’s web.”

This excellence was the result of carefully following the methods of the ancient Roman settlers, who established immense sheep farms in various parts of the country and set up woolen factories at the old capital, Winchester. They undoubtedly appreciated the splendid breed of sheep which they found on the island and their rich yield of long, silky fleeces.

The raw wool imported from England came in three qualities: "*Buona*" (fine), "*Moiana*" (soft), and "*Locchi*" (wool from stillborn lambs). The prices per sack for Scottish wool were: twenty English marks for fine qualities, twelve marks for coarse, and nine marks for stillborn lamb's wool (using English coinage).<sup>2</sup>

One hundred English pounds were equal to about one hundred and forty Florentine pounds, and each English sack contained about fifty-two <term>stones</term> <note>The OCR reads "pounds," but historically a wool sack contained 52 stones (364 lbs), which matches the Florentine weight mentioned next.</note>. For ease of transport by mule, the sacks were packed in two equal bales—each weighing about two hundred and fifty Florentine pounds.

The exports of raw wool from England assumed vast proportions and excited the jealousy and opposition of local producers and manufacturers. The annual shipments from Great Britain to Florence in the fourteenth century—and indeed earlier—filled 2,800 sacks or bags and had an average value of £25,000 to £30,000.

Troublesome Acts of Parliament were passed to limit the operations of the Florentine traders. Edward III invited dyers, fullers, and weavers from Flanders to settle in his dominions and teach his people their methods; at the same time, he directed that

<margin>15th Century</margin>
In 1455, during the reign of Henry VI, a law was enacted forbidding Italian merchants from purchasing wool, woolen yarn, and cloth anywhere except in London, Southampton, and Sandwich. A few years later, these regulations were made even more stringent by Parliament’s absolute refusal to allow any sales to Italian wool merchants.

and restricted local merchants from shipping bales or bags to any foreign ports except Calais. All these repressive measures led Italian merchants to commission blockade-running ships; by these risky means, valuable shipments were successfully delivered to Italy and elsewhere.

Such embargoes could not be tolerated, so the Florentine shippers appointed Bindo da Staggio—a resident of London and a favored person <note>original: "*persona grata*"</note> at Court—as their ambassador to plead for a relaxation of the prohibitive regulations. The outcome was favorable to the foreign traders. To secure their advantage, two wool merchants—Francesco de’ Strozzi and Gierozo de’ Pigli, both residents of London—were appointed Consuls of the Florentine colony in England.^1

In 1483, a Royal decree was issued to regulate sales to Florentine merchants, which again restricted their trade. Under Henry VII, more enlightened policies prevailed, and in 1486, a commercial treaty between England and the Florentine Republic was signed. By this treaty, English merchants undertook to transport enough wool every year to supply all the states of Italy, and Florentine traders promised to buy no wool unless it was carried in English ships. In return, the Florentines obtained corresponding privileges regarding the import into England of refinished <term>redressed: cloth that has been processed, sheared, or finished after the initial weaving</term> foreign cloth and dyed Florentine textiles.^2 In 1493, modifications were made to the treaty. Greater freedom was allowed in purchasing raw wool for use only in Florence, but her merchants were forbidden from reselling their imports, except for six hundred bales annually to the Venetians.

<margin>

The reigns of Henry VIII and Elizabeth were filled with laws both favoring and opposing the Florentine woolen-cloth merchants. The former monarch encouraged their enterprise and had personal dealings with the Frescobaldi, Bardi, Corsi, Cavalcanti, and other leading merchant houses. However, Elizabeth’s policy was repressive, and under her rule, the export of raw wool was once more

At the same time, no such restrictions or prohibitions affected the export of Spanish and Portuguese wool. From a document dating to the year 1326, we learn that prices ranged as follows:—$^1$

*   A whole fleece of “Garbo” wool—without the skin—one hundred gold florins.

With England serving as the greatest wool-producing country in Europe from the thirteenth to the fifteenth centuries, commercial relations with the Florentines developed rapidly. At first, trade with English growers was conducted only through French and Flemish markets and was transported overland—because of this, English wool was called “*lana francigena*” <note>original: "lana francigena"; Latin/Italian: "French-sourced wool"</note>.

<margin>
Trade
opens at the
ports
</margin>

After Florence gained possession of the ports of Livorno <note>also known as Leghorn</note> and Porto Pisano, the bales were shipped directly from London or Southampton—the latter being the primary wool-shipping hub. One of the favorite trade routes went from London to the coast of France by sea, then up the rivers Gironde and Dordogne as far as Libourne; from there it went overland by way of Montpellier to Aigues-Mortes in Provence. From that point, it traveled by canal and sea to Porto Pisano, then by riverboat up the Arno to Signa <note>OCR: "Segna"</note>, and finally by road to Florence! Another route went by way of Bruges in Flanders, through Germany to Basel, and over the Alpine passes.

The expenses of land transport were enormous and added immensely to the value of the wool by the time it reached the hands of the craftsmen in Florence. The freight from London to Leghorn or Porto Pisano was two *soldi* per mule load, and the charges for porterage, trans-shipment, repacking, and other costs along the way added

<margin>15th Century</margin>

In the fifteenth century, a ship canal intended to connect Florence with the sea was planned by merchants of the "Calimala" and "Wool" Guilds. Leonardo da Vinci actually conducted elaborate surveys and drafted plans for the project. The scheme, however, fell through because the Republic had other expensive projects underway.

During the thirteenth century, Florentine manufacturers were engaged almost exclusively in weaving coarse quality cloth made from native wool. These went by various names: <term>bigello</term> (coarse camlet or frieze), <term>frustagno</term> (fustian), <term>arabasio</term> (canvas cloth), <term>pignolato</term> (rough, hard cloth), <term>schiavina</term> (blanketing or "slave-cloth"), <term>villaneschi</term> (peasants’ serge), <term>baracane</term> (coarse camlet), <term>moscolato</term> (a moss-like mixture), and other rough and inferior descriptions.

"These fabrics," writes Villani, "were coarse and of low value; indeed, they had not yet learned to finish them with the skill they later acquired." <note>Villani, vol. xi. c. 94.</note>

One variety of the native manufacture was certainly of finer texture. It was called <term>tintilano</term> (fine-grained cloth), made from the silky fleeces of young lambs. It was further distinguished as <term>locchi</term> (made from the wool of still-born lambs) and <term>moiana</term> (soft and light). This woven material was greatly esteemed for the tight-fitting body hose and drawers worn by men, and Boccaccio refers to it as being thoroughly Florentine. <note>Boccaccio, "Novelle" III, Day 7.</note>

<margin>The Guild welcomed skilled people who made machinery</margin>

The wool industry thrived not only under the sponsorship of the <term>Umiliati</term> <note>a religious order that specialized in wool production</note>, but also through the energy of the Consuls of the "Wool Guild." They welcomed artisans from Greece and elsewhere who were skilled in making carding frames, weaving looms, and the other machines and appliances required by the craft.

<margin>In depth with additional cultural interest</margin>
The business policy of the Florentine manufacturers attracted a great number of foreign workmen. The Government of the Republic granted all of these the same exemptions and privileges which had been bestowed upon the *Umiliati*.¹ <note>The Umiliati were a religious order that played a vital role in establishing the medieval wool industry.</note>

This immigration made it absolutely necessary—for the sake of public health and to avoid overcrowding in the neighborhoods already inhabited by the craftsmen—to allocate new areas to the newcomers. Hence, we find that settlements of mechanics and makers of carding combs <term>carding-combs</term> <note>tools used to untangle and clean raw wool fibers before spinning</note> were established in Oltrarno. <gloss>—> suburbs</gloss> <note>Oltrarno literally means "beyond the Arno," referring to the district on the south bank of the river.</note>

<margin>Growth of the road</margin>
By the end of the thirteenth century, Via Maggio, Via San Felice in Piazza, and Fondaco San Spirito—located in *Borgo San Jacopo*, around San Martino and San Procolo, in the Vigna, and near Porta Rossa—had received a new population. When added to the original woolworkers in that quarter, these residents later became a very powerful factor in the destinies not merely of the Craft, but of the Republic at large. Many of the more skillful foreign artisans were also located in the *botteghe*—small shops—of the Via de' Pellicciai and around the headquarters of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries."²

Indeed, when the wool industry was at the height of its prosperity, Florence appeared to be one vast drying and stretching ground. Cloth of all kinds and colors waved in great lengths in every quarter and gave the streets an extraordinary appearance!

<margin>size of the guild</margin>
More than thirty thousand workers were engaged in the manufacture of wool cloth—all, or nearly all, of whom worked in connection with the “Guild of Wool.” Villani <note>Giovanni Villani (c. 1276–1348), a famous Florentine chronicler.</note>, speaking of the year 1308, says there were two hundred workshops belonging to the Guild in Florence and its immediate surrounding territory <term>contado</term> <note>The rural area under the jurisdiction of a city-state.</note>, where seventy to eighty thousand pieces of wool cloth were manufactured. The value of this output amounted to two hundred thousand gold florins. Thirty years later, there were three hundred wool cloth factories, which produced more than one hundred thousand pieces of cloth.

<margin>profit <unclear>levels</unclear></margin>
At the levying of the <term>Catasto</term> <note>A Florentine tax census based on an assessment of property and income.</note>—the income tax—in 1427, it was found that there were one hundred and eight *large* factories to be taxed; and in the census of 1460, the number had risen to two hundred and twenty-three wholesale houses doing an enormous business. These figures do not include the *small* factories, the number of which varied, but which were always at least as numerous as the leading houses.

In that same year, Benedetto Dei relates that Florentine woven cloth was sold extensively in Rome, Naples, Sicily, Constantinople, Pera, Adrianople, and all over the East. At the same time, wool yarn spun in Florence was not permitted to be sold to foreign customers.

Trade was flourishing in the final years of Lorenzo de’ Medici, as fourteen thousand pieces of cloth made from Spanish wool called “*Garbo*,” were woven in one year and sold abroad for twenty-one gold florins per piece. In the same year, five thousand pieces of cloth made from fine English wool called “*San Martino*,” were woven and earned sixty gold florins per piece.¹

The Consuls resided in the very heart of the city, within the precincts of Or San Michele. Their residence—the ancient Palazzo de’ Comprobbisi—was connected to the Shrine and Granary across the street by an arched, covered stairway built in the sixteenth century. From the massive, battlemented tower, they could oversee the operations of their workers in the immediate neighborhood, as well as the wagons and strings of mules carrying the materials of their craft in and out across the bridges. It was called the “*Archivio de’ Contratti*”—the “Registry of Contracts”—because the registers of commissions made on behalf of the Guild were preserved within it.

This tower still stands and bears the sculpted arms of the Guild. These arms were also displayed upon the *Gonfalon* <term>a heraldic banner or ensign</term> and skillfully united the religious devotion of the Florentine people with the symbols of their city and their craft. They were: a white “*Agnus Dei*” <note>Latin: Lamb of God</note> on a red field, carrying a white banneret with a red cross, positioned under four blue lilies and a wool-comber’s iron rake.

The interior of the Residence was richly decorated. The <note>Circled in pencil in original</note>Hall of Audience, which occupied the entire first floor, had a finely painted ceiling with plaster moldings supported by massive marble pillars, and the walls were covered with frescoes. A wide staircase led to an upper story, which was lit by large stained-glass windows. Upon a slab of *pietra serena* <term>a dark gray sandstone used extensively in Florentine architecture</term> were the sculpted arms of the Guild, with an inscription:

### THE GUILD OF WOOL

This date coincides with the restoration of the Guild's headquarters in the year 1308.

The Guild possessed not only palaces, houses, shops, and farms, but also six large cloth-stretching grounds <note>Original: *tiratoli*; these were large structures or open spaces used for drying and stretching cloth on frames.</note> at Orbetello, located between the Via degli Alfani and the Via della Pergola, on the Lungarno dell'Aquila, along the Via dei Servi, the Via San Piero Gatolino, and the Via dell'Uccello; they also owned many fulling mills.<sup>1</sup>

The "Wool Guild" owned and rented many factories in the *contado* <term>the rural territory or countryside surrounding a city</term>, including the Castagnolo factory on the road to Pisa. This was sold to the Della Stufa family in 1220—a remarkably early date that indicates the very early expansion of the wool industry. Many convents and family residences, located within easy reach of the Consuls' headquarters, served as workrooms for busy laborers under the Guild's sponsorship. In 1340, the monastery of Santa Maria della Disciplina was occupied by the famous Capponi family and sheltered a large number of wool spinners and weavers.<sup>2</sup>

</margin>
Two questions constantly gave rise to new legislation: wages and foreign competition. The workers knew perfectly well what enormous profits the wool merchants and manufacturers made in their dealings with foreign markets. They understood without the least difficulty that, while their employers had control over the best supplies of raw materials, the prices for Florentine cloth remained the highest everywhere. They also rightly judged that this preeminent position was due very largely to their own individual and collective skill in craftsmanship.

Joining forces, the workers of the two guilds—the "Calimala" <note>The Guild of Finishers of Foreign Cloth</note> and the "Wool Guild"—placed the question of wages at the very top of their negotiations with the merchants.
