<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Another element also contributed to the urgency of the matter—the constant rise in prices for the necessities of daily life. This reaction by shopkeepers and grain dealers to the steadily increasing market rates for wool and cloth created a double economic burden for the working classes. The only relief they could find was to demand better pay and, when employers remained stubborn, to go on strike.

Strikes were a regular feature of Florentine life, and they frequently escalated into political feuds and revolutionary uprisings. The peak of this unrest was the *Ciompi* Rising <note>The Ciompi Revolt of 1378 was a rebellion by unrepresented textile workers (the *popolo minuto*) against the ruling merchant elite; the term *Ciompi* likely referred to the "carders" of wool.</note> in 1378. The *Ciompi* were, for the most part, laborers employed by the “Guild of Wool,” and they generally succeeded in obtaining all they asked for.

<margin>① ② Secondly</margin>
Alongside meeting the workers' demands, employers found themselves facing a steady decline in prices due to competition from foreign-woven cloth. The convergence of these two opposing forces—rising labor costs and falling product prices—led directly to the decline of the Florentine wool industry, which had always been built upon a somewhat unstable foundation.

A greed for profit had led Florentine entrepreneurs to establish factories in many parts of Europe. In these locations, in addition to accumulating huge stocks of raw wool, they manufactured large quantities of woolen cloth. These establishments effectively became technical schools where the local workmen were trained in the methods used in Florence.

Furthermore, the natural mechanical talent of British and Flemish workers led to improvements in loom design and the various tools required by the industry. Consequently, a class of artisans emerged who were equal in skill and adaptability to their Florentine counterparts. While wood was perhaps a less critical natural resource than it was in Tuscany, iron and coal were far greater assets in England and Flanders than in the Arno Valley.

<margin>16th century</margin>
Thus, by the sixteenth century, Florence found itself matched by ambitious rivals, and her wool merchants and manufacturers

The industry had to contend with the superiority of foreign wool, combined with a leveling of manufacturing techniques. 

They sought a remedy through a policy of protectionism. While this offered a temporary solution to the challenges facing members of the Wool Guild, it eventually led to disastrous consequences.

Cantini <note>Lorenzo Cantini (1765–1839) was an Italian historian known for compiling the laws of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.</note> provides a long list of articles and materials used in the wool industry which, in the sixteenth century, were forbidden from being exported through the city gates without special permission from the Guild Consuls. These items included: wool scraps and waste fibers; white and colored wool thread; cuttings of woolen cloth; pressed wool used for felt; woolen rags; iron screens for beating wool; carding combs and teasels <term>teasel: a dried flower head used to raise the nap on cloth</term>—both old and new; iron looms, stays, and shuttles; finishing cards for serge fabrics; white and red wine dregs (lees) in barrels <note>Wine lees were used as a mordant in the dyeing process.</note>; madder <term>madder: a root used to produce red dye</term> in bags; white moss or lichen; woad <term>woad: a plant used to produce blue dye</term>—fresh or dried; all crimson and red dyes—liquid or powder; brazilwood <note>A wood used to produce red dye.</note>; gallnuts <note>Used in making ink and dyes.</note>; indigo; rock alum and alum scum; vitriol; cloth soap; presses or boards for bales; lead seals and labels, and so on.

The prosperity of the wool industry continued to decline significantly throughout the sixteenth century. This was largely due to hostile legislation passed by the rulers and governments of foreign countries. For example, a law passed under Edward IV <note>King of England from 1461–1470 and 1471–1483.</note> stated: “No person below the rank of Baron shall wear any type of woolen cloth manufactured outside the King’s dominions, nor any sable furs, under penalty of a £10 fine.” During the reign of Cosimo I—the first Grand Duke—the number of Florentine business houses associated with the “Wool Guild” was reduced to 166. By the end of the century, only 88 remained to testify to the industry's former prosperity.

The decline of the wool industry, as well as the general commerce of Florence, was characterized by habits of idleness brought on by a long period of uninterrupted prosperity. *“To act the gentleman”* <note>original: “Fare il Signore”</note> meant that if someone wished to be considered important,

--- Page 244 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Florentine wool industry's decline, moving from economic and protectionist causes to the social and cultural shifts—specifically the desire for aristocratic status—that led merchants to abandon their trades.</meta>

### THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

All it took was to stop actively participating in trade and adopt the manners of those in a higher social class! This was undoubtedly a prominent characteristic of the Florentine people throughout the Renaissance; it was the natural, yet destructive, result of life in a purely commercial community where everyone belonged to the middle class. No branch of trade felt this more than the wool industry, with its large number of workers, and the tightening grip of decline took a firm hold on the members of the "Guild of Woolen Merchants."

The *Via degli Arazzieri*—named after Arras in Flanders <note>Arras was a major center for tapestry production, so much so that the word "arras" became a synonym for tapestry in English and "arazzo" in Italian.</note>—recalls almost the last desperate effort to revive the prosperity of the "Wool Guild." In 1543, Grand Duke Cosimo I wished to decorate his new palace with woven tapestries. He asked the city’s wool manufacturers to carry out the commission, but unfortunately, technical skill and commercial initiative were dying, if not already dead, and no one would take the job. 

Cosimo then persuaded several tapestry workers from Flanders to settle in Florence. He established a weaving factory for the public benefit in a building later called the "*Uffizio dell' Ipotece*" <note>Office of Mortgages</note>. Under the direction of Johannes Rotter—better known by his Italian name, Giovanni Rosto—the industry grew quickly. The Florentine painters Bronzino and Salviati designed cartoons <term>cartoon: a full-scale preparatory drawing used as a model for a tapestry</term> for the weavers. The finished pieces bore Rotter’s (or Rosto’s) mark: a piece of meat roasting on a spit <note>A pun on his Italian name, *Rosto*, which resembles the word *arrosto* (roast).</note>. Fifty years later, Cosimo II brought master weavers from Paris, and before long, Florentine tapestries surpassed all similar works. A magnificent collection can be seen in the *Palazzo della Crocetta*.

The final ruin of the wool industry was caused by the establishment of the "Military Order of the Knights of St. Stephen" in 1561 <note>Though the text attributes this to Cosimo II, the order was actually founded by Cosimo I in 1561; Cosimo II was a later Grand Duke.</note>. Many wealthy merchants and manufacturers—hoping to secure the lifelong honor and status of the military cross and its privileges for their families—founded commanderies <term>commandery: an administrative manor or estate belonging to a military order</term>. Fearing they would lower their social standing, they refused to continue practicing their trade.

### THE GUILD OF WOOL

The same Prince <note>Referring to Grand Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, mentioned on the previous page.</note> achieved a complete revolution in the statutes and the status of the Guild in that same year. The old order of magistrates was abolished, and four new Consuls were appointed who held office for only four months. Their powers were limited to overseeing civil cases between members of the Guild involving disputed sums exceeding thirty pounds.

A Council was created entitled the Congregation of the Conservators of the Wool Guild <note>original: *Congregazione dei Conservatori dell’ Arte della Lana*</note>. It was composed of a Senator (who was not a member of the Guild), a merchant, and two manufacturers. This Council was presided over by the Superintendent of the Guild <note>original: *Provveditore dell’ Arte*</note>, assisted by a legal official styled as the Judge of the Guild <note>original: *Giudice dell’ Arte*</note> acting as an advisor. The functions of this Council dealt with criminal cases between members of the Guild.

Periodic efforts to revive the dying organization were all in vain. The spirit of enterprise had departed from the failing industry. The stones that mischievous apprentices and quarrelsome artisans had once hurled at one another—and at everyone else—were left to lie in the streets and the corners of the squares <note>original: *Piazzas*</note>, until blades of green grass and moss spread a mantle of idleness and sleep over them.

Busy fulling-mills <term>fulling-mill: a water-powered mill used to clean and thicken wool cloth</term> and humming looms were left to rust and rot. The beautiful blue lilies in the garden of the “Lamb of God” <note>original: “*Agnus Dei*”; the Lamb of God was the heraldic symbol of the Wool Guild</note> had faded, and the sharp teeth of the woolcomber’s rake had lost their shine and their bite!

The exact date of the suppression of the “Guild and University of Wool” <note>original: “*Arte e Università della Lana*”</note> is not known. However, during the reign of Ferdinand I, the Residence of the Consuls was closed and handed over to the Canons of the Church of Saint Michael in the Orchard <note>original: *Or San Michele*; the central grain market and later the guild church of Florence</note>.

Rome in the Middle Ages was the actual ruler of all material interests, just as she was the teacher of all moral conduct. It was a principle of the Papacy that: “Wherever Christianity prevails, everything, by divine right, belongs to the successor of Saint Peter.” Her faithful sons never thought to dispute her claims, and consequently, wealth flowed into her coffers in a constantly increasing stream.

The offerings of pilgrims, the revenues of vacant benefices <term>benefice: a church office that provided an income to its holder</term>, the contributions of Peter’s Pence, the fortunes of the Cardinals, the tributes of dependent States, the plunder of Jews and heretics, and other sources, required skillful and experienced management.

# BANKERS AND MONEY-CHANGERS

Other cities competed for control of the Papal treasure. The title "Papal Money-Changers" <note>original: "*Campsores Papæ*"</note> was first claimed by the Sienese, even though they belonged to the Ghibelline party <note>The political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor against the Pope</note>.

The victory of Montaperti—which made the Ghibellines masters of Tuscany, with the exception of Lucca—nevertheless led to their humiliation in another area. In 1260, Pope Alexander IV excommunicated the Sienese and decreed that no debts should be paid to them until they had made peace with the Church. This excommunication became effective after the Sienese had ravaged Radicofani, a territory belonging to the Papal See.

However, the Papal administration’s <note>original: Curia</note> deep-seated dislike of changes of any kind ensured that the Sienese bankers kept their privileges regarding the Holy See. As late as 1263, Sienese agents were still acting as Papal representatives in England, Flanders, and elsewhere.

Florence strongly resisted the continuation of the Pope’s favors to her rival and asserted her superior claims as the supporter of the Guelphs—the Pope’s party. Besides this, managing the vast Papal treasures was perfectly suited to the sharp commercial instincts of her citizens; Florence also stood like a toll-house on the main highway to Rome.

Commercial relations had existed between Florence and the states of Europe from very early times. Agents of the “Merchants of Tuscany” <note>original: "*Mercatores Tuscie*"</note>—as they were called in King John’s reign—visited the great trade fairs held in Champagne and other French commercial centers at the end of the eleventh century, bartering their woolen fabrics for raw wool and conducting financial negotiations.

The first record of a mission of Florentine bankers to England was in 1199, when Otto degli Gherardini settled there and acquired property and status. When the Pope placed the kingdom under an interdict <note>An ecclesiastical censure that prohibited most church services</note>, as many as sixty-nine different Italian banking houses were represented, collecting Peter’s Pence <note>A tax of a penny per household paid to the Papal See</note> and otherwise profiting from the country's wealth.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers, moving from Florence's early commercial competition with Siena to the establishment of the gold florin and the rise of Florentine banking as the foundation of modern finance.</meta>

->THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

The issuance of the gold florin by the Republic of Florence in 1252 proved to be a decisive step in the race for financial supremacy among the city-states. Until that date, every state and every banker had dealt largely, if not exclusively, in debased silver money—not only in Italy but throughout Europe. The Florentines discovered that honesty was the best policy, and the world accepted them and their convenient new coin as the standard for international commerce.<sup>1</sup>

Everywhere, Florentine merchants pursued an enterprising strategy, while the Sienese and others continued to haggle using old-fashioned methods. Additionally, the constant struggles between the cities of the Tuscan League led to a shift in public sentiment. As the influence of Florence grew higher and higher, the "peace-at-any-price" party gained the upper hand, and the people of Siena and Lucca gradually withdrew from the contest. The bankers of Florence thus secured their exclusive claim to the title and position of "Papal Money-Changers" <note>original: "*Campsores Papæ*"</note>.

In this capacity, as well as in their dealings with foreign courts, it is no exaggeration to say that Florence established the modern system of banking. Her merchant-bankers are regarded as the fathers of the financial methods used today.

Many names were given to these merchant-bankers at various times: *Cambiatori* (Bankers), *Banchieri* (Changers), *Tavolieri* (Petty-cash dealers), *Prestatori* (Lenders), *Feneratori* (Discount-brokers), *Usurai* (Usurers), and—in a derogatory sense—*Cani Lombardi*, meaning "Lombard bloodhounds!" <note>original: "*Cani Lombardi*"</note><sup>2</sup>

***

The origin of the "Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers" can be found in the wealth of the three great manufacturing guilds: the "Calimala" <note>The Guild of Refiners of Foreign Cloth</note>, the "Wool" guild, and the "Silk" guild. These wealthy merchants needed a safe place to deposit their capital. In accordance with a persistent Florentine characteristic—which always sought impartial assistance outside their own specific group—

# BANKERS AND MONEY-CHANGERS

interests—they discovered what they wanted in the incorporation of the fourth Great Guild. Dante summarizes this:

> “Commerce and Exchange combined made Florence great.” ¹

Her citizens soon discovered, however, that lending money was a far more profitable pursuit than manufacturing commercial goods; and, quite early in the thirteenth century, Florence became the banking center of Europe. The surplus capital which her bankers were able to hold in reserve was the guarantee and the security of her merchants.

One of the earliest records of the banking business in Florence dates to the year 1194, when the Marquis Aldobrandino d’Este was obliged to turn to Florentine capitalists for money to support the faction and policy of Pope Innocent III. In return for the loan he then received, he pledged all his available property as collateral.

Perhaps the first mention of the bankers as forming an *Arte* <term>Guild or professional association</term> is in a document from 1201. This document describes a grant of land made by the Commune of Florence to a certain Gonnella di Guidaccio, in which the consuls of the “Guild of Bankers” are named.

The signatures of the consuls of the Guild of Bankers—together with those of the other guilds of Florence—on the 1204 treaty with Siena also indicate that the corporation was in existence and fully operational before the end of the twelfth century.

Between 1220 and 1230, agencies of Florentine bankers were established in many parts of Europe, forwarding remittances to Rome directly or through the parent houses in Florence. In this business, they were joined by Sienese merchant-bankers, and they were specifically associated together in 1233, when Pope Gregory IX issued a “Rule” <note>A formal decree or administrative order</note> authorizing them to collect the papal revenues in France, England, Spain, and Flanders.²

->THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

Through their manufactured articles, the Florentine Merchant-Bankers, by the middle of the thirteenth century, had secured the key to the wealth of all nations.

The general commercial activities of the Florentine bankers undoubtedly led to some confusion, as they were conducted in friendly rivalry with the enterprises of the merchants of the “Calimala” and the Guilds of “Wool” and “Silk.” There was likely a system of fraternal cooperation <note>The original uses the word "Freemasonry" to describe a cooperative network or secret mutual-aid system between the guilds.</note> at work among them, whereby each and all of them acted simultaneously as dealers in wool and cloth and as operators in money and financial securities.

The earliest Statutes of the Guild preserved in the Archives of Florence date to the year 1299. They consist of thirty-four paragraphs. An earlier code, which was compiled in 1280 but no longer exists, appears to have been the foundation for all subsequent Statutes. <note>original citation: Pagnini, vol. ii. p. 132, etc.</note>

The commission of Merchants and Judges, which was assembled at the end of the thirteenth century for the purpose of reviewing the Statutes and Bylaws of all the Guilds and Crafts, compiled the Code already described. This code was adopted between 1301 and 1309 by the “Calimala” Guild; in 1307, the commission also drafted special regulations and rules for the “Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers.”

This Code was amended and expanded to seventy-three sections in 1334. Two copies of the latter have been preserved, written in a particularly beautiful hand; one is in perfect condition, but the other has suffered greatly from being handled by thousands of researchers who, in earlier times, had reason to consult its rulings.

The officers of the Guild were the same in number and name as those of the other Guilds, except that a special official was appointed whose title was <term>*Esecutore*</term>—Executor, or perhaps Prosecutor. It was his duty to take legal action against debtors, as well as to manage properties in the names of heirs during their minority, and to generally oversee the affairs of deceased merchants. Regarding the first part of his duties, the <term>*Esecutore*</term> had the authority to—

Rubric 56 is very curious and demonstrates the jealousy that existed at the time between the Ghibelline nobles and the Guelph merchants. It decrees that, “should any noble of the city or *Contado* <note>The surrounding territory or countryside governed by the city.</note> of Florence presume to enter the Residences or the Offices of the Guild uninvited, he would thereby incur a fine of ten *lire* and would not be released until he had paid in full.”

Another Rubric—No. 70—is also strangely punitive. The Consuls were permitted to keep a rack and other instruments of punishment at the Headquarters, which were used by the Judges attached to the Guild during their oral examinations of defendants accused of concealing the truth about financial transactions. This process was grimly described as “enabling the Judge to deliver a just judgment!”

The Judge, or Syndic, was also subject to harsh treatment under Rubric No. 71. He was fined one hundred pounds for every instance of judicial corruption that could be proven against him after an inquiry by a panel of neutral Judges!

Strict rules regarding admission to the Guild were established in the Statutes. Before engaging in the profession of banking, candidates were required to enter their names on the Matriculation Roll <term>The official register or enrollment list of members</term>. They had to undergo a rigorous examination before the Consuls, who reviewed each of the necessary personal qualifications. Approval by this Board led to the payment of the Admission Fee, which was quite high in proportion to the capital involved.

<margin>¹ Statutes of the People of Florence, volume ii. 10. <note>original: "Statuta Populi Florentiae"</note></margin>
The father, grandfather, and even the great-grandfather shared the same legal liability for a descendant engaged in trade as if they had actually acted as his guarantor. To escape this responsibility, they were required to make a formal legal disclaimer of liability. Individual independence was obtained only after a public legal process before the Council of the Consuls of all the Guilds.¹

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Bankers and money-changers belonging to the Guild alone were recognized by the State, and they were assigned positions in one or another of the markets—generally in the *Mercato Nuovo* <note>The New Market</note> and along the *Via de' Tavolini* <note>Street of the Little Tables</note>. This privilege gave the right to a table and a chair, which were placed conveniently for the transaction of business. The table was covered with a green cloth, and upon it were placed the ledger and a layer of clean parchment for entries of the day's business. On one side was the "Bank," which consisted of a pouch or bag of gold and a wooden or metal bowl full of small coins for change. The pouch was usually a very decorative ornament made of expertly stamped or painted leather, embroidered in silk—perhaps by some sweetheart—and generally bearing the banker's coat of arms or monogram. This custom of the money-changer's table gave a special name to the registered bankers of the markets: "The Company of the Table."

There were, of course, many unlicensed money-dealers, for every Florentine who had a spare gold florin was always ready to lend it to his neighbor at a rate of interest agreed between the two. The operations of these men were more or less shady, but were in a way useful, if not indispensable, given the speculative tendencies of the citizens and the constantly busy state of trade. They were allowed to place tables in the markets, but without cloths and without chairs. Old documents distinguish between the two classes as: "With a canopy or a cloth, or without" <note>original: "Cum vela, vel tapeto, vel sine"</note>.

In *The Game of Chess* <note>original: "Giuoccho delle Scacchi"</note>, published in 1493 by Antonio Miscomini with the commentary of Jacopo de' Cessolis and several woodcuts, the Florentine banker-money-changer is represented as the King’s Pawn.

> "The fourth pawn is set before the King and is created in the form of a man holding a scale in his right hand and a weight in his left, with a table in front of him. At his belt is a purse full of money, ready to give to the merchants of cloth, linen, and wool, and of all other merchandise. And—"

<page-num>178</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

members of the Guild, and such persons were forbidden to conduct public money transactions in the markets.

The statutes of the Guild ordered, moreover, that the daily entries in the “Table” ledgers should, invariably, be made in clear cursive characters, using Roman rather than Arabic numerals, and with no capital letters, paragraphs, or marks of punctuation.

Until the time of the Medici rise to power, Florentine accounts were kept by single-entry bookkeeping, although the double-entry system of the Venetians was recognized as superior. To safeguard and verify the simpler method, duplicate books were endorsed and deposited in strongboxes; these were called *Books of the Board* <note>original: "Libri dell’ Asse"</note>, or *Red, White, and Black Books* <note>original: "Libri rossi, bianchi, neri"</note>, and so on, according to the color of the cover. Each volume contained, on the first page, an invocation of God and a dedication of the owner and the scribe to the protection of Heaven. Of these books, which were made of ordinary Florentine-made cotton paper and bound in leather, nearly all traces have disappeared. The Alberti family certainly still possesses many of the ancient banking books of their ancestors, and there are, in addition, several volumes and sheets in the *Riccardiana Library* <note>original: "Biblioteca Riccardiana"</note> belonging to the Peruzzi Company from the years 1292–1343, the latter being the year that bank suspended payment.

From these daybooks, copies were made at set times into the *Master Journals* <note>original: "Libri Maestri"</note>—formidable volumes with parchment leaves and heavy wooden or leather cases, secured and locked with metal fittings. These volumes were preserved at the offices of the Guild for consultation and correction, and many of them still exist today.

The Florentine bankers and merchants made their cash calculations in *pounds*, *shillings*, and *pence* <note>original: "lire, soldi, and denari"</note>—the origin of the British £. s. d. Twenty shillings went to the pound and twelve pence to the shilling. The market values of these coins were constantly fluctuating; therefore, the standard coin for all important transactions was the gold florin, first minted in 1252.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers in Florence, shifting from record-keeping methods to the etymology of banking terms, guild oversight, and the history of their headquarters.</meta>

<page-num>179</page-num>
<header>BANKERS AND MONEY-CHANGERS</header>

The bankers and money-changers of Florence gave us many modern financial terms: *cassa*—cash; *banco*—bank; *bancarotta*—bankruptcy; *giornale*—journal; *debito* and *debitore*—debt, debtor, and "Dr"; *credito* and *creditore*—credit, creditor, and "Cr"; while *detto* is the origin of our "ditto" and "do."

Every year, the Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild.</note> convened a conference with the financial officials of all the guilds and the Priors of the monastic orders to reconcile disputed accounts and to establish regulations governing currency values and loan interest for the current year. Each year, the Consuls also held a consultation with several of their predecessors in office to review the names, reputations, and business methods of all the money-changers and money-lenders operating in the city. Any dealer in money who had become notorious or unfair in his terms was removed from the Register, and his name was posted as a delinquent at the guild's offices.

The residence of the Consuls and the headquarters of the "Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers" were established at an early date in the *Mercato Nuovo* <note>New Market</note>, near the *Porta Santa Maria* <note>Saint Mary's Gate</note>. This building was destroyed by fire in 1304, but in its place, an edifice was erected that far surpassed all the other consular residences in dignity and splendor—as was appropriate for the wealth and influence of the guild members. The interior was decorated with multicolored ceilings, and the walls were draped with rich hangings of embossed and gilded leather. Many fine oil paintings and noble marble statues were displayed alongside magnificent cabinets—the work of expert carvers and inlayers—and beautiful stained-glass windows.

Over this building was a bell, placed there by the charitable concern of a wealthy money-changer named Giovanni della Gheradesca. Rung twice a day, it signaled the opening of financial business and announced the closing of the money market. In <gloss>?</gloss>1516 <note>The date 1516 has a question mark written above it in the original document.</note>, when Cosimo I installed the clock in the market, the "Bankers' Bell" was moved to the top of the *Casa del Saggio* <note>original: "Casa del Saggio"; the Public Assay Office for gold and silver</note> and continued to ring the guild's cashiers in and out of work.

The Guild's coat of arms was displayed on the facade of their headquarters and was, of course, emblazoned on the <term>Gonfalon</term> <note>A heraldic banner or ensign.</note> entrusted to the Guild’s standard-bearer in 1266. These arms clearly signified the Guild’s purpose: a red field scattered with gold <term>florins</term> <note>The primary gold coin of Florence, first minted in 1252.</note>.

In 1343, an excellent system of dowries for young citizens of both sexes was established. Parents and friends loaned money to the State for roughly fifteen years, and they received guarantees of repayment within specific time limits. At first, the interest rate was 18 percent, which naturally attracted many depositors. The administration of this fund was entrusted to the Consuls and Council of the "Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers." The Guild elected special officers who also oversaw matters of bail and security; any shameful neglect of duty or dishonest stewardship was rigorously punished by fines and imprisonment.

Professionally, bankers were remarkably pious! Not only did every head of a household begin the day's work with family prayers, but the bank's business was also opened by a gathering of the entire staff for religious exercises. No class of citizens attended Mass and other church duties more regularly than the bankers and money-changers. Their profession also demanded charity; as they prospered, they gave alms accordingly. The traditional belief that those who deal in the most worldly matters must store up the most "heavenly treasure" was a constant consideration.

The dates when the great banking families of Florence first made their mark were approximately as follows: Acciaiuoli (1252), Alberti (1244), Bardi (1215), Buonaparte (1260), Frescobaldi (1252), Pegolotti (1317), Peruzzi (1260), Sassetti (1260), Scali (1235), and Villani (1298). Unfortunately, the diaries, account books, and parchments of almost all these families have been lost; most of what we know is gathered from the private records of...

As early as 1228, there were banks in Florence belonging to the Benevieni, Lamberti, Alamanni, and Ugolini families, who were already doing business with France, England, and Flanders. In 1264, the houses of Simonetti, Bacarelli, Ardinghi, and Spinelli had agents in London whose chief business was the collection of <term>Peter’s Pence</term> <note>An annual tax or donation paid by landowners to the Pope.</note>. Branch banks were opened by Giovanni Vanno and his company at Dover and Canterbury in 1302, as well as in London.

The Peruzzi family had sixteen such agencies: Pisa and Genoa in 1302; Paris in 1303; Avignon and Chiarenza, in the <term>Morea</term> <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, in 1305; Tunis and Venice in 1306; Naples and Rhodes in 1310; London and Bruges in 1312; Castel di Castro (Cagliari) in 1332; Barletta on the Adriatic and Palermo in 1335; and Majorca in 1336. By the middle of the fourteenth century, the number of their agents reached one hundred and thirty.

<margin>} 2</margin>
The <term>Papal Schism</term> <note>A period from 1378 to 1417 (though the author cites 1305–1377, likely referring to the Avignon Papacy) when there were rival claimants to the title of Pope.</note> gave the Florentine bankers rare opportunities to reap "golden harvests." The contributions of the faithful were unavoidably diverted into two rival channels. Much money was either entirely lost or misapplied, and this confusion added immensely to the business and the commissions of the <note>original: "Campsores Papæ"</note> **Papal Money-changers**. The houses of Mozzi, Bardi, Acciaiuoli, Scali, Spini, and Alberti rose to eminence during this period.

Two extant books show that in 1348, the company of Jacopo and Caroccio degli Alberti was employed in collecting Peter’s Pence and other ecclesiastical dues in the name of the Avignon Pope; they had agencies in Paris, Bruges, Venice, Siena, Perugia, Brussels, Naples, and Rome.

Other Florentine bankers whose names were well known in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries included the Strozzi, Medici, Capponi, Salviati, da Uzzano, Albizzi, Badesi, Bartolini, Corsini, Dini, Ricci, and Covoni families.

Perhaps the most famous of them all were the Bardi, who made their mark as enterprising merchants along with the Caval—

They were involved in the feud between Cosimo de' Medici and Luca Pitti in 1434 and, along with the Castellani, Ardinghelli, Rondinelli, Brancacci, Guardagni, Baldovinetti, and others, were exiled for many years. This severe treatment, however, resulted in the title of the heads of the Guilds being changed from <term>Priori delle Arti</term> <note>Priors of the Guilds.</note> to <term>Priori di Libertà</term> <note>Priors of Liberty.</note>, so that the people "might," as Machiavelli says, "at least preserve the name of the thing they had lost."¹

On May 29, 1311, the Bardi Company, which consisted of nine partners, appointed legal representatives in France, England, Ireland, Tuscany, Lombardy, and Germany. In August of the same year, another such official was appointed for Cyprus and Rhodes.²

The power of the Bardi Company grew enormously, as did their generosity. They certainly strictly maintained their monopolies, which were numerous and diverse; but, at the same time, they opened branch offices everywhere and provided employment to many small firms and individuals. Builders, dealers, merchants, tradespeople, and others shared in the success of their business relations. To be connected with a house like that of the Bardi meant not only enjoying significant social and personal comfort and profit, but also gaining the respect and confidence of everyone they encountered.³

Villani calls the Bardi, the Peruzzi, the Acciaiuoli, the Buonaccorsi, and the Scali families: "The Pillars of Commerce and of Christianity."

In 1315, an enterprising <term>Ministro</term> <note>Agent or manager.</note> of the Bardi Company in Flanders, Francesco Balducci, obtained certain privileges for Florentine merchants from the Duke of Brabant: (1) a reduction of the import duty on silk per shipload, and (2) a maximum tax of two <term>denari</term> <note>Small silver coins.</note> per one hundred and twenty pounds of wool. In 1324, he went on behalf of his company to Cyprus, where a high tariff had been placed on all Florentine merchandise. He

Such agents were not men of inferior position or ability. The heads of the large banking houses were too well aware of business opportunities to appoint any representatives who did not possess the very highest qualifications. Among them, we find descendants of the great houses of Donati, Guicciardini, Villani, Strozzi, Soderini, Machiavelli, Pazzi, Portinari, and many others. In later years, seven of these agents served in their time in the office of <term>Standard-bearer of Justice</term> <note>original: "Gonfaloniere di Giustizia," the highest executive office in the Florentine Republic.</note>, and as many as twenty-seven held the high dignity of <term>Prior</term> <note>A member of the city's supreme governing council.</note>.

All of the agents or couriers were not only registered members of the Guild, but their names were also recorded on the Foreign Agents’ Roll. In addition to generous fixed salaries, they received ample funds for their travel expenses, as well as letters of recommendation and credit. Each one carried a medal, or token, bearing the heraldic emblem of his house as a further mark of official responsibility.^1

Some idea of the annual salaries paid to agents, couriers, and clerks of the great banking houses may be gathered by consulting the books of the Peruzzi Company for the years 1335–1338.^2 The amounts range from ten <term>lire</term> and three <term>soldi</term>—paid to an <term>apprentice</term> <note>original: "discipulo"</note> named Giusto di Beno Battelli—to three hundred and twenty-two <term>lire</term> paid to an agent, Bartolo Uguccioni. <note>The lira and soldo were units of Florentine currency.</note>

No more interesting and exciting scene could be witnessed in old Florence than the daily transactions of the bankers and money-changers.

...ebbs and flows. All around are the agents and travelers of the firm, either just returned from, or starting off to, Armenia, China, and the East, or London, Paris, Antwerp, and other Western capitals.

Those returning home are seated, busily revising their financial statements of business conducted and consulting their order books in preparation for their inspection by the cashiers at the counter. Some are walking up and down, exchanging greetings and information with the couriers about to start on outward journeys. The atmosphere is full of bustle and excitement—men are bragging about their travels and showing off the quirks and eccentricities they have picked up along the way, while others are boasting of what they are about to achieve and are strutting back and forth!

The heads of the firm are either meeting privately in their offices, discussing high finance, or perhaps are haughtily making their way in full official attire to participate in some important affair of state in the Council at the <term>Palazzo Vecchio</term> <note>The "Old Palace," the seat of government in Florence.</note>.

If the Bank has a <term>Loggia</term> <note>An open-air gallery or porch.</note> or <term>Borsa</term> <note>An exchange or clearinghouse.</note> attached to it—a vestibule or clearing office—the scene is even more animated. In addition to the regular staff, customers of all sorts and kinds are popping in and out, and voices are discussing in shrill tones the state of the money market and the rise and fall of stocks, and so on.

Under the portico of the <term>Mercato Nuovo</term> <note>The "New Market," built in the 16th century as a center for the silk and gold trades.</note> especially, bankers, merchants, and their clients gather. Speculators and risk-takers—"Bulls and Bears"—are there just as they are in our day in the vicinity of the Stock Exchange.

> "The shares of the <term>Monte</term> <note>The state-funded public debt or pawn office.</note> are at thirty. Can we do business?" cries one. "Say, this time next year, I’ll sell or I’ll buy as you like."
>
> "What’s your price?" is the reply. "What premium do you propose?" <note>1</note>

Stock changed hands constantly, and accordingly a tax of two silver florins was imposed upon every transfer, which proved the government's fondness for levying money for State purposes in every imaginable...

direction, and also established the regularity of the contract. "**Jobbing**"—as we call it <note>Speculative trading or acting as a middleman to profit from price fluctuations.</note>—was in full swing in the *Mercato Nuovo* <note>The "New Market."</note> all through the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. In the year 1371, a tax of two percent was established and imposed upon every completed bargain.¹

The palaces of the great banker families were a distinctive feature of the street architecture in old Florence. Sometimes an entire street was occupied by members of a single family, for example: Via de' Peruzzi, Via de' Tornabuoni, Borgo degli Albizzi, Borgo de' Greci, Via de' Bardi, and Via de' Cerchi <note>Literally: Peruzzi Street, Tornabuoni Street, etc.</note>.

The **Peruzzi Bank**, at the beginning of the fourteenth century, consisted of three brothers who lived with their wives and children in the Via de' Peruzzi. The combined families numbered thirty-one people, who were served by more than twenty domestics of all grades. The annual expenditure of these united households reached the considerable figure of three thousand gold florins, equivalent to £1,500 <note>In the late 19th century, when this was likely written, £1,500 was a very large sum; today, 3,000 gold florins would represent a massive fortune in gold value alone.</note>.

Much of the expansion of Florence's banking business was directly due to the wanderings of **Guelphic exiles** <note>Members of the Guelph faction, who supported the Pope against the Holy Roman Emperor; they were frequently exiled during political shifts.</note>, who temporarily became agents for their firms in foreign lands.

**Charles of Anjou**, before he set out from France on his way to Italy, not only received many loans from Florentine bankers and merchants but also surrounded himself with Florentine judges, notaries, doctors, apothecaries, armorers, saddlers, and others. Four hundred exiled Guelphs—mostly Florentine bankers—formed his bodyguard. Through his influence, the majority of the trade in Naples passed into the hands of Florentine merchants. Exclusive shipments of wine, grain, and oil from Manfredonia and Ravenna were made by these same enterprising traders under Charles's patronage.

Towards the end of the fourteenth century, Florentine commerce had made such an immense advance that an entire body of statutes and regulations dealing with financial matters came into existence. Among them was a series of laws enabling all mercantile affairs to be conducted with greater speed by avoiding legal red tape and releasing merchants’ credits from mortgage and seizure. At the same time, attempts were made to organize a formal code of laws concerning perjury, fraud, and bankruptcy.

The vast scale of the banking business that Florentines were conducting in the fifteenth century drew a remarkable admission from the reluctant lips of the ruler of a rival republic—Venice. Doge Tommaso Mocenigo declared that:
> “Florence is drawing out of Venice 392,000 gold ducats a year!”

Troubles came in their turn, and by 1422 there remained only seventy-two firms engaged in banking and money-changing, and these were for the most part small houses. Further shrinkage followed until, in 1474, no more than thirty-two banks were able to keep their doors open. This low point marked the beginning of the decline of Florentine commercial prosperity.

The extreme complexity and variety of monetary values that existed in the Middle Ages and early Renaissance in every city and town of Europe made the existence of an association of exchange agents an absolute necessity.

The foreign coinage that found its way to Florence was remarkable for its variety and fluctuation in value. The standard piece of Naples was the *Carlin*; of Venice, the *Mark* or *Ducat*; of London, the *Pound sterling*; of Paris, the *Livre Tournois* <term>The "Tours pound," a standard French currency based on the weight of silver</term>; and of Rhodes and Tunis, the *Besan* <term>Also known as a Bezant, a gold coin originally from the Byzantine Empire used widely in Mediterranean trade</term>. All these were current in Florence.

<page-num>187</page-num>
<header>->BANKERS AND MONEY-CHANGERS<-</header>

While Jews and Greeks on one hand, and Venetians and Genoese on the other, were the primary drivers of monetary expansion during the Middle Ages, Florence was undoubtedly the center of all banking interests during the Renaissance.

The remarkable ease of exchanging cash values for paper credit is entirely due to Florentine initiative. This system revolutionized and energized the conduct of commerce, not only in Florence itself but throughout the known world.

“*Lettere di Cambio*” <note>original: "Lettere di Cambio" — Letters of Exchange</note>—letters of exchange or credit—became an essential means of transacting international business for bankers and moneylenders. Transporting gold and silver bullion grew increasingly risky, and its weight made transit difficult. The constant loss of value in common coinage was another major drawback to dealing directly in cash. These excellent and convenient money drafts provided a ready and secure way to trade using credit. They were first used in Florence in 1260, though they may have originated in Venice during the mid-twelfth century, where their use was limited to specific business houses that traded with one another.

The system of “Letters of Credit” made sending money to distant places—even as far as Jaffa or Tana <note>Tana was a major medieval commercial port on the Sea of Azov, near the mouth of the Don River.</note> on the Sea of Azov—relatively easy. For instance, if a Florentine citizen wanted to send, say, two hundred pounds to Antwerp, he only had to walk into the office of a “Calimala” <term>The Calimala Guild was the guild of finishers and merchants of foreign cloth.</term>, “Wool,” or “Silk” merchant. With a few words sent by courier to an agent in that city, the merchant ensured the payment was made.

The use of “Letters of Credit” enabled massive financial operations, such as those of the Bardi and Peruzzi families. Up until the year 1340, they placed nearly a million and a half gold florins—equivalent to £750,000—at the disposal of King Edward III <note>King Edward III of England famously defaulted on these massive loans in 1345, which contributed to the eventual bankruptcy of the Bardi and Peruzzi banking houses.</note>.

A table of time limits between Florence and the major cities of Europe and the East—copies of which were displayed in all the banks—showed the number of days required for shipments...

The days occupied by the couriers of the Florentine merchant and banking firms in traveling were as follows: Rome and Genoa, five to six days each; Milan, Venice, and Naples, ten to twelve; Paris, Bruges, and Barcelona, twenty to twenty-five; London, Sicily, and Constantinople—twenty-five to thirty.

The brokerage fees authorized by the Guild varied according to the standard value of the money employed, whether gold or silver; the average amount was from ten to fifteen percent. Probably one of the principal causes which contributed to making Florence so prosperous was the system of loans at interest. <note>Peruzzi, p. 81.</note>

In Florence, it was a sound system of finance rather than a greedy love of money that influenced her commercial policy. Very early on, her merchants discovered that capital borrowed at a high rate of interest was not the most efficient way to advance their operations. Doubtless there were speculators and even "plungers"—to use a modern term—who craved money for its own sake, but these men were held in little esteem, and their methods were not generally attractive.

At first, the church authorities opposed the lending of money at interest, and making a profit upon a temporary loan was deemed <term>usury</term> <note>The practice of lending money at unreasonably high rates of interest, often condemned by the medieval church.</note>. Even until the end of the fourteenth century, "it was considered usury for anyone to make a loan which was not drawn up on an official document, and where, in the document itself, it was not stated that the loan was made for free." <note>Lapo Mazzei, "Letters" <note>original: "Lettere"</note>, vol. i. 246.</note>

The companies accepted the contract and provided the necessary sum, either in full or in part, raising the remainder from the citizens under specific conditions and at a reasonable interest rate. Another method was used when the state wanted to force citizens to take up a loan: the total amount required was publicly announced, and a portion was assigned to every street based on the wealth and number of its inhabitants. After each person's share was determined, the money was delivered to the State Treasurer, who repaid the creditors from the proceeds of customs duties when the loan expired. To make this easier, contributors were also granted a specific quantity of salt at six *lire* <note>The local currency.</note> per bushel and were permitted to sell it at the standard fixed price, which was higher.

Lending money to the state for a fixed term at a specific interest rate led to the creation of a new government office in 1222, which became popularly known as *Il Monte* <note>original: "Il Monte"</note>—"The Money-pile!" Instead of requesting loans from banks as had been the previous custom, the government divided the funds needed for the public treasury into portions based on each citizen's tax assessment, and everyone was expected to contribute their full share. The interest rate credited to each contributor in the *Monte* ledgers varied from three to twenty-five percent. This ledger was known as *Il Libro de' Settamilioni* <note>original: "Il Libro de' Settamilioni"</note>—"The Book of Seven Millions"—named after the amount of the original loan.

In 1307, the Republic’s credit was pledged to the bankers, the *Calimala* <note>The Guild of Cloth Merchants, one of the most powerful in Florence.</note>, and the *Parte Guelfa* <note>The political faction supporting the Pope, which held significant financial power.</note> for the sum of seven million gold florins. During the war with Arezzo, the "Guild of Bankers and Money-changers" extended the state credit for eight million gold florins; this amount was repaid by a *Provvisione* <note>original: "Provvisione"</note> <term>Provvisione</term> <note>A legislative decree or order in council issued by the Florentine government.</note> in 1307.^1

Their resourcefulness was the result of their systematic training in the flexibility of capital. When one strategy appeared to have achieved its goal, these alert capitalists were never at a loss for another.

Until the middle of the fourteenth century, State revenues were raised without difficulty through customs and duties on contracts called "<term>Gabelle</term>" <note>Excise taxes or consumption taxes.</note>. Among the <term>Provvisioni</term> <note>Legislative decrees or acts of the Florentine government.</note> of the year 1290 is one that shows how the "<term>Gabella</term>" was collected and how the different Guilds not only contributed as organizations, but also how individual members were appointed to handle the collection. Millers, bakers, masons, carpenters, tailors, and barbers of the <term>Contado</term> <note>The rural territory and villages surrounding the city of Florence.</note> were specially taxed; each man paid forty <term>soldi</term> <note>A silver coin; twenty soldi made one lira.</note> a month, with the tax spanning two months.<sup>1</sup> In 1336, however, the expenses incurred in many military expeditions were far too heavy to be met by ordinary taxation. A national debt—as we would call it—was created through forced loans and was called "<term>Prestanza</term>" from <note>original: "præstigium"</note> tribute.

The distribution of the required amount was quite arbitrary but depended on seven separate assessments of the property owned by each individual. An average was calculated, which was the sum required from each citizen of sufficient wealth. Failure to pay this tax within seven days led to the delinquent's name being entered in a book called "<term>il Specchio</term>"—"The Looking Glass"—and he was subjected to fines and legal disqualifications.

Several registers for the "<term>Prestanza</term>" are preserved in the Archives of Florence. One—a paper book in good condition—has the following entry:

> "In the name of God, Amen. The public debt in 1344 amounted to thirty thousand gold florins, which the State could not pay. To resolve the debt, a “<term>Monte</term>”—or Public Bank—was established so that patriotic citizens might contribute their share. Each depositor received in exchange credit or a promise to pay, which became a negotiable asset that could be transferred from one person to another, much like our modern check system.

Once the “<term>Prestanza</term>” <note>A forced loan or tribute.</note> had served its purpose, there was no difficulty in further manipulating State revenues to absorb private wealth. In 1345, a “<term>Monte Comune</term>” was raised to satisfy the greed of the Duke of Athens <note>Walter VI of Brienne, who briefly ruled Florence as a dictator.</note> and his faction. Through this system, all loans made to the Republic were merged into one consolidated fund or debt.

which was made to bear interest at five percent and was secured against state revenues. This was effectively the creation of government stock, as every person interested in the loans was entitled to buy, sell, pledge, or exchange their share as they wished. Market prices in the ***Mercato Nuovo*** <note>The New Market, the financial and banking center of Florence.</note> fluctuated according to the rise or fall of the State’s credit. The Florentine ***Monte Comune*** <note>Common Mountain; the consolidated public debt.</note> was the first national debt, as such, ever established.

The ***Arbitrio*** <note>Arbitrary assessment.</note>—an individual valuation—and the ***Decima*** <note>The Tenth.</note>—a general percentage of property—were other methods used by the State to raise loans quickly and easily, acting on the advice of the Consuls of the **Guild of Bankers and Money-changers**. The former was a tax based on the estimated earnings of the citizens. It was very unpopular and failed to achieve its intended purpose. Cosimo I finally abolished it after it had existed for sixty years. The latter—the *Decima*—was a tax of ten florins for every hundred gold florins of an individual’s net income. Because it was a rate of one-tenth of the income, it gained its name. Assessments were subject to a review every three years. Fraudulent tax returns led to the confiscation of any property not listed in the records.

The ***Catasto*** <note>A comprehensive tax census and income tax.</note>—the Income Tax—was named after the book in which the names of all taxpayers, along with descriptions and values of their properties, were recorded. It was devised by Filippo Giacciacetto but actually introduced by Giovanni de’ Medici in 1427. The name was derived from *accatastare* <note>original: "accatastare" — to accumulate or pile up</note>. It was the most elaborate and thorough register of people and property ever undertaken by any civilized state and stands as a monument to the financial skill of the Florentine people. Each person’s exact financial position was calculated from every perspective, and the final total was charged at a rate of half a florin for every hundred gold florins. The *Catasto* operated very smoothly and did much to increase the popularity of the Medici family. Between 1427 and 1453, the loans raised amounted to the enormous sum of 6,374,000 gold florins, contributed by seventy-six banks;

family, over successive generations, manipulated public accounts. While pretending to be friends of the people, they were able—without any sense of guilt—to help themselves quite generously to the contents of the public treasury!

Lorenzo "the Magnificent" <note>original: "il Magnifico"</note> was the first of the Medici to entirely abandon all connections with business and banking interests. At the same time, his time in office marked the end of Florence's financial freedom—which seems like a paradox, but is nonetheless a fact!

The wealth accumulated by the merchant banking families can be judged by the example of the Medici, whose dominance in the political and social life of the State was a significant factor. Giovanni de' Medici left behind 179,221 gold florins, Cosimo I left 235,137, and Piero left 237,982; meanwhile, every leading member of the family gave massive charitable gifts to the city and its inhabitants—Cosimo alone, it is said, gave away more than 500,000 gold florins! ^1

The interest rates paid on borrowed capital varied significantly, not only in general use but also according to specific classes of the population. Looking back to the days of Justinian <note>The Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman Law in the 6th century.</note>, when fixed rules and rates were first established, it is quite interesting to learn that people of rank and influence usually paid four percent on loans. Meanwhile, merchants were charged eight percent, and unfortunate dealers in grain and other food supplies were forced to pay <term>mulcted: penalized or heavily charged</term> eleven percent! ^2

Authorities tried to find a middle ground, and an attempt was made to charge a general rate of six to seven percent. This succeeded for a time until 1345, when the Duke of Athens <note>Walter VI of Brienne, a brief and unpopular ruler of Florence.</note>—seeking revenge because the merchants and bankers were unenthusiastic about his cause—declared that Justinian's original rates should be restored.

The fluctuating value of the gold florin caused a similar sliding scale in interest rates. Regarding state loans, the interest varied considerably depending on the time and circumstances. In 1345, the creditors of the "Monte Comune" <term>The "Common Mountain," the consolidated public debt or communal bank of Florence.</term>

received five percent, while between 1349 and 1380, the rate paid was between twelve and twenty percent.¹

On the other hand, the rate for extraordinary business transactions was moderate. The Bardi Company charged the King of Sicily only two percent, and in Seville, their price was only five percent. The Peruzzi Company made similar charges.

The wide extent and importance of the banking and trading interests of the Bardi and Peruzzi companies is evidenced by the interesting fact that the King of Armenia reduced the usual dues by half for merchandise cleared to or from Florence in the names of either of those houses. The King’s official permit had his gold seal attached by a broad green silk ribbon.

Money-changers and money-lenders appear to have been frequently at odds in their operations. To the former were due almost all the statutes passed after 1394 affecting the status and privileges of the latter. These became so oppressive that all interest was looked upon as theoretically usurious <term>usury: the practice of lending money at interest, which was often condemned by the Church as a sin</term>, though practically as much as fifteen percent was permissible.²

Dante is very severe in his "*Inferno*" <note>Italian: "Hell"; the first part of Dante Alighieri's 14th-century epic poem, the Divine Comedy.</note> upon the crime of unjust usury, describing it as prostituting the fair role of Nature and Nature’s laws:

Money lending became a precise science, a fine art, a fraud, and a farce in turn. Men sharpened their wits to acquire money—honestly, if possible—by practicing every imaginable trick. Church dignitaries were just as eager as the common people to borrow and lend, with the sole goal of their own eventual profit. If a money-lender died who had been known as a shrewd fellow, burial was refused to his remains until a payment had been made to the bishop! Men were urged to make honorable terms with heaven before they died by handing over significant sums or property to the care of those who held the Keys of Heaven <term>Keys of Heaven: a reference to the spiritual authority of the Catholic Church</term>!

It was not impossible to maintain an appearance of respectability, and even holiness, in money-dealing. The terminology of the period presented disgraceful and questionable transactions under pleasant-sounding names, such as: *dono di tempo* <note>Italian: "gift of time"</note>—quick returns; *merito* <note>Italian: "merit"</note>—slight recompense; *interesso* <note>Italian: "interest"</note>—smart gain; *cambio* <note>Italian: "exchange"</note>—tit-for-tat; *civanza* <note>Italian: "benefit"</note>—unexpected profit; *baroccolo* <note>Italian: "petty graft"</note>—sly advantage; *ritrangola* <note>Italian: "usury"</note>—trifling advance on a price, and so on.¹

Sacchetti tells the story of one Sandro Tornabello, who had a greedy love of money. Meeting an old creditor who threatened to arrest him for an unpaid account—which had actually been settled by his father, though no record had been kept—he visited his notary. The notary advised him to let the man proceed against him in the usual way. When the bailiff arrived to take him into custody, Sandro proposed that he should pay the official half of the three-hundred-gold-florin claim in exchange for dismissing the lawsuit in the *Podestà's* <term>Podestà: the chief magistrate or city official in medieval Italian cities</term> Court! ²

Boccaccio directed many sharp shafts of sarcasm at the monetary hypocrisies of his day: *Qui è poca civanza e men guadagna* <note>Italian: "Here there is little profit and even less gain."</note>, "He who steals a trifling benefit, thereby acquires an..."

. . . ample gain!"¹ And he sums up his indignation in the expression—"Gross usury!"² <note>original: "Grossa usura!"</note>

"That man," wrote Machiavelli, "will never be regarded as good who, for the purpose of always making a profit from an occupation which he carries on, proves himself rapacious, fraudulent, and violent."³

Constant efforts were made to restrain usurious interest. Unhappily, they were usually rendered useless by the actions of the Government, which aimed at extracting the highest possible rates from citizens who dealt directly with its officials. In 1420, usury—or, as we would now call it, interest upon money—was so high and so arbitrary that the State took steps to issue fixed rates and prices. One decree ordained that no more than five *denari* <term>denari: a small currency unit, twelve of which made a soldo</term> might be charged per *lira* <term>lira: a unit of currency composed of 20 soldi</term> per month.

A banker's ledger of the year 1427 is still preserved. It belonged to the company of Guiliano di Nannino dei Bardi and Piero di Francesco Piccioli, and reveals the fact that the interest upon a capital of 2,928 *lire* amounted to 878 *lire* a year—a rate of nearly thirty percent! A goldsmith, Oderigo da Credi by name, borrowed twenty *lire* for six months and paid four *lire* in interest; in addition, he deposited his rich green doublet, lined with velvet, as a guarantee for the repayment of the amount!

The demands of money-lenders—whether licensed by the Guild or unlicensed operators in the Market—became so excessive at the end of the fifteenth century that not only was the State forced to issue repressive *Provvisioni* <term>Provvisioni: legislative decrees or legal provisions issued by the Florentine government</term>, but the influence of the pulpit was also arrayed in violent opposition.

Between 1430 and 1436—when the city gates were once more opened to the Jews—the "Guild of Bankers and Money-changers" forbade all money-lenders under its authority to ask for more than four *denari* for a *lira* per month—a rate of twenty percent.

The Republic provided the preaching friars—particularly the Augustinians and Dominicans—with plenty of material for fierce verbal attacks. They targeted the "*Monte Comune*" <term>Monte Comune: The Public Debt or state fund</term>, where subscribers paid a tax of ten percent based on their annual income valuations. The way this tax was collected placed a heavy burden on the working and poorer classes. In their distress, they turned to the Jewish community for help, as their numbers in the city had grown and their financial activities had largely escaped the notice of the authorities.

The suffering caused by these financial demands on poor families stirred the passion of a famous preacher at the end of the fifteenth century. Preaching in the church of Santa Croce in 1488, Bernardino da Feltre spoke out on behalf of the struggling citizens and fiercely condemned the greed of Jewish moneylenders. He proposed establishing a Pawnshop <note>This refers to the *Monte di Pietà*, a charitable institution that lent money at low interest rates to the poor.</note> where the impoverished and distressed could find fair treatment. This proposal was eventually realized, though not until 1495, after Matteo Strozzi led a raid against the Jews, who were then banished from the city.

Savonarola threw himself completely into the struggle between might and right. He championed the cause of the people and advocated for the removal of the greedy and wealthy oligarchy that threatened the liberties of Florence. His preaching had a massive impact and led to the creation of two factions in the city: the "*Arrabbiati*" <note>literal: "the Enraged"; the aristocratic party of reaction</note> and the "*Piagnoni*" <note>literal: "the Weepers"; the supporters of Savonarola’s reforms</note>. Under the influence of the Friar <note>Savonarola</note>, the "*Tribunale della Mercanzia*" <term>Tribunale della Mercanzia: The Merchants' Court, which oversaw commercial disputes</term>, which had become ineffective, was restored. He achieved a level of unprecedented power and eventually caused significant losses for the wealthier citizens, which completely transformed the landscape of Florentine business and society.

The reputation of Florentine bankers for brilliant financial operations, supported by their record of honest conduct and fair management, spread far and wide. Many states and cities throughout Europe invited members of the Guild to manage their public finances and oversee the minting of coins. From—

<meta>This page continues the history of Florentine financial influence across Europe, moving from the internal religious and social debates about usury and poverty in Florence to the Guild of Bankers' international operations and their role as creditors to European monarchs.</meta>

<page-num>199</page-num>
<header>BANKERS AND MONEY-CHANGERS</header>

By the end of the twelfth century, the management of finances and mints in London, Naples, Halle, Aquileia, and many other places was controlled by the Florentines.

Among the earliest recorded loans to foreign states made by the "Guild of Bankers and Money-changers" were those to Faenza in 1257, Arezzo in 1278, and Città di Castello in 1290.

Before the end of the reign of Henry III, Florentine bankers had established a strong presence in England. They issued "Letters of Credit" to ambassadors, and bills of exchange were monopolies under their control. Money was scarce and was raised only with difficulty; consequently, not only Henry III but also the first three Edwards <note>The author refers to Edward I, Edward II, and Edward III.</note> turned to Florence for financial assistance.¹

Edward I incurred heavy expenses in Palestine, but he received help from Florence. Interest was rarely promised in such negotiations because it was equated with usury, and moneylenders were treated as heretics; therefore, the king paid £10,000 to the Frescobaldi family as compensation. He also appointed their London agent to correct errors made by London banks and named him "Director of the Currency" of the Kingdom. This same firm and many others also provided the Queen and several nobles of the Court with cash advances, receiving duties on wool, hides, and other local products as security for payment.

The Salimbeni and Peruzzi companies had similar dealings with Edward II and also with the Dukes of Burgundy.

The peak of Florentine prosperity was reached in 1336, when its population reached 180,000 inhabitants, and fifteen hundred nobles were enrolled in the membership lists of the Greater Guilds! The value of the currency was 400,000 gold florins (equivalent to £200,000), and the annual state revenue reached 300,000 gold florins (£150,000), while ordinary spending was only 40,000 gold florins (£20,000).

At this time in her history, Edward III was at war with France. Needing supplies, he applied to the "Guild of Bankers and Money-changers" of Florence through their banking—

The Bardi, Peruzzi, Frescobaldi, and Scali families took the lead in supplying the monarch’s needs through their agents resident in London. In exchange, they received the <term>farming of the customs</term><note>The practice of purchasing the right to collect and keep tax revenues for a profit.</note> of the kingdom, the superintendence of all royal revenues, and the monopoly on exporting wool.

The expansion of Florence's financial business produced, as might be expected, irregularities and misfortunes. For example, the speculative operations of the Scali company led to a suspension of payments in 1326. Their failure amounted to 400,000 gold florins and, although the most significant, was by no means the only disaster in the Florentine money market. Moreover, it caused misery and litigation far and wide. Among the creditors were the <term>Holy See</term> itself and the two Queens of Naples—Sancia and Joan. The Spanish Cardinal Pietro di Santa Sabina appealed to the Pope in Avignon, Clement, and together they pressured the government of Florence to compel the company to pay the claim. However, their debt to the Papal chair was upwards of seven thousand gold florins, and the only result was the issuance of an <term>Interdict</term><note>An ecclesiastical censure that prohibits certain church rites and sacraments from being performed in a city or for a group.</note>, directed not only against the bankers in particular but against the entire city; this was not removed until 1347.

In 1339, like a "bolt out of the blue," an English royal decree was <term>promulgated</term><note>formally proclaimed; original: "promulged"</note>, suspending the payment of money due to the Crown's creditors. This caused the Bardi and Peruzzi companies alone a loss of 1,355,000 gold florins—nearly £700,000—a colossal sum which Villani <note>Giovanni Villani (c. 1276–1348), a famous Florentine chronicler and bank official.</note> quaintly says was "worth as much as the kingdom itself."<gloss>1</gloss>

This was a disaster of the first order, and the entire banking interest of Florence reeled from the blow. "All Christendom," says the old chronicler, "came to suspect and distrust every merchant and every bank." The catastrophe led to the collapse of other banks. Between 1340 and 1345, the failures of the Acciaiuoli, Buonaccorsi, Corsini, Cocchi, Antellesi, da Uzzano, and other influential companies created a succession of crises which had far-reaching results.

The devastated banking houses liquidated their assets in full. Their credit, lands, houses, and all available possessions were sold, but at an enormous sacrifice—representing a loss of at least thirty percent. The Bardi family succeeded in paying their creditors seventy percent of what was owed, but the Peruzzi family did not fare as well, only managing to pay fifteen to twenty percent.

Giovanni Villani—whose writings are so frequently quoted in this volume—was a banker by profession. He served as the Director of the Mint while he was a member of the <term>Signoria</term><note>The supreme governing council of the Republic of Florence.</note>. He went bankrupt along with the Acciaiuoli, Buonaccorsi, Corsini, and Cocchi families, and was caught up with many other bankers and banking companies in the great collapse of the Bardi and Peruzzi. Being completely ruined, he was, according to the law, imprisoned for life. He was one of the victims of the terrible plague which ravaged Florence in the year 1350!

From another source, we find that the members of the "Guild of Bankers and Money-changers" were also heavily affected. The King of Sicily—imitating the King of England—refused to honor his obligations, which included debts to the unfortunate Bardi and Peruzzi of over 200,000 gold <term>florins</term><note>The standard gold currency of Florence, valued at approximately £100,000 in the author's contemporary terms.</note>.

Troubles arrived in rapid succession, and one more blow was struck against the stability of Florentine finance when the King of France, continuing the traditions of his family, persecuted and expelled all the Florentine merchants and bankers from his realm!

These financial crashes and political defeats were followed by a calamitous plague—the "Black Death"—which killed one-third of the population of the city and its suburbs. The Revolt of the <term>Ciompi</term><note>A violent uprising of the lower-class textile workers in 1378 that challenged the power of the major Guilds.</note> in 1378 also led to the destruction by fire and looting of the palaces and offices of many leading bankers. In fact, the fourteenth century closed over a broken and bereaved Florence, and men wondered whether recovery was possible, and whether, like a phoenix, she would ever rise again.

## CHAPTER VII

# THE SILK GUILD

### *THE GUILD OF SILK, OR "ST. MARY’S GATE"* <note>original: "L'Arte della Seta, or 'Por Santa Maria'"</note>

I. **ORIGIN.**—Early history of the silk industry. Introduced into Tuscany around 1200. The father of the silk industry in Florence. The pavement of the Baptistery. Guild incorporated at the end of the twelfth century. A costly material. Early "Membership Register" <term>original: Libro di Matricola</term>. Alternative title. A splendid residence.
II. **CONSTITUTION.**—Customs lead to regulations. Codification. "The Old Statute" <term>original: Il Statuto Vecchio</term>. Congregation of Deputies <term>original: Congregazione de' Deputati</term>. Officers. "Ancient and Modern Memoirs" <term>original: Memorie antiche e moderne</term>. Guild registers. Membership enrollment. "Wholesale silk-merchants" <term>original: Setaiuoli grossi</term> and "retail silk-merchants" <term>original: Setaiuoli minuti</term>. Agents. Relations with other guilds. An entirely new code, 1557.
III. **DEVELOPMENT.**—Trade associations. Affiliated industries. "Silk-waste preparation" <note>original: "Rottura della Seta"</note>. Silk-workers from Lucca. Lombardy dyers. Importance of the mulberry tree. Sir Richard Dallington's testimony. Processes. Balducci Pegolotti's instructions. Silk velvet and the Velluti family. Lapo Mazzei and the "Treatise on the Craft of Silk." Directions for dyeing. Prices of raw silk. Weights. Sizes. Sale prices for silk pieces. Workers in gold and silver. "The Goldsmiths' Guild" <term>original: L'Arte degli Orefici</term>. Goldsmiths' apprentices. Rich clothing of Florentines. Beautiful lace. "Work of the Nuns" <term>original: Opera de' Monache</term>. Embroideries. Gold filigree. Veil-makers. Painted silk. Immense trade and wealth. Royal patronage. "Field of the Cloth of Gold." The Guicciardini family. Song of the Silk Girls.

The silk industry was brought from India to Europe during the reign of Justinian. It is said that in the year 550, two monks who had just returned from the East presented some silkworm eggs and cocoons to the Emperor at Constantinople. They had brought them concealed inside a bamboo cane and, at the same time, demonstrated the methods of hatching and unwinding used in China.<sup>1</sup> These worms were the ancestors of all those varieties that supplied Europe with raw silk for nearly a thousand years.<sup>2</sup>

The Emperor immediately recognized the importance of these natural curiosities and their potential in the world of commerce; he took the monks under his special protection. Turkey thus—

<header>THE GUILD OF SILK</header>

...became the mother of silkworm cultivation and silk manufacturing in Europe.

The first expansion of the silk industry’s reach was into Greece during the eighth century, occurring at almost the same time the Moors introduced it into Spain. Greek emigrants, colonizing the shores and islands of the Mediterranean, further increased the trade in silk.

The date that silkworms and cocoons were introduced into Italy, though somewhat late, produced significant results. In 1148, King Roger of Sicily led an expedition against Thebes, Athens, and Corinth; after conquering them and the surrounding territory, he took several Greek artisans skilled in manufacturing silk brocade and gold-work back to Palermo as spoils of war. These people settled wherever the King placed them and immediately began their various trades.

Within fifty years of the silk industry's establishment in Palermo, many silk workers had emigrated to the Italian mainland. A significant group traveled by sea to Leghorn and Pisa, and from there to Lucca, Milan, and Venice—in each of these cities, silk manufacturing was actively underway by the late twelfth century.

Exactly how silkworms and the production of silk goods first reached Florence remains uncertain. It is probable that the suitability of the Arno Valley for cultivating mulberry trees was known to the inhabitants of Lucca and shared by them with the new settlers.

However, the earliest silk worker in Florence whose name was recorded was a Neapolitan—named Napoleone after his birthplace—who is described in records from the year 1200 as a “merchant in silk cloth.” In any case, before the end of the twelfth century, not only the precious silkworm <note>original: "verme"</note> but also its essential food, the mulberry leaf <note>original: "erba di vermini"</note>, had been introduced into the Florentine countryside <note>original: "Contado"</note>.
