<meta>This page discusses the early development of the Florentine silk industry in the 13th century, comparing its profitability and risks to the established wool trade.</meta>

<page-num>206</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Naturally, for a long time, the manufacturing of silk fabrics was primarily dependent on the import of raw silk. Regardless of how this began, there are extensive records showing the flourishing state of this new industry in the first decade of the thirteenth century.¹

The brocades first woven by immigrant silk-workers from Lucca and Naples followed classical patterns learned in Greece and passed down through generations, though they were modified by the influences of the Sicilian environment.

Some of the earliest, if not the very first, specimens of silk brocade made in Florence are especially interesting because they reproduce the designs of the magnificent <term>tessellated</term> <note>a mosaic pattern made of small square stones or tiles</note> pavement of San Giovanni Battista, which was completed in 1204.

It must be frankly acknowledged that the silk trade did not thrive as successfully in its early days as the wool trade did. There were key differences between the two. First of all, the cultivation of silkworms involved much greater risks than the raising of sheep, and the value of raw silk in foreign markets was far higher than that of wool.

The manufacture of fabrics made from silk, gold, and silver represented a much higher material value and required more expensive processing than woolen cloth. The capital required—even for small-scale operations—was also greater. On the other hand, the sale price of silk goods did not offer as high a profit margin relative to production costs as was seen in woolen manufacturing.

The profit on spun silk was considerably lower than that on spun wool. For example: a pound of raw Spanish wool, which cost about two and a half *lire*, could be manufactured into fine cloth worth forty *lire*; meanwhile, a pound of raw silk, before dressing, cost at least thirty *lire*, and the simple silk fabric woven from it sold for no more than one hundred and twenty *lire*.² The addition of gold and silver thread or cord naturally increased production costs significantly, while the final prices did not increase by a proportionate amount.

¹ <note>original: "L'Osservatore Fiorentino"</note> "*The Florentine Observer*," vol. iv. p. 103.         ² *Pagnini*, vols. ii. and iii.

<page-num>207</page-num>
<header>THE GUILD OF SILK</header>

The silk industry therefore grew slowly but steadily, and by the beginning of the thirteenth century, a large number of looms were in operation. Consequently, manufacturers began to organize themselves into companies and corporations.<note>Ammirato, Lib. i. p. 67.</note>

The origin of the "Silk Guild" is contemporary with that of the "Wool Guild" and the "Calimala Guild." The Consuls of these three guilds signed the peace treaty with Siena in 1204. Again in 1224 and 1229, the signatures of the Consuls of the "Silk Guild" were added to the treaties with Volterra and Orvieto, along with those of the other consuls. By 1224, the guild was sufficiently established that a moral code was issued to govern its members.<note>Cantini, "Legislazioni," i. 176.</note>

A <term>codex</term> <note>an ancient manuscript in book form</note> from the year 1225, belonging to the "Por Santa Maria," is preserved among the city archives.<note>"Archivio dell' Arte della Seta," Letter G.</note> It is titled the *Register of Membership* <note>original: "Libro di Matriculo"</note>, and it is the earliest existing membership roll. It records that Claro, son of Guido Arlotti of Oltrarno; Simbaldo, son of Bartolo Caccialupi, son of Caccia, of the Porta Santa Maria; Cardinale, son of Marcoaldo of Santa Cecilia; Dono Spinelli; and Arrigo di Renucciai of the "Calimala District" <note>original: "Pressa di Calimala"</note> were registered in that year. The roll continues until 1233 and contains three hundred and sixty other names; it is mentioned again under the date 1308, when the statutes for all the guilds underwent a thorough revision.<note>Pagnini, vol. ii. 108.</note>

The original full title of the guild was: *The Guild and Association of Silk of the City of Florence* <note>original: "Ars et Universitas della Seta Civitatis Florentinæ"</note>. This title—along with the guild's coat of arms—still appears on the tower of its headquarters, which stands on the Via Capaccio. These heraldic symbols consist of two closed and barred doors—undoubtedly borrowed from the Porta Santa Maria, one of the gates in the first city wall of old Florence. <term>Amorini</term> <note>decorative figures of chubby infant boys or cupids</note> and wreaths were later decorative additions.

The alternative name of the guild—"The Guild of Saint Mary's Gate" <note>original: "L'Arte della Porta Santa Maria"</note>—which has come into use...

This building was known as the *Palazzo de' Lamberti*, and it was assigned to the use of the Silk Guild by the State. Within it also were the headquarters of the ***Parte Guelfa*** <note>the Guelph Party; the dominant pro-papal political faction in Florence</note>, which powerful political association extended special patronage to the "Guild of Silk." This Residence was, perhaps, the most splendid of all the Guild Palaces of Florence. Established in the old church of San Biagio—formerly *Santa Maria della Porta*—the artists employed by the Guild covered the exterior of the building with fine stucco, which they then lavishly decorated in fresco and what they then called ***sgraffiti*** <note>original: "sgraffiti"</note>—finely scratched designs. The Audience Hall contained superb oriental alabaster columns, gorgeous mosaics, beautifully tooled gilt bronze work, rich silken hangings and embroideries, and brilliantly stained-glass windows.

Goro Dati speaks of the splendid display the Guild Consuls made at the annual Feast of San Giovanni:—

> "All along the Via Porta Santa Maria, magnificent brocades of silk and gold were displayed over the shops and offices of the silk merchants, bearing the emblazoned arms of ten kingdoms, whose sovereigns and courtiers were clothed with the products of the Florentine silk-looms."

As was the case with the other Guilds, many bylaws and regulations had, from time to time, been adopted by silk manufacturers and merchants. These were of a somewhat contradictory character because, while the development of the silk industry had been comparatively slow, many new ideas and methods had been introduced into Florence. At the general revision of the Guild laws between 1301 and 1309—when the General Code for all of them was drafted—the technicalities of the silk trade were examined, and a council of experts was empanelled to adopt a full Constitution for the "**Por Santa Maria**."

Their work had progressed so far by 1328 that a significant step was taken toward codifying the Statutes of the Guild. The original number of four Consuls was restored, and was more—

Their powers were only slightly inferior to those held by the Chief Magistrates. One of the Councillors was a notary, and the two others were chosen from among leading manufacturers who had not previously been officially connected with the Guild.

In 1335, a complete Code of Statutes was issued. These were written in Latin on parchment in the form of a book, which was later referred to as “*The Old Statute*” <note>original: "Il Statuto Vecchio"</note>.

The procedures for electing officers were the same as those used for officials of the “*Calimala*” Guild <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth</note>, and their duties and functions were also similar. All high offices were required to be filled exclusively by individuals of Florentine parentage and birth who were generally recognized as leaders among silk manufacturers and merchants.

The Tribunal of the Guild was composed of the four Consuls, along with two *Guardians* <note>original: "Conservatori"</note>, who respectively supervised the civil and criminal affairs of the Guild. The business of this Court was twofold: 1. The direction of everything pertaining to the silk trade; and 2. The administration of justice to every person connected with the Guild.

Among the higher officials was the *Council of Deputies* <note>original: "Congregazione de’ Deputati"</note>, which handled all questions and matters relating to the practical development of the silk industry and the interests of the various groups of workers employed. The Deputies—whose number varied from time to time—were representatives of the subordinate trade associations connected with the Guild.

The two *Administrators* <note>original: "Provveditori"</note> were the managers of the Guild's goods and property. The *Chancellor* <note>original: "Cancelliere"</note>, or Keeper, was responsible for the registers, documents, and charters of the Guild. Two Inspectors were appointed annually by the Consular Tribunal to conduct regular and strict inspections of the factories, workshops, and homes of individuals associated with the Guild. They recorded the timing, weight, and value of all deliveries of raw silk and manufactured goods at various stages as they moved from masters to workers. Furthermore, they were instructed to monitor the moral conduct, technical skill, and hard work of every operative and to report these findings to the Consuls. <margin>Statutes of the Silk Guild, Section 34.</margin>

The Inspectors' annual report also included detailed returns on the description and condition of the machinery used, as well as notes on all new inventions and innovative methods. Under them served two Assistant Inspectors, whose attention was primarily focused on quality testing and ensuring the accuracy of weights and measures. They were instructed to carefully examine every bale of raw silk, every reel of silk thread, and every piece of silk fabric regarding its length, width, weight, color, and other qualities.

The Tribunal held many valuable archives. One of these contains an "**Ancient and Modern Memoir**" <note>original: "Memorie antiche e moderne"</note>, which fills several volumes. <margin>Pagnini, volume 2, page 132.</margin> These archives also include two registers of membership from the years 1247 and 1289 written on parchment; similar registers from 1368 and from 1397–1480 written on paper; voter lists from 1374–1418; a register of payments to the Palace of San Michele in Orto <note>The building known today as Orsanmichele, which served as a grain market and guild shrine</note> for the years 1345 and 1346; membership books for the years 1328–1520; a list of Consuls from 1435–1500; and many volumes and tracts dealing with wills, codicils, donations, and other matters belonging to members of the Guild. They also contain legal proceedings and endless details concerning the work and the workers of the Guild, along with inventories of goods and various other records. Most of these are preserved in the great libraries of Florence.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Florentine Silk Guild’s administrative and organizational structure, moving from the record-keeping of the Tribunal to the specific requirements for membership and the hierarchy within the guild classes.</meta>

<page-num>211</page-num>
<header>THE GUILD OF SILK</header>

The standards for admission followed the lines of the <term>Calimala</term> <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants of Foreign Cloth</note> and Wool Guilds, at least regarding personal qualifications and entrance fees. Nevertheless, the act of enrollment <note>original: "Matriculation"</note> did not necessarily grant access to the general benefits of the Guild. Candidates were usually enrolled as members of a specific branch within the Guild's operations and under its control. Consequently, a man was required to state the exact trade he intended to follow and to provide the Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the Guild</note> with a demonstration of his skill in that calling before he was granted full membership.¹

The members of the Guild were divided into two classes: the **Major Silk Merchants** <note>original: "Setaiuoli Grossi"</note> and the **Minor Silk Merchants** <note>original: "Setaiuoli Minuti"</note>. The first group was required to possess capital of at least twelve thousand gold florins. They held the privilege of manufacturing silk fabrics at their own discretion and selling them wholesale, both within Florence and abroad. All merchandise they sold required the official stamp of the Guild. They were forbidden from selling retail or in any way underselling the retail silk dealers. The **Major Silk Merchants** formed the aristocratic section of the Guild, and many of them were among the wealthiest and most influential citizens.

The **Minor Silk Merchants**, who were also called "master silk workers," were those who sold all items related to the silk industry in retail quantities; most of them were also practical silk spinners and weavers. They were also required to have a capital qualification, but the amount was not fixed, though it was considerably less than that required for the **Major Silk Merchants**. Indeed, many were permitted to enter the Guild with no financial qualification at all, as manufacturing skill and business aptitude were regarded as equivalent to capital. These **Minor Silk Merchants** were not permitted to spin or weave silk without a license from the Consuls, although they were allowed to own the machinery and tools of their craft without being taxed. Their shops and warehouses also required licenses, and their manufactured goods required the official stamp of the Guild.

<page-num>212</page-num>

The other Guilds largely employed the services of *Sensali* <note>brokers or agents</note>, but the *Por Santa Maria* <note>The Guild of Silk</note> was far too vigilant regarding the interests of masters and workpeople to tolerate the unnecessary involvement of middlemen. Consequently, in 1376, a decree <note>original: "Provvisione"</note> was passed, prohibiting anyone from acting as a broker or dealer who had not taken an oath before the Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the Guild</note>, or the Notary of the Guild, swearing that he would do nothing contrary to the spirit and the letter of the Statutes. Moreover, such an individual was bound by the payment of a security deposit and by the provision of two reliable guarantors <note>original: "sureties"</note>. The matter was further addressed in Section <note>original: "Rubric"</note> 18 of the Statutes, which expressly states that no person connected with the Guild was permitted to have dealings with *Sensali* whose names were posted as defaulters upon the notice board of the Court of Commerce <note>original: "Tribunal of the Mercanzia"</note>.

With respect to the system of account payments, the Silk Guild only allowed eight months' credit, except among its own members; but in 1429 the limit was extended to one year for amounts exceeding twenty-five pounds.<gloss>1</gloss>

Merchants of the *Calimala* <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants of Foreign Cloth</note> and *Por Santa Maria* were forbidden to exchange shops or offices, or to share them. No silk merchant was permitted to deal in foreign cloth within the boundaries of the State, nor overseas, unless by special permission from the Consuls of the *Calimala*.

The Statutes of the "Guild of Silk" were revised in 1386, and again in 1415, when many alterations and additions were made in accordance with the progress and prosperity of the Guild. In 1557, an entirely new Code was issued <note>original: "promulgated"</note> under the rule of the Medici.

# THE GUILD OF SILK

Most of these workers lived and worked near the small street called Silk Alley <note>original: "Vicolo della Seta"</note>. It ran alongside the Church of Santa Maria next to the Lamberti Palace, where, in later years, the wealthy Acciaiuoli family built a magnificent palace. In this crowded quarter of the city was the meeting place for everyone involved in the silk industry, and outsiders were often treated rudely if they dared to walk through its boundaries.

Column Street <note>original: "Via della Colonna"</note> featured a massive stone column that supported the roof over a large drying terrace, where silk fabrics were dyed and stretched. Surrounding this building were many warehouses belonging to the Guild and the homes where the workers lived.

The Retail Silk Merchants <note>original: "Setaiuoli Minuti"</note> did not have the power to set wage scales; instead, they were required to apply to the Wholesale Silk Merchants <note>original: "Setaiuoli Grossi"</note> for the terms approved by the Consuls. Once every year, in June, the Consuls issued a "Silk Price List" <note>original: "Rottura della Seta"</note>. This current price list governed both buyers and sellers alike, preventing inflated wages and speculative price quotes.¹

According to Section 84 <term>Rubric: A specific law or section within the Guild's statutes.</term> of the Statutes, no one was allowed to engage in any industry related to the manufacture of silk without a written and endorsed license from the Consuls of the Guild.

Among the protective regulations concerning personal liberty, Section 62 decreed that no silk worker—or worker in gold and silver—could be evicted from his house or his shop without a specific sentence from the Consuls in Council.

Under Section 21, pawnbrokers were forbidden from accepting raw silk, silk fabrics, or the tools and objects used and required for the trade.

No Guild worker, male or female, was permitted to leave the city or go beyond the surrounding countryside <note>original: "Contado"</note> unless they carried a written permit. This was only granted under strict conditions regarding the purpose and duration of the trip; Section 84 indicates the penalties incurred for disobedience.

Many sections deal with the treatment of silkworms, eggs, and—

...cocoons. For example, cocoons were not to be handled between the ringing of the evening bell and the morning prayers <note>original: "matins"</note>.

In 1315, a significant boost to the strength and efficiency of the Guild workers occurred with the arrival in Florence of many silk and gold craftsmen from Lucca, following its sack by Uguccione della Fagiola. This migration was caused by the harsh, restrictive laws imposed by the victorious Florentines. There was undoubtedly a reason for this policy—the shattering of the local industry in Lucca and the growth of the Florentine Guild! At first, the immigrants were treated with suspicion by their rivals and were not permitted to settle in the silk quarter of the city.

The Wholesale Silk Merchants <note>original: "Setaiuoli Grossi"</note>, however, knew exactly what they were doing. While Section 84 <term>Rubric: A specific law or section within the Guild's statutes.</term> of the Statutes contained a provision that prohibited Florentine workers from communicating or conducting business with the newcomers, the Consuls ordered them to be housed in the Prato district and provided them with homes and workshops.

This group of immigrants was not the only one that helped increase the population and develop the silk industry in Florence. Quite early in the thirteenth century, a number of dyers migrated from Lombardy and took up residence just beyond the Porta San Gallo in a building belonging to the monastery of the Augustinian monks.¹

Naturally, a rivalry developed between this group and the dyers already working under the Guilds of "Calimala" <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth.</note> and "Wool," as well as the workers employed by the manufacturers of the *Umiliati* <note>A religious order famous for their involvement in the wool industry.</note> in the Borgo d'Ognissanti. However, they received proposals from the "Guild of Silk" and joined that organization on the condition that they worked exclusively with silk and silken goods.

This Lombard company became very prosperous under their new circumstances and was known far and wide for its hospitality and charity. They established shelters for dyers,

Those who were over fifty years of age were provided for in an institution they named the *Gerolocomio*—perhaps meaning a "Home for the distressed and aged." In this home, pensioners lived with their families, who were dependent upon the pensioners' earnings.

Later, another Company of Dyers migrated to Florence. They also came from Lucca, undoubtedly tempted by the high wages paid to the laborers employed by the "Guild of Silk." Under their banner—which depicted Christ upon the Cross, clothed from head to foot in a long silken robe—they settled in houses belonging to Ser Girolamo Baldesi, near the Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova.

The policy of admitting skilled foreign workers was as excellent as it was far-sighted. Every trade is bound to profit immensely from the infusion of new blood, and this proved to be conspicuously true for the "Guild of Silk" and its workforce.

The importance of the mulberry tree in relation to the manufacture of silk cannot, of course, be overestimated. For nearly two centuries, however, the Florentine silk merchants made little to no effort to cultivate the tree in the area surrounding Florence. They were content to gather the silkworm eggs and cocoons through their agents in the East and elsewhere; these agents transported them along with huge shipments of mulberry leaves.

The success or failure of the silk trade depended entirely upon the supply of raw material. Consequently, as the industry became increasingly prosperous, it became necessary for manufacturers to find more sources of production. Therefore, at the end of the fourteenth century and early in the fifteenth, many *Provvisioni* <note>original: "Provvisioni" — Legislative acts or decrees.</note> were passed by the Consuls and Council of the "Guild of Silk" to increase the cultivation of the mulberry. These decrees were approved by the State Council and appear to be the first evidence of the tree's introduction into Tuscany. In 1440, it was enacted by law that on every *podere* <note>original: "podere" — A small farm or agricultural estate.</note>, at least five mulberry trees were to be planted annually until the number of trees in healthy growth reached fifty.

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

The trees thrived wonderfully, and manufacturers reflected upon their previous lack of foresight. Two classes of farmers were especially interested in breeding silkworm food, and they were enrolled under two designations by the Consuls of the Guild: *Padroni de’ Terreni* <note>original: "Padroni de’ Terreni" — landowners of land suitable for growing mulberry trees</note> and *Maestri di Mori e di Foglie* <note>original: "Maestri di Mori e di Foglie" — "Mulberry growers and purveyors of mulberry leaves"</note>. The Guild acquired the land of the former through direct purchase or lease and employed the latter to carry out the cultivation under rules and bylaws specifically established for that purpose.

The success of the new enterprise was immediately evident. The climate suited the tree admirably, and the yield matched that of other lands in richness and luxuriance, while the silkworms benefited immensely from their fresh and succulent food. Likely, the scientific methods of these wise cultivators contributed much to this favorable result. Moreover, other silk-manufacturing cities in Italy began to send their merchants and dealers to Florence to buy silkworms, cocoons, and mulberry leaves. The "Guild of Silk" met this trade with a protectionist spirit, and in 1442, a *Provvisione* <note>original: "Provvisione" — a legislative decree or provision</note> was passed forbidding the export of everything connected with the manufacture—specifically naming worms, cocoons, raw silk, and mulberry leaves.

Sir Richard Dallington, an intelligent English traveler in Italy in the middle of the sixteenth century, writes the following about the cultivation of silkworms and mulberry trees, and the general prospects of the silk industry <note>1</note>:

> "I will speak of the mulberry, because mentioning it naturally leads to a discussion of the silkworm, which is another of the greatest commodities of Tuscany. In the months of May and June, this worm labors... when [the eggs] are laid in the sun, they hatch; however, for want of heat, and to have them hatch early, people will hatch them in their bosoms. As soon as they hatch into worms, they are given mulberry leaves..."

...upon which they feed exclusively, and for this purpose, a great many trees are planted daily: the leaves are sold at four *quattrini* <note>original: "quattrini" — small Italian copper coins</note> per pound. . . . For the rest of the year, they are only kept in warm and enclosed places where they may be endangered by neither cold nor thunder, for either destroys them. When the worm has spun itself into a cocoon <note>original: "bottome"</note>, they put it into warm water to find the end of the silk thread; but if they wish to preserve the worm for breeding <note>original: "seed"</note>, then they find the end without putting the cocoon into water (for this kills the worm). . . . And whereas previously the silk workers of Florence, in addition to their own supply, were usually accustomed to buy as much silk from Naples, Lombardy, and Greece as yearly amounted to three hundred thousand ducats <note>original: "duckets"</note>, it is now thought that they shall soon have enough of their own. . . . It is estimated that every year Florentine <term>rashes</term> <note>original: "Rashes" — a smooth, twilled fabric, usually made of silk or wool</note> are made to the value of two million ducats, and silks and cloths of gold and silver to the value of three million. . . .

In spite of the increase of mulberry plantations and silkworms in Tuscany, it was necessary for the Florentine manufacturers to import both leaves and worms extensively from abroad, and especially from the Rhone Valley.

At various times, especially during epidemics, much suspicion was directed toward the possibility of the introduction of fever and other ailments by means of the raw silk and cocoons imported from the East. It was also commonly said, in later days, that the cultivation of the mulberry was harmful: — "for in most places where it has been planted, plague and sickness have broken out!"

Perhaps of all the processes, the most important were those which dealt with the earliest stages of the manufacture — the treatment of the cocoon. No cocoons containing dead worms, or double cocoons, or any which had suffered injury or discoloration in transit, were allowed to pass the tables of the *Conduttori* <note>original: "Conduttori" — overseers or inspectors who managed the initial reception of raw materials</note>, who were the first to deal with cocoons in their rough state.

Steaming in hot water — by the *Calderai* <note>original: "Calderai" — boiler-men or workers who managed the heating of the silk kettles</note> — was the next step.

The weft-thread was composed of two or three strands of raw silk that were not "thrown" <term>The process of twisting silk filaments into a thread strong enough for weaving</term>, and this gave the material its silky appearance and feel.

No doubt the introduction of raw silk to Florence was due, in the first instance, to the agents of the merchants and bankers. As they traversed lands and seas, they never failed to pick up novelties of all kinds, and especially such objects as appeared likely to be profitable commercial assets. Thus, samples of unwound cocoons and thrown silk found their way into consignments of foreign produce.

The finest quality of raw silk was imported from Spain, which, in the fourteenth century, was valued at from two *lire* and ten *soldi* to eleven *soldi* per pound. Out of nineteen or twenty other varieties, that of Catanzaro was the least highly esteemed.

Balducci Pegolotti, in his *Manual of the Florentine Merchant or Treatises* <note>original: "Manuale del Mercante Fiorentino o Divisamenti"</note>, gives instructions for preserving silk during transit. He speaks of "raw silk which comes in bales and is of many kinds and qualities; but of whatever kind it is, it must be smooth to the touch, and according to the quality, the thread must be fine, round, and free from fluff, dross, and knots. . . ."

> “It is also necessary to ensure that it is not rubbed. This means that on the road, when it is brought by beasts of burden or in wagons, the bales must not come into contact with hedges, the wagon, or the ground, so that the canvas or outer covering is not torn and the silk exposed. . . .”

> “To preserve silk well, it must be packed tighter than any other merchandise and kept in a place neither too damp nor too dry, covered with good matting. If it is kept this way, it will never be spoiled.”

One other element contributed to the fame of Florence as a silk market. Many couriers and agents brought home with them natives of the countries through which they traveled. These people brought with them, into the service of their new masters, secrets and methods known only in the East; by the terms of their purchase, they were held in a state of semi-slavery and gave their time and abilities to the pursuit of their craft for the benefit of their masters.

Thus, in a relatively short time, beauty of design, richness of coloring, and fineness of workmanship raised the value of Florentine silk immeasurably. Just as in the case of foreign cloth reprocessed by Florentine workers, the output of the silk looms of Florence commanded much higher prices in the European markets than did the similar products of any other city or country.<sup>1</sup> Her craftsmen excelled those of Lucca, Milan, Naples, Pisa, Genoa, Bologna, and Ferrara, as well as those of Bergamo, Bassano, Vicenza, Verona, Padua, and other centers of the silk industry in Lombardy.<sup>2</sup>

The two most important branches of silk manufacturing—properly speaking—were plain silk and silk-velvet or plush. The invention of velvet was due to the enterprise of the Velluti family—hence the name <note>The Italian word for velvet is *velluto*</note>—who were already doing a thriving business in the thirteenth century. Inconvenienced by a lack of space in their original workshops off the *Vicolo della Seta* <note>Silk Alley</note>, they moved, along with other families and workers engaged in the same kind of silk manufacturing; and, somewhere around 1285, they crossed the river and established themselves in more spacious quarters in Oltrarno <note>The district "beyond the Arno" river</note>. The Velluti family built large warehouses and factories in a new street, to which they gave the name *Via de' Velluti*. This street soon became an important thoroughfare, and, because many other rising families built fine—

A Chronicle exists—the original manuscript of which is owned by the current Duke of San Clemente, Simone Velluti Zate—that deals with the history of his family and its success in trade; it was started in 1300 by Donato di Lamberto dei Velluti. Many pages are missing from the first part, and there is the following suggestive note by Paolo Velluti, who continued the Chronicle: "Whatever has been erased on these pages, I have done so to wipe out the memory of the feuds and vendettas of the men of our house." <note>Donato Velluti, *Chronicle*, 1300–1370.</note>

A light type of silk tissue was frequently made called *Drappi delle Ermisini*—sarcenet—which allowed for the mixing of inferior and diluted materials, a sort of "shoddy silk." This production was discouraged and, under certain conditions, forbidden, as it damaged the reputation of Florentine silk manufacturers. Silk tissue, which was sold everywhere by weight, was woven in pieces measuring normally twenty *ulne*—lengths equal to a forearm. <note>Cantini, volume 7, page 176. An *ulna* or *braccio* was a standard unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches.</note>

Lapo Mazzei, the notary, makes several moralizing remarks in his "Letters" regarding the ethics and goals of Florentine business methods. He quite optimistically claims that they had more noble things in mind than mere financial gain, and he cites a "Treatise on the Silk Guild" (<note>original: "Arte della Seta"</note>), written by an anonymous member of the Guild. The manuscript is kept in the Laurentian Library in Florence. The author provides not only excellent rules and recommendations for running the industry successfully but also the "better way" of conducting worldly business—by making arrangements with heaven!

The methods for dyeing crimson and black, for instance, are as follows:

***Crimson***:—"To dye crimson, the silk must be left for a day—or ideally a day and a night—in an alum solution. In the morning, wash out the alum in a trough of clear water and wrap the material in clean linen cloths. Have a cauldron of hot water ready with a moderate amount of lye in it. Add half of the crimson dye, which has been well ground and sifted, and bring the mixture to a boil. It is very important not to use too much lye. Inexperienced dyers are often too generous with it, fearing that the solution in the cauldron is not thick enough. This, however, will result in a yellowish color, making the process useless."

"Dip the alumed silk carefully into the cauldron, then take it out and place it back in the alum bath for an hour or two. Remove it once more and dip it into the cauldron again. Finally, take it out, wash it thoroughly, and rinse it several times. <meta>This page continues the technical instructions for dyeing silk from a historical manual of the Florentine silk industry, specifically focusing on the black dyeing process and the economic rates for various types of raw silk and labor.</meta>

<page-num>226</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Black dye weakens the fabric, so instead of boiling the silk in it, pour the boiling solution over the material. Take it out and set it to cool as many times as necessary, until the sample indicates that the process is finished. When this has been done three times, place the material in the cauldron so that it is completely covered, and let it soak all night—then take it out and wash it. Prepare a pan with washing-soap dissolved in it, put the material in, and soap it well. This soaping process makes it lustrous, bright, and soft; otherwise, it would remain dark and harsh, and would be prone to splitting.

Many kinds of silk require great care when dyeing them black, such as the silk of Bruges and others with weak fibers. If these are boiled in black dye, they become so fragile that they are useless. This is not the case with Spanish silk and other sturdier qualities.

The second table deals with the “Winding of Silk.” All masters who employ silk-winders are required to pay the following prices per pound: For all double skeins, five piccioli per pound; for raw silk, six piccioli; for the <term>woof</term> <note>The crosswise threads in a woven fabric.</note> used in weaving, seven piccioli; for single white skeins, eight piccioli; for white sewing silk, six piccioli; for the woof for <term>Taffeta</term> <note>A crisp, smooth, plain-woven silk fabric.</note>, nine piccioli; for raw knotty silk, seven piccioli; for fine <term>Raso</term> (<note>original: "Raso"</note>)—lustrous silk or satin—ten piccioli. When these services were recorded on credit and paid for after the work was completed, these prices were increased by fifty percent.

Other qualities and descriptions of silk fabrics are also quoted in the "Manual," <note>Likely referring to a merchant's handbook or trade manual of the period.</note> but the preceding examples will suffice to show the values that generally prevailed in the sixteenth century.

During the fourteenth century, the full title of the Guild was: <note>original: "L’ Arte della Seta e di Drappi d’Oro, e degli Orafi"</note>—"The Guild of Silk and Cloth of Gold Manufacturers and Goldsmiths."

The addition of "Goldsmiths" to the title of the Guild points to the importance of that group of artists and craftsmen. Working in precious metals established a new profession for artistically inclined Florentines—a profession that ranked as an equal to, if it did not actually surpass, the Company of Painters (attached to the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries") and the Society of Sculptors and Architects (affiliated with the lesser "Guild of Masters in Stone and Wood").

Gold and silver work became so popular that a special Guild came into existence in the early fourteenth century, which bore the title <note>original: "L’Arte degli Orefici"</note>—"Guild of Workers in Gold and Silver." Every boy who displayed artistic talent was apprenticed to a goldsmith, and thus almost every

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the incorporation of the Goldsmiths into the Silk Guild (Por Santa Maria) and details the regulations governing the production and sale of gold and silver goods in Florence.</meta>

<page-num>229</page-num>
<header>THE GUILD OF SILK</header>

Many of the famous painters, sculptors, potters, and decorative workers of all kinds were enrolled members of “The Guild of Goldsmiths.” In the middle of the century, there were actually as many as forty-four goldsmiths’ shops upon the Ponte Vecchio—a position assigned to them by the Council of State—the united rentals of which amounted annually to more than eight hundred gold florins.^1

In 1322, three examiners were appointed by the “*Por Santa Maria*” <note>The gate and district that served as the headquarters for the Silk Guild.</note> to look into the statutes and regulations of the subordinate “Guild of Goldsmiths.” The result of their inquiries led to the admission of the master craftsmen to full membership in the Greater Guild on the same terms as the existing members. All disputes between masters and apprentices were to be decided by the Consuls of the Silk Guild.^2

Goldsmiths were authorized to work with all metals, but every article made had to be submitted for approval to appointed inspectors, and each item passed required the stamp of the maker’s name and his trademark. For gold work, the metal employed had to be of equal value to that used for the gold florin <term>florin</term> <note>The standard gold coin of Florence, known for its high purity and consistency.</note>; however, gold worked into wreaths and personal ornaments required the addition of sulfur. No goldsmith was allowed to practice his craft outside his own dwelling-house or workshop.

The Consuls of the Silk Guild had the right to visit and inspect workers, finished work, and materials in preparation whenever they chose to do so.

Severe measures were taken from time to time to prevent the use of imitation or low-quality gold and silver thread. For church vestments especially, care was taken to ensure that the gold and silver were of the best quality, coming from Cyprus, Olivio, and Cologne <note>original: "Colonia"</note>. Ecclesiastics and the Superiors General of the monasteries were forbidden from using anything but the best metal for the decoration of altars, sacred images, etc.; they were also forbidden from selling such objects to second-hand dealers and pawnshops.

In the early fifteenth century, the weaving of what was called "spun cloth of gold" was introduced by members of the Guild who had traveled to the East and learned how to manufacture this magnificent fabric.¹

According to Gino Capponi, the introduction of gold and silver-tissue spinning and weaving occurred in 1422. He also claims that the best gold thread came from Sicily and Cyprus.²

Alongside its production by Florentine silk looms, there was a significant enrichment of the clothing of private citizens and the state robes of public officials.

As early as the year 1296, two rich pieces of cloth of gold were manufactured in honor of Cardinal Pietro di Piperno and were valued at thirty-nine gold florins. The robe of Filippa di Giotti Peruzzi—worn on her marriage to Carlo degli Adimari—was made of fine silk velvet embroidered in gold and cost two hundred and sixty-nine gold florins. Her traveling dress cost twenty gold florins more and included a rich silk <term>gonnella</term> (a petticoat or skirt) and a <term>guarnacca</term> (a full, embroidered morning gown).

Despite the great prosperity of this trade, the "Guild of Workers in Gold and Silver" had only a very brief existence. During the revision of the Silk Guild’s statutes in 1335, it was suppressed, and its members were transferred with full and equal rights and privileges into the larger corporation.³

"The Guild of Goldsmiths"—<note>original: "Arte degli Orafi"</note>—as distinct from the "Guild of Workers in Gold and Silver"—<note>original: "Arte degli Orefici"</note>—continued its operations and became one of the most important and wealthy corporations in Florence during the sixteenth century.

Among the famous goldsmiths were Andrea Arditi, Bernardo Cenni, Lorenzo Ghiberti, Tommaso degli Ghirlandajo, L. Nero, Antonio di Sandro, Antonio Salvi, Paolo Uccello, Benvenuto Cellini, and Filippo Brunelleschi. The latter was enrolled in the

The history of the "Silk Guild" <note>original: "Santa Maria"</note> is distinct from these works, which form a subject separate from the industry of silk and precious-metal weaving.

There is no doubt that in Florence, the goldsmith's art stood very high during the times with which we are dealing. The goldsmiths were artists; therefore, most of the workers in chiseled gold and silver, and the engravers of gold and precious stones, attained a high reputation. It may be truly said that the work of the Florentine goldsmiths far surpassed, in exquisite detail and originality of design, that of any other city.

...the introduction of a new and beautiful art: lace-making. This art found many devotees particularly in the convents, where the nuns taught their lay sisters the elegant techniques of using bobbins and stilettos <term>stiletto: a small, sharp-pointed tool used for piercing eyelets in embroidery or lace</term>. Savonarola rebuked the members of religious orders for "devoting their time to the pointless creation of gold laces with which to adorn people and houses." This exquisite work—examples of which can be found in every important collection of vestments—is still called "nun’s work" <note>original: "opera de’ monache"</note>.

Henry VIII of England and his queens were very fond of Florentine lace. He granted two Florentine merchants the privilege of importing for three years "all kinds of fringes and trimmings <term>parsements: decorative braids or trimmings, often made of gold or silver thread</term>, worked in gold and silver and other materials."

The embroiderers and embroideries of Florence were more famous than any others. Philip, Duke of Burgundy, was a great patron and collector of cloth-of-gold fabric sewn with pearls, corals, and other valuable materials. Antonio Pollaiuolo and many other painters and goldsmiths designed small cartoons <term>cartoons: full-scale preparatory drawings intended to be copied into a different medium, such as tapestry or embroidery</term> to be worked into silk fabrics and ornaments. One artist, Paolo—a Venetian settled in Florence—spent twenty-six years embroidering altar hangings for the Baptistery. These depicted the life of Saint John the Baptist and looked exactly like paintings done with a brush.

Women especially excelled in this artistic craft, and their energies were directed toward making ecclesiastical vestments in which the richest fabrics were covered with gold filigree work and gems. Pope Paul III gave many commissions to Florentine embroiderers.

Another very beautiful art was the painting and decorating with gems of fine muslins and laces. The Florentine veil-makers <note>original: "Velettai"</note> were celebrated not only for their taste but also for their skill in weaving mixtures of silk, wool, and cotton with the finest strands of metal.

Ideas were undoubtedly gathered and patterns drawn from Eastern fabrics imported from the Orient. For a long period, these influences were apparent in the work produced, but in the fifteenth century—if not earlier—a marked independence

A departure from restraint and convention is noticeable in the output of the Florentine workshops and studios.

Painting on silk and satin was greatly admired in old Florence. This form of decorative art developed in two directions: first, the blending of colors, purely in the style of a master painter; and, second, mosaic painting, in which the colors were not mixed together but laid side by side in patches. This added much to the richness of the effect because strips and borders of the material were left showing. In all the sacristies <term>sacristy: a room in a church where vestments and sacred vessels are kept</term> of Florence, and many more throughout Europe, exquisite examples of this method are preserved. No doubt the development of this art was due to the fashion of painting the gonfalons <term>gonfalon: a heraldic flag or banner, often suspended from a crossbar</term> of the Guilds and Companies, and the shields and bucklers of knights. The baldachinos <term>baldachino: a ceremonial canopy over an altar or throne</term> of churches and the frontals <term>frontal: a decorative cloth covering the front of an altar</term> of altars were generally treated in this manner with adornments of gold and silver lace.

Manuscripts written in 1487 by Balducci Pegolotti and by Giovanni da Uzzano, which describe the *Catasto* <term>Catasto: the Florentine system of land registration and tax assessment established in 1427</term> of 1427, preserve many very interesting details concerning the silk trade. Several detailed instructions are given concerning the methods of manufacture, and lists are added regarding the quality, weight, and value of different sorts of raw silk. <note>Manuscript No. 17, 1427, Laurentian Library.</note>

The "*Por Santa Maria*" <note>The Guild of the "Gate of Saint Mary," the primary guild overseeing the silk trade.</note> contributed greatly to the wealth and magnificence of Florence during the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries. "In 1472," says Benedetto Dei in his *Chronicle* <note>original: "Cronica," pp. 22-44.</note>, "the number of workshops belonging to the Guild was eighty-four, where the industry of weaving cloth of gold, silver brocade, and silk tissue of every color and texture was carried on." More than sixteen thousand operatives and master workmen were employed in the manufacture of silk and its related industries within the city and the *contado* <term>contado: the rural territory or countryside surrounding an Italian city-state</term>.

Silk fabrics were dispatched to Lyons, Geneva, Antwerp, Naples, Rome, Sicily, Provence, Romania, Spain, the Levant <term>Levant: the region along the eastern shores of the Mediterranean</term>, Morocco, Barbary <term>Barbary: the coastal regions of North Africa</term>, and elsewhere. Surprisingly, no shipments of such goods were made to England and Germany for general

Royal patronage, however, was not lacking, for Henry VII of England—always a supporter of talented and scholarly foreigners—appointed Leonardo Frescobaldo and Antonio Cavallari in 1516 as suppliers of gold and silver cloth to the Court, each with a salary of £20. A letter from Henry VII still exists, addressed to the *Signoria* <term>Signoria: the supreme executive council and governing body of the Republic of Florence</term>,¹ recommending Antonio Corsi. Corsi was a Florentine agent who enjoyed high favor with the King and was being sent to Florence "to purchase enough gold cloth and silks to load three mules."

<margin>² British Museum Manuscripts, 2481.</margin>
The household account book of Henry VIII contains records of payments to several Florentine banker-merchants—including the Frescobaldi, Bardi, Corsi, and Cavalcanti families—for pieces of cloth of gold.¹ These were undoubtedly required to furnish the magnificent uniforms and decorations for the famous "Field of the Cloth of Gold" <note>A grand diplomatic summit held in 1520 between Henry VIII and Francis I of France, named for the sheer abundance of gold-woven fabrics used in the tents and clothing.</note>, as well as for the personal use of the King and the Court in England.

Ser Antonio Guidotti—the negotiator of loans for the King who was knighted for his successful financial strategies—was a major promoter of the silk industry. In a letter to Thomas Cromwell written in 1536, he offered to bring a group of silk weavers from Messina to England. He was a Florentine himself and employed many craftsmen from his native city.

During the fifteenth century, Duke Filippo Maria Visconti of Milan was also a patron of the Florentine silk industry. He invited silk workers to settle in Milan to instruct the local citizens in the details of manufacturing. Despite prohibitions against workers leaving Florence, some accepted the Duke's generous terms: "a liberal monthly salary, full political rights, and ten years of tax exemptions, both for themselves and for any agents who might work with them."

The founders of the famous French factories for silk and velvet at Lyons, Montpellier, Avignon, and other centers were undoubtedly Florentines. Traditions and traces of their work...

A notable family, the Guicciardini, held a prominent place in the Silk Guild. The historian, statesman, and courtier Francesco Guicciardini—who was active in the middle of the sixteenth century and whose literary works are frequently quoted in this volume—owned a share in a silk factory along with Jacopo and Lorenzo di Bernardo Segni and their company. His *Political and Civil Memories of Florence* <note>original: "Ricordi Politici e Civili di Firenze"</note> was written during the siege of Florence by the Emperor and the Pope in 1529–30.

Sir Richard Dallington, in his *Survey of the Grand Duke’s Estate*, makes lengthy references to the silk industry and to the cultivation of silkworms and mulberry trees. The late date of this record—1596—suggests that this same Grand Duke and his two immediate predecessors, through their uncalled-for and unwise interference in the silk industry, as well as in the other trades of Florence, practically caused the ruin of the commercial life of the splendid old city and its wealthy merchants.

Signs of decline in the trade appeared in the middle of the sixteenth century. Foreign competition, a more general spread of the industry, and the improvement of transportation may be cited as reasons; however, the primary contributing factors were undoubtedly the amazing prosperity of the city and the self-indulgence of its citizens.

In the Middle Ages, the science of medicine was in a deplorable state, and knowledge of chemistry was quite elementary. Surgery was hardly practiced at all; because it was considered impious to dissect a dead human body, anatomy was practically unknown.¹

Herbalists and dealers in herbal remedies <term>simples</term> were held in higher esteem than medicine-makers, apothecaries, and distillers. As a science, the practice of medicine did not extend beyond the use of horoscopes,

...the examination of urine and a few carefully guarded secrets, of which the Jews were the primary keepers.¹

The use of the knife [in surgery] had practically died out. Cauterization <term>cautery</term> and the setting of bones represented the whole of experimental surgery. The extraction of teeth, bloodletting <term>phlebotomy</term>, and all such minor operations were complacently left to the skill of the ever-present barber, or doubtfully committed to the questionable care of the casual quack <term>empiric</term>.

The influence of the occult sciences upon human destiny and human suffering always excited the imagination of the curious. The alchemist’s robe, the astrologer’s wand, and the doctor’s spectacles signaled the possession of mystic powers, which were admired by the gullible. Wealth seemed to be linked to fame in the exploitation of medicine and its sister sciences, and that was quite a sufficient recommendation in the eyes of shrewd businessmen.

The lamp of science had undoubtedly been kept burning in the monasteries, but its glow did not illuminate the darkness of the outside world. Consequently, when the founding of universities became a hallmark of the era, much that was known only in secret chambers and cells began to be revealed to the growing intelligence of mankind in general.

Bologna, Ravenna, Padua, Salerno, and other centers of enlightenment and leadership opened their doors to an expectant world. Among the earliest faculties sought there were the sciences of practical medicine and experimental surgery. Many a young Florentine went there, carrying his parents’ hopes. In due time, these pioneer adventurers returned home again to preach and practice what they had heard and seen in school and hospital.

The earliest mention of physicians in the Florentine Archives² is dated 934, when it is noted that one “Amalpertius,” a deacon of the Church, was also a doctor <note>original: "medico"</note> and was addressed as “Lord Master” <note>original: "Domino Messere"</note>. In 1070, “Britulus” is named, “who was a...

<meta>This page continues the history of medical professionals in Florence, shifting from the general rise of university faculties to the specific records of early Florentine doctors and the formal organization of their Guild and College.</meta>

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

"...well-known doctor." Piero, the Abbot of the Badia, mentions "Giovanni, our most esteemed doctor and friend," in 1090.

The names of many doctors and physicians were recorded in the following years. They were organized into a Guild in the early twelfth century. This was likely due to the same reasons that led to the formation of the Merchant Guilds: the benefits of collective action and mutual support.

The fact that the Consuls' signatures were included alongside those of other Guilds in the anti-imperial League of Tuscan cities proves that a Guild of Doctors was already an active body in 1197. Florence led this league, and they signed as representatives of "The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries." This fact also shows the union of two classes of men in one community. Although they were quite different in social status, they each depended on the other for their livelihood and professional opportunities.

Around the year 1218, we find the first evidence of a College of Doctors and Apothecaries. It was established much like the ancient Roman and Imperial *collegia* <term>guilds or corporations</term>. Its members included not only doctors, apothecaries, physicians, and chemists, but also surgeons and midwives. However, these last two groups were considered quite insignificant and held subordinate positions.

Taddeo d'Alderotti was the founder of the Florentine School of Medicine. He was born in Florence in 1223. His father—a grain merchant—sent him to study at Bologna. He first focused his attention on Greek literature and philosophy, eventually becoming a professor in that faculty. He gained great fame for his translations of Aristotle's *Ethics* and his commentaries on Galen and others. Dante mentions "Taddeo’s learning." <gloss>1. *Paradise* <note>original: "Paradiso"</note>, Canto xii.</gloss> He was deeply attracted to Hippocrates and the history of human disease. As recorded in Dante's *The Banquet* <note>original: "Convito"</note>, he earned the nickname "The Hippocratean" <note>original: "l' Ippocratisto"</note>.

The date of Taddeo's establishment as a professor of medicine...

Taddeo's arrival in Florence is uncertain; but two circumstances seem to point to the year 1278. Records exist that provide the name of one of his earliest Florentine pupils—Dino del Garbo, who later became a preacher in the Cistercian Order—and also state that in that year, Taddeo combined the teaching of medicine with the trade of a corn-merchant <term>corn-chandler</term> in the public granary at Or San Michele.

Dino del Garbo’s son, Tommaso, was also a pupil of Taddeo, and Filippo Villani discusses both at length in his *Life of Taddeo d’Alderotti* <note>original: "Vita di Taddeo d’Alderotti"</note>.

Taddeo’s fame was great. Among his patients was Pope Honorius IV, who suffered from gout so severely that it completely prevented him from saying Mass. After his health was restored, His Holiness gratefully bestowed six thousand ducats (roughly £3,000) upon the great doctor. Taddeo’s reputation, and his fees as well, rose immensely. From wealthy merchants, he demanded as much as fifty to one hundred gold florins for a brief consultation! <note>original reference: L’ Osservatore Fiorentino (The Florentine Observer), vol. i. 134, p. 301.</note>

Other famous professors of the medical and surgical faculties in Florence were Giambattista Torregiano and Michele Vieri, both of whom were pupils of Taddeo d’Alderotti.

No records appear to state the exact relationship between the Guild and the College or School; however, it is certain that the latter was subordinate to the former.

---

A Statute of the Guild lays down that: "no doctor may be admitted as a member of the College, nor be allowed to practice, unless he has first been publicly examined by the Consuls of the Guild." <note>original reference: Statuti, Lib. iv. Act ii. Stat. 53 (Statutes, Book 4, Act 2, Statute 53).</note> This was likely a mere formality, since the candidate had already obtained his degree and qualification at his university. The requirement probably referred to the candidate's social standing and, likely, to the high opinion the applicant held of himself!

Another Statute names the apothecary members of the Guild but imposes no examination, unlike the requirement for the doctors.

The activities and importance of the Guild grew proportionately. In 1282, at the second election of Priors <note>Priors (Priori) were the chief magistrates or executive officials of the Florentine Republic</note>, one of the men chosen was a member of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries."

A few years later, in 1296, the Matriculation Roll <term>an official register or list of members</term> of the Guild was graced with its most celebrated name in the history of Florence—the immortal writer of *The Divine Comedy* <note>original: "Divina Commedia"</note>, Dante Alighieri.

A very distinguished member of the Guild, who enrolled <term>matriculated</term> in 1333, was Matteo Palmieri. He was also a writer of poetry; his "*Citta di Vita*" <note>City of Life</note> is very reminiscent of the work of Dante. He realized the highest ambition of all Florentines by being appointed ambassador; his mission was to the Court of the King of Naples. "The ambassador," says a quaint old historian—Giovanni Battista Gello, who was a tailor by trade but also a free student in the university—"behaved himself very wisely, and the king asked what kind of man he was in his own country, and it was told him that he was an apothecary. 'If the apothecaries,' said the king, 'are so wise and learned in Florence, who are their physicians?'"¹

A Code of Statutes was issued by authority in 1313. Its provisions corresponded in general terms with those of the "Calimala" <note>The Guild of Merchants, Cloth Finishers, and Foreign Trade</note> Statutes of 1301–1309, and additions were made in 1316, and again in 1349. Complete revisions of the statutes, regulations, bylaws, and of the whole constitution of the Guild were performed in 1415 and 1468, and further additions were made in 1558 and 1571.

In the revision <term>recension</term> of 1415, it was enacted that no one under the age of fifteen years should be apprenticed to a doctor of medicine, surgeon, barber, midwife, or anyone else who had care of the sick. All such persons were required to establish their reputation for honesty, morality, and mental and physical fitness before being enrolled <term>matriculated</term>.²

Doctors were permitted to enter into partnership with apothecaries on mutual terms: the former sending patients to the latter with their prescriptions, and the latter recommending patients to the former.³

Under all these laws the number of Consuls was always four. They had unlimited jurisdiction over all physicians and apothecaries, as well as over all surgeons, midwives, herbalists, distillers,

In Jacopo di Cessolis' moralization on the "Game of Chess"—published by Antonio Miscomini, and already referred to—the character of a Doctor-apothecary is represented by the Queen's Pawn as follows:<sup>1</sup> 

> “The pawn that is set before the Queen represents the Physician, Spicier, and Apothecary. He is formed in the figure of a man and is seated in a master’s chair; he holds a book in his right hand and an ampoule or a box of ointments in his left. At his belt <term>girdle</term> are his instruments of iron and silver for making incisions, examining wounds and injuries, and lancing abscesses <term>apostumes</term>; by these things, surgeons are recognized. By the book, physicians are understood, as well as all grammarians, logicians, and masters of law, geometry, arithmetic, music, and astronomy. By the ampoule are signified the makers of pigments, spice-sellers, and apothecaries, and those who make confections, candies <term>confytes</term>, and medicines made with precious spices. By the iron tools and instruments hanging from the belt, the surgeons and master craftsmen are signified.”

The Residence of the Consuls of the Guild was one of the finest in the city. It was formerly the Palazzo de' Lamberti, located at the corner of the Via di Sant' Andrea, and was massive and imposing in appearance. The Hall of Audience was especially handsome; it was adorned with fine marble sculptures and a beautifully painted ceiling. Each of the allied or subordinate Guilds, or divisions, contributed some characteristic decoration: painters, illustrators <term>miniaturists</term>, porcelain-makers, haberdashers and silk agents, perfumers, etc. The ceiling is now preserved among the treasures of the Museo di San Marco. On the facade of the Residence, the coat of arms <term>escutcheon</term> of the Guild was displayed—the Madonna and Child supported by two pots of growing Annunciation lilies. The same device was repeated in white upon a red field on the Guild's banner <term>gonfalon</term>.

During the first half of the thirteenth century, there were no more than sixty doctors, physicians, and surgeons out of a total population of nearly one hundred thousand. However, their importance—not to mention their arrogance—increased as their numbers remained small. 

<image-desc>A woodcut-style illustration depicting a medical scene in an architectural setting featuring two arches. On the left, three men in long academic robes and caps stand together. In the background, two small windows within the arches show tiny figures looking out. Below the image is a caption: "DOCTORS IN CONSULTATION.—1500".</image-desc>

->DOCTORS IN CONSULTATION.—1500<-

Their roles were much more theoretical than practical. For the most part, they were content to wear the clothing <term>habiliments</term> specific to their profession and pose as men of science, rather than actually practicing the medical field to which they belonged.

<summary>This page notes that despite their small numbers in 13th-century Florence, doctors held significant social influence and often prioritized professional appearance and theory over practical medical work.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the medical profession in Florence, focusing on the prestigious attire, social privileges, and the close, often commercial, relationship between doctors and apothecaries.</meta>

<page-num>244</page-num>

### THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Doctors who had graduated from a university never appeared in public except in full, long robes decorated with scarlet and <term>vair-skin</term> <note>a type of expensive fur made from the bluish-gray back of the northern squirrel</note>, in the style of knights; a fur hood hung from their shoulders, similar to those worn by Capuchin monks. A velvet cap or hat and gloves completed their professional costume. Generally, they were accompanied by a groom leading a horse, which they usually made a show of mounting in the <term>Mercato Vecchio</term> <note>the Old Market, the center of Florentine public life</note>.

Like doctors of law and men over seventy years of age, doctors of medicine were exempt from serving in the military companies of their <term>sestieri</term> <note>the six administrative districts of Florence</note>.

It was a common enough custom in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries for doctors of medicine to establish their professional residence and consulting room at an apothecary’s shop. A mutual agreement was reached whereby the doctor prescribed only drugs sold by his own apothecary. In later times, when the dignity of the profession had suffered somewhat at the hands of commercial interests, doctors set themselves up as independent retailers of drugs; however, such "double-dealing" does not appear to have been very profitable for either them or their patients.

The diagnosis of physical ailments, as well as the casting of psychological horoscopes, had little to do with the actual treatment of sickness. The doctor, seated upon his horse or settled into his easy chair with spectacles on his nose, pompously prescribed a remedy, writing it out in nearly illegible handwriting, which became a frequent source of errors in the administration of drugs.

Professional etiquette required, first of all, the feeling of the pulse and the examination of the tongue; these medical courtesies were performed as readily in the open market as in the consultation room. The next stage was the elaborate wrapping of an afflicted limb in linen cloths dipped in water and the entrusting of the patient to the "tender mercies" of the apothecary.

That irreverent talker Nello the barber—so amusingly described in *Romola* <note>a historical novel by George Eliot set in 15th-century Florence</note> mocking the doctors and apothecaries—asks: "What sort of inspiration do you expect to get from the..."

->DOCTORS AND APOTHECARIES<-

...scent of foul-smelling herbal decoctions?—to say nothing of the fact that you no sooner pass the threshold than you see a doctor of medicine, like a gigantic spider disguised in fur and scarlet, waiting for his prey, or even see him blocking up the doorway, seated on a scrawny horse inspecting saliva."¹

Petrarch had a jovial appreciation for the doctors of his day: "Whenever I see a doctor approaching, I already know everything he is going to say to me," he laughingly exclaimed. "Eat a pair of young chickens, drink plenty of warm water, and use the remedy that the storks teach us!"² <note>original: "remedium quod ciconiae docent." This is a reference to enemas; storks were popularly believed to use their long beaks to inject water into their own rectums to cleanse themselves.</note>

A very favorite process for any malady of the head—whether a simple headache or more serious ailments—was to shave off all the hair and then hold the bare scalp to the scorching heat of a blazing fire! An excellent <term>embrocation</term> <note>a liquid or lotion rubbed on the body to relieve pain or stiffness</note> for any part of the body was considered to be soap made of myrrh, boiled in water infused with crushed ivy flowers, and mixed with egg yolk.

For a stiff neck, or stiffness of the bones and limbs, a wash was used compounded of wine and tincture of asafetida, which was rubbed in with such force that the skin began to bleed, or the bone of the skull was laid bare!

The favorite poultice was made of honey and asafetida with betony powder and other ingredients, applied hot. Warm drinks—sweet and nauseous—were commonly consumed, and men in armor were plied with steaming potions to ward off the cold shock of the steel they wore.

Persons suffering from fever were advised to plunge into cold water! Profuse bleeding was stopped by <term>cautery</term> <note>the practice of burning the flesh to stop bleeding or prevent infection</note>—specifically by binding the source of the blood with a stout cord and setting it on fire with a candle!³

Obstructions in the ear were treated with hot poultices for thirty days; if relief was not obtained, sharp blows were administered to the unoffending ear! "This practice,"—as it was quaintly—

Water treatment, accompanied by the application of syrups and laxatives, was a favorite remedy for all stomach ailments and skin diseases. For the wealthier citizens, a course of baths at Siena was prescribed. This was quite ironic, for the average Florentine loved nothing more than to humiliate his old defeated enemies by parading with a lordly step up and down those crooked streets; consequently, such medical advice was followed with great enthusiasm!

For the poorer classes, who could not afford a Sienese vacation <note>original: "villegiatura"</note>, there was the bath in the gallery <note>original: "loggia"</note> of the Old Bridge <note>original: "Ponte Vecchio"</note>. This was fed by the water of the Arno River, the medicinal virtues of which were always loudly praised by the medical and pharmaceutical faculties. They claimed it was a specific cure for all the ailments of the poor, and it was said in old Florence, as it was of the deep ocean:—"The sea washes away all human ills." ³

The humble cabbage was highly praised—as were all the vegetable treasures of the garden and the field in their turn—as a cure-all for all the aches and pains of suffering humanity. It was eaten raw or cooked, and even the water in which it was prepared was considered a health-giving drink.⁴

The following is a satirical rhyme that an old chronicler attributes to many a despairing patient of the old Florentine doctors:—

> "There is neither herb nor root,
> Nor any remedy to boot,
> That can keep death away by even a foot!" ⁵

One of the most famous physician-surgeons of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries was Master Niccolo di Francesco Falucci, who was titled the "most learned doctor" <note>original: "Medicus doctissimus"</note>. He wrote many treatises—the most highly regarded being the "Practice of Niccolo of Florence" <note>original: "Pratica di Niccolo da Firenze"</note>, for such was his common name. Among medicines...

The death of Lorenzo de' Medici in 1492 was certainly hastened by his medical treatment. As if to emphasize the high human value of the patient's life, they lavishly prescribed a potion of crushed pearls and rubies!

# DOCTORS AND APOTHECARIES

No very celebrated Florentine surgeon made his mark before the sixteenth century. The greatest master was probably Antonio Benevieni, a member of a scholarly family.

The low regard in which practitioners were held in the fifteenth century, at least, is colorfully described by the author of *Romola*:

> "Is it the Florentine fashion," asks Master Tacco of Nello the barber, "to put the masters of the science of medicine on a level with men who perform carpentry on broken limbs, sew up wounds like tailors, and cut away growths as a butcher trims meat? To put a manual art such as any craftsman might learn—one which has been practiced by simple barbers like you—on a level with the noble science of Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna...!"¹

Villani, in his 1300 record of the population of Florence, states that there were sixty doctors and surgeons whose names were entered on the <term>Matriculation Roll</term> <note>the official membership register</note> of the Guild.

The fees paid to doctors and surgeons were not fixed by the College rules or the Guild statutes. They varied considerably and were perhaps proportional to the patients' wealth and the doctors' reputations.

The State paid its medical assistants a meager rate for professional work involving government officials and criminals. For example, in 1292, <term>Ser</term> <note>a title of respect, similar to "Master" or "Sir"</note> Guido di Jacopo and <term>Ser</term> Orlando di Giovanni were called in to treat the feet of five men injured in the <term>pillory</term> <note>a wooden framework with holes for the head and hands, used for public punishment</note>. Their payment was a miserable sum of fifty <term>soldi</term> <note>a medieval Italian silver coin</note> each! On the other hand, established practitioners received between two and five gold florins for a standard consultation. Both famous and less well-known physicians were also willing to accept payment in kind, such as merchandise, wine, and farm produce.

The high fees paid to Taddeo d'Alderotti were not unique; for instance, in 1336, Bonifacio Peruzzi hired the celebrated doctor <term>Messere</term> <note>an honorific title meaning "Sir" or "Master"</note> Alberto of Bologna to cure his sore throat and paid him sixty gold florins.²

->### THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

Despite the laws and limitations restricting the occupations of both doctors and apothecaries, many traveling charlatans made their way daily through the streets of Florence. They came mostly from Padua and the surrounding cities, intent on claiming some of the excessive wealth of the rich Republic. Mounted on sturdy ponies with large saddlebags, they rode into the markets as if they were ordinary merchants. Their stores of secret medicines were well-hidden to escape the watchful eyes of the gatekeepers. They stayed far away from the apothecary shops and slipped away whenever Florentine medical dignitaries approached. However, here and there, bribes of fat chickens and plump pigeons were handed over to those who, in return, harvested small coins from the gullible for worthless salves, pills, and powders.

George Eliot wrote of one such person: "Let any gentleman," says the *doctor* <note>original: "Medico"</note>, "smell this box, and he will find a genuine scent of medicines—not, indeed, of crushed gems, rare Eastern vegetables, or stones found inside birds . . . and here is a paste which always has a pleasant smell and is a certain cure for depression <note>original: "melancholia"</note>, having been prepared under the alignment of Jupiter and Venus, and I have seen it soothe spasms."¹ <gloss>George Eliot, *Romola*, chapter 16.</gloss> Nevertheless, under certain conditions regarding the practitioner and the remedy, quacks were recognized as members of the affiliated and subordinate <term>Arte de' Ciurmadore</term> <note>Association of Registered Empirical Practitioners of Medicine; literally, the "Guild of the Swindlers" or "Charlatans"</note>.

The <term>Mercato Vecchio</term> <note>Old Market</note> was the favorite meeting place for quack doctors. Their loud voices, promoting one remedy or another, added a daily note of discord to the terrible noise of that busy market; yet no one else gathered so many wide-eyed listeners and cash-paying customers.

A real Florentine doctor, by contrast, held his head high. He was granted the title of <term>Messere</term> <note>a title of respect, similar to "Master" or "Sir"</note>, and sometimes that of <term>Algebrista</term> <note>Algebraist</note>, because one of his privileges was the solution of difficult problems connected with ancient science—

<page-num>251</page-num>

->DOCTORS AND APOTHECARIES<-

The doctor was interested in astrology. He always considered himself a superior individual and never stooped to social intimacy with his lower-ranking fellow guild members—the apothecaries.

The reason for uniting a professional class and a commercial class—represented by the apothecaries—within a single corporation can be seen in how much they depended on one another. This was always the case in old Florence; the aristocratic temperament of her people was constantly at odds with their democratic tendencies.

While apothecaries were viewed by their more distinguished guild members much like poor relations or inferiors, their importance to the commercial and social economy of Florence was undeniable. They were not considered men of science; at least in early times, they were not required to pass any educational exams beyond being able to read the terrible handwriting of the *Messeri Medici*—"Gentlemen Doctors" <note>original: "Messeri Medici"</note>. They were seen as assistants to the medical faculty and as useful agents for selling various small goods.

In the early days of the Commune <note>The government of the city-state of Florence</note>, apothecaries simply bought and sold medicinal herbs that grew near Florence and were brought to market daily by country folk. Later, apothecaries were required to obtain a license before opening a shop or store, and every applicant promised "to keep his shop open daily, except on feast days, and to sell only genuine products."¹ Each was also required to deposit a sum of money with the Guild Treasurer—the amount varying by circumstance—as a guarantee that would be returned to their relatives upon their death.

The impressive commercial success of the *Calimala* <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Foreign Cloth Merchants</note> and Wool Guilds opened vast new fields for research and for acquiring precious pharmaceutical treasures. The "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries" became a powerful force in the Republic, and its members joined enthusiastically in the race for com-
