commercial supremacy. In all the traveling companies of the period, apothecaries were found who brought home their spoils in triumph. Fine cloth finished by skilled Florentine workers and other European goods were accepted in the East in exchange for drugs and spices.

The sale of medicines and their ingredients was strictly limited by the Guild's authority to the shops of duly qualified apothecaries. No citizen was permitted to sell or display any foreign drugs or spices unless they were also a member of the Guild.

The sale of drugs and spices was carefully regulated to protect the public from fraud and life-threatening dangers. Every year, the Guild's Consuls appointed a *Sindaco* <term>Sindaco: An inspector or auditor</term> to visit all apothecary shops and the storerooms of any doctors who kept medicines and other supplies for their patients.¹ They had the power to seize and destroy any goods that did not bear the Guild's official stamp or that violated the bylaws, even if they did bear the seal. At the same time, the names of those guilty of such offenses were posted at the Guild's offices. These individuals were forbidden from practicing their profession or trading their goods for a period determined by the Consuls.

One of the best-known apothecaries' shops was the *Farmacia del Moro*—"The Moor’s-Head Pharmacy." It stood at the corner of the Borgo di San Lorenzo and was founded early in the sixteenth century. Here, Antonio Francesco Grazziani—whose nickname was "*il Lasco*" <note>original: "il Lasco"</note>, meaning "the idle dog"—ran a chemist's business. Despite this, he was a poet and a novelist. His family moved from Staggia to Florence in the fourteenth century, and he was registered on the Apothecaries' enrollment lists. He is famous as the founder of the "*Accademia della Crusca*" <note>The academy founded to maintain the purity of the Italian language</note>, which standardized the polite speech of Tuscany.

<page-num>253</page-num>

<header>DOCTORS AND APOTHECARIES</header>

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, Cosimo de' Medici welcomed a large group of Greek scholars. One of the earliest signs of their influence was the translation into Italian of an ancient manuscript concerning the science of surgery. This was followed by excerpts from other manuscripts written by ancient naturalists.¹

Cosimo also employed these new teachers to prepare a new Florentine *Pharmacopoeia* <term>Pharmacopoeia: An official book containing a list of medicinal drugs with their effects and directions for use</term>, which included local formulas and others collected from various medical schools in Europe or extracted from ancient knowledge. To support his medical staff, he founded a laboratory of botanical science, where he energetically studied herbs.²

This was the first Florentine laboratory, or school of critical research, where apothecaries could learn to improve the simple and unscientific methods they had previously followed when compounding medicines.

Another famous laboratory, or pharmacy, was established under the sign of "The Lily" late in the fifteenth century.³ There, the Rosselli family—Romolo, Stefano, and Francesco—operated as apothecaries and also wrote several learned treatises on medical and surgical subjects. Through Cosimo Rosselli, the family also showed evidence of artistic talent. A Dominican father, Agostino del Riccio, who wrote a "Treatise on Agriculture," mentions the apothecary Stefano Rosselli with particular honor, stating: "The city of Florence owes a debt of gratitude to this noble man, because he has cured many citizens with the secret remedies he prepared in his shop."

In the cloister of the monastic church of Santa Maria Novella, a *Spezieria* <note>original: "Spezieria"</note> or drug store was opened for manufacturing medicines and producing medicinal oils, ointments, and perfumes, under the direction of a council of chartered apothecaries. The *Farmacia della Pecora* <note>original: "Farmacia della Pecora"; "The Sheep's Pharmacy"</note> in the *Mercato Nuovo* <note>original: "Mercato Nuovo"; "New Market"</note> was another important establishment for dispensing medicines under the control of "The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries."

The **Golden Pine** <note>original: "*Pinadoro*"</note> was a well-known apothecary's shop and was the training school for many a famous Florentine—Perino del Naga <note>likely a reference to Perino del Vaga, the famous painter and pupil of Raphael</note> among them. Each of the monasteries had its **pharmacy** <note>original: "*Spezieria*"</note>, or dispensary as we say, where medications, condiments, and many necessary comforts were distributed for free, or at a very low price, to sick and needy applicants. The members of the religious orders were highly skilled experts in the subtle arts of pharmacy and undoubtedly used their skills to advance the cause of religion.

Regarding the number of apothecaries <term>Apothecary: a person who prepared and sold medicines and drugs; a precursor to the modern pharmacist</term> whose names were enrolled on the registration records of the Guild, Giovanni Villani records that, in 1300, there were nearly one hundred. Benedetto Dei gives the number of registered apothecaries in 1479 as sixty-six—the decline being due, undoubtedly, to trade competition, which caused the smaller and less enterprising men to go out of business.

The **shops** <note>original: "*botteghe*"</note> of the apothecaries were among the most ornamental and attractive of the many shops in Old Florence. Their internal arrangement followed strictly traditional lines. At least two rooms were required: the one facing the street or market was the shop itself, while the room behind served for mixing and preparing the vast variety of items offered for sale and for housing apprentices and assistants.

Across the center of the shop ran a counter with drawers and cupboards. Upon it, along with **ointment pots** <note>original: "*letti*"</note>, **tasting cups** <note>original: "*tazzine*"</note>, and **vials** <note>original: "*fiole*"</note>, were displayed small and interesting articles such as perfumes, gloves, sachets, buckles, and knick-knacks of all kinds from overseas. Upon a firm pedestal stood a large mortar made of metal or earthenware, with strong external ribs like masonry buttresses to withstand the heavy pounding of ingredients. On a side table were sets of **childbirth gift sets** <note>original: "*Vasi di puerperali*"</note> and **dessert dishes** <note>original: "*canestralle*"</note>.

Behind these, along the walls, were shelves of wood holding in proper order earthenware **cylindrical drug jars** <note>original: "*albarelli*"</note> and **pitchers** <note>original: "*boccali*"</note>—dry drug jars...

All these items bore the owner’s initials, coat of arms, or name, along with the name of the drug or contents painted upon a ribbon-style decoration. Small flasks, bottles for medicines, and little boxes for pills were arranged in convenient stacks, all showing evidence of artistic taste. The walls of the shops were decorated with painted majolica tiles, carved and painted wood, and tapestry or leather hangings. Comfortable benches for customers were placed near the counter on clean, braided straw matting. Generally, small metal flags were hung outside the door, much like inn signs, bearing the owners' names and special notices, while *albarelli* <term>Albarelli: tall, cylindrical ceramic jars used to store medicinal herbs and ointments</term> further signaled their profession.

A branch of the Apothecaries’ business—and a significant one, given the large population of Florence and its *Contado* <term>Contado: the rural territory surrounding and controlled by a city-state</term>, and the frequent outbreaks of fire, flood, famine, and plague—was that of the undertaker. Funerals, at least for the wealthier citizens—whether nobles or merchants—were conducted by the Apothecaries. They provided every necessity: coffins, biers, pallbearers, funeral palls, torches for use in the street, candles for church services, decorative trappings, ornaments of all kinds, funeral meats, burial drinks, and all other accessories. Strangely, the most popular refreshments at funerals were the same as those still offered at rural burials in Great Britain: *confetti* <note>In this historical context, small sugar-coated sweets or sponge cakes</note> and *alchermes*—a spiced liquor flavored with cinnamon and cloves.

In every *bottega* <term>Bottega: a shop or workshop</term>, a price list or tariff of funeral expenses was displayed. These costs were categorized to suit every budget, and the relatives of the deceased were visited at their homes to finalize arrangements, much like today.

Apothecaries who served as undertakers did not have the best reputation for honesty or fair pricing. When one member of the profession hung a "Melon" as a shop sign, it was met with mocking laughter as a fitting symbol of the shameless tricks of the trade!

Public records and the *Prioristi* <term>Prioristi: registers recording the names of those who served as Priors, the high magistrates of Florence</term> and *Zibaldoni* <term>Zibaldoni: personal commonplace books or journals used for recording daily events, accounts, and news</term>—private notebooks for jotting down interesting news items at the moment, which were carried and used by Florentines of every class, age, and sex—contain numerous paragraphs relating to burial ceremonies. None of the latter were more scrupulously recorded than those of the Alberti, Cavalcanti, Peruzzi, Rucellai, and Valori families.

For example, among other items in the account <note>Valori MS., p. 23.</note> of the burial of Monna Piera de’ Valori Curonni in 1365, are biscuits and sweetmeats, a cloth baldaccino <term>Baldaccino: a ceremonial canopy, typically made of rich fabric, held over a coffin or dignitary</term>, poles for carrying the coffin, wax candles for the night watch, sweet herbs for perfuming the room, torches for the street procession, and so on. The amount paid to Giovanni di Bertoldo, the Apothecary, for all these reached fifty-three gold florins. An additional account for tapers, candles, and torches used at the interment—also supplied by the same undertaker—came to eleven gold florins. The fees paid to the lady’s two doctors—Messeri Niccolo da Mantova and Piero de’ Pulchi—for “medical attendance and for certifying the death” amounted to seventy gold florins.

The expense of the funeral of Niccolaio di Jacopo degli Alberti, who died in August 1377, was enormous. “He was buried,” says the old chronicler, “at Santa Croce, with the greatest honors in tallow and wax.” The sum total came to three thousand gold florins—nearly £1500!

In fact, the serious expenses associated with funeral ceremonies led to restrictive legislation by the State, and the “Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries” was called upon to investigate the matter. Many regulations were adopted throughout the fifteenth century, and at length, some new statutes were enacted in 1536 which dealt with torches, candles, and various other objects modeled in wax. These confirmed the Guild's exclusive right to make, keep, and sell all such things, and further limited the trade in illuminations and fireworks—which at the period had become indispensable additions to all funerals—to members of the Guild.

By far the most fashionable and lucrative department in the Apothecaries' shops was that of Perfumery and Haberdashery. Indeed, the perfumer's private room—with its delicious odors and rich stores of attractive trifles—was a dangerous rival to the gossiping salon of the versatile barber.

When a man required a tonic, it was common practice for him to drop into his chemist's shop. There, in addition to the usual local news, he was able to discuss interesting items from foreign lands, handle samples of scents and silks from the East, taste curious sherbets and essences, and chat to his heart's content with the fashionable socialites of the emporium. High-born gentlemen and well-to-do country women <term>contadine: country or peasant women</term> thronged these busy markets, lending their elegance and their eccentricities to the lively scene. Flirtations and secret meetings were the order of the day behind shady slatted blinds and amid cushioned couches, while the discreet and spectacled master busied himself not with their gossip, but with their petty cash.

The widespread use of perfumes was a characteristic of the prosperity of Florence and of the luxury of her citizens. Almost everyone became a connoisseur of delicate and pungent odors. The fashion was introduced from Spain, which provided the recipes that became the rage, bearing names such as "Princess Isabella" <note>original: "Infanta Isabella"</note> and "Lady Florence of Ullhoa" <note>original: "Donna Fiorenza del Ullhoa"</note>.

<note>1 "Dithyramb on the Orange Flower" (original: "Diterambo sul Fiore d' Arancio").</note>
Count Lorenzo Magalotti tells us that a pair of small silk sachets filled with these delights sold easily in Florence for four hundred gold florins. The Count also wrote a sonnet entitled "To the Orange Flower,"¹ wherein he enthusiastically lists the fascinating ingredients of his own favorite perfume: orange blossom, honeysuckle, roses, jasmine, lilies of the valley, elderflowers, sweet mint, thyme, and geranium blossoms. He gives a recipe for the manufacture of a delicious fragrance: "Take," he says, "the empty skin of an orange, with a little powdered benzoin <term>benzoin: a fragrant balsamic resin from trees in East Asia, used in perfumes and incense</term>, two pounded cloves, and a small stick of cinnamon; cover them with the finest rose water, and set them to boil upon a brazier."

Magalotti also discourses upon the charms of *Buccheri* <term>scented clay vessels</term>, and says solemnly: "What a delight it would be to boil four or five pieces of Guadalajara clay in a Sorceress's jar with Cordova water! <note>original: "put to boil in a Bucchero della Maga, with Cordova water, four or five pieces of Bucchero di Guadalaxara"</note> Such a mixture would keep its perfume for a year if wrapped in amber-scented leather with a penny's worth <note>original: "denaro"</note> of quinine extract <note>original: "lacrima di Quinquina"</note> and would be both food and drink combined!"

Under the general term *Merciai*—Haberdashers—which, by the way, was added to the title of the Guild in the year 1282, and which, from then on, was known as "*L'Arte de' Medici e degli Speziali e de' Merciai*"—"The Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Haberdashers"—were included many small dealers of fancy goods.

*Merciai* strictly meant traders who purchased raw silk in the Levant and Persia and shipped it to Florence. They were also keen on picking up endless articles that promised profitable sales at home. They contributed greatly to the splendor of marriage feasts, which in the fifteenth century were celebrated without fear of laws restricting luxury <term>sumptuary laws</term>. The weddings of Baccio Adimari and Lisa Ricasoli in 1420, of Bernardo Rucellai and Nannina de' Medici in 1460, and of Lorenzo de' Medici and Clarice Orsini in 1469 were remarkable for the richness and variety of the beautiful presents of Eastern origin—embroidered cushions, belts, purses, veils and fringes of fine silk, inlaid thimbles and needle-cases, ivory combs, feathered fans, and various other items. The wedding trousseau of Giovanna de' Medici, in 1466, excelled all others in the skillful beauties of its unnamed trifles of rare and excellent workmanship, sought out from the endless stores of the Apothecaries.

Throughout the fifteenth century, as the fame of Florence spread further and further abroad, her merchants and her apothecaries engaged in an increasingly friendly rivalry to exploit the treasures of distant lands. The "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries" dispatched travelers and agents into every known land, who quickly sent back valuable shipments of goods. Everything of an aromatic nature or pleasing to the eye, as well as every ingredient useful in the *Pharmacopoeia* <note>A book containing a list of medicinal drugs with their effects and directions for their use.</note>, became articles of trade and commerce.

Every ship from the East that entered the harbor of Leghorn <note>Modern Livorno.</note>, or sailed up to the quays of Pisa, brought immense stores of precious Oriental merchandise. These were unloaded and promptly packed onto the backs of mules or placed in shallow riverboats and sent directly to the shops of the apothecaries.

The number of *Sensali* (agents) and *Mezzani* (middlemen) was very large. They were either engaged in foreign travel, or

<page-num>264</page-num>

at depots in Italy and abroad, or in Florence itself. By the middle of the thirteenth century, the Guild fully recognized and generally employed these assistants. From time to time, regulations were put into effect that limited both the number and the activities of people acting as agents and salesmen. Furthermore, anyone engaging in these occupations was required to obtain the approval of the Consuls of the Guild.

The cooperative nature that characterized all trade ventures in Florence was also evident among agents and salesmen. Consequently, it is not surprising to find that by the middle of the fourteenth century, a subordinate corporation had been established: the Guild of Agents and Middlemen <note>original: "L'Arte de' Sensali e di Mezzani"</note>. This association held no independent political power and was entirely under the direction of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries." Upon enrollment or admission, each member received a metal token which he was required to wear while exercising his trade. He was also permitted to display this same badge over the door of his home or office.

Agents and salesmen were not allowed to conduct sales of any kind without the authority of the Greater Guild. Breaking this rule resulted in a fine for each offense of one <term>soldo</term> <note>A small silver coin used in Florence.</note>, and repeated violations led to expulsion.

Florentine commerce increased so greatly during the fifteenth century that the leading apothecaries, in addition to their staff of travelers, established banking agencies in all the major population centers. This was especially true in those countries which produced the wide variety of goods used in their trade.

These "Professional Banks"—if we may call them that for want of a better name—became significant business houses and were heavily involved in granting loans to members of the Guild to support exploration expeditions. They also took on the character of general money-lending offices and, because they were well-managed, became very prosperous ventures.

<meta>This page transitions from the commercial activities of agents and banking to the cultural and intellectual patronage provided by the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries, specifically highlighting its connection to famous writers, artists, and explorers like Dante Alighieri.</meta>

With something of the inclusivity of a nurturing mother <note>original: "Alma Mater"</note>, the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries" extended its protective patronage to many objects and interests not, at first sight, necessarily associated with medicine, surgery, and drugs.

Literature, painting, and geographical discovery all benefited from the fostering care of the Guild. If a man had a book, a paint pigment, or a plan for an adventure, he had nothing to do but drop in at one of the major pharmacies of old Florence. There, he could socialize with others of his kind and chat affably with the dignified and bespectacled doctors. After persuading the patient but observant apothecary, he rarely departed without having obtained what he asked for.

Dante, Cimabue, and Toscanelli may be rightly called the fathers of these glorious families of writers, artists, and explorers, who have shed such undying fame upon their nurturing mother <note>original: "Alma Mater"</note> and have illuminated all lands and all periods by the brilliance of their genius.

The writers of the Renaissance, whose influence began and flourished in Florence, form a paradise of celebrities who have placed the "Fair City" upon the highest throne of the Hall of Fame <note>original: "Valhalla"</note> of Learning.

> ->"Boccaccio's Garden and its fairyland<-
> ->The love of joy and the gallantry,"<-

The city's sons used the pen with the same magnificent spirit of enterprise and success as their brothers used the loom. Her writers, her merchants, and her bankers together built up her fortune and her glory.

Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) was the son of a notary belonging to the <term>sestiere</term> <note>One of the six districts or wards into which Florence was divided.</note> of Por San Piero. He was sent to study law at Bologna and philosophy at Padua; but, having no taste for either subject, he enrolled in 1296 in the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries." His choice may have been dictated by his fondness for literature, because books were among the wares sold exclusively in the pharmacies.

Dante Alighieri entered public life soon after his marriage in 1295 and took an active part in the debates of the magistrates. In 1300, he was elected Prior and was instrumental in causing the exile of the Blacks and the Whites <note>original: "Neri and Bianchi"; these were rival factions within the Guelph political party in Florence.</note>. This led to his own exile upon a trumped-up charge of "barratry"—the financial misuse of office—as well as extortion and illegal profits.

Even if Petrarch (1304–1374) and Boccaccio (1313–1375) were never formally enrolled <term>matriculated: formally admitted or enrolled as a member of a guild or organization</term> into the Guild, their sympathies lay with its charitable and beneficial character. Their writings were nowhere more accessible, and their clever sayings more constantly repeated, than in the apothecary shops of their beloved Florence.

Matteo Palmieri (1364–1427), apothecary and poet; Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1475), physician, astronomer, architect, and writer; Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), surgeon, philosopher, and writer; and Antonio Benivieni (1453–1542), physician and man of letters, were among those who were enrolled in the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries." But who could possibly list the names of that entire mighty Florentine phalanx of literary men who have brilliantly honored not only their Guild, their city, and their time, but the great world at large for all eternity!

No effort appears to have been made to establish a separate corporation specifically for the enrollment of men of letters, which was also the case for painters.

The printing, making, and selling of books and other literary material—as well as wood and copper block engraving—were recognized as belonging to the professional "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries."

Bernardo Cennini—Ghiberti's partner in designing and casting the famous Baptistery Gates—was the first Florentine to print using movable type. His earliest book, *A Commentary on Virgil*, was published in 1471.

We owe the typeface called *Italic* to Aldus Manutius (1450–1516). It was modeled after the handwriting of Petrarch. The cutting of the type was done by Francesco da Bologna—Francesco Raibolini—the painter-goldsmith, who signed himself, indiffer-

In 1472, Piero da Moguntia—another German—issued Giovanni Boccaccio's *Filocopo* in Florence. Five years later, Nicholaus of Breslau printed Bettini’s *Holy Mountain of God* <note>original: "Monte Sancto di Dio"</note>; and in 1481—under his assumed name of Niccolo di Lorenzo of Florence—he published an edition of Dante's works. This was the finest example of Florentine printing that had appeared up to that time. The first mention of wood-engraving in Florence appears in an entry for the *Catasto* (income tax) of 1430. This record states that an unnamed craftsman reported "many woodblocks for the printing of playing cards and images of saints useful to him in his profession" as taxable property. However, no surviving print is older than 1490, a date which appears on a bird's-eye view of Florence currently kept in Berlin.

Jacopone da Todi's *Hymns of Praise* <note>original: "Laudi"</note>—printed by Francesco Buonaccorso—and similar books of devotion appeared in 1490 with woodblock illustrations. In the same year, Buonaccorso—who was related to Savonarola through his mother—published the eloquent Friar's <note>original: "Frate's"</note> tract, *The Book of Widowed Life* <note>original: "Libro della Vita viduata"</note>. Savonarola himself flooded Florence with illustrated tracts and sermons. These were produced in two or three special workshops where they were designed and executed; publishers applied to the masters of these shops when they required woodcuts for their publications. Luigi Pulci's *Morgante Maggiore*, which contains more than two hundred woodcuts, was published in 1500. Many old Florentine woodcuts dated between 1516 and 1546 are signed by Giovanni Benvenuto, a leading publisher and member of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries."

The earliest Florentine copperplate engraving was probably a "Paschal Table for finding Easter from the year 1461," of which there is a copy in the British Museum. The first illustrated books published in Florence that contained copperplate engravings were the *Holy Mountain of God* <note>original: "Monte Sacro di Dio"</note> and Dante's works. ...was responsible, and examples of his skill as an engraver may be seen at the Berlin Museum. Filippo Lippi, who served as a Consul of the Painters' Guild several times, produced fifteen plates for the *Life of the Madonna*, published in 1482.

Apparently, the mechanical challenges of printing text and plates on the same page were too great even for the skilled Florentine artist-craftsmen. Consequently, between 1472 and 1490, fewer than two hundred illustrated books were published in Florence. Another reason for this limited production was likely the general preference for illuminated manuscripts; in these works, no scribes <note>original: "Scrivani"</note> surpassed those of Florence for beautiful and accurate handwriting. The art of writing and decorating manuscripts required two types of artists: manuscript writers and capital-letter designers <note>original: "Miniatori-caligrafi"</note>, and illuminators <note>original: "Miniatori-pittori"</note>. As early as 1150, Florentine scribes were famous for their fine, clear, and accurate penmanship. By the start of the fourteenth century, the pen began to be replaced by the brush.

The last of the great master copyists was Vespasiano da Bisticci (1421–1498). He was a member of the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries and published a book titled *The Lives of Illustrious Men*. He is remembered today as the first modern bookseller, and his shop near the New Market <note>original: "Mercato Nuovo"</note> was the first store dedicated exclusively to supplying printed books.

A vast number of craftsmen were involved in the book industry: typefounders, press-makers, paper and parchment dressers, typesetters, printers, illustrators, engravers, binders, cloth-shearers, vellum-stretchers, and boss-carvers <note>Artisans who carved decorative metal studs or fittings for book covers</note>. All these artisans were subject to strict regulations regarding their workmanship, and their work underwent rigorous censorship by officials from the Great Guild before publication. There do not seem to have been separate organizations for these specific workers; instead, they were likely members of the subordinate association of bookmakers and booksellers <note>original: "Librai"</note>.

In the Early Renaissance, the great Comacine Guild <note>An influential guild of itinerant stonemasons and builders</note> em—

### DOCTORS AND APOTHECARIES

...embraced workers in all the decorative arts—architects, builders, mosaic-workers, workers in gold and bronze, carvers in wood and stone, painters, etc. The *Master Painters* <note>original: "Magistri pittori"</note> formed the fourth branch of that famous Guild until the beginning of the fourteenth century, when painter communities were founded outside the parent organization.

Every state and every town where the Comacine Masters <note>A guild of master masons and architects active in Italy during the Middle Ages</note> worked had its Lodge of Painters. One spirit moved the brethren in friendly rivalry and produced individual styles, to each of which the name of "School" was given. Thus Cimabue, Giotto, Lorenzetti, Memmi, Gaddi, Aretino, and others worked together and apart, each with their own characteristic style.

Every wall space not allocated to the sculptor or the mosaic-master was smoothed and plastered to receive the pigments of the painter. Scratch where you will—at Fiesole, in San Miniato, or in Santa Croce—plaster peels off and reveals a painting by a Comacine Master. The Spanish Chapel <note>original: "Cappella degli Spagnuoli"</note> at Santa Maria Novella is an intact treasure-house of Comacine frescoes.

Somewhere around 1297, the Florentine painters—being dependent on the Apothecaries and their agents in foreign lands for their supplies of pigments—placed themselves under the banner of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries," though they had no distinct organization.

The first incorporation of the Painters appears to date from 1303 and was the natural result of the commercial economies of the period. Certain rules and regulations were compiled, but the first serious enactment of Statutes was accomplished in November 1339, when the "Guild of Painters" <note>original: "L'Arte de' Pittori"</note> became a duly constituted corporation. At the same time, it was ruled that the new brotherhood should be dependent upon the Greater "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries" and should possess no special political or social pre-eminence.¹

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

In 1349, a further development of the Guild of Painters took place, and its members enrolled themselves as the "Company and Fraternity of Saint Luke" <note>original: "Compagnia e Fraternita di San Luca"</note> under the special protection of the Virgin Mary, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Zenobius, and Saint Reparata. The headquarters of the members were moved to the disused church of San Matteo, and they added an alternative title—"The Confraternity of Painters" <note>original: "La Confraternita de’ Pittori"</note>—while acknowledging their dependence upon the great Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries. The Confraternity included among its members not only creators of pictures, frescoes, and designs, but also decorators of stone, wood, metal, glass, stucco, leather, and so on.

The Statutes of the Guild,¹ which were properly registered before a notary on August 18, 1354, established the governing body: four Consuls, four Councilors, two Treasurers, and two Secretaries. These officers were generally men of the highest artistic skill—for example, Luca Della Robbia, although not a master of pigments <note>A painter</note> in the ordinary sense of the term, served as Consul several times. He was, moreover, elected thirty times as a member of the Council, three times as a <term>Syndic</term> <note>A legal representative or magistrate of the guild</note>, and twice as Treasurer.

The matriculation fee was only five *lire*, and other payments from members were on the same modest scale. One statute provided: "that those who registered themselves on the membership roll—whether men or women—should be contrite and confess their sins; and that while they were members of the Guild, they should go to confession and take Communion at least once a year."

All members were required to recite five Our Fathers <note>original: "Paternosters"</note> and five Hail Marys <note>original: "Aves"</note> daily; however, if their memory failed them, the omission had to be made up the following day. Complaints were common in 1406 that members of the Guild were neglectful of their religious duties and their obedience to officers. Penalties included temporary confinement in the Guild House and money fines—starting from twelve <term>denarii</term> <note>Small silver or copper coins</note>—for each neglect of duty.

# DOCTORS AND APOTHECARIES

> “O you of the gentle spirit who are lovers of Art and devoted to its pursuit, adorn yourselves with the garments of love, modesty, obedience, and penance.”

St. Luke’s Day was a famous festival in Florence, when all the finest pictures not actually in their permanent locations <note>original: "in situ"</note> were collected from the studios and exhibited in the cloisters of La Nunziata. In this observance, we see the origin of the Academy of Saint Luke <note>original: "Accademia di San Luca"</note>, renamed in 1562 by Cosimo I as the “Academy of the Fine Arts” <note>original: "Accademia delle Belle Arti"</note>. Here, he united the three Fine Arts—Sculpture, Painting, and Architecture—under the splendid motto: <note>original: "Levare di terra al cielo nostro intelleto"</note> “To raise our intellect from earth to heaven!”

Genius indeed! What pen could name all the great lights of that era, much less do justice to the magnificent procession of the Painters of Florence? If Benvenuto Cellini wrote:
> “Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael Sanzio, and Michelangelo Buonarroti are the Book of the World,”

who shall add honors to their names, or who shall tell the glories of their brothers in art?

Under the patronage of the “Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries,” many eminent artists turned their attention to stained glass. Ghiberti, Ghirlandajo, Perugino, Lorenzo di Credi, Pierino del Vaga, and Vivarini were only a few of those who designed subjects and also performed the process of staining.

They ground their pigments very fine, mixed them with water containing gum or some other adhesive, sketched in light dark-touches and shadows, and then fired the glass in a kiln. When cool, colors were applied and dotted over the surface and left to dry. A soft brush was passed over the picture, highlights were scratched out, and the sheet was fired again.¹

The glass-worked glories of the Cathedral <note>Duomo</note>, Santa Croce, Santa Maria Novella, San Spirito, La Nunziata, Or San Michele, and many another shrine of religion and art owe their creation to these renowned masters. Working with them were Moise—in 1350—and Domenico di...

Turning lastly to the discoverers and explorers of lands and seas, who were all under the patronage <note>original: "Ægis"</note> of the Guild, we encounter two great Florentines—Paolo Toscanelli and Amerigo Vespucci—among a host of worthy compatriots in adventure.

Paolo Toscanelli, the son of a physician, was born in 1397. After reading the classics in the "Florentine Studio" <note>The University of Florence</note>—where Boccaccio used to expound upon Dante—he graduated from the University of Padua. On his return to Florence in 1425, he became a member of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries" without paying fees, by right of his father <note>original: "beneficio patris"</note>. He took up the study of natural science, especially devoting himself to astrology—which he called "the crazy daughter of a wise mother, astronomy." Under his philosophy, the Milesian theory regarding the spherical form of the earth was revived. His opinions, together with the ever-increasing needs of Florentine commerce for new dyes, new drugs, and new spices, prompted the idea of reaching Prester John <note>original: "Prete Janni"</note>—the fabled land of herbs in the West.

The route traced on his map by Toscanelli enabled Christopher Columbus to set foot upon the New World. The many letters which passed between Toscanelli, the King of Portugal, Columbus, and many other notable figures have a romantic as well as a scientific interest. Alas, he never lived to see the crowning achievement of his life's work; he died in 1482, just ten years before the discovery by Columbus. He was buried in the Church of Santo Spirito. The mantle of Toscanelli fell upon the shoulders of Amerigo Vespucci, who was born in Florence in 1451. He was the son of a notary but entered a commercial career <note>original: "mercantile life"</note> in one of the Medici Companies of Adventurers, becoming the Cadiz agent for that firm in 1492. He was introduced to Christopher Columbus and contracted to provide supplies for two of his expeditions. The famous explorer spoke of him as: "a very worthy man" <note>original: "*imo hombre muy de bien*"</note>—"a very reliable sort of fellow!"

In 1497, King Ferdinand of Portugal <note>Historical note: While the text names Ferdinand of Portugal, Vespucci's 1497 voyage was likely under the Spanish crown; the author may be referring to King Manuel I for later Portuguese voyages.</note> entrusted him with the command of an exploring expedition, and he returned to Florence for information and assistance. While in his native city, he was enrolled as a full member of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries." He afterward sailed to the New World, taking with him Hojeda <note>Alonso de Ojeda</note>, Pinzon, and Cabral—all famous Portuguese explorers—and had the satisfaction of discovering the coast of the Northern Continent, to which he gave his own name, *Amerigo*—"America." The news of his success caused immense excitement and enthusiasm in Florence. For three days and three nights, the entire city was decorated with wreaths and banners and illuminated with torches and lamps. Vespucci died at Seville in 1512. His portrait, painted by Ghirlandajo, was discovered in a fresco at the Church of Ognissanti in Florence.

Because of the very nature of their work, explorers and navigators were positioned so that they could not form a cooperative society of their own. Membership in the Great Guild, which patronized and funded <note>original: "subsidised"</note> their efforts, was sufficient for their needs.

->. . . . .<-

And it truly was a "Great Guild"; for although the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries" held no higher place in the guild hierarchy of Florence than sixth, it was second to none in the nobility of its aims and the splendor of its achievements.

### CHAPTER IX

## THE GUILD OF FURRIERS AND SKINNERS

->*The Guild of Vair-dressers and Furriers* <note>original: "L'Arte de' Vaiai e Pellicciai"</note><-

I. **Origin.**—The wearing of skins and furs. Carolingian kings. Early craftsmen. Guild added to the Seven Greater Guilds in 1197. Few early records. Antonio Pucci's *Centiloquio* <note>A 14th-century poem summarizing the history of Florence</note>.

II. **Constitution.**—Avoidance of confusion with tanners and other leather workers. First Consuls appointed in 1270. Guild books. Various divisions of guild members. Officers. Low fees for enrollment <term>matriculation</term>. The "Tax of the Little Torches" <note>original: "Tasso di Torcetti"</note>. "Squeezers" or "Pepper-boxers!" <note>Nicknames for specific guild or tax officials</note>. Street regulations regarding trade processes. Sumptuary laws <term>laws regulating luxury and spending</term> affecting furs.

III. **Development.**—Types of skins and furs. Meaning of the guild's double title. Values. Processes. Treaties. Exports. An early restrictive law. Wearing vair <term>a patterned fur from the grey squirrel</term> and other furs marked the prosperity of Florence. The "fool in vair!" Curative properties of fur. Cinderella <note>Referring to the theory that her "glass" slipper was originally "vair" or fur</note>.

IV. A discussion of the dress of the Florentines during the Renaissance.

The wearing of skins and fur was undoubtedly the earliest fashion in clothing used by the primitive races of mankind. We naturally associate such coverings with savage and semi-civilized life. What could be more natural or easier—when winter storms grew cold, or old age and sickness thinned the blood—than to kill an animal and use its skin <term>pelt</term> to protect the human body?

Woven garments are the clothing of civilization and peace. Consequently, when fierce warlords from the north overran the fair plains of Italy in the early Middle Ages, no one was surprised to see their strong limbs dressed in the furs of the animals they had killed along their route. Of Ansprand <note>original: "Ausprando"</note>, King of the Lombards in 772, it is recorded that he arrived clothed in fine skins and rare furs.¹

¹ Paul the Deacon <note>original: "Paolo Diacono"</note>, Book VI, chapter 35.

<header>GUILD OF FURRIERS AND SKINNERS</header>

The Carolingian <term>the dynasty of Charlemagne</term> kings followed the same fashion, and Charlemagne himself used to wear thick otter-skins in winter. In the summertime, when he went hunting, he wore practical sheepskins. During his official travels through Italy, he generally wore a large robe lined with vair <term>a patterned fur from the grey squirrel</term> and fox-skin. His officers and courtiers were dressed in a similar fashion, and their appearance undoubtedly impressed the quick-witted Florentines, giving them ideas which they were quick to put into practice.¹

The early inhabitants of Tuscany—their former industries having been scattered—were forced to clothe themselves, for both peace and war, in whatever was most readily available and offered the least temptation to their robber enemies. Consequently, at the time of the founding of the Guilds, many remnants of a troubled past remained in their clothing styles, and skins and furs were very much in fashion.

The first mentions of Furriers and Skinners in the Archives of Florence are the following:

> “1050—*Sethimus*—furrier <note>original: "pellicarius"</note>.”
> “1075—*Vivulo*, son of Stephen <note>original: "filius Stefani"</note>—furriers <note>original: "pellicarii"</note>.” ²

Under the date 1054, there is the following entry: *A fur cloak* (?) <note>original: "Crosna"</note>, *with a fox-skin hat* <note>original: "cum Capello de Vulpe"</note>; and in 1077, “*A fox-skin garment*” <note>original: "Vesta una de Vulpe"</note>—perhaps mantles or cloaks made of fox-skin. In the former year, the value of the fur garments is recorded at five hundred *lire*. In 1197, there is a record of a worthy Rector of Santa Maria Novella who wished to pawn “*his red-deer skins*” <note>original: "pelles suas lupi cerverii"—though "lupi cerverii" typically refers to lynx, the author identifies it here as red-deer</note>!

The earliest specific mention of the “Guild of Furriers and Skinners” was in 1197, when its first incorporation took place alongside the Guilds of “Judges and Notaries” and “Doctors and Apothecaries.” Already, the four principal Guilds—“*Calimala*” <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers</note>, “Wool,” “Bankers,” and “Silk”—were in existence and were exercising significant influence in the Commune.

Why the “Guild of Vair-dressers and Furriers” <note>original: "Arte de' Vaiai e Pellicciai"</note> was chosen for incorporation above the “Guild of Linen” or that of the “Masters of Stone...”

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

It is quite impossible to say why this guild was chosen to fill the seventh place in the Guild Hierarchy, rather than, for example, the guild of "Oil and Wood" or that of the "Butchers." Its craftsmen were likely of a more ancient lineage, or perhaps they represented a higher social class in the public’s estimation. Alternatively, they may have formed the most significant industrial class outside the exclusive circle of the three leading commercial corporations.

In any case, in 1266, the formal title of "Guild" was bestowed upon them, along with their armorial banner—the *Agnus Dei* <term>Lamb of God</term>, holding a white flag with a red cross in the corner of a blue field. Their Consuls and other officers were granted the same rank and priority as the officials of the other Greater Guilds. After this date, records of the Guild are abundant, concerning both its status and its activities in the industrial life of the city and the *Contado* <term>the surrounding territory or countryside</term>.

At a conference of Guild Consuls held in April 1280, the attendees included Salvi Aldobrandini, Feo Bonci, Baldo Calderusci, and Cambio Rusticucci, who were Consuls of the "Guild of Skinners." <note>original: "Le Consulte," i. 27</note> Among those who attended and spoke at a similar conference in December 1293 was Caruccio della Verra of the "Guild of Furriers." He was one of the city's most distinguished citizens, though very little is known about him except that he traveled far and wide. In May 1296, the Consuls of the Guild took an active part in discussions concerning the Hospital of San Gallo. Along with the Consuls of the "Bankers and Exchangers" and "Doctors and Apothecaries" guilds, they were appointed as guardians and overseers.

Antonio Pucci sings of the Guild in his "Songs of the *Mercato Vecchio*" <term>Old Market</term> as follows:

> "Florence, the home of widespread trade,
> Counts twenty-one guilds in all;
> Of equal rank, and the seventh place
> The 'Furriers and Skinners' we call." <note>original: A. Pucci, "Centiloquio"</note>

. . . . . . . . . . .

Originally, only two Consuls were elected to preside over the affairs of the Guild. However, between 1270 and 1280, the number was increased to three, and later—after the revision of the Statutes between 1301 and 1309—to four. They held office for four months, and their names were drawn from an urn containing slips of paper, as was the general practice.

As established in the constitutions of the other Guilds, the Consuls took notice of all civil and criminal cases between members of the Guild. They also granted enrollment <term>matriculation</term> to candidates and supervised member subscriptions and other corporate property.

The *Consigliere*—Chancellor—was entitled to certain fees:
* For each person enrolled: ten *soldi* <term>Florentine silver coins</term>.
* For written agreements between a master and an apprentice: ten *soldi*.
* For each license to keep untanned skins or hides: ten *soldi*.
* For each cancellation of enrollment and resignation of membership: ten *soldi*.
* For the appraisal of stock in any retail shop: ten *soldi*.
* For each written agreement between slaughterer-skinners and leather-tanners: ten *soldi*.
* Various other smaller fees. 

The Chancellor’s term lasted one year, and the occupant was ineligible for immediate re-election.<sup>1</sup>

The *Provveditore*—Director—was required to keep the following Guild books fully updated: 
* A journal of debtors and creditors, along with the salaries and expenses of the Consuls and other officials. 
* An enrollment register <term>Matriculation Register</term> containing the payments and obligations of the persons enrolled in the city. 
* A similar register for the *Contado* <term>the surrounding territory or countryside</term>. 
* A notebook containing the registered trademarks of all tanners and dealers in leather, and so on. 

He also received fees, though smaller in amount, for the same purposes as the Chancellor.<sup>2</sup>

<meta>This page continues the description of the administrative officers of the Guild of Furriers and Skinners, moving from the Chancellor and Director to the Chamberlain and specialized inspectors, while also listing the various trades categorized under this Guild.</meta>

### THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

The *Cameriere*—or Chamberlain—was responsible for the Guild's finances. He managed the accounts for the rents of slaughterhouses, skinning houses, tanyards, pits, leather-dressing workshops, and the shops and stalls of everyone involved in the trade. It was also his duty to manage the Guild's charitable contributions and to provide relief to distressed craftsmen and their families. These last two officers were elected for a one-year term but were eligible for re-election.

The *Stimatori*—Inspectors—and the *Tassatori*—Taxing Masters—consisted of two officials for each role. They were elected every six months and were instructed to keep the two divisions of Guild members as distinct and separate as possible, at least regarding the specific details of their various occupations.

In the first group were the:
* *Vaiai*—Miniver-dressers <note>Miniver refers to a type of white or spotted fur, usually ermine or squirrel, used for lining garments.</note>
* *Pelliciai*—General Furriers
* *Conciatori di pelli col pelo*—Dressers of skins with the fur attached
* *Incettiatori di bossette*—Dressers of lambskins

In the second group were the:
* *Cuoiai*—General Leather-dressers
* *Conciatori di cuoio grosso*—Dressers of heavy leather
* *Conciatori di sottili*—Dressers of fine leather
* *Orpellai*—Leather embossers and gilders

A third division was added in later times, comprised of:
* *Calzolai*—Shoemakers
* *Pianellai*—Slipper-makers
* *Collettai*—Collar and belt makers
* *Coloristi di pelli*—Leather-stainers
* Various minor but artistic crafts, including, perhaps, the *Pelacani*—dog-clippers! <note>The term *pelacani* literally translates to "dog-skinners" and often referred to tanners of lower-quality hides.</note>

There was also a fourth class containing:
* *Sellai*—Saddlers
* *Brigliai*—Bridle and rein makers
* *Cintiai*—Makers of sword-belts and bandoliers <term>bandoliers</term> <note>Shoulder belts with loops for carrying ammunition or tools.</note>

However, some of these workmen appear to have also been associated with the Lesser Guild of *Galigai*—Tanners—and the overlapping interests of the two Guilds likely led to some confusion. Nevertheless, the trade of tanning was a distinct industry, and no member of the "Guild of Furriers and Skinners" was permitted to participate in it. In the same way...

## GUILD OF FURRIERS AND SKINNERS

Shoemakers employed by the Guild were workers of luxury goods only, which required the addition of fur to be completed.

The matriculation fee was very low—specifically, four *soldi* <note>A *soldo* was a medieval Italian silver coin.</note> to each Consul and two to the Chancellor. However, the guarantee required to prove a candidate's qualification for enrollment was fixed at ten to twenty gold florins. An annual poll tax was levied by the State upon every registered member of the Guild; this tax earned several suggestive nicknames: "The Pepper Tax" <note>original: "*Tassa del Pepe*"</note>—"Pepper-boxes," or "The Squeezer Tax" <note>original: "*Tassa de' Torcetti*"</note>—"Squeezers"!

It was forbidden to mix local products with skins and furs from "beyond the mountains" (outside the borders of the State), or to treat any skin or fur with sulfur, dye, or oil. Skins that had been snipped, or those stretched out using glue or lime or any other media, were not to be bought or sold.

All violations of these and similar regulations were punished with fines and the seizure of goods, and the wrongdoers were liable to be expelled from the Guild.¹

Furriers and skinners were forbidden to buy or sell knives and tools of all kinds used in the craft at wholesale from or to the common people <note>original: "*Popolo Minuto*"—referring to the lower working classes</note> or to any unemployed person. However, such persons were permitted to purchase small quantities of cat and rabbit skins and stoat fur for the linings of garments.

The primary name of the Guild, "*Vaiai*," comes from the word *Vaio*—meaning speckled or variegated—as applied to the dark gray fur or coat of the stoat and squirrel.² A *Vaiaio* was a furrier who dressed such skins. These small animals were abundant in the forests surrounding old Florence, providing both sportsmen and craftsmen with an attractive and profitable occupation. The color of the animal's back was much darker than that of the belly, which, in young creatures, was a dazzling white—and was highly valued for that reason. This variety of color led to the use of—

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

...three terms were used for the fur: the back-fur and the entire coat of older animals were called “<term>Miniver</term>”; the rarer white belly piece was named “<term>Ermine</term>,” because it resembled true <term>ermine</term>; and “<term>Rosetello</term>” was the name given to the brown and yellow fur of spring growth.

The second part of the title of the Guild, “<term>Pellicciai</term>,” indicates the union of two industries—the dressing of furs and the treatment of skins; although, for that matter, <term>Pellicciaio</term> also meant “Furrier.” The Latin name, as written by the Notaries of old, was <term>Pelliparius</term> <note>original: "Pelliparius"—a Latin term for a skinner or tanner</note>, which indicated a dresser of skins after the tanning process had been completed.

The skins offered for sale in Florence, intended for purchase and treatment by the workers employed by the “Guild of Furriers and Skinners,” were usually those of wolves, lambs, polecats, foxes, deer, lynxes, and rabbits, along with the furs of <term>miniver</term>, marten, sable, and <term>ermine</term>.

<term>Ermine</term> and sable were rare commodities, and they commanded high prices—indeed, they were almost unknown until the late fifteenth century. Like marten fur, they were used for borders, trimmings, and decorations, and were never used for entire garments. Only very wealthy and ostentatious men had their state robes lined with these costly furs. Later in the history of the furrier industry, these same distinguished figures added the skins, furs, and tails of rare Eastern animals to the splendor of their attire.¹

The Guild dealt only indirectly, and in a secondary capacity, with heavy skins such as those of horses, cattle, mules, donkeys, goats, and sheep. These formed the staple of the tanning industry and provided materials for processing by members of the minor Guilds, such as the “Saddlers,” “Shoemakers,” and “Buckle-makers,” etc.

When counting by the hundreds in this manner, a strange and perhaps typical custom existed: starting the count with a head start of four to ten. This was likely because each word of the standard religious or saintly prayer said at the beginning counted as one skin or fur in the tally!

In the <term>Gabella</term> <note>A tax or duty on consumer goods</note> of 1402, the following rates were charged on skins and furs offered for sale in the city—per hundred, dressed: *Vair* <note>original: "Vaio"</note> and *Polecat* <note>original: "Faina"</note>—two pounds; *Sucklings* <note>original: "Lattizi"</note>, *Ermine* <note>original: "Ermellino"</note>, and *Marten* <note>original: "Martora"</note>—three pounds. Because <term>vair</term> <note>The fur of a species of squirrel with a gray back and white belly</note> was used so extensively, it was naturally a major target for taxation. This occurred not only through the annual special <term>Gabella</term>—which was collected for extraordinary state needs—but also at the city gates as a standard customs duty on imports.

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Raw fur was prepared for use by softening the pelts, skins, or hides with sweet olive oil and then trampling on them in tubs filled with fine hardwood sawdust heated to body temperature. The pelt was then removed and drawn over sharp knives to scrape away bits of flesh or other clinging substances. In this way, even the thickest hide was made as soft and flexible as the thinnest kid leather used for gloves.

The furrier then sorted the treated skins according to the color and texture of the hair and cut them to the required patterns. Next, the pelt was nailed to a board while damp and stretched with pins. The final step was trimming and softening the edges.

Most of the guild's workshops and showrooms were located along the elegant *Via de' Pellicciai* <note>The Street of the Furriers</note>. No street in old Florence was more attractive, and nowhere else did so many fashionable men and women gather daily to admire and desire the magnificent furs displayed by the guild's merchants. Here, families like the Lamberti, the Toschi, the Cipriani, the Pilli, and others competed with one another in the variety of their stock and the excellence of their dressing methods and styles.

Trade in skins expanded significantly and became very important. Treaties were established with Ferrara and Mantua regarding exports and imports. In 1307, an agreement was signed between the Commune of Florence and the Counts of Mugnone regarding the creation and maintenance of a specific trade route between Florence and Bologna. The costs of this project were funded by taxes based on the value and weight of the goods transported along it. Among these taxes was a fee of one pound for every load of fox or cat skins.

The value of the mixed furs exported by the <term>Guild of Furriers and Skinners</term> was immense, and transport convoys were in constant danger of being attacked and robbed. Among the legal <term>reprisals</term> <note>Legal authorizations to seize goods from citizens of another city to compensate for a debt or theft</note> issued by the <term>Priors</term> <note>The high-ranking magistrates of the Florentine Republic</note> of Florence on this matter was one sent to the Council of State in Siena in 1329, seeking...

restitution for two bales of <term>miniver</term> <note>A type of white fur used for lining and trimming garments, typically squirrel belly</note> blankets, consigned by Florentine merchants from Grosseto to Siena, or financial compensation based on the ruling of the joint Court of Arbitration.

Luigi Cibrario <note>An Italian historian and statesman</note> records many entries regarding the exports and values of furs processed by the “Guild of Furriers and Skinners” in Florence. For example, under the date 1367, eighty-seven marten skins for the lining of a cloak for Amadeo VI of Savoy, to be delivered in Rome, cost twenty-seven gold florins.

Everyone wore furs of varying value, and even the strict dress codes observed in religious houses were relaxed until luxury and showiness in clerical clothing became a scandal. A council held in London in 1127 passed a decree forbidding abbesses and other holy nuns from wearing skins of any kind except those of lambs, cats, and rabbits.¹

In 1225, Cardinal Sant’ Angelo regulated the habits <note>monastic clothing</note> of monks, decreeing that none were allowed new fur garments more often than every three years, and these were not to be lined with the skins of fox, leopard, or young lambs. Two types of capes were permitted—one of white fur for the summer, and one in darker shades of gray for the winter; only the winter capes were of a large size that reached to the ground.

In the thirteenth century, everyone wore a *pelliccia*—a short cloak—lined with <term>vair</term> <note>The skin of a species of squirrel with a blue-gray back and white belly</note>, ermine, or other fur. Many wealthier citizens also owned long cloaks lined with vair and bordered with even finer furs. Caps of *latiazzi*—young vair skin—and of vair mixed with other furs, were in general use.

The fur-lined tunics of soldiers—especially the cavalry—influenced civilian fashion. Men and women alike appreciated the comfort and elegance of clothing that was tight-fitting yet flexible. The popularity of wearing fur increased along with the use of silk decorations, marking the prosperity of Florence and the luxury of its merchants and citizens.

The former were called <note>original: "abiti di riguardo"</note> "garments of distinction," and were also adopted by church officials—a custom which has remained until our own day in the capes worn by canons and other high-ranking clergy.

Boccaccio, who was always observant of customs and fashions, says: "Highly valued are the garments lined with <term>vair</term> <note>A type of squirrel fur, often arranged in a heraldic blue-and-white pattern</note> upon which the sword of knighthood often falls."¹ To provide a contrast, and to show the Florentines' fondness for ridicule and their hatred of citizens who put on airs of dignity, that incomparable critic Antonio Pucci tells how in his day: "they dressed the fool in vair."² This refers to Villani’s story about Giudetto della Torre, who sent a jester to mock the cowardly Matteo Vincenti of Milan. The fool returned with an answer that pleased Giudetto so much that he awarded his witty messenger the fur-lined robe of a baron and gave him a fine riding horse as well!³

In a very curious pamphlet written by a man named Charrier and published in Paris in 1634, many strange customs and superstitions regarding the wearing of fur in the sixteenth century are recorded. He says: "Bachelors <note>likely referring to knights-bachelor</note>, Doctors of Law, Emperors, and Doctors of Medicine are dressed in the furs which represent the mysteries of Theology, the principles of politics, and the secrets of medical science!" "For the use of furs cures headaches and stomach aches; rheumatism, which resists even the most powerful remedies, is removed by the skins of cats, lambs, and hares."

Charrier goes on to claim with pride that: "of all the decorations which luxury has invented, there are none so glorious, so majestic, and so precious as fur." "The privileges and honors of Furriers and Skinners," he adds, "rightly surpass those of all other trades!"

### *DRESS OF THE FLORENTINES DURING THE RENAISSANCE.*

The question of dress was always more or less important in the ethics of Florence. Since the chief industries and the bulk of the commerce of the city and the surrounding countryside <term>Contado</term> were intimately concerned with the materials from which clothes are made, it is a subject that cannot be overlooked in any true appreciation of the life and work of the Guilds.

In the twelfth century, Florentines preserved many of the customs of their Roman ancestors.¹ They continued to wear the wool shirt, or vest, with the large round cloak, or toga, made of their native wool. These garments were plain and undyed for the use of the lower classes, and colored and ornamented for wealthier people.

In his "*Paradiso*" Dante speaks of primitive Florence in this way:

> “Florence, within her ancient city walls,
> Which still call her to morning and noon prayers,
> Was chaste and sober, and lived in peace.
> . . . . . . . . .
> I saw the sons
> Of Nerli and of Vecchio, well content
> With plain leather jerkins, and their wives handling
> The spindle and the flax; O, how happy they were!” ²

Ricordano Malespini records that, up to the year 1260, Florentines did not look down on coarse fabrics; many were satisfied to clothe themselves in skins and to wear fur caps and low leather shoes. The men wore a tight-fitting garment made of woven goat hair dyed scarlet. Everyone wore belts, generally of fine leather, to which the better-dressed added buckles. The

---

Women used to cover their heads with cloth or linen mantles and veils.

The habits of the religious orders were adapted from the dress of the peasantry, which consisted of a tunic or shirt of rough frieze <term>a coarse, heavy woollen fabric with a nap on one side</term>, reaching well below the knees, with a woollen belt. The legs were bare, but in winter and wet weather, leather buskins <term>sturdy, calf-high boots</term> were worn by all classes and orders.¹

The manners and general life of the people of Florence toward the end of the thirteenth century² were marked by gravity, sobriety, and frugality. Their simple food cost them little, as they did not care for rich eating. Each household lived very much by itself, and public entertainments were rare. Nevertheless, they were a cheerful race, and, while they were above all things serious and earnest about business affairs, they were fond of mirth, song, and dance in their proper seasons. Certainly, some of their ways were somewhat rough and rude, but in their dealings with strangers, they showed marked consideration and courtesy. In speech, they were not eloquent, but simple chatting gave them more pleasure than a polished oration or a witty dialogue.

Both men and women were coarsely dressed, mostly in leather jackets <term>jerkins</term> and skirts, with treated skins for extra covering. The wealthier citizens favored valuable furs, but these were worn without vanity. Small, tight-fitting leather caps or woven woollen berets <note>original: "berrette"</note> were worn by both sexes. All wore plain stockings, and when they were not barefoot, they had heavy boots and shoes of leather. The richer married women wore tight petticoats of coarse red "Ipro" or "Camo"—*Camoiardo*—cloth, gathered at the waist with a leather belt and metal buckle. In winter, some also put on fur-lined mantles with hoods attached—called *tasselli*—to cover the head. The poorer women wore gowns of rough green *Cambiagio* fabric made in the same way as the garments of their more wealthy sisters.

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The younger women practiced great restraint and rarely married until they were well over twenty years of age. A hundred *lire* <term>the currency of Florence</term> was considered an ample dowry for a bride, while two or three hundred was regarded as a splendid fortune by a lucky bridegroom.

Among the prohibitions—both sumptuary <term>laws regulating luxury and extravagant spending</term> and otherwise—enacted from time to time for the members of the Guilds to follow, was an Order of the Priors in 1296 regarding the display of coats of arms. It reads as follows:

"No one shall dare to establish a private club, society, or company with unauthorized arms. No one shall bear painted arms except according to the Statutes of his Guild or the Order of the Commune. Every Master of a Trade, along with his sons, brothers, and nephews, is permitted to wear and use the painted arms and signs of his Craft. No one should presume to bear painted arms that are not used by his family house. Upon payment of the prescribed fee of two hundred *lire*, any man may adopt the arms of King Charles in addition to those of his own house. No *popolano* (tradesman) may use the arms of a *magnifico* (merchant or magistrate) or keep them in his house unless he is a servant <note>original: "famulus"</note> or a member of that person's household. Nevertheless, painters may color arms, and tailors may sew them onto garments; likewise, armorers and shield-makers may engrave them in metal and leather. All such badges are permitted to be displayed for sale by the *Rigattieri* (retail dealers) in their shops."

As artistic craftsmanship advanced, a more refined taste in personal attire and adornment emerged. The excellence of the material and how well it fit the human figure led to both simplicity in arrangement and better correctness in cut and shape. Excessive use of color was replaced by artistic contrast, a unified effect, and restrained decoration.

Woolen fabrics were considered proper wear for ordinary days, while silk fabrics became the clothing for celebration and festivity. Everyday costumes were usually unadorned but still artistic, as the quality of the cloth and even the construction of the clothing were matters of great importance.

Older people wore the stately, neck-to-ankle *lucco* <term>a long, voluminous Florentine gown</term> made of scarlet silk for ceremonial occasions; however, in everyday life, they wore it in black silk or the finest black serge <term>a durable twilled fabric</term>. Around the neck was wrapped the white silk or woolen *becchetto* <term>a long scarf or streamer attached to a headpiece</term>, while the grey-haired head was covered with the large *berretta* <term>a square or round cap</term> and its hanging red curtain.

Young men of about eighteen years old wore surcoats made of black serge or *rascia* <term>a coarse, rough wool cloth</term>—which reached down to their heels and were sometimes lined with *taffeta* <term>a crisp, smooth silk</term>. In winter, the surcoats belonging to the sons of wealthy families were lined with fur or padded with rich silk brocade. *Ermisino* <term>a light, thin silk from the East</term> was worn by rising Doctors of Law. Their trousers, made of wool or silk depending on the season and the wearer's wealth, were tight-fitting and slashed <term>cut with decorative slits to show the fabric underneath</term> at the knee and hip. The colors were a matter of personal taste. On their heads, they wore the "civic cap" <note>original: "La berretta alla civico"</note>, made of black serge or *rascia* and lined with silk; the hanging curtain was often green. Another form of headwear was the *cappuccio* <term>a hood or cowl</term>, used by older people and by everyone during the winter. This was also made of cloth but was trimmed with fur. Men on a journey wore a *gabbano*—a felt cloak. Clothes were changed most scrupulously every Sunday, with clean garments being worn for the first time to Mass.

The dress of the peasantry was sparse but practical. Luca Della Robbia, in his twelve "Rondels" of the Seasons, has shown us the Tuscan countryman at work in the different duties of his calling.<sup>1</sup> A plain shirt of wool, linen, or a blend of both, tied at the waist, covered the body, leaving the head and legs bare. Woolen stockings were added in winter, and leather shoes were put on for digging and felling timber. When going to town or to Mass, they wore long, buttoned-up gowns or tunics without sleeves; the shirt sleeves showed through the armholes, and a leather belt was added, or not, as the wearer pleased. Peasant women in the fields were dressed in dull-colored clothing made of rough woolen cloth or coarse linen canvas; however, when going to market or to Mass, they—

The workers of the city were dressed in garments best suited to their various industries. These were never mere rags, but were made specifically for their purpose and were sometimes put on over their everyday clothes. Both men and women were proud to be seen in the uniform of the Guild to which they belonged. Wool, linen, canvas, and leather were the materials used. The senior workmen were also careful to display the crest or coat of arms of their Guild upon their tunics. However, wearing such decorations on headwear was forbidden, as it was seen as displaying a political or trade badge that might incite public disorder.

Merchants, Judges, Notaries, Doctors, and Apothecaries <term>pharmacists</term> all wore garments of distinctive and appropriate shape, color, and richness. Such costumes were compulsory for both their public professional duties and their private lives.

Magistrates in the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries were known by their long grey or yellow overcoats and scarlet *berrette* <term>square or round caps</term> with red hanging flaps. Adornments of gold and silver, silk and velvet, and fur and leather were introduced later. The *Podesta* <term>the chief magistrate of the city</term>, the *Gonfalonieri di Giustizia* <term>Standard-bearers of Justice</term>, the Captains of the People, Priors or Consuls, and other dignitaries were dressed in scarlet and gold, with fur linings and trimmings on their cloaks. They usually wore red *cappucci* <term>hoods</term> or *berrette* with deep hanging flaps, all trimmed with miniver <term>a white fur from the belly of a squirrel</term> and laced with gold. Their stockings were scarlet, and their boots were made of light tan or black leather embroidered with gold. The Consuls' headgear resembled cardinals' hats, and they wore uncut diamonds and sapphires. Pearls were reserved for the exclusive use of the *Podesta* and *Gonfaloniere di Giustizia*, whose state robes were decorated with golden stars.

An excessive taste for wearing finery emerged during the fourteenth century, around the year 1330, and the attention of serious-minded men was drawn to these extravagant trends. Eight citizens were appointed to patrol the city and report on the private spending and household management of individual families. The wearing...

...certain kinds of dress, regarded as excessive, were forbidden. The only people who seem to have escaped this condemnation were the wives of knights and doctors—both of law and of medicine.

Restrictions were placed on the extravagance of state ceremonies and on the expenses of wedding feasts. It was ordered that bridesmaids and other guests should dress simply, and that the bride’s trousseau should be on a modest scale.

Sumptuary laws <term>laws limiting private expenditure on food and luxury items</term>, which were passed from time to time, dealt largely with all forms of clothing-related extravagance. The tax census <term>Catasto</term> of 1427 was especially severe against the pride and ostentation of clothing. One regulation was as follows: 
> “No female—woman or girl—of whatever rank or status, married or unmarried, shall dare or presume, in the city of Florence or in its surrounding territory <term>Contado</term>, to wear any sleeve, bodice, cloak, robe, or other garment lined with the fur of any animal, whether domestic or wild, coarse or fine, by whatever name it may be known. . . .”

Another regulation enacted that no person of any rank or status, nor any tailor, dressmaker, squirrel-fur <term>vair</term> merchant, or furrier, shall dare or presume to cut, make, line, or cause to be cut, made, or lined, any of the following garments: *long tunics* <note>original: "cioppe"</note> and *peasant blouses* <note>original: "cottadite villani"</note> in which fur is a major component.

The wearing of gold embroidery and jewelry was strictly regulated; nevertheless, women were “allowed to wear gold, silver, and gilded embroidery upon the collars of their garments—to a depth of one-third of a cubit <term>braccio</term>.”¹

Damasks, patterned silks, and brocades were forbidden for everyday wear, and the colors and decorations of the robes that were permitted were restricted to those of simple design. The following were some of these laws:
> “No one shall presume to wear more than one pound of silver in garlands, buttons, or anything else upon their head or person . . . in addition to this, they may wear a silver belt, weighing, along with the..."

No woman is permitted to own more than two silk dresses at the same time. Sleeves and linings are not to be made of silk or fur, but of wool, linen, or cotton.

“They shall not dare to wear any open lace-work <term>intaglio</term> of more than a cubit <term>braccio</term> <note>Approximately 23 inches</note> in width . . . nor any fringe of gold, silver, or silk on the dress, except upon the bodice. . . . The hem of the garments may be decorated, but no skirt may be more than ten cubits <term>braccia</term> in circumference.” Many other details follow, prescribing with remarkable precision every part of both male and female clothing.

In the matter of jewelry—ostentation was to be avoided. “Women shall not presume to wear . . . more than two rings, and the rings shall not have more than one pearl and one other precious stone.”

With respect to the wedding chests <term>Cassoni</term>, strict orders were given; for example: “No one shall dare to include jeweled necklaces in the caskets of women or girls when they are promised or betrothed, nor shall they be given garlands or brooches of pearl, precious stones, gold, or silver.”

Some of the sumptuary measures <term>laws regulating consumption and luxury</term> passed and enforced have already been mentioned in earlier chapters, as well as the way the people circumvented and avoided them. The pressure became so excessive and irritating that a backlash was the only possible outcome.

Gradually, the enforcement of these clothing reforms slackened, and in the fifteenth century, they ceased to have any force. This was not only because of the difficulty of maintaining them but also because of the vastly increased import and manufacture of costly objects and fabrics.

In the frescoes at *Santa Maria Novella*, we see the new fashions that had just arrived, and the mural paintings in other city churches and palaces continue this history of clothing. Strangely enough, men set the fashion in those days, but

The unpredictable changes in men's fashion—or the lack thereof—were quickly adopted by women. Knights <note>original: "Cavaliers"</note> wore tight-fitting tunics with the long points of their wristbands lined with squirrel fur <term>vair</term> reaching down to the ground. Fashionable women followed their lead and adjusted their styles accordingly.

It became fashionable to wear multi-colored stockings <term>hose</term> striped with three or four different colors. Shoes had very long, pointed toes, and the wearers' legs were so tightly wrapped with ribbons and laces that they could barely sit down. Young men went about in silken or woolen tights and wore silk or velvet mantles hanging from their shoulders. Their hair hung down their backs, and long feathers were stuck into their jaunty red caps. Women improved upon these styles, and their skirts were skin-tight—getting in the way of their feet.

Sacchetti <note>Franco Sacchetti, a 14th-century Italian novelist</note> says, “Some women had their dresses cut so low that their armpits were visible; they would then give a jump to make the collars rise up to their ears!”

The wedding outfit <term>trousseau</term> and the marriage feast of Giovanna de' Medici were remarkable for the splendor of the robes and decorations. <note>Guido Biagi, “Private Life of the Renaissance Florentines.”</note> Four leading merchant princes of the city—Misters <note>original: "Messeri"</note> Manno Temperani, Carlo Pandolfini, Giovannazzo Pitti, and Tommaso Soderini—were the bride's attendants. Each was dressed in festive clothing made of crimson silk and scarlet cloth lined with white fur <term>miniver</term>. The bride herself was gowned in cloth of gold with an ermine mantle, while her dinner dress was made of white *zetana*—a very thick satin—adorned with pearls and trimmed with sable and ermine.

Rich furs were worn by all the guests. The fifty noblewomen and fifty noble youths who formed the bodyguard of the beautiful Giovanna competed with one another in decorating their tight-fitting jackets edged with sable. Their wide sleeves, with pointed wristbands lined with white fur <term>miniver</term> and ermine, reached the floor, and their shoes were embroidered with gold and bordered with sable fur.
