In the later years of the Republic, personal adornment and extravagance in dress reached a phenomenal height. Doctor Biagi says: “In 1467, for the State Tournament, Benedetto Salutati decorated the harness, headgear, and the trappings of two horses with 170 pounds of pure silver, which he had commissioned from the hands of Antonio Pollaiuolo. Furthermore, around the robes of the heralds, he strung 30 pounds of pearls—the greater part of which were of great value!”

Many amusing stories are told by the topical writers of the Renaissance concerning fashions and their constant changes. “Poor Mister <note>original: "Messere"</note> Valore di Buondelmonte, an old man of the traditional school, was forced by his relatives to change his cloak and hood. Everyone marveled and stopped him in the streets, asking: ‘Oh, what is this, Messer Valore? I do not recognize you! What is the matter with you? Do you have the mumps?’ When ruffs <term>large, pleated collars</term> became fashionable, Salvestro Brunelleschi, while eating some peas with a spoon, instead of putting them into his mouth, slipped them inside his ruff and scalded himself!” ^1

Under the Medici, no limits were set on personal freedom regarding clothing and ornaments. Only one law was passed—under the Grand Duke Ferdinand II—prohibiting specific types of dress, furniture, and other household and private matters, but it was repealed after a nine-month trial period.

## CHAPTER X

### THE GUILDS OF BUTCHERS, BLACKSMITHS, AND SHOEMAKERS

->*THE GUILDS OF THE BUTCHERS, THE SMITHS, AND THE SHOEMAKERS* <note>original: "LE ARTI DE' BECCAI, DE' FABBRI, E DE' CALZOLAI"</note><-

I. BUTCHERS.—War-lords, graziers, and slaughterers. Limited pastureland of Tuscany. Customs duties and evasions. Clever salesmen. Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note>. Old Bridge <note>original: "Ponte Vecchio"</note>. Heads must be attached to carcasses. Delicate Florentine palates. Fishmongers and fish. Fines and litigation. "Cheats!" and "Wooden-shoes!"

II. SMITHS.—Tuscany rich in minerals. St. Eloy. Descendants of nobility. Primitive forges and smelting yards. "Old iron and brass for sale!" Renaissance wrought ironwork. A money-grabber. Renowned workers in metals. The Acciaiuoli family.

III. SHOEMAKERS.—"Nothing like leather!" Many associated trades. Dependent upon the Guild of Tanners. Shoemakers warned not to give shelter to wandering men. Lining of armor. <term>Buskins</term> <note>calf-high or knee-high boots made of leather or cloth</note> worn by all classes. Flirtations.

### I. THE GUILD OF BUTCHERS <note>original: "L'ARTE DE' BECCAI"</note>

In every list of the Florentine Guilds, the "*Guild of Butchers*" <note>original: "Arte de' Beccai"</note> leads the Second Division, or Lesser Guilds, and occupies the first place among the Five Intermediate Guilds.

The term *Beccai* was originally applied to the highest families in Italy. The war-lords, who set out from Germany in the Middle Ages, took possession of the richest resources of the lands they traveled through—seizing cattle and livestock of all kinds, and robbing castles and villages with impunity. It is said that Dante’s use of the word in this sense greatly offended Francis I.

Something of the same feeling seems to have been shared by the Renaissance Florentines, who strove to distinguish between *Beccai*—graziers—and *Macellai*—slaughterers. In any case, the Guild was, at its first beginning in the thirteenth century, composed of

<keywords>Guild of Butchers, Guild of Smiths, Guild of Shoemakers, Arte de' Beccai, Tuscany, Mercato Vecchio, Dante, Renaissance, social hierarchy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Guild of Butchers, transitioning from their origins as German war-lords and wholesale dealers to their formal incorporation and status among the Florentine Guilds.</meta>

# GUILD OF BUTCHERS

wholesale dealers; the corporation of retail butchers was a later arrangement.

The earliest mention of a "butcher" in the Archives of Florence is of one "Martin the Butcher" <note>original: "Martinus—beccadore"</note> in 1110, but whether he was a member of a guild like the one in Paris—to which King Philip granted a charter in 1162—no one can say.¹

It is true that in every European country during the Middle Ages, "butchers" played a leading role, not only in the arena of commercial enterprise but also in political activity. This pre-eminence was partly due to hereditary backgrounds and traits, and partly to effective physical development. Bodily strength and force of character were always essential attributes for success in life generally, and these were particular marks of the *Beccai* <note>Butchers</note> of Florence.

There can be no doubt that two motives largely influenced the incorporation of the *Beccai*. First, the breeders and graziers of cattle and sheep needed to protect themselves, their lands, and their livestock from the attacks of robber captains and cattle raiders. Secondly, they wished to control the supply of meat and keep retail butchers and slaughterers out of the wholesale market.

The latter precaution was soon recognized as unwise because, with the rapid growth of the population, retail butchers became a necessity. Establishing friendly terms between the two sections of meat merchants proved to be the best policy.

The first distinct mention of the "Guild of Butchers" <note>original: "Arte de’ Beccai"</note> was in 1236, when the *Buonuomini* <note>The "Good Men," a board of officials</note>—who managed the reorganization and classification of the Florentine trades—placed it eighth in the order of the Guilds and named it first among the Fourteen Lesser Guilds. This priority of position was due to the influential character of the corporation's first members. They were not merely simple country breeders and peasant traders; many among them were prosperous city manufacturers and merchants. These rich men found that possessing *poderi* <note>farm estates</note>—

...and livestock, providing safe and profitable investments for their capital. This economic condition offers an interesting parallel to the much earlier absorption of the landed *Grandi* <note>Nobles</note> by the city *Popolani* <note>Commoners/Guild members</note>—a reflexive movement of great political importance.

The "Guild of Butchers" kept its primary rank during the revision and expansion of the Guilds in 1266. By that date, the two sections—the *Beccai* <note>Butchers</note> and the *Macellai* <note>Retailers/Slaughterers</note>—had likely discovered the benefits of cooperation and mutual respect.

In the list of Guilds revised in 1280 and 1282, the "Guild of Butchers" was awarded a further distinction. It was placed first among the "Five Intermediate Guilds," which were for many years classified among the "Twelve Greater Guilds."

This arrangement proved the importance and influence of the butchers' brotherhood in the Commonwealth, and it also led to the addition of a powerful company to the city’s militias. No Guild company carried its *gonfalon* <note>a heraldic banner or ensign</note> more proudly, or was capable of performing better in times of crisis, than these slaughterers, who were natural-born fighters.

By the end of the thirteenth century, the Guild's position and character were fully recognized. No brotherhood possessed a finer or more lavishly furnished residence than the one that housed its Consuls next to Or San Michele. Furthermore, no banner flew more proudly than theirs: a black goat on a yellow field—the Guild's coat of arms.

From the beginning, the *Beccai* faced a major natural challenge that required both intelligence and resources to overcome. The Arno Valley was a fertile garden, and land could hardly be spared for grazing grass. The uplands and the Tuscan hills provided only poor pasture—enough perhaps for raising sheep for wool, but unsuitable for fattening livestock for meat. Consequently, flocks and herds had to be driven to distant locations where richer grazing could be found.

Traveling back and forth, in and out of Tuscany, required heavy spending on shepherding and involved paying customs duties at the frontiers of foreign states. The risks of travel and the losses along the way...

<summary>This page describes the rise of the Guild of Butchers in Florentine society, highlighting their high rank among the guilds, their military prowess, and the geographical challenges they faced in sourcing livestock.</summary>
<keywords>Guild of Butchers, Beccai, Macellai, Five Intermediate Guilds, Twelve Greater Guilds, Or San Michele, Arno Valley, Tuscany, livestock trade, Florentine militias</keywords>

--- Page 407 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the economic challenges faced by the Guild of Butchers, specifically focusing on the costs of importing livestock from the surrounding uplands and the complexities of gate taxes and smuggling.</meta>

->### GUILD OF BUTCHERS<-

The costs were great, and everything conspired to drive up the selling price of livestock and meat. At the same time, an embargo was placed on, and maintained against, the export of livestock beyond the *Contado* <term>the rural territory surrounding the city</term>. The first recorded restriction of this type occurred in 1285.^1

With such a considerable importation of livestock and meat, it is understandable that many stories were common in the markets about clever tricks used to avoid paying the gate dues <term>taxes paid at the city gates</term>. It was not an uncommon practice to place *two* carcasses on the back of a mule or donkey and cover them well with greenery so that only *one* was visible and paid for! The risk of discovery, however, was serious. If caught by an over-diligent official, both the beast of burden and its load were confiscated; meanwhile, it was common knowledge that the seized carcasses were shared among the staff of the *Dogana* <term>customs house</term>! A *Provvisione* <term>a government decree or ordinance</term> was passed in the thirteenth century which ordered the arrest of the dishonest dealer, but he usually settled with the authorities by paying a fine!

The gate customs against commodities of all kinds significantly affected the interests of livestock dealers and retail butchers. Toward the end of the thirteenth century, while the selling price of a fat ox ranged from twelve to sixteen *lire*, the tax on the animal amounted to ten percent. In 1319, the *Gabella* <term>an indirect tax, specifically the tax on livestock at the gates</term> levied upon the breeders and butchers, brought in a high total of 1,185 gold florins—nearly £600.^2

Indeed, as a rule, it was more profitable to slaughter the animals outside the city and transport the carcasses and the hides or fleeces separately.

This issue of customs was constantly resurfacing. The need for organized efforts to counteract restrictive legislation made the services of the Consuls of the Guild <term>the elected chief magistrates of the guild</term> extremely important, not only to the members of the Guild but to the entire community of the city.

->### THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

Florence early on became a profitable center for the meat trade in Tuscany, which grew to significant proportions in the early years of the fourteenth century. The annual average of livestock for slaughter that entered the city was as follows: four thousand bulls and cows, sixty thousand sheep and lambs, and twenty thousand goats and bucks.^1

A decree from Duke Charles of Calabria, issued on May 16, 1327, ordered the "merchants of the <term>Guild of Butchers</term> <note>original: "Beccai"</note>" to drive more oxen and cows out of Apulia to provide provisions for the city.

Livestock breeders were required to go to the market themselves and drive only their own animals. Brokers or middle-men were not allowed to act as intermediaries between the breeders and the retail butchers. This injunction remained in effect for well over a hundred years, from 1346 to 1477.^2

The driving of cattle—whether to the slaughterhouses or elsewhere—was subject to strict regulations, and each animal was taxed. Larger cattle were taxed at eight to twelve <term>denari</term> <note>a small silver coin or unit of currency</note>, and small animals at four *denari* per head. Each animal had a label or ticket attached to its horn or throat with the owner's name written on it.^3 Cattle brought in from outside the territory by foreigners and sold in the market or at the city gates had to be slaughtered and the meat put on display that same evening. Wholesale butchers were strictly forbidden from selling to street hawkers until the amount of fresh meat typically required daily by the citizens had been provided and sold to the regular retail dealers.

Shrewd salesmen were in the habit of underselling the official daily market prices by four *denari* per pound. This evasion of the regulations was not only tolerated but actually encouraged by the authorities. It is difficult to understand the intention behind this inconsistency, though it may have been due to a paternalistic desire that all citizens—even the very poorest—might enjoy a better diet than was normally possible, at least during public festivals.^4

For a long period, the <term>Old Market</term> <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> was the principal center...

market of the Butchers. Around its four sides, open stalls were placed where meat for retail sale was displayed. Keeping meat for sale inside a house or store within the city was strictly forbidden, and covered shops were not allowed until well into the fourteenth century.¹

The new Ponte Vecchio, built by the State in 1345 at a cost of sixty thousand gold florins, featured a double row of shops. Forty-four of these were claimed by and granted to the "Guild of Butchers," and they remained occupied by its members until 1490, when the goldsmiths obtained them from Cosimo I.

Retail butchers in the market were not permitted to enter into partnerships with cattle dealers. They could not keep more than one assistant. They were required to live within five hundred yards of the Piazza Santa Croce, near which the <term>shambles</term> <note>slaughterhouses</note> were located.² Every butcher, before he was licensed to either slaughter or display meat, was compelled to be enrolled or registered in the "Guild of Butchers."

During the Patronal Festival of St. John <note>original: "San Giovanni"</note> in June, there was always a great increase in the supply of butcher's meat, which required many extra workers. At all such festivals, the prices to be charged by the <term>Macellai</term> <note>Butchers</note> were fixed by the Consuls of the Guild, and a price list was ordered to be displayed at every stall. The Guild's license was also required for all temporary assistants, and the amount of their wages was set by the Consuls.³

The <term>Macellai</term> could only buy fat cattle at the weekly public sales, and they were, by a <term>Provvisione</term> <note>legislative decree</note> of 1415, obliged to slaughter the animals within eight days of purchase. The slaughtering and dressing of meat were subject to strict regulations. These processes could only be carried out in certain localities outside the city and at fixed hours. The tax demanded by the State for the slaughtering of beasts was the same as the tax fixed for killing bears and wild boars, though the amount varied considerably over time.

-># GUILD OF BUTCHERS<-

The sale of pigs was completely prohibited in the Old and New Markets and in front of the <term>Podesta's Palace</term> <note>the residence of the city's chief magistrate, now known as the Bargello</note>. Fat pigs were not allowed to be kept in any residential house in the Borgo d'Ognissanti or any area bordering the river.¹

Butchers were forbidden from carrying beef tripe, the heads of bullocks and rams, or the hides of recently slaughtered animals through the <term>Mercato Vecchio</term> <note>Old Market</note>.²

Butchers, slaughterers, and innkeepers who sold fresh meat and cooked cuts were required to appear before the market authorities every January. They had to provide a security deposit of fifty *lire* and swear an oath to practice their trade honestly and loyally.

Tripe-sellers—whether men or women—sausage-makers, and cooks who prepared "snacks" at the smaller inns were also ordered to appear every January before the Notary of the Captains of <term>Or San Michele</term> <note>a grain market and shrine that served as the headquarters for many Florentine guilds</note> to swear obedience to the Guild Statutes.³

In a way that reflects an early refinement in the culinary tastes of the people, their preference for delicate meats became increasingly pronounced as the Renaissance progressed. For example, although beef and mutton were of excellent quality and cheaper, they were held in lower regard than veal and lamb. This preference has been noted by many writers, both serious and overly critical. This created a temptation for the guild of butchers to substitute coarser cuts for these finer delicacies—a temptation many of them succumbed to. However, such tradesmen gave the entire profession a bad name and reinforced the public's negative opinion regarding unfair business practices.

To prevent fraud and the substitution of meats, the Guild Consuls required that the carcasses of lambs and calves always be displayed for sale at the butcher stalls with their heads still attached.⁴

Associated with the butchers were the <term>Pescivendoli</term> <note>Fishmongers</note>, who were formally organized and governed by strict bylaws.

Fresh fish could only be sold in the loggia near the **Ponte Vecchio** and at certain butcher shops that were specially licensed by the market authorities. These shops were equipped with tanks where the fish had to be kept, as displaying them wholesale on stalls was strictly forbidden. Poisoning fish in the rivers or marshes was a criminal offense and was punished severely.¹

Tench <note>original: "Tinche"</note> from the lake in the **Val di Chiana** <note>a valley in eastern Tuscany</note> was sold at the following rates: large fish—weighing one pound or more—at two *soldi* per pound; small fish—weighing less than a pound—at one *soldo* and eight *denari*. Tench from the River Po <note>original: "Pado"</note> and from **Lombardy** followed the same prices. Tench from Bientina <note>original: "Brentina"</note>, Fucecchio <note>original: "Gusciana"</note>, and other places—being less highly regarded—were sold at lower rates. Eels from Val di Chiana and other localities varied in price from three *soldi* to one *soldo* and four *denari*. Lampreys, sardines, and other small fish were sold in bulk. Fees were levied on all fish at the city gates and quays at a certain percentage of the wholesale market price.

Innkeepers, butchers, and fishmongers were not allowed to enter into partnerships with people living in the country for the supply of fish; they were required to go to the markets or shops like everyone else.² Cooks were prohibited from buying fresh fish and then reselling it while still raw. Like all other citizens, they were also forbidden from keeping fish in aquaria, water-baskets, or other enclosures for indefinite periods.³

By order of the Captains of <term>Or San Michele</term> <note>the guild headquarters and market center</note> and other market magistrates, fresh meat, fresh and salt fish, and all perishable food items could not be offered for sale for more than a single day.⁴

The councils of the <term>Podesta</term> <note>the city's chief magistrate</note> and the <term>Captain of the People</term> <note>a high official representing the interests of the commoners</note>, and later the State Council of the <term>Signoria</term> <note>the supreme governing body of Florence</note>, were overwhelmed almost daily by people complaining about the poor quality of the meat and fish offered for sale in the market and the fraudulent practices of the butchers. In 1281, a case was addressed in which Brunetto Latini—Dante’s Master—proposed that the <term>Fourteen</term> <note>original: "Quattordici"; a governing council of Florence</note> should appoint expert inspectors who would, without being recognized, make random purchases of meat and fish. This was intended to detect any possible fraud or irregularity on the part of the retail dealers.¹

Heavy fines were imposed upon all unskillful and untidy workmen, and especially for carelessness in the disposal of offal, fish bones, and other waste. The bundling of hides and fleeces and their prompt removal from the <term>shambles</term> <note>slaughterhouses and meat markets</note> were strictly required. No class of tradesmen reveled so thoroughly and constantly in legal disputes as did the <term>Butchers</term> <note>original: "Beccai"</note>, the <term>Meat-sellers</term> <note>original: "Macellai"</note>, and the <term>Fishmongers</term> <note>original: "Pescivendoli"</note>—and somehow or other, they generally won their cases!

At the enactment of the General Code of Statutes for all the Guilds in 1301–1309, and again in 1346 and 1415, the “Guild of Butchers” maintained its position in the hierarchy of the Guilds. Under the Medici family, the importance of the Guild was constantly affirmed and duly acknowledged. For example, in the Parliament held on August 18, 1343, in the Church of Santa Maria del Fiore, Francesco di Giovanni, a member of the “Guild of Butchers,” was nominated to represent the <term>Common People</term> <note>original: "Popolo Minuto"</note>. He served alongside Filippo de’ Bardi and Tegghia de’ Bonacotti—representatives of the <term>Nobility</term> <note>original: "Grandi"</note> and the <term>Wealthy Merchant Class</term> <note>original: "Popolo Grasso"</note> respectively—to consult on public security. At this conference, by the way, the final step was taken by the <term>Governing Council</term> <note>original: "Signoria"</note> to expel the Duke of Athens <note>Walter VI of Brienne, a brief but tyrannical ruler of Florence</note>.

Under the Medici, the Guild thrived amazingly. The prosperity of all the citizens led to the increased enjoyment of all pleasures—those of the table always being foremost. During the celebration of <term>Jousts</term> <note>original: "Giostre"</note> and other festivals, hospitality was general and profuse: everyone feasted themselves and their neighbors, greatly to the financial profit of the <term>Butchers</term> <note>original: "Beccai"</note>.

On the enrollment of the Fourteen Lesser Guilds into four "Universities" <note>administrative groupings of guilds</note> in 1534, the <term>Guild of Butchers</term> <note>original: "Arte de’ Beccai"</note> was placed first in

They held a high rank in the premier University, along with the <term>Oil-merchants</term> <note>original: "Oliandoli"</note> and the <term>Bakers</term> <note>original: "Fornai"</note>—the city's other two food-supplying Guilds. The title “<term>The University of Saint Peter’s Gate</term>” <note>original: "Universita di Por San Piero"</note> was given to this union, a name derived from how close the Guilds' activities were to the gate of that name.

By the members of the Greater Guilds at large, the <term>Guild of Butchers</term> <note>original: "Arte de’ Beccai"</note> was looked upon with disdain. No citizens were held in lower esteem than the indispensable breeders and slaughterers of cattle. In fact, the proud manufacturers of the “Guild of Wool” ridiculed the Butchers for being dishonest and dubbed them <term>petty thieves</term> <note>original: "ladroncelli"</note>!

On their part, the Butchers were accustomed to return the "compliment":

> “You <term>Ciompi</term> <note>The lower-class laborers in the wool industry</note> care only for the wool which you fleece from your customers, while we, as honest men, sell good, healthy meat to feed you and make you fit for your work!” <sup>1</sup>

In any case, the Butchers of Florence did not have a good reputation for fair dealing, but in this regard, they shared the same reputation as the <term>Wine-merchants</term> <note>original: "Vinattieri"</note> and the <term>Innkeepers</term> <note>original: "Albergatori"</note>!

The Florentines of former times were mostly moderate in their consumption of meat. Sir Richard Dallington, writing at the close of the sixteenth century, says:

> “The working people average no more than <term>fourteen pounds</term> <note>original: "a stone weight"</note> of fresh meat per man per year.” <sup>2</sup>

This is probably considerably below the actual figure, for other travelers noted with astonishment and admiration the quality of eating and drinking enjoyed by all classes of the community.

Indeed, it is fair to say that much of the physical strength and vigor of the citizens—whether rich or poor—was, in great measure, due to a generous and nourishing diet. This opinion is confirmed when one remembers that meat-eating peoples have always been the rulers of cities and empires—namely the Romans, Florentines, and Britons!

## II. THE GUILD OF BLACKSMITHS <note>original: "L'Arte de' Fabbri"</note>

When focusing on Tuscany’s metalworkers, one must remember that the region is exceptionally rich in minerals—particularly lead, tin, copper, lignite, and iron oxides. The Etruscans were among the ancestors of the Florentines, and their skill in working iron and gold, in particular, placed them in the highest ranks of metalworking. They undoubtedly learned their art from Greek colonists and, in turn, became teachers to the Romans.

The island of Elba was an important source of mineral wealth long ago in ancient times, and the prosperity of the city of Popolonia was largely due to the mechanical arts of its citizens. At Monte Amiata, there was mercury, and other deposits included boracic crystals, Siena earths <note>Earth pigments such as raw and burnt sienna</note>, and salt.

While marble of endless variety and richness abounded all over the country—especially at Carrara and Massa—there do not appear to have been any coal deposits in Tuscany.

The earliest form of an iron forge was merely an excavation on the windward side of a hill or ridge. The exact date of the invention of cast iron is uncertain, but it was being produced by the fourteenth century. The discovery of this process was due to the adoption of larger furnaces and higher-pressure bellows.

Steel was developed in the middle of the sixteenth century. It was noted by Biringuccio in 1540 and described by Agricola in "*On the Nature of Metals*" <note>original: "De Re Metallica"</note> in 1561. They observed that a bar of wrought iron, if kept immersed for a long time in molten cast iron, became <term>steel-plated</term> <note>original: "acierated"</note> by absorbing the carbon from the cast iron.

Saint Eligius was regarded as the patron saint of blacksmiths. He worked as a journeyman in a smithy, but after gaining the attention of King Dagobert <note>King of the Franks, r. 629–639</note>, he was appointed as the court treasurer and master of the mint. In the year 640, he was promoted to the Bishopric of Noyon. Among his charitable works was the founding of a monastery for smiths at Solignac, near Limoges; in connection with this, he also established a school for metalworkers.

Many extraordinary stories are told of the saintly Blacksmith <note>St. Eligius (Saint Eloi), the patron saint of metalworkers</note> and his spiritual powers. On one occasion, at any rate, he is reported to have performed an astonishing miracle. A horse brought to his smithy to be shod became possessed by a demon, who caused him to buck and kick so violently that no one could shoe him. St. Eligius determined to finish the job; he immediately chopped off one of the horse's legs and, having nailed a shoe to the hoof without difficulty, he instantly restored the severed limb, thereby defeating the Evil One!

After the death of the Countess Matilda, the industries of Florence and all of Tuscany prospered exceedingly. Her artisans, no less than her merchants, displayed admirable enterprise and resourcefulness. Many of the descendants of ancient noble houses, who had fallen on hard times because of the competition from the *Popolani* <note>The wealthy merchant class or "well-to-do citizens"</note> and the *Popolo Minuto* <note>The "small people" or lower-class workers</note>, joined forces with the common citizens. The crafts that most attracted them were those that appealed to their warlike instincts, and they enrolled themselves as apprentices in the trade associations that dealt in metal, stone, and wood.

Smithing was by far the most popular handicraft, as one may easily understand by noting the great number of noble names that appeared early on the Membership Rolls of the "Blacksmiths," the "Locksmiths," the "Armourers," and the "Masters of Stone and Wood." These young men brought to their adopted work the strength and muscle developed by an active life in the open air.

The Archives of Florence contain the following records from the eleventh and twelfth centuries:

> “1038, Olivus, *faber* <note>original: "faber"—Blacksmith</note>.”
> “1141, Bernerius, son of Barlittario <note>original: "fil. Barlittario"—Bellfounder</note>.”
> “1146, Uguccione, *Calderarius* <note>original: "Calderarius"—Coppersmith</note>.”

In the year 1038, as many as six Blacksmiths are named; in 1065, two more appear; and in 1080, six others are listed, all practicing their craft within the bounds of the *Contado* <term>the rural territory surrounding the city</term>. In 1174, a piece of land in

The *Arte de' Fabbri* <term>Guild of Blacksmiths</term> ranked tenth in the list of the guilds in 1236, and it retained that position in the revisions of 1266, 1280–82, and 1301–09. In 1415, however, the “Guild of Blacksmiths” ranked ninth, displacing the “Guild of Shoemakers.”

---

Little or no trace remains of the early statutes of the guild. What has been preserved—as was the case with the other Lesser Guilds—is written in a mixed jargon of low Latin and abbreviated vernacular that is very difficult to decipher. A document from 1274 states that the Smiths then had twelve <term>Rectors</term> <note>administrative officers</note> who, according to the regulations of the guild, received salaries ranging from eighteen to six <term>denari</term> <note>small silver coins</note> for their terms of office.¹ Because this number was found to be too large, only six Rectors were elected the following year. The number of <term>Consuls</term> <note>the highest-ranking executive officers</note> varied from three to five in later times. The larger number indicated prosperous times and *vice versa* <note>original Latin: "the opposite being true"</note>.

At a council of Consuls and <term>Capitudini</term> <note>heads of the various guilds</note> held in 1286, a petition was presented to the Priors of the Guilds on behalf of the Rectors of the “Guilds of Blacksmiths” and “Locksmiths.” It requested, first, that no one should be permitted—within the confines of the city and the <term>Contado</term> <note>the rural territory or countryside surrounding the city</note>—to set up a smith’s forge, a smelting furnace, or a puddling yard for the manufacture of metal wire, thin plates, and metal objects, except for members of the two guilds, under penalty of a fine of one thousand <term>lire</term>.

The second article in the petition requested that no one, except members of the said guilds, should be allowed to process metal wire into sheets or do metalwork of any kind within the same limits, except under a fine of one hundred *lire*. The third article required that all such manufactured goods should be confiscated and destroyed, whether they were found in smithies and shops or loaded

<meta>This page continues the detailed regulations for the various branches of the Blacksmiths' Guild (Arte de’ Fabbri), specifically focusing on quality control for metalworkers, price controls for farriers, and public conduct rules for scrap-iron dealers.</meta>

<page-num>310</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

<term>Fornaciai</term> <note>Furnacemen or kiln-workers</note> and <term>Calderai</term> <note>Coppersmiths</note> were subject to strict rules regarding the location, construction, and contents of their furnaces and cauldrons. Inspectors visited all foundries and iron workshops from time to time to ensure that the quality of the metals and the proportions of the mixtures were precisely maintained. Fines were imposed for inferior materials and poor workmanship, and any improper alloy—whether in the furnace or the casting bath—was confiscated. 1

<term>Manescalchi</term> <note>Farriers</note> were forbidden from charging ordinary citizens more than three to four *soldi* for a shoe for a horse, a mule, or a pony. The price of a shoe for a young mule or a donkey was two *soldi* and six *denari*. Very large shoes were charged as much as six *soldi*. Removing a shoe, or a part of one, cost one-third of these amounts. Farrier shops were required to be open from dawn to dusk every day, except for Sundays and Festivals, when it was forbidden to do any farrier work. 2

<term>Ferravecchi</term> <note>Scrap-iron dealers</note> were restricted in how they conducted their business. They were not allowed under any circumstances to go through the streets shouting: “*Old iron or old brass for sale!*” <note>original: “Ferro vecchio, vel rame vecchio a vendere!”</note> Offenders were punished with fines of fifty *lire*, and they were required to provide a security deposit of fifty silver florins to guarantee their good behavior. Smiths worked only for ready money and allowed no credit. 3

An idea of the Guild’s financial position can be gathered from the fact that in the general taxation of the Guilds in 1321, the <term>Arte de’ Fabbri</term> <note>Blacksmiths' Guild</note> was assessed a sum of four hundred *lire*—a relatively small amount—while the Furnacemen were charged a separate assessment of ninety-two *lire*.

The Statutes of the Guild were revised and expanded in 1344, 1415, 1472, 1525, and 1541. The final date records a proposal to unite the Blacksmiths of Florence and Pisa.

When Cosimo I, the first Grand Duke, established four “Universities” to include the Fourteen Lesser Guilds, the third was named the “*University of Manufacturers*” <note>Universita de’ Fabbricanti</note>—the University of Iron—

The residence of the Guild’s Consuls was located behind the Mint <note>original: “Zecca”</note>, just off the Via de' Lamberteschi. On its facade were several finely molded and hammered iron torch-sconces and banner-holders. In the latter were placed the standard <note>original: “Gonfalon”</note> of the Guild, which bore the coat of arms assigned to the Blacksmiths by Count Guido Novelli in 1266—a pair of furnace tongs on a white field.

->. . . . .<-

The wrought-iron work of the Italian Renaissance was essentially unique <note>original: “sui generis”</note>. Gothic models were unknown, and the influence of Byzantine craftsmen and the masters of antiquity was very faint. It appears the common method of working was to beat out a thin, flat metal surface and then punch holes through it or stamp designs upon it. No finer example of this flat-work exists than the screen at Santa Maria Novella, which is dated 1366.<gloss>1</gloss>

At the beginning of the fourteenth century, metal casting had become a staple industry in Florence. Among the early workers—who were both artists and craftsmen—were Cione, Ugolino, Giglio, Piero, Leonardo, and Nofai. In 1343, the Duke of Athens, fearing personal violence, introduced a novel form of window protection: iron gratings or bars. He commissioned the “Guild of Blacksmiths” to install these defenses at his palace. The fashion grew, and window gratings eventually became some of the finest examples of the blacksmith’s skill. This trend was further developed in 1506 and the following years by Michelangelo, who introduced what were called “kneeling gratings”—that is, bowed iron protections for windows.

The “Masters of Stone and Wood” imposed their style of craftsmanship upon their fellow metalworkers, and many wrought

iron lanterns and countless other objects are handled as though the material were stone or wood. This style was shown in its ultimate perfection by a famous member of the Guild, Niccolo Grosso (1455–1509). Vasari calls him “*Il Caparra*” —“Money Grabber” <note>original: "*Il Caparra*"</note> —from his habit of demanding payment for his work in advance! His specialty was <term>fanali</term>—flare-baskets or lanterns—such as those that still exist on the walls of the Strozzi, Guardagni, Pazzi, Borgherino, Riccardi, and Quaratesi Palaces.

The grille-work of Florence is unsurpassed outside of Tuscany. The primary features of Florentine workmanship include the fineness of the iron wire and bars, perfection in hammering, the beauty of scrolls and curves, the realistic nature of floral ornaments, the high quality of the bosses and masks, the neatness of the joints and knobs, and the grace of the molded volutes with their curling tendrils.

The exquisite grilles in the Campo Santo at Santa Croce, which were installed in 1371, consist of punched ironwork with chiseled caps, bases, and moldings; they were finished through patient work with files and pincers. It is interesting to note once again the influence of the “Masters of Stone and Wood” in the iron joinery and carving, which resemble fine woodwork more than traditional blacksmithing.

In contrast to the ornate work of Flemish and German craftsmen, Florentine smiths always maintained a restraint and dignity that were perfectly in keeping with their natural temperament.

The fifteenth century saw the art of metalworking reach its peak. The great sculptors were accustomed to employing the services of blacksmiths to forge and cast their splendid bronze works. A vast number of intelligent craftsmen were busy creating metal doors and gates for the Baptistery and the Cathedral <note>original: "Duomo"</note>—the timeless and precious creations of the Pisani, L. Ghiberti, and Luca Della Robbia.

Other skilled members of the Guild assisted Donatello, Verrocchio, Giovanni da Bologna, and Benvenuto Cellini in producing the masterpieces <note>original: "*chefs d’œuvre*"</note> that bear their names. These were men of the forge and bellows, men of the anvil and hammer, men

<header>GUILD OF BLACKSMITHS</header>

Using soldering irons and smoothing files, they all worked with the typical Florentine diligence and intelligence.

Combining wrought-iron work with brass and bronze was a Tuscan innovation. Countless objects fall into this category: wall sockets, shields displaying Guild coats of arms, tavern signs, baptismal font covers, reading desks, candelabra, door knockers, gargoyles, weather vanes, architectural ornaments, and household items. Even the workmen’s tools were never entirely without decorative features.

The iron fixtures—brackets and rings—attached to the walls of palaces and other buildings were designed to hold torches. They were equipped with iron rings for athletic torch-bearers to grip as they secured their flaming trophies into the sockets. They were also used to support banner poles during festivals. These items demonstrate how artistic design was adapted for common objects.

Fanlights, balcony railings, firebacks and firedogs, frames of all kinds, and many other objects that required both strength and elegance formed another category. Once again, the smiths looked to the “Masters of Stone and Wood” and sought their models and patterns in floors, wall panels, and ceiling vaults, or even in *intarsiatura* <note>wood inlay</note> or mosaic.

Among the curiosities of the blacksmith’s craft were the iron tongs used for stamping the festival cakes of the Guilds, which were eaten on the Feast of Saint John the Baptist and on the anniversaries of the Guilds. The stamps created images of saints or Guild emblems; for example, the Blacksmiths' cakes featured an embossed hammer in the center, while the Butchers' had a cow or a ram, and so on.

<margin>✓ Smiths wore thick and heavy leather aprons while working, which they could tie tightly around their legs with leather straps cut from the same hide. A blacksmith's entire set of tools cost about one gold florin, or about twelve shillings in our currency.</margin>

By the sixteenth century, the smiths of Florence were enjoying the peak of their craft’s excellence and refinement. Every workman was an artist, capable of working from any design submitted to him, or to

They created original and beautiful objects with spontaneous creativity. Two specialized lines of superior metalwork were portrait medallions, historical plaques, and bronzes. Those whose fame among metalworkers is most widely known were: Niccolo Fiorentino, Giamgallo Poggini, Bertoldo, Petrellino, Niccolo Domenico, Antonio del Pollaiuolo, Andrea Guazzoloti of Prato, Domenico Poggini, Antonio Averlino, Michelozzo Michelozzi, and, last but not least, Donatello, whose dates range from 1460 to 1557.

In any school or nation, nothing surpasses the delicacy, naturalness, brilliant composition, and high finish of the works by these *“Masters of metal.”* Examples of their skill may be seen in every archaeological and art museum, but none is as rich as the Bargello in Florence.

The names of many descendants of famous noble families were enrolled in the annals of the “Guild of Blacksmiths.” To mention one among many, the Acciaiuoli were steel manufacturers—as their name implies <note>The name Acciaiuoli is derived from the Italian word *acciaio*, meaning steel</note>—who came from Brescia in the year 1160 and rose to high status. After the banking disasters in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, Niccolo restored the honor of his house while he ruled the Kingdom of Naples. He married the widowed Empress of Constantinople, built the Certosa <note>A Carthusian monastery</note> near the Porta Romana, and founded a School of Liberal Arts for studious apprentices.

### III. THE SHOEMAKERS’ GUILD <note>original: "L'Arte de' Calzolai"</note>

In every land, footwear—both useful and ornamental—plays an important role. Protection during working hours and decoration during times of leisure are both necessary and attractive.

<margin>✓</margin>
As to who first wore coverings on their feet, nobody knows and probably nobody cares; however, no age and no nation has ever been without them. Every conceivable material—both natural and manufactured—has been utilized, and man's skill has been called upon throughout all time to create adaptive designs.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Shoemakers' Guild (Arte dei Calzolai), focusing on the historical importance of leather and the early archival records of the guild's ranking and organization in Florence.</meta>

<page-num>315</page-num>
<header>GUILD OF SHOEMAKERS</header>

Leather has always been the ideal material for boots and shoes of all kinds. Strong, waterproof, flexible under pressure, and easy to clean, it has surpassed all other competitors. The craft of shoemaking has also enriched countless artists of the <term>last</term> <note>A "last" is a mechanical form shaped like a human foot, used by shoemakers to fashion and repair shoes</note>, while the whims of Fashion have demanded artistic workmanship and added to both the joys and sorrows of human life.

Early in the Middle Ages, Tuscan leather was famous, and even before the Renaissance, Florentine shoemakers had established a reputation and acquired wealth. A document exists in the City Archives which records that, in the year 1139, one "John, son of Peter, who is called the Shoemaker <note>original Latin: "Johannes filius Petri qui vocatur Calzolarius"</note>, bestowed a donation upon the *Hospital of the Shoemakers* <note>original Italian: "Spedale de' Calzolai"</note>, in the Val di Pesa, near Florence."

Very little information can be gathered from the City Archives regarding the beginning and progress of the Shoemakers' Guild. The earliest sets of statutes have been lost, and the later records are either very fragmentary or written in an abbreviated and illegible manner. Furthermore, they are written in a language not easily understood by modern readers and students—being partly Latin and partly the local dialect.

At first glance, the "Guild of Tanners" should have occupied the place in the hierarchy of the guilds that is held by the Shoemakers, both because of the more general nature of its interests and the social importance of its members.

The earliest mentions in the Archives of people working in the shoemaking trade are as follows:
> "1087. Rusticus—Shoemaker <note>original Latin: "Calzolarius"</note>."
> "1113. John—Wooden-clog maker <note>original Latin: "Johannes—Zocolarius"</note>."

In the first list of the guilds—that of 1236—the "*Shoemakers' Guild*" <note>original Italian: "Arte de' Calzolai"</note> is placed ninth in order. This position was maintained during the revisions of the Guild Statutes in 1266, 1282, and 1301–1309. However, in 1415, the "Guild of Blacksmiths" was promoted above the Shoemakers, who were then moved down to the tenth rank in the guild hierarchy. This remained the final position of the Guild.

When Cosimo de' Medici grouped the Fourteen Lesser Guilds into four "Universities" in 1534, the second was styled

The "University of the Masters of Leatherwork" <note>original Italian: "Universita’ de’ Maestri di Cuoiame"</note> included the three Guilds of Shoemakers, Tanners, and Saddlers in their proper order.

The number of Consuls varied between three and six. This was a common feature among the chief officers of the guilds in general, and it was probably due to the nature of the business that engaged the Consuls' attention in the General Council from time to time. Their residence was in the Chiasso de’ Baronelli, almost next door to the headquarters of the "Guild of Skinners and Furriers." The Guild's coat of arms was displayed there, as well as on their banner <note>original: "Gonfalon"</note>, and consisted of alternating red and white stripes.

The enrollment fee was very low—nearly the lowest of any such payments made for guild membership. Under the year 1290, the Archives of Florence record that one Ricchus Borredicti, a shoemaker of the Parish <note>original: "Popoli"</note> of San Giorgio and a Syndic <term>A syndic was a legal representative or business manager for a corporate body like a guild.</term> of the Guild, received forty soldi per person for the entrance of new members.

2. *Zoccalai*—Wooden shoemakers (clog-makers).
3. *Zoccholi*—Sandal-makers.
4. *Ciabattini*—Cobblers, who were considered an inferior class.

The Statutes of 1415 contain the following sections <note>original: "rubrics"</note>: "Shoemakers, slipper-makers, and any other persons selling fine skins, scraps, or any kind of leather, are warned not to offer common dressed goatskins as Spanish morocco <note>High-quality goatskin leather originally from Morocco, often imitated by inferior processing.</note>, and not to pass off inferior leathers as better qualities. A fine of eighty soldi was charged for each instance of such substitution." ^1

"Shoemakers are forbidden to open their shops or keep their assistants at work on Sundays and festivals. The Guild Consuls are required to make all Master craftsmen swear to observe this regulation, subject to a penalty of one hundred lire for each offense. ^2 To avoid unfair competition and trade disputes with the 'Guild of Tanners,' shoemakers and all members of their guild are strictly ordered not to process, or have processed on their premises, horse skins or cattle hides." ^3

"Sandal and clog-makers seem to have been a somewhat transient group, for in one of the sections, there is an amusing warning to shoemakers and other respectable members of the guild not to shelter any such wandering characters. No chests, coffers, boxes, or trunks were to be left unlocked or open, lest any poor fellow should hide inside them. The objective was undoubtedly to prevent Masters from profiting from the illegal work of unauthorized workmen. Perhaps, even with all the elaborate rules and regulations that favored fair trade, lower-level workers were subject to 'sweating' <term>'Sweating' refers to the exploitation of laborers through long hours and very low wages, often in poor conditions.</term>." ^4

"Leather shoes are not to be sold if made of horse and goat skin mixed and advertised as being made of horsehide only. Thigh pieces of armor <margin>*</margin> may be lined with goatskin, and kid leather is permissible as a decorative addition to shoes and footwear generally." ^5

In December 1292, the Heads or Consuls of the *Arte de' Calzolai* <note>Guild of Shoemakers</note> took part in the deliberations of the Consuls of the Seven Greater Guilds, and again in December 1293 with the Consuls of the Twelve Greater Guilds.¹

That the dignity of the Guild and its Consuls was equal to that of the other trade corporations is proved by the appointment in 1301 of Benedetto da Carlona, a sandal-maker, as one of the Priors of the *Sestiere* <term>Sestiere: One of the six districts or wards of Florence</term> of San Spirito.

On the other hand, the financial position of the Guild was inferior. In 1321, when a proportional tax was levied upon the Guilds, the sum required from the “Shoemakers” was only one hundred *lire*, compared to two thousand gold florins contributed by the “Guild of Wool” and fifty gold florins by the “Guild of Carpenters.”

The *Zibaldoni* <term>Zibaldoni: Commonplace books or informal notebooks containing various records and anecdotes</term>, and other private records, are remarkably lacking in mentions of the “Guild of Shoemakers.” It is, however, recorded that one of its members became famous at the siege of Capraia in 1249, when the Guelphs were besieged by the Emperor Frederic II. Giovanni del Tosco—who had been one of the "ancients" <term>Ancients: 'Anziani,' high-ranking city officials or elders</term> and was a man of wealth and influence—went to the gates of the town and shouted that the place could only hold out for one more day. This so greatly discouraged the besieged that they surrendered unconditionally. Two years later, del Tosco paid for his treachery. He entered Florence among other returning exiles, but upon being recognized, he was stoned to death by the people, and his body was thrown into the moat!

## CHAPTER XI

### THE GUILDS OF MASTERS OF STONE AND WOOD, AND OF RETAIL CLOTH-DEALERS AND LINEN MANUFACTURERS.

#### *The Guilds of the Masters of Stone and Wood, and of the Retailers* <note>original: "LE ARTI DE' MAESTRI DI PIETRA E DI LEGNAME, E DE' RIGATTIERI"</note>

##### I. MASTERS OF STONE AND WOOD

ORIGIN.—The great <term>Comacine Guild</term> <note>A powerful medieval guild of stonemasons centered around Lake Como</note>. <term>Freemasons</term>. <term>Travelling lodges</term> <note>original: "Ambulatory lodges"</note>. <term>Grandi</term> <note>The old noble families of Florence</note> and artisans. In any book dealing with the subject of Guilds, it is quite impossible to overlook that great organization of the Early Middle Ages—*“The <term>Comacine Guild</term> of Masters.”* The origin

The origin of this Brotherhood is lost in antiquity; it was probably a survival of ancient Jewish and Egyptian times. <note>Leader Scott, "The Cathedral Builders," p. 10.</note> Fugitive craftsmen from all parts of Italy, driven from their homes and trades by invading barbarians, sought refuge upon the little island of Comacina in Lake Como. The Lombard chieftains extended protection and patronage to them. The settlement became known as the *Casari* or *Casarii*—house-builders <note>original: "Casari or Casarii"</note>. Muratori first discovered traces of its existence in an edict dated November 22, 643, signed by King Rotharis the Lombard. This edict mentions the "Comacine Masters" <note>original: "Magistri Comacini"</note> as being designers and superintendents of buildings and builders, whom we may classify together under the modern term "architects."

These Master-builders, whose creative skill is evidenced across all of Italy, had formed themselves into a vast University by the year 590 for mutual protection and advancement, though they had no central college or fixed residence. According to their motto, their "Temple was made without hands."

> "The old records," writes a quaint and concise writer, <note>Desagulier, "Constitutions of the Free Masons."</note> "of Masons afford many hints of their Lodges existing from the beginning of the world among civilized nations. . . . Masons were always favored by the prominent and became necessary for their great undertakings in any sort of materials—not only in stone, brick, timber, and plaster, but even in cloth or skins, or whatever was used for tents, and for all sorts of architecture. . . . Painters and sculptors were also always considered good Masons as much as builders, stone-cutters, bricklayers, carpenters, joiners, upholsterers, or tent-makers."

Two early patrons of the Comacine builders were Queen Theodolinda, who in 737 instructed them to draw plans for and proceed with the construction of the Cathedral of Monza, and Saint Calixtus, to whom the Cathedral of Friuli is due.

...and 1000 A.D. were the handiwork of the Comacine Masters, several institutions were established: 1. *Scholæ*—Schools for novices; 2. a *Laborerum*—a workshop for laborers; and 3. an *Opera fabbrica*—an office for architects. <note>original: "Opera fabbrica"</note>¹

The workers employed by the Guild were divided into two classes: *murarii* (builders) and *operarii* (laborers).

The Senior Master-builder was called the *Capo Maestro* <note>Italian: "Head Master"</note>, and he was assisted by two or more *Soprastanti* (supervisors). These assistants were responsible for drafting specifications and managing the financial affairs of the members. Consequently, all the organizational structure required for a properly established craft guild was already in place, and at an early date, the Comacine Masters were recognized as members of a worldwide Order of Freemasons.²

Members of these Lodges, regardless of their rank, were treated as a privileged class and were exempt from local military service. They also enjoyed the freedom to travel and the right to seek employment wherever they chose.

The term “Freemason,” as applied to Master-builders, first appears in manuscripts from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In these documents, terms such as *Sculptores lapidum liberorum* <note>Latin: "sculptors of free stones"</note> and *Latonii vocati fremacconi* <note>Latin/Medieval Italian: "stone-cutters called freemasons"</note> were used interchangeably to describe those who worked with freestone. Master craftsmen in stone and wood were originally classified as Freemasons and were considered a separate class from ordinary stonemasons and common carpenters.

Formal enrollment—matriculation—made a significant difference in status between a master and a common laborer. For this reason, the intermediate "Guild of Masters in Stone and Wood" in Florence was named in a way that perfectly suited both historical fact and local custom.

The actual work of a *Maestro di Pietra* (Master of Stone) involved virgin stone—that is, freestone—rather than marble. A clear distinction was made between a worker in *lapis liber* <note>Latin: "free stone"</note> and a worker in *saxum vivum* <note>Latin: "living rock"</note>. The former was considered a simple stonemason, while the latter was a skilled sculptor or "Master."

Regarding woodworkers, a “*Master of Wood*” <note>original: "Maestro di Legname"</note> was someone capable of constructing scaffolding and building roofs, while a “*Master of Carving*” <note>original: "Maestro d’ Intaglio"</note> was a woodcarver or inlayer. This division into four classes of craftsmen was completed by a fifth group called the “*Masters of Design*” <note>original: "Maestri del Disegno"</note>, who served as architects.

Every mobile “Lodge” or permanent “Temple” of the Guild or Order was staffed by representatives from each of these categories. As projects became more long-term, the rules and conditions governing building operations became increasingly permanent. One such permanent center was established in Florence during the thirteenth century, at a time when massive construction projects were underway.

The stone-cutting and woodworking crafts were likely the earliest trade corporations in medieval Florence. Under Charlemagne, who visited Florence many times, the industry grew steadily; during the reign of Lothair, it flourished throughout Tuscany.¹

During the period when the *First People* <note>original: "Primo Popolo"</note>—the middle class composed of united nobles and merchants—was gradually being established, another alliance was formed: that between the disinherited sons of ruined noble families <note>original: "Grandi"</note> and working artisans. Descended from lineages of military captains, many young men had to set aside their family pride and join honest craftsmen rather than beg for food. Since they were trained to serve in the ranks of the *Condottieri* (leaders of mercenary troops), tools of labor were as easy for them to handle as weapons of war.

The two professions that most appealed to these men were stonemasonry and woodworking. This is evident from the Guild's membership registers, where the names of ancient noble families appear repeatedly.

It is nearly impossible to provide an exact date for when the Florentine Lodge of Freemasons—the Master Builders of the great Comacine Guild—merged into the “*Guild of the Masters of Stone* <note>original: "Arte de’ Maestri di Pietra"</note>...

“…and of Wood” <note>original: “e di Legname”</note>. The use of the word “Lodge” comes from the custom of holding meetings of the brotherhood in the “*Loggie*” <note>covered porticoes or arcades</note> or porches of houses. The first mention of Master-builders—including both masons and woodworkers—in the Florentine archives occurs in the year 1038, when “John, who is called the wood-turner” <note>original: “Johannis qui tornario vocatus est”</note> is named. In 1094, the first record of a stone-mason appears as follows: “Baldus (?) of the Marble Court” <note>original: “Baldus (?) curtis de Marmorio”</note>. They undoubtedly worked alongside many fellow craftsmen. Throughout the eleventh and twelfth centuries, the *Schools* <note>original: “Scholæ”</note>, the *Workshops* <note>original: “Laborerum”</note>, and the *Works Offices* <note>original: “Opera Fabbrica”</note> were administered under steadily improving leadership and with better equipment.

The *Schools*, while focusing primarily on the essential elements of construction, gradually provided their pupils with the technical skills of architecture, sculpture, and even painting. Sons and nephews of Masters were entitled to enrollment by hereditary right without serving a novitiate <term>a period of apprenticeship or probation</term>, but outsiders were subjected to a rigorous preparatory course. Certain Masters were appointed to teach pupils and apprentices privately in their own studios, as well as through the public projects of the *Schools*. These teachers were chosen from among the most distinguished individuals who had progressed through the *Workshops*.

The *Workshop*, or shop for workmen, provided employment opportunities for every registered and approved member who had not yet been promoted to the rank of Master. In the old manuscripts, these men were called “brothers” <note>original: “fratres”</note>; they were, in a sense, the graduates of the guild’s education system. A successful tenure in the *Workshop* opened the way to professional commissions and fame. It was here that genius could flourish, and brotherly rivalry led to magnificent results.

<margin>➤</margin>
The *Works Office* <note>original: “Opera Fabbrica”</note> served as the headquarters for the Master-builders. All plans, specifications, and estimates were prepared and displayed there. Contracts were signed between the patron and the builder, and down payments <term>earnest money</term> were exchanged. This office also managed the registration of workpeople and their assignment to various construction tasks. Communications between the *Works Office*...

In the early years of the thirteenth century, separate associations appear from time to time in the public records, for example: "Master Wood-cutters" <note>original: "Maestri dell' Ascia"</note>, "Master Bricklayers" <note>original: "Maestri di Muratori"</note>, and "Architects" <note>original: "Maestri d' Architetti"</note>.

In the classification of the guilds in 1236 and 1266, "Bricklayers and Stone-masons" <note>original: "Muratori e Scarpellini"</note> appear tenth on the list; this was the earliest name for the Guild of Master Builders in Florence.

The title "Masters of Stone and Wood" <note>original: "Maestri di Pietra e di Legname"</note> was first used in 1282, but its origins date back to the year 1260. Jacopino Rangoni of Modena was then the *Podesta* <term>the chief magistrate or city administrator</term> of Florence, and he took energetic measures to prepare for the war with Siena.

Twelve Captains of War were chosen—two for each *sestiere* <note>a district or one-sixth part of the city</note>—to raise companies of cavalry and infantry. Of these companies, two were composed of men skilled in the use of picks, axes, saws, planes, and other similar tools. They were given the name "Masters of Stone and Wood" <note>original: "Maestri di Pietra e di Legname"</note>. They formed the vanguard of the city's companies—the position of both conflict and honor.

During the revision of the statutes and bylaws of all the guilds in 1282 and between 1301 and 1309, these companies maintained their military organization while integrating the system of industrial incorporation. Thus, they became a powerful and enterprising order within the hierarchy of the guilds.

The guild was further honored in 1293 by Giano della Bella. Just before leaving the office of Prior <term>one of the high-ranking magistrates of the city</term>, he pushed a decree <note>original: "Provvisione"</note> through the State Council to increase the Chief Magistrate's personal guard to one thousand men. He called upon the consuls of the "Guild of Stone-masons and Wood-workers" to provide the first, or leading, company of two hundred men, fifty of whom were to be armed

with heavy picks." Naturally, these military units consisted of skilled stonemasons and woodworkers rather than Master Builders. Regarding the latter, the historian Villani records that at the beginning of 1299, at least 146 men held the Guild's license as Master Builders, overseeing the work of more than 2,000 practicing stonemasons and woodworkers. Furthermore, some of these masters were appointed to manage the foreign workmen who crowded into the city and petitioned the Guild officials for employment.

Renaissance Masters—whether they were designers or architects, scaffold or roof specialists, stonemasons or bricklayers, sculptors or carvers—were the direct descendants of ancient woodcutters and stone carvers. Consequently, an inherited instinct was visible in the games and hobbies of their children. Young children enthusiastically built miniature palaces and churches with the same passion shown by their parents and older brothers. Every alley <note>original: "Chiasso"</note> and courtyard <note>original: "Cortile"</note> became, for the time being, a brickyard or a mason's workshop, while many a future "master" displayed his skill and creativity using mud, sand, and wood shavings!

The Consuls of the Guild are recorded as participating in the negotiations organized in 1280 by Cardinal Latino dei Frangipani, acting as a Papal Legate <term>a personal representative of the Pope</term>, for the purpose of reconciling the Guelph and Ghibelline factions <note>The Guelphs supported the Pope and the Ghibellines supported the Holy Roman Emperor</note>. These Consuls, along with those from the Guilds of "Calimala" <note>The merchants of foreign cloth</note>, "Wool," "Bankers and Money-changers," "Skinners and Furriers," and "Retail Cloth Dealers," did not support the negotiations. Consequently, nothing was achieved except for a further increase in the power of the Guelph Party <note>original: "Parte Guelfa"</note>.

During the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, there seem to have been three Consuls; at least, that number is cited as attending the joint conferences of the Twelve Major Guilds. They undoubtedly performed the same roles as the Comacine <note>Referring to the Comacine Masters, a prestigious guild of stonemasons from the Lake Como region</note> Master-in-Chief <note>original: "Capo Maestro"</note>. For assistants, they also had two supervisors <note>original: "Soprastanti"</note> who held the titles of "Chancellor" <note>original: "Cancelliere"</note> and "Chamberlain" <note>original: "Camerlingo"</note>—mirroring the officials in the other Guilds.

cautions and notices that were issued from time to time to improve the organization and discipline of the craftsmen. One example will suffice. In June 1456, the Superintendent <term>Provveditore</term> issued the following notice: "It is ordered that under no circumstances shall any Master work outside the Works Department <term>Opera</term> without the discussion and consent of all four Directors <term>Operai</term>. If anyone absents himself without this permission, he shall be considered dismissed."1

The office of Superintendent <term>Provveditore</term> was no easy job, due to the constant disputes between masters and workers; however, he was assisted by two arbitrators <term>Buonuomini</term>, who served as mediators in trade disputes and also audited the Guild’s accounts.

When "Masters" were unhappy with their pay—since all commissions were handled in the name of the Guild and were not paid directly by patrons to individual workers—or when workers went on strike, it was customary to call for help from independent parties. For example, in the Cathedral Works <term>Opera del Duomo</term>, all disagreements were brought before the Consuls and Council of the "Wool Guild," which was in charge of the various projects. They requested estimates and progress reports, and after lengthy discussions, matters were usually settled by compromise, setting standard rates for pay and timelines.

Regarding issues affecting the Guild’s internal operations, the members of the Building Works Office <term>Opera Fabbrica</term> and the instructors of the Workshop <term>Laborerum</term> formed a deliberative council. All Masters were bound to the Workshop <term>Laborerum</term> by contract. Sometimes they were paid by the day, and at other times, they agreed to piecework.

Of course, many men—both skilled and unskilled—were employed at various times for the vast building contracts undertaken by the Guild. These men were not enrolled in the primary Craft Guild <term>Craft-major</term>, but were instead organized into trade unions or associations for the duration of the works, each with its own specific officers and regulations, though all were subordinate to the Guild itself.

When Francesco Talenti was <term>Head Master</term> <note>Italian: *Capo Maestro*</note>, many meetings were held to settle matters of detail. In June 1353, one such meeting ordered the removal of the scaffolding from the new Baptistery. In August of the same year, wooden scale models of the <term>Bell Tower</term> <note>Italian: *Campanile*</note> were ordered to be made to judge dimensions and decorative features. 

The following month, the “Masters” were anxious about the financial position of the Guild. A Notary was appointed to pressure the <term>Signoria</term> <note>The governing council of Florence</note> for the payment of one hundred and fifty *lire* due to the Guild. Furthermore, he was to consult with the <term>Auditors</term> <note>original: "Regolatori"</note> and the captains of the <term>Misericordia</term> <note>A prominent Florentine charitable brotherhood</note> regarding the settlement of certain legacies left in the wills of deceased members of the Guild.¹

At another meeting in the following year, the *free supply of wine* to master-builders and architects while they were engaged in work was cut off because the Guild funds were so low!

At the revision of the Constitutions of the various Guilds in 1415, the “Guild of Masters of Stone and Wood” received its share of amendments. Many <term>regulations</term> <note>original: "Rubrics"</note> were passed affecting workers and others.

Pavers, brick-kiln workers, masters of stone and wood, and laborers were bound to make and keep strictly accurate measurements of quantity and to maintain a consistent quality in their work. Surveyors were appointed to examine and test all deliveries of stone and brick and to inspect every stage of building operations thoroughly. Inferior material and inefficient workmanship were met with prompt punishment. The surveyors themselves were subjected to penalties if they performed their duties in a merely superficial manner; indeed, they were liable to be expelled from membership in the Guild.²

Kiln workers and brickmakers were generally instructed to fill their kilns with only the highest quality lime. They were also to ensure that the bricks they fired were free from defects and were accurately and properly shaped according to standard requirements. Every brick had to be stamped on all four sides with the coat of arms of Florence, and the length of the sides had to be exactly four times the width of the ends. The ends had to be finished smoothly so that they could be joined as neatly and tightly as possible. Tiles, troughs, and square edging pieces followed these same standards.

Wall measurements were taken with an iron yard-measure that matched the exact length of the “Calimala” <term>measuring rod</term> <note>Italian: *canna*</note>. Clay pits and lime works were under direct State supervision. Rents and fees were paid for the right to operate them, and State taxes were collected at the city gates on loads of bricks and tiles. These were categorized by shape and purpose as <term>bricks</term> <note>Italian: *mattoni*</note>, <term>floor tiles</term> <note>Italian: *mezzane*</note>, <term>roof tiles</term> <note>Italian: *tegole*</note>, <term>flat paving bricks</term> <note>Italian: *pianelle*</note>, and <term>large square bricks</term> <note>Italian: *quadrucchi*</note>.²

Strict regulations governed the location and dimensions of brick kilns. All such structures were required to be located more than three miles outside the old <term>surrounding territory</term> <note>Italian: *Contado*</note>, and they could not exceed a height of nine <term>cubits</term> <note>Italian: *braccia*, roughly an arm's length</note>.³

The price of bricks per thousand and the weekly wage scales were regularly determined by the Consuls of the “Guild of Masters in Stone and Wood.” These rates were posted in all the brickyards and workshops of the city.⁴

According to the Statutes of 1415, specific regulations were established regarding timber. Wood stocks could not be kept simply for resale through brokers. The amount of wood allowed in workshops had to be strictly proportionate to the work currently in progress. Masters of wood and their apprentices were required to work only with timber that bore the official stamp of the Guild. Much greater

<page-num>331</page-num>
<header>MASTERS OF STONE AND WOOD</header>

Freedom to work was extended to foreign workers, although they were required to be affiliated with the Guild and to submit to the rulings of the Consuls. Incentives were offered especially to Lombard workers, who were provided with rent-free housing for a time and were permitted to bring in their tools and equipment free of customs duties.¹

The wages of an ordinary stone-mason or bricklayer were one *lira* a day, with half a *lira* for his laborer. A carpenter’s average wage was the same. These amounts compared favorably with the wages of agricultural laborers, who could rarely earn more than ten *soldi* a day.

The Residence of the Consuls was in the Chiasso di Baronelli, not far from the Loggia de’ Lanzi. Over its portals were sculpted the arms of the Guild, which were, of course, also displayed upon its banner—a white axe upon a red field.

In the neighborhood of Florence, two or three kinds of stone were easily accessible:

1.  **Pietra forte** <note>literally "strong stone"</note>—a durable sandstone with lime-based ingredients. It was excellent for building purposes and for paving, but was generally found only in small pieces. The most frequently used quarry was at Camfora, outside the Porta Romana.

2.  **Pietra serena** <note>literally "serene stone"</note>—or *Macigno*—a silica-based sandstone of a dark grey or bluish-black color with unique black patches, which takes on a bronze hue over time. Benvenuto Cellini <note>a famous Florentine sculptor and goldsmith, 1500–1571</note> says this stone is found in the hilly country around Florence—especially at Settignano, Signa, Montelupo, and Fiesole. "It is," he adds, "distinguished by its beauty and fine texture, and is easily worked; but, as it does not resist water or withstand exposure to the open air, it is best suited for indoor work and statues kept under cover."

3.  **Pietra morta** <note>literally "dead stone"</note> is also mentioned by Cellini, who praises its rich tan color and its softness and ease in chiselling. It with—

...stands up to winds, rains, and the effects of time, and it is excellent for ornamental work and for window and door frames.

“There is,” says Sir Richard Dallington, “dug out of the Tuscan hills a kind of freestone, exceedingly hard, and in color—depending on the nature of the location where it is quarried—white, red, or black. Many very gallant and stately palaces in Florence are built of all these varieties. They also have marble pits in many places—white, blue, and multicolored—of excellent quality.” The old chronicler also speaks of the well-paved streets, which were “long, straight, wide, and beautifully laid with *hastia*”—broad paving stones—“so that no weather makes them muddy.” 1

Statuary marble came chiefly from Massa and Carrara, but Michelangelo, at the request of Pope Julius II, also worked with marble from Seravezza. The prospecting, quarrying, and transporting of the huge blocks required by the stone masters of Florence demanded great ingenuity and engineering skills from the members of the Guild.

Rare marbles used to enrich monuments and for mosaic work were also imported from far and wide. Many costly examples came directly from Rome—the ancient “*Marmorata*” <note>the district in Rome where imported marble was landed and stored</note> being the marble emporium of the world.

Regarding the timber needed for scaffolding and general construction, as well as the finer woods used in decorative work, there was no difficulty with the supply. The Arno Valley was an arboretum of all kinds of trees. Pines, oaks, elms, and plane trees supplied the builders, while walnuts, ashes, briars, and many others provided the carvers with everything they needed. Furthermore, the wise rulers of the city constantly created plantations of useful trees to replenish harvested areas. In 1534, for example, Duke Alessandro converted river mud and sandbanks into the shady *Cascine* <note>now a large public park in Florence</note>, and he and his successors planted many a *podere*—farm lands—with trees and shrubs.

Arnolfo’s fame, however, rests mainly upon his work at Santa Maria del Fiore <note>the Cathedral of Florence</note>, where he acted as chief architect and builder from 1294 until the day of his death in 1310. <note>*Archivio del Duomo—Antica Necrologia di Santa Reparata*, Document 12.</note> The Palazzo Vecchio also acknowledges him as its creator. It was indeed a masterstroke of engineering which incorporated the old Foraboschi tower—later called the <term>Torre della Vacca</term> <note>Tower of the Cow</note>—and crowned it with its crenelated stone cap!

An entry in the archives records the state's grant of certain privileges to him in 1300—freedom from taxation and a seat in the Signoria <note>the governing council of Florence</note>—"for his industry, his experience, and his talent." He is styled: "Chief Master of the labor and work of the church of the Blessed Reparata." <note>original: "Caput Magister laborerii et operis ecclesiæ beatæ Reparate." Provv., No. X., p. 235.</note> A special feature of his style was the use of panels or slabs of various colored marbles, an example followed by all his successors.

From 1340 to 1348, Giotto was <term>Capo Maestro</term> and Consul of the Guild. For his glorious <term>Campanile</term> <note>bell tower</note>, four master masons were sent to Carrara in 1350 to buy marble.

Other famous master builders and Consuls were Taddeo Gaddi, who rebuilt the <term>Ponte alla Carraia</term> <note>the Carraia Bridge</note> in 1337 and prepared plans for the new Ponte Vecchio and Ponte alla Santa Trinita; and Andrea Orcagna, who built the shrine of Or San Michele and the pillars of Santa Maria del Fiore.
