The Guild's registers record the names and commissions of many master builders up until the year 1418. Among them were Simone Giovanni del Pino, who in 1363 carved the twisted red marble columns in the windows of the Cathedral <note>original: "Duomo"</note>; Taddeo Ristori—a member of the Cione family—who was the architect of Or San Michele and the Loggia dei Lanzi in 1336; and Giovanni Stefani, a noted 1381 builder of scaffolding and a specialist in foundation work.

In 1349, Brother Lorenzo erected the Speaker's Tribune <note>original: "Ringhiera"</note> outside the Palazzo Vecchio at a cost of one thousand gold florins. Ten years later, the plans for the facade of the Cathedral were made public. These were the joint work of the following Guild members: Neri di Fioravante, Benci di Cione, Francesco Salvetti, and Niccolò Tommasi, who, along with Taddeo Gaddi and Andrea Orcagna, formed a special commission for that purpose. We may assume all of these men were serious and capable architects and master builders; however, in 1418, there is a record of one Piero d'Antonio. Although he was elected as a Consul and <term>Capo Maestro</term> <note>Chief Master</note>, he was nicknamed "<term>Fannullone</term>" <note>original: "Fannullone"</note>—meaning a braggart or an idle fellow!

Six master builders competed in 1418 for the commission to build the dome of the Cathedral; among them were Nanni di Banco, Lorenzo Ghiberti, and Donatello. However, none of them were successful, and the commission was instead given to Filippo Brunellesco, who, notably, was not a member of the Guild of Stone and Wood. He had matriculated into the Silk Guild <note>original: "Arte della Seta"</note> in 1398, and later, in 1404, had enrolled as a member of the new Goldsmiths' Guild <note>original: "Arte degli Orafi"</note>, which was a subordinate corporation of the greater Silk Guild.

The selection of Brunellesco to build the dome, and also to complete the lantern in 1434, caused great offense to the "Masters of Stone and Wood." They insisted that he enroll in their Guild, but to demonstrate that a man did not need to be a freemason <note>a member of the stoneworkers' guild</note> to build a church, Brunellesco ignored their protests and never paid his fees! He was caught by the law—the Masters of the Works <note>original: "Laborerum," likely referring to the Opera del Duomo</note> sued him for debt, and the successful architect was imprisoned! The offender’s cause was nevertheless championed not only by the Silk Guild <note>original: "Por Santa Maria"</note>, but also by the "Wool Guild"—the former doubtless on account of his membership therein, and the latter probably due to its stewardship of the Cathedral works. He was released, while a scapegoat was found in an unfortunate but nameless member of the "Guild of Masters of Stone and Wood," who was thrown into Brunelleschi's cell without a trial on a fabricated charge of being an idle fellow!

The story of Columbus and the egg may, with much more probability, be attributed to Brunelleschi in relation to the famous dome of the Cathedral <note>original: "Duomo"</note>. The art of building a dome <note>original: "cupola"</note> like that of the Roman Pantheon had been lost, and Brunelleschi rediscovered it. None of the scientists consulted by the authorities could do it, but he proposed that the man who could make an egg stand upright upon a flat base should be chosen as architect. With a gentle tap, he broke in one end and thus easily set it up upon the slab!

Regarding Brunelleschi’s achievement, the familiar Tuscan proverb is applicable: "Rounder than Giotto's O" <note>original: "Piu rondo che di l’O Giotto"</note>—meaning anything more perfect is impossible. Indeed, the reverberation of sounds is extraordinary. No echo is discernible, but words and music appear to be carried up through the lantern and never return again!

The construction of the dome <note>original: "cupola"</note> put the builders of scaffolding to the test. The whole city seems to have taken the matter in hand, for public meetings were held where everyone was asked to express their opinions. Models in brick, plaster, and wood were projected to scale, both with and without scaffolding. Very ingenious plans were devised for the hoisting of heavy material, including those by Antonio da Vercelli—a leading Master of Wood <note>original: "Maestro di legno"</note>. Ognissanti dates to 1256, La Nunziata to 1258, Or San Michele to 1285, Santa Maria Novella to 1279, Santa Croce and San Spirito to 1295, and San Marco to 1299. San Miniato al Monte—originally built under Charlemagne in 774—was rebuilt in 1093 and was significantly expanded in the thirteenth century through the generosity of the <term>Calimala Guild</term> <note>The powerful Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth.</note>.

Master builders also turned their attention to civil architecture in the thirteenth century. Designs for all these projects were drafted, and cost estimates prepared, by the first descendants of the ancient <term>Comacine Masters</term> <note>A medieval guild of master stonemasons and architects originally from the Lake Como region, influential in spreading Romanesque and Gothic styles.</note>; the work was then carried out by their sons and grandsons through their labors. Several palaces were erected: the Bargello in 1258, the Badia between 990 and 1285, and the Palazzo Vecchio in 1294. Bridges were also constructed: the Ponte alla Carraia in 1218, the Ponte Santa Trinita in 1252, the Ponte alle Grazie (also known as Rubaconte) in 1237, and the Ponte Vecchio between 1080 and 1333. City gates included those at Al Prato, San Gallo, and San Ambrogio in 1284, and the Porta Ghibellina in 1290. Hospitals were established as well: San Gallo in 1218, Santa Maria Nuova in 1267, and San Bartolommeo in 1295. The city walls were rebuilt and expanded between 1285 and 1299, and the <term>Stinche Prison</term> was built in 1260.

Regarding architecture, the fourteenth century was notable for the completion and decoration of many magnificent buildings. Sculptors working in stone, wood, and metal, as well as mosaic masters, terra-cotta craftsmen, and fresco painters, were all working diligently under the authority of the Guild. This was the era of the greatest masters of the fine arts. Even the most humble laborer felt the influence of their personalities, and even the simplest tasks were marked by a combination of boldness and elegance. Even the very tools they used were decorated with artistic features.

The master planners also had their work cut out for them in laying out the city with fine squares and well-paved streets, as well as removing unattractive and cramped buildings. The <term>Piazze</term> (squares) included: San Giovanni in 1300, Santa Maria Novella in 1302, and the Piazza della Signoria in 1307. The <term>Loggie</term> (covered galleries) included: the Bigallo in 1330, the Lanzi in 1334, the <term>Zecca</term> (the Mint) in 1361, and the Mercato...

Other *Operai*—Masters of Works—took charge of the interior decoration of churches, palaces, Guild residences, and the private homes of wealthy citizens. Splendidly designed and decorated wooden ceilings were a prominent feature. The ceiling in the Laurentian Library (*Biblioteca Laurenziana*), created by Tasso and Carola, shows the exceptional skill of these master wood-carvers. The favorite style was the "King Post" truss, which was often concealed by decorative paneling. Rood screens <note>Partitions between the chancel and the nave of a church.</note> and shrines, the work of Donatello and Brunellesco, can still be seen in the Church of Santa Croce.

The fifteenth century was famous for the construction of superb palaces, which wealthy families built in a spirit of noble competition. The master builders and their workmen were busier than ever. Florence rang with the purposeful music of the trowel, the chisel, the hammer, and the plane. Massive scaffolding transformed the entire city into a huge lumberyard, yet from this emerged artistic and grandiose edifices that will command admiration and imitation for all time.

The Antinori, Borgherini, Guadagni, Guicciardini, Niccolini, Panciatichi, Pandolfini, Pitti, Pecori-Geraldi, Rucellai, Serristori, Torrigiani, and Uguccione palaces, along with many others, followed in quick succession. In 1430, the Palazzo Riccardi was completed for the Medici family. The old Strozzi, Albizzi, Pazzi, and Buondelmonti palaces had been burned to the ground by the *Ciompi* <note>The "Ciompi" were lower-class textile workers who led a popular revolt in 1378.</note> in 1378, and now—like a phoenix—new structures rose in their place. The protection of city buildings, the construction of lordly villas in the *Contado* <note>The rural territory or countryside surrounding the city.</note>, and the dedication of country shrines all required the skillful labor of architects and sculptors.

An examination of these masterpieces of fifteenth-century domestic architecture reveals the striking fact that every characteristic of the Florentine people has been preserved and immortalized in stone, wood, and metal. Solidity, boldness, and dignity are joined with elegance, simplicity, and restraint; the result is a unique style, somewhat inaccurately called “Rustic” <note>Also known as "rustication" or *bugnato*, a style of masonry using large, rough-hewn blocks with deeply recessed joints.</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the construction of 15th-century palaces to the "Finished Renaissance" of the 16th century, highlighting the influence of Michelangelo Buonarroti and the continued contributions of the "Masters of Stone and Wood" in both artistic decoration and military defense.</meta>

<page-num>339</page-num>
<header>MASTERS OF STONE AND WOOD</header>

The sixteenth century has been called the period of the "Late Renaissance," but we should rather designate it as the "Finished Renaissance." Florence was fully built; her architecture was complete. She was adorned with statues and carvings in stone, wood, and metal, and little more was required for the decoration of the beautiful city.

There remained only the tasks of placing the capstones on her architecture, adding the finishing touches to her sculpture, removing the scaffolds, and unveiling her latest art treasures. These duties were undertaken by the most commanding personality of the century—Michelangelo Buonarroti. The son of a city magnate, born into wealth and culture, he was a motherless child raised by a simple mason's wife at Settignano. In this way, he personally represented all the noblest traits of citizenship.

The models for Michelangelo’s life’s work were the well-proportioned, virile figures of his daily companions. Consequently, his ideals in architecture, sculpture, and painting realized the highest aspirations of the masters of all time.

During the siege of Florence by Pope Clement VII in 1529, Michelangelo was appointed Commissary-General of the Republic's forces. He gathered the "Masters of Wood and Stone" around him, and with their assistance, he constructed earthworks and defensive walls that were quite remarkable for their precise and scientific design.

The century was also marked by a craze for wax-modeling. Every man with artistic tastes set out to be a *wax-worker* <note>original: "Ceraiuolo"</note>. No class took to the art with more earnestness than the "Masters of Stone and Wood." Apprentices were instructed and encouraged in its pursuit, and in a very short time, an entire school of artists had arisen who displayed their skill in portraiture and other fine work. One of the most famous modelers and portraitists was Orsino, who made many wax casts of the features of Lorenzo de' Medici—*the Magnificent* <note>original: "il Magnifico"</note>.

The cutting of gems and cameos became a specialty of the

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Masters of Stone and Wood," shifting from Michelangelo’s specific contributions to a broader catalog of the guild's most illustrious members and their lasting impact on the city of Florence during the Renaissance.</meta>

<page-num>340</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Florentine sculptors flourished during the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries. Among the more famous gem engravers were Giovanni and Bernardino Peruzzi (1300–1379); Giovanni delle Corniole, known for his portrait of Savonarola (1494); Pietro da Pescia, a friend of Michelangelo (1513); and Domenico da Pola (1527). All of these men were registered members of the "Guild of Masters of Stone and Wood."

The Florentines dedicated themselves to the pleasant task of building upon the work of their ancestors and fully enjoying the glory of their surroundings. The Medici family were experts in the art of entertainment, and the open squares and narrow streets were frequently filled with daily pageants. The citizens took great pride in their magnificent buildings and noble bridges, for their fathers had built them, and they were now their guardians.

To provide a simple list of the members of the "Guild of Masters of Stone and Wood" who made themselves, their guild, and their city famous—or to compile a basic catalog of their achievements—would be an unnecessary task. To see their memorial, one only needs to "look around," just as one does in St. Paul’s Cathedral regarding Sir Christopher Wren. <note>Wren's epitaph in St. Paul's reads: "Lector, si monumentum requiris, circumspice" (Reader, if you seek his monument, look around you).</note>

Nevertheless, the following masters, along with those already mentioned, gave character and life to their era: Jacopo della Quercia, Benedetto da Maiano, Mino da Fiesole, Desiderio da Settignano, Il Cronaca, Baccio d’Agnolo, and Baccio Bandinelli, along with the families of Della Robbia, Rossellini, Sansovini, Pollaiuoli, Ammannati, and San Gallo (also known as Giamberti).

Leon Battista Alberti (1405–1472) stands out as a monumental figure—an architect, sculptor, painter, and engineer. His work, *On Building* <note>original: "De Re Ædificatoria"</note>, was the first systematic treatise on art since the time of Vitruvius <note>A Roman author and architect (c. 80–15 BC) whose work heavily influenced Renaissance architecture</note>; his ten books on architecture, sculpture, and painting are considered absolute classics.

Lorenzo Ghiberti, Luca della Robbia, and Donatello were "the three brightest stars of the Renaissance," while Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael Santi, and Michelangelo Buonarroti constituted "the School of the World!"

All of Europe felt the impact of these energetic craftsmen. The Emperor’s Court attracted many Florentine masters, while in Paris, Francis I welcomed Leonardo da Vinci, Benvenuto Cellini, Primaticcio, and other members of the Guild with royal honors. <note>Vasari, *Lives of the Artists*, vol. 4, page 262, note.</note>

<margin>Artistic settlements of Italians, primarily from Florence, were spread throughout England, particularly around Winchester and Southampton. Their members worked in various materials—including stone, bronze, wood, and leather—in many public buildings and private residences. The demonstration of their skill was a massive revelation and a powerful inspiration for local craftsmen.</margin>

Piero Torrigiano arrived in 1513, and with the assistance of his *school* <note>original: "Schola"</note> at Westminster, he built the magnificent tomb of Henry VII and Queen Eleanor—a flawless example of Florentine Renaissance art. <note>The author likely means Elizabeth of York, who is buried with Henry VII; Eleanor of Castile’s tomb is also in Westminster but was built earlier.</note> It is said the Master paid his assistants at the Abbey three gold florins a month each during the first year, and forty ducats plus room, board, and horse rental for each subsequent year.

Antonio di Lorenzo, Toto della Nunziata, Benedetto da Rovezzano, Giovanni da Maiano, Pietro Baldi, and Giovanni Utricci—along with the "famous engravers Ruccieri and Ambrogio"—were all highly encouraged by Henry VIII and Cardinal Wolsey, and <margin>✓</margin>were employed at Windsor, Oxford, and Hampton Court. <note>J. A. Gotch, *Architecture of the Renaissance*, vol. 1, page xxii.</note>

The wooden screens and choir stalls in King’s College Chapel, <margin>✓</margin>Cambridge, were carved by Florentine Masters of Wood. The Tuscan "Rustic" style became the foundation for a native school of architects and carvers; many country estates still stand today as evidence of how those skilled guild members prepared the way for what we now call the "Elizabethan style."

"Those English beasts"—as Torrigiano called our ancestors of that time—were, despite his bitterness, among the most appreciative patrons of the Florentine arts and crafts. When Elizabeth I visited Greenwich in 1583, Roger Manners, writing to...

---

The decline in the fortunes and enterprise of the Guild can be traced to the appointment of Brunelleschi <note>original: "Brunellesco"</note> in 1434—after his release from prison—as chief architect for all the public buildings in Florence. This move proved to be a death blow to the great Masonic Guild. While its influence remained, its organization was broken up into separate corporations. The great workshop <note>original: "Laborerum"</note> was closed, and the schools <note>original: "Scholæ"</note> dwindled to very modest proportions.

Lorenzo de’ Medici tried hard to revive the Guild’s work by opening and generously endowing a School of Sculpture in his garden at Villa Larga, and it certainly achieved a degree of success. Regardless, this school <note>original: "Schola"</note> is responsible for collecting and preserving all the finest models and examples from nearly three centuries of splendid achievements by the “Masters of Stone and Wood.”

---

<margin>✓</margin>
It is necessary to say a few words about pottery and to explain why historical authorities are silent regarding the existence of a Corporation or Guild of Potters.²

<margin>✓</margin>
The potter’s art was, of course, as familiar to Florentines as any other. It was the custom on many farms <note>original: "poderi"</note> in the countryside <note>original: "Contado"</note>, throughout history, not only to make utensils for ordinary domestic and business purposes but also to fashion figures out of the heavy clay <note>original: "tenacious subsoil"</note> of the Arno valley. Some of these figures were of ambitious sizes and were finished in colors within the city workshops. Modellers in terra-cotta included Bicci di Lorenzo (1373–1452) and the Della Robbia family (1430–1529). All these men were artists and members of the “Guild of Workers of Stone and Wood.” Consequently, the more artistic styles of pottery were regarded as the domain of sculptors, while the

The more basic products of the potter's wheel were categorized as items to be sent to pharmacies and grain dealers' shops.

There was, perhaps, no opportunity for a separate guild composed solely of workers in clay and glaze. Furthermore, the highest quality types of earthenware were of foreign origin; for instance, the finest pottery was made from the opaque white clay of Siena, commonly known as "St. John's Earth."

Conversely, the first artificial porcelain known to have been produced in Europe was made in Florence around the year 1580 under the patronage of Francesco de' Medici, the second Grand Duke of Tuscany (who died in 1587). This porcelain was composed of a soft or hybrid paste, unlike the material required for hard pottery. The factory was located in the Boboli Gardens but only operated for a few years. Its standard trademark, stamped in blue, featured the dome of the Cathedral <note>original: "Duomo"</note> with the letter "F" underneath.

## II. THE GUILD OF RETAILERS <note>original: "L’ARTE DE’ RIGATTIERI"</note>

->A. Retail Cloth Dealers.<-
->B. Linen Manufacturers.<-

The history of the two branches of this guild—the twelfth in the hierarchy of the guilds—is quite difficult to untangle because of the confusing and inconsistent records found in the Florentine Archives.

The earliest records of the various trades and occupations included under the jurisdiction of the guild are apparently as follows:

> “1032. *The House of Florence the Tailor* <note>original: "Casa Florentii Sarti"</note>—Shop of a Tailor.”
> “1084. *Bonus, son of John, hawker* <note>original: "Bonus, fil. Johannis, baro"</note>—Hawker <term>baro: a street-peddler or traveling merchant</term>.”
> “1191. *Martin, linen-maker* <note>original: "Martinus, pignolajno"</note>—Maker of fine linen.”
> “1211. *Ristoro, son of Piero, purse-maker* <note>original: "Ristoro, fil. Pieri—buorsajo"</note>—Pouch-maker.”
> “1211. *Albizi of Ferrara, rag-seller of the Lung' Arno* <note>original: "Albizi di Fferrare, pezzaio di Lung’ Arno"</note>—Rag seller.”

Indeed, the “Guild of Retail Dealers” seems to have grown...

...out of the fact that many minor crafts, which were somewhat similar in character, gradually formed themselves into a union based on the typical Florentine cooperative principle for mutual benefit and defense.

One would have thought the “Guild of Linen Manufacturers” would have held a prominent position alongside the guilds of the related wool and silk industries; however, for some reason that remains impossible to explain, the flax growers and linen makers had to accept a secondary role.

### A.—The Guild of Retailers <note>original: "L'Arte de' Rigattieri"</note>

This guild was very broad in scope and included retail traders of almost every kind among its members. In old Florence, there was always a significant number of men who were not exactly “idlers,” but who, having likely joined their fathers' guilds, did not fully commit to those specific industries. Some of them undoubtedly lacked focus, but many felt they could be more successful than they would be by remaining in the traditional ranks of their family professions.

The continuous growth of commerce—along with the arrival of appealing goods and the creation of new demands—introduced new interests and opened up new career paths. The *Sensali* <term>Sensali: commercial brokers or agents</term>, or agents of the Greater Guilds, noted novelties during their travels and learned foreign customs; their sharp business sense taught them that these could be profitably brought to Florence.

Furthermore, it was clear that the activities of the Greater Guilds were wholesale in nature, and that the large-scale employers of labor had neither the space nor the opportunity to sell small quantities. Consequently, shops gradually opened where citizens and visitors could buy useful and decorative items at retail. The buyers of silk remnants and wool or linen cloth from the workshops saw a profit margin in selling such items in the open market. Scraps, off-cuts, and waste materials had their own value; even old clothes, rags, and trimmings of fur and hide became tradable assets.

<summary>This page describes the formation of the Guild of Retailers as a union of minor crafts and explains how the shift from wholesale to retail commerce allowed for new business opportunities in Florence.</summary>
<keywords>Guild of Retailers, L'Arte de' Rigattieri, Linen Manufacturers, Sensali, commerce, retail trade, Greater Guilds, Florence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the organization of the Guild of Retailers, explaining how various minor crafts consolidated into a single union and detailing the economic shift from wholesale production to retail commerce.</meta>

Buyers also traveled around to purchase the woven and knitted work of hardworking housewives.

Many items offered for sale by the Apothecaries appeared to fall into the category of "odds and ends"; consequently, a certain number of traders entered the market daily as peddlers or barterers.

In some of these occupations—for example, selling silk and cloth remnants, articles of clothing, and strips of leather—a significant fortune could be amassed. Sons of merchants, and even the merchants themselves, entered these new lines of trade in large numbers. The respect in which such dealers were held grew until the necessity of forming a union for the mutual defense of common interests became obvious.

Conditions of life and work in old Florence were surprisingly similar to those that govern our own time. Men made fortunes "around the corner," in all sorts of unusual ways, and from all kinds of unexpected sources. Knowing how and what to buy was an essential first requirement for every salesman, whether he was a wealthy merchant of the *Calimala* <note>The *Arte di Calimala* was the prestigious guild of merchants who refined and sold imported cloth.</note> or a poor hawker of haberdashery.

<insert>✓</insert> The *Arte de' Rigattieri* <note>original: "Arte de' Rigattieri"</note>—the Guild of Retail Dealers—was first incorporated in 1266 and received its banner, which was colored half red and half white. The *Arte de' Linaiuoli* <note>original: "Arte de' Linaiuoli"</note>—the "Guild of Linen Drapers"—was incorporated with it.

At the same date, the guild's place in the order of precedence was fixed as twelfth in rank, immediately after the "Masters of Stone and Wood." Consequently, when the Five Intermediate Guilds were called into conference with the Greater Guilds, the Guild of Retail Dealers was always included. However, this distinction of position was somewhat diminished by the fact that the Retail Dealers were regarded as a "sandwich" guild, serving as a link to the Nine Lesser Guilds.

The Consuls of the guild are recorded as voting in 1293 among the Consuls of the twelve Greater Guilds. The statutes of the *L'Arte de' Rigattieri della Magnifica Città di Firenze* <note>English: The Guild of Retailers of the Magnificent City of Florence</note>—to give...

The *Parchment Codex* <term>original: *Codex Membranaceo*</term>,<sup>2</sup> dated March 1295, contains two manuscripts, numbered "No. 1" and "No. 19" respectively. The former contains the Statutes and other regulations of the Retailers <term>original: *Rigattieri*</term>, Linen-drapers <term>original: *Linaiuoli*</term>, Tailors <term>original: *Sarti*</term>, and Cloth-sellers <term>original: *Venditori di panne*</term>, and begins with the dedication:— "In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. This is made and composed in honor of Almighty God, of the Virgin and St. John the Baptist, by the men who are Consuls and Rectors of the 'Guild of Buyers' <note>original: *Arte del’ Ementium*</note> (Remnant-dealers?), vendors of cloth, and vendors of fur linings."

The manuscript is well written, as are most of the records of the period, but the language used—which was common to all such documents—is a mixture of corrupt Latin with many abbreviations and local colloquialisms, making it almost, if not entirely, illegible.

The earlier sections of the manuscript deal, as usual, with the Statutes and rules for the election of Consuls and other Guild officers. One regulation <term>original: rubric</term> deals with apprentices convicted of theft, who were punished with a fine of twenty-five gold florins and the cancellation of their apprenticeship contracts <term>original: indentures</term>.

Several regulations prescribe observances for the burial of members—such as the burning of ceremonial candles in the room where the deceased lay, and the display of banners—bearing the coats of arms of the Guild and of the family—at the doors of the deceased’s house, and so forth.

Tailors <term>original: *Sarti*</term> are specifically named in the manuscript. They are not to make or use materials mixed with tow <term>original: *Struppa* or *stoppa*</term>—fine hemp or flax waste—and coarse cotton <term>original: *Bambix* or *bambagia*</term>, such as was used for lamp wicks. In short, "mixed tailoring" <note>original: *Sartia mista*</note>—mixtures of every sort—were forbidden.

The second manuscript is the document dealing with, and settling, the purchase of a house—it is titled "Purchase of the Retailers' Residence" <note>original: *Compra de residenza de Rigattieri*</note>, etc.; but it goes on to name the Linen-drapers <term>original: *Linaiuoli*</term>—the flax weavers—as the actual owners of the property on behalf of

The retail dealers were not allowed to sell *Zendado*—the richest silk taffeta—or *Imbacciacinato*—highly-raised brocade—to any of the *Popolo Minuto* <note>original: "Popolo Minuto" — the "little people," or the lower-class commoners</note>. The fine for breaking this rule was fifty *lire*. This was accompanied by the withdrawal of the dealer’s selling license and the confiscation of the illegal merchandise.²

Retail dealers—frequently called members of the *Arte de’ Boldagiori* <note>original: "Arte de’ Boldagiori" — the Guild of Retailers and Linen-merchants</note>—were permitted to sell woolen cloths of the following descriptions: *Romagniuolo* (Roman weave), *Bigello* (frieze), *Burello* (coarse cloth), *Cremonense* (Cremona weave), *Pignolati* (fine linen), and all other kinds except redressed foreign cloths, whether they were processed in Florence, Milan, or elsewhere. They were forbidden from selling decorated or stamped pouches, caps, belts, fine silk scarves, veils, and any sort of material weighing more than one pound. Small metal basins, mortars, pieces of ivory, and other small articles were to be sold by weight at a fixed price per pound.³

Along with the retail dealers and linen drapers, the following were generally grouped: *Pennaiuoli* (stationers), *Copertolari* (coverlet-sellers), *Farsettori* (doublet-makers), and *Coltellinai* (cutlers), together with dealers in raw flax, hemp, canvas, and string nets. Their shops were not to be opened before the ringing of the bell for morning matins and had to be closed before four o'clock in the afternoon.⁴

All tailors were directly under the jurisdiction of the *Ufficiali della Grascia* <note>original: "Ufficiali della Grascia" — the Surveyors of Markets and Trades</note>, who carefully inspected and recorded the quantities and qualities of the woolen and linen cloth they kept in their shops. Not only was this regulated, but the price they were permitted to charge for every garment they made was fixed. The State also levied a specific tax on each value. For example, a *Roba* (a robe made of fine red cloth) paid a tax of five *lire*; a *Cottardita* (a tunic of blue cloth) paid three *lire*; a *gammurra* (a petticoat or gown with stitching in the front and buttonholes in the back) paid two *lire* and five *soldi*; and a *Guarnello* (a fustian gown for a...)

No tailor was permitted to pawn wool or linen cloth, or cloth made of a wool and flax blend—whether it was cut or uncut. They were also forbidden from pawning any garment—finished or unfinished—or anything else belonging to the trade. Fines of twenty-five *lire* or more were imposed not only on the reckless tailor but also on any person who accepted the pledge.<sup>2</sup>

Dishonest and runaway tradesmen were, of course, found in every guild, but the "Guild of Second-hand Dealers" <note>original: "Arte de’ Rigattieri"</note> likely produced the highest number of such unfortunate individuals. When such a man fell into hardship, he was not the only one to suffer; his business partners and his family were also declared offenders and fined. A specific case is recorded in the archives dated January 17, 1330. It notes that the partners of a merchant and craftsman in the "Guild of Second-hand Dealers"—who specialized in selling old wool and linen scraps and belonged to the parish <note>original: "popoli"</note> of Santa Cecilia—were declared outlaws after the merchant went bankrupt.<sup>3</sup>

and many other kinds of woolen materials.
    They were also permitted to trade in all types of silk goods and sewing silks. Ivy berries—used for the red dye called *grana* <note>original: "grana"</note>—and dried kermes—from which the crimson dye *chermisi* <note>original: "chermisi"</note> was derived—as well as gold and silver in the form of cakes, powder, flakes, and leaf, were all included. Pearls and jewelry of all kinds, veils, thin capes, and fichus <note>term: light triangular scarves or neckerchiefs</note>, every sort of gilded leather and tinsel work, were also displayed for sale. Many other items, far too numerous to list, were sold by the *Rigattieri* <note>original: "Rigattieri"; the Retail Dealers</note>, though each required the specific permission of the Council of State and remained under the direction of the Consuls and officials of the Guild.

### B. The Guild of Linen Manufacturers <note>original: "L’Arte de’ Linaiuoli"</note>

    Linen is likely the oldest manufactured material still in domestic use. Thousands of years ago, the art of weaving linen cloth was known and practiced in India, Egypt, and Greece. Linen was also known to the people of the Stone Age and to the prehistoric lake dwellers. The Romans held flax in high regard for their personal clothing.
    Apuleius, the wise monk of the fifth century, says pointedly:
> "Wool, being the discharge of a sluggish body taken from a sheep, was considered unholy clothing even in the times of Orpheus and Pythagoras; but flax—that cleanest product of the field—is rightly used for man’s innermost garments."

--- Page 473 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the trade regulations of the Retailers' Guild (Arte de’ Rigattieri) to the history and techniques of the Guild of Linen Manufacturers, focusing on the origins of flax cultivation in Italy and the involvement of religious orders.</meta>

<page-num>351</page-num>

->**LINEN-MANUFACTURERS**<-

Every monastery on the plains of Italy had its own flax patch, and the monks encouraged the peasants living around them to cultivate this useful little plant, with its thin green blades and delicate blue flowers. The members of these religious orders <note>original: "The Religious"</note> furthermore engaged themselves everywhere in the manufacture of linen thread and cloth, and they provided instruction to their neighbors in the secrets of the craft.

<margin>/</margin>
Church sacristies <note>term: a room in a church where vestments, altar linens, and sacred vessels are kept</note> became treasuries of fine linen because, under Canon Law, this material was the only one permitted for use in the ritual of the Mass and for other religious functions.

<margin>✓</margin>
From the perspective of household management, linen was known to be practically indestructible; consequently, both nobles and peasants alike found it to be the most durable material for everyday use.

The cultivation of flax was very common in the Arno Valley <note>original: "Vale of Arno"</note> throughout the period of the Renaissance. In extent, it rivaled the cultivation of the vine and the olive, but it far exceeded both in the intelligence and labor demanded of its cultivators. Specific methods of plowing, manuring, sowing, and harvesting were in operation which have remained in practice until today.<sup>1</sup>

<margin>✓</margin>
The four processes of the harvest were as follows:
1. **Pulling**—When the plant had developed seed-capsules <note>term: "bolls" refers to the rounded seed pods of the flax plant</note> and turned brown, it was pulled up by the roots—never cut.
2. **Rippling**—The seed-capsules were removed in the field using a combing frame with iron teeth. Two men worked together: one gathered the seeds while the other handled the stalks.
3. **Retting**—There were two kinds: water retting and dew retting. In the first method, pure water from the Arno River was used without any addition of lime or iron. The flax stalks were laid flat in bundles in hollowed-out dams or pits four feet deep. On top of the last layer, a cover of freshly cut rushes was placed, over which heavy stones were positioned. Fermentation quickly began, causing the fiber to separate from the stalk as the outer sheath fell away.

The dew **Retting** required the bundles of flax to be opened and spread upon closely grown grass, without any protection from the sun, wind, or rain, and in full contact with the air and dew. This was, of course, a slow and tedious process, and it was only used by the less enterprising farmers.

***

<sup>1</sup> *Encyclopædia Britannica*, "Flax," 1900.

<page-num>352</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

3. [The third process was performed by] harvesters; 4. **Scutching**—In this stage, the fiber of the flax was separated by hand from the wood or stalk. It was then passed between grooved wooden or iron rollers, which required very careful adjustment. This was necessary to avoid, on one hand, creating tangled knots <note>original: "matted skeins"</note> or lumps, and on the other, crushing the flax too completely, which resulted in broken fibers and the production of lint. Flax treated in this way was ready to be placed on the market. In the fourteenth century, the average price for one hundred pounds of raw flax was five gold florins.<sup>1</sup>

The first mention of the "Guild of Linen-Manufacturers" seems to be in 1236, when the *Arte de’ Linaiuoli* was placed sixteenth in the hierarchy of the Guilds. It was probably the offspring of a humble association of flax growers and linen-thread spinners.

An early record of the linen industry is found in the Florentine Archives from the same year, 1236. It notes that Guido, the Abbot of Coltibuono, received a loan of one hundred and fifty *lire* from Iacopo, son of Bellioto dei Albertischi. This loan was for the payment of a debt owed to Buonosegno Malcristiano, who had sold the crops which fed the Abbot’s household and provided the flax for their clothing.

When the Guild Statutes were reformed in 1266, the name of the Guild does not appear; however, the *Arte de’ Rigattieri* <note>term: The Guild of Retailers or Second-hand Dealers</note> is listed. Again, in the revisions of 1280–1282, the *Arte de’ Rigattieri* appears, but there is no mention of the *Arte de’ Linaiuoli*.

The Florentine State Archives contain a record from 1294 regarding a company of four merchants trading in *lino* (flax), *accia* (linen thread) <note>original: "hemp"</note>, *stoppa* (tow) <note>term: the coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp used for spinning or as oakum for caulking</note>, *capecchi* (waste fibers) <note>original: "flocks"</note>, and every type of material for the manufacture of linen, as well as everything else pertaining to the trade. This firm had one warehouse in the house of the Cipriani family in the parish district <term>popolo: an administrative and religious district centered around a parish church</term> of San Pietro Bonconsiglio; another in the house of Petracchio de’ Cipriani and his partners in the *popolo* of Sant’ Andrea; and a third in the house of the Admidei in the *popolo* of San Stefani. Each partner in the business contributed one hundred and fifty *lire* to the capital; the senior member of the firm was named Matteo di Beliotto.<sup>2</sup>

<meta>This page continues the history of the Linen-Manufacturers' Guild (Arte de’ Linaiuoli) into the 14th century, detailing its administrative reorganization and its relationship with the Greater Guilds and the Retailers' Guild.</meta>

->**LINEN MANUFACTURERS**<-

At the General Revision of the Statutes of all the Guilds—1301–1309—there was still no mention of the old *Arte de’ Linaiuoli* <note>original: "Arte de' Linaiuoli"; translated: Linen-Manufacturers' Guild</note>; but in 1340, a body of regulations and laws appeared for the "Guild of Linen-Manufacturers." These rules, which were based on the common model of the statutes of the *Calimala* Guild <note>The powerful guild of merchants who imported and finished foreign cloth.</note>, were accepted unanimously by the flax workers.

Between 1340 and 1350, the Guild was exceedingly flourishing, and the linen manufacturers shared in the city’s general prosperity to such an extent that negotiations began for their inclusion among the Greater Guilds.

The Consuls and the Council of the Guild undertook a thorough revision of the Guild's statutes. The result of their labors was a disappointment for the members’ ambitious goals, for they were denied entry into the Seven Great Guilds and had to be content with merging with the twelfth guild in the hierarchy, the *Arte di Rigattieri* <term>The Guild of Retailers and Second-hand Dealers</term>.

Nevertheless, the *Linaiuoli* retained the right to elect their own officers without any restrictions and to issue bylaws for the members' compliance, regardless of their articles of association with the "Guild of Retail-Dealers."

Enrollment in the Guild was conducted under the same terms as in the Greater Guilds—so far as *men* were concerned; but, unlike them, *women* were admitted with full privileges and duties. The fees for enrollment were twenty-eight *lire* for candidates residing in the city and fourteen *lire* for those living in the *Contado* <term>The rural territory or countryside surrounding Florence</term>.

From 1342 onward, the officers included two Consuls, one Chancellor, and two *Provveditori* <term>Managers</term>. Two leading members from the agricultural side were appointed *Veditori delle Coltrici* <term>Inspectors of the flax fields</term>. They not only inspected the seed, the soil, and the labor, but also made agreements with the custom-house officials regarding the *Dogana* <term>customs</term> duties payable by growers. They delivered written agreements to the landowners and to the peasants, which were endorsed by the gatekeepers of the city. These documents dealt with the weights and condition

of the bundles of cut flax. In busy years when the area under cultivation was extended, assistant *Veditori* <term>Inspectors</term> were elected.¹

The Staff of the Guild was further increased by the appointment of six *Misuratori*—Surveyors of Weights and Measures—at the flax-grounds, at the city gates, and in the market. They were generally chosen from the smaller manufacturers of linen. *Stimatori*—Valuers—usually two in number, were elected to examine the peasants' pledges as the rightful growers of the flax cut for sale, to appraise the value of the processed flax, and, in disputes about the quality of the linen cloth, to decide its value. The officials of the Guild also included four *Donzelli*—Porters—who were specifically employed at the Residence and Office of the Consuls.

As in the case of the sister industries, the growers of flax and the manufacturers of linen suffered from the existence and intrusion of *Sensali* <term>Middlemen or Brokers</term>. These agents, as we might call them, received the reports of the *Stimatori* and fixed the actual sale prices of raw processed flax, spun thread, and woven linen—whether of local or foreign origin. They were bound by the articles of their admission as *Sensali* to submit copies of these values each month to the Consuls for their official approval.

No flax worker was permitted to purchase the raw produce directly from the grower, but only through six senior *Sensali* appointed by the Consuls; sales of linen came under a similar regulation. Breaches of these bylaws were severely punished—fines were enforced ranging from one *lira* <note>original: "one lire"</note> and twenty-five *piccioli* <note>The picciolo was a small copper coin, the smallest denomination of the Florentine lira.</note> for a first offense, to one hundred *lire* in a more serious case.

The *Sensali* appear to have been unusually protective of their rights and of their fees; and *Provvisioni* <term>provisions or statutes</term> and *Bandi* <term>proclamations or decrees</term> were constantly enacted for or against their interests. Every piece of linen cloth woven in Florence required the official stamp of the Guild, and a *bullettino* <term>label or tag</term> had to be attached, marked with the length, width, quality, and any special features. Imported pieces also required the seal of the Custom-House authorities, and only cloth marked in this way was permitted to be

# LINEN MANUFACTURERS

Any retail dealer or salesman offering other cloth pieces or linen thread was liable to fines ranging from five *lire* upward, depending on the severity or deceitfulness of the offense.

The Consuls designated the specific locations where manufacturing could be carried out and where stalls or shops for the sale of linen cloth and thread could be opened. The neighborhood surrounding the Church of San Lorenzo and the Via dei Servi <note>Street of the Servants</note> were specifically set apart for the operations of the linen industry. Public sales were held in the Market every Wednesday and Saturday.

In the fifteenth century, <term>fustian</term> <note>a heavy cloth made of cotton and flax</note> cotton cloth was used for church <term>chasubles</term> <note>the outermost vestment worn by a priest during Mass</note>. The Cistercian Order of Monks was forbidden from wearing any other kind of fabric. <term>Fustian</term> was also generally in style for <term>doublets</term> <note>a man's close-fitting padded jacket</note> and <term>jackets</term> for laymen.

In the Florentine manufacturing process, the <term>spindle</term>—onto which the thread spun from the <term>distaff</term> (or rack) was run—was usually about twelve inches long. After the <term>bobbin</term> was attached, a <term>whorl</term> <note>a weighted pulley used to maintain the speed of the spindle</note> made of stone or glazed terra-cotta was fixed to the top of the spindle to provide stability during the rotating movement. These whorls were often the work of talented artists; indeed, great masters such as the Della Robbia family did not think it beneath them to mold, paint, and glaze them beautifully for their female friends who wished to make their spinning wheels ornamental. Many such objects are found in art collections today, but they have often been mistakenly labeled as "Terra-Cotta Beads"!

Elegant related industries also emerged, and women of leisure, as well as ordinary workers in linen thread, took up the art of <term>Lace-making</term>. In this craft, the nuns were soon recognized as expert teachers. Their work was known in the market as "*punto tagliato*"—meaning <note>original: "punto tagliato"</note> "cut point"—so called because pieces of the linen base were cut out and the holes were worked with a needle and thread. Flax thread and silk tissue were generally used for ordinary lace, but a very delicate and yet strong fiber—from the aloe plant—was preferred for the finest work. This aloe thread is still used today for sewing together the well-known Florentine <term>straw plaits</term> <note>OCR "show plaits"; likely a reference to the "treccia," or straw braids used in the Florentine hat industry</note>.

He speaks much of "*sculpted*" <note>original: "scolpi"</note> work—carved in relief—which was actually a very high-relief point lace. This was not only woven or handmade on cushions but was also trimmed with fine scissors and cut to enhance its three-dimensional, sculpturesque appearance.

When Catherine de' Medici entered Paris as a bride, she introduced Florentine point lace, which became a widespread fashion at the French court. In 1545, a sister of Francis I purchased sixty ells of fine Florentine lace <note>original: "soixante aulnes fine dantelle de Florence"</note>. Similarly, in 1559, Madame Elizabeth of France added trimmings and narrow lace made of white Florentine thread <note>original: "passements et de bisette en fil blanc de Florence"</note> to her trousseau upon her marriage to Philip II.

During the great social upheaval of 1378 caused by the **Rising of the Ciompi** <note>a rebellion of unrepresented laborers in Florence</note>, many groups of ambitious craftsmen rose to prominence. Within the Second Operative Guild, established under the leadership of Michael Lando, an **Association of Flax Weavers** <note>original: "Arte, or Associazione de' Linaiuoli"</note> took an active role under the common banner of "**Justice**" <note>original: "Giustizia"</note>. These people were likely only workers in flax and linen, rather than merchants or large-scale manufacturers. The formation of this organization was further proof of the industry's importance and the prosperity of the "Guild of Linen-Manufacturers."

The residence of the Consuls and the general offices of the two united guilds were located in the large **House of Anzio** <note>original: "Casa d' Anzio"</note> in the Piazza de' Sant' Andrea, at the corner of the **Old Market** <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note>. In 1387, the foundation stone of a fine new building was laid. When completed, this edifice became the headquarters of the "**Guild and University of Second-hand Dealers, Linen-manufacturers, and Tailors**" <note>original: "Arte e Universita de Rigattieri, e Linaiuoli, e Sarti"</note>—as it was then titled—with heraldic shields mounted above the main door. The coat of arms was very simple: a shield divided vertically into two halves, red and white. The Audience Hall was one of the most magnificent in the city, filled with marble statues, wood-carvings, and colorful decorative paintings by emerging artists. A Guild record from 1466 survives, stating that the residence "is splendidly adorned with every artistic treasure."

The shops of Guild members, as well as their private rooms, were notable for their elegance and rich decoration. The wealth of the Guild was further demonstrated by the commission...

This work was entrusted to Donatello in 1411 and to Fra Giovanni Angelico in 1433 to enrich the church of Or San Michele.

During the final general reform of the Guilds in 1415, the union of the two guilds remained in effect, even though the name of the *Linaiuoli* <note>Linen-drapers</note> did not appear. This arrangement and name—"*Arte de' Rigattieri*" <note>Guild of Retailers or Second-hand Dealers</note>—continued until the year 1534.

Throughout these strenuous years, the flax industry of Florence made remarkable progress, keeping pace with the city's general development and prosperity. However, it was quite late in the industrial history of the "City of Merchants" that the linen manufacturers finally came into their own. At the end of 1534, under the rule of the Medici family, the "*Università de' Linaiuoli*"—the University of Linen-drapers—emerged. This guild, which had hidden its name for three hundred years, now rose to prominence and led a union of Lesser Guilds: the *Vinattieri* (Wine-merchants), *Albergatori* (Innkeepers), the *Sarti* (Tailors), and its long-time senior partner, the *Rigattieri*.

The guild continued to flourish until 1537, when the new order of things introduced by the Medici significantly altered and modified the character of Florentine industry. Incentives and monopolies were created and abolished almost simultaneously. The advancement of new ideas and the introduction of new methods signaled the end for the old shopkeepers. One by one, their shutters were closed, and the era of guild life became extinct.

### I. THE GUILD OF THE WINE-MERCHANTS <note>original: "L’ARTE DE’ VINATTIERI"</note>

“Tuscany is exceptionally well-suited for agriculture” was an old and commonplace saying; similarly, in a specific sense, her soil and climate were perfectly adapted for cultivating the vine. The undulating nature of the terrain, with its rolling uplands,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the history of the Wine-merchants' Guild, specifically focusing on the geographic conditions and early history of vine cultivation in Tuscany.</meta>

<header>GUILD OF WINE-MERCHANTS</header>

An altitude averaging about four hundred feet above sea level is ideal for perfecting the grape.

Tuscan red wine is the richest and most famous wine in the world. When you consider that the area around Florence produces more than half of this prized vintage, the vine's importance to the city is immediately clear.

In early times, growing this valuable plant was very precarious. While grain crops can be grown with little difficulty even during political unrest and armed conflict, fruit requires periods of peace and stable land ownership to reach maturity.

This was the state of affairs in Tuscany throughout the Middle Ages. However, the vine was native to the Arno Valley and grew wild on the hillsides. Men traveling on military expeditions or peaceful business plucked the delicious clusters to quench their thirst. If they had even a short break while the fruit was ripening, they would press the juice to fill their large skins and bulky gourds with a rough but refreshing wine.

As times became more stable and the peasants gained some freedom, individual farmers began to focus on the wild vines growing across their land and homes. The laborer who dug, fertilized, pruned, and watered the plants enjoyed the rich results of his hard work.

Landowners quickly recognized the potential of this harvest and encouraged their farmworkers to develop it. Indeed, some of these prominent men, having a keen eye for business, established thorough cultivation systems intended for profitable sale. The law of *Mezzaria* <note>A system of sharecropping where the produce is divided between the owner and the tenant.</note>—"going halves"—was applied to grape growing: the first half went to the landowner, and the second half to the tenant farmer.

In the early days, the annual harvest undoubtedly brought joy first to the owners and producers; whatever was

to spare, they bartered or sold immediately to their neighbors or their friends in the city or elsewhere. A commerce so primitive in its beginning developed quickly as harvest followed harvest, and the vine-growers' profits grew larger in their yearly accounts as they added the business of city wine-merchants to their vineyard occupations.

The methods adopted in the thirteenth century, or even earlier, were almost exactly those which generally prevail today. Where the vine grew, there it remained. With the least amount of labor, the plants were trained up the stems of living trees; where these were absent, *Testucchi* <note>Italian: testers or wooden supports</note>—wooden supports—were fixed under the heavy branches. These were of two kinds: espaliers (lengths of trellis work) and single posts set up at certain distances apart.

In the vineyards of the wealthier owners, the *Testucchi* gave way to substantial stone or brick pillars, which were called *Pergole*. In either case, the plant was allowed to grow as it pleased, forming a distinctive and beautiful feature of the landscape. It was also encouraged to yield as many bunches of grapes as possible, as the art of lopping or close pruning was unknown to the Tuscan vine-growers.

The location and the direction the vineyard faced exerted a powerful influence upon the yield in both quality and quantity. On the hill terraces, which were built with infinite care and patience, the grapes produced a drier and more alcoholic wine than on the lowlands. A southern aspect resulted in a sweeter and richer vintage.

At first, the people in the *Mercato Vecchio* <note>The Old Market in Florence</note> probably brought in and sold their vintages along with their other country produce. Gradually, the custom emerged of separating wine from other market commodities and opening shops specifically concerned with its sale. Each important landowner found this a convenient way of dealing with his share of the year's yield; he either occupied a wine shop himself or appointed some friend or agent to open one. In this way, no

<header>GUILD OF WINE-MERCHANTS</header>

...doubt the business of wine-merchant came into existence. The first record of such an individual in the city archives is as follows: “1070—*Paganus, qui vocatur vinadro*” <note>Latin: "Paganus, who is called the wine-seller"</note>.

Whether this good man had what we would call a license, no one can say, but he apparently sold only beverages in his little wine shop. In the absence of earlier records, we must regard him as the father of Florentine wine merchants. Paganus had many followers whose names appear in the archives, but at the end of the twelfth century, there is a new kind of entry: “1189—*Marcellus—tabernarius*” <note>Latin: "Marcellus—Tavern-keeper"</note>. This worthy citizen, unlike his neighbor at the wine shop, sold both food and drink. He was an important person in the eyes of his peers, and because there is no record of an earlier predecessor, he must be considered the first restaurant owner in Florentine history.

Thus, by the end of the twelfth century, there were two distinct classes of wine sellers, both of whom were dependent on the harvest of the vintage. However, the year 1211 reveals a third class through an entry in the archives: “*Servodeo—osste*” <note>Italian: "Servodeo—Host"</note>—host or landlord—the first recorded ancestor of the innkeeper proper.

Not much can be learned about the exact constitution of the guild from the statutes that have survived destruction. The first mention of <term>officers</term> <note>The governing officials of the guild</note> is in a petition which the *Rettori* <note>The Directors or Rectors of the guild</note> presented to the Council of State on April 3, 1291. They were seeking the refund of a sum of money owed to the guild as a rebate for a tax they had recently paid.^1

The guild certainly followed the example of the other guilds and, early in the fourteenth century, adopted many of the statutes enacted for the “*Calimala*” <note>The powerful Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth</note> Guild. At the same time, they added specific <term>rubrics</term> <note>Legal headings or specific rules</note> of a specialized character that were necessary for the guild's efficiency and the well-being of its members. In the years 1339 and 1341, alterations and additions were made to the statutes, and a register of <term>matriculation</term> <note>The formal enrollment of members into the guild</note> dating up to the year 1335 has been preserved.

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

One of the earlier laws decreed that wine merchants were forbidden from having more than two casks of wine tapped at the same time in their vaults or cellars for retail sale. These casks had a fixed capacity and were required to hold one type of red wine and one type of white wine. Wine in large quantities was usually sold by the barrel or cask. Two casks constituted the load for a pack-horse or mule. The largest liquid measure in Florence was called the *Cogno*, which was equal to ten casks.

The general revision of the Guild Statutes in 1415 included <term>rubrics</term> <note>Heading or section of a legal document</note> enacted for the benefit of "the Guild of Wine-Merchants," and many of these are interesting.

The porch of San Giovanni Battista was a favorite gathering place for the poor and for beggars. Wine merchants were strictly forbidden from selling wine or other beverages there, or within fifty yards of it. <margin>Rule 85, 1415.</margin>

Wine merchants were not allowed to have vine-pits or wine-presses within the city limits, nor vats for <term>must</term> <note>Unfermented grape juice</note>. They were not permitted to treat grapes or wine-mash with water or other liquids in any place where the smell or waste would cause a public nuisance. <margin>Rule 86, 1415.</margin>

Every utensil, jug, and measure was required to be stamped with the coat of arms of the city and to bear the quantity it held, whether a *Terzeruola* (quart), a *Metreta* (pint), or a *Mezzetta* (half-pint). Failure to follow this rule led to a fine of one hundred <term>soldi</term> <note>A Florentine silver coin; 20 soldi made up one lira</note>.

Wine shops were forbidden from taking in travelers or selling beverages to be consumed on the premises. They were not to supply bread, wine, meat, cooked fish, or any other food. Wine sellers were not allowed to stand opposite the Palace of the Priors or the House of the Captain of the People, nor within a distance of two hundred <term>arm's-lengths</term> <note>Approximately 400 feet; based on the "braccio," a Florentine unit of about 23 inches</note>. No wine shop was permitted in the neighborhood of the Monastery of San Giovanni Evangelista. <margin>Rule 90, 1415.</margin>

# GUILD OF WINE-MERCHANTS

No wine merchant was allowed to provide food, whether in the city or in the *Contado* <note>The surrounding territory or countryside governed by Florence</note>, either in a retail wine shop or in his own house. Anyone selling wine to citizens after the final stroke of the Compline bell <note>The final church service of the day, usually around 9:00 PM</note> incurred a penalty of one hundred *lire*. The sale of provisions was also forbidden within fifty arm's-lengths <note>A "braccio" or arm's-length was approximately 23 inches</note> of any wine shop or wine cellar. ^1

Wine merchants and tavern keepers were not permitted to display bushes or signs made of laurel, olive, or any other tree on the front of their premises. <note>In the Middle Ages, an evergreen branch or "bush" was the traditional sign of a tavern</note> ^2 Both new and old wines were required to be transported in wooden barrels. Each barrel had to bear the official seal of the Podesta <note>The chief magistrate and administrator of the city</note>. ^3

No victualler <term>victualler</term> <note>A person licensed to sell food and drink</note> was permitted to make or buy unfermented wine or raw wines fortified with spirits during the harvest season until the feast of All Saints <note>November 1st</note>, under a penalty of ten *lire*. Furthermore, no wine merchant or innkeeper could sell such beverages to the public before that festival. ^4

The Matriculation Registers of 1335 and 1415 show that the following wine merchant families, among many others, enrolled their sons in the guild: the Albizzi, Ricasoli, Strozzi, and Guicciardini families of Florence proper; the Niccolini of Carmignano; the Pucci of Siena and the Val d'Elsa; the Salviati of Pisa; the Toscanelli of Pontedera; the Cocconi of Montepulciano; and the Caspelli of Pontassieve. These names are significant not just for their fame, but because they indicate how widely the guild's membership was distributed. In reality, these members were landed gentry who owned many acres of vineyards and olive orchards, and who engaged in the profitable and pleasant trade of wine merchant at the same time.

In the first List of Guilds from 1236, we find the terms <term>vinadro</term> <note>original Italian: wine-seller</note>, <term>tabernarius</term> <note>original Latin: tavern-keeper</note>, and <term>osste</term> <note>original Italian: innkeeper</note> all merged into the "Arte de' Vinattieri"—"The Guild of Wine Merchants." This association lasted for fifty years, as the naming of the guild remained the same in—

Under the year 1267, there is a curious entry in the Archives indicating a sort of merger between the Guilds of Bakers, Wine-Merchants, and Innkeepers. For some purpose that is not clearly stated, "Ciprianus Pane, son of Vincente, a tavern-keeper of the *sestiere* <note>One of the six administrative districts of Florence</note> of St. Pancratius <note>Italian: San Pancrazio</note> and former Rector of the said Guilds, was appointed Syndic <term>syndic</term> <note>A legal representative or agent for a group</note> by the votes of twenty-three members. The first split in the constitution of the "Guild of Wine-Merchants" took place in 1282, when the order of the twenty-one Guilds was reorganized. In the list of Guilds, the thirteenth place was still occupied by the *Arte de' Vinattieri* <note>Guild of Wine-Merchants</note>, but the fourteenth was occupied by a completely new corporation titled the *Arte degli Albergatori Maggiori*—the "Guild of the Greater Innkeepers." It was likely found that selling food <term>victuals</term> in wine shops was inconvenient, or perhaps the influx of foreign visitors required management on a larger and more professional scale.

The order established in 1282 was maintained through all subsequent revisions of the statutes until 1539. At that time, Grand Duke Cosimo I established the fourth "University" <note>A combined administrative body for multiple guilds</note>, which included the "Guilds of Retail-Drapers and Linen-Manufacturers," "Wine-Merchants," and "Innkeepers," under the name *Universita e Arte de' Linaiuoli* <note>University and Guild of Linen-Manufacturers</note>.

The residence of the Guild's Consuls was located next to the side door of the Church of St. Stephen <note>Italian: San Stefano</note> on the Via de' Lamberteschi. Over the entrance, a shield was displayed—as was customary—bearing the Guild's coat of arms: a blue cup on a white field. This same emblem appeared on the *gonfalon* <note>A processional banner or flag</note> entrusted to the Guild's standard-bearer in 1266.

As far as can be gathered from scattered accounts in many sources, the grape harvest in Renaissance Tuscany was very much the same as it is today. On the first day, the estate's peasants and hired laborers from the city accompanied the vine-growers into the vineyards with shears and baskets.

White grapes were picked first and left to dry in the sun for several weeks until the juice began to drip from them. This produced *Vino Santo*—the favorite white wine for special occasions and the one required for use in the Mass.

The best black grapes were cut and left to ferment by themselves, while those of lower quality were thrown into large wooden vats. When full, the vats were pulled by white oxen to the fermentation house. There, twice a day for a week, bare-legged [workers]...

<meta>This page continues the description of the Tuscan grape harvest and wine-making process, moving from the collection of different grape varieties to the pressing of the fruit and the specific types of wine favored by the citizens of Florence.</meta>

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Young men and women stamped and danced upon the fruit to their hearts' content. The first extraction of this juice—which had, of course, been fermenting all the while—was poured over the richer black clusters placed carefully in the winepress. The rest of the mixture, called <note>original: "il Primo Vino"; the First Wine</note>, was the beverage of the well-to-do citizens. Second and third qualities were also produced—the latter by the addition of water, which is why it was called <note>original: "il Mezzo Vino"; the Half Wine</note>, the drink of the common people. The winepress was made of wood and was strongly, though clumsily, constructed with a large wooden screw and flat wooden slabs.

The Florentines of old were a pleasure-loving people, despite the many serious traits in their character. Nothing pleased them more than to sit in the wine shops after their meals to sing, dance, gamble, and drink to their hearts' content; but, like sensible men, they knew when they had had enough!

The wines most in demand at these jovial scenes were *Vernaccia*, *Leatico*, *Trebbiano*, and *Vino Santo*. They were all sweet and aromatic, with a rich and flashing golden color, yet they were not so potent as to interfere with the full enjoyment and exhilaration of their devotees.

To this list must be added the sweet wines of *Montecalcino*, *Pescianico*, and *Verdea*, mentioned by many writers. *Carmignano*, *Pomino*, and *Chianti* were equally celebrated—the latter, grown on the sides of the rocky hills around Siena, was both red and astringent, as well as white and luscious. The wine of *Artimino* had the character of modern claret, while *Montepulciano*—by far the most famous—combined a luscious flavor with aromatic sharpness and a remarkably brilliant purple color. The finest blend of Tuscan wine was the one that has been held in the highest regard for more than four hundred years, namely: seven-tenths <term>Sangiogheto</term> <note>now known as Sangiovese</note> grapes, two-tenths *Canaiuolo*, and one-tenth *Malvasia* or *Trebbiano*.

The average amount of wine consumed annually in Florence in the middle of the fourteenth century was upwards of 55,000 <term>cogni</term> <note>an ancient liquid measure used in Florence</note>—measures each containing ten barrels. In years of public rejoicings, the total reached 65,000 *cogni*.

->WINE MERCHANTS AND INNKEEPERS 367<-

And wine was cheap in those days. Mazzei <note>Mazzei, i. 158, 395.</note> says that he had “heard of an entire vineyard offered for sale for sixty gold florins!” The wine served to the Priors <note>The high officials of the Florentine Republic.</note> during their term of office cost only thirty gold florins (£15), a sum that demonstrated the moderation of their Excellencies!

The Florentines' extraordinary obsession with regulating quantities, qualities, weights, volumes, and prices extended to even the smallest trifles. Nothing that could be considered a marketable commodity was overlooked. The common, cheap drink of the peasantry—clover juice—was untaxed in the countryside <note>original: "Contado"</note> but was taxed within the city. <note>Perrens’ “History of Florence,” vi. 492.</note>

The value of the wine industry and the wealth of the wine merchants were demonstrated in a peculiar way in the year 1435. During the patronal festival of Saint John the Baptist <note>original: "San Giovanni Battista"</note> the previous year, the massive canvas and silk awnings—which had been provided since early times by the “Guild of *Calimala*” <note>The guild of cloth finishers and foreign cloth merchants.</note> to cover the Square of Saint John <note>original: "Piazza di’ San Giovanni"</note>—were almost completely destroyed by fire. To help the “*Calimala*” merchants cover the heavy expense of restoration, the Council of State passed a decree on April 14, 1435. This decree placed a tax for three years on all wines sold in barrels in the Wine Square <note>original: "Piazza del Vino"</note>. From each year’s gross revenue, fifty-two gold florins were to be deducted as a courtesy to Master <note>original: "Messere"</note> Bino de’ Pecori, Prior of the Monastery of San Piero Scheraggio, and twenty-nine gold florins were to be paid to the tax collector.

No sign of the fame and prosperity of Florence as the "Mother of Commerce" was more distinct or characteristic than the founding and incorporation of a Guild of “Innkeepers.”

The origin of the "Guild of Innkeepers" is not difficult to trace; its actual incorporation, and its inclusion in the hierarchy of the Guilds of Florence, took place in the year 1282. Up to the year 1282—as has been related in the history of the "Guild of Wine Merchants"—wine shops for the sale of beverages only, and taverns for the supply of food and drink, sufficed for the needs of the city. From the available sources, we are able to gather some interesting facts and obtain definite knowledge of how the Guild functioned.

It appears that Innkeepers were treated rather harshly regarding the acquisition of what we now call licenses. The tax levied by the State upon the *Camere Locande* <note>original: "Camere Locande" — lodgings for strangers</note>—as the inns were sometimes called—was quite heavy. As much as forty, fifty, and even eighty gold florins were extracted every third year, at which time all Innkeepers were compelled to appear before the officials of the *Dogana* <term>Customs House</term> to submit their accounts.

Three-year leases seem to have been the usual custom. Any man might bid for a particular inn and could even outbid the current occupier, who, in such an event, was forced to vacate his house. This auction was marked by a quaint custom: the lighting of a candle. It was only lawful to place a bid while the candle remained burning.

While the sale of native wines was restricted to the shops of the Wine Merchants and the houses of the Tavern-keepers, Innkeepers were granted a monopoly on the import of foreign wines, both for immediate consumption and for storage.

Strangers visiting Florence and seeking accommodation were instructed by the officials at the city gates to apply at the Guild offices at the *Canto* <term>corner</term> of the *Via de' Speziali* <note>Street of the Apothecaries</note>. Certain inns were set aside specifically for the reception of foreigners, and others for natives of Tuscany living outside the city boundaries. All these hostelries were directed to advertise their readiness to accept visitors by displaying a bottle of wine in a doorway or window.

### GUILD OF INN-KEEPERS

...to display, whether inside or out, any public sign other than the Guild's coat of arms; no one was allowed this privilege unless they had paid all Guild dues, State taxes, and any fines that had been incurred over time.

Innkeepers were strictly forbidden from admitting people of ill repute under any pretext. There were also strict regulations regarding the food and drink provided by hosts to their guests; for instance, no host, innkeeper, cook, or anyone else was permitted to cook liver, sausages, kidneys, or sweetbreads in their house, inn, or kitchen, nor could they offer them for sale. <note>Rubric 222, 1415.</note>

Innkeepers were strictly ordered not to sell wine or any other beverages to the poor. They were prohibited from competing with the Wine Merchants. While they could sell drinks to guests staying in their houses, they were not allowed to sell to the general public. All wine had to bear the stamp of the Custom House. <note>Rubric 92, 1415.</note>

Regarding the housing of pack mules and horses, no stables were allowed directly beneath the windows of rooms used by guests. Specific streets and areas were designated for this purpose; for example, the Via *Lontanmorte* <note>original: "Lontanmorte" — Street of the Distant Dead</note> contained rows of stables for baggage animals and sheds for storing loads. The number of visitors grew so large that by 1290—only eight years after the Guild was incorporated—there were eighty-six innkeepers and retail wine merchants in Florence and its *contado* <term>the rural territory surrounding the city</term>.

Gambling was forbidden in inns, taverns, and hostels within the city and the countryside, just as it was prohibited in all locations within three hundred *braccia* <term>a Florentine unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches</term> of any public road.

The headquarters of the Consuls of the "*Arte degli Albergatori Maggiori*" <note>original: "Arte degli Albergatori Maggiori" — Guild of the Major Innkeepers</note> was located in the Palazzo Lamberti Simonetti on Via de’ Cavalieri, opposite the Palazzo de’ Pilli. The facade was elegantly carved from hard stone. The architrave featured four coats of arms, including the Guild's emblem—a red star on a silver background. Inside, the Council Chamber featured a beautiful fifteenth-century painted ceiling supported by marble...

Among the ancient inns which were destroyed in 1878 during the clearing of the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> and its neighborhood, were the following:

**The Camel** <note>original: "del Cammello"</note>, near the Rose Gate <note>original: "Porta Rosa"</note>, formerly the Soldanieri Palace.

**The Crown** <note>original: "della Corona"</note>, on the Way of the Proconsul <note>original: "Via del Proconsolo"</note>, in the house of the Buonafi family. In 1427, it was held by Ambrogio di Giovanni, nicknamed "the Little Roman" <note>original: "Romanello"</note> because of his imitation of Roman manners and cuisine.

**The Glove** <note>original: "del Guanto"</note>, on the Way of Saint Romeo <note>original: "Via di San Romeo"</note>. This inn was a gathering place for workers in kidskin and fine leathers.

**The Marciana** <note>original: "della Marciana"</note>, at the corner of the Archbishop’s Way <note>original: "Via dell’ Arciveccordo"</note>, in a house belonging to the Pecori family.

**The Moor** <note>original: "del Moro"</note>, on the Way of the Cow-herd <note>original: "Via Vacchereccia"</note>, the property of the Fantoni family and a famous lounge for the superior silk-workers—the *Major Silk Merchants* <term>Setaiuoli Grossi</term>.

**The Bones** <note>original: "dell’ Ossa"</note>, on the Way of the Plaza <note>original: "Via del Piazza"</note>, belonging to the Bizzini family.

**The King** <note>original: "del Re"</note>, in the Plaza of the Macci <note>original: "Piazza de’ Macci"</note>, the property of the Macci and, later, of the Garliani families.

**The Saint Louis** <note>original: "di San Luigi"</note>, at the corner of the Street of the Straw <note>original: "Via alla Paglia"</note>, belonging to the Marignolli family.

The families named here were all members of the "Guild of Innkeepers." Their houses were registered in the Guild books, and they received periodical inspection visits from the Guild officials.

On the Way of the Apothecaries <note>original: "Via de’ Speziali"</note> were four much-frequented hostelries: **The Lily** <note>original: "del Giglio"</note>, **The Stag** <note>original: "del Cervo"</note>, **The Swallow** <note>original: "della Rondina"</note>, and **The Falcon** <note>original: "del Falcone"</note>. Near Saint Martin <note>original: "San Martino"</note> stood the popular hostelry of **The Baboons** <note>original: "delle Bertucche"</note>, so called because of the preference of its worthy hosts for the rare and curious animals brought to Florence by her merchants and their agents from foreign lands. It was also a favorite center for the *Cerretani* <term>itinerant charlatans or conjurers</term>, whose command of racy dialect and colorful insults was unlimited.
