Indeed, good food was available to anyone with the money for it almost anywhere in the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note>, even though the grimy-looking basements and dark, cavernous rooms were not particularly inviting. If you wished, you could catch the pleasing aroma of stuffed boar’s head and well-fattened venison as you passed the open doorways.

Supper clubs were always the fashion in old Florence, and none maintained their popularity with greater brilliance than the "Society of Poetic Suppers" <note>original: "*Societa delle Cene poetiche*"</note>. Members of the club followed two primary rules: 1. The menu <note>original: "Bill of Fare"</note> was a nightly competition in clever poetic jokes; 2. Each member, in turn, was responsible for ordering the supper. The social meetings of this club were held at Fico’s Tavern <note>original: "*Osteria*"</note> in the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note>. The owner of the land was a member of the Adimari family, who also owned another well-known inn in the Old Market called "Of the Pig" <note>original: "del Porco"</note>—perhaps meaning "Wild Boar." This establishment was worthy of its name due to the excellence of its risotto <note>original: "*Risoto*"</note> and the skillfully crafted delicacy of its salami <note>original: "*Salame*"</note>. No tavern <note>original: "*Osteria*"</note> had such a large following of artists and fashionable young men. And no regular customer <note>original: "habitué"</note> was more cheerful or more brilliant than Sandro Botticelli, the leader of a merry group of artists and companions.

The window sills and doorway of Fico’s were usually decorated with dishes of fried meats <note>original: "*Fritti*"</note> and small birds on spits. Inside, there were large open fires for grilling and frying. Salami <note>original: "*Salame*"</note> and figs were usually served as appetizers <note>original: "*hors-d’œuvre*"</note>. The favorite fish was tench <note>original: "*Tinche*"</note> from the marshes, fried in oil with rosemary leaves; however, *arnotti*—a river fish served in vinegar—was nearly as popular.

When in season, thrushes stuffed with sage and bread were always very welcome; but fig-peckers <note>original: "Beccafichi"</note>—stuffed with mushrooms and toast—were by far the most popular bird dish.

# GUILD OF INN-KEEPERS

The tavern was also known as the "Inn of the Malvasia Wine" <note>original: "*Osteria della Malvasia*"</note>. A great specialty there was *Macciana* or *Maccheroni*—crisp macaroons that paired very well with the favorite beverage.

Andrea del Sarto, known by the title "Andrea the Unerring" <note>original: "*Andrea senza errore*"</note>, had another side to his character. He belonged to the celebrated artists' club called the "Society of the Cauldrons" <note>original: "*Societa del Calderai*"</note>, whose members excelled at modeling foodstuffs <note>term: comestibles</note> in wax and chiseling them in stone. They created every sort and kind of food in the style of a modern Italian chef's highly decorative sugar confectionery!

"The Florentine Supper" <note>original: "*La Cena Fiorentina*"</note> became a proverb, as the fame of the city's cooks and the cheerfulness of her guests grew so immensely. In 1388, no cuisine in all of Italy was nearly as famous; not only did her dinners and suppers surpass all others, but her delicious preserves <note>term: confitures</note> and tasty snacks between meals—washed down with delicate and luscious red and white wines—recalled the historic days of the Greek gourmets <note>term: epicures</note>.

Nothing pleased the successful members of the Guilds more than to sit in their loggias <note>term: *loggie*; open-sided galleries or architectural porches</note> overlooking the Market or the streets, inviting their friends to join them for light refreshments to the admiration of the passersby. For more substantial meals, the custom was to adjourn to some well-known inn and feast upon the good things served by the worthy landlord.

By 1472, a passion for costly banquets had set in, both public and private. These functions were marked by such extravagance and luxury that the notable entertainments of the noble and wealthy Romans almost seemed insignificant <note>original: "paled"</note> by comparison. Arrayed in the richest garments and adorned with gold and precious stones, the powerful leaders of the city reclined upon the softest silk and fur. Waited upon by small armies of attendants in bright uniforms—both white and those of color—each great man vied with his neighbor in the magnificence of his hospitality and the literary and poetic sophistication of his guests.

Such festivities reached their peak during the public festivals of Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of the city's patron saint, St. John the Baptist <note>original: "San Giovanni"</note>.

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Battista. Each Guild had its Commemoration with its own procession, games, music, and banquets. Rich men were also accustomed to showing off their wealth through the lavish entertaining of their poorer brethren. These celebrations were usually held in connection with marriage feasts and similar events; they were managed by some well-known innkeeper whose cook was famous for his culinary skill.

A goose baked in the oven and stuffed with garlic and quince was considered an exquisite dish in the days of Francesco Sacchetti. <note>Sacchetti (c. 1335–1400) was a Florentine writer and poet.</note> The same lively author relates that at a supper given by the *Gonfaloniere* <note>term: the chief magistrate of the Florentine Republic</note> in his palace for a celebrated physician, the first dish brought to the table was a calf's belly, followed by boiled partridges and stewed sardines. According to Boccaccio, Chichibio—the cook for the Gianfigliazzi family—served his master a roasted crane. Leeks were ordered as a special dish by the regulations of the Chapter of San Lorenzo when the canons <note>term: members of a cathedral or collegiate church</note> were in residence. Sweet tarts were served with the roast meat and counted as a single dish. Saffron was a common condiment in both soup and other recipes. As an appetizer, liverwort <note>term: a type of herb</note> was eaten first. Soup was flavored with marjoram and other herbs. Kid <note>term: young goat</note> was served boiled in white wine. On great occasions, boiled peacock was displayed with the feathers still on, though it was not actually eaten. Wine and fruit jellies, colored and molded into various shapes, were considered dishes of honor.

The salaries or fees paid to cooks varied depending on the occasion that required their services. For a banquet at the conferring of a knighthood, the fee was two gold florins; for a wedding breakfast, one gold florin; for a meal of twelve settings, twenty to thirty *soldi*, and so on.

# GUILD OF TANNERS

Furriers. The medieval practice of wearing skins and furs—both by warring raiders from the north and by the peaceful inhabitants of Tuscan lands—prompted early efforts to make such primitive coverings strong and durable.

Alongside abundant animal life, both wild and domestic, great groves of majestic oaks flourished on the hillsides, while patches of humble mallow grew in the marshy lands and along the river reeds. Oak bark and the reddish madder <note>original: "*robbia*"</note> provided a ready supply of materials for tanning and dyeing. It only required the developing ingenuity of the people living along the banks of the Arno and on the hills of Fiesole to apply these natural riches toward creating a highly useful and profitable leather industry.

In the absence of earlier records, we must recognize a man named Paganuccio as the father of the leather workers of Florence. In the State Archives dated 1098, he is called a "Galligario," or "Tanner" <note>original: "*Galligario*"</note>; this appears to be the first mention of the industry.

In the Roll of the Guilds from the year 1236, the Guild of Leather-dressers and Tanners <note>original: "*Arte dei Cuoiai e Caligai*"</note> is ranked eleventh overall, making it fourth in order among the Lesser Guilds. A Latin document dated August 9, 1245, mentions a society of tanners known as the "Sons of the Tanner" <note>original: "*Filii Galigai*"</note>.

The Florentine Archives record a meeting held on December 11, 1276, in the church of SS. Apostoli, attended by forty-two tanners—all of whom were inhabitants of the parish <note>term: *popoli*</note> of SS. Apostoli. The business conducted was the nomination of a Syndic <note>term: a legal representative or business manager</note> by the Rectors <note>original: *Rettori*</note>. This official was tasked with taking out a loan on behalf of the Guild to pay the taxes levied on its members that year and to cover the Guild's general expenses. These expenses included the salaries of officials, the rent of premises for Guild business, river freight charges, and various other items. At the same meeting, provisions were also made for the rent of the Residence of the Rectors (or Consuls) and for certain...

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

"...workshops and a leather warehouse." At the same time, agreements were reached where members of the Guild could purchase materials required for their industry at a two percent discount off retail prices.

The revision of the Title and Statutes of the Guilds in 1282 considerably altered the former and confirmed the latter. The name "Leather-dressers and Shoemakers" <note>original: "*Cuoiai e Caligai*"</note> disappeared, and instead we find "The Guild of Master-Tanners" <note>original: "*L'Arte dei Galigai Grossi*"</note>. Furthermore, the Guild was now placed sixteenth in the order of precedence. No one can say for certain why this demotion occurred. It is possible that the increasing prosperity of the city favored other groups more, such as the "Masters of Stone and Wood," the "Retail Cloth-Drapers and Haberdashers," the "Wine-Merchants," the "Inn-keepers," and the "Salt-Merchants—or General Provision Dealers." All five of these Guilds were ranked before the Tanners.

In the fourteenth century, no change was made to the position of the Guild. A minor corporation, probably affiliated with the "Guild of Tanners" <note>original: "*Arte de' Galigai*"</note>, came into existence in 1327 called the "Company of Scabbard-makers" <note>original: "*Compagnia de' Vaginari*"</note>. Of the three operative Guilds formed during the Revolt of the *Ciompi* <note>the *Ciompi* were disenfranchised wool carders who led a popular rebellion in 1378</note> in 1378, the third was made up of "Sheep-shearers," "Patchers of Skins and Hides," and "Sandal-makers," in addition to other minor crafts. All of these had relationships with the "Guild of Tanners."

The official order of the Guilds in 1415 raised the "Guild of Tanners" <note>original: "*Arte de' Galigai*"</note> one step in precedence over the "Salt-Merchants," who from then on were styled the "Guild of Oil-merchants" <note>original: "*Arte degli Oliandoli*"</note>. At the final grouping of the Lesser Guilds in the year 1534, when four "Universities" <note>term: *Universita*—in this context, a large corporate body or federation of multiple guilds</note> were created, the second of them included the "Shoemakers" <note>original: "*Calzolai*"</note>, "Tanners" <note>original: "*Galigai*"</note>, and "Strap-makers" <note>original: "*Coreggiai*"</note>. This body bore the title of the "University of Masters of Leather" <note>original: "*Universita de' Maestri di Cuoiame*"</note>.

The "Tanners" undoubtedly had dealings with "Skinners and Furriers," "Shoemakers," and "Saddlers" all along, but apparently no specific details of such interactions have been preserved.

# GUILD OF TANNERS

From the fragmentary references to the "Guild of Tanners" in the Archives of Florence—and as a result of the wholesale destruction of documents during the *Ciompi* riots <note>The *Ciompi* were disenfranchised wool carders who led a popular rebellion in 1378</note> and other city disturbances—very little information can be gathered regarding the Constitution of the Guild. Among the archives, however, is a Registration Roll for the year 1320, which gives little information beyond a record of names. It is obvious that there were earlier codes and rolls than this one, but probably no complete set of Statutes was issued until after the General Revision of 1301–1309.

The title of Consul was not bestowed upon the chief officer of the Guild until the 14th century; before that period, he was merely called the *Capitudo* <note>original: "*Capitudo*" (Latin for "Head")</note>. His residence was in the *Via delle Torri*, near the Buondelmonti tower, where the coat of arms of the Guild was carved—a white field divided by a broad red stripe—the same device appearing on the Guild's *gonfalon* <term>a processional banner or flag hanging from a crosspiece</term>.

The *Sensali* <note>original: "*Sensali*" (brokers or agents)</note> numbered four, and were practical and experienced workers in every description of leather. They were appointed by the Consuls and held office for a year. They fixed the price of skins, hides, and raw leather, as well as the rates for tanning, dressing, etc., and kept registers of all workers employed by the Guild. They received a percentage on all imports of skins and hides—for each hundred pairs of skins and hides from India, Greece, England, and Norway, seven *lire*; for each roll of leather dressed abroad, one *lira*, and so on. The consignments were made to the *Sensali*, and they distributed them to the various tanners and dressers.<sup>1</sup>

No tanner, currier <term>a craftsman who dresses, finishes, and colors tanned hides</term>, or scrap-leather dealer was allowed to offer the hides of oxen, cows, and other large animals for sale within the city and the *Contado* <term>the rural territory or countryside surrounding the city</term> unless they had been soaked in brine and cold water for eight months, or for at least three months in hot water. The fine for a violation was two hundred *lire*.<sup>2</sup>

All such persons were warned against dressing hides with cinders or ash, or treating leather with any tanning mixture that would become a nuisance to the neighborhood. Leather could

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

...must not be sold in the market or at the tanyards if it was not perfectly dry, well-cured, and free from decay, under threat of fines of no less than one hundred *lire*. <note>Statute Rubric 227, 1415</note>

Tanners and scrap-leather dealers were forbidden from burning the hoofs and horns of cattle, as well as the hard calluses on horse skins and cow hides, for use in the currying <term>the process of leveling, softening, and coloring leather</term> process. <note>Statute Rubric 78, 1415</note>

All leather workers were forbidden from working in secret. Every tanyard and dressing shop was inspected regularly. Strict regulations were enforced regarding offal and other unpleasant or unsanitary materials. Scraps and waste were required to be burned or removed. Skinning dead animals was not permitted within the city, and the boundaries of this prohibition were constantly expanded until, by the sixteenth century, no *Beccai* <note>original: "*Beccai*" (slaughterer-skinners)</note> was allowed to practice their trade within a ten-mile radius of the Palazzo Vecchio. <note>Cantini, vol. xi, pp. 106–107</note>

A standard outfit for a "Tanner" and "Currier" cost the substantial sum of eighteen gold florins; this price likely included expenses related to the distance of their operations.

<margin>✓</margin>
The methods used by Florentine tanners appear to have been as follows: first, the raw hides were salted to prevent decay, then soaked in a weak lime solution for about three months to prepare them for de-hairing and fleshing. Next, they were placed in pits between layers of coarsely ground oak bark until the pits were full, at which point a thick layer of bark was placed over them. No water or other liquids were permitted to enter the pits. These bundles were taken out and turned several times, with fresh oak bark added each time. This tanning process lasted approximately eighteen months.

<margin>✓</margin>
In the early days, oak bark was the only tanning agent used, and there was an unlimited supply. Thick oak forests surrounded Florence, which provided not only the...

<header>GUILD OF TANNERS</header>

The “Galigai” <note>original: “*Galigai*” (Tanners)</note> used this material not only for their work, but also to feed the fires and furnaces of all the houses and workshops in the city and the surrounding countryside <note>original: “*Contado*”</note>.

However, quick-witted Tanners disregarded the rule regarding the introduction of water. Knowing the benefits of the Arno River, they freely used water sprays and were able to ensure the skins rapidly absorbed the tannin.

The next process was “handling,” in which the hides were transferred to larger pits and then turned over every day in a liquid solution <term>also known as "ooze"</term> made of oak bark. This process lasted five or six weeks. In later times, madder <note>original: “*robbia*”</note> and other liquid dyes were introduced into the tanning process to thoroughly saturate the skins that were intended to be finished in color. For the final step, the skins were hung over large wooden bars immersed in the tanning and dyeing mixture.

The drying process was the most difficult and uncertain stage regarding the desired result. Drying them too quickly led to discoloration and cracking, while a process that was too slow caused molding and unevenness. The drying shed was a wooden building equipped with many openings at the sides to allow air currents to pass through while blocking the direct rays of the sun.

The standard test for dryness was to hold a mirror or some other highly polished object close to the hanging skin. If moisture condensed on the bright surface, the Tanner knew the piece was not ready; if it did not, the piece was finished <note>original: “*vice versâ*”</note>.

Foreign tanned and curried <term>the process of leveling, softening, and coloring leather</term> skins and hides were imported to make shoe soles and sandals, but Florentine Tanners treated them with baths of brine and oak. Sometimes, to reach the market more quickly, they shortened the re-soaking period, but they incurred fines and penalties for doing so.

<margin>/</margin>
The preparation of parchment was an important and profitable branch of the currying industry. Until 1209, its use for writing was limited to monasteries and notaries, but from then on, sales were opened to the general public. High-quality sheets were usually rare and expensive, but in Florence, the same skill that characterized her people’s expertise in other industries was...

...not lacking in the production of superior quality or in an adequate supply.

White parchment, smooth and nearly transparent, was best suited for fine calligraphy, and it held gold and silver leaf better than skins that had been stained yellow or purple. Only the very finest quality of kidskin was used for this purpose, while other varieties were used for more general and rugged purposes—for example, the binding of books.

The market prices were moderate, which accounts for the high number of commonplace books <note>original: *Zibaldoni*</note> and other private diaries, as well as public records and business journals. The Stationers <note>original: *Cartolai*</note> were a trade corporation affiliated with the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries"; they sold the products of the parchment-makers and always appear to have had a large stock on hand, from which they exported prepared skins to every European country.

<margin>✓</margin>
Bookbinding was an important branch of the leather industry, but no one can say for certain whether it was undertaken by the "Guild of Tanners," by the "Guild of Saddlers," or by an association of leather workers employed by the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries"—or perhaps by all three separately. Regardless, the skill possessed by the Florentine leather workers and stampers could not have been put to better use, and from the very beginning, Florentine books were produced in exceptionally attractive forms.

The most common bindings were made of white, smoothly dressed sheepskin and polished vellum <term>high-quality parchment made from calfskin</term>, either perfectly plain or with ornamental markings in black ink and gold. Tooling leather covers for books—that is to say, the art of impressing small dies in a running or connecting pattern—undoubtedly originated in Florence. Rich skins—often with the fur retained and closely clipped—were used and paired with clasps made of silver and copper. About the middle of the sixteenth century, books were—as an old rhymer put it:

> "Bound very handsomely in leather covers,
> Or of satin damask, or else of pure velvet."

Tommaso Maioli of Florence was a famous book collector...

# GUILD OF TANNERS

...who stamped his treasures "Of Maioli and his friends" <note>original: "*Il Maioli et Amicorum*"</note>. His style of binding established the fashion of the day for its delicate and rich materials and workmanship. His favorite material was the finest white kidskin, decorated with gold. However, his simple and elegant style soon gave way to an almost overwhelming abundance of decorative detail. Consequently, Florentine books of the sixteenth century are notable for their varied and elaborate bindings. Craftsmen utilized every possible material—including wood, silver, ivory, parchment, enameled plaques, papier-mâché, and embroidered fabrics—and added embellishments of pearls, precious stones, and goldwork.

It is, of course, impossible to describe in detail the various uses for the leather produced by the skilled Florentine Tanners. In short, they provided the raw materials for essential craftsmen such as shoemakers, saddlers, bookbinders, shield-makers, wall-decorators, chair-upholsterers, and many others. Painters, modellers, sculptors of low-reliefs, and many other artistic craftsmen looked to the Tanners for the material upon which to showcase their beautiful workmanship.

A particular specialty of the leather-workers' trade was making the hides of various animals soft and flexible for molding through repeated soaking and boiling in the tanning pits. <term>*Cuoio-lesso*</term>—boiled leather, as it is called—was shaped by pressure while damp. Its surface was then stamped and carved with ornaments of all kinds, in both high and low relief, similar to the style of wood-carving. This decorative process was known as "block stamping."

Articles made of leather treated this way were usually stained black or a rich, dark madder-brown. Examples can be found in every collection of art treasures, including: bellows, book-covers, chair-backs and seats, writing cases, picture frames, door panels, wall friezes and hangings, pouches, bags, and various types of boxes. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, <term>*Cuoio-lesso*</term> was also used by armorers to make parts of suits of armor, such as elbow guards,

The Guild continued its successful career well into the sixteenth century. However, because Francis I of France and other royal patrons encouraged craftsmen to settle in their territories, Florentine tanners and leather-dressers were among those who found homes in foreign lands. By joining with native workers there, they continued their industry abroad, which consequently left Florence poorer.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the agricultural foundations of Tuscany, detailing the land tenure system and the daily lives and labor of the peasantry as observed by historical chroniclers.</meta>

<page-num>386</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

The form of land tenure in Tuscany during the Renaissance, which is still largely in use today, was the *Mezzeria*—"share and share alike." It was a result of the feudal system and preserved many of its features. Each estate was divided into several *poderi* <note>small farms or agricultural plots</note>, averaging between thirty and forty acres. Half the produce went to the landlord, and the other half was kept by the *Mezzadro* <note>peasant-farmer</note>. There was, however, a silent understanding that the year's harvest was split into three portions, one of which was always kept out of the official count!

The *Mezzadro* held his land through a contract with the landlord. Although this was officially only binding for one year at a time, it was treated practically as a lifelong interest and was commonly passed down from father to son.

Sir Richard Dallington, speaking of the sterility of the Tuscan soil and the extraordinary patience and diligence of the peasantry in cultivating "fruits, herbs, and grain," says<sup>1</sup>:

> "The nature of the soil is generally light and sandy. But because of the nearby cities and great towns, and the large population, the land is heavily worked <term>forced</term> <note>original: "much forced"</note> and made more fruitful. For there are those who spend their entire lives doing nothing but traveling up and down the cities with their donkeys, gathering dung from the streets and carrying it to the land of those with whom they have a contract."

He also refers to the system of dividing the *poderi* and says:

> "The countryman will plow <term>stirre</term> <note>original: "stirre"</note> eighteen of them with his two yokes of oxen—one yoke feeding while the other works—in a single day. He receives four *crazie* <note>small Tuscan coins</note> each for his labor, which is three halfpence sterling; so he and his beasts earn about four shillings and sixpence sterling per day. . . ."

The same old chronicler goes on to say:

> "On the hillsides they grow acorns, olives, and chestnuts. Acorns," he continues, "they eat, and so do their pigs. They do not eat the olives but crush them to export the oil. Chestnuts serve as the countryman's bread, as—"

***

1 "Survey of the Estate of the Great Duke," pp. 30-36.

"...water is his drink." He also remarks that Florentines appeared to be excessively fond of greens <term>green-stuff</term>, and says: "Herbage is the most general food of the Tuscans, at whose tables a salad <term>sallet</term> <note>original: "sallet"</note> is as common as salt is at ours." In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, figs also formed a profitable source of revenue for the cultivator; the best kinds were called "Brugiotti."

The landlord met the expenses necessary for the upkeep of the farm buildings and for the planting of trees. He was also a part-owner of the teams <term>spans</term> of oxen used on the *podere* <note>small farm or agricultural plot</note>, and in addition, he paid the taxes on the land. On the other hand, the *mezzadro* <note>sharecropping farmer</note> paid for any labor that was beyond his own strength; such payment generally consisted simply of board and lodging. The *mezzadro's* usual helpers were his younger brothers and his sons, who lived in rather cramped conditions <term>hugger-mugger</term> <note>original: "hugger-mugger"</note> in the farmhouse. Hired laborers were not in high demand <term>at a discount</term>, as they were usually unemployed townsmen or extra workers <term>spare hands</term> who had doubtful reputations.

On each *podere* stood a roomy farmhouse <term>labourer farmer's cottage</term>, a stable and yard for cattle, a shed for fodder, a vat-house for grapes, and an oil press—all of which were the property of the landlord.

The *mezzadro* knew exactly the capabilities of each portion of his holding and understood the proper rotation of crops. His principal crops <term>objects of cultivation</term> were vines, olives, wheat, beans, and millet for animal feed <term>forage</term>, which kept him busy throughout the year. Mulberry trees, chestnuts, and oaks—along with flax, hemp, fruit, and vegetables—also required his care and labor.

While he looked after his pigs, his wife <term>spouse</term> tended <term>minded</term> the poultry; she also made the butter and the cheese and grew her flowers, sweet herbs, and other items for the market. She was assigned the care of the bees and the processing <term>rendering</term> of the honey. Many a housewife <term>goodwife</term> also had her trays and drawers of silkworms and silk cocoons <note>a practice known as sericulture</note> under the patronage of the "Guild of Silk." She also spent much of her time spinning flax, plaiting straw, and assisting her husband in making wicker baskets.

Cattle and sheep breeding were only indirectly part of the peasant farmer’s work. Generally speaking, around Florence, herds and flocks were the property and business of the <term>Beccai</term>—wholesale breeders and butchers—and mostly grazed almost wild through the Maremma, the lowlands by the sea. Horses, however, along with mules and goats, required the attention of the <term>mezzadro</term> <note>sharecropper</note>, along with his oxen and his dogs. He used the dogs to watch his crops and livestock and to alert him to intruders.

The Tuscan peasants were a robust, well-developed people with handsome brown faces and intelligent expressions. The vitality born of a healthy, outdoor life and constant hard work and exercise led to sobriety and simplicity, which produced a natural courtesy of manner.

Donatello’s “David”—the first nude bronze of the Renaissance—truthfully represents a Tuscan peasant boy just entering manhood. Leonardo da Vinci described it as a “perfect figure.” Michelangelo’s “David” was modeled after just such a youth: alert and aware of his strength and excellent physical condition. Many handsome farm boys, like the shepherd boy of Israel, found their way into Florence daily with market produce. These two statues are quite typical of the race to which the young peasants belonged.

Leonardo, himself a son of the soil, possessed immense physical strength and high spirits. He used to go out into the <term>poderi</term> <note>small farms</note> and chat with the farm laborers. Nothing pleased him more than to make well-built youths jump, wrestle, and climb trees so that he could observe their muscular beauty and translate their bodily perfection into his pictures. In 1506, he painted a handsome young man sitting on a grassy mound, his head crowned with vine leaves. The form is purely Florentine, and the physical beauty of every part reflects the fine qualities of the Tuscan peasant. Although the picture is titled “Saint John the Baptist,” it is more accurately a representation of a vine-trimmer and an olive-presser—a Renaissance “Bacchus”!

The great Florentine <note>Leonardo da Vinci</note> was also in his element when telling groups of lounging peasants ridiculous stories which convulsed them with laughter, for then he swiftly sketched their poses and expressions.

And if these great artists have preserved for us the traits of manly character and vigor, the Della Robbia family, Raphael, Andrea del Sarto, and many more besides have given us the no less striking charms of the *contadine* <note>peasant women</note>, both old and young. The terra-cottas of Luca Della Robbia, in particular, reproduce faithfully the two types of Renaissance women. Stateliness of posture and solemnity of manner are characteristic of the silent country life of the hills, where the drama of nature is always being enacted. In the other type, the casual nature of town life in the valley, where all is gay and busy, lends confidence to their bearing. The “Madonna and Child” of the Via dell’ Agnolo is at once the true representation of a healthy, radiant peasant woman and her baby, and the symbol of the intelligence of the Renaissance.

The peasants of the *Contado* <note>the rural territory surrounding the city</note> and beyond were happy people, and eased the monotony of their daily toil with jests and songs.<sup>1</sup> As soon as one ended what he knew, another burst forth with the melody, each vying with his neighbor in friendly rivalry. Whoever could sing the most songs was acclaimed the leader. Parties of singers used to frequent the fairs and public games and exhibit their vocal powers, receiving as their reward many a flowing bowl of good red wine and a supper fit for a king at one or another of the hospitable inns! These popular songs were known by the name of “Cantastorie” <note>literally "story-singers" or narrative ballads</note>, and none went with a better swing than those which they sang on May mornings.

Something of what a countryman looked like in the fifteenth century may be seen in a woodcut of the Rook’s Pawn in Jacopo de Cessolis’s “*The Game of Chess*” <note>original: “Giuoccho delle Scacchi”</note>. “This type of person,” he says, “is depicted . . . in the shape of a man holding a spade or shovel in his right hand, and a rod in his left hand. The spade or shovel is for digging and working the earth with, and

"...the rod is for driving or leading all the animals into the pastures. He also ought to have in his belt a curved hatchet to cut off the excess growth of the vines and trees. . . ."

The cultivation of the olive tree was a very important branch of country life. Planting, irrigating, pruning, and shaking the trees required constant attention, for no tree is more unpredictable in its yield. The olive groves of Tuscany rivaled the vineyards in total area under cultivation. Wealthy citizens owned scores or even hundreds of trees, while the humblest *contadino* <note>original: "contadino"; a peasant farmer</note> had his two or three.

->"DELLAVORATORE"—FARM LABOURER. FIFTEENTH CENTURY<-

Agricultural methods are slow to change, for even today, the techniques for shaking and collecting the dark purple-green fruit are exactly those of five hundred years ago. Large canvas sheets are spread upon the ground under each tree, into which nimble youths climb, armed with long thin sticks, to shake each branch and cluster gently so that the berries are not damaged.

# GENERAL PROVISION DEALERS

...by their fall. In ordinary years, the value of the yield from each tree-beating averaged ten to twelve gold florins, equal to £5 or £6 in our money.

Tuscan olive groves were always more or less troubled by infestations of the dreaded *Mosca olearia* <note>original: "Mosca olearia"; the olive fruit fly</note>, the olive pest. Various methods were employed year after year to check its destruction, which sometimes caused the entire failure of the crop and, moreover, weakened the trees for future harvests.

The methods used for extracting the oil were very similar to those now in use all over Italy. Each *podere* <term>farm or smallholding</term> had its own olive press and clearing mill—usually heavy constructions of wood and iron—which were operated by both hand and ox power. In the fifteenth century, the price of good average olive oil was six *lire* and ten *soldi* per barrel—equal to half the load of a pack-mule or donkey. The best oil was produced at Lucca, Calci, and Buti, to the north of Florence.

That there was an ample and constant supply of all kinds of fruit for consumption in Florence is confirmed by the characteristic summary that Buonaccorso Pitti gives in his "Chronicle" of the fruit trees in his garden. He says:

> "On April 24, 1419, which was my birthday, I counted all the fruit trees in my garden and vineyard. I found that, excluding hazelnuts, they totaled five hundred and sixty-one: sixty-four fig trees, one hundred and six peach trees, eighty plum trees, fifty-eight cherry trees, twenty-four almond trees, twenty-five apple trees, and sixteen pear trees. There are, besides, six orange trees, seven pomegranates, two quinces, four walnuts, and nine *Amarini* <term>bitter cherries</term>. In addition to sixty olive trees in full production, there are a great many more fruit trees of all kinds which have not yet borne any crop, but perhaps they will if the drought does not trouble them." <sup>1</sup>

The *Fattore* <term>bailiff or estate manager</term> was the owner’s agent; he supervised the working of the different farms and rendered his master an account twice a year. These men were sometimes cruel to the...

Indeed, it was a common custom for an estate manager (<term>Fattore</term>) to be enrolled in one of the Guilds (<term>Arti</term>), such as the "Wine-merchants" <note>original: "de’ Vinattieri"</note>, the "Oil-merchants" <note>original: "degli Oliandoli"</note>, or the "Innkeepers" <note>original: "degli Albergatori"</note>. This practice also spread to the wealthier sharecroppers, who were thus able to carry on a combined trade as both growers and salesmen.

In 1379, he leased a piece of land—or *farm* <note>original: "podere"</note>—on the condition that the tenant should give him at Christmas one hundred and fifty pounds of pork, along with a pair of capons and five dozen eggs; and at Easter, another pair of capons and five dozen eggs. In addition, the farmer was required to deliver by his wagon the shares of wheat, oats, and oil, and half the share of wine which were due to him as the owner. The farmer also had to tend certain vines belonging to his landlord and had to break in two teams of oxen each year, which he had to partially purchase.

Land sales were generally conducted at Or San Michele, where a number of *Surveyors* <note>original: "Agremensori"</note> were in daily attendance. Their fee was one gold florin for each sale completed, along with what we would now call a stamp duty of nine *soldi* <note>a small Florentine currency unit</note>.

***

This Guild—the eighth in order of precedence among the fourteen Lesser Guilds—was essentially the Guild of the market people. Under its white banner, decorated with the highly appropriate coat of arms of the Guild—a red lion standing guard <note>original: "gardant"</note> under a green tree—were gathered not only wealthy growers of olive trees, owners of fruitful orchards, makers of farmhouse cheese, and hunters keen for game, but every variety of large and small dealers in the countless necessities of daily life.

The Guild provided a common union for people engaged in agricultural occupations, in the same way that the "*Guild of Retailers and Second-hand Dealers*" <note>original: "Arte de' Rigattieri"</note> provided a comprehensive organization for citizens involved in small industrial trades.

The precise date of the first registration of the "*Guild of Oil-merchants and Provision Dealers*" <note>original: "Arte degli Oliandoli e Pizzicagnoli"</note> is, as with most of the other Guilds, completely uncertain. Early records have disappeared, and the first historical mentions of the trades united within the Guild seem to be as follows:

> "1021. *Florentius*—*straw-seller* <note>original: "paliarius"</note>."
> "1084. *Bonus, son of John* <note>original: "Bonus f. Johannes"</note>—*hawker* <note>original: "baro," a variant for "barullo"</note>."

"1104. Bonizo—oil merchant <note>original: "olearius"</note>."
"1139. Lupaccia—fruit and vegetable dealer <note>original: "lo tricco"</note>."

In the first list of the Guilds, dating from the year 1236, the **Guild of Oil-Merchants and Provision Dealers** <note>original: "Arte degli Oliandoli e Pizzicagnoli"</note> is placed fifteenth. The revision of 1266 preserved the same order but granted the "Guild of Oil-Merchants and General Provision Dealers" appropriate armorial bearings.

The list of Guilds made in 1282 makes no mention of the **Guild of Oil-Merchants and Provision Dealers**; instead, in the fifteenth position, we see the **Guild of Salt-merchants** <note>original: "Arte dei Venditori del Sale"</note>. This was still the designation of the Guild in 1295, the year in which the "Guild of Salt" is named in the Archives. The reason may be found in the fact that as the city grew in population, so did the status of those merchants and dealers whose business relations were of the greatest value to the citizens.

At the reorganization and rearrangement of the Guilds in 1415, the fifteenth place was taken by the **Guild of Tanners** <note>original: "Arte de' Galigai"</note>, and the "Guild of Oil-Merchants and General Provision Dealers" was moved to sixteenth. Why this loss of precedence occurred is impossible to say; regardless, the Tanners maintained their superiority until the final dissolution of the Guilds in the sixteenth century.

There is an entry in the Archives of the **Merchants' Court** <note>original: "Mercanzia"</note> dated 1328, regarding a judgment delivered against a certain grain merchant <note>original: "Granaiuolo"</note> of the "Guild of Bakers," and in favor of the Consuls of the "Guild of Oil-merchants." The title of the Guild is given in full, and it includes a variety of curiously linked industries: grain merchants <note>original: "Biadaiuoli"</note>, cheese merchants <note>original: "Casciaiuoli"</note>, glassblowers <note>original: "Bicchierai"</note>, ropemakers <note>original: "Funai"</note>, and soap-boilers <note>original: "Saponai"</note>. In 1380, the grain merchants joined with the oil merchants and ceased to be a separate association.

There is no doubt that the “Guild of Oil-Merchants and General Provision Dealers” followed the example of the other crafts by adopting the Statutes of the “Calimala” <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants</note> from 1301–1309 as a code of moral and commercial conduct, making certain adjustments for their own circumstances.

Because the early records and acts of the Consuls or Councils have been lost, we cannot determine the exact number or the duties of the various officers. Nor can we find a complete list of all the trades and professions that were allied under the banner of the Guild.

The fact that the guild’s headquarters was located in the basement of the *Palazzo de’ Lamberti* suggests that the chief officials eventually held the rank of Consul. The upper part of that building was occupied by the Consuls and Courts of the “Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries.” It is, however, of special interest to note that Savonarola established his famous “Mount of Piety” <note>original: "Monte di Pieta"; a charitable institution that offered low-interest loans to the poor</note> in the same basement—which was also known as “The House of Pigli” <note>original: "La Casa di Pigli"</note>—to counter the high interest rates and greed of the Jewish moneylenders.

Fortunately, the Statutes of 1415 have been preserved. In them, we see ample evidence of the guild members' importance, prosperity, and excellent governance.<sup>1</sup> The following are some of the interesting details gathered from reading those three large volumes:

All provision dealers, whether they were members of the “Guild of Oil-Merchants and General Provision Dealers” or not, were required to use weights and measures that strictly followed established standards. Furthermore, they were required to present them to the state’s official inspectors. All measuring containers had to be approved by the Consuls of the Guild, and patterns of those approved items were kept at the headquarters to be used as models for imitation.<sup>2</sup>

Under no circumstances were these dealers allowed to sell fresh fish; they could only sell varieties that had been salted or dried. Eggs, cheese,

Chickens, mushrooms, small birds, venison, and game of all kinds were all marketable commodities on their stalls.¹

The export of foodstuffs from Florence—both the city and its <term>Contado</term> <note>the surrounding rural territory or countryside</note>—was very strictly prohibited. Included in the prohibition were: grain of all kinds, ears of corn, vegetables, olives and olive oil, livestock, oxen, pigs, wine, fresh meat, fish, raw hides, fruits, cheese, and provisions of every kind.²

It was strictly forbidden to offer grain for sale mixed with chaff, seeds, or any other matter. Wheat stalks were not to be soaked in water to make them swell before being displayed in the market. <term>Granaiuoli</term> <note>corn-chandlers or grain merchants</note> guilty of such conduct were fined heavily. They were, moreover, required to declare the place of origin for their merchandise and were absolutely forbidden from substituting a crop from one locality for one coming from another.³

Vegetable dealers, whether men or women, were not allowed to offer for sale any sort of grain in quantities exceeding two <term>staioi</term> <note>bushels</note> unless they had a special license from the officials of <term>Or San Michele</term> <note>a building that served as both a granary and a center for Florence's guilds</note>. No dealers in vegetables were permitted to purchase fruit or vegetables before the hour of <term>Nones</term> <note>the ninth hour of the liturgical day, roughly 3:00 PM</note>, nor were they allowed to frequent public places where wholesale salesmen gathered before that hour. Women were forbidden from hawking green produce through the streets. Green nuts were also forbidden to be sold. It was strictly prohibited to carry through the streets, or to offer for sale, more than three bunches of unripe grapes. Ripe wine grapes were also forbidden as marketable commodities.⁴

On Sundays, and all through Holy Week, the sale of green produce in the <term>Mercato Vecchio</term> <note>the Old Market</note> was absolutely prohibited. All fruiterers and dealers in vegetables were required to appear in the month of January each year before the Market Officials and swear an oath to carry on their business honestly, peacefully, and diligently.⁵

The sale of certain articles was absolutely forbidden in the squares, bridges, and certain other localities: olives, fruit, vege-

vegetables <note>original: "tables"; likely an OCR error for vegetables given the preceding page's reference to "green produce"</note>, grass, straw, cheese, eggs, fish, geese, small birds, chickens, foxes, hares, and venison. Hawkers of such goods were not allowed to stand in front of the market stalls or street shops of established tradesmen.

Poultry, vegetables, fruit, eggs, game, venison, and other similar produce could not be offered for sale in the markets or shops if they originated from outside a nine-mile radius of the city. Thrushes and blackbirds were strictly forbidden from being offered for sale in Florence at any time. Quails could be sold only during August, September, and October.¹

No innkeeper, vegetable dealer, or anyone who traded in such goods was allowed to buy the following food items in the streets, on bridges, or in the squares: pigs, kids <note>young goats</note>, calves, chickens, pigeons, eggs, cheese, and joints of fresh meat, or sows with litters. This last prohibition also applied to butchers. Pork butchers were not allowed to use the same slaughterhouses as those occupied by the *Beccai* <note>the Guild of Butchers, who primarily handled beef and mutton</note>. Indeed, pigs could only be slaughtered between September and March. In the shops of the Guild, every kind of salted meat was available for sale, as well as salted and dried fish.²

If any fruiterer or poulterer, regardless of their status, dared to buy mushrooms, cheese, eggs, chickens, any kind of poultry, or venison—or to loiter where such things were offered for sale—before the hour of <term>Nones</term> <note>the ninth hour of the liturgical day, approximately 3:00 PM</note>, whether they had a license or not, or to wait within two hundred yards of the market, he or she was liable to a fine of ten <term>lire</term> <note>the local currency of Florence</note>. If he or she could not or would not pay, the man was imprisoned for a month, and the woman was beaten through the streets with a stick!³

All provision dealers were required to appear every year in the month of January before the market authorities and their notary to pay a sum of fifty silver florins as security for their honest dealings with the poorer people. They were subject to the same regulations as millers and bakers regarding the sale of grain and cooked meats.⁴

<meta>This page continues the detailed market regulations from the 1415 Statutes of Florence, transitioning from the sale of poultry and meat to the quality control of olive oil, candles, and fuel materials.</meta>

<page-num>398</page-num>

The olive oil they offered for sale had to be pure, clear, and sweet-smelling, and meat products of every kind required accurate labeling—the substitution of inferior grades for superior qualities was strictly monitored. If any food item was found to be spoiled or moldy, the dealer was punished with a fine of twenty *lire*.¹

The measurements for oil were the same as those for wine, and every cask, jar, bowl, pitcher, bottle, or other vessel had to be clearly marked with the quantity it was supposed to hold. No oil merchant was permitted to have more than four jars of olive oil in his shop at any one time, and these had to be labeled with the names of the olive grove and the grower. Direct trade of oil between private individuals was forbidden, as was the practice of peddling it through the city streets.²

Provision dealers who supplied candles were required to ensure that they were made of good tallow <note>rendered animal fat used for making candles and soap</note> and had functional cotton wicks. All inferior types were seized and destroyed by the Market officials. The boiling and melting of tallow for candle-making was forbidden within sixty yards of any major street.³

Sellers of straw, firewood, and other fuel materials were required to appear every January before the Market officials to solemnly promise to observe all the regulations and bylaws affecting their trade; failure to appear resulted in a fine of fifty *lire*. Additionally, no flammable material was permitted to be stored for sale within the city walls.⁴

Warnings were also issued to those who packed loads of straw and flammable materials. The load for each donkey was not to exceed two hundred pounds in weight and had to be packed compactly and evenly. Vegetable dealers and others in similar trades were also cautioned about the volume of firewood they brought into the city. No timber more than two yards long or weighing more than two hundred pounds was permitted for any single animal.⁵

Restrictive laws were also in effect regarding the amount of fuel a citizen could purchase. For private houses, no more than two donkey loads were allowed; at factories and—

In the meat markets <note>original: "shambles"</note>, larger quantities were permissible. No one was allowed to peddle coals, pitwood, straw, or any other such materials from carts or pack animals.<sup>1</sup>

The barge and boatmen of the Arno River were subject to strict regulations and bylaws. Once a year, in the month of January, they were required to provide a security deposit of one hundred *lire* as a guarantee that they would not load, carry, or land any contraband or merchandise that violated state laws. They were forbidden from loading for export grain, vegetables, olive oil, fruit, bulls, oxen, pigs, wine, or cheese—if it exceeded one hundred pounds in weight. They were also prohibited from exporting salted meat, fish, lake-tench <note>a species of freshwater fish</note>, more than a bushel of baked bread, mushrooms, and all other food items designated for local consumption by the officials of Or San Michele <note>a building in Florence that served as both a grain market and a guild headquarters</note>.<sup>2</sup>

Despite all these careful, and even restrictive, measures, the working classes and even many wealthier citizens were known for disregarding standard dietary rules. Poor-quality food, meat from ill-fed animals, and bad ingredients were given as little thought as the simple and hygienic rules of cooking were in poorly managed homes. Many <term>Provvisioni</term> <note>Italian: legislative decrees or provisions</note> were passed against suppliers who provided low-quality food to the poor and against unsanitary conditions in the preparation of public meals.

The Statutes of the Guild were revised and expanded in 1345, 1415, and 1529. During the final reorganization of the Lesser Guilds in 1534, the “*Arte degli Oliandoli e Pizzicagnoli*” <note>Guild of Oil-merchants and General Provision Dealers</note> was included in the first of the four "Universities" alongside the *Beccai* <note>Butchers</note> and the *Fornai* <note>Bakers</note>. This association was named the “*Universita di Por San Piero*”—the “University of Saint Peter’s Gate.”

In the writings of Franco Sacchetti, Simone della Tosa, the Peruzzi Codex, the "*Libro di Montaperti*" <note>The Book of Montaperti</note>, the accounts of the Alberti family, the <term>Provvisioni</term> <note>legislative decrees</note>, and other sources, we find a great number of interesting details about the values and prices of commodities of all kinds in Florence during the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries.¹

The best cheese came from Lucardo, in the Val d'Elsa, "where they make good cheese," as the common report had it. Much was also imported from Sicily and Sardinia, as well as from Apulia, but a tax of ten <term>soldi</term> <note>a silver coin and unit of currency</note> was charged on all such foreign supplies for every thirty pounds of weight.

On October 13th, 1330, notice was given to the officials of the <term>Mercanzia</term> <note>the Merchants' Court or guild council</note> of the arrival at Leghorn <note>the port city of Livorno</note> of a ship laden, among other things, with three hundred and fifteen jars or casks of clear olive oil, eighty-five of unrefined oil, and forty thousand pounds of Apulian cheese.²

The market people suffered greatly at the hands of these nimble gentry <note>referring to the aggressive tax or toll collectors</note>. Sir Richard Dallington says:
> "I saw a poor country-woman, who came to the gate to pay her toll for a basket of lettuce she brought in: one of the 'foxes'—who I think could smell a goose, for he could not possibly see one—searched under the herbs, and finding a dead one without feathers, sent the poor woman away half dead with sorrow, without her goose!"¹

While Florentines were moderate in their consumption of butchers' meat, they were very fond of a preparation called "*Mischiasto*"—desiccated beef—imported from Barbary <note>the coast of North Africa</note>. This meat powder was on sale at all the shops of the Guild.

The worldly wisdom of the Florentines in their talent for striking good bargains is amusingly illustrated by a proverb <note>original: "wise saw"</note> of the period regarding the purchase of grain:
> "When you *buy* oats, look out that the measure is not filled too quickly, for it will always sink two or three percent; but when you *sell*, fill quickly and your oats will grow!"²

The monopoly of salt was in the hands of the State, which owned the ancient pits at Volterra, Portoferraio, and Castiglione; but the retail sale of this indispensable commodity devolved upon the "Guild of Oil-Merchants and General Provision Dealers." Its supply was so important to the community at large that in 1266 the Guild became popularly known as the "*Arte dei Venditori del Sale*" <note>original: "Guild of Salt-Merchants"</note>.

The price charged for salt at the Guild shops varied with the circumstances of the time, for the legislators of the Republic fastened new taxes more readily and heavily upon it than upon any other article.

The processing of salt was equal to the high standard of the other industries of the city, and Florentine salt merchants became famous. A document dated November 16, 1564, is in the possession of the Paganelli family, by which Queen Elizabeth of...

England granted to Tommaso Baroncelli of Florence the privilege of introducing the art of refining and bleaching salt to England, as it was practiced in Florence, along with a monopoly on manufacturing white salt for a period of twenty years.

The "*Arte degli Oliandoli*" <note>the Guild of Oil-merchants and General Provision Dealers</note> was, after all, not entirely confined to Florence, but extended its branches far and wide. General provision dealers have long been known in England under the title of "Italian Warehousemen." In the shop of any such merchant today, one may see most, if not all, of the various items that used to keep the salesmen of old Florence busy in supplying daily needs.

## II. THE GUILD OF HARNESS-MAKERS <note>original: "L'Arte de' Coreggiai"</note>

Few things were regarded with more pride among Florentines of the Renaissance than the art of horsemanship. To begin with, owning a riding horse was considered a passport to good society; however, regarding the use of mounts by the *Masters* <note>original: "Messeri"</note> of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries," those notable men made very little attempt to ride a horse simply for the sake of riding!

The curriculum of all the physical education schools of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries included skill in equestrian exercises. Agnolo Pandolfini—acclaimed by his fellow citizens as "The Peaceful Citizen" (1360–1446)—kept twenty highly bred and trained horses at his villa at Segni. He was an expert in every kind of physical exercise and pursued every fashionable sport; he also trained his sons, his apprentices, and his servants to follow in his example.

Vittorino da Feltre (1397–1446), the founder of the celebrated physical education school at Mantua, also included horsemanship and hunting in his list of mandatory exercises for the noble youths entrusted to his care.

The great Duke Federigo of Urbino—himself a pupil of Vittorino—was proficient in all manly sports. He took up the profession of arms and joined the troop of the <term>Condottiere</term> <note>a leader of mercenary soldiers</note> Niccolo...

<page-num>403</page-num>
<header>GUILD OF SADDLERS</header>

Piccinino <note>Niccolò Piccinino (1386–1444), a famous Italian mercenary captain</note>. He bore honorable scars on his body as proof of his prowess, for during a joust outside the town gate, he had the misfortune to lose an eye and break his nose!

Among the exercises necessary for a gentleman, as laid down by Count Baldassare Castiglione in his world-famous book, *The Courtier* <note>original: "Il Cortigiano"</note>—published in 1531—was horsemanship. "I would have it," he says, "that a gentleman should be a perfect horseman in every respect—skilled in riding, running at the ring, and tilting... hunting the wild boar and bull..."

In the days of ancient chivalry, when not engaged in active warfare against foreign enemies, young warriors found outlets for their exuberant vigor in tournaments. These were at first bloody combats where one, and sometimes both, of the combatants were killed. Such bloody encounters were suppressed by religious decrees <note>Sacred Canon</note> from Rome, and less lethal pastimes were established instead. To these, the Florentines applied the title jousts <note>original: "Giostre"</note>.

The great jousts were held during the principal Church Festivals. The tilting ground was of considerable size to allow the horses a free gallop. Each knight had to ride three courses. Tilting at the Saracen <note>original: "Il Saracino"</note>—the Moor, similar to our "Turk's Head"—offered opportunities for fearless horsemanship.

To "win his spurs" was the ambition of every squire and, indeed, the dream of every youthful page. The squire could wear only short and plain silver spurs, while the knight was spurred in gold. The use of spurs was a mark of independence and authority.

As this was the fashion of the times, there was immense scope for the employment of manual skill in the making of saddles, bridles, stirrups, and all the accessories of the stable and the racecourse. Saddlers, harness-makers, shield-makers, scabbard-makers, and the like had their hands full of commissions. These, of course, required greater skill and provided greater profit than the ancient manufacture of ordinary cart and carriage harnesses and equipment.

“There are,” says Brunetto Latini, “horses of all kinds—chargers, or tall horses, for combat; others for gentle exercises use palfreys—which are also called amblers and hackneys; others again employ pack-horses to carry loads.”<sup>1</sup> Mares were never used for riding purposes—indeed, to offer a mare to a knight was considered an insult: they were reserved for pulling carts and carrying packs.

Horse-dealers and horse-brokers formed a significant portion of the Guild: at least Guild members were the recognized agents between the stock breeders in the *Contado* <term>the rural territory surrounding the city</term> and beyond, and the horse buyers of the city. In this trade, they were undoubtedly partners, in a sense, with the *Albergatori*—Innkeepers—many of whom owned or rented stables for the feeding and resting of travelers’ horses and mules.

The numbers of pack animals and draft horses were, of course, considerable on the trade routes between the sea and Florence, and upon the more distant lines of communication with France and Germany. Merchants and commercial travelers looked to the dealers and brokers of Florence, and the neighboring cities and townships, for their relays of convoy animals.

The Archives of Florence contain several records of Saddlers and allied craftsmen, for example:
> “1031. *Martinus—Cabellarius*” <note>original: Cabellarius</note>—Horse-dealer.
> “1073. *Aezo—Sellarius*” <note>original: Sellarius</note>—Saddler.
> “1076. *Barone—Scutarius*” <note>original: Scutarius</note>—Shield-maker.
> “1101. *Sichelmus—Stafarius*” <note>original: Stafarius</note>—Stirrup-maker.
> “1211. *Ristoro, son of Pieri—Buorsajo*” <note>original: Buorsajo</note>—Pouch-maker.

These various branches of the leather industry and others like bookbinding, gauntlet-making, and many luxury trades—having a common material and serving the needs of the fashionable and literary classes of society—were quite naturally drawn together for the mutual advantage of all.

The “*Arte de’ Coreggiai*” <note>The Guild of Saddlers and Harness-makers</note> first appears in the list of Guilds in 1236, when it was placed twelfth in the order of the Fourteen Minor Guilds.

<header>GUILD OF SADDLERS</header>

The Guild maintained the same status during the revisions of 1266 and 1280–1282. In the latter year, the title of the Guild was expanded to become the "Guild of Saddlers, Harness-makers, and Shield-makers" <note>original: "L’Arte de’ Sellaiai e Coreggiai e Scudai"</note>. In 1285, an Association of Bridle and Reins-makers was recorded as an incorporated branch of the Guild under the title of the "Guild of Bridle-makers" <note>original: "L’Arte de’ Frenai"</note>.

Among the minor associations affiliated with the Guild was the "Horse-dealers and Jobbers" <note>original: "Prestatori di Ronzoni"</note>, which is frequently mentioned between 1309 and 1316. In 1321, another company is mentioned—the "Scabbard-makers" <note>original: "Vaginari"</note>.

The Guild must have prospered, for by 1415 it no longer occupied its very low position in the hierarchy of the guilds; instead, it had advanced to tenth place among the Lesser Guilds.

As was the case with all the Guilds, both Greater and Lesser, the first regular Statutes were established between 1301 and 1309. These were revised and expanded in 1342, 1415, and 1501. The usual Guild officials served under Consuls. The number of Consuls varied as circumstances required, but there were always more of them than in some other Lesser Guilds, as they represented the various associated trades.

The Saddlers were organized into six classes:
1.  Makers of saddles, stirrups, and harness for heavy hauling.
2.  Makers of carriage reins and bridles.
3.  Gold and silver spur-makers and horse armorers.
4.  Makers of wooden saddle-bows and pack-frames.
5.  Curriers <term>craftsmen who dress and color tanned leather</term>, who covered the wooden frames with leather.
6.  Saddle-painters and decorators.

The Shield-makers were also subdivided:
1.  Workers in metal frames.
2.  Turners who made the wooden foundations.
3.  Craftsmen who stretched and lined the shields with leather.
4.  Embossers and painters.

The other members of the Guild were similarly subdivided, including the harness-makers, scabbard-makers, gauntlet-makers, bookbinders, and others.

In 1530, under Cosimo I, the "Guild of Saddlers and Shield-makers" was merged with the "Shoemakers" and the "Tanners."

The coat of arms of the Guild consisted of two red stripes on a white field. These were displayed on the banner first presented to the Guild in 1266, and they also appeared on the Residence of the Consuls.

Regarding saddles, their use for military purposes began with the introduction of steel and iron armor. Men in armor could not maintain their balance without support; consequently, for combat, they were provided with leather seats featuring flaps designed to wrap around the rider's thighs to give him a steadier seat.

Saddles were gradually equipped with: (1) the tree <term>the solid structure that forms the base of a saddle</term> or stretcher upon which the leather was fixed—this was made of wood; (2) the seat itself; (3) the skirt; and (4) the flaps. The "tree" was usually made of beechwood set upon an iron framework.

<page-num>407</page-num>

# GUILD OF SADDLERS

Pigskin was the standard leather used, but dishonest saddlers were not above using imitation skins, as many a horseman discovered to his own expense!

Saddlers also made pillions <term>cushions for a second passenger behind the main saddle</term> and litters <term>enclosed seats or beds carried by horses or men</term> for ladies and the sick. They also produced saddlecloths and horse-caparisons <term>ornamental coverings for horses</term>, hiring embroiderers and leather-stampers for decoration.

Saddlers were also involved in cutting and sewing bridles, reins, and stirrup straps for riding horses, as well as heavier harnesses for draft teams <term>animals used for pulling heavy loads</term> and pack animals. For these items—which needed to be both light and strong—they used uncolored strips of hardened, well-seasoned leather that had also been pressed.

Stirrups originated in France and came in various shapes and sizes to suit military and civilian riders. Tournament stirrups were bulky and heavy, but highly decorated and reinforced with iron supports. These were essential for combat—whether on the battlefield or in tournaments <note>original: "lists of chivalry"</note>—though ordinary horse riding was done without them.

The list of iron hardware <term>original: "ironmongery"</term> used by saddlers is quite extensive: buckles, bits, snaffle chains, headpieces, collar steels, saddle bearings, gearing chains and bolts, civilian spurs, all types of straps, whips, whip-bands, and more.

Regarding shields—the production of which belonged to the Craft of Saddlery—these were kite-shaped or triangular in the twelfth century. Smaller shields of similar shapes were introduced in the thirteenth century, featuring holes cut into the upper right corner to serve as a rest for a spear or lance. Round bucklers <term>small handheld shields</term> were held in the hand during the fourteenth century, while pear-shaped shields were worn on the arm. By the fifteenth century, knights' shields featured a central bulge and were about two and a half feet long.

Florentine shield-makers used various names for different types of bucklers, such as: the round shield <note>original: "*Rotella*"</note>, the oblong shield <note>original: "*Scudo*"</note>, and the small arm shield <note>original: "*Brocchiere*"</note>.

...and bulging; the *Targa*—a large square or round shield; and the *Pavese*—a shield that covered the whole body.

The materials used were iron, copper, wood, and leather, though usually in combination. When two materials were used, the shield was bound with an iron rim. Tournament shields were a specialty of the Florentine shield-makers <term>original: "Scudai"</term> and were made more for display than for actual use. They were elaborately adorned with paintings, embossed with plaster <term>original: "gesso"</term> moldings, or inlaid with patterns of wood and metal. They were often decorated by first-rate artists.

Pouches, purses, and gauntlets all fell under the category of <term>Saddlery</term>. Their manufacture and decoration formed an attractive trade that was quite profitable for the skilled craftsman. Each class of citizen had a distinctive shape of pouch or purse, and it was possible to identify the wearer's Guild by the shape they favored. Civilians used to display their coats of arms, or those of their Guild, on their pouches—*scarselle* <term>Florentine pouches or purses worn on the belt</term>, as they were called.

This custom sparked great rivalry and considerable variety. The more stylish a man was in his dress and in the style of his belt, pouch, and gauntlets, the more respect he received in public.

Dante refers to this fashion in the *Inferno*:

> "...hanging from his neck each wore a pouch
> marked with various colors and emblems,
> on which it seemed their eyes were feeding." <sup>1</sup>

*Scarselle* and leather gauntlets were sold by the retailers <term>original: "Rigattieri"</term> as well as by the saddlers, who also made all kinds of gloves.

These pouches were often works of art, where the finest efforts of the leather-dresser or the cloth-stitcher were colored with the pigments of renowned artists and decorated with the embroidery of skilled silk-workers and goldsmiths. They were hung from the belt on the right side, or from the—

As time went on, more and more care was spent on finishing and adorning leatherwork. As a case in point, it is recorded that in the middle of the fifteenth century, the Saddlers of Florence had introduced a lower standard of workmanship. Fashion demanded pictorial decoration on saddles, shields, book covers, and other leather objects; consequently, the "Guild of Painters" intervened and passed a rule <note>original: "rubric"</note> which forbade their members from painting or decorating any kind of leather except the very best ox-hide or pigskin—and under no circumstances were they allowed to use inferior colors.¹

### III. The Guild of Locksmiths <note>original: "L’Arte de’ Chiavaiuoli"</note>

The Renaissance demanded finer and more artistic workmanship from all types of artisans than had been sufficient in medieval times. No industry felt this influence more strongly than that of the metalworkers. Because of the bulk and nature of their materials, as well as the heavy requirements of their trade, the "Guild of Blacksmiths" was entirely unable to produce the countless elegant objects that skilled hands could craft from common metals.

As early as the fifth century, Ampelius, the monk-historian, mentions a "Corporation of Locksmiths" in his *Legends of the Saints*, citing the complexities of their craft. Another monk-historian, Theophilus, in his *Handbook of Various Arts* <note>original: "Diversarium Artium Schedula"</note>, published in the early part of the twelfth century, provides descriptions of methods for embossing, damascening <term>the art of inlaying different metals into one another for decoration</term>, and other work in iron, steel, copper, and bronze. He further adds a list of locksmiths’ tools, including hammers, chisels, screw-jacks, saws, scrapers <note>original: "scalpers"</note>, engraving tools <note>original: "burins"</note>, etching needles, burnishers, and so on.

In the twelfth-century Archives of Florence, there are the following records regarding locksmiths:
->“1108. Florentius—Locksmith <note>original: "Clavajulus"</note>”<-

In the first list of the Guilds from 1236, the “Guild of Locksmiths” <note>original: "Arte de’ Chiavaiuoli"</note> was ranked tenth among the Fourteen Lesser Guilds. This position was maintained in 1266, but between 1280 and 1282, the Guild was promoted to sixth place and received an extension of its title, namely: “The Guild of Locksmiths and Ironworkers—Old and New” <note>original: "L’Arte de’ Chiavaiuoli e Ferraiuoli-Vecchi e Nuovi"</note>.

In 1301–1309, when the statutes underwent a strict revision to align with the general adoption of the model code prepared for the “Calimala” <term>The Guild of Foreign Cloth Merchants</term> merchants by all the Guilds, an alteration was made to the name of the Guild as follows: “The Guild of Locksmiths, Ironworkers, and Braziers” <note>original: "L’Arte de’ Chiavaiuoli, Ferraiuoli, e Calderai"</note>. In 1415, the original style of 1236 was restored, and the Guild was ranked eleventh among the Fourteen Lesser Guilds.

Many trade associations were affiliated with the Guild, for no industry provided more opportunities for varied craftsmanship, both useful and decorative. These associations ranged from groups of highly skilled artists in metal—both precious and common—to the lowest social classes. For example, in 1311, the “Scrap-iron Dealers” <note>original: "Ferravecchi"</note>—a recognized trade in its own right—were incorporated, and in 1327, “Engravers in Copper” <note>original: "Incisori in Rame"</note> were included in the Guild membership.

If the custom mentioned by Ampelius the Monk in the fifth century—the election of two Consuls, which he calls “the good old Republican title”—was continued in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries by the Locksmiths of Florence, then the Guild was entirely in line with the other trade corporations regarding its chief officers.

It is taken for granted that much, if not all, of the system implemented in the "Workshops" <note>original: "Laborerum"</note> of the "Guild of Masters of Stone and Wood" was adopted by the masters of iron and copper.

Tests of craftsmanship were required before admission to the Guild. The candidate not only had to produce samples of his work, but he was also required to provide evidence of his skill to the Consuls. He did this by demonstrating his dexterity in using all kinds of tools, manipulating various types of metals on the spot.

The residence of the Guild Consuls was a small house opposite *Or San Michele* and adjacent to the offices of the "Guild of Wool." Carved on the wall, as was customary, were the Arms of the Guild—a large black key—which also appeared on the red field of the Guild’s banner <term>gonfalon</term>.

---

Some idea of the Guild's progress and prosperity can be gained by comparing the amount it contributed during the taxation of the Guilds in 1325. This tax was raised to pay for the military enterprises of the Republic. The Guild contributed eighty gold florins—exactly the same amount as the "Guild of Masters of Stone and Wood." This sum exceeded the amount raised by the "Guild of Tanners and Skinners." This measure of development holds true regarding the number of Guild members, their financial resources, and their skill and reputation.

Workshops for artistic metalworking were abundant in old Florence. Sometimes two or three trades shared the same premises and worked side by side. In Fico’s basement in the *Mercato Vecchio* <note>Old Market</note>, there was a furnace for glass-blowing alongside a shop for locksmiths and gimlet-grinders. There, one could purchase a flattering hand-mirror or an elegant flower vase, and inspect the latest fashions in metal belt-clasps, dress buttons, belts <term>cinctures</term>, purse fittings, and other personal ornaments.

Florence soon became a rival to the grand city of Milan in the art and craft of locksmithing. Indeed, on at least one occasion, she won the prize—when Cardinal Wolsey ordered from Florence...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the specialized products of the Florentine metalworkers, specifically those produced by the Guild of Locksmiths, and describes the aesthetic characteristics of their work.</meta>

<page-num>412</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

two thousand sets of <term>horse-harness</term> <note>the equipment and gear for a horse</note>, with embossed and <term>damascened</term> <note>metal inlaid with gold or silver patterns</note> metal work. The price was sixteen shillings per set—a large sum in those days.

Much of the fineness and delicacy of Florentine <term>locksmithery</term> was undoubtedly due to the sunny, invigorating climate of <term>Tuscany</term>. In the very characteristic workmanship, there is an entire absence of deep furrows and profound shadows, while <term>low relief</term> <note>carving or casting where the design stands out only slightly from the background</note> and lightness of touch are evident in every object. The designs are full of life and cheerfulness. If the mask of tragedy scowls menacingly, there is something about its expression which suggests merely a passing mood. The features of comedy never cease their merry laughter: every smile, every dimple, and every blush is exactly marked with a sympathetic touch.

In nothing so much as in the making of <term>locks</term> and <term>keys</term>, and the <term>hinges</term> of doors and cupboards, did the nimble-fingered artisans in metal exhibit this atmospheric influence in the perfection of their skill and adaptability.

These articles were almost always constructed in connection with wood and leather; hence <term>locksmithery</term>, <term>joinery</term> <note>fine woodworking and furniture making</note>, and <term>curriery</term> <note>the processing and dressing of tanned leather</note> marched hand-in-hand, absorbing and assimilating similar ideas and methods. For an example of this statement, one only needs to compare the <term>tongued and grooved</term> work of the Middle Ages with the <term>framed and mortised</term> treatment of the <term>Renaissance</term>. The long, over-strapped hinge of a door or chest was changed into the dove-tailed “<term>bull-hinge</term>,” as it is called.

The making of locks attained such a degree of excellence that they were considered rare objects of art and were transported with the utmost care from place to place. The designs most commonly produced in Florence were <term>armorial bearings</term> <note>coats of arms and heraldic symbols</note>, lettering, and <term>grotesques</term> <note>fanciful or fantastic decorative figures</note>, with conventional <term>foliage</term> and <term>ribbon work</term>—all in sympathetic relief. Keys followed the same pattern: they were first distinguished in Florence as “male” and “female”—the former had solid shanks, while the latter were hollowed out or barrelled.

The models of these objects, and others similar in character, were always made in wax. The <term>wax-modellers</term> of Florence...
