<page-num>413</page-num>

<header>GUILD OF LOCKSMITHS</header>

The work of these craftsmen excelled those of all other cities of art. It is perhaps curious that they never formed themselves into a specific Guild or Corporation of their own. Their finest workmanship resulted in glorious bronze medallions, which are the pride and joy of artists, craftsmen, and collectors alike. They are remarkable for the lowness of their relief; nothing more delicate was ever achieved by the hand of man working in metal.

The following are some of the more prominent masters of bronze who worked in the shops of the Locksmiths: Antonio Avertino, Giovanni Petrecini, Michelozzo Michelozzi, Andrea Guazzalotti, and Niccolò Fiorentino in the fifteenth century; and in the sixteenth, Benvenuto Cellini, Giovanni da Bologna, Francesco di Sangallo, Antonio Pollaiuolo, Domenico Poggini, and the Gianpaolo brothers—all of whom were <term>matriculated</term> <note>officially registered or enrolled</note> members of the Guild.

The <term>damascening</term> <note>the art of inlaying different metals into one another, typically gold or silver into steel or bronze</note> of metal—a beautiful art—consists of inlaying gold and silver upon steel and bronze. The method used in Florence was that introduced from the East, namely the spreading of the stamped-out design laid flat and close upon the surface of the metal. Pressure and blows were applied under both heat and cold. <term>Artificers</term> <note>skilled craftsmen</note> called it <note>original: "All' Azzimina"</note> "in the Persian style"—meaning "like a coat of mail"—and <note>original: "Alla Gemina"</note> "in the twin style"—meaning "after the original."

The finest work of this description was exhibited in the magnificently wrought iron cabinets, inlaid with gold and silver, which became a fashion among wealthy citizens in the sixteenth century.

Benvenuto Cellini is very warm in his praise of the damascening of steel by Florentine craftsmen. He says: "With their needle-like chisels, they turn up every twist and curve of the most intricately overlapping acanthus leaf. Their introduction of little singing birds and playful animals seems to make the bare metal a living entity."

The embossing of metal was by no means the least admirable product of the Florentine Locksmiths. In this art-craft, they competed with the workers in leather and the carvers of wood.

Indeed, all three classes of workmen became so skilled that, when tasked with a subject to be crafted in each of the three materials, they aimed to produce a unified result where no one could tell at a glance which part was metal, wood, or leather!

Few craftsmen were greater in this beautiful trade than Francesco dal Prato di Girolamo. He worked in the style of Michelangelo <note>The original text refers to "Michele Agnolo," a common archaic spelling for Michelangelo</note>, who perhaps introduced the technique to Florence from Germany.

The greatest artists did not consider it beneath them to create the simplest objects. For instance, Benvenuto Cellini made salt-cellars, Jacopo Sansovino made inkstands, Donatello made mirror frames, the Pollaiuoli family made candlesticks, and so on. To realize that these objects were as strong as they were beautiful, one only needs to recall the feat of Leonardo da Vinci, who reportedly wrenched off door-knockers with only one hand to win a wager. A favorite style of door-knocker was a chiseled figure of a naked child—much like the lovely *bambini* <note>original: "bambini"; Italian for "infants" or "children"</note> of the Della Robbia family—holding a scroll inscribed with "*Salve*" <note>original: "Salve"; Latin for "Welcome" or "Greetings"</note>.

The clever members of the "Guild of Locksmiths" have left behind endless objects for posterity to admire and imitate. Some of the most striking evidences of their artistic leanings combined with practical convenience were everyday working tools. Unlike today, these were not merely—and often obtrusively—utilitarian. Instead, they were designed and made by men who taught the eternal lesson that the useful and the ornamental need never be separated.

Many humble but indispensable household tools feature beautiful decorations. For example, there are cloth-smoothing irons with handles shaped like coiled snakes, and carpenters' compasses with impressed and chiseled floral designs. There are also nutcrackers, trays, and scent-caskets with delicately fine pierced work. Farriers' tools <note>tools used for shoeing horses</note> feature richly embossed designs. Sixteenth-century surgical saws have handles made of ivory inlaid with silver and amber, while other instruments have ebony handles decorated with inlays and small bronze plaques. Snuffers <note>tools used to extinguish or trim candle wicks</note> were embellished with patterns in stamped diaper <note>a repetitive geometric or floral pattern</note>. Drilling braces, pincers, fire-irons, knives, forks, spoons, skewers, thimbles, candle-prickets <note>a type of candlestick with a sharp spike to hold the candle</note>, hand-planes, and the tools and instruments used—

<summary>This page explores how the Guild of Locksmiths integrated high art into everyday utilitarian objects, from door-knockers to surgical tools. It highlights the involvement of legendary artists like Donatello and Cellini in creating decorative household items.</summary>
<keywords>Guild of Locksmiths, metalwork, decorative arts, Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, door-knockers, household tools, craftsmanship, Florence</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the argument that the utilitarian tools produced by Florentine trades were elevated by artistic design, focusing specifically on the impact of the Guild of Locksmiths.</meta>

<page-num>415</page-num>

<header>GUILD OF LOCKSMITHS</header>

in all the trades of Florence, were all of them made for work but adorned by art.

In short, the Locksmiths’ Art was an absolute affirmation of all the mighty powers of the Renaissance. Without the clever metal craftsmen, much of the charming revelation of that precious awakening would not have existed. The "Guild of Locksmiths" supplied the instruments with which the secrets of ornamental craft and useful art have been revealed to a delighted world. They gave spatulas to sculptors, paint-boxes to painters, compasses to architects, sextants to explorers of nature, pestles and mortars to doctors and apothecaries, combs to silk carders, fine frame wires to silk weavers, smoothing irons to "*Calimala*" <note>The *Arte di Calimala* was the powerful guild of cloth finishers and foreign cloth merchants.</note> cloth finishers, needles to lace-workers and embroiderers, and sensitive scales to coin-makers at the Mint—along with many more indispensable implements and apparatus.

When Cosimo I, the first Grand Duke, established his four Universities of the Crafts in 1534, the "Guild of Locksmiths" was incorporated as the third in rank, along with the "Blacksmiths," the "Masters of Stone and Wood," the "Armorers and Swordmakers," and the "Carpenters." The name of this combined organization was "*L’Università de’ Fabbricanti*"—the "University of Artificers" <note>original: "L’Universita de’ Fabbricanti"</note>.

### I. THE GUILD OF ARMORERS AND SWORDMAKERS
<note>original: "L’ARTE DE’ CORAZZAI E SPADAI"</note>

ALTHOUGH the primitive arms of the Etruscans came originally from Greece and were famed for their excellence of pattern and manufacture, and although the legions of the conquering Roman armies crossed and recrossed Tuscany and impressed the durability and workmanship of their weapons and armor upon the subjected races, it is a matter of certainty that Florentine arms and armor were directly influenced by Germany.

In Italy, the business of making armor and weapons—especially swords—was a specialty of Milan and other towns in

Lombardy. The patterns and workmanship shown in these workshops were undoubtedly Teutonic <note>Germanic in style</note>, but in the skillful hands of Italian workmen, the plain and practical instruments of attack and defense received the addition of artistic decoration.

One of the earliest famous armorers in Milan was Galvano Fiamino, who, by 1288, had established a great reputation for making helmets, breastplates, shields, and other pieces of body armor in burnished metal. The Giulino family was also famous for making steel armor, but they specialized particularly in defensive armor for horses.

From the eleventh to the fourteenth century, armored men wore only iron shirts <note>Referring to chainmail hauberks</note>. In the thirteenth century, crossbows were generally used with a variety of arrows, for example: sharp, short darts <note>original: "Verrettoni"</note>, medium-length bolts with ball-shaped points <note>original: "Moschette"</note>, and long four-feathered shafts <note>original: "Quadrelli"</note>.

Before the invention of gunpowder in the middle of the thirteenth century, the machines used for artillery were as varied in type as they were extraordinary in form. Their manufacture required the services of armorers and metalworkers, as well as the assistance of carpenters, rope-makers, and other craftsmen. After gunpowder was applied to artillery in 1280, this class of offensive weapons became a distinct and widely practiced industry. With the introduction of firearms, a rival class of workmen emerged—gunsmiths—who gradually replaced armorers as the science of warfare developed.

Throughout the fourteenth century, knights continued to use the lance, sword, and battle-axe. Foot soldiers were armed with short swords, bows and arrows, darts, short axes, slings, knives, daggers, and javelins. Scale armor was rarely, if ever, used after the fourteenth century.

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Tuscan infantry were armed with steel or iron breastplates, but they wore no armor on their backs. They carried iron pikes set upon stout wooden poles seventeen feet long, along with swords that had rounded points. Head...

Armor was not worn. Arquebuses <term>early muzzle-loading firearms</term> made their appearance only at the beginning of the sixteenth century.

The work of armorer-smiths seems to have reached its highest point of excellence in the second half of the fifteenth century. The influence of the Renaissance was felt in the richness of decorative features rather than in the quality of the metal used.

Also very evident was the progress made—both intellectual and artistic—in the products of the armorers’ shops. Ill-fitting pieces gave way to well-molded articles, much in the same way that poorly made cloth garments never leave the workbench of an observant and diligent tailor.

Bronze armor was introduced during the sixteenth century and was worn until the year 1558. Its adoption was mainly due to the fact that it was much easier to keep clean than steel. Black armor followed on the heels of bronze armor, and its somberness brought into fashion the splendid decorative qualities of gold and silver damascening <term>the art of inlaying different metals into one another to create patterns</term>. Embossed and fluted armor was the latest adaptation of defensive dress and became fashionable at the end of the sixteenth century, used more for state functions and parades than for use in the field or at the joust.

As early as the end of the eleventh century, armorers existed in Florence—if not much before that period. The archives contain the following entries:

> “1090. Johannes, son of Rodolfo—dagger-maker <note>original: "fil. Rodolfo—pugnitore"</note>”
> “1128. Florentius—armorer <note>original: "Spaliarius", literally a maker of shoulder-guards</note>”

Workmen who had been trained in the Milanese workshops found their way to Florence, along with many other craftsmen, when her sun began to rise so gloriously in the early Renaissance.

Florentine armorers, along with those of Pisa and Pistoia, very soon attained fame for being proficient in the art of making arms and armor. To the latter city <note>Pistoia</note> belongs the distinction of having manufactured the first “pistol”—a lethal weapon with a wheel lock and a barrel a foot long. The growth of the industry led

...naturally to an incorporation of the artisans, and so it is not surprising that in the first list of the Guilds—that of 1236—the Guild of Armorers and Sword-makers <note>original: "Arte de' Corazzai e Spadai"</note> finds a place.

Certainly, the rank of the "Guild of Armorers and Sword-makers" was very humble—eleventh among the Fourteen Lesser Guilds. This position was maintained in 1266, but in the List of 1280–82, the Guild displaced that of the "Locksmiths" and retained that rank in 1301–1309 and right on until 1415. In that year, the "Armorers and Sword-makers" gave way to their rivals in the industry of artistic metalwork and even lost one more place, ending up as the nineteenth out of all the Twenty-one Guilds.

Upon the last reorganization of the Lesser Guilds in 1534, the "Armorers and Sword-makers" were grouped with the other workers in metal, stone, and wood—the "Blacksmiths," "Locksmiths," "Masters of Stone and Wood," and "Carpenters"—under the comprehensive title of "The University of Craftsmen" <note>original: "L'Universita de' Fabbricanti"</note>. This was the third of the four "Universities" <term>large administrative bodies formed by merging several smaller guilds</term> incorporated under the Grand Duke Cosimo.

In a document of the thirteenth century, to which no date is attached, it is stated that "those who hammer their metal plates and make steel cuirasses <term>pieces of armor covering the torso</term> are a Guild apart, and exercise their craft under Consuls or Rectors, like the other Guilds of Florence."

Another entry, dated 1303, names nineteen individuals "who are declared to be more than two-thirds of the members of the Guild, and who in a full meeting elected two Consuls or Rectors." Among other matters that came before these officials was a dispute between the "Armorers' Guild" and that of the "Escutcheon and Shield-makers' Guild" <term>escutcheon: a shield or emblem bearing a coat of arms</term>. They appointed two members of the Guild to act as arbitrators. The disputants, who, it is stated, had—or ought to have had—a common banner, held different opinions as to who should pay for a new one and who should have the care of it. The decision reached charged the "Armorers" with two-thirds of the cost and the "Escutcheon and Shield-makers" with the remaining one-third. Further,

Since the latter had held possession of the Banner for a full year, the former was granted custody of it for two consecutive years.

Another disputed matter—the share of grain which the two Guilds were required to contribute to the Florentine army in the field—was settled in the same manner.

Very little information can be found in the Archives and Records of Florence regarding the constitution of the Guild.

Statutes were first issued in 1300; until that date, custom and convenience seem to have been sufficient for the purposes of government and development. These were revised in 1305 following the model of the "*Calimala*" Code <note>The "Calimala" was the prestigious Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth</note>. Additions and alterations were made in 1314–1316, 1321, 1342, and 1463, following the same pattern as the "Guild of Carpenters."¹ Among the Statutes of 1315 was one requiring every horseman serving in a campaign to provide himself with a helmet, breastplate, gauntlets, <term>cuishes</term> <note>armor protecting the thighs</note>, and leg-pieces—all made of iron by recognized armorers of Florence.

Naturally, many related industries were included in the Guild's membership, but it is difficult to determine their exact relationships with one another. One such association is recorded between 1309 and 1316: the "*Compagnia degli Arcariai*" <note>original: "Compagnia degli Arcariai"</note>, or the "Company of Makers of Bows and Arrows."

Armorers were expected to supply general camp equipment as well as the arms and armor of the soldiers. *Trabacche* <note>original: "Trabacche"</note>—bell tents—and *Padiglioni* <note>original: "Padiglioni"</note>—pavilions—were made of heavy canvas and, in the early days, were provided by the soldiers themselves. These pavilions were often enormous, beautifully decorated with painting and embroidery, and adorned with many flags.

...promised to pay Nato Melliorati and Pela Lapi—business partners and citizens and merchants of Florence—a sum of seventy *lire*, payable within a month, for a certain shipment of goods: belts, hats, breeches, <term>bucklers</term> <note>small round shields</note>, helmets, and swords. In the Tax List of 1321, when the Guilds were taxed in proportionate charges for the benefit of the State, the Guild of Armourers and Sword-makers <note>original: "Arte de' Corazzai e Spadai"</note> is recorded as paying one hundred and fifty *lire*—a very small sum indeed compared to the contribution of two thousand gold florins by the Wool Guild <note>original: "Arte della Lana"</note>. In the same list, the Company of Bow-makers <note>original: "Compagnia degli Arcariai"</note> is charged separately the very modest sum of eight *lire*—the smallest amount of all.

In the days of the *Condottieri* <note>mercenary military leaders</note>, when the spirit of warfare and the plague of banditry went hand in hand, deadly weapons and body armor were in great demand. Florentines, however, were an industrial people, not a warlike folk, and they managed their battles by proxy.

Vast sums of money were paid for the arming, mounting, and provisioning of the organized groups of mercenary troops. These troops, led by Florentine commanders or foreign captains, defended the honor of the "City of the Lily" <note>a nickname for Florence</note> and proclaimed her power over reckless opponents. Such leaders included Uguccione della Faggiola, Castruccio Castracane, Bartolommeo Colleoni, Giovanni de' Medici (of the Black Bands), Guarnieri, and Hawkwood.

Each *Condottiere* regarded his troop—and some of them numbered thousands of soldiers—as the deciding factor in peace and war, and took the utmost pains to keep his armaments up to date.

Every young Florentine of noble birth was trained in schools like the one at Urbino, and quickly adopted the teachings of Castiglione’s *The Courtier*. "I would have," the Count wrote, "a perfect gentleman be of good physique and well-proportioned in..."

Although the prices of these items are not included here, we can gather from a price list dated 1372 that it was a significant financial undertaking to equip a knight with body armor, weapons, a horse, and banners. A *ronzone* <note>original: "ronzone" — a warhorse or charger</note> cost between forty and fifty gold florins, and its daily upkeep in a public stable cost at least one-fifth of a gold florin. A pair of spurs cost half a gold florin, a bridle cost three-quarters, and an engraved bit cost nearly one full gold florin. For a page, a mule cost twenty gold florins, a pair of stirrups cost half a gold florin, and the bridle cost three-quarters. A <term>sumpter-horse</term> <note>a packhorse for carrying luggage</note> for a servant cost at least twenty-five gold florins.¹

If Milan was the recognized market for functional battle armor, Florence was no less famous as the source of ornamental weapons. Its "Armorers and Sword-makers" were primarily employed in making equipment for knights to use in *Giostre* <note>original: "Giostre" — jousts or tournaments</note>. These were items of great beauty and high value, intended for show rather than for durability or practical use.

As early as the year 1260, young Florentines of all social classes were in the habit of going out to Peretola—a famous jousting field three miles away—to practice with the lance and sword in friendly competition. The ancient rule had been that only noble-born young men and famous soldiers were eligible to take part in these contests; indeed, the right to carry weapons was denied

the lower classes. Under the rule of the Medici, however, the *Giostre* <note>original: "Giostre" — jousts or tournaments</note> were opened to all social classes.

These tests of skill, strength, and agility were always held during the major Church festivals. Jousting grounds were established in the city's larger squares and in all the more important surrounding villages.

One of the most famous duels to the death took place during the siege of Florence in 1530, when the giant Dante da Castiglione faced Bertino Aldobrandi, a renowned Florentine champion. With one crushing blow, Aldobrandi—despite having a crippled right arm—split his opponent's helmet and skull all the way down to the shoulder!

Another celebrated Florentine, Leon Battista Alberti—renowned forever for his proficiency in many arts and sciences—was also a great athlete. He thought nothing of leaping onto the back of a galloping horse while wearing full armor!

This gave much encouragement to the craft of the armorer, and the members of the “*Arte de’ Corazzai e Spadai*” <note>The Guild of Armorers and Sword-makers</note> became extremely skilled and also extremely wealthy.

The headquarters of the Guild's Consuls was in the Piazza del Duomo, in the same building as the offices of the “Misericordia” <note>The Archconfraternity of Mercy, a historic Florentine charitable organization</note>. One of the armorers' most important workshops was located on the Via de’ Spadai (Street of the Sword-makers), next to the Church of Sant’ Andrea in the *Mercato Vecchio* (Old Market) and adjacent to the famous market shrine of the Madonna. The Guild's coat of arms was displayed over both buildings: a red sword and a blue cuirass <term>a piece of armor protecting the torso</term> on a white field.

In 1472, a “Treatise on Military Arts” by a Florentine named Giovanni Valturio was published. It contains the first mention of guns and similar engines of war being manufactured by the “Guild of Armorers and Sword-makers.” Until 1474, the Florentines only had iron guns drawn by oxen—used more or less for show—since these primitive weapons required several hours to cool after every shot before they could be used again! The Republic’s standing army was small and possessed no artillery.

### II. THE GUILD OF CARPENTERS
<note>original: "L’ARTE DE’ LEGNAIUOLI"</note>

The Guild of Carpenters was one of the least esteemed in the hierarchy of the guilds. In every official list, it occupied the second-to-last position, taking precedence only over the "Bakers' Guild" <note>original: "Arte de’ Fornai"</note>. It is quite impossible to state the reasons for this perceived inferiority. Possibly, the relationship between this guild and the "Masters of Wood"—who were incorporated into the "Guild of Masters of Stone and Wood" <note>original: "Arte de’ Maestri di Pietra e Legname"</note>—was such that the latter group attracted all the more skillful and artistic workers, as well as the wealthier and more influential ones.

It is very likely that the rougher woodworkers were originally peasants from the rural district <note>original: "Contado" — the countryside surrounding a city</note>, accustomed to felling trees and preparing them for the master builders in the city. Some were also undoubtedly gatherers of firewood and loose timber. Such men would be quite capable of building, however crudely, the huts and cottages where they lived, as well as the sheds and barns where they sheltered their cattle and stored their harvests.

Whatever the Guild of Carpenters failed to achieve in terms of high social status within the guild economy, they certainly possessed in terms of their ancient origins. Their claim to an early existence as a trade is indisputable.

In the days of Charlemagne, there are records of a "Society of Carpenters" in Tuscany, known by the designation of "*Fabritignarii*" <note>Latin: "workers in wood"</note>. The robber-captains in the warlike times before Countess Matilda <note>Matilda of Tuscany (1046–1115), a powerful medieval ruler and supporter of the Papacy</note>—like her ancestor Boniface, who was created the first Marquis of Tuscany <note>original: "Torscia or Toscana"</note> in 828—found plenty of work for them. These craftsmen were kept busy clearing forests, planting stockades, and manufacturing pike handles, bows, and arrows. In later years, many descendants of these rugged ancestors, who were skilled at working with timber, became members of the first carpenter associations in Florence.¹

Between 1209 and 1213, mention is made of certain workmen known as “*coopers*” <note>original: "Bottariai"</note> and “*trough-makers*” <note>original: "Madiellariai"</note>. Reference is made in 1327 to two other allied trades: “*chest and cradle-makers*” <note>original: "Cunatori"</note> and “*varnishers*” <note>original: "Verniciatori"</note>.

In the lists of guilds from the various revisions of the statutes in 1236, 1266, 1280–82, 1301–1309, and 1415, the “*Guild of Carpenters*” <note>original: "Arte de’ Legnaiuoli"</note> is ranked twentieth. In the latter year, it was titled the “*Guild of Master Carpenters*” <note>original: "Arte de’ Legnaiuoli Grossi"</note>.

In the early days, a set of carpenter's tools cost a man very little. For example: a broad-axe cost 5 *soldi* <term>soldi: small silver or copper coins used in medieval Italy</term>, a plain saw cost 3 *soldi*, a plane cost 4 *soldi*, an adze cost 2 *soldi*, and a square, a spokeshave, and a chisel cost 1 *soldo* each!

---

The statutes of the guild were first issued in 1300. As was the case with the guilds of “armorers,” “locksmiths,” and “saddlers,” which were in a similar position, these statutes were written in handwriting so difficult to read that no one has yet succeeded in fully explaining the details of its constitution. The general code, which was drawn up between 1301 and 1309 for use by all the guilds and adapted to their specific requirements, was adopted by the carpenters in 1305.

We seem to have no information regarding the specific officials elected to manage the guild's affairs. It is certain that there were consuls, just as in the other guilds. This is proven by the fact that their headquarters was located on the Via de’ Lamberteschi, next door to the *Mint* <note>original: "Zecca"</note>, over which their

->The guild's coat of arms was emblazoned with a green tree and a red house on a white field.<-

No carpenter or wood dealer in the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> was allowed to move timber at night, under the penalty of a ten *lire* <term>lire: the plural of lira, the basic monetary unit of Florence</term> fine. They were forbidden from placing their workbenches outside their houses or creating litter in the public streets. Items in the process of being made—such as benches, chairs, and chests—were not permitted to block the footpaths.

Any structures projecting into the street or Market-place were subject to measurement. Anything that exceeded the *canna* <term>canna: a traditional Italian unit of length, approximately 2 meters</term> used by the "Calimala" <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers, which maintained the city's standard weights and measures</note> had to be removed, and the owner incurred a fine of ten *lire*. In the New Market <note>original: "Mercato Nuovo"</note>, wooden frames with hooks for stretching and drying wool cloth were prohibited. Likewise, along the Old Bridge <note>original: "Ponte Vecchio"</note>, tubs, boxes, blocks, and other wooden articles or obstructions were forbidden; offenders were fined ten *lire* for each offense.

Carpenters were forbidden from working in the two main Markets and also in front of the church of Or San Michele. Any absolutely necessary work in those locations had to be completed within three days, and every care had to be taken to remove shavings, sawdust, and debris without delay. No carpenter was allowed to leave timber in front of his workshop for more than three days, though he did have the right to use a space one foot wide beyond his wall to store wood he was currently using.¹

Whether a clear line can be drawn between the professions of the "Masters of Wood" and those of the "Carpenters" is a matter of opinion. Apparently, the former Guild undertook scaffolding, roofing, paneling, and all such important matters requiring strict architectural knowledge, along with the design and possibly the execution of artistic decorations. The "Carpenters" were likely more concerned with framing, flooring, fitting, and repair jobs, while much of their time was occupied with cabinet-making.

Renaissance furniture was by no means the least significant aspect of their craft...

...the construction of every significant object of artistic craftsmanship. In the varied forms of bedsteads, cupboards, chests—for marriage outfits and other purposes—couches, chairs, tables, picture frames, and more, Florentine workmen gained a high reputation for skill and thoroughness.

Until the fifteenth century, with few exceptions, the dining table was nothing more than a loose board, or boards, laid upon trestles—hence the term "festive board." Regarding chairs, until the end of the first decade of the sixteenth century, the only chair set at the table was the one occupied by the master of the house, the bishop or general of a monastery, or the head of a business house. "Taking the chair" is an expression directly traceable to this custom, referring to the place of honor. Only gradually did the long, hard benches disappear, replaced by chairs that were first made of plain wood, then seated with leather, and finally upholstered.

And who is not familiar with the splendid *Cassoni* <term>Cassoni: large, ornate Italian chests, often given as wedding gifts</term>—marriage coffers—belonging chiefly to the sixteenth century? With their grandeur of outline and sturdy workmanship, the entire school of Florentine painters, man by man in turn, adorned them with superb paintings. These formed, in a way, a continuous history of the men and women, the manners, and the fashions of the Renaissance.

Cabinetmakers were not satisfied with crude effects or simple treatments, but added enrichments of all kinds. Veneering was the precursor to mosaic work, and it was a skill mastered early in Florence. At first, it was limited exclusively to the addition of various sorts of cane and foreign wood. Gradually, a more solid surface became the fashion, and almost imperceptibly, Florentine mosaic became the signature style of her carpenters and woodworkers.

In this art, the surface of the wood is no longer visible, or only visible in part. Upon the plain timber foundation is laid a solid mass of stone and metal—columns of lapis lazuli, malachite, and jasper, with gilt capitals and decorative wreaths, and...

### GUILD OF CARPENTERS

Pedestals of gilt bronze are paired with medallions made of agate, carnelian, bloodstone, and onyx. Through a natural progression, this inlay or encrusting work was applied to stone foundations; this resulted in the class of artistic work commonly known as "Mosaic." Grand Duke Ferdinand I introduced this style from Milan in the year 1580 for the decoration of the Medici tombs at San Lorenzo.

Another form of artistic carpentry was especially popular in the sixteenth century—the overlaying of ivory onto an ebony background. This was called "Scagliuola" <term>Scagliuola: While usually referring to a plaster technique imitating marble, the author here applies it to intricate ivory and wood inlay</term>, and it represented the final expression of the artistic taste of the Renaissance.

Walnut and pear were the favorite woods used by woodcarvers, who likely belonged to the "Masters of Wood," while the workmen of the "Carpenters' Guild" performed the roughing out of panels, borders, balustrades, and so on.

The secrets of manufacturing Florentine picture frames have never left the beautiful city on the Arno. Wood gilding was a fine art just as much as woodcarving was. The moldings were covered with red lead and then with coatings of the thinnest white glue—which was thicker on the parts to be burnished—and sometimes as many as ten coats were applied.

Polishing woodwork, whether on flat or carved surfaces, was also a serious art. A mixture of turpentine and beeswax was brushed carefully and repeatedly over the surface and then rubbed down with hard brushes. Olive oil was poured generously over the parts, and then heavy, heated irons were applied; the whole process was finished with the swift manipulation of soft leather and silk waste.

Gesso—which was a very ancient process—was revived in Florence in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Cennino Cennini, in his *Treatise on Painting* <note>original: "Trattato della Pittura"</note>, sheds much light on the different methods of working with this material.

The material consisted of calcined chalk, or whiting, mixed with a viscid liquid such as glue or size. This formed an excellent...

This was an excellent medium for low-relief and was frequently used by carpenters and cabinetmakers to decorate ceilings, marriage chests (<term>cassoni</term>), wall panels, tournament shields, and many other types of furniture. In the workshops, the term “<term>Pastiglia</term>” <note>A decorative technique using a paste made of white lead and binder to create raised patterns</note> was applied to this moldable substance, which was applied almost like paint using hog-hair brushes and metal spatulas. Indeed, this form of decorative art was essentially relief painting, occupying the attention and energy of many craftsmen with an eye for beauty.

<term>Intarsiatura</term>—also known simply as “<term>Tarsia</term>”—was used for the floors and walls of rooms and consisted of a simple inlay of various types of wood. The term “<term>Certosiatura</term>” <note>A specialized inlay technique using small geometric pieces of wood, bone, metal, or mother-of-pearl</note> was applied to the finest varieties, especially the inlaid work installed in churches and religious houses. This gave rise to the name “work of the ‘Certosa’” <note>A Carthusian monastery</note>. This provides interesting proof that the monasteries played their part in the advancement of arts and crafts.

A common practice was to glue together long rods of various kinds of wood and, once dry, saw through the block, revealing a checkered pattern. The favorite combination was black or very dark wood paired with the palest white grain, which produced the effect of a checkerboard and was very popular in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

The fact that the Guild was prosperous and its members were profitably employed is proven by the Guild's position regarding taxation. In 1321, for example, the Carpenters were taxed a proportionate amount of fifty gold florins; the Guild ranked tenth in terms of wealth among the entire twenty-one guilds!

The names of several esteemed craftsmen and their specific branches of carpentry have been preserved. For example: Antonio Leopardi was a well-known maker and inlayer of tables (1450–1525); the d'Agnolo family—Bernardo the father, and his sons Domenico and Giovanni—were celebrated as designers of inlay work and as woodcarvers in the churches of Florence (1460–1563); and the Tasso brothers—Domenico and Giovanni—who worked with Michelangelo, were renowned woodcarvers.

### III. THE GUILD OF BAKERS <note>original: "L’ARTE DE’ FORNAI"</note>

Despite Tuscany's natural prominence as an agricultural region, its inhabitants were surprisingly unappreciative of their advantages regarding the cultivation of grain.

Vines, olives, mulberries, and flax seem to have occupied the attention of old-time farmers to the relative exclusion of grain crops. This is all the more remarkable because the Florentines' instinctive foresight in making money actually failed them in this matter. Possibly industrial pursuits engrossed them more, as they offered better prospects for financial success.

The *Contado* <term>The rural territory or countryside surrounding the city</term> produced little grain—certainly no more than three or four months' worth of food for the population. Montepulciano, Arezzo, the higher parts of the Val d’Arno, and the area around Pisa were the most favorable local granaries. Provisioning a city the size of Florence with its rapidly growing population was a very serious business.

A "Magistracy of Abundance," or *Annona* <note>original: "Annona"; a government body responsible for the grain supply and preventing famine</note>, as it was called, existed from very early times, though no records of its institution...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Florence's grain supply and the history of the "Annona" (food supply office), following the description of the limited grain production in the surrounding Tuscan countryside of Montepulciano and Arezzo.</meta>

<page-num>433</page-num>
<header>GUILD OF BAKERS</header>

have been preserved. Originally, this magistracy was composed of eight *Capitudini* <term>Heads of families or guild leaders</term>, but in 1352, their duties were assumed by the Council of State.

The officials of the "Annona" <term>The government office responsible for the grain supply and food logistics</term> were chiefly occupied with buying and importing foreign grain. During normal times, their operations were conducted in Romagna (the region north of Siena) and in Sicily. However, in years of famine, they sought supplies from more distant locations like Egypt, the Barbary Coast <note>The coastal regions of North Africa</note>, and the East.

This system, however, created a monopoly, and the execution of government contracts became a source of oppression and scandal. No regular reports were issued regarding supply and demand. Prices were not fixed, and financial losses were never investigated. As long as the daily supply of foreign grain in the public market of Or San Michele <note>The central grain market and shrine in Florence</note> amounted to fifty or sixty loads at an ordinary price, no questions were asked.

On the other hand, all the roads leading into Florence from the rural districts were placed under the surveillance of six officers. Their duty was to ensure that no obstacles hindered the easy movement of grain.

Nevertheless, taxes were imposed at the city gates on all loads of grain coming from districts not directly under the rule of Florence. Many tricks were adopted to evade these taxes. Messengers, spies, and agents in disguise intercepted convoys to either purchase the loads on the spot or relabel the consignments before they reached the city. Successfully smuggling in grain packs entitled the bold driver and the skillful agent to immunity from arrest for debt and other privileges.

Many statutes, rubrics, and *Provvisioni* <term>Legislative acts or provisions enacted by the Florentine government</term> were issued by the government between 1296 and 1299 to regulate this contraband commerce. <note>original: "Provv. vi. 126; viii. 98; x. 39."</note>

The current prices for grain naturally varied according to circumstances. For example, between the years 1224 and 1232, the price range was between fifteen and two *soldi* <term>shillings or small silver coins</term> per *staio* <term>a dry measure approximately equal to a bushel</term>.

The annual fixing of the price of grain, flour, and bread was—

The subject of a very quaint and primitive ceremony: "The Officers of Abundance," <term>Ufficiali dell’Abbondanza: The magistracy responsible for the city's food supply</term> as they were called, climbed to the top of the ancient Granary of Or San Michele just before the harvest. There, they settled the year’s prices based on the impressions they gathered from viewing the countryside from that vantage point—the greener the crops appeared, the higher the rates were set! <note>original: Cantini, iii. 60. Reference to Lorenzo Cantini's "Legislazione Toscana."</note>

Corn <note>In this historical context, "corn" refers to grain in general, such as wheat or barley, rather than maize.</note> in the market at Or San Michele was sorted into four categories:
1. *<term>Calvello</term>*—a large-grained barley that would not pass through the standard sieve; this was the highest priced.
2. Sicilian wheat—second in value.
3. *<term>Grano Comunale</term>* <term>Ordinary grain</term>—the most recent Florentine harvest, which was sometimes mixed with barley.
4. *<term>Grano Grosso</term>* <term>Coarse grain</term>—lower-quality varieties of grain.

All grain intended for human use was displayed for sale in *<term>Bigoncie</term>* <term>large baskets or trays made of rushes or wood</term>, each generally holding seven or eight *<term>staii</term>* <term>A Florentine measure of dry volume, roughly equivalent to two-thirds of a bushel</term>. In times of plenty, as many as three hundred of these containers could be seen in the corn market.

Another duty of the officials was to circulate among the sacks, bags, and baskets of grain brought into the market for sale, making a personal examination of both quantity and quality. The amount of wheat required for daily consumption in 1427 was one hundred *<term>moggi</term>* <term>A large unit of dry measure; one hundred moggi would be approximately 2,400 bushels</term>. Daily, when the great "*<term>Vacca</term>*" <note>The "Cow," a nickname for the great bell in the tower of the Palazzo Vecchio</note> struck the hour of nine, the "Officers of Abundance" took their seats on a platform within the *<term>Loggia</term>* <term>An open-air gallery or porch</term> of Or San Michele. From there, they oversaw the orderly distribution of the certified stock.

In front of the Shrine of the Madonna of Or San Michele, an office was established—consisting of a desk and a bench—where one or more notaries sat daily at specific hours. These legal officials were appointed for the purpose of receiving the affidavits of corn-chandlers <term>grain merchants</term> and drafting contracts. These were written in strict terms to bind both buyer and seller to act honorably, and to prevent the sale of inferior goods and the artificial inflation of prices. Any disputes that arose on the spot were referred to the notary, who was frequently accompanied by a Dominican <note>A friar of the Dominican Order, likely acting as a moral arbiter or witness</note>...

In times of scarcity or distress, well-intentioned merchants and others were accustomed to sending in wagons laden with grain <note>In this historical context, "corn" refers to grain in general.</note> to be sold to the poorer citizens as the “Officers of Abundance” directed. Very often, too, wealthy and ambitious men—in order to...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of grain management in Florence, specifically focusing on the "Officers of Abundance" and the low social standing of the Bakers' Guild due to strict government regulation.</meta>

<page-num>436</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

curry favor with the public, placed supplies of grain at the disposal of the Officers for free distribution.

Sometimes, when the pressure of poverty became severe, people clamored and fought around the Granary-shrine for daily rations of wheat. Among the relics of the "good old days" preserved for years in the Sacristy was a terrifying instrument in the shape of an axe and a wooden block. The block used to stand by the platform where the "Officers of Abundance" presided under the Loggia, and it was used in the very summary method these officials resorted to when they quietly chopped off a finger or two from the hands of the more unruly claimants!

The effect of the intervention of the "Officers of Provisions" <note>original: "Uffiziali della Grascia"</note> and the "Officers of Abundance" <note>original: "dell' Abbondanza"</note>—the market authorities—was not entirely helpful in lowering the price of food. The constant succession of new men and new laws caused confusion and difficulty. Because of this, the sales of grain in the markets and the shops of the grain-dealers <note>original: "Granaiuoli"</note>, as well as the prices of flour and bread at the bakehouses of the members of the "Guild of Bakers," varied significantly and constantly.

The overwhelming influence of the "Annona" <note>The government office responsible for the grain supply and preventing famine.</note> had a great deal to do with the subordination of the "Bakers' Guild" <note>original: "Arte de' Fornai"</note>. Members of the Guild were completely dependent upon the Board's good offices—or bad—in the conduct of their trade.

While at Pisa the "Guild of Bakers" ranked among the Seven Greater Guilds, in the Florentine hierarchy it came last of all the twenty-one corporations! This low ranking supports the stories of the bad reputation of the trade in general in the capital city.

Certainly, in reading through the records of the Council of State of Florence, one is struck by the frequency with which the "Guild of Bakers" and its members appear as offenders. It was constantly necessary to take measures against them, as well as against "the Guild of Butchers," because of "the dishonor they do the community and the Chief Magistrate <note>original: "Podesta"</note> by the bad quality of the flour and the mutton they offer for sale."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the low social standing of the Bakers' Guild in Florence, providing historical evidence from Council speeches and early archival records regarding its organization and ranking among the other guilds.</meta>

<page-num>437</page-num>
<header>GUILD OF BAKERS</header>

The reason for the low regard in which the Guild was held is illuminated by a speech made in the Council of the Captain of the People on January 30, 1282, by Bernardo Rossi—a baker. He maintained that

> “there were many wealthy citizens who had financial interests in the trades of milling and baking, but who took no part in the business themselves. By the high prices they charged for flour, they encouraged working bakers to mix in inferior grains; and by the high rents they demanded for the lease of bakehouses, they compelled the tenants to make excessive charges for inferior bread. This second accusation was coupled with the use of dishonest weights. This state of things,” he went on to say, “affected the poorer classes more than the wealthier citizens, and consequently excited popular prejudice against the mistreated bakers, rather than against the greedy capitalists!” $^1$

There are no records of the actual date the Guild was established; indeed, the early Archives of Florence—at least those that have been preserved—contain only very limited mentions of milling and baking, and almost none regarding a Corporation of Craftsmen.

It goes without saying that occupations so essential to the public well-being were actively and widely practiced from the earliest times. Doubtless, a great many customs and methods had developed over time, and from these, more or less regular codes of procedure and conduct were naturally established.

In the Archives, there are early mentions as follows:

-> “1028. *Ursus . . . pistor*—a Baker.” <note>original: "pistor"</note> <-
-> “1147. *Bernardus—Mugnarius*—a Miller.” <note>original: "Mugnarius"</note> <-

In the year 1236, the “Bakers’ Guild” <note>original: *Arte de’ Fornai*</note> was officially listed with the rest of the twenty-one Guilds and placed seventh in the order of the fourteen Lesser Guilds. This prominent position was retained for only a few years, for in 1282, the “Guild of Bakers” appears last of all the Guilds, and it remained there until the end.

In 1534, the Guild received a sort of promotion when it was included with the Guilds of "Butchers" and "Oil-Merchants and General Dealers" in the *University of Por San Piero*—the first of the four Unions of Lesser Guilds established by Grand Duke Cosimo I.

Whatever special features or unique officers the Guild may have had in its earlier days seem to have disappeared by the end of the thirteenth century. At that time, the Guild fell into line with the others

and adopted the reformed Statutes of the "*Calimala*" <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in Foreign Cloth</note> Guild of 1301–1309 as a model for its own new constitution.

In the beginning, the chief officers were likely styled *Capitudini*—meaning "Heads"—rather than "Consuls," although their official residence was called "consular." This residence was a fine house located in the *Chiasso del Buco* <note>a narrow alleyway</note> near the *Mercato Vecchio* <note>The Old Market</note>. Upon its facade was emblazoned a white star on a red field—the coat of arms of the Guild, which was assigned to the *Arte de' Fornai* <note>The Guild of Bakers</note> by the Priors in 1266.

From the start, a distinction was made between the two different classes of citizens who made up the membership of the Guild: the *Mugnai* (millers) and the *Fornai* (bakers). The former

<page-num>439</page-num>

The former were engaged in grinding flour at their mills in the *contado* <note>the rural territory surrounding the city</note>, or along the riverside, and in carrying their full sacks to the corn market at Or San Michele. The latter were employed in kneading and baking bread and in selling it at retail.

Millers were forbidden from retailing flour in Florence for their own profit. Three pounds of grain were allocated to the bushel. Millers were expected to deliver the ground flour within three days of receiving the grain. $^1$

The wholesale storage of grain and flour—which would have a tendency to drive up market prices and allow it to be sold at higher rates during times of scarcity—was absolutely forbidden. Persons evading this prohibition were liable to have their entire stock confiscated and to see their names exposed to public infamy. $^2$

Much of the public criticism that was directed at the bakers should probably be blamed on the millers. Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), famous Italian author of the Decameron</note> hints many times that, despite their well-lined jackets and clean white aprons, the millers were generally considered sharp dealers, if not outright cheats. It was said that they invariably kept back half of the flour produced by every grinding! $^3$

In 1296, full powers were granted to the Priors to draft a statute against this dishonest dealing, as well as a *provvisione* <note>an ordinance or administrative decree</note> to determine the retail price of bread. $^4$ This was all the more necessary given the great variations that existed in the value of grain, flour, and bread at different periods. In 1224, for example, a *staio* <note>a dry measure approximately equal to a bushel</note> of wheat cost fifteen *soldi*; whereas during the great famine in 1328, the price rose to one gold florin—equivalent to ten shillings. $^5$

A statute was passed fixing the price at four *denari* for a *staio*—one-third of a sack of grain—worth of bread; but because fuel—which was always a somewhat scarce commodity—cost more in winter than in summer, it was impossible to sell at one price all year round. Naturally, people wished to buy at the lowest price...

summer prices. Consequently, any price increase by the bakers led to disputes and sometimes even to people raiding their shops. The bakers complained that they were the ones being treated unfairly and appealed to the State for protection. Finally, it was agreed that the bakers should charge four *denari* <note>a small silver or copper coin</note> in the summer and five in the winter for the same quantity of bread.

Villani <note>Giovanni Villani (c. 1276–1348), a Florentine chronicler</note> says the bakers benefited from this new arrangement and turned as many as one hundred and fifty loads of grain into bread every day. Each loaf had to be stamped with the baker's mark. Any bread offered for sale without a stamp was immediately seized by the "Officers of Abundance" <note>Italian: *Ufficiali dell'Abbondanza*, the magistracy responsible for the city's food supply</note>, and the offending baker was forced to pay heavy fines.¹

Bakers, however, felt the weight of heavy taxation, because they had to pay a tax not only on the flour they baked but also for the privilege of keeping their shops open and their ovens heated.² The constant changes in local bylaws were a great burden to the bakers. For instance, a man might bake and sell bread of a specific quality and weight one day, only to have it declared illegal the next.³

Kneaders of dough and bread-bakers were not allowed to work on Sundays or other solemn religious holidays. Anyone doing so was fined forty *soldi* <note>a silver coin worth twelve denari</note>. However, the "Sportello" <term>a small window or hatch used for retail sales</term> could be opened on such days after Mass for the sale of bread.⁴

Makers of macaroni and vermicelli were required to obtain their licenses in the month of January, and all unlicensed baking was fined ten *lire* for every sale made.⁵

Citizens were warned not to purchase or keep large quantities of bread unless they were innkeepers. Bread for the family had to be purchased fresh daily, and no private individual or person not associated with the Guild was allowed to sell bread under any circumstances.⁶ Foreigners visiting Florence and residing—

for a period, they were permitted to bake, cook, and sell as they pleased, regardless of the embarrassing regulations which hampered the Florentine bakers.

Bakers never extended credit beyond the value of ten lire, and they were required to provide the Consuls of the Guild, at specific times, with lists of their customers and the amount owed by each.

Bread was by no means the only commodity which bakers were allowed to sell; they also dealt in all kinds of flour, as well as bran and every description of sifted grain. Consequently, a sort of rivalry developed between them and the *Granaiuoli*—Corn-chandlers—who were associated with the *Arte degli Oliandoli* <note>The Guild of Oil-merchants and Provision-dealers</note>.

A very important and popular branch of the bakery business was that of the *Panattieri*—Pastry-cooks—but this was a later development in the art of baking. Pastry made with eggs, butter, sugar, milk, and flour, however, is never mentioned in records before the end of the sixteenth century, when a company of pastry-cooks migrated from Milan to Florence and introduced their special delicacies.

In the *Canti Carnascialeschi*—Carnival Songs—where all the Guilds and Crafts are celebrated or parodied, there is no mention of pastry-cooks. First sung by Berni <note>Francesco Berni (c. 1497–1535), an Italian poet known for his humorous and satirical verse</note> in his *Orlando Innamorato*, pastry provided the gourmet with delights he had never even dreamed of:

> "To live luxuriously in every way
> Requires the help of foreign cooking.
> Pastry pairs well with your savory dishes and with your
> Poultry, boiled and roast, and with baked meats." ¹

It goes without saying that the pastry-cooks' shops were, in later times, irresistible attractions to the cheerful Florentines. Many a pretty young *contadina* <term>peasant woman or country girl</term>, walking along with her lover, picked up some tasty treat or other. Just off the hot iron plates of the oven and temptingly set out in dainty wicker baskets were such delicacies as *berlingozzi*—puff-pastry—and *cialdoni*—thin spiced wafers.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Bakers' Guild, detailing the specific pastries they produced, the regulatory oversight by city officials and the Captains of Or San Michele, and the guild's overall prosperity and social standing in Florence.</meta>

*ciambelle*—jam rolls, *bericuocoli*—gingerbread cakes, *bracciatelli*—crisp sweet biscuits, *lasagne*—macaroons, and many other delights, along with whole cakes and confectionery of all descriptions.

All bakers and pastry-cooks—whether men or women—were required to display a sign over their bakeries and shops decorated with the Lily of Florence in blue.¹ Once a year, in the month of December, they were required to appear before the Officials of Or San Michele <note>Or San Michele was a major Florentine landmark that served as a grain market, a shrine, and the headquarters for guild administration</note>, and to swear solemnly that they would practice their trade well, truly, and honestly. They vowed to commit no fraud against the State or the public, but to observe, strictly and intelligently, all the regulations of their Guild and the laws of the State.²

The weights and measures used by members of the Guild were subject to the inspection and correction of the officials appointed by the "Captains of Or San Michele," who also had the power to examine and test the weight and quality of all bread baked in Florence.

Within the first month of taking office, the Podestàs <note>The chief magistrates of the city-state</note> and Captains of the People caused a careful inquiry to be made into the location, construction, and safety of all public and private bakeries and ovens. All nuisances or states of disrepair were pointed out, and time was given for their repair. Failure to comply with the directions of the officials led to fines of one hundred *lire*, or more.³

Attention was also paid to the amount of fuel—wood or other flammable material—stored by each baker, and strict rules were ordered regarding its storage and protection from fire.⁴

The Guild—despite various obstacles and interference—flourished immensely. The members built fine bakeries and shops, as well as palatial residences which they furnished handsomely, thereby encouraging many a rising artist and craftsman. In their Sunday and holiday dress, they were not a bit behind their more aristocratic fellow-guildsmen, while in their hospitality and the standard of their meals, they were second to none.

The lungs of Florence's commerce were the two markets—the <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> Old Market and the <note>original: "Mercato Nuovo"</note> New Market. The domestic trade of all the guilds and crafts was transacted within their boundaries for more than five hundred years. Here, a constant clamor for profit rose up day after day. Men, and women too, worked as only those busy Florentines of the past knew how, striving both for individual success and for the prosperity of their beloved city. The sharpness of her traders and peddlers, as well as the alertness of her manufacturers and merchants, are best reflected in the words of *Boccaccio*:

> “Those who have no possessions are little better than mindless cattle; he who has the most is considered the most worthy.” <note>1</note>

<note>1</note> *Boccaccio*, “One Hundred Novels” <note>The Decameron</note>, Day 8, Tale 10, folio 195.

<page-num>445</page-num>

-># LIFE AND WORK IN THE MARKETS<-

The Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> was the most historic site in Florence. As the first part of the city to be built, it was geographically the center of the municipal area. It became the seat of the most ancient legal tribunal, the social residence of the old aristocracy, and the commercial hub of the known world.¹

An old tradition identifies the Old Market as the exact spot where the fierce Fiesoleans <note>people from the nearby hill town of Fiesole</note> of ancient times, coming down armed from their strongholds in the hills, traded with the peaceful inhabitants living along the riverbanks.

Dante says that Etruscans, Romans, and Lombards had all spoken of the Old Market before 1150. Around that date, one of the earliest important buildings was erected: the tower of the Caponsacchi family.

Among the traditions of the Old Market, perhaps the earliest relates that Conrad II visited Florence in 1037 and took up residence in the marketplace. There were already well-known residents of the Market: a wealthy nobleman, Count Martino <note>original: "Conte di Martino"</note>; a rich merchant, Rufo; and certain prosperous artisans, Olivo and Giovanni. It is said that Conrad seized the dwellings of these last three and gave them to the canons of San Giovanni <note>the clergy of the Baptistery of St. John</note>, who had championed his cause.

The earliest historical record identifies the year 1079 as the date when the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> received its name. Markets appear to have been held in various parts of the ancient city, and old woodcuts show trade happening just outside the doors of San Giovanni Battista <note>Saint John the Baptist</note>; however, such "trading spots" were informal and lacked official regulation.²

Surrounding the Old Market were the houses or palaces of many of the leading inhabitants: the Adimari, Amieri, Agolanti, Alamanni, Alfieri, Altieri, Caponsacchi, Cacciaguide, Macci, Manfredi, Medici, Nerli, Pegolotti, Sizi, Soldanieri, Tosinghi, Tornaquinci, Vecchietti, and others.

The Tosinghi Palace <note>original: "Palazzo Tosinghi"</note>—also called "The Palace" <note>original: "Il Palazzo"</note> because it—

<header>LIFE AND WORK IN THE MARKETS</header>

In the Old Market, their Ghibelline <note>a pro-imperial political faction in medieval Italy</note> towers looked down upon many a strange scene, but none were as uncanny as the shrouded figure of Ginevra di Niccolo degli Amieri knocking helplessly at the great door of her father’s house. Married to Francesco Agolanti, she fell ill with the plague in 1400 and was laid out for dead. Funeral rites were duly performed, and the poor young wife was left in her grave; however, she had only fainted. Awakening in alarm, she cast off her burial clothes, wrapped the shroud around herself, and hurried to her husband’s house. Terrified by what he was convinced was a ghost, he fled from her. All her friends, frightened, refused to help her, and the poor girl was likely to die from exposure and hunger when a childhood lover appeared on the scene. Ginevra returned his passionate embrace, and Antonio Rondinelli led her to her second wedding; and, as the storybooks say, “they lived happily ever after!” The Street of the Dead <note>original: "Via della Morta"</note> was named after Ginevra’s awakening.

At the corner of the Market, where the Street of the Apothecaries <note>original: "Via degli Speziali"</note> begins, was a shrine with an altar named the “Oratory of Saint Mary of the Trumpet” <note>original: "Oratorio di Santa Maria della Tromba"</note>. It was built to commemorate the ministry of Saint Peter Martyr, and especially as a thank-offering for his miracle in exorcising the Devil, who, in the form of a black horse, had terrified the neighbors. In 1361, the care of the shrine was entrusted to the “Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries.” It was decorated with a painting of the Madonna and Saints by Jacopo del Casentino. Mass was said daily, and devout passers-by offered prayers to the Mother of God and the Saints. Furthermore, every poor criminal condemned to death was dragged past this image of the Madonna and compelled to kneel on his way to execution.

The *Mercato Vecchio* <note>Old Market</note> was distinguished by its own language—truly a jumble of all the dialects of the countryside <note>original: "Contado"</note>, mixed with popular versions of classical Latin.

While Dante established the Tuscan language of the Early Renaissance and laid the foundation of the Crusca Academy <note>original: "della Crusca"</note>—the refined speech

Regarding the Florentines—Boccaccio,¹ Sacchetti, and Pucci looked back to ancient customs and have preserved for us the common language—the Florentine Language of the Old Market <note>original: "La Lingua Fiorentina di Mercato Vecchio"</note>—used by rich and poor alike. Francesco Sacchetti has been rightly called "The Echo of the Old Market." Born in 1335 into the family of Benci d'Uguccione, he died in 1410. His short stories <note>original: "Novelle"</note> are valuable records of the local slang used in the Market.

Brother Passavanti, of the "Order of Preachers" <note>the Dominicans</note> and chaplain to Archbishop Acciajuoli, in his *The Mirror of True Penance* <note>original: "Specchio della vera Penitenza"</note>—written in support of the *Accademia della Crusca* <note>the primary institution for the study of the Italian language</note>—criticizes Tuscans, and especially Florentines, for their constant use of slang, for shortening their words, and for the artificial tone of their voices. He calls it "the idiotic style of the Old Market," which, as he says, "has sacrificed both grace and liveliness, but which, nevertheless, has preserved honorable traits."

<margin>² *The Delights of Tuscan Scholars*, vol. 6, p. 267, etc.</margin>
Antonio Pucci, the unique street poet of the markets who delighted in the "satirical-humorous" style of poetry <note>original: "Satirico-giocoso"</note>, has provided us with a vivid picture of life and work in the Old Market.² His poem, *The Properties of the Old Market* <note>original: "La Proprietà di Mercato Vecchio"</note>, written very early in the fourteenth century—long before the "Chronicle of Villani" was ever put to paper—is composed of many stanzas. A few of these, freely translated, are as follows:

> "Our Old Market provides plenty of food for everyone,
> And surpasses all other markets with rich and fine produce;
> You could not find its equal outside of Florence, even if you wished!
>
> It is greatly blessed with busy activity;
> At every corner, there is a church for holy reflection,
> While streets branch out in every direction.
>
> Doctors are nearby for every human ailment;
> Flax merchants display yarns and linen cloths as well;
> Nearby are pork butchers—and pharmacists too.
>
> Here they sell fine glassware, plates, and sturdy pitchers;
> Taverns, too, offer food and drink temptingly laid out,
> And pretty serving girls, with whom to flirt, no doubt!"

He may well speak as he does in the last verse, for the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> was called "The Garden of Florence" <note>original: "Giardino di Firenze"</note> precisely because it was always full of abundance and delights, and because it was the fertile source of the life and enterprise of the entire community.

Pucci first describes—as all devout Florentines would—the religious temples. Saint Mary in the Capitol <note>original: "Santa Maria in Campidoglio"</note>—located just behind the old fish market—adjoined a popular tavern, the Tavern of the Cross of Malta <note>original: "Osteria della Croce di Malta"</note>, the social meeting place for members of various associations of commercial travelers. Its site was that of the ancient Roman Capitol. Saint Peter of Good Counsel <note>original: "San Piero Buonconsiglio"</note>—shortened to *San Pierino*—at the southwest corner, was founded in the eighth century and served as both a sanctuary and a parliament house for the "Guild of Judges and Notaries." It had a small outdoor pulpit from which orators usually addressed general audiences and legal scholars delivered public lectures.

Saint Thomas <note>original: "San Tommaso"</note>—at the northeast corner—later became the church of the Medici family. "The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries..."

Apothecaries used this temple for private and public devotions. Many of the wool merchants also used to attend the early daily Mass here. Saint Andrew’s <note>original: "Sant' Andrea"</note>—the senior parish church of Florence—was a very ancient building, having been founded as a convent for nuns in 852. Nearby was the little square of Saint Andrew <note>original: "Piazzetta di Sant' Andrea"</note>, where members of the Linen Merchants' Guild used to gather. The guild’s chapel and altar were located inside the church. Merchants of the Calimala Guild <note>The guild of merchants who refined and traded foreign cloth</note> also used to stop in as they passed to say their prayers.

In the center of the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note>, a fine column of oriental *cipollino* <note>a green-veined marble</note> was erected, which had been taken from the Baptistery of Saint John <note>original: "San Giovanni"</note>. In 1430, a marble figure symbolizing Abundance—Donatello’s "*Dovizia*"—was placed upon it. Two iron rods ran up the shaft: one was connected to a bell that rang at the opening and closing of the day’s business; the other rod loudly jangled a similar bell to warn everyone that thieves and criminals were prowling about!

Before dawn, rumbling wheels carried in the day’s supply of country produce. The clatter of iron hooves on the large, flat stone paving mingled harshly with the angry shouting of drivers and dealers. The barking of country dogs and the yelping of city strays—perhaps struck by vigorous farmhands or stepped on by late-night revelers—clashed with the cackling of geese and the bleating of lambs and calves.

The Florentines of old were early risers. Before the bells for "Lauds" <note>the dawn prayer service</note> had finished ringing in the belfries, artisans were already crowding the church entrances. They would briefly attend a hurried low Mass as they made their way to the smithy, the tannery, or the loom. Indeed, work began at daybreak all year round; even before the darkness of night had passed, many flickering lanterns danced across the grim old marketplace.

Spinners make their way to Saint Bigio <note>original: "San Bigio"</note>, while carders and weavers hurry to their workshops from the Oltrarno <note>The district "beyond the Arno" river</note>. Goldsmiths' assistants appear in tidier clothing, alongside dyers and tanners with stained hands, arms, and clothes, and many other respectable working men and women—greeting one another with kind words of cheer or playful, taunting cries.

As the day progresses, simple housewives in their plain wool gowns and linen kerchiefs, with baskets on their arms and children at their breasts, line up along the rows of market stalls ready to shop—seeking their husbands' breakfasts and other domestic needs. The <term>Albergatori</term> <note>original: "Innkeepers"</note> are also up early to find cheap food for their wives to cook for their hungry guests.

The <term>Messeri</term> <note>original: "Masters" or "Sirs"</note> of the Great Guilds pick their way through the chattering, haggling crowd as they go to and from their palaces. Since most of them owned pleasant villas in the suburbs, where a true <term>villeggiatura</term> <note>original: "country retreat"</note> could always be enjoyed, they loved the Old Market despite all its dirt and noise. To every Florentine, it was the source of his life, the foundation of his fortune, and the stage for his pride.

Some of these dignitaries <note>original: "Magnificos"</note> are heading to the headquarters of the Consuls of their Guild, or to the offices of their various companies, to meet travelers and agents from abroad. Others are going to see how their laborers are progressing in the workshops and to inspect new machines and methods. Many are also bound for the Palace of the Podestà <note>The seat of the city's chief magistrate</note> or to the Palazzo Vecchio <note>The town hall of Florence</note> to conduct state affairs or advance their own political interests. Each wears the <term>lucco</term> <note>a long, hooded gown worn by Florentine citizens</note>, or robe, of his social class, featuring its own distinctive marks.

Judges and Notaries, dressed in the robes of their professions, also make their way with appropriate dignity to their seats in the Courts—carefully avoiding all familiar talk and joking greetings as they pass.

Silence was unknown in the Old Market. Early and late, by night as well as by day, all year round, its many voices rose up far beyond the rooftops of the houses and climbed away

<header>LIFE AND WORK IN THE MARKETS</header>

As noon approaches, the activity of the Market rises even higher. Groups of playful apprentices begin to pour into the Square, set free until the bell tolls them back to their work. With empty stomachs and hungry mouths, they snatch and toss onions and chunks of bread and cheese to one another, throwing down their *piccioli*—small coins—though just as often as not, they throw down no money at all! They surge forward, munching as they go, and cutting down many a fat sausage hanging in their path on the stalls of the pork butchers. The protests of the *contadine* <note>original: "contadine" — peasant women or female farmers</note> and the salt-meat sellers go unheeded. Their empty flasks and drinking cans replenished with good *Trebbiano* <note>a popular variety of Italian wine</note> at wine shops along the way, they jostle back and forth—a merry, noisy, mischievous throng—to finish their frugal meal on the steps of Santa Maria in Campidoglio, and then to play impromptu games of *Calcio* <note>an early form of football or soccer</note> or *Pallone* <note>a traditional Italian ball game</note> among the stalls and tethered beasts, heedless of the place or circumstances.

Artists too, and craftsmen, with a brief respite for their hands, flock into the Market precincts—dirty, hungry, and tired. Some are intent on dining simply in the open on fruit and eggs, perhaps with Donatello, Luca della Robbia, and their social circle; and some, with better-lined pockets, are intent on richer fare with the Ghirlandai and Pollaiuoli, and with men of fashion—a Rucellai, an Alberti, or a Medici.

The siesta is not forgotten, and many a muscular limb and curly head of hair lie flat on the steps, or even on the bare ground—in later days with "fragrant weed" <note>tobacco</note> or a smoking pipe between their teeth. But, listen! The work bell rings, and in an instant, the dreamers rise and stretch themselves, and hurry back to their tasks again.

But, "*Accorr 'uomo! Accorr 'uomo!*"—"Help! Help!" <note>original: "Accorr 'uomo!" — literally "Run, man!" or "Help, man!"</note>—sounds out alike for a runaway horse and for a personal assault. Once taken up, the cry became, often enough, the signal for the prompt closing of shops and dwelling houses as conflict broke out between class and class or trade and trade. Riots in the Market were normal events. Perhaps a clumsy porter, or a pack mule, accidentally kicked a member of the Ricci family, who at once struck the offender, and he in his turn was beaten with blows from every Albizzi <note>The Ricci and Albizzi were powerful and often rival families in Florentine politics</note> within reach...

reach, until the two families and their adherents were involved in a grim death struggle.1

Rival trades were accustomed to joining in massive brawls over the smallest incidents. The dyers and the finishers of the "Calimala Guild" <note>The guild of finishers and merchants of foreign cloth</note> fought to the end in disputes with the workers of the "Guild of Wool," and so forth.

Stone-throwing was always a common tactic. Many times the street boys—"hooligans" both young and old—bent on mischief, formed skirmish lines in front of the opposing parties.

The *Podesta* <note>the chief magistrate or city administrator</note> and the other magistrates sat for long, tiring hours dealing with the troubles of the Market. Legal opponents were as aggressive as they were numerous. Often, no other remedy was quicker than to throw everyone involved into the town’s stocks to cool their tempers! These unfortunate souls, it goes without saying, became the targets of ridicule for everyone passing by. Sometimes the poor wretches suffered serious physical injuries, but the Market overseers would usually punish the attackers by placing them side-by-side with their victims!

Was that busy marketplace ever cleaned and tidied? It was certainly decorated—but with the kind of debris that only increased the litter. Vegetables, trimmed right next to where they were grown, underwent further cleaning here. Chestnut shells lay thick around the carts of *Brucciata* <note>likely referring to vendors of roasted chestnuts, from the Italian "bruciate"</note> and his fellow roasters. Scraps of cloth and linen, and leftover bits of silk and velvet, along with many tufts of fur and leather shavings, were tossed here and there. Waste, filth, and rags competed with crime, violence, and disorder to present a disgusting and repulsive sight to both noble and common travelers.

Despite all this chaos and dirt, strict rules governed not only the traders in the Old Market but also their customers; violations of these rules were treated with severity. Those accused—whether guilty or not—were usually tied to the column in the center of the Market, wearing dunce caps on their heads and signs on their chests stating the nature of their offense!

# LIFE AND WORK IN THE MARKETS

Serious infractions of the Market Bylaws were punished by periods spent in the stocks, with a heavy iron collar locked around the neck and attached by a chain to a post!¹

The market porters—who were exceptionally strong men—were, of course, under strict rules and subject to special bylaws. For instance, no man was allowed to carry loads weighing more than two hundred pounds for a distance of two hundred and fifty yards, and his wage was fixed at six *denari* <note>small silver coins</note>. For greater or shorter distances, and for lighter or heavier loads, the payment was to be proportional <note>original: "pro rata"</note>. Refusing to pay the official rate, attempting to overcharge, or disputes about weight and distance resulted in the offender being imprisoned for a month.

As the sun sets, the country people prepare to head home in groups, but they pause as quiet crowds slip into the four churches at the sound of the Vesper bell. There, while mechanically counting their prayer beads, they mentally calculate their day’s earnings!

If a lull falls over the busy trade scenes, it only serves as cover for the activities of unfortunate beggars, while dice-players, gamblers, and rogues of every sort emerge from their hiding places. Homeless boys, who used to shout together during brutal street games, steal whatever they can find; meanwhile, little children running home from school share their frights and stories through bitter tears and rippling laughter.

As evening quickly approaches, many groups of interested listeners gather around the seats of the storytellers, for there were few things Florentines enjoyed more than stories—whether of romance or war. Laughing one moment and crying the next until salt tears ran down everyone’s cheeks, the speaker’s emotion touched their hearts. Everyone reached into their meager pockets for a coin of some kind to toss into the performer’s outstretched cap.

At times, strange exhibitions entertained the busy workers during their leisure hours. For example, in 1413, a great sensation was caused by the capture of a mermaid or siren in the Mediterranean.

Night settles down upon a sleeping city, while ghostly *sbirri* <note>police officers or watchmen</note> steal along the streets with clanking, iron-tipped staffs and glowing lanterns.

All the public's needs for food and drink were supplied in the Old Market.
