In the same way, the butchers' stalls were later felt to be unsuitable and a source of clutter in the Market, so they were moved to the shops upon the Ponte Vecchio <note>Old Bridge</note>.

### LIFE AND WORK IN THE MARKETS 457

The trade was managed by dealers in the Old Market <note>Mercato Vecchio</note>. This proved to be a nuisance, and as early as 1177, a small fish market was opened in a shed built at the Lung' Arno end of the Old Bridge <note>Ponte Vecchio</note>. Grand Duke Cosimo I rebuilt the Fish Gallery <note>Loggia del Pesce</note> and installed the inscription:

> *“The fish market, which until this time used to be frequented during Lent at the Old Bridge.”*
> <note>original: “Forum piscarium q. usq. ad huc temporitur Quadragesimalibus ad Pontem Veterum frequentabatur.”</note>

Attached to this fish market was a small market for the sale of fruit and vegetables that could not find room in the Old Market.

Poultry, game, and pork—both alive and dead—were brought to market daily by the country people and were sold at the shops of the Oil-merchants' Guild <note>Arte degli Oliandoli</note>. The cries of these creatures added significantly to the hubbub of the scene. Falcons, goshawks, and other birds of prey were not allowed to be sold publicly, while enthusiasts and lovers of songbirds—among the latter being Leonardo da Vinci—went about buying up the little birds just to set them free again!

Greengrocers were allied with the poulterers, and no stalls in the market were more cheerful than those daily decorated with flowers, fruit, and vegetables. The *Giglio* <note>lily</note>, of course, was the primary favorite—the famous iris-lily of Florence—but roses and carnations <note>originally "pinks"</note> filled the air with fragrance, as did the bunches of sweet herbs and lavender. Painters like Botticelli and his colleagues have preserved the forms and colors of the floral treasures from the hillsides and gardens of the *Contado* <note>the rural territory surrounding the city</note>.

There was no shortage of fruit, and the variety was endless. Yellow apricots shared top honors with pine nuts and prickly pears; brown medlars, piled up in baskets, sat next to what looked almost like strawberries but were actually luscious arbutus berries. Children spent their *piccioli* <note>small copper coins</note> on the glossy brown berries of the *Giuggiolo* (jujube tree) and the oval cherry-berries.

In the summertime, water-melon sellers reaped rich harvests, but many a thirsty soul preferred the tart juice of the *Nespolo* <note>loquat or medlar tree</note>—the

yellow medlar—or the freshly made lemonade from the lemon squeezers of the *Vicolo de' Limonai* <note>Alley of the Lemon Sellers</note>.

Nuts were also in universal demand, and none were more delicious or more popular with the apprentices than the little kernels of the stone pine. Raw and roasted chestnuts were always a Florentine favorite. *Pinocchiato* <note>pine nut candy</note>—pine seeds eaten with honey and sugar—were always welcome.

Vegetables were as plentiful as they were decorative. Strings of crimson chili peppers, piles of scarlet tomatoes, and heaps of purple *Petronciani*—eggplants <term>originally called pumpions or mad-apples</term>—mingled with mounds of golden pomegranates, cabbages of all colors, creamy marrows, yellow *Ceci* <note>chickpeas</note>, and beans of all sorts and sizes. There were tender sprays of dark green fennel, strange-looking *Fungi* <note>mushrooms</note> with succulent *Radicchio* <note>endive</note>, and tasty *Gobbi*—the market name for *Carciofi* <note>artichokes</note> because of their "hunchbacked" appearance—along with many other delicious herbs.

Cries of "*Salate! Salate!*" <note>Salads! Salads!</note> daily filled the air, for all Florentines knew how to make and enjoy a salad; meanwhile, everyone made a point of patronizing the traveling vendors of salted lupine seeds.

The famous *Cavolaja* <note>cabbage woman</note> lived under the Vecchietti Palace; she made her fortune by coming into the market every day to sell the produce of her little *podere* <note>small farm</note>. When she died, the bells of the four market churches and of Santa Reparata were rung from All Saints' Day until Ash Wednesday—just as she had requested in her will. She was buried with great ceremony in the Baptistery in Bishop Rannucci’s tomb.

In sunny weather and during winter rains, covers were permitted over the market stalls, and awnings were allowed over the shop fronts. However, none of these could extend beyond the width of the stalls, nor more than five yards beyond the buildings.<sup>1</sup>

For example, in the "Petition of the Guilds," presented to the Signoria <note>the governing body of Florence</note> in 1378, clause 15 runs as follows:— "That Giovanni de' Mone, an honorable citizen of Florence who is always dedicated to the service of the Commune and has already been awarded the belt of knighthood, shall receive three hundred gold florins annually for the rest of his life. These funds shall come from the market dues paid by butchers and retail dealers of meat and poultry."¹

These dues were actually the annual rents paid for the shops <note>original: *botteghe*</note> that were arranged all around the Old Market, located directly in front of the entrances to the houses and palaces. Giovanni de' Mone was a corn merchant <term>originally called a corn-chandler</term> who, along with Guido Bandiera and Salvestro de' Medici, was knighted by the acclaim of the common people <note>original: *Popolo Minuto*</note> during the Ciompi Revolt <note>original: *Ciompi* rising</note>.²

The merriest and busiest shops in and around the Old Market were those of the apothecaries and the parlors of the barbers. All the fashionable people of the day gathered at the apothecaries' to flood the city with gossip, while men congregated alone at the barbers' to hear and tell the latest scandal.

The business of the Florentine barbers <note>original: *Barbieri*</note> was typically conducted outdoors during fair weather. Each barber had the right to place a chair, a shaving basin, and a mirror outside his shop. They were permitted to stay open on Sundays and employ their apprentices, but they were not allowed to place their shaving stools and other tools of their trade outside their doors on those days.

On Sundays and festivals, they were forbidden from going to or sending someone to shave customers in their homes. Among other restrictions, barbers were strictly forbidden from working by candlelight. If any customer ventured to wash his hands or face in public, the helpful barber was fined ten *soldi* <note>a small silver coin</note> for each offense!³

"...the grandson of a barber"—as he liked to call himself. His shop <note>original: *bottega*</note>, in 1408, was located close to the headquarters <note>original: "Residence"</note> of the Consuls of the "**Calimala Guild**"; it became the most celebrated barber shop <note>original: "shaving saloon"</note> of the century.

Burchiello, who joined <term>matriculated into</term> the "**Calimala Guild**" in 1432, was something of a poet. He wrote verses about the current events of the day in the common language <note>original: "vernacular"</note> and style of the Old Market. Indeed, he is rightfully famous as the creator of the "**Burchiellesque Language**" <note>original: *Lingua Burchiellesca*</note>—the unique social slang of Florence. Nothing was more popular than his witty verses and sharp jokes—though perhaps they were sometimes a bit coarse <note>original: "strong"</note> and unsuitable for general repetition! They were published in Florence in 1480, becoming one of the earliest works produced by the printing press.

His sharp razor kept time with laughter and chatter. Many an elegant gown <term>lucco: a long, heavy Florentine outer garment</term> and many pairs of tight-fitting hose were splattered by soapsuds flying from the mouths of men roaring with laughter! Even so, no one could provide a cleaner shave than Master <note>original: *Messere*</note> Domenico Burchiello, and in the fifteenth century, at all events, a clean-shaven face was the fashion. George Eliot gives these words to the Florentine barber Nello: "Here in Florence, we do not like to see a man with his nose sticking out over a waterfall of hair."¹

By far the most popular hairstyle in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries was known as the "**Zazzera**."² The hair was cut square at the shoulders and not thinned out toward the bottom. A stylish finish was added with curling tongs, as the locks of hair were arranged like a halo or, as they described it, "like a moon in a mist." This style was known as the "Florentine cut" *par excellence* <note>above all others</note> in Paris, London, and elsewhere! It is said that Machiavelli was shrewd enough to appreciate the delicacy of the barber’s art; he saw in the barber's precise handling of the finest details <note>original: *il pelo dell' uovo*, literally "the hair of the egg," usually meaning being over-meticulous; the author equates it to the English idiom "the skin of one's teeth"</note> a sharpening of his own mental faculties.

Barbers and apothecaries were rivals in the Market. However, the barbers would joke about the crowds flocking to "**The Moor**" <note>original: *Il Moro*</note> and other famous apothecary shops <note>original: *botteghe degli Speziali*</note>, suggesting they were lacking in...

...the joys which only a sharp razor and a lively wit could provide!

Antonio Alamanni, born in 1480, was a follower <term>disciple</term> of Giovanni Burchiello and kept up the tradition <note>original: "cult"</note> of “*La Burchia*”—the Burlesque. He also produced topical melodies and established “*La Trottola*”—songs of playful banter. It must have been a very funny sight to watch the grimacing Alamanni, arm in arm with his eccentric and serious friend Antonio Magliabecchi—the great Librarian—crossing the Marketplace with Giovanni Pegolotti following along behind! Pegolotti was the inexhaustible author of jokes and insults <note>original: "gibes"</note> at the expense of the clergy and the medical profession <term>faculty</term>; he was impulsive <note>original: "capricious"</note> and bizarre, but entirely characteristic of the lighter side of life in the Market.

Music too, both vocal and instrumental, was not missing from the outskirts <term>purlieus</term> of the Old Market. Living in a hilly country by a swiftly running river, the Florentines were naturally gifted with sweet and full-toned voices and with accurate musical ears—the “*Voce Toscana*” <note>Tuscan Voice</note> became a proverb. Dante has preserved the name and the fame of Belacqua, a musical instrument-maker in the Market, and of Casella, his skillful musician friend.1

The Old Market <note>original: *Mercato Vecchio*</note> was a treasury of local traditions and stories. One—“The Legend of the White Hen”—is as follows: There was in the Old Marketplace of Florence an ancient house and shop; over the door was a stone carving <note>original: "figure, in bas-relief"</note> of a good fat hen to show that eggs could be bought there. The old woman who kept the shop was called Furicchia, and she was a mystery to her simple-minded neighbors. She always had an enormous quantity of eggs on hand, but where they came from, nobody knew. She did a splendid trade and rapidly became rich—especially as her eggs had the power <note>original: "virtue"</note> of curing sick people and bewitched children.

One day a poor but high-born Florentine lady, who was very jealous of Furicchia’s prosperity, determined to discover the secret. She visited the little shop and found its mistress out, but she heard a hen clucking in a cupboard:—

The name “Mercato Nuovo” <term>New Market</term> was first applied as an extension of the Mercato Vecchio <term>Old Market</term> in the fourteenth century. The demolition of many houses and towers exposed a site within easy reach of the Old Market at a time when daily trade <note>original: "barterings"</note> was overwhelming its capacity.

The growth of the silk industry, and the vast number of crafts and trades associated with it, required a nearly separate marketplace <term>mart</term>. Along with the increase in industrial output, the “Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers” found the Old Market very unsuitable for conducting their daily financial business. Consequently, an area was cleared of debris <note>original: "rubbish"</note> and surrounded by fine buildings—residences, shops, and offices. The primary families living in the New Market were the Cavalcanti, Giandonati, Infangati, and Mangiatori. Among the offices

A branch agency of the “Calimala” Guild was newly established there, where the banking business of the “French Merchants” <note>original: "Mercanti Francesca"</note> was primarily conducted.

A loggia <term>an open-sided gallery or arcade</term> was built on one side of the market. Here, the “Guild of Bankers and Money Changers” established an exchange where couriers and agents could be officially registered, and where those already employed could gather to submit their accounts and compare daily reports from foreign stock exchanges <term>Bourses</term>.

Tables with seats for money-changers were arranged all around the market. The tables of the registered guild members were covered with green cloth, while those of unlicensed changers were simply bare boards. During the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, nearly a hundred of these “banks” were established. The number of banks was limited by the available space in the market, for the Florentines strictly adhered to the tradition of staying in specific locations. It was not until the sixteenth century that bankers dared to expand their businesses to other squares <term>Piazze</term> and along the streets.

The New Market <term>Mercato Nuovo</term> differed from the Old Market <term>Mercato Vecchio</term> in that no food <term>comestibles</term> was sold within its boundaries. However, the sale of flowers was permitted, especially for church festivals and public ceremonies—a type of trade and a charming tradition that continues to this day.

Cosimo de’ Medici—“The Father of his Country”—was always loyal to his native city and his family. He noticed that the Florentine loggia was inferior to the stock exchanges <term>Borsa</term> of Amsterdam and other capital cities, and he decided to build a more impressive structure. Two architects were commissioned for the project, Bernardo Tasso and Buono Talenti, but Tasso performed most of the work, and the current beautiful building was completed in 1548. Beside one of the pillars stands the famous bronze boar, looking calmly at the cool fountain; it was cast by Pietro Tacca, a student of Giambologna <note>original: "Giovanni da Bologna"</note>.

The loggia was a magnificent sight every day during the hour of “Tierce” <term>the third canonical hour, approximately 9:00 a.m.</term>. It was filled with noble merchants in their formal robes and distinguished foreign visitors, swarming like bees and

In the center of the New Market <term>Mercato Nuovo</term>, the "*Carroccio*"—the ancient Florentine battle chariot—used to stand for thirty days before the Republic’s armies marched out to meet the enemy. Kept in the Baptistery, it was drawn into the New Market during times of trouble by two milk-white oxen covered with bright red cloths. The red and white banner of the people was raised over it, and Mass was said daily at an altar built upon its square platform. A guard of young men, all dressed in white, kept watch around this *Palladium* <term>a sacred object providing protection</term> of the city.¹ The use of the "*Carroccio*" began early in the thirteenth century, when it preceded the Florentine army on their way to Siena in 1230. Surprisingly, the sacred car was last used in another war against that same city, during which it fell into the hands of the Sienese, who destroyed it.

In place of the "*Carroccio*," the Signoria <term>the governing council of Florence</term> ordered a marble design to be set into the center of the market where the car had been accustomed to stand. This took the shape of a wheel with six alternating spokes of black and white marble embedded in the paving.

On this spot, at a later date, a stone pillar or post was erected. Bankrupts were tied to this post and publicly beaten three times with every mark of personal humiliation. Without a doubt, the modern custom of "hammering" a delinquent on the London Stock Exchange had its origin in this Florentine practice!

There was no way for a man to obtain a discharge from his debts except by undergoing this degrading flogging. If there was one thing the banking community of the New Market feared and hated more than any other, it was, of course, failure. A man or a business house that could not meet its payments was an object of universal contempt and persecution. The same treatment was also...

...punishment was administered to all citizens who persisted in “playing games with cards and dice, which distract honest men from work.” <note>Ademollo, i. 179.</note>

However, a special privilege was allowed by custom and law to debtors, who were free from arrest as long as they remained within the boundaries of the Market.

Another law was passed and generally observed which contributed to the dignity and the liberty of the *Mercato Nuovo* <term>New Market</term>—no person carrying weapons was permitted to enter. In times of public unrest, no doubt, this regulation was suspended; nevertheless, the militia of the “Guild of Bankers and Money-changers” were always on guard to defend the interests and fight for the privileges of the money market.

Many goldsmiths’ workshops were established in the basements of the houses bordering the Market. The studio of Giovanbattista Sogliani—Benvenuto Cellini’s third master—who allowed his distinguished pupil to share his workspace, was located here. They conducted such a thriving business that they required three shops, which were held from the “Guild of Goldsmiths” by Salvadore and Michele Guasconti, workers in precious metals. <note>J. A. Symonds, “Life of Benvenuto Cellini.”</note>

It was not the fashion to tip one's hat in old Florence, and this was nowhere more evident than in the Market. Even the *Messeri* <term>Sirs/Gentry</term> of the “Doctors” and the “Judges” Guilds were received with little courtesy; after all, were not the regular visitors also mostly members of honorable Crafts and possessed of full civic rights, or aspiring to them?

There was a good deal of “I’m-as-good-as-my-neighbor” attitude among the *genti* <term>people</term> of Florence. To salute an equal implied inferiority; to tip one's hat to a superior—well, there were none in the opinion of these artisan-aristocrats! All were members of a great and progressive industrial and commercial Republic, where the humblest citizen had the power to attain the highest positions of dignity. Ceremonious customs arrived with the rule of the Medici and marked the decline of Florentine greatness.

On the other hand, quite a few were the gestures of contempt—

The thumb was pushed between the first two fingers of the hand and then pointed at the disrespected person. Dante refers to this gesture in his *Inferno*:

> "When he had spoken, the wretch raised his hands

And certainly, our English expression—"don't care a fig"—has its origin in this Florentine custom.

However, as in all human affairs, sad days befell the markets. Riot, famine, flood, fire, and plague, in rapid succession, punished the antics and the crimes of reckless and treacherous citizens. The cry of <note>original: "All' Arme! All' Arme!"</note> "To Arms! To Arms!" resounded many times from one side of the busy marketplace to the other, re-echoing down the streets and lanes until it was caught up at the riverside and wafted across to the Oltrarno <term>the district "beyond the Arno" river</term> and right over the <term>Contado</term> <gloss>the surrounding rural territory under the city's jurisdiction</gloss>.

In 1304, terrible encounters were witnessed between the *Bianchi* and the *Neri*—the "Whites" and the "Blacks"—under the leadership of the Cerchi and the Donati families respectively. Fierce popular passions were aroused, and many a sturdy craftsman, as well as many a noble merchant, lay soaked in his own lifeblood. Whole families were wiped out, and industries were hindered and destroyed. Fire was set to the houses of the rival factions, and the Cavalcanti and Gherardini families of the markets were burned out of their homes.

Again in 1312, party strife broke out with renewed frenzy, and the Guelphs and Ghibellines <note>The two primary rival political factions in medieval Italy.</note> fought out their feuds in the markets. Workers and people from the countryside joined in the fray, and every workman used his axe, his knife, his mallet, and his saw in the bloody work of civil war. "Men," says Dino Compagni, "kill each other regardless of the law." <note>2 Dino Compagni, "Chronicle," p. 312.</note>

The fourteenth century found Florence torn and distraught—

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

tournaments and shows reduced the daily Market throng. The whole city went mad with excesses, and the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> and the New Market <note>original: "Mercato Nuovo"</note> were the scenes of wild debauchery.

The festivities, however, were abruptly halted in November 1333, when a fierce storm raged for four whole days and nights. The terrified citizens, sobered by the catastrophe, sought sanctuary in the churches until those too were inundated by the flood. The Market was four feet under water, and many houses collapsed; the bridges over the Arno were washed away. A great many people were drowned, and many cattle were carried off. When the waters subsided after a week of destruction, they left behind a foul-smelling slime that covered everything. This slime emitted a terrible stench and caused a plague to break out in the cramped houses of the city. The wells and springs were also polluted, and stores of grain, hay, and other food supplies were ruined. Famine seemed ready to complete the fateful work of an avenging Providence.

"*The Center of Florence*" <note>original: "Il Centro di Firenze"</note> became a social and political slogan in the middle of the 19th century. Decay, filth, and immoral habits had combined to give the Old Market and its surrounding areas a bad reputation. Plans for restoration or improvement were proposed and then abandoned; questions of private compensation and public convenience were weighed against one another. Financial burdens became the downfall of many sensible suggestions. At last, people grew tired of a project that seemed impossible to solve, and the demand for the demolition and removal of ancient buildings became fierce and urgent.

The city government yielded, not unwillingly, to the demand, and the grim work of destruction began. At first, the demolition workers plied their trade tentatively and timidly; but as they grew bolder and disregarded all respect for antiquity, a vast area was cleared of buildings.

The palaces, towers, shops, and taverns of the Old Market have disappeared. Its four churches are gone, and the *Column* <note>original: "Colonna"</note>...

The Column of Abundance <note>original: "della Dovitzia"</note>, with all its winding stories of a busy past, has been torn down.

The living lungs—though congested—which had breathed the life of centuries in and out of Florence, "the Beautiful and the Busy," have ceased their functions forever! The Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> was no more!

Memories of deeds from the distant past, and perhaps the ghosts of notable people long dead, still linger and mingle in a strange maze of "Hell" <note>original: "Inferno"</note> and "Paradise" <note>original: "Paradiso"</note>. Time and distance have softened the cries of the traders and silenced their tramping feet. A faint figure glides away, and a hushed voice proclaims: "The Old Market once stood here!"

### CHAPTER XVI

## THE STREETS, THE SQUARES, AND THE BRIDGES, WITH SOME OF THEIR STORIES

STREETS:—A maze of streets and lanes. Description of Florentine houses. Linen windows. Street noises. Children’s games. Straw matting. Fires—Pace da Certaldo’s <note>Pace da Certaldo (mid-14th century) was a merchant who wrote a book on good manners and household management.</note> expedient. Via di Calimala and its state awnings. “Rowdy Row.” Bernardo Cennini’s printing office. Gorgeous banners of the Por Santa Maria. Apprentices and their tricks. Artists’ workshops. A great blaze. Buffalmacco’s <note>Buonamico Buffalmacco was a 14th-century painter and legendary prankster.</note> jokes. The Devil of the Market <note>original: "Il Diavolo del Mercato," a bronze statue by Giambologna.</note>. A street of palaces. Narrow alleys <note>original: "chiassi"</note>. Dark deeds. Charles Dickens.

SQUARES:—Piazza della Signoria, the focus of official life. Giants at the gates. Palace of Merchandise <note>original: "Palazzo della Mercanzia"</note>. Loggia of the Lancers <note>original: "Loggia de’ Lanzi"</note>. Piazza di San Giovanni and great religious festivals. Pall-mall <note>original: "Palla e Maglio," a traditional lawn game.</note>. The Crusades. The Ball Game <note>original: "Il Pallone"</note>. Santa Croce. Florentine Football <note>original: "Il Calcio"</note>. Annual fairs. Love potions.

BRIDGES:—Old Bridge <note>original: "Ponte Vecchio"</note>. A bridegroom done to death. Butchers and goldsmiths. Carraia Bridge <note>original: "Ponte alla Carraia"</note>. Loads of wool. A link between past and present. Rubaconte Bridge <note>original: "Ponte Rubaconte," now known as the Ponte alle Grazie</note>, or Bridge of the Graces. Shop signs featuring animals. The quay of the sand-men. Bridge of the Holy Trinity <note>original: "Ponte alla Santa Trinita"</note>. Trysting place for lovers. Dante and Beatrice.

Scenes and stories:—Street violence. Bordone Bordoni. Wedding bells. Practical jokes. Horse races in the Cathedral <note>original: "Duomo"</note>! Solemn processions. Our Lady of Impruneta <note>original: "Madonna dell’ Impruneta"</note>. The Misericordia <note>A historic Florentine charitable brotherhood.</note>. Festival of St. John the Baptist. Banners. Towers. The Prize Race <note>original: "Il Palio"</note>. Pranks and tricks! <note>original: "Burle e Beffe!"</note>. The curfew. The spirits of the past.

A TOTAL maze of streets and squares, with tall, irregularly built houses of every kind and status, extended all around the markets. Mostly paved with large, hard, flat stones—and here and there a stretch of river cobbles set on their roughest ends—they served as the sturdy yet noisy stage where the comedies and tragedies of old Florence were performed.

The houses of Florence bore many designations—for example: *Palazzo* (a town mansion), *Palagetto* (a smaller building), *Casolaro* (an old palace inhabited by many poor people), *Casa* (an ordinary house), *Casella* (a small dwelling), *Bottega* (a shop), and *Loggia* (a porch or arcade).

# THE STREETS, SQUARES, AND BRIDGES

Some of the buildings were all that remained of the grim castles belonging to the <term>Società delle Torre</term> <note>Tower Societies: Associations formed by noble families in medieval Florence to build and defend fortified towers.</note>. Others displayed the notched battlements characteristic of the conflict between the Guelphs and Ghibellines <note>The two primary rival political factions in medieval Italy.</note>. As a rule, the ground floors featured arcades—or at least massive pillars and arches supported the upper floors—leaving dark, cave-like depths where sunlight rarely glinted.

During the day, these arcades and <term>loggie</term> <note>open-air galleries or porches</note> were crowded with small merchants selling every imaginable commodity, creating a never-ending cacophony of voices pitched at every possible key.

At night, and during times of domestic or political unrest, large doors or shutters and strong iron bars were typically slid into position to ensure the security of the residents and their property.¹

Many disreputable gambling dens flourished in those dark entryways. Tables for "Chess" and for "Woman" <note>original: "Woman," likely a literal translation of the Italian game *Dama*, known in English as checkers or draughts.</note>—the two popular games—were laid out, along with others for risky and unnamed games of chance. Players sat on rough benches while idle and immoral people gathered around to bet on the play. An accusation of cheating or a run of bad luck threw the gamblers, spectators, and the owners of the tables into a furious rage. Knives were quickly drawn, and before the cry of "*Accor’ uomo!*" <note>original: "Accor’ uomo!" — an Italian cry for help meaning "Help, someone!" or "To the rescue!"</note> could reach the outside world, some poor wretch would be lying on the ground, killed.

The fronts of many of these grand old houses appeared quite shabby, despite their massive stones and heavy ironwork. Their windows—if one can call those various openings for light and air "windows"—were covered only with dirty strips of oiled linen stretched tightly over wooden frames. Glass windows were a luxury reserved for the wealthy, and even many of the <term>Magnificos</term> <note>Magnificoes: Powerful and wealthy citizens of Florence.</note> were content to live in the same semi-darkness as their poorer neighbors.

The street noises were unbearable. There were the loud shouts of merchants promoting their many goods, the fierce cursing of pack-animal drivers and carters, the insults exchanged by jostled peddlers and passersby, vulgar and indecent snatches of song and jokes, and the howling of un-

# THE STREETS, SQUARES, AND BRIDGES

—it was undoubtedly the ancestor of our game "Oranges and Lemons." Two strong youths or maidens, clasping each other’s hands tightly, stood and tried to encircle the waists of passers-by as well as their playmates, asking each captive which party he or she belonged to. The prisoner was released only to hold onto the end of the line of their chosen side. When enough recruits were obtained, the two lines pulled as hard as they possibly could, with the winners tugging their weaker opponents wherever and however they <term>listed</term> <note>listed: desired or pleased</note>.

Filled with people in every sort of costume—rich and poor, old and young, merry and grave—all day long, no time was ever taken to sweep away the litter and the dust. Fortunately, rain ran in rivulets and periodically washed the gutters free of refuse; however, this cleansing swept the people's <term>porkers</term> <note>porkers: pigs</note>, which rooted in the dirt, into the basements of the houses, making the disorder beyond description. The straw matting on the floors of both rich and poor alike harbored both dirt and vermin!

The interiors of the houses were swept only once a week—on Saturdays—so one can well imagine the accumulation of filth that choked every corner and coated the tangled veils of enormous spiderwebs! <gloss>1</gloss>

The dwellings of the Florentines were very susceptible to fire. Their linen windows <note>Windows were often covered with oiled cloth or parchment rather than expensive glass.</note>, the wooden framework of their fittings and doors, and the vast amount of drying clothes—both wool and linen—waving their length from the top stories, all combined with many other factors to encourage fires. Furthermore, the safety measures against sudden outbreaks of fire were poorly designed.

Pace da Certaldo—a fourteenth-century writer—advised everyone "to keep at least twelve large canvas bags handy in which to put your things whenever there is a fire in your neighborhood, and also a thick piece of rope long enough to reach the ground to help you escape through a window!" <gloss>2</gloss>

## I. STREETS

Of all the streets that opened into the Old Market (*Mercato Vecchio*), the Calimala Way (*Via di Calimala*)—sometimes called the French Road (*Strada Francesca*)—was by far the most important. Not only did the most prominent merchants frequent it daily, but it also gave its name to the greatest of all the Guilds. Its principal building was the Palace of the Cavalcanti, which the family handed over to serve as a residence for the Consuls of that Great Guild. On the feast day of the city's patron saint <note>St. John the Baptist.</note>, the entire street was covered with a ceremonial awning of blue canvas, richly embroidered.

This was always the rallying point for both the friends and the foes of the merchants. At times, the solemn footsteps of respected city elders and their quiet, serious conversations gave way to the hurried march of the armed *Ciompi* <term>Ciompi: The disenfranchised textile workers who led a famous revolt in 1378.</term>, who sought—first with protests and then with fire—the removal of some trade injustice or the granting of some political privilege. <margin><note>original: "L'Osservatore Fiorentino."</note> The Florentine Observer.</margin>

At the end of the Calimala Way, where it entered the New Market (*Mercato Nuovo*), there was a narrow lane leading to the Shoemakers' Street (*Via de’ Calzaiuoli*). It was called "*Il Baccano*"—"Rowdy Row!"—because of the loud and vulgar shouts made by apprentices to attract customers to shop there. In 1470, a change came over the scene, and the discordant voices of disorderly lads gave way to the metallic music of the first type-foundry in Florence. Here, Bernardo Cennini established himself as a printer and publisher, using machines that have since revolutionized the world. The first banking house of the Medici was also located in "Rowdy Row." From "Rowdy Row" to the little Garbo Way (*Via del Garbo*) <note>Named for the high-quality wool produced there, known as "Garbo" wool.</note> was only a pace or two. There, shortly after printing became the "stepmother of learning," the first Florentine Booksellers’ Row was established.

The St. Mary’s Gate Street (*Via Por Santa Maria*) was second to none in importance, wealth, and romance. Here was the residence of the great Silk...

# THE STREETS, SQUARES, AND BRIDGES

The Guild, whose façade used to display the finest banners in the city, and whose Consuls and merchants walked with heads held high and pockets full of gold florins, were prouder than their peers. And precisely because of this arrogance, the street was famous for its practical jokers, who used crossed chains and unexpected obstacles to trip up the most elegant of these fine people!

A favorite trick of the apprentices and pranksters of Saint Mary's Gate Way <note>original: "Via Por Santa Maria"</note> was to place tubs or buckets of dirty water in front of the merchants' doors and in the deep shadows of the Amidei Tower <note>original: "Torre degli Amidei"</note> and the other towers. When an unsuspecting pedestrian fell into one, it was a signal for loud laughter, while boys at the corners—skilled at throwing stones—launched dangerous volleys! It was in Saint Mary's Gate Way <note>original: "Via Por Santa Maria"</note> that Benvenuto Cellini, when only sixteen years old, fought off five opponents who had dishonorably attacked his brother.

In the street leading from the Saint Mary's Gate <note>original: "Por Santa Maria"</note> to the Signoria Square <note>original: "Piazza della Signoria"</note> was located the ancient church of Santa Cecilia, where the two great Guilds of Wool and Silk held joint meetings for their mutual benefit. Sometimes these conferences led to riots because of the mutual jealousy of individual members.

Shoemakers' Way <note>original: "Via de’ Calzaiuoli"</note> was originally divided into three parts: Amidei Road <note>original: "Corso degli Amidei"</note>, Painters' Way <note>original: "Via de’ Pittori"</note>, and Cheesemongers' Way <note>original: "Via de’ Caciaiuoli"</note>. The latter was always smelling strongly of the goods of the cheesemongers—members of the "Oil-merchants' Guild" <note>original: "Arte degli Oliandoli"</note>—and many a gourmet wandered along, intent on tasting the food. Painters' Way <note>original: "Via de’ Pittori"</note> appealed to the people’s artistic instincts, just as the other appealed to their sense of smell. The new name came from the prosperity of the "Shoemakers’ Guild," and their cutting, hammering, punching, and other noisy trade details were constantly in progress. In Shoemakers' Way <note>original: "Via de’ Calzaiuoli"</note> was the Macci Palace <note>original: "Palazzo Macci"</note>, the residence of the Duke of Athens <note>Walter VI of Brienne, who briefly ruled Florence as a dictator in 1342–1343.</note> during his term as Chief Magistrate. The shops of those who made leggings <term>body-hose: tight-fitting garments covering the legs and lower torso, a precursor to modern tights.</term> and stockings were also in this street. This manufacture was a specialty...

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

...of Florence, so that when Charles V entered the city in 1506, wearing light breeches, he was hailed as a true Florentine! <sup>1</sup>

Just beyond the Bigallo <note>The Loggia del Bigallo</note>, in Shoemakers' Way <note>original: "Via de' Calzaiuoli"</note>, Donatello, Luca Della Robbia, Michelozzo, and Masaccio worked as brothers for the common cause of art and craft.

The Corso was the strategic boundary between the Cerchi and the Donati families. Cerchi Way <note>original: "Via de' Cerchi"</note>—a charming narrow lane—ran parallel to Shoemakers' Way. At the corner where Shearers' Way <note>original: "Via di Cimatori"</note> joined it, a stone pillar stood displaying three circles—the coat of arms of the formidable "Whites" faction. It was part of their loggia. The Borgo degli Albizzi, at the other end of the Corso, contained the houses of the "Blacks" faction.

During a street fight between these hostile parties in the year 1302, a great many candles were burning at the shrine of Or San Michele. One evening, the flames ignited some wax votive offerings hanging there. The blaze so greatly excited the common people that, grabbing the burning fragments, they madly set fire to all the houses in the neighborhood!

Just beyond the Church of San Pierino of the Market was Glove Alley <note>original: "Vicolo del Guanto"</note>, where lived the dressers of kid and calfskin and the makers of gloves and gauntlets. It was a favorite meeting place for gentlemen and young women looking for elegant handwear. Sometimes the narrow lane was called Little Lion Alley <note>original: "Vicolo del Leoncino"</note>, named after its noted inn and world-famous banking house.

In Melon Way <note>original: "Via di Mellone"</note>—now Ricasoli Way—thirteenth-century artists, craftsmen, and playful jokers gathered. Tafi, wearing a long gown and feeling almost dizzy from fixing mosaics within the dome of the Baptistery, had to put up with the daily teasing of Buffalmacco—the master prankster. Giotto cast a shadow from his uniquely shaped cap down that way after finishing his difficult work on the "Gospel of Labor" <note>referring to the relief sculptures</note> on the Bell Tower <note>original: "Campanile"</note>, with his chisel and his measuring tool tucked into his belt. Jostling them came many an enthusiastic comrade, with song, jokes, gossip, and shy...

# THE STREETS, SQUARES, AND BRIDGES

...glances from cheerful young women at the street doors excited many a beating heart!

In Vaccherecia Street <note>original: "Via di Vaccherecia"</note>, the musical tinkling of goldsmiths’ hammers and niello engravers’ drills softened the harsher sounds of engravers’ scratching needles and burnishers’ rasping files. The Pollaiuoli family, along with Maso Finiguerra and many others, created pleasant and profitable harmonies in metal, amidst the chatter of Brunelleschi <note>original: "Brunellesco"</note> and his close companions. Nearby, in Saint Giles Street <note>original: "Via di Sant’ Egidio"</note>, at the Della Robbia House, Ghiberti cast his glorious gates. Meanwhile, from Cellini’s furnace next door in Pergola Street <note>original: "Via della Pergola"</note>, came the celebrated "Perseus" of the Loggia dei Lanzi—a statue famously cast with the addition of pewter vessels to the molten bronze.

Andrea del Sarto and Franciabigio had their shop at the corner of Or San Michele Square <note>original: "Piazza dell’ Or San Michele"</note>, a famous gathering place for artists and wits. Bursts of laughter often stopped passersby and prompted many curious people to step across the dark threshold in search of fun. Fra Bartolommeo della Porta—the premier painter of Florence—took his name from his birthplace near the Roman Gate. There, his faithful companion Albertinelli eventually traded his brush and palette for the wine flasks and glass beakers of a wine merchant <note>original: "Vinattiere"</note>.

Furriers' Street <note>original: "Via de’ Pelliccieri"</note>—with its palaces and towers belonging to the Lamberti, Toschi, Cipriani, Pilli, and other families connected to the "Guild of Skinners and Furriers"—was also frequently visited by goldsmiths. In this historic street, master painters also lingered as they chose the finest pieces of vellum for their miniature illustrations or the best-grained wood panels for their paintings of the Madonna.

Moving from the elegant and refined trades of Furriers' Street to the dirt and stench of Fire Street <note>original: "Via del Fuoco"</note>—just around the corner from the headquarters of the "Guild of Wool"—was only a short distance, but it felt like a world away. With its shrine and image of the Virgin Mary and her ever-burning lamp—a religious offering intended to prevent a city fire—the Street of the Furnaces was always as grimy as could be. Charcoal dealers, iron...

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Moulders and traders who worked with fire were always a hardworking and noisy group.

At the corner of Vecchietti Street <note>original: "Via de' Vecchietti"</note> and Old Iron Street <note>original: "Via de' Ferrivecchi"</note>—where the Cavolaia Palace <note>original: "Palazzo Cavolaia"</note>, or the "Cabbage-woman’s Palace," once stood—was placed the eerie bronze figure of the *Market Devil* <note>original: "Il Diavolo del Mercato"</note>, cast by Giovanni da Bologna. It was a fitting location for it—the site of the labors of scrap-iron dealers, who argued and swore all day long! The main workshops of the "Armourers" and "Locksmiths" were nearby—scenes of noisy machinery and talkative mechanics.

Bardi Street <note>original: "Via de' Bardi"</note> was and remains a characteristic thoroughfare of the city, where every layer of stone, wooden door, and heavy piece of iron speaks of wartime and old-world romance. Its palaces are gone—destroyed by fire, looting, and floods—but the spirits of hardworking, busy woolworkers and clever bankers still remain.

Ricci Lane <note>original: "Chiasso de' Ricci"</note>, Erri Lane <note>original: "Chiasso de' Erri"</note>, and many other narrow alleys and passages in the busy center of old Florence were full of human interest. Almost blocked from the sunlight by the closeness of the overhanging eaves of buildings on opposite sides, the silent warning to travelers—"you may only pass if we wish it"—seemed just as effective at stopping movement as the notorious street chains used during times of unrest and rioting.

Strange entryways and courtyards existed—bordering the lanes and streets—well-suited for tragedy and forgotten events. Secret histories and plots, as well as noble projects and literary memories, fill those narrow, busy streets with both the romance and the reality of a living humanity.

> "Magnificent, stern, and somber," wrote Charles Dickens, "are the streets of beautiful Florence."

<header>THE STREETS, SQUARES, AND BRIDGES</header>

The square served as the meeting place of the armed groups of the guilds during times of unrest. Dominated by the Old Palace <note>original: "Palazzo Vecchio"</note>—built in 1298—it was a secure residence for the Priors <note>The city's executive magistrates</note>. The tower—world-famous—is that of the old Foraboschi Palace. It earned the name of the *Tower of the Cow* <note>original: "Torre della Vacca"</note> because the great bell of Florence was hung there—the bell whose notes called citizens to fight or to work, depending on whether the times were warlike or peaceful.

"The Giants at the Gates," as they were fittingly called, were heroic marble statues of "David" by Michelangelo and "Hercules slaying Cacus" by Baccio Bandinelli. Over the great portal of the Palace, one may still read the proud inscription carved in the fifteenth century: "*King of Kings and Lord of Lords*" <note>original: "Rex Regum et Dominus Dominantium"</note>. Along the front of the Palace ran the *Ringhiera*, or public speaker’s platform, which was completed in 1349.

Close at hand was the Badia—the official residence of the Podestà <note>The chief magistrate of the city</note>—where the "Banner of the People," half red and half white, was kept. Not very far away was the Bargello, the Palace of the *Captain of the People* <note>original: "Capitano del Popolo"</note>; he was responsible for the custody of the Banner of the Republic—the *Giglio* or Lily of Florence.

On one side of the square was the Merchants’ Palace <note>original: "Palazzo della Mercanzia"</note>—the Chamber of Commerce—which was effectively the parliament of the guilds. At a corner of the square originally stood the Church of San Piero Scheraggio, which was removed to make way for the *Uffizi*—or Government Offices. Next to it is the Loggia dei Lanzi, begun in 1374 by Orcagna and named after the mercenary lancers <note>The "Lanzi" were German mercenary pikemen/lancers</note> of Grand Duke Cosimo I in 1541.

Beyond the Old Palace was the great Neptune Fountain—constructed by Baccio Bandinelli—and called by Florentines "*The Great White Figure*" <note>original: "Il Biancone"</note>. By time-honored custom, they always said a respectful goodbye to this statue before starting on a journey abroad.

The Square of Saint John the Baptist <note>original: "Piazza di San Giovanni Battista"</note> was the most historic square in Florence and the one most deeply respected by the citizens. It was the setting for all the major public religious festivals. In 1283, the Rossi family and their supporters, to the...

A group of one thousand people, all dressed in white under a leader called "the Lord of Love," performed a series of miracle plays <note>Religious dramas based on the lives of saints or biblical stories</note> during the Festival of the Patron Saint.

Marriages of prominent citizens were sometimes held in the open square. For example, in 1419, Salvestro di Messere Filippo Adimari married Lisa del Abbatacchio de' Ricasoli with great magnificence in the presence of Pope Martin V. The bridegroom's best man was the *Condottiere* <note>A commander of mercenary troops</note> Braccio da Montone, a successful adventurer and Lord of Perugia.

This circumstance inspired a bit of mocking doggerel verse:

| | |
|---|---|
| "Brave Braccio <note>original: "*Braccio valente*"</note> | Conquers every nation. <note>original: "*Vince ogni gente.*"</note> |
| But Pope Martin <note>original: "*Il Papa Martino*"</note> | Isn't worth a penny!" <note>original: "*Non vale un quattrino!*"</note> |

This reflected how the poverty and gentleness of His Holiness failed to impress the practical-minded Florentines.

In 1526, when a new military force of young knights was raised to oppose another Pope—Clement VII—a richly decorated altar was placed in the center of the square. There, officers and ordinary knights publicly took an oath of allegiance to the Republic in the presence of the magnificent Signoria <note>The supreme governing body of Florence</note>.

To mention both significant and minor events together—a fair number of bullfights were held on this nearly sacred ground for the entertainment of foreign princes and ambassadors. Furthermore, in 1453, a Goose Fair was established as an annual event on the Feast of All Saints. This was greatly to the benefit of the members of the "Guild of Oil-merchants and Provisioners" <note>original: "Arte degli *Oliandoli*"</note>, who celebrated a major festival as a result.

The Piazza di San Marco contains within its monastery and library the most enduring monuments to Cosimo de' Medici—known as "the Father of his Country." Memories of the virtuous Archbishop Saint Antonino and of Fra Angelico, the "Divine" painter, also linger fondly there. However, in stark contrast to these religious associations, the square also served as a playground for the city's young men. ...was a wooden bat like a flat club, the wicket was a single stump, and runs were scored much like in modern single-wicket cricket. The "**Palla**" <note>Italian: "ball"</note> was a small hard ball. This was undoubtedly the ancestor of the British national game, brought to England's public schools and colleges in the sixteenth century during the time of the so-called "Tuscan Fever," when so many Florentine customs took root in Great Britain.

The Piazza di Santa Maria Novella was always the scene of religious fervor and warlike romance. It was here in 1287 that the banner of the Florentine Company of the Second Crusade was unfurled. The Bishop had entrusted this banner to the proud Pazzino de' Pazzi in the neighboring church of San Donato alla Torre. Pazzino also rode back to this square at the head of his knights, wearing the mural crown <term>A headpiece representing city walls, awarded to the first soldier to climb the wall of a besieged city</term> placed upon his brow by Godfrey of Bouillon.

To show his gratitude to Almighty God, Pazzino set aside a sum of money to pay for a permanent annual memorial of his command's exploits. This festival is still celebrated on Holy Saturday with the ceremony of the **Sacred Fire** <note>Also known as the *Scoppio del Carro*, or Explosion of the Cart</note>, but it has since been moved to the Piazza del Duomo.

In this famous square, the ringleaders of the city’s riots used to gather. Brave were the speeches and stout were the hearts of those fierce "**Wooden Shoes**" <note>The *Ciompi*, or lower-class laborers, who wore wooden clogs</note> as they shouldered their tools and weapons and rallied to the cry, "**Long live the People!**" <note>original: "*Evviva il Popolo!*"</note>

Sports and pastimes also found a home and many devotees under the shadow of the glorious church. "**Il Pallone**" <note>A traditional Italian ball game; literally "the large ball"</note>—the ancestor of Rackets and Court Tennis—was the favorite game. The ball was tossed up merrily against the massive walls and decorative stone windows until practicality and a sense of decorum led the players to move their games to the Cascine <note>A large public park in Florence</note>.

The Piazza di Santa Croce was second to none in the magnificence of its pageants or the romance of its history. In the early days, it was given over to the solemn chants of monks and the harmless play of children; eventually, it became the setting for the city’s welcome and entertainment of her most distinguished visitors.

To it was given the name of the "Hill Fair" <note>original: "*Fiera collina*"</note> by the peasant women <note>original: *contadine*</note>, who came yearly out of the hill country of Pistoia and the Casentino to sing their mournful hymns to the Virgin Mary and to sell their yarn and dried mushrooms. The yarn was the product of the previous year’s home industry, carried in large bundles on their strong backs. Once their devotions were finished and sales were made, the rest of the day was dedicated to pleasure in the booths and among the other attractions of the fairground.

It was a festival for mothers and children, filled with every innocent trick and delight. Quack doctors, magicians, and peddlers shouted their medicines, tricks, and bargains from their various stations. Mysterious pills to soothe headaches, earaches, and perhaps even heartaches, were available cheaply enough; antidotes against drowning, fire, and similar strange misfortunes were also moderately priced.^1

But the Square, which was quiet enough at other times, was the pleasant scene of much kind-hearted charity from the holy Servite Brethren <note>A mendicant religious order founded in Florence in 1233</note>. There too, in later days, many a returned explorer told stories of adventure and success to his fellow citizens and the members of his Guild—the Doctors and Apothecaries.

The Brunelleschi and Onion Squares <note>original: *Piazze de’ Brunelleschi, and di Cipolle*</note> were always very popular. In the former, also called Chestnut Square <note>original: *Piazza di Marroni*</note>, were candied-chestnut vendors and the shops of the "Guild of Second-hand Dealers" <note>original: "*Arte de’ Rigattieri*"</note>. There, the newest tasteful knick-knacks to decorate a young woman’s room attracted many a loving couple. The latter square, located just behind the Strozzi Palace, was the trading ground for the less fragrant but ever-popular onions. The salesmen displayed them on the large stone benches that surrounded the Square. While fashionable people rarely risked a visit, many an amorous young city girl crept secretly along to obtain a love potion from one of the old women who sat there meditating and talking to themselves.

### III. BRIDGES

The building of bridges has always been regarded as a sign of vigorous political and commercial life. Florence easily took the lead over other cities through its early enterprise in bridging the Arno River. Much of the life and business of the city was carried out upon, as well as over, its four substantial bridges, whose stones were polished by the hurrying feet of craftsmen and their pack animals.

The most famous bridge, as well as the oldest—the *Ponte Vecchio* <note>The Old Bridge</note>—dates back to Roman times, when the Roman-Etrurian road was carried over the river on a stone archway. The first structure was washed away, but in 1080, another bridge was built across—a kind of forerunner to the Renaissance. The changes in fortune of the *Ponte Vecchio* were countless and varied in their impact, and they aptly illustrate the fortunes of the city itself. Flood, fire, plague, and bloodshed swept those ancient piers and attacked those venerable structures more times than can be remembered.²

It was on this bridge, at the foot of the mutilated statue of Mars—the city’s earliest *Palladium* <note>A statue or object believed to provide protection or safety for a city</note>—that on Easter Day in 1215, a handsome bridegroom was dragged from his richly decorated horse and stabbed to death by the daggers of the enraged Fifanti family. Buondelmonte de’ Buondelmonti had jilted a daughter of the Amidei family and had married Beatrice Donati instead; it was Mosca de’ Lamberti who said, “Let him die!” This murder gave rise to the two great political factions: the Guelphs and Ghibellines.

The current, most interesting bridge was built by Taddeo Gaddi in 1345 at a cost of sixty thousand gold florins. On a buttress, the original inscription can still be seen:
->Gaddi made me; I am the Old Bridge. <note>original: “Gaddi me fece, il Ponte Vecchio sono.”</note><-

In 1378, in recognition of his devotion to the cause of the *Popolo Minuto* <note>The "little people" or the lower classes/unskilled laborers of Florence</note>, Salvestro di Messere Alamanno de' Medici was awarded—along with his knighthood—the annual rent of all forty-four shops built upon the bridge by the leaders of the *Ciompi* <note>The wool-carders' guild and the namesake of the popular revolt of 1378</note> government. In 1281, this produced only the small sum of five hundred *lire*, but a century later, the shops were worth at least a thousand gold florins a year.

At first, these shops appear to have been occupied by anyone who came along; however, from 1422 to 1490, they were rented exclusively by members of the "Guild of Butchers," whose trade had outgrown the Old Market area. Under Cosimo I, the *Capitani di Parte Guelfa* <note>Captains of the Guelph Party, a powerful political and administrative body</note> signed an order for the butchers to leave the bridge, and the goldsmiths were installed in their place.<gloss>1</gloss> Since then, the bridge has echoed with the hearty voices of cheerful young apprentices, calling out to all who pass by to purchase the beautiful trinkets their skilled hands have crafted.<gloss>1</gloss>

In 1564, Cosimo I constructed the covered corridor <note>The Vasari Corridor</note> which connects the Pitti and the Uffizi palaces, completely altering the appearance of the venerable bridge.

The *Ponte Alla Carraia*—alternately built, washed away, and rebuilt—was the bridge of the laborer. No bridge was so crowded with workers hurrying to and from the wool factories of the "Umiliati" <note>A religious order known for their work in the textile industry</note> and the merchants of the "Wool Guild."

Its very name signifies a toilsome enterprise, for its approaches were daily blocked by loaded carts and burdened pack-mules. Its earliest name, however, was "*Il Ponte Nuovo*" <note>The New Bridge</note>, a title it held during the early years of the thirteenth century. The first bridge was made of wood and erected in 1218. The *Ponte alla Carraia* is, metaphorically, the link between the medieval isolation of monastic influences and the Renaissance freedom of the arts and crafts. Gaddi's bridge <note>Designed by the architect and painter Taddeo Gaddi</note> was finished in 1337 and cost seventy-two thousand gold florins.

The *Ponte Rubaconte*—first built under the Podestà <note>The chief magistrate of the city</note> Ruba—

The Ponte Rubaconte—built by Messere Lapo, the master of Arnolfo di Cambio, in 1237—suffered like the other bridges, but it eventually came to be regarded as the most fashionable bridge in Florence, and its houses were tall and handsome.

There is a record in the Archives dated August 22, 1297, regarding the leasing of fourteen or fifteen shops newly built upon the Ponte Rubaconte. The average annual rent was fixed at between five and forty *lire*, depending on how close the shop was to the Via di Por Santa Maria. Among the traders on the bridge were six strap and stirrup-makers and five pouch or purse-makers—all members of the "Guild of Saddlers." Each shop was required to display a unique sign, and these signs all featured animals. For example, there were: "The Two Lions," "The Unicorn," "The Wolf," "The Leopard," "The Stag," "The Cat," "The Panther," "The Bear," and "The Camel."<gloss>1</gloss> In 1333, when a disastrous flood swept away the other four bridges over the Arno but spared the Ponte Rubaconte, the name was changed to the Ponte alle Grazie <note>Bridge of the Graces</note> as a token of thankfulness to the Almighty, and a prayer chapel was built over the center arch.

On the Oltrarno <note>the "other side of the Arno" river</note> side of the bridge was the Piazza de' Mozzi. Tommaso de' Mozzi built his palace where the riverbank was later reinforced by the Via dei Renai, or the Quay of the Sandmen. The sandmen were a very vigorous group, though they were rumored to be prone to personal violence and robbery. Nevertheless, they served as models for Michelangelo's "*Slaves*" and Benvenuto Cellini's "*Perseus*," and their trade association was a significant one among its peers.

The Ponte alla Santa Trinita was the last of the four bridges to be built. It is said that the Frescobaldi family—who, along with many other merchant families, settled in the formerly poor suburbs of Oltrarno in 1252—built a private wooden bridge across the river from the Borgo San Jacopo. This was a favorite meeting place for lovers. Young men used to lounge upon the bridge, and because it was not crowded with houses and shops, its parapets...

looked directly out upon the Lungarno <note>the embankments along the river Arno</note> to the right and left. From there, the young women of their choice—or otherwise—could be seen walking modestly hand-in-hand along the pavement by the river walls. Dante <note>Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), the famous Italian poet</note> was not the only Florentine youth who saw and loved his Beatrice <note>Beatrice Portinari, Dante's muse</note> there!

---

Chronicles of factional fights are not the only interesting records in the history of the streets and squares of Florence. Many of the old narratives are quite amusing and entertaining. At one time, for example, robbery with violence became widespread and intolerable. Houses and individuals alike were attacked, and the entire scheme was organized according to an elaborate system.

A gang of thieves organized themselves to strip the city bare. Many of them carried musical instruments and serenaded the occupants of houses, who felt obligated to unbar their doors and windows and bow to their visitors. However, while they were thus engaged, the musicians' accomplices forced an entrance and, of course, ransacked the premises!

A charming and unique feature of their exploits was the recruitment of well-connected children who were available to accompany them as dancers, singers, collectors, and the like. Some of these children were posted at the ends of streets about to be "burglarized" to warn travelers not to venture there, as danger was brewing! One of the leaders was a young man called Bordone Bordoni, who was well-connected and wealthy. He was finally caught and beheaded, and his band of prowling criminals was scattered.

Wedding bells also rang out from the informative bell towers as cavaliers, with jingling spurs and restless horses, pranced along to their weddings with beautiful maidens of noble appearance and high birth. The rustle <term>frou-frou</term> of silken skirts and the shimmer of flashing gems sweep many times across the pages of the history of old Florence.

Florence. Where eye spoke to eye and heart beat for heart, striped awnings and festoons of greenery stretched right across the narrow streets. Proud coats of arms were displayed on house fronts, colorful banners waved high above, and beautiful, valuable tapestries and furs hung over balconies and windowsills.

The Via della Vigna <note>Street of the Vineyard, a famous street in Florence</note> was crowded from one end to the other with people in holiday dress and spectators of the show. Everything was festive for Romola <note>A reference to the heroine of George Eliot’s novel *Romola*, set in 15th-century Florence</note>, Caterina, or some other lovely bride. Then, once the marriage ceremony was over—amidst music, flowers, and sunshine—the tournament <term>Tilting-match: a jousting competition</term> would attract the crowds.

On such days, the aroma of fine vintages filled the air, as red and yellow wine ran deep through the streets and lanes; meanwhile, workmen, servants, and beggars were treated to plenty of good food and drink. <note>Footnote 1: G. Biagi, “Private Life of Renaissance Florentines.”</note>

Holidays were also days of mischief for high-spirited young Florentines. Emboldened perhaps by gambling and wine, or simply by an excess of youthful energy, groups of festive youths used to race through the city, entering houses and breaking up the many parties inside, or forcing the hosts to keep "open house" and admit them to the feasts.

As Benvenuto Cellini <note>1500–1571; a famous Florentine goldsmith and sculptor known for his rowdy autobiography</note> records, young aristocrats would resort to practical jokes that sometimes became outrages against public decency and religious holiness. It was considered a top-tier prank to snatch the ink-pots of passing Notaries and, rushing with them into the churches, pour the ink into the holy-water basins! Raids were also made upon the fearful pharmacists <term>Apothecaries: health professionals who formulated and dispensed remedies</term>, where asafoetida <note>a pungent, foul-smelling resin</note> and other stinking concoctions were seized to be mixed with the incense supplies in the church vestries! However, no sport equaled the "jest" and desecration of driving livestock from the market into the churches, or racing on horseback around the Tribune <note>the semicircular or polygonal area at the end of the church</note> at the Cathedral <term>Duomo: the Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore</term>!

But days of gloom, silenced by the sound of heavy footsteps, often came to the good people of Florence. The solemn—

The funeral songs of monks tramping in from La Pineta <note>The Pine Grove</note> with the sacred image of the *Madonna dell'Impruneta* <note>Our Lady of Impruneta, a revered icon of the Virgin Mary often carried in times of crisis</note>—brought in a procession to the Duomo <note>Cathedral</note> to seek divine favor during a disaster or catastrophe—brings all men to their knees. With a hastily marked cross upon the breast and a whispered "*Ave*" <note>original: "Ave"; Hail Mary</note>, working men and women kneel for a moment side by side on the pavement with their employers and their rulers. The Guilds are prostrate before the emblems of the Christian faith. Church candles are all ablaze, while the loom lights are extinguished; hands once skillful in the crafts now drop rosary beads one by one in a silent, reverent pause.

> “May God, Saint Mary, and the Saints—especially the good Saint John—avert the plague or stop it; give needed rain, or dry up the floodwaters; defend the right against the public enemy; and settle the feuds of rival houses: may God protect Florence!”—

Such were the prayers that pierced the blue Tuscan vault of heaven.

Still other sights, affecting and arresting, were witnessed day in and day out in old Florence. Through spacious squares and narrow streets pass the silent, hooded bearers of the sick, the dying, and the dead. The *Misericordia* <term>Mercy: a charitable lay brotherhood dedicated to caring for the sick and burying the poor</term> Brethren have, from time immemorial, picked up a poor body in some dingy corner—an outcast or a waif, perhaps the victim of another or of his own hand. Passing through the buyers and the sellers in the busy markets, they have struck a pathetic chord in many a rugged heart, calling forth the quiet cry "*Miserere nobis Domine*" <note>original: "Miserere nobis Domine"; Lord, have mercy on us</note> from many a somber mouth.

The Festival of San Giovanni Battista <note>Saint John the Baptist</note>, the Patron of Florence, was always an occasion of rejoicing in the markets and the streets. The ceremonies of the day began in front of the Palazzo Vecchio, in the Piazza della Signoria, where everyone, from nobles to commoners, dressed in holiday attire and went to pay their respects to the *Gonfaloniere di Giustizia* <term>Standard-bearer of Justice: the highest-ranking magistrate in the Florentine government</term> and the other magistrates. These dignitaries, arrayed in robes of state, took their places upon the *Ringhiera* <term>The railed stone platform in front of the Palazzo Vecchio used for public addresses and ceremonies</term> early in the day.

One hundred gorgeous banners were unfurled and displayed by as many richly dressed *gonfalonieri* <term>standard-bearers</term>. They represented not...

not only the various *sestieri* <term>sestieri: the six administrative districts of Florence</term> of the city and the Twenty-one Guilds—with the banners of allied trade companies and religious brotherhoods—but among them were many trophy flags: the captured emblems of defeated cities.

After the greetings were finished, the Magnificos <term>Magnificos: the high-ranking leaders and prominent citizens of the city</term> led a massive procession to the Baptistery to lay their offerings upon the altar of the Saint. A splendid feature of the parade was the succession of brightly decorated floats belonging to the various Guilds, each accompanied by its Consuls <term>Consuls: the elected chief magistrates or leaders of a guild</term>, officers, and a full attendance of members. Famous artists were hired to decorate the floats; for example, Andrea del Sarto painted one for the "Guild of Wool," and Piero di Cosimo another for the "Guild of Silk." The floats were pulled by richly decorated horses and oxen, and many carried curious towers made of wax, painted and adorned, which were designed to rotate.

At San Giovanni <note>The Baptistery of San Giovanni (St. John the Baptist), the patron saint of Florence</note>, expensive offerings were dedicated by the Officers of State, the Consuls, and the wealthier citizens; meanwhile, even the poorest person presented a humble tallow candle <note>a cheap candle made from animal fat</note>, which they had purchased at one of the Apothecaries' <term>Apothecaries: pharmacists who, in Florence, belonged to a major guild and sold wax and candles alongside medicines</term> shops.

The wax towers were always greeted with delight, but often with jokes as well. Usually, young men at the house windows along the route tried to tip over the towers and the boys inside them using long poles. Others changed the joke by snatching candles and lamps out of the hands of those in the procession, using long wands or rods. Such rascals were nicknamed "*bel Ceio*" <note>original: "bel Ceio"; a Florentine slang term for an impudent or foolish fellow</note>, meaning "impudent, stupid fellow"; nevertheless, their pranks were always tolerated.

For the Festival, the entire Piazza di San Giovanni was covered with a massive awning of light-blue linen canvas at the expense of the *Calimala Guild* <note>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants of Foreign Cloth, one of the wealthiest in Florence</note>. It was made of five pieces, three of which covered the square and the space between the Baptistery and the Duomo <term>Duomo: the Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore</term>—the middle strip in front of the doors featured the embroidered coat of arms of the Republic. The other two pieces were stretched over the side of the *Misericordia* <term>Misericordia: the headquarters of the charitable brotherhood mentioned on the previous page</term> office and formed a canopy for San Giovanni. The purpose of the awning was, primarily, to provide shelter from the heat of the midsummer

At noon, a general feast was held. Every tavern and eating-house in the Market and its adjacent streets was crammed with hungry, thirsty, and lively revelers; perhaps each person realized for himself a favorite saying of the Market people:— "Caught like a flea in a bundle of tow <term>tow: the coarse, tangled fibers of flax or hemp; the phrase implies being caught in a dense, chaotic crowd</term>!"

Then, after the briefest of naps under the Market's *loggie* <term>loggie: open-air arched galleries or porches</term>, or elsewhere in the shade, everyone moved off to find a place for the *Palio* <term>Palio: a traditional high-stakes horse race</term>—the great annual horse race. The course lay right through the city from the Porta al Prato to the Porta alla Croce, along the Borgo degli Albizzi, the Via Vigna Nuova, and the Borgo d’Ognissanti.

The *Palio* always formed a primary feature in all public celebrations. If a victory had been won over Siena, Lucca, Pisa, Prato, or any other rival city, horse races were the natural and popular accompaniments. They were held immediately under the walls of the defeated stronghold by the victorious troops, as well as in Florence by the peaceful citizens.

Once this spectacle was over, a further move was made, either to the sports ground at Peretola, or to the Piazze della Croce and Santa Maria Novella, to view the *giostre* <term>giostre: jousts or tournaments</term> and games. The merry, noisy, sweaty crowd of the city—increased by the arrival of visitors from the *Contado* <term>Contado: the rural territory and villages surrounding the city</term> and the neighboring towns—passed to and fro with *burle* and *beffe* <term>burle and beffe: traditional Italian words for jokes and pranks</term>.

An ancient Carnival song went like this:

> "To the Calcio <term>Calcio: a historic, often violent form of football originating in 16th-century Florence</term> field, up comrades and away.
> The bounding football there invites us all to play;
> No game is so full of sport to fill the day."

Oh, how the remaining historic palaces, ancient shops, well-worn streets, and busy marketplaces speak to us! In solemn tones, they tell of the sternness and grandeur, as well as the playfulness and the violence, of those distant scenes in old Florence.

Those sturdy, massive buildings are like the tightly packed ranks of the city's armored militias. Their open doorways and hidden basements bring to mind busy laborers. The solid towers—built with the square-headed merlons <note>Likely a typo for "merlons" (the solid part of a battlemented parapet).</note> used by the Guelphs <term>Guelphs: a political faction in medieval Italy that supported the Pope</term>, or the forked ones favored by the Ghibellines <term>Ghibellines: a political faction that supported the Holy Roman Emperor</term>—stand as memorials to the watchful captains of the Guilds and the proud nobles of the Signoria <term>Signoria: the governing body of the Republic of Florence</term>. Now, these structures appear aged and weathered.

# CHAPTER XVII

## THE RELIGION OF THE GUILDS

Humanism. Greek ideals. Roman methods. Pleasure, ambition, and avarice. The Church non-aggressive. The Pope’s party: the People’s party. <term>The Pope’s Bankers <note>original: "Campsores Papæ"</note></term>. Types of the great artists of Florence. The Baptistery. Early system of birth registration. Religious associations. “The Watchers and Servants of Mary.” The <term>Humiliati <note>original: "Umilitati"—a religious order known for their work in the wool industry</note></term>. Public participation in daily “Hours.” No cant, no hypocrisy! The Madonna. Prayers before business. Obscure “Beatitudes.” “Candle-spikers” and “Breast-beaters.” Poor and rich alike affected. Private chapels. The Charterhouse of Val d’Ema <note>original: "Certosa di Val d’Ema"</note>. “Apostles of the Lord.” Days of religious obligation. The <term>Sportelli <note>original: "Sportelli"—likely referring to the service windows or hatches used for distributing charity or goods</note></term>. <term>Votive offerings <note>original: "Ex votos"</note></term>. Facilities for attending Mass. Free thought. Religious equality. Platonic philosophy. Writings of Leonardo da Vinci, Leon Battista Alberti, Francesco Guicciardini, Niccolo Machiavelli, and others. Church festivals. “The Feast of Love.” Superstitions. Saint John the Baptist <note>original: "San Giovanni Battista"</note>. Lorenzo de’ Medici’s image. Miracles of healing. “How to extinguish a big blaze!” Cleanliness next to godliness. The “Evil Eye.” The <term>Brevi <note>original: "Brevi"—devotional charms or written amulets</note></term>. Large families. Fatalistic tendencies. Monks and nuns. <note>original: "Firenze la Prima!"—Florence the First!</note> The Council of Florence. The Inquisition. Savonarola. Sermons. “Imitate Barletta!” <note>A reference to Gabriel Barletta, a famously expressive 15th-century Dominican preacher</note>. Burial customs. Michelangelo’s torch. The <term>Patarines <note>original: "Paterini"—a religious movement often viewed as heretical by the Church</note></term>. The “Black Company.”

The religion of the thirteenth-century Florentines was simple humanism. The blending of the various strands of human life that formed the Tuscan race also produced a spirituality that inspired men and women with vigorous devotional feelings.

A people so notable for their sharp minds and physical vigor could not help but be strongly influenced by religious instincts. As they were essentially practical in all matters concerning human progress, the Florentines were ready to adopt any spiritual truths that resonated with them.

Along with a simple trust in the widely accepted traditions of their people and land, there was a firm adherence to Greek ideals and Roman methods.

<header>THE RELIGION OF THE GUILDS</header>

In the days when the law of might was superior to the law of right, and when households were broken up and men became fugitives, the scattered remnants of a warlike people held on to all they knew of noble aims, energetic will, and effective achievement. Into their personalities entered the characteristics of Dante’s three strange animals—the nimble panther, the proud lion, and the gaunt-looking wolf—representing pleasure, ambition, and greed.1 While the actions of the priesthood were aggressive in most states and cities in the Middle Ages, the religious orders who settled in Florence were remarkable for their reserve and restraint. This characteristic was probably caused by the spirit of freedom that breathed through Tuscany from an early date, which was indeed the guiding influence in all her dominance in later years. Hermit clergy in their cells on hillsides and by riverbanks—the self-denying pioneers of Catholic Rome—played their part nobly in softening and refining the minds and lives of the wild people they lived among. The favorable attitude of the Papacy did much to control and subordinate the passions of the lower classes, and to encourage and foster the goodwill of the ruling citizens. The Pope’s party also became the party of the People and, under the title of <term>Guelphs <note>The political faction in central and northern Italy that supported the Pope against the Holy Roman Emperor</note></term>, stood for liberty and progress. The Church of Rome was regarded as a political government to negotiate with, rather than a spiritual institution to submit to.

Florentines were essentially of a non-theological cast of mind; religious doubts and differences of belief had little or no interest for them. Rome, always wise and able to feel the public pulse and recognize the popular temperament, never infringed upon the liberties of the city. If Popes occasionally launched their <term>interdicts <note>A sentence by the Pope that excludes a person or district from church ceremonies and sacraments</note></term>, they were soon persuaded to remove them and to consult the people’s prejudices and wishes. Meanwhile, they profited significantly from the wise industrial enterprise and far-reaching commercial policy of their followers.

It goes without saying that the Florentines were emotional—the
