The Greek and Etruscan heritage in their blood provided this characteristic, just as clearly as Roman and German reserve shaped their stoicism. There was much of the Greek spirit in the expression of their religious feelings. Beautiful forms, fine features, and graceful movements were always held in deep reverence. Simplicity, naturalness, and grace marked both their public functions and their private devotions.

The singing boys and girls of Luca Della Robbia’s *Cantoria* <note>The "Singing Gallery" sculpted for the Florence Cathedral</note>, along with the trio of "Davids"—Donatello’s goatherd, Verrocchio’s city apprentice, and Buonarroti’s <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti</note> young giant-hero—preserve the handsome types of youth from those days. Masaccio, Ghirlandaio, and Botticelli have captured, with their rare pigments, the features of the men and women who worshipped God and honored the ideal of perfect manhood.

Saint John the Baptist <note>San Giovanni Battista; specifically the Baptistery of Florence</note> was the earliest center of the religious life of Florence. There, in the midst of the stalls and carts of market people—with business being conducted almost within the sacred doors—stood the venerable temple of God. Like the heart in a human body, it was sanctified by the baptisms, first vows, earliest Masses, marriages, and funeral rites of the entire population.^1

The black and white beans, respectively, registered a person simultaneously as a child of God and a citizen of the Commune. Prayer and commerce were close companions, joined together in every contract and statute just as they were in every church ceremony and civic festival.

Candles were burned there as well—not merely for meaningless show or lighting, but as a practical way of making arrangements with heaven.

Catechisms and sermons were taught and preached by priests—who were sons of the people—to their own kin with a freedom and sincerity as profound as the characters of their listeners. Everyone worked as hard at their religious duties as they did in their daily occupations. They believed that, just as they formed groups and companies for industry and commerce—

# THE RELIGION OF THE GUILDS

...just as they prospered through the connection of mutual interest and respect, so too did their association in worship provide comfort and spiritual renewal. The voices of laymen and the performance of lay-led devotions were heard and seen in every sacred building, as people took the time to count their prayer beads and recite their "Our Fathers" <note>original: *Pater-nosters*</note>.

The Monastery and the Church of the Annunciation <note>original: *La Nunziata*</note>, for example, were built by the Servites—an order of working monks founded in 1239 by seven wealthy and noble citizens of Florence. They were in the habit of meeting daily to sing the "Hail Mary" <note>original: *Ave Maria*</note> in the chapel of San Zenobio, which then stood on the site of Giotto’s Bell Tower <note>original: *Campanile*</note>. It is said that their piety and charity were so notable that passers-by in the streets pointed them out as the "Watchers and Servants of Mary" <note>original: *Guardatori e Servi di Maria*</note>. The walls of their sanctuary quickly became covered with votive offerings from people of all walks of life who shared similar passions.

Great as the influence of the "Humble Brethren" <note>original: *Umiliati*</note> was upon the industrial life of the Florentines, it was even more significant in its religious and charitable aspects. Their example and teaching appealed powerfully to all classes of the population. As intellectual equals to merchants and manufacturers, the "Humble Brethren" <note>original: *Umiliati*</note> were also the equals of artisans and laborers in manual skill. They were laymen, and as such—having no special class distinctions—they were in full harmony with the human concerns of their neighbors. They were brothers in labor and, at the same time, fathers in religion.

The "Humble Brethren" <note>original: *Umiliati*</note> demonstrated daily how it was both possible and beneficial to combine hard work and worship. To fear God and to honor fellow men was the foundational principle of this faith. The daily recitation of "The Hours" and various lay devotions in their chapel attracted both masters and workers alike. There was something robust about their way of serving God which agreed perfectly with the instincts of the Florentines.

Very soon, this same spirit of sobriety, morality, and devotion sprang up within groups and families. Churches were visited regularly, and serious men and women joined their hearts...

and soul in the daily religious services <note>original: offices</note>. This was nowhere more remarkable than at the church of Santa Reparata. The clergy, always tactful, understood the spirit of the people and freely admitted them to the choir and the lectern. Huge books of psalms <note>original: psalters</note>, with their large black square notes, were placed at the entrance of the sanctuary so that men and boys could stand around and join their voices with the clerical recitations. This excellent practice was continued in the new church of Santa Maria del Fiore, and even today, it is still considered a special and highly valued privilege by the respectable men of the city.

The example set by the "**Humble Brethren**" <note>original: *Umiliati*</note> had an equally admirable effect on the charitable instincts of the people they lived among. Their ready sympathy for every kind of suffering and misfortune, their loving care for children and the elderly, and their own self-denying lives won the affection and imitation of everyone they encountered. The thirteenth-century Florentines were almost brutally intolerant of mere overly sentimental or weak-spirited charity <note>original: mawkish sentiment and maudlin ministration</note>; instead, they were deeply moved by everything that was manly and noble. A high-minded piety and a thoughtful approach to charity became the guiding lights for their lives and work.

Florentines shared with all other Catholics a profound devotion to the Madonna, honoring her through many different titles. Early art had established her personality and power in both the minds and the sight of her followers. For example, the entire city celebrated a holiday when Cimabue’s famous painting was ceremoniously escorted through the streets to its place in the Rucellai Chapel in the church of Santa Maria Novella.

Saint Mary of Cigoli <note>original: Santa Maria di Cigoli</note>, near San Miniato al Monte; Saint Mary of the Woods <note>original: Santa Maria della Selva</note>; Saint Mary of Springtime in Fiesole <note>original: Santa Maria Primavera di Fiesole</note>; Saint Mary of Impruneta <note>original: Santa Maria dell’ Impruneta</note>; and Saint Mary of the Oratory of Saint Michael <note>original: Santa Maria dell’ Or San Michele</note> were all, in turn—and often simultaneously—the objects of enthusiastic devotion.

enterprise, and were accustomed to crowd around the altar of their favorite Madonna to seek her patronage and aid.

The little chapel of *Santa Maria alle Grazie*, located on the bridge of that same name, was crowded with worshippers every day. The sanctuary was so small that the candles offered on one day had to be removed to make room for the next day's offerings.

Perhaps the most famous Madonna of them all was that of "**Impruneta**." During the early years of the sixteenth century, in times of political excitement, the "**Black Madonna**"—as she was also called—was carried from her shrine along the seven miles of road to the *Porta Romana*. She was accompanied by immense crowds of clergy and citizens, with mounted guards provided by the Seven Greater Guilds. At the Gate, she was taken into the care of the monks of *Santa Trinita* <note>Holy Trinity</note>, who carried her in a solemn procession and placed her upon a throne in the center of the *Duomo* <note>Cathedral</note>. There she remained until the social unrest had subsided, and where she received the respectful visits of thousands of residents. 

Her special role <note>original: prerogative</note> was the calming of popular passion and the peaceful administration of the city. Consequently, it became a rule to bring the Madonna into the cathedral before each election of the *Signoria* <note>the governing council of Florence</note>, "so that God may give us good and wise leaders."¹ The "Madonna of Impruneta" was also believed to have the power of healing the sick, curing those wounded in battle, and driving away evil spirits. The road leading up to her shrine was traveled daily by groups of Guild members seeking a <term>healing</term> <note>original: guerison</note> or offering a gift of thanks.

Next to the worship of the Madonna came, oddly enough, irregular devotions to the least authentic and most obscure figures in the calendar of saints. Florentines cared little about the Pope's official approval <note>original: Papal *imprimatur*</note> in such matters; when they felt like it, they simply dubbed this or that individual a "Blessed Soul!" <note>original: "Beatitude!"</note>

The "**Humble Brethren**" <note>original: *Umiliati*</note> naturally produced many saintly figures who were great in both prayer and hard work. Among these was San Gherardino di Villamagna—a popular monk who taught in the wool shops; and

San Barduccio—a virtuous wool-carder who simply did his duty to God and to man.

The portraits and features of such blessed examples of industrial excellence, reproduced by "Masters in Wood and Stone" <note>sculptors and architects</note>, or in metal and paint, were always depicted with the halo of sainthood.

Every family had its patron saint, following the example of the patrons of the guilds. These were often obscure citizens who were the founders of the family’s name and reputation. They were honored with a form of ancestor worship through the annual commemoration of their worthy lives and meritorious deaths.

The peasants of Marignolle canonized a blind poet whose verses had enchanted them, as well as a poor village girl who had lost her belt and her purse and found them in answer to fervent prayer. At the graves of people such as these, their relatives and friends burned candles and sang litanies. These rural traditions spread far and wide, and almost every village had its cottage chapel, its orchard shrine, or its roadside votive offering <note>original: *ex voto*</note>. These devotees were mockingly called "candle-spikers" <note>original: *spigolistri*</note> and "breast-beaters" <note>original: *picchiapetti*</note> by the profane, who regarded them all as hypocrites!

These devotions did not only affect the peasantry and the poorer townspeople; they also spread their charm over the residents of many country villas—the homes of wealthy Florentines. At Montebuoni lived the Buondelmonti, the Gherardini, the Fenzi, and the Machiavelli families; at Signa dwelt the Alberti, the Altoviti, the Morelli, the Cavalcanti, the Pitti-Leparelli, the Passerini, and other rich merchant princes.

The Medici villa was at Poggio a Caiano; the Strozzi and the Borgherini families had country houses at Bellosguardo; and at Peretola lived the Panciatichi and the Vespucci. The Capponi, the Nerli, the Gianfigliazzi, and the Sacchetti were at Marignolle; and at Legnaia—where the best vegetables sold in the Old Market <note>original: *Mercato Vecchio*</note> were grown—resided the Rinuccini, the Caducci, the Artinini, and others. All these families, and many others as well, have left magnificent evidence of their pious devotion and noble charity.

...in frescoed churches and sculptured cloisters—which were also witnesses to the wealth and influence of the Guilds.

The Certosa di Val d'Ema <note>a Carthusian monastery near Florence</note> especially attracted members of the Guilds. Some were old and approaching death, while others were in the prime of life; however, all were weary of the stress and turmoil of commerce and industry. Yearning for quiet, they sought the peace of God within those silent courtyards through acts of self-humiliation. You can see what those craftsmen looked like in real life by observing their features, characteristically sculpted in glazed terra-cotta busts by Giovanni Della Robbia on the walls of the cloister. The Acciaiuoli family has left a significant legacy at the Certosa. Niccolò Acciaiuoli endowed the monastery and dedicated it to Saint Lawrence, the patron of his Guild, and bequeathed his precious marbles, paintings, and bronzes to it.

At times, a somber mood affected both the rich and the poor in the city and its suburbs. Men and women adopted monastic clothing <note>the habit</note> and walked with downcast heads while reciting pious phrases. At home, they spent their free time praying and repeatedly making the sign of the cross to keep their solitary hours virtuous. They called one another "Brother" and "Sister" and spoke of the society to which they belonged as "The Apostles of the Lord."

Sacchetti and writers like him did not spare these gloomy religious enthusiasts; both he and Boccaccio nicknamed them "*Buonapostoli*" <note>original: "Good Apostles"</note>—suggesting they were "good" only in the sense that they showed as much of the "old Adam" <note>human sinfulness or original sin</note> in their daily lives as anyone else!¹ To call them hypocrites might perhaps be too harsh, but at the very least, they were almost the only individuals in Florentine history whose beliefs and practices could truthfully be described as "cant" <term>hypocritical or sanctimonious talk</term>.

Both sanctimony and bigotry were distasteful to the Florentines of old. They were far too sincere and straightforward in character to tolerate anything that favored superficial religious respectability or professionalized piety.

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

Days of religious obligation were strictly observed in old Florence. Church authorities precisely defined not only the individual duties of citizens regarding attendance at Mass and other services, but they also instructed members of the Guilds to visit the churches as a collective body.¹

On holy days, no public business of any kind was permitted between early Mass and Vespers <note>evening prayer services</note>. Times of fasting and abstinence were marked by a total halt to labor and the closing of workshops and market stalls.

Drivers of carts and other vehicles, as well as mule and horse teamsters, were forbidden from transporting merchandise or working their animals. <term>Farriers</term> <note>blacksmiths who shoe horses</note> were allowed to shoe horses and mules under exceptional circumstances, but they were forbidden from forging iron. Cattle and horses could receive medical treatment, and naturally, there were no restrictions on feeding and watering livestock.

Haberdashers, tailors, shoemakers, cobblers, pork butchers, cattle slaughterers, and retail cloth dealers were specifically warned to keep their businesses strictly closed all day. <term>Quacks</term> <note>original: "Cuirmadori"</note>—charlatans of all kinds—were penalized for taking money during prohibited hours.

The <term>wickets</term> <note>original: "Sportelli"</note> of the apothecaries (for selling medicines) and of the retail butchers (for selling fresh meat and fish) were allowed to be partially open. The stalls of poulterers and game dealers, along with those of certain fresh pork sellers, were permitted to be half-open between Mass and Vespers. “<term>To keep the shop half-open</term>” <note>original: "Stare a sportello"</note> and “<term>My shop is only half-open today</term>” <note>original: "La mia bottega sta a sportello oggi"</note> were common sayings regarding days of obligation.

Bakers, sellers of macaroni and vegetables, and fishmongers were permitted to hawk their goods in public places without restrictions all year round. Millers were allowed to work on days of obligation when it was necessary for public convenience—but only behind closed doors—and they were forbidden from delivering flour.

...open for the sale of religious objects and *votive* images <note>original: "ex voto"; offerings given in fulfillment of a religious vow</note>, but on no account were they to sell other goods or candles for secular purposes.

Chestnut roasters, while not allowed to roast them in public, could do so at home, and they were permitted to offer them for sale between Mass and Vespers <note>the evening prayer service</note>. Hawkers of small objects could not sell their wares by stealth during prohibited hours; if caught secretly bartering, they were thrown into prison and their goods were confiscated.

Doctors, surgeons, and barbers were required to stay indoors on holy days and fast days, and were strictly forbidden from seeking patients or clients in the streets. Taverns and inns that sold food and drink were kept closed until midday. Domestic servants, except for those of color <note>a reference to the historical presence of enslaved or servant people of African or Eastern descent in Renaissance Italy</note>, were free after Vespers; masters and mistresses were urged to provide opportunities for their dependents to attend Mass.¹

The churches were the homes of the people, for no city could boast so many that were both beautiful and expressive of personal devotion. The Republican sentiments of the population—rich and poor alike—were nowhere so evident. In every group of kneeling worshippers at Mass, or in any congregation listening to the impassioned words of a preaching friar, the noble, the merchant, the tradesman, the artisan, the peasant, and the beggar knelt and stood shoulder to shoulder, each as the peer of the other. Religious equality was always a hallmark of Florentine citizenship.

Free thought was undoubtedly permitted in Florence, and it existed to such a degree that the Academy of Florence raised Platonic philosophy to a position of high honor in the religious hierarchy of the State. The officers of the Guilds—men of culture, merchant princes, and successful businessmen—generally embraced the spirit of theological inquiry. No gathering or reunion of such persons was complete without a debate in which Christianity and Paganism each had their supporters.²

Yet it is clear, from a careful study of the writings of men such as Leonardo da Vinci, Leon Battista Alberti, Francesco Guicciardini, and many others, that pure skepticism was far from the minds of those quick-witted creators of Florence.

The depth and strength of the commercial and industrial classes' commitment to the faith of the Church is shown by the abundance of shrines and religious objects in the streets and squares.

Many still have hanging lamps where the devotions of a religious people once flickered. These objects are not merely the crude products of poorly skilled peddlers; they are masterpieces <note>original: "chefs d’œuvre"</note> by masters of stone, wood, iron, and terracotta.

Nevertheless, the people of the Renaissance were significantly influenced by a pagan spirit, for many came to regard Christianity as a guide for private morality rather than a controlling power over public or corporate life. Machiavelli emphasizes this repeatedly in *The Prince* and *The Discourses*.

### THE RELIGION OF THE GUILDS

The phrase originally spoken by Gino Capponi—"those who love their country more than the salvation of their souls are wise"—was often on his lips. He also vividly contrasted the power that ancient religious rites had over the lives and characters of the Romans with the weakness of the Papal authority <note>original: "the Keys," referring to the Keys of Saint Peter, the symbol of the Papacy</note> over the morals and intellect of the Florentines of his day. This wavering between so-called Christian morality and political necessity was a danger and a deception in the lives of many prominent Florentines.

There was also a striking mixture of the serious and the worldly in the religious observances of the citizens. If they went, as was their custom, on the first Sunday of every month to say their prayers and recite the Rosary <note>original: "count their beads"</note> at San Gallo—located just beyond the city gate—it was so that the craftsmen and their friends could spend a merry afternoon and evening eating, playing, dancing, and courting!

The Feast of the Epiphany—or "*Befana*" as they called it, named after the doll carried about on the Eve—provided both religious services and pleasant entertainment. Every house, workshop, convent, and church had its Christ Child figure <term>Bambino: an artistic representation of the infant Jesus</term>, which was sometimes beautifully dressed by artists. During the day, every child carried their sacred doll around, exhibiting it in fierce competition with others. At dusk, these figures were placed on window sills or in doorways, flanked by burning candles and brightly painted paper lanterns. Pageants and processions of the Three Holy Kings passed through the streets while "Bethlehems" <note>nativity scenes</note> were decorated at the Altars of the Nativity. These were visited by merchants and artisans, nobles and commoners, young and old, as if on a solemn pilgrimage.

The first of May was the "Feast of Love." After hearing Mass and making offerings at the Shrines of Orsanmichele <note>original: "Or San Michele"</note> and the Basilica of the Annunciation <note>original: "La Nunziata"</note>, apprentices and their sweethearts headed for the hills and woods to spend the day in romantic games.

<header>->THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-</header>

Many city boys won their country girls, but many were also jilted on that bitter-sweet May Day!

The choice of a young man or woman was heatedly debated within the family circle, because for the Florentines, marriage was as much a business contract as it was a union of hearts. Florentine mothers were frequently engaged in match-making. Alessandra Machinghi degli Strozzi used to go to Mass every morning at Santa Maria del Fiore <note>The Cathedral of Saint Mary of the Flower, also known as the Duomo.</note> to get a good look at the girls her son Filippo admired; she would return with critical remarks, which she urged him to take seriously. While a good figure and a pretty face went a long way toward winning a mother's approval, even more decisive factors were family influence and financial resources.¹

Superstition—which is what the occult science of nature was called—played a significant and visible role in both the individual lives and the collective activities of the Florentines.

Mars—the earliest patron of the city’s destiny—had devoted followers in every social class, despite being replaced by Saint John the Baptist <note>original: "Saint Giovanni Battista"</note>. For years, his statue adorned the temple on the Citadel; later, what remained of it after the barbarian invasions was placed upon the Ponte Vecchio <note>The "Old Bridge" in Florence.</note>. While his damaged statue looked out over the rushing river below, Florence was triumphant. His destruction, however, was believed to bring unheard-of woes upon the city. So, when the disastrous flood of 1337 finally occurred—claiming almost all of Florence as its victim and carrying away both the bridge and the *Palladium* <term>Palladium: a sacred object or statue believed to provide protection to a city or nation.</term> together—loud lamentations arose to appease a vengeful God.

The attributes of the warrior god—his strength, his boldness, and his victory—were transferred to the peaceful Forerunner <note>Saint John the Baptist.</note>, whose character included the saintly virtues of the Gospel. Monastic tradition and popular imagination, which enjoyed blending similar personalities, linked Saint Sebastian to Apollo, Saint Mary to Venus, and turned Mercury into the valiant Saint George.

Every unusual event was exaggerated and attributed to supernatural influences; for instance, a comet in the sky was seen as an omen of war and blood—

shed; lights shooting across the sky at night like falling stars signaled personal danger to distinguished men; thunder under a clear moon threatened business and trade; the fall of a monument or a piece of masonry pointed to family troubles, and so forth.

No one was in the least surprised, when Lorenzo de' Medici died, to hear that his votive wax statue in the church of the Annunziata <note>original: "La Nunziata"</note> had fallen and shattered into pieces. The news spread quickly from person to person: "The votive image has fallen in the Most Holy Annunziata!" <note>original: "Boto, caduto in Santissima Nunziata!"</note> and some added, "May God pardon him," "Rest his soul," and "The price of wax will rise!"—referring, no doubt, to the grand funeral ceremonies that would follow for the departed prince.

The folklore of the Florentines included ghosts, witches, spells, and werewolves; but many of their so-called superstitions were harmless and even childish. If a woman, for example, lost her cat, her best remedy was to burn a candle to the Madonna—preferably at the church of Or San Michele. If a man could not avoid starting a new business venture or making a deal on a Friday, he was careful to slip into the nearest church to say a hurried "Our Father" <note>original: "Pater-noster"</note>.

Green was regarded as the color of the "unspeakable Turk" <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire, then seen as a major threat to Christendom.</note> and even suggested the pale color of Hell <note>original: "Inferno"</note>; consequently, no self-respecting citizen would willingly wear clothes dyed that color, although it was considered acceptable for a hood or cap.

A person's lost sanity could be recovered by placing the miter of Saint Zenobius—the holy Bishop of Florence in the fifth century, whose memory was and still is highly respected—on the head of the unfortunate individual. Another certain cure was to dress a deranged person in the cloak of Saint Giovanni Gualberti, the Abbot of San Miniato who died in 1073. The miracles performed by these two blessed patrons of Florence provided Ghiberti, Ghirlandaio, and Benedetto da Rovezzano with subjects for their artwork.

> "In the Name of the Father—Shadrach; ✠ In the Name of the Son—Meshach; ✠ In the Name of the Spirit—Abednego." ¹ <note>The original text uses "Adenago," an archaic variant of Abednego, one of the three men in the fiery furnace from the Book of Daniel.</note>

Any uncanny or unusual noise sent both young and old in search of holy water, with which to sprinkle the area and thus exorcise the disturbing spirit. If a murderer could, without being moved, eat his supper while sitting on the body of his victims, he was excused from execution.

Strange views were held regarding the cure for ailments: for example, jumping three times over a skein of boiled twine, and rubbing a person with oil dripping from the framework of church bells, were considered effective remedies and were very commonly practiced!

Poorer Florentine mothers also had a superstitious dread of children having clean hands and feet! The more dirt the little toddlers acquired while grubbing in the gutter, the more likely they were to escape illness and death. When washing became absolutely necessary, it was followed by visits to the shrine of a favorite Madonna, where a "Hail Mary" <note>original: "Ave"</note> was said to avert the evil consequences of such unavoidable cleanliness!

The cult of the Evil Eye was followed by all classes of the community, but sometimes the hasty gesture of the pointing fingers <note>Likely referring to the *mano cornuta* or "horned hand," a gesture intended to ward off bad luck or the Evil Eye.</note> led to retaliation with a knife or stone! No people were quicker to resent an imagined insult than the laborers in the markets and streets of Florence. Any leading citizen whose name came to be even accidentally associated with the city’s misfortunes, or with personal and party suffering, was always a target for the "pointing finger and the cross." Sometimes the superstition held true against every member of his family. Thus the Soderini—Niccolò, Lorenzo, and Piero—were regarded with suspicion and aversion. This custom likely originated in the general fear and contempt of the Jewish people. Regardless, no one would think of passing through the Ghetto—the Jewish district adjoining the Old Market <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note>—without making the protective sign.

Everyone wore a little crooked horn made of brass, bone, or coral suspended around the neck by a silken or woollen cord. They were accustomed to touch this horn if any "evil shadow" seemed about to cross their path. This token was often accompanied by a small silken or cotton bag called a "*Breve*," which frequently contained nothing more than harmless powder! Conjurers and charlatans readily sold such charms to their simple-minded audiences. "Wear this next to your breast," they said, "and it will help you in danger and in love." Many a young woman took her "*Breve*" to her confessor to obtain the blessing of the Church upon her destiny.

The course of human life was regarded largely as an experience of the inevitable. The Florentines considered that man was born primarily to reproduce his kind, and secondarily to resign his offspring absolutely to the mercies—tender or otherwise—of the overruling powers.

Having twenty or more children was considered a perfectly natural condition of family life. If the children lived to maturity, the parents fervently exclaimed:

> "Heaven be praised"; and, if they died in childhood, they sanctimoniously declared: "Yes, and for everything, heaven be praised. Amen!" <note>G. Biagi, p. 57.</note>

This fatalistic tendency also showed itself in their dealings with aged and distressed dependents. Gregorio Dati, in his "Secret Book" <note>original: "Libro Segreto"</note>, writes about the epidemic of 1426:

> "The pestilence was in our house. It began with our manservant Piccino; within three days, our slave Martha died. On the first of April, my daughter Sandra died, and on the fifth, Antonia. We left the house and moved into the one opposite. In a few days, Veronica died. Again we moved, and went to live in Via Chiara. Here Vandecca and Pippa were taken ill, and, on the first of August, both went to heaven. They all died of the plague. Heaven help them!"

In a letter written in the same hand a few months later we read: "Piero is still alive, so he must endure it and go beg. It would be best, of course, if heaven would take him!"

Religious people were everywhere—indeed, they occasionally made up an unusually large part of the entire population. In the beginning of the sixteenth century—the "Golden Age of Florence"—there were more than one hundred monasteries and convents, with perhaps thousands of residents, in addition to the large number of secular clergy <term>secular clergy: priests who work in the world among the people rather than in a monastic order</term> who served the parish churches.

The high-ranking clergy—from the Archbishop down to the youngest priests—were, as a rule, members of prominent Florentine families. The noblest citizens willingly gave up their sons for the work of the priesthood. There was always a certain amount of resentment expressed against foreign clergy, and the men admitted to Holy Orders were, as a rule, motivated by patriotic and popular goals. "Florence first" <note>original: "Firenze la prima"</note> was their motto. This positive state of religious affairs encouraged nothing but good in the interactions between the Altar and the Home.

The Council of Florence, held in the Duomo <note>The Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore</note> in 1439, was notable not only for the prestige of the people attending its discussions and the agreement of its decisions, but also for the deep respect and sympathy of the general public. Perhaps this was due to two causes: the popular elements within the structure of the Council, and the fact that merchants and artisans were so busy with their worldly professions that they had little time or desire to study matters of religious doctrine.

There was very little opportunity in Florence for the work of the "Holy Office of the Inquisition." Only one confirmed burning is recorded: that of Giovanni da Montecatini in 1450. Whether the reason for this lack of persecution was found in the certain orthodoxy of the people, or in their absolute indifference to...

Whether this was due to dogmatic questions, no one can say. It is likely that the unspoken policy of the Vatican—to avoid interfering with the religious passion of a population so successful in the worlds of commerce and industry—played a significant role in keeping the city safe from the horrors of the stake <note>Execution by burning for heresy</note>. Only during the period of Savonarola's dominance did ecclesiastical disputes reach a critical and dangerous stage.

Perhaps no movement moved the great heart of Florence as deeply as the arrival of the great preaching friars in the fifteenth century.

->SAVONAROLA PREACHING DURING LENT IN SANTA MARIA DEL FIORE<-

Girolamo Savonarola and his brothers loudly proclaimed, "Jesus Christ is King of Florence!" At the time, the city was suffering under an almost unbearable weight of tyranny, jealousy, and corruption <term>venality: the condition of being open to bribes or bribery</term>. The greed for money, the pride of life, and the pretense of culture were leading men to view commercial integrity, political freedom, and domestic virtue through a distorted lens.

Savonarola fought against the Medici family and their seizures of power with all his energy, preaching tirelessly against the excess of worldly power in high positions. He generally formulated his doctrines as follows:

...as follows: 1. The fear of God in the reform of personal liberty and habits; 2. The love of religion in the submission of everyone; 3. Peace among men and the forgiveness of injuries; and 4. Government based on sound Republican principles.

The eloquence of the famous Friar <note>original: "Frate"</note> created a three-fold division among the population: 
- "*Palleschi*"—named after the balls on the Medici coat of arms (often associated with pawnbrokers)—was the name adopted by the supporters of the Medici.
- "*Frateschi*" or "*Piagnoni*"—translated by the author as "Tears and Treachery" <note>literally "The Weepers"</note>—were the party of Savonarola.
- "*Arrabbiati*"—perhaps "Irreconcilables" <note>literally "The Enraged"</note>—was the name for the general group of opponents.

Florentines loved sermons, but they preferred those that dealt least with religion. Their highly cultured intellects were more attuned to skeptical emotions and sarcastic remarks. At first, Savonarola failed to move them; it was not until he began to use metaphors that they rallied to his preaching. His vehemence and somewhat brusque manner and speech had originally offended them.

The preachers who drew the largest audiences were those who belonged to the school of Gabriele Barletta of Naples, about whom it was said: "No one knows how to preach if he cannot imitate Barletta." His eloquence was fantastic, crude, and extravagant.

Savonarola's doctrines were ridiculed by more profane men. A large number of young men—apprentices, students, and wealthy idlers—banded together to mock the impassioned eloquence of the Friar and his companions. The "*Compagnacci*," as they were dubbed by the populace—meaning "good-for-nothing fellows" <note>literally "Bad Companions"</note>—revived old Bacchanalian revels as a counterpoint to the bands of children sent out to strip citizens of their worldly vanities. They poked fun at the asceticism and self-abasement of the monk's followers. "If," they said, "Savonarola enters the fire, he will undoubtedly be burned; if he refuses to enter it, he will lose all credibility with his followers."$^1$ Marini Sanuto—an observant Venetian of the Savonarola era—

the deceased person’s name, age, and occupation at the Palazzo Vecchio <note>The town hall of Florence</note>. The corpse was first moved to the "Guardamorto" <note>A room for the dead; literally "death-watch"</note> at the corner of the Piazza di San Giovanni, but within eighteen hours, the relatives were obliged to accompany it to the grave.

Mourning colors were brown or dull red, though some people wore the unlucky green. Requiem Masses <note>original: "Mortuary Masses"</note>, held in the presence of the departed, became customary in the thirteenth century. People of all classes were very careful to have the bodies of relatives who died in foreign lands brought home for burial <note>original: "interment"</note>.¹

Notorious criminals and those who had been denied absolution <note>Formal forgiveness of sins by a priest</note> received little respect in death. Their bodies—unwashed and without shrouds—were thrown naked into ditches like dead dogs. The unknown and unclaimed dead found in the city or river were given to the hospitals and to sculptors for anatomical study. It is said that Michelangelo used to study in a room lent to him by his early patrons, the monks of Santo Spirito, with a flaming torch stuck into the chest of a corpse!

Criminals used to be harshly treated, for small offenses no less than for great crimes. Those condemned to death were left to the "tender mercies" of the jailers, and no provision was made for their spiritual needs. Many citizens made efforts to improve <note>original: "ameliorate"</note> these sad conditions, but nothing was actually accomplished until 1361. In that year, twelve young Guildsmen—influenced by a religious enthusiasm that remained as a trace of the "Paterini" <note>A religious movement or sect, sometimes considered heretical, that emphasized poverty and reform</note> influence—went boldly to the Signoria <note>The governing body of Florence</note> and asked for a piece of waste land outside the city, near the Piazza di Santa Croce, where executions were carried out. On this site, they built a chapel where the condemned could hear Mass before ascending the scaffold, and beneath the walls of which their bodies could be decently buried.

## THE PATRONAGE OF THE GUILDS

From the very first rise of Florentine prosperity—when money began to flow into the pockets of her merchants and her craftsmen as smoothly as the waters of the Arno flow under the arches of her bridges—principles of charity guided the hands of generous donors.

Human nature, human needs, and human failings always held a primary place in the Florentine economy. Therefore, it was not only the kind-hearted householder and the sympathetic wife who gave of their wealth in private charity. The Guild members, in their corporate capacity, also gave a portion of their profits. Even the State followed this example, treating generosity as an essential part of its identity, as seen in the word "Liberty" <note>original: "Liberta"</note> inscribed on the shields of the city's leaders.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the patronage provided by Florentine Guilds, shifting from the list of specific chapels and societies to the underlying philosophy of civic and religious duty as articulated by Machiavelli and Guicciardini.</meta>

<page-num>517</page-num>

->THE PATRONAGE OF THE GUILDS<-

Among the maxims of Machiavelli, regarding the duties of religion and charity that fall upon the State, are the following:—

> “Governments,” he says, “that wish to keep themselves free from corruption must, above all else, maintain religious ceremonies in their pure form and always hold them in the highest reverence. Among all the qualities that distinguish a citizen in his country, the most important is being liberal and generous—especially in the construction of public buildings, such as churches, monasteries, and shelters for the poor, the sick, and for travelers.”¹

The Statutes of all the various Guilds, in addition to a formal dedicatory preface, contain in their opening entries lists of pious trusts undertaken by the Guilds. These include explicit directions on how, where, and when appropriate observances are to be performed.

This is quite in keeping with the character of the people of Florence. Although such provisions appear somewhat superficial or even hypocritical to us, they were not viewed that way at all in old Florence.

The close union of religion and work was as natural as it was conventional. It did not represent a mindless obedience to dogma or doctrine; on the contrary, it showed a healthy understanding of spiritual power within the republic of industry.

In the same way, the Florentines of old lacked any sense of "professional Christianity" or fake piety. The Catholic Faith offered everyone a reasonable and practical means of grace that seemed perfectly suited to their needs, their labor, and their rest.

There was a great deal of mutual sincerity as well as a vast amount of individual sympathy in all the religious exercises of those sensible and alert people. Next to the man himself came his usefulness to the State; the love of human progress was the keynote of the religion of Florence.

Lorenzo Guicciardini writes the following:— “Whoever in Florence

...anyone who wishes to be well-liked by the people must avoid a reputation for ambition. As one would expect, the lead in religious projects was taken by the Master Guild—the "<term>Calimala</term>" <note>The Guild of Merchants, Finishers, and Refiners of Foreign Cloth.</note>. When the ancient Basilica of San Miniato al Monte fell into disrepair, it was only natural that an appeal should be made to wealthy citizens to undertake its restoration. This church was originally built in 1013 from the ruins of the third-century Oratory of St. Peter by the Emperor Henry, Queen Cunegonda, and Archbishop Hildebrand. The Guild stepped into the breach, spending both money and labor upon its decoration. In addition to the structural work, Spinello Aretino painted the fresco of Saint Bernard, and Luca Della Robbia installed glazed terra-cotta medallions of the Virtues, all at the Guild's expense.

Dante mentions San Miniato in his "*Purgatorio*":—

> "That steep hill where the chapel stands, 
> Looking grandly down over the Rubaconte." ² <note>The Rubaconte is the old name for the bridge now known as the Ponte alle Grazie.</note>

Many rules in the Statutes of the "<term>Calimala</term>" Guild provide for these works, and even earlier records—dating before 1220—exist which show the devotion of the Merchants of Foreign Cloth to religious interests. The Guild retained the privilege of repairing and guarding San Miniato al Monte until Piero de' Medici took it out of their hands.

The restoration of the Baptistery of San Giovanni—one of the most ancient churches in Florence and originally a Temple of Mars—was undertaken by the "<term>Calimala</term>" Merchants. A new building was completed in 1150, primarily at their expense. "Already," says an early historian, "in the middle of the twelfth century, certain merchants of the Commune gave money to assist..."

# THE PATRONAGE OF THE GUILDS

"...building up the battered old church."¹ In 1451 they erected the façade, and later on, employed the most famous artists of the day to perform the wood-carving and *intarsiatura* <note>wood inlay</note> of the choir.

In 1292, when every citizen of Florence, young and old, was inspired with religious enthusiasm by the miracles performed at the shrine of Or San Michele, the "*Calimala*" Guild—fully in tune with the spirit of thankfulness and generosity then created—undertook once more the repair and the completion of the Baptistery.

Old columns and worn-out stonework were removed and replaced by splendid marbles brought at great cost from the East. Mosaics were started in the tribune by Giacomo da Turrita and continued by Andrea Tafi—the greatest of all the mosaic masters. Much of this elaborate work was done while the feud between the Buondelmonti and Amidei families was at its height.

Andrea Pisano, in 1339, and Lorenzo Ghiberti, in 1452, installed the famous bronze doors which bear their names. Andrea was enrolled as a freeman of Florence as a reward and was admitted into the "*Calimala*" Guild. The latter commission was intended as a thank-offering for the passing of the great plague. The workmanship is characteristic of the intelligence of the people of Florence, for the faces and figures are "the people of Florence" <note>original: "la gente di Firenze"</note> in miniature.

The interior was enriched by costly offerings—the product of the silk loom, goldsmith's tool, sculptor's chisel, and painter's palette—provided in religious competition by "the Merchants of Calimala, the wisest and most powerful in Florence."

Every year, eight days before the Patronal Festival, six <term>Buonomini</term>—or Deputies—were designated by the Consuls to attend the Baptistery on the morning of the Feast. There, they were to receive the offerings made at the Altar of the Saint, in money and goods, by each registered member of the Guild and by well-disposed members of the other Guilds. The Bishop was always careful to remind the Consuls of their duty in this regard, and he frequently joined the *Buonuomini* <term>the "Good Men," a committee of advisors or overseers</term> in person, or appointed his deputy to assist in their sacred duties.¹

In 1341, the Guild, eager to beautify the city and wishing to enlarge the Piazza di San Giovanni, purchased a plot of land near the Archbishop's Palace.² The Consuls had already, in 1338, bought two houses belonging to the Adimari family near San Cristofano; they gave these to the Cathedral Chapter in exchange for the canons' houses near the Archbishop's tower. In 1339, they acquired a third house for the sum of seventy-three gold florins from the brothers and sons of a man named Martellino; the title deeds were drafted by the Guild's notary, Ser Giovanni Ugolino. These several buildings were demolished, and their sites were added to the Piazza, which added much to the dignity of the ancient Baptistery.

The salaries or wages paid to those employed by the Guild for various public works were quite modest. For example, the Superintendent of Works at San Giovanni Battista received only twelve *lire* a year. Payments to builders and others appear to have been made through foremen, who were required to provide accounts of work completed, along with reports on the moral conduct and diligence of those under them. All money was paid according to a fixed scale, with deductions made for any misconduct or negligence.

The Cathedral—originally known as Santa Reparata—had fallen into a state of ruin and desperately needed restoration. Consequently, a decree was issued by the State Council in 1294, which commanded the immediate construction of a new church. Among the instructions given to the architect, Arnolfo di Cambio, was a requirement to design a church "of such magnificence that neither the effort nor the genius of man shall be able to invent anything that shall surpass it."³

The amount raised by the two taxes was completely inadequate. Therefore, the Consuls directed that every factory and shop—both wholesale and retail—connected with the Guilds should place a donation box at all entrances and exits. Visiting merchants, buyers, and strangers in general were invited to deposit offerings into these boxes. Initially, a specific amount was requested—one *denaro* <term>a small silver coin</term> per person. Because of this, the contribution was named the "**Deodenaro**"—"God’s penny." In one year, this produced the significant sum of two thousand gold florins.²

Between 1282 and 1527, the "**Wool Guild**" <note>original: *Arte della Lana*</note> spent a total of four hundred and fifty thousand gold florins (equivalent to £225,000) on the Cathedral of **Santa Maria del Fiore**!

**Savonarola** also lent his influence to the Cathedral Completion Fund. He decreed that all wills, upon reaching probate <term>the legal process of proving a will</term>, must bear a Cathedral stamp costing seventy *soldi* <term>shillings</term>. He allowed no letters of administration <term>legal authority to manage an estate</term> to be granted until this condition had been fulfilled. It is said that this provision remains in force in Florence today.

By a decree of the **Signoria** <term>the governing council of the Florentine Republic</term>, the supervision and maintenance of the Chapel of the Holy Miracle in the Church of **Saint Ambrose** <note>original: *Sant’ Ambrogio*</note> was assigned to the "**Arte de’ Giudice e Notai**"—the "**Judges’ and Notaries’ Guild**." Every year on the Feast of the Holy Miracle, which was celebrated during the octave <term>the eight-day period following a festival</term> of *Corpus Christi* <note>The Body of Christ</note>, the Consuls and officials of the Guild formally attended High Mass and collected the offerings of the members. A type of court was held in the chapel, where any members who had been accused or suspended for minor offenses or breaches of the guild rules were pardoned. At the same time and place, they reviewed the guild's public charitable works and distributed alms to those in need.

# THE PATRONAGE OF THE GUILDS

The Guild was established under the title, "**Chapel of the Guild of Saint Apollinaris**" <note>original: "Cappella dell’ Arte di Sant’ Apollinare"</note>. The Consuls of the Guild assumed legal control of the chapel and the right to nominate a chaplain in the year 1448, when the virtuous Antonino was Archbishop of Florence.

The chapel was originally built and painted at the expense of a man named Bartolomeo, son of Costello di Giacherio, from the parish of Saint Apollinaris. He was a furrier by trade and a member of the Guild. In his will, he requested to be buried in his own vault beneath the Chapel of Saints Bartholomew and Christopher. The chapel was endowed with the proceeds from several pieces of land—including olive groves, orchards, woods, and vineyards—totaling thirty-nine *staiori* <term>an old Italian land measurement</term> (acres). It also included three cottages in the parishes of San Martino da Guigabanda and San Stefano da Calcinaia. <note>1 Manni, “Sigilli,” Inventory made 1589.</note>

The chaplain, or rector, was required to celebrate a weekly Mass and a High Mass on the Feast of Saint Bartholomew for the eternal rest of the pious founder's soul. This provision was still being faithfully observed in both 1636 and 1663, as certified by the chapel’s registrars at those times. The Guild’s coat of arms was displayed over the chapel and was also carved onto the facade of the church.

At **La Nunziata** <note>The Basilica of the Santissima Annunziata in Florence</note>, the chapels included those belonging to the "**Shoemakers’ Guild**" <note>original: "Arte de’ Calzolai"</note> and the subordinate "**Painters’ Guild**" <note>original: "Arte de’ Pittori"</note>, also known as the "**Society of Saint Luke**." The latter featured frescoes painted by **Vasari** and **Pontormo**. Furthermore, wealthy guild members donated countless artistic treasures to the church—magnificent works by **Andrea del Sarto**, **Ghirlandaio**, **San Gallo**, **Alesso Baldovinetti**, the **Rossellini**, **Giovanni da Bologna**, **Perugino**, and **Bandinelli**.

The "**Company of Saint Joseph**" <note>original: "Compagnia di San Giuseppe"</note> was a religious fraternity for members of the "**Carpenters’ Guild**" <note>original: "Arte de’ Legnaiuoli"</note>. It was founded during the era of the **Duke of Athens**, when he sought to gain supporters from the Lesser Guilds. # THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

The headquarters for the relief of distressed carpenters was nearby, in the old palace of the Carnesecchi family.<sup>1</sup>

Almost all the trade associations and industrial companies subordinate to the official Guilds had their own religious confraternities. These organizations had their specific patron saints, altars, and sacred rituals, which were typically combined with offices for administering charity and promoting art.

In 1300, the “Society of Dyers” owned a church, a guild house, and a hospital on the Via de’ Malcontenti, at the site where the Capuchin monastery was more recently located. Their coat of arms can still be seen on the front of the building.

The example set by the Florentine guild members and trade unionists regarding religious and charitable practices was enthusiastically followed by various groups of foreign workmen. These laborers flocked to Florence from every European country and settled down with their wives and families, or else married Florentine women and established new households.

At the Church of the Annunziata <note>La Nunziata</note>, the companies of Flemish and German artisans had their own altar dedicated to Saint Barbara. There, they gathered for daily and weekly Masses, prayed the rosary <term>told their beads</term>, and made their confessions. At Santo Spirito, the merchants and artisans from Lorraine <note>a region in modern-day France</note> had a chapel in the sacristy of the church, which was dedicated to Saint Felix <note>San Felice</note>. They also maintained a separate burial ground within the sacred precincts.

Among the minor associations was the “Society of Lombard Cooks.” They enjoyed many privileges, both religious <term>sacred</term> and secular <term>profane</term>. They were accustomed to reciting their daily prayers <term>their hours</term> first in San Piero del Mugnone on the Via San Gallo; however, they later moved their devotions to a chapel within the church of their patron saint, San Carlo <note>Saint Charles Borromeo</note>, in the Piazza d’Orsanmichele <note>Piazza del Or San Michele</note>.

# THE PATRONAGE OF THE GUILDS

They established religious confraternities and founded chapels and altars in various town churches. These were almost always dedicated to Saint John the Baptist; everywhere, traders, agents, and workers gathered periodically for religious exercises and wise counsel in the local chapel dedicated to the saint.

The devotional corporate life of the guilds centered on the guild shrine of Or San Michele <note>San Michele in Orto</note>. The very name reveals its origin—the "Garden Chapel"—for, as far back as the eighth century, holy monks from Lombardy dedicated a small church to the patron of their country, the Archangel Michael, and planted trees around it. Rebuilt around the year 1000 and established as a parish church for the expansion of the city between Santa Reparata and the river, the garden was still preserved and tended by Cistercian fathers. A square <term>piazza</term> was formed by the Uberti, Abati, Cavalcanti, Caponsacchi, Macci, and other rising families who built their houses around the church.

Despite the encouragement of the popes—especially Innocent III and Innocent IV—the venerable building fell into great disrepair. This reached such a state that, in 1249, the city government <term>Signoria</term> signaled its intention to demolish it. This was carried out in 1284; because of the lack of space in the Old Market <term>Mercato Vecchio</term> for hay and grain dealers, it was decided to build an open-sided gallery <term>loggia</term> in the middle of the square to serve as a grain market.

Arnolfo di Cambio was commissioned to provide a plan, which he did; he also undertook the construction of the Church of San Carlo di Mercato to replace the older shrine. Arnolfo’s work was destroyed by fire in 1304. The new market gallery was opened in 1317, with Taddeo Gaddi serving as the architect. He worked with the best kind of high-quality sandstone <term>pietra forte</term> <note>original: "pietra forte", literally "strong stone"</note>. He and his assistants were placed under the special supervision of the "Por Santa Maria"—the Guild of Silk.

Formally moved to an alcove under the gallery <term>loggia</term> and fixed to one of the supporting pillars <term>pilasters</term>, the Sacred Picture continued to carry out its beneficial mission until it became a daily object of devotion for great numbers of pilgrims.

The devotion to the *Madonna of the Garden* <note>original: "Madonna del Orto"</note> grew so significantly that in 1291 a Confraternity was founded, which included many members of the Greater Guilds and other influential citizens. They called themselves “*The Company of Or San Michele*” <note>original: "La Compagnia del Or San Michele"</note>—but were more familiarly known as “*The Company of the Pillar*” <note>original: "La Compagnia del Pilastro"</note>.

The Statutes of the Company contained forty chapters, which were mainly concerned with the collection and use of the offerings from pilgrims. These consisted of many objects of value, as well as goods and votive wax images. A Notary was in constant attendance to record the names of visitors, enter the amounts of their donations, and chronicle the results of their religious devotions. He also enrolled the names of new associates of the Company and kept a list of those who, when dying, desired the prayers of the faithful.

Every day “Lauds” were sung by the lay brothers, who attended in rotation <term>rota</term>, which led to a new name for the Company: “*The Singers of Saint Mary*” <note>original: "Laudesi di Santa Maria"</note>. Formal speeches <term>allocutions</term> were constantly delivered by the brothers to groups of worshippers, counseling piety and charity; personal visits were also made to the bedsides of the elderly, the crippled, and the dying. Processions of the brothers were held every year to the Churches of Santa Croce, Santa Maria Novella, San Marco, San Spirito, del Carmine, and La Nunziata, where litanies and hymns were sung. The streets through which they passed were decorated and crowded with shared devotion from spectators.

Undoubtedly, the greatest glory of the “Company of Or San Michele” was the generosity of its charities, which benefited not only the residents of the city but also those who lived far away in the rural districts <term>contado</term> and beyond.

Hymns were sung simultaneously, and those who came to buy and those who sold alike left their offerings. Thus, into the intense commercial life of the Florentines entered a new and enthusiastic spirit—that of tireless piety. The offerings in money received in 1348 reached the massive sum of three hundred and fifty thousand gold florins <term>the standard gold currency of Florence</term>.

In 1350, a staff of priests was assigned to the Oratory, where they performed daily Masses at the church's altars. Nine years later, the church was decorated with the exquisite Tabernacle by Orcagna <note>Andrea di Cione, a celebrated Florentine painter, sculptor, and architect.</note>. The ancient records state that, "the members of the 'Confraternity of Or San Michele,' having accumulated very great wealth, decided to build a tabernacle for the Madonna."

By an ancient decree of the State Council, it was mandated that all property bequeathed to hospitals had to be sold within two years, and its value devoted to pious causes. Failure to follow this law caused the inheritance to pass to the "Confraternity of Or San Michele." <note>Varchi, *Storia fiorentina*, Book II, page 109.</note>

At one time, the annual income of the Confraternity amounted to eighteen thousand gold florins from estates directly inherited or forfeited, and seven thousand gold florins from other sources. During the devastation of the plague in the middle of the fourteenth century, legacies and gifts produced, in a single year, the sum of one hundred and twenty-five thousand gold florins. <note>Scipione Ammirato, *Istorie fiorentine*, Book I, page 373.</note>

The greatest respect and reverence was paid not only to the Shrine but to its surroundings. The tethering of donkeys, pack animals, and cattle under the Loggia <term>an open-sided gallery</term> or by the columns, or anywhere near the building, was punished with fines of forty *soldi* <term>Florentine silver coins</term>. No trash or merchandise was allowed to be left within the sacred area under penalty of similar fines. <note>Regulation 252 of the 1415 Statutes.</note>

The first united action by the Guilds regarding Or San Michele took place in the year 1406. The building, which was rectangular in shape, had niches built into its exterior walls. Inside one of these, the "Guild of Silk" obtained permission to erect a marble statue of their patron saint—Saint John the Evangelist. In fact, the statue was never completed.

...and was not installed until two hundred years had passed, when Baccio da Montelupo, a pupil of Michelangelo, finished it.

The application of the "Silk Guild," however, roused the Consuls of the other Guilds, and they secured from the Signoria <term>the governing council of the Republic of Florence</term> the right to regard the building as the exclusive property of the Guilds of Florence.

Each Guild—both major and minor—offered to provide a statue for the exterior and a painting for the interior. At the same time, the members of each Guild bound themselves to make an annual collection on the festival of their Patron Saints; this money was to be handed over to the "Company of Or San Michele" for distribution among the poor and the sick. As a sign of ownership, the Consuls of the Guild were pledged to receive a visit from the Signoria once a year on Michaelmas Day <term>September 29th</term>, and then and there to toast them with offerings of wine—newly made and blessed.

The "Calimala Guild" <term>The Guild of Cloth Finishers and Merchants in foreign cloth</term>—always at the forefront of good works—commissioned Lorenzo Ghiberti in 1406 to sculpt their Patron Saint, Saint John the Baptist. In 1428, it was placed in its niche, being the first statue actually installed in position.

The "Wool Guild," following their example that same year, placed a bronze figure of Saint Stephen—also by Ghiberti—in the third niche on the west side. The first niche on the south side, belonging to the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries," was the most richly decorated of them all. Simone da Fiesole sculpted the coat of arms of the Guild—the Madonna and Child—within a lavish framework of statuettes. This statue was subsequently removed twice: once in 1493, after a fanatical Jewish man threw a stone at it, and again during the reign of Grand Duke Ferdinand, because a rumor spread that it possessed miraculous powers, and crowds were drawn to worship at the new shrine.

The "Guild of Furriers and Skinners" had Saint James as their patron, and Nanni di Banco or Niccolò d’Arezzo was commissioned to create the statue. The third niche was occupied by Saint Mark, a work by Donatello commissioned in 1411 by the

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

The "Guild of Retail Cloth-dealers and Linen Merchants" commissioned their statue and set it up in 1430.

On the western front of the church, the statue of Saint Eligius—the patron of the "Guild of Blacksmiths"—sculpted by Nanni di Banco, was installed in 1431. The next position was originally assigned to Saint Lawrence, the patron of the "Guild of Bakers." However, because their funds ran low, they yielded their niche to the "Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers." In 1419, this guild employed Michelozzo Michelozzi to create a statue of Saint Matthew; in 1422, Lorenzo Ghiberti became his partner in the work.

Undoubtedly the finest statue of the entire series, and one of the masterpieces <note>original: "chefs d’œuvre"</note> of the Renaissance, was located on the north side: Saint George. It was sculpted by Donatello in 1416 for the "Guild of Armorers and Sword-Makers." This splendid figure perfectly preserves all the physical attributes of a manly young Florentine—alert, serious, strong, and virtuous. When Michelangelo saw it, he exclaimed in delight, "Walk!" <note>original: "Cammina!"—the OCR "Communa" is a transcription error for the famous anecdote where Michelangelo told the lifelike statue to "March" or "Walk."</note>.

The "Guild of Masters in Stone and Wood" erected a group of four sculptors martyred under Diocletian <note>Known as the "Four Crowned Martyrs" (Santi Quattro Coronati)</note> in the next niche between 1417 and 1420. Nanni di Banco carved them, but Donatello adapted them to fit into their designated spaces.

"Saint Philip," who comes next, was also sculpted by Nanni di Banco. He was commissioned by the "Guild of Hosiers"—an ambitious corporation that was not included in the primary hierarchy of the twenty-one guilds. In 1408, the Guild of Butchers commissioned their patron, Saint Peter, as the next in order. Donatello was again the sculptor. Their coat of arms appeared in a medallion above the niche as <term>the Goat</term> <note>original: "il Becco"</note>, which is said to have given them their name <term>Butchers</term> <note>original: "Beccai"</note>.

In addition to Saint John the Baptist of the <term>Cloth Finishers' Guild</term> <note>original: "Calimala"</note>, the east front of the church features Saint Luke, the protector of the "Guild of Judges and Notaries." This was a bronze work by Giovanni da Bologna from the late sixteenth century. A fine group occupies the next niche, "Christ and Saint Thomas," erected at the expense of the <term>Merchants' Court</term> <note>original: "Corte della Mercanzia"</note>—the Chamber of Commerce.

# THE PATRONAGE OF THE GUILDS

—and completed in 1483 by Verrocchio, following a dispute over terms with Ghiberti and Donatello.

All around the four sides are medallions and low-relief sculptures <term>bas-reliefs</term>: the former reproduce the coats of arms of the guilds, and the latter are mostly scenes from the lives of the different patron saints. The curious lean-to archway joining the shrine to the residence of the "Guild of Wool" was an afterthought.

The interior of Orsanmichele is very striking. The walls and pillars were richly painted by artists in the fifteenth century at the expense of the various guilds, who also contributed funds for the rich stained glass. The Tabernacle of the Madonna is one of the most magnificent monuments of the Renaissance. Orcagna has given his masterpiece the appearance of having been carved out of a single piece of marble. The altar itself, dedicated to the patron saint of Florence <note>While St. John the Baptist is the patron of the city, this altar specifically honored the miraculous image of the Virgin</note>, was erected by the Signoria <term>the governing council of Florence</term> in 1349. The whole building is a unique example of the life, thought, and work of the great guild system of Florence, and it preaches eloquent sermons to the religious and the industrious alike.

Begging <term>mendicity</term>—unknown in the earlier years of the Renaissance—became, through the natural decline of worldly things, a scourge and a scandal over time. Loafers, cripples, beggars, and the other human atoms of an impoverished underclass <term>submerged tenth</term> infested the markets, the bridges, and the doors of monasteries, palaces, and churches. Orsanmichele, by reason of the immense concourse of worshippers and pilgrims, became their favorite gathering ground. A mass of human misery assembled there daily, which invited both pity and disgust. At one time, as many as eighteen thousand destitute and disreputable persons are said to have crowded the portals of the shrine.

Dante speaks of the begging community in pathetic terms:

> "So those blind beggars that have lost their all
> Frequent the churches to supply their need." <gloss>1</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the description of the beggar population in Florence, specifically those congregating at sites like Orsanmichele, and transitions into the private religious patronage of wealthy merchant families in churches like Santa Croce.</meta>

# THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE

The beggars were infinite in their variety and wickedness, creating a tradition in the annals of Florence that persists to this day. Writers of the time sought to shame this public disgrace and rid the city of these "undesirables" through mockery and sarcasm.

Sacchetti’s story of the “Three Blind Beggars” is highly entertaining. They agreed to beg in specific, separate districts of the city and split their total earnings. They met at a small tavern in the suburbs and immediately began to argue and beat each other. In their struggle, they accidentally smashed much of the furniture in the room; when the landlord arrived to stop the brawl, they beat him as well. The worthy landlady, however, was something of a fierce woman <term>virago</term>, for she thrashed the four of them and made off with the beggars' loot!¹

The members of the Guilds, acting as organizations, offered many donations to religious causes and the decoration of churches. However, wealthy nobles and merchants were not satisfied with this alone; many made generous individual contributions and hired leading artists to decorate chapels and altars. Indeed, there seems to have been a fierce rivalry between influential citizens in building artistic memorials connected to church services.

These memorials—which are both the enduring records of commercial prosperity and the most splendid achievements of art—exist in every sacred building in Florence. They are especially prominent in the magnificent churches of Santa Croce, Santa Maria Novella, and San Lorenzo. At Santa Croce, the choir belonged to the great Alberti family, and the surrounding chapels belonged to the Cavalcanti, Pazzi, Bardi, Peruzzi, Riccardi-Guigni, Soderini, Morelli, Baroncelli, Castellani, Medici, Rinuccini, Tosinghi-Spinelli, Ricasoli, Conti-Bardi, Pulci, and Niccolini families.

This is a list of famous merchant-princes such as no other city could produce, and it serves simultaneously as a roll of honor for glorious artists. It includes the great names of Giotto, Margaritone,

One family—the Pazzi—further honored their name in 1410 by building the adjacent and beautiful chapel of Santa Maria Maddalena. It was built according to the plans of Brunelleschi <note>original: "Brunellesco"</note> and contains Perugino’s masterpiece <note>original: "chef d’œuvre"</note>, "The Crucifixion," which was commissioned in 1493.

In Santa Maria Novella are the chapels of the merchant-princes: the Rucellai, Strozzi, Filippo Strozzi, and Gaddi. These art patrons employed Cimabue, Orcagna, Uccello, Filippino Lippi, Ghirlandaio, Bronzino, Bernardo Rossellino, Benedetto da Maiano, and Neri di Bicci to beautify their family shrines.

The Spanish Chapel <note>original: "Cappella degli Spagnuoli"</note>—the name was perhaps given because Spanish merchants and artisans gathered in the chapel for their daily Mass and devotions—is unrivaled for its frescoes by Taddeo Gaddi, Simone Martini <note>original: "Simone di Memmi"</note>, Andrea da Firenze, and Antonio Veneziano. It serves as further evidence, if any were needed, of the prosperity of the Florentine Guild members, of their wholehearted encouragement of the fine arts, and of their admirable devotion to the service of the Church. In 1470, following the designs of Leon Battista Alberti, Giovanni Rucellai erected the fine façade of Santa Maria Novella at his own expense and to the honor of God; it remains the noblest example of Tuscan Gothic ever built.

San Lorenzo, with its Sacristies, is the superb memorial to the Medici family. Its reconstruction, however, after the devastating fire of 1417, was undertaken by the Medici and seven other merchant families as a thank-offering for their success in business and in the State. It was due to Giovanni de’ Medici that San Lorenzo became his family's shrine. Brunelleschi, Donatello, and Filippo Lippi collaborated on the new building and its decoration, while Michelangelo <note>original: "Michael Angelo"</note> made the "New Sacristy"—built in 1529 by Giulio <note>original: "Guilio"</note> de’ Medici (Pope Clement VII)—a treasure-house of sculpted masterpieces.

### CHAPTER XIX
## THE CHARITY OF THE GUILDS

A large subject. The *Calimala* Guild <note>The Guild of Foreign Cloth Merchants</note> serves as an example for the rest: Monasteries, hospitals, schools, homes for the elderly and the mentally ill, poorhouses, and more. *Hospitals* <note>original: "Spedali"</note>—including Saint Eusebius, Saint Mary and Saint Gall, Saint Mary New <note>original: "Santa Maria Nuova"</note> and its pharmacy, Saint Lazarus, Saint Mary of the Stair <note>original: "Santa Maria della Scala"</note>, Ortebello, Saint John, Saint Matthew and the notary Lapo Mazzei, Saint John of God, Saint Paul, the convalescent hospital of “Saint Mary’s Gate” <note>original: "Por Santa Maria"</note>, and the Hospital of the Innocents <note>original: "degli Innocenti"</note>. A home for widows. A hostel for young men. The generosity of Niccolo da Uzzano and Francesco da Mantoa. Marriage dowries. The *Mercy* <note>original: "Misericordia"</note>—its origin and development. The *Company of the Bigallo* <note>original: "Compagnia del Bigallo"</note>. A dead body. Sylvanus of Samosata. Brother Peter of Verona <note>original: "Fra Pietro da Verona"</note>. The *Paterines* <note>original: "Paterini"</note>. The *Congregation of Saint Martin* <note>original: "Congregazione di San Martino"</note>. Archbishop Antonino. *The Shamefaced Poor* <note>original: "I Poveri Vergognosi"</note>. A list of the first twelve *Good Men* <note>original: "Buonuomini"</note>. Money boxes. The *Good Men of the Stinche Prison* <note>original: "Buonuomini della Stinche"</note>. The *Good Men of Saint Bonaventure*. Bankrupt merchants.

It would be impossible, except at very great length, to list all the charitable and religious works of the Guilds during the Renaissance. Perhaps a brief list of such benefits associated with the “Calimala Guild” will serve as an example for the rest and support the claim that the Florentines were inspired by the noblest human instincts.

The “Calimala” statutes and other records confirm that the “Merchants of Foreign Cloth” maintained the following charitable institutions in and around Florence:

*Monasteries*:—at Montecalvoli, Ripoli, Saint Donato in Torri, Faenza <note>original: "Faventia"</note>, Le Mura, Borgo San Lorenzo in Mugello, Saint Mary at the Meadow <note>original: "Santa Maria al Prato"</note>, Saint James in Chains <note>original: "San Jacopo in Vincoli"</note>, Bibbiena, Maiano, Saint Matthew of Arcetri, Saint Lucy in Quaracchi, Saint Giles <note>original: "Sant’ Egidio"</note>, Hill of the Cross <note>original: "Podio della Croce"</note>, Saint John the Baptist in Mugello, Holy Spirit <note>original: "San Spirito"</note>, the Carmine, etc.

->Bella Gionnina <note>OCR reads "Gionalina"</note>, New Saint Mary’s <note>original: "Santa Maria Nuova"</note>, Saint Eusebius <note>original: "Sant' Eusebio"</note>, Saint Mary of Cafaggio <note>original: "Santa Maria di Cafaggio"</note>, Saint Lazarus <note>original: "San Lazaro"</note>, Saint Minias on the Mountain <note>original: "San Miniato al Monte"</note>, Saint John the Baptist <note>original: "San Giovanni Battista"</note>, etc. etc.<-

And what the premier Guild did on such a generous scale, all the other Guilds imitated. According to their own financial means, they achieved equally impressive records of charity.

Monasteries were endowed for a variety of purposes. They served not only as sacred sanctuaries for religious persons who dedicated their whole time to divine worship, but they were also retreats from the world for many weary workers from the markets and the shops.

Some of them were schools for the young, teaching both religious and secular <note>original: "profane"</note> knowledge, while in others the brothers were taught useful crafts. Many were also homes for the elderly, the disabled, and the mentally ill; some were hospitals for the sick, and others were shelters for the needy.

At first, their caretakers were members of the clergy—both the monks and the local priests—along with holy and devout women. Later on, laypeople were entrusted with these charitable duties in partnership with the religious orders, and eventually, the clerical element was entirely replaced.

For example: In 1344, the Duke of Athens, during his term as Chief Magistrate <note>original: "Podestaship"</note>, gave the sole charge of the Hospital of Saint Giles <note>original: "Spedale di Sant' Egidio"</note> to the **"Calimala"** Guild <note>The Guild of Foreign Cloth Merchants</note>. In 1350, the State placed the Monastery of Saint Barnabas <note>original: "San Barnabo"</note> under the exclusive care of the **"Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries."** These lay holdings were later confirmed by Papal decrees <note>original: "Bulls"</note>.

Every significant building project and every large industrial business had its own staff of trained charitable assistants. At Saint Minias on the Mountain, Saint John the Baptist, and Saint Mary of the Flower <note>original: "Santa Maria del Fiore," the Florence Cathedral</note>, the workers and their families were cared for in both health and sickness, and were placed under disciplined and beneficial regulations.

Machiavelli records the spirit of his time regarding such matters: "Public works," he says, "should be carried on—"
