In 1338, there were thirty fully equipped hospitals—both large and small—in the city, providing more than one thousand beds to accommodate the sick, the needy, and the elderly.

By the time of Lorenzo de’ Medici, at least forty hospitals of various kinds were in active operation, with a total annual income from investments alone of more than sixty thousand gold florins. During this same period, the monasteries and convents numbered over one hundred large houses and many smaller ones.

The following is a list of the more notable charitable institutions managed by the Guilds:

### 1. *Hospital of Saint Eusebius.* <note>original: "Spedale di Sant’ Eusebio"</note>

The Hospital of Saint Eusebius in the Prato d’Ognissanti was probably the earliest charitable institution founded in Florence for the relief of human suffering. Originally, the building was a convent for the Nuns of Saint Anne, and members of the Donati family were among its early benefactors. In 1186, the nuns added the care of the afflicted to their religious duties; they maintained this pious responsibility until the year 1278, when the Captain of the Guelph Party <note>original: "Parte Guelfa"</note>, with the consent of the Papal See, relieved the nuns of their charitable functions. He entrusted the care of the sick to a joint commission of the *Umiliati* <term>a religious order specializing in wool production</term> and merchants from the "Calimala" <term>Refiners of Foreign Cloth</term> and "Wool" Guilds, under the direction of the monastery's administrator <term>Mercato</term>.

### 2. *Hospital of Saint Mary of San Gallo.* <note>original: "Spedale di Santa Maria di San Gallo"</note>

Early in the thirteenth century, Guidalotto di Volto dall’ Orco founded this hospital for the relief and support of the poor and of pilgrims. In 1218, he bequeathed his endowment to the Church, which greatly expanded the institution, particularly as a refuge for young children abandoned by their parents. In 1292, the hospital was placed under the protection of the "Guild of Silk Merchants" <note>original: "Merchants of Porta Santa Maria"</note>. New buildings were erected in a garden belonging to the Guild near the Piazza dei Servi; however, due to a "scarcity of money" <note>original: "scarsezza de’ denari"</note>—as the record quaintly puts it—they

The buildings were not finished until 1444, under the direction of Francesco della Luna. In 1463 the "Foundling Hospital of San Gallo" <note>original: "Brefotrofio di San Gallo"</note>—as it was then called—was amalgamated with the Hospital of Santa Maria degli Innocenti <note>Hospital of Saint Mary of the Innocents</note>.

### 3. *Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova.* <note>original: "Spedale di Santa Maria Nuova"</note>

The Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova—which still exists—was founded in 1285 by Folco Portinari, two years before the marriage of his daughter, Beatrice (immortalized by Dante), to Simone de' Bardi. Dante describes Portinari as "a man of exceeding goodness." He held, in turn, all the highest offices of state and was often elected Consul <term>the highest administrative leader</term> of his guild—the "Calimala" <term>the Guild of Refiners of Foreign Cloth</term>. The hospital was opened on January 23, 1288, with seventeen beds. In 1329, bylaws were established for the governance of the hospital. Two wards were created—one for men and one for women—which were visited daily by members of the first rank of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries."

A medical school was attached to the hospital in 1350, and a library of medical books, a museum of drugs—consisting chiefly of foreign substances organized by the apothecaries—and an anatomical theatre were also added.

The patronage of the Greater Guilds ensured the charity’s permanence and financial stability. Indeed, the amount of donations was so substantial that in the fifteenth century, the governors at one time had an annual revenue of more than fifteen thousand gold florins. In 1348, the year of the Great Plague, a sum of at least twenty-five thousand gold florins was contributed to the hospital's funds.¹

### 4. *Hospital of San Lazaro.* <note>original: "Spedale di San Lazaro"</note>

In the year 1338, the "Calimala Guild" built this hospital outside the Faenza Gate <note>Porta a Faenza</note> in a hamlet called Campoluccio. They endowed it with food, clothing, and medical treatment for the elderly and

the sick and poor. This institution carried on its charitable work until 1529 when, during the famous siege of Florence, it was demolished to make way for the fortifications designed by Michelangelo.

### 5. *Hospital of Saint Mary of the Ladder.* <note>original: "Spedale di Santa Maria della Scala"</note>

The Hospital of Saint Mary of the Ladder was founded in 1306 by Cione di Lapo Pollini, a member of the Santa Maria Novella chapter of the "Guild of Wood-carvers." It was modeled on a hospital established at Siena in the ninth century for travelers and people in distress. Cione was essentially a cobbler—the humble trade of the lowest-ranking division of the "Guild of Shoemakers." His connection with the Wood-carvers' Guild is not very obvious; perhaps social status, if not the trade itself, had its influence. However, it was a common practice for a member of an inferior Guild to seek honorary enrollment in one of a higher degree.

Regardless, the benevolent operations of the hospital, along with the upkeep of its buildings and other affairs, were taken over by a "Company of Shoemakers." This group—established in 1502—was known as the *Company of Saints Crispin and Crispinian* <note>original: "La Compagnia di SS. Crespino e Crespigniano"</note>. Their offices, used for the relief of poor craftsmen, were in the old Palazzo Marucelli. There, assistance was freely given to German and other foreign workers in leather shoes and slippers, as well as to jobbing cobblers. In 1531, the Hospital of Saint Mary of the Ladder was incorporated into the Hospital of Saint Mary of the Innocents <note>original: "Santa Maria degli Innocenti"</note>.^1

### 6. *Hospital of Ortebello.* <note>original: "Spedale del Ortebello"</note>

Niccolo degli Alberti—a wealthy wool merchant—founded a charity in 1377 for the benefit of elderly poor women who were to act as nurses to unfortunate young mothers. It was perhaps the earliest Florentine maternity hospital <term>original: "Lying-in Hospital"</term>, and was originally reserved for workers in the wool industry.^2

### 7. *Hospital of Saint John.* <note>original: "Spedale di San Giovanni"</note>

Bonifazio Lupi, Marquess of Soragna, who was one of the famous <term>mercenary leaders</term> <note>original: "Condottieri"</note> employed by the Republic of Florence in the wars against Pisa, built a hospital in 1377 for the mentally ill. It was given the name "Bonifazio’s Asylum" <note>original: "Manicomio di Bonifazio"</note>. It was the only asylum for these unfortunate people, who until then had been confined to the <term>Stinche</term> <note>A notorious Florentine prison, originally used for debtors.</note>—the debtors' prison! The construction and endowment cost twenty-five thousand gold florins and served as a thank-offering for the freedom of the city, which a grateful public had granted to their successful general. At his death, Lupi also left an annual income of seven hundred gold florins and entrusted its administration to the <term>Calimala Guild</term> <note>The powerful guild of merchants who imported and refined foreign cloth.</note>.¹

### 8. *Hospital of Saint Matthew.* <note>original: "Spedale di San Matteo"</note>

Toward the end of the fourteenth century, Lemmo da Montecatini—a banker—began building a hospital for poor rural people visiting Florence. He dedicated it to Saint Nicholas and, upon his death in 1389, left it a generous endowment. Early in the fifteenth century, the "Guild of Bankers and Money-Changers" took over the completion of the buildings and the administration of the charity. The name of the guild's patron saint—Saint Matthew—was added to the original dedication, but it eventually became known simply as the <term>Hospital of Saint Matthew</term> <note>original: "Spedale di San Matteo"</note>. Its specific purpose also changed, and it became an asylum for elderly men and women. The Consuls of the Guild were appointed as the sole governors, while every member of the guild was taxed <term>proportionally</term> <note>original: "pro rata"</note> to contribute toward the maintenance costs. One of the hospital's administrators was the well-known notary Lapo Mazzei. He left behind several interesting letters concerning the subject of charity. "There are many merchants," he says, "who, after their annual accounts are settled, come to me to ask which charities are the most deserving, so that they may wisely allocate certain portions of"

### 9. *Hospital of Saint John of God.* <note>original: "Spedale di San Giovanni di Dio"</note>

In the same century, around 1411, Simone Vespucci endowed the Convent of Saint Mary of Humility <note>original: "Santa Maria dell' Umilita"</note>, in the Ognissanti district <note>original: "Borgo d'Ognissanti"</note>, for poor and infirm workmen. After the death of its founder, it was placed under the direction of the Captains of the <term>Bigallo</term> <note>A prominent Florentine charitable confraternity.</note>. In 1580, the Hospital was transferred to the care of the Order of Saint John of God—better known as the "Brothers of Good Fellowship" <note>original: "Frati dei Bene Fratelli"</note>—and received its new name.

### 10. *Hospital of Saint Paul.* <note>original: "Spedale di San Paolo"</note>

Within the building that became known as the "Hospital of Saint Paul," a body of Franciscan Pilgrim Fathers had settled; the house served as a resting place for religious persons traveling to and from Rome. In 1413, the monks opened a wing as a <term>lay convalescent hospital</term>, which, in 1457, was transferred to the care of the Proconsul and the Consuls of the "Guild of Judges and Notaries"—the coat of arms of the Guild are still visible on the front of the building. Around 1500, the sick poor were admitted, and the scope of the foundation was enlarged. Another change awaited the hospital, for at the end of the sixteenth century, the sick patients made way for other residents. An industrial school for girls, specifically devoted to the silk trade, was established within its gates by the Grand Duke <term>Piero Leopoldo</term> <note>Peter Leopold (1747–1792), Grand Duke of Tuscany and later Holy Roman Emperor.</note>.

### 12. *Hospital of Saint Mary of the Innocents.* <note>original: "Spedale di Santa Maria degli Innocenti"</note>

Perhaps the best-known hospital in Florence today is the "Hospital for Foundlings," featuring a portico splendidly decorated with medallions of infants <note>original: "bambini"</note> by Andrea Della Robbia. Inspired by a moving speech given in 1421 by the scholar Leonardo Aretino regarding the urgent problem of the rise in illegitimate births in Florence, the <term>Signoria</term> <note>The supreme governing body of the Republic of Florence.</note> decided to build a foundling hospital where such unfortunate children could be received and nursed.

Designs for the building were prepared by <term>Brunellesco</term> <note>Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446), the architect famous for the dome of the Florence Cathedral.</note>, and the hospital opened for its young residents in 1444. The Signoria entrusted its management to the wealthy and growing "Silk Guild." By 1579, there were sixteen hundred children in the hospital. A sum of ten thousand gold florins was raised to apprentice boys between the ages of twelve and sixteen to ship captains in Livorno.¹

In 1430, at the corner of the <term>Piazza Santa Maria Novella</term> and the <term>Via della Scala</term>, Lisa di Ranieri Paganelli—the wife of Gentile di Vanni degli Albizzi and a member of the "Wool Guild"—founded a home for four destitute widows from the poorest class of wool workers in <term>Oltrarno</term> <note>The district of Florence "across the Arno" river.</note>.

In association with the University of Florence, Niccolo da Uzzano—a wealthy merchant of the <term>Calimala Guild</term> <note>The guild of refiners of imported woolen cloth.</note>—bequeathed money in his 1432 will to build and endow a hostel. This hostel was intended for fifty poor but honest and promising young men from Florence. He appointed the consuls of the "Calimala" Guild as his trustees. Da Uzzano was quite the

The most prominent citizen of his day, the leader of the aristocratic party and the opponent of the ambitions and aims of the Medici <note>Niccolò da Uzzano (1359–1431), a powerful Florentine politician.</note>. His selflessness and absolute loyalty have been memorialized by Machiavelli, who attributes to him the saying: “God deliver this city from private tyranny.”¹ <note>original: "private usurpation"</note>

To the Hospital of Saint Mary of the Staircase <note>original: "Spedale di Santa Maria della Scala"</note>, he left six hundred gold florins “for providing dowries for girls and supporting children”; to the Hospital of Saint John the Baptist <note>original: "Spedale di San Giambattista"</note>, two hundred gold florins; to the Hospital of Saint Gall <note>original: "Spedale di San Gallo"</note>, two hundred florins; to the Company of the Bigallo <note>original: "Compagnia del Bigallo"</note>, four hundred gold florins to be distributed to the occupants of the debtors’ prison, along with eight bushels of bread a month for twenty years; and many bequests to churches for their completion, decoration, and repair.²

The Linen Manufacturers were not a bit behind the other guilds in their religious and charitable inclinations. Two members of the guild—Antonio di Antonio and Giuliano Carracci—left certain sums of money in their 1475 wills to be invested for the benefit of the daughters of deceased <term>matriculated</term> <note>Formally enrolled or registered as a member of a guild.</note> members, to serve as dowries upon their marriage. The choice of the maidens was made annually by the entire body of living members—as was the approval of the fortunate suitors—and preference was always given to young men registered in the guild.³

It is interesting to note that every <term>popolo</term> <note>A parish or administrative district in Florence.</note> or parish in Florence provided a number of “marriage portions” for deserving poor girls of good character.

Adimari family. Here they spent their leisure time gambling, drinking, and blaspheming. In 1240, while still a young man, Pietro Borsi joined this corrupt group. He had been raised with care and religious devotion, and he was deeply shocked by the sights and sounds around him. Becoming bold one day, he approached a group of the ringleaders of this shameful behavior and rebuked them. He suggested it would be a good thing if they imposed a small fine on themselves, and on everyone else who frequented the area, every time a man swore—since the Florentines always considered blasphemy a serious sin. 

His proposal was taken seriously, which encouraged him to plead that the men form a society to help the sick and the needy. This was also agreed upon. With the money raised from these fines, they purchased six <term>stretchers</term> <note>original: "litters"</note>—one for use in each of the city's six <term>districts</term> <note>original: "sestieri"</note>—to carry victims of street accidents and the sick to hospitals, and the dead for burial. Donations in cash and goods poured in; for instance, during the Great Plague of 1348, the public gave thirty-five thousand gold florins in charity to the fraternity.

They purchased part of the house where they used to meet and converted it into a street hospital with an attached <term>chapel</term> <note>original: "Oratory"</note>. In 1250, without any formal ceremony, the former group of blasphemers transformed into the "Company of the Brothers of Mercy." They adopted a distinctive uniform to protect the brothers while they performed their charitable duties and to prevent unwanted curiosity or disruptive public displays. At first, this was a dull red color, but black was eventually chosen as more suitable.

Around the year 1350, plans were approved to build a <term>covered gallery</term> <note>original: "Loggia"</note> where brothers engaged in their daily acts of mercy could rest for a while. It was also a place where lost or abandoned children could stay until claimed by their parents or a kind benefactor. This was simply an expansion of the charitable work carried out since

No longer restricted to the humblest ranks of society, the descendants of noble families and the sons of wealthy Guild members gladly joined the Order. They wore the habit <term>distinctive religious clothing or uniform</term> of the society, performed its duties, and shared its privileges. They considered themselves fortunate to be allowed to play a part in easing the terrible burden of human suffering. A rota <term>duty roster or schedule</term> was organized, and a bell was hung in the Loggia <term>an open-sided gallery or porch</term>. When it rang, the Brothers scheduled for duty in the streets would hurry to provide their services.

Mass was held every morning in the Oratory, and Litanies <term>a series of prayers or petitions</term> were sung by the Brothers in attendance. Their devotions were focused on the pious intentions of the members and the peace of the souls of the deceased. Collection boxes for donations were placed in several parts of the city, each decorated with a picture of a *Pieta* <note>original: "Pieta"; an artistic representation of the Virgin Mary cradling the dead body of Jesus</note>. They carried the inscription: "Give alms for the poor and needy sick," and a Brother-guardian stood by each box in his uniform. It is said that the box placed outside the Baptistery received more than five hundred silver florins <term>a currency used in Florence</term> and small coins in a single day.

In 1425, the *Misericordia* <term>Brotherhood of Mercy</term> joined with the *Compagnia del Bigallo* <term>Company of the Bigallo</term>. However, the merger did not work well because the members of the Bigallo refused to carry the sick.

A tragic event led to the reorganization of the "Brothers of Mercy." Early in 1475, the corpse of a man was found in the *Via de Macci* <note>Macci Street</note> with no one to bury it. A passing market porter threw down his load and, reverently placing the dead body on his shoulders, staggered with it to the *Palazzo Vecchio* <note>The Old Palace; the town hall of Florence</note>. He deposited the body at the feet of the *Gonfaloniere di Giustizia* <term>the Standard-bearer of Justice, the city's chief magistrate</term>.

This act convinced the *Misericordia* to end their connection with the *Compagnia del Bigallo*. They decided to once again undertake the burial of the dead and resume their other specific organizational duties. At first, the bodies interred by the Brothers were buried in a pit which they dug and fenced in on the site of the *Torre della Guardamorto* <note>Tower of the Watcher of the Dead</note>, which had been destroyed by the Ghibellines <term>a political faction that supported the Holy Roman Emperor</term>. ### *The Company of the Bigallo.*

Another charitable organization, very similar to the “*Misericordia*,” grew out of a religious movement from the Middle Ages. This group played an active role in the lives of the Guild members during the Renaissance.

In the seventh century, a man named Silvanus of Samosata, a fanatical disciple of the Apostle Paul, denied the Incarnation of Christ. His followers became outright Manichaeans <term>followers of a dualistic religious system that saw the world as a struggle between light and darkness</term>. One of them arrived in Florence in 1212 and claimed the title of Bishop. Many converts—mostly Ghibellines <term>the political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor</term>—joined his cause. He was a simple, enthusiastic working-man from Milan named Filippo Paternono.

Dominicans and Franciscans joined forces against these heretics. Led by a young monk—Fra Pietro da Verona, better known as Saint Peter Martyr—the “Society of the Captains of Holy Mary” was formed from the ranks of young knights to suppress the members of this sect.

The suffering these misguided people endured earned them the name “*Paterini*” <term>Patarines</term>. In 1245, the Captains, wearing white robes, attacked and defeated them, finally driving them from the city. The victors erected the Column of Saint Felicitas <note>original: "Colonna di Santa Felicita"</note> and the Cross at Trebbio <note>original: "Croce al Trebbio"</note> as symbols of the triumph of the Catholic Faith.¹

---

¹ Dino Capponi, vol. i. p. 32.

<page-num>550</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

For their part, the scattered "Paterines" <term>a heretical Christian sect often associated with the Cathars</term> accepted their defeat and wisely redirected their energy into a more sensible path. In and around Florence, there were a number of small hospitals and asylums that were poorly funded and badly managed. The Paterines took charge of these and established their headquarters in one located on the road to Arezzo, which was called "*Il Bigallo*" <note>The Bigallo</note>.

Many members of the Guilds, especially the Lesser Guilds, sincerely sympathized with the suffering of these "poor heretics." They gave their support and even joined forces with the new hospital workers, who adopted the name "*La Compagnia del Bigallo*" <note>The Company of the Bigallo</note>.

At first, they gathered for collective worship in the small church of Saint Mary of Saint Gazzio—or Saint Cajo. However, after correcting their theological errors, they were eventually granted a chapel in Santa Maria Novella for their religious devotions and for the administration of their charities.

For generations, the influence of Paterine beliefs <note>original: "Paterinismo"</note> was felt in the minds and lives of many wool-carders and dyers in the *Oltrarno* <term>the district of Florence located "across the Arno" river</term>. This likely contributed to their indifference toward public opinion and their political restlessness. In the religious character of the average Florentine working man and woman, there was a significant amount of the strictness found in later Methodists!

### *The Congregation of Saint Martin* <note>original: "La Congregazione di San Martino"</note>

Because of its perpetual succession of new governments, the continually shifting power of political parties, and private rivalries between families, Florence was exposed to greater fluctuations in fortune than the inhabitants of industrial centers who are merely victims of the unpredictability of trade.

Men who held power, office, and the ability to create wealth one day were liable to face legal charges the next, resulting in fines, imprisonment, exile, and even death. The result of this state of affairs was a large amount of misery, which was nobly...

<meta>This page continues the description of charitable efforts in Florence, specifically focusing on the hidden poverty of the upper classes and the founding of the Congregation of Saint Martin by Brother Antonino.</meta>

<page-num>551</page-num>
<header>THE CHARITY OF THE GUILDS</header>

[Well-born and in] poverty, carefully concealed. The finest palaces often enough sheltered the greatest suffering. Born into nobility and delicately raised, their inhabitants were the pathetic victims of unfortunate circumstances.

Private, discreet charity failed to reach these victims of misfortune until the year 1435, when Brother <note>original: "Frate"</note> Antonino di Niccolo Pierozzo <note>Known as Saint Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459)</note> was elected the first Prior of the Monastery of San Marco. He immediately took up the apostolic mission of benevolence, for he saw and understood the suffering around him. He thought very seriously about how to help the "shame-faced poor" <note>original: "i poveri vergognosi"</note>—the victims of poverty who were too ashamed to beg—as they were called.

The good Prior sent for twelve of the most upright men in Florence—men of all social classes, including a merchant, a manufacturer, a banker, a wool-carder, a furrier, a silk-winder, a shoemaker, and others. These members of the Guilds were presented with the harrowing details of the local distress, and he shared his ideas for their relief.

The twelve "Good Men" <note>original: "Buonuomini"</note>, touched to the heart by Brother Antonino's revelations and by his genuine selflessness, warmly offered themselves as assistants in carrying out the charitable program. In this way, an institution arose in 1441 that still survives and prospers: "The Congregation of Saint Martin" <note>original: "La Congregazione di San Martino"</note>. It was named after the small church of that name where the meetings—both for prayer and for discussion—of the "good men" were held.

The names of the first "Congregation" have been preserved:
Michele di Messere Piero Benini.

Nofri d' Agnolo—*Drappiere* <note>Cloth-dresser</note>.
Primerano di Jacopo—*Calzaiuolo* <note>Hosier</note>.
Giovanni di Baldo—*Lanaiuolo* <note>Woolen-draper</note>.
Pasquino d' Ugolino del Vernaccia—*Setaiuolo* <note>Silk manufacturer</note>.

They established a central office in a room in the Abbey <note>original: "Badia"</note>, granted to them by the City Council <note>original: "Signoria"</note>, where, along with a store of medicines and surgical appliances, members of the "Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries" were always in attendance, accompanied by both male and female nurses. In 1470, however, Primerano di Jacopo presented the Congregation with a house in the Square of Saint Martin <note>original: "Piazza di San Martino"</note>, to which the agencies of the Good Men <note>original: "Buonuomini"</note> were moved.

Outside the Church of Saint Martin and the Office of Charity, money boxes were placed to receive offerings from passersby. The former was put in its place by Prior Antonino, and is still in its original position <note>original: "in situ"</note>. The alms gathered in this way were divided each month among the twelve Good Men <note>original: "Buonuomini"</note>, who, in pairs, visited each of the six districts <note>original: "sestieri"</note> of the city and made direct distributions among impoverished and fallen nobles and merchants and their families.

"The Good Archbishop"—as he was affectionately and popularly called—forbade the Congregation to hold capital or to purchase land and other securities after his consecration in 1446 as the fifth Archbishop of Florence. At the same time, he counseled the Good Men <note>original: "Buonuomini"</note> to conduct their charitable work without charging the Congregation for any costs. Every donation given in kind was quickly converted to its best marketable cash value, and the money was distributed promptly and without distinction of any sort. The story of the foundation and early work of the Congregation of Saint Martin <note>original: "Congregazione di San Martino"</note> was preserved upon the walls of the Church of Saint Martin.

## "FLORENCE WEALTHY THROUGH HER INDUSTRY!"
<note>original: "Firenze Ricca Per Industria!"</note>

### (FLORENCE PROSPEROUS THROUGH HER INDUSTRIES)

It was an old saying that: “The Sienese are the richer in land, the Florentines in industry,” and this may be compared to Aristotle’s maxim: “The more barren the soil, the richer the city.”

In a sense, this was true of Florence and of Tuscany—although the fruitful Vale of Arno can in no way be called barren—perhaps in the sense implied in the couplet:

-> "Neither such beautiful silk, nor fine gold,
Do the industrious Florentines cause to be woven!" <note>original: "Ma ne si bella seta, ne fin oro. Nai Fiorentini industri tesser fanno!"</note> <-

-> . <-

-> "Not for lovely silk nor for finest gold,
But for her industry the fame is told
Of busy Florence!" <-

Yes, it was industry that made her fortune!

The Florentines were perhaps the very first people who kept a register of baptisms. Every baby born in Florence was, from the earliest times, baptized by immersion in the great font at San Giovanni. Originally, a box was placed near the font, in which the sex of each child presented was recorded by dropping in beans—black for a boy and white for a girl. An old chronicler says this "became a very unreliable and very dirty habit, as accumulating dust destroyed the color of the beans."<sup>1</sup> In 1450, a better method was adopted for registering the population—the keeping of written records of all baptisms performed within the Baptistery.

Some idea of Florence and her population at different periods in her history can, of course, be gathered from historians.

During the period of Totila's invasion of Tuscany in the sixth century, Florence was a large city, numbering more than sixty thousand souls. In Dante's time, she numbered as many as one hundred and fifty thousand inhabitants, including those in the *Contado* <term>the surrounding rural territory or countryside</term>. An attempt was made in 1233 by the *Podesta* <term>chief magistrate</term>, Torcello di Strado, to take a census of the population. All the male inhabitants of Florence were ordered to appear before the notaries of their several *sestieri* <term>city districts or wards</term> to declare whether they were nobles, knights, doctors, judges, merchants, men of leisure, soldiers, tradesmen, mechanics, artisans, laborers, and so on.

Villani says that in the year 1300, there were 90,000 inhabitants in the city enjoying the full rights of citizenship. There were 1,500 wealthy *Grandi* <term>members of the noble class</term>, and 25,000 people capable of bearing arms. Foreigners passing through the city numbered about 2,000. In the elementary schools, there were between 8,000 and 10,000 children.

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Between 1,000 and 1,500 boys were studying arithmetic, and 500 to 600 were studying grammar and rhetoric.

The churches and religious houses numbered one hundred and ten. In twenty-four nunneries, there were five hundred religious women, and there were also ten monastic houses for the regular clergy. Thirty hospitals and poorhouses provided aid and shelter to more than one thousand sick and needy people, who were served by more than three hundred monks or nurses.

Within the city, there were many palaces and substantial private buildings, as well as public edifices. The *Contado* <term>the surrounding rural territory</term>—within which there were more than 80,000 armed men—was full of villas and handsome country residences, surrounded by fine gardens and fruitful orchards. Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533), a famous Italian poet</note> refers to this evidence of the wealth of Florence:

> “While gazing on your villa-studded hills,
> It would seem as though the earth sprouted palaces.”

Villani <note>Giovanni Villani (c. 1276–1348), a Florentine chronicler</note> also provides many very interesting notes regarding the industry and commerce of Florence in the first half of the fourteenth century. The taxes collected at the city gates represented, on average, fifty-five to sixty-five tuns <term>large casks of approximately 250 gallons</term> of wine, four thousand fat oxen and calves, sixty thousand sheep, thirty thousand pigs, twenty thousand goats, and three to four thousand loads of melons.

The factories, warehouses, and other buildings belonging to the “Guild of Wool” <note>the *Arte della Lana*</note> numbered more than two hundred; in these, seventy to eighty thousand pieces of cloth were manufactured, valued at 1,200,000 gold florins. There were more than 30,000 wool workers in total. The value of foreign woven cloth imported by the “Calimala” Guild <note>the *Arte di Calimala*, which specialized in refining and finishing foreign cloth</note>, after being refined and finished in Florence, was well over 300,000 gold florins. There were eighty exchange banks. The value of the gold coinage in circulation was about 350,000 gold florins, in addition to 20,000 pounds in weight of small silver and bronze money.

The morals and legal rights of the inhabitants were overseen by members of the “*Arte de’ Giudici e Notai*” <note>the Guild of Judges and Notaries</note>—eighty-four...

# “FLORENCE IS RICH THROUGH INDUSTRY!” <note>original: “FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA!”</note>

There were judges and six hundred notaries or lawyers, while the citizens' bodily health and well-being were attended to by sixty physicians and surgeons, who handed them over to the hundred apothecary shops for doses and medicine. To ensure an ample supply of bread, one hundred and fifty bakehouses and just as many bakers were busily at work.

Within fifty years of Villani’s <note>Giovanni Villani (c. 1276–1348), the Florentine chronicler</note> calculation, the population had decreased in an extraordinary fashion. Years of plague, flood, and fire followed in quick succession—so much so, indeed, that in the year 1348, the first of these terrible scourges alone accounted for forty thousand deaths, which was nearly one-half of the total number of inhabitants!

Fluctuations occurred as the years rolled on, but by 1478, signs of permanent decrease were apparent; the census showed a total of only seventy-one thousand people of all kinds and conditions in the city. Fifty years later, in 1532—the year the *Campana* <note>The "Bell," specifically the Great Bell of the Republic used to summon citizens</note> was silenced and the Republic ended—the population had returned to the levels of Totila’s Florence <note>Referring to the 6th-century Siege of Florence by the Ostrogoth king Totila</note>, namely 67,000. By then, "Ichabod" <note>original: "Ichabod"; a biblical reference meaning "the glory has departed"</note> was written large over the workshops of the once-busy city, and her population was on a downward slide; the lowest figure—fifty thousand—was reached in 1574.

The financial prosperity of the Republic in the middle of the thirteenth century is shown by extracts from the annual accounts of receipts and expenditure. <note>Villani, book 11, chapters 91-94.</note> The average income totaled three hundred thousand gold florins, while expenses were less than fifty thousand. A yearly balance on the right side of the account of nearly £130,000 was no mean profit.

The total revenue averaged more than 300,000 gold florins per year during the ten-year period from 1366 to 1376.<sup>1</sup>

The nearly endless variety of commercial goods shipped to and from Florence in the early years of the fourteenth century can be seen in an inventory of goods sent from Pisa to Florence in 1321.<sup>2</sup> The following are some of the items listed: cloth scraps, saltwater fish, scrap iron, palm branches, a bundle of veils and shawls, books, washed wool from Tunisia, sugar, chests full of men’s clothing, pike-staffs <note>Long wooden poles with metal tips used as weapons</note>, hanks of drawn silk, silkworm eggs, raw silk fiber, wine from Siena, saddles, donkeys, mattresses, and so on.

In another inventory, the following are listed: 915 pieces of gold and white tinsel for embossing leather, a package of new keys, a leather traveling bag, velvet saddlebags, seven balls of raw Sardinian lamb’s wool, dog collars, linen gloves, Greek wine, a bale of horse brushes, a bundle of miscellaneous items from Bulgaria, and so forth.

Throughout most of the fifteenth century, the average price of wheat was one *lira*, two *soldi*, and eight *denari* per bushel. Wine—both red and white—cost twenty-seven *soldi* and eight *denari* per barrel; oil was six *lire* and ten *soldi* per barrel; and fresh meat from the butcher cost between two and four *soldi* per pound.

Artisans, bankers, and merchants were the architects of the Republic's wealth. The records of the *Gonfalonieri* <note>The "Standard-bearers of Justice," high-ranking civic officials</note> and other state officials include the names of men from all walks of life. Every citizen contributed his portion to the public treasury and bore his share of the common burden. In this regard, it is interesting to note that the amounts collected from direct taxation in each of the six *sestieri* <note>The six administrative districts or "sixths" of the city</note> varied; however, the higher payments did not necessarily come from the wealthier districts, but rather the opposite.

In 1340, the total sum raised through this method was 100,000 gold florins, divided as follows: *Oltrarno*—the working-class district—28,000; *San Piero Scheraggio*—the administrative district—25,000; *San Piero*...

Maggiore—12,000; San Pancrazio—13,000; Borgo d’ Ognissanti—12,000; and Porta del Duomo—11,000.

This equality—or indeed, the superiority—of the contributions from the *Popolo Minuto* <term>Literally the "little people"; the working class and members of the lower guilds</term> to the Public Treasury had a significant impact on the manners, dress, and food of the people. The responsibility of supporting the State improved the character and demeanor of every class of the population. There was a "leveling up," as we call it, throughout the whole of Florentine society. The hovel became a small house; the small house became a town residence; and the town residence became a palace. Fittings, furniture, decorations, utensils, and so on, all followed suit, ennobling both festive banquets and simple, home-cooked meals alike.

<header>->FLORENCE IS WEALTHY THROUGH INDUSTRY!<-

Silverware, for example, until well into the fifteenth century, was regarded as showy—even on the tables of the wealthier citizens. At most, only forks, spoons, and cups were permitted to be made of precious metals; other vessels were made of brass, including candlesticks, basins, and dishes. Nevertheless, it was quite common to engrave the owner's coat of arms or crest in silver upon each of these articles.

At public banquets, however, these restrictions were ignored. No community could offer such royal magnificence in their table settings as the merchant-princes of Florence. They took pride in the fact that, while they maintained the traditional rules of simplicity and thrift in their private lives, they surpassed reigning monarchs in extravagance during their public entertainments. <note>Borghini, "*Discourse on Florentine Currency*," <note>original: "Discorso della Moneta Fiorentina"</note> vol. 2, p. 163.</note>

This characteristic had always been very prominent in the private lives and public service of the merchants. None were too proud to work with a shuttle, scale, knife, or other tool in the practice of their craft, while simultaneously using their other hand to direct the great policies of the State.

Perhaps the wealth and importance of Florence were never more strikingly displayed than during the Jubilee of Pope Boniface VIII in 1300. The city sent a magnificently equipped embassy to Rome, representing every era of her history. Not only that, but through her bankers and merchants living in or doing business with foreign states, she managed to ensure that the representatives officially sent to the Papal Court for the Jubilee ceremonies by almost all the European powers were actually Florentines. 

Vermiglio Alfani represented the Emperor of Germany; Simone de' Rossi represented the Emperor of Byzantium; Musciatta Franzesi represented the King of France; Ugolino de' Cerchi represented the King of England; and so on. Florence herself was directly represented by Palla de' Strozzi. A large retinue of knights, superbly mounted and dressed, escorted the ambassadors, who were all outfitted in the state uniforms of the countries they represented.

Boniface, astonished by the magnificence of the procession, and...

[Pope Boniface VIII,] astonished at the opulence of the gifts brought to his feet, cried out, as an old manuscript records:

> “Whatever kind of city is this Florence?”

No one was found ready with an answer, but at last a Cardinal—fearing the Pope's displeasure—timidly remarked:

> “Your Holiness, the city of Florence is a good city.”
> 
> “Nonsense,” replied the Pope, “she is by far the greatest of all cities! She feeds, clothes, and governs us all! Indeed, she appears to rule the whole world! She and her people are, in truth, the fifth element of the universe!” ^1 <note>This famous statement refers to the ancient belief in four elements (earth, air, fire, and water); the Pope suggested Florence was a fifth essential component of the world.</note>

Of all the rich men of Florence in the fourteenth century, Niccolò degli Alberti was probably the wealthiest. He died in 1377, possessing at least three hundred and forty thousand gold florins—roughly £150,000—an enormous sum in those days!

In 1422, Florence was considered the richest city in Europe: every useful trade and decorative art flourished exceedingly. No less than two million gold florins were in active circulation—an amount that was not reached in London until the year 1838! The expenses of the wars with Genoa, Pisa, and Leghorn <note>Modern Livorno.</note> amounted, in 1427, to two and a half million gold florins—further proof of the city's prosperity and wealth.^2

In the same year, the number of *Sopportatori* <term>Ratepayers: Those who paid the "Catasto" tax.</term>—those who contributed to the year’s “Catasto” <term>A system of wealth and property assessment for taxation introduced in 1427.</term>—reached 37,225; by 1470, they numbered 40,238. The Revenue at the end of the century totaled 345,540 gold florins—without taking into account the “Decima” <term>A ten-percent tax on income from real estate.</term>—and the Expenditure was 226,000. The average yearly yield of the latter tax between, say, 1470 and 1520, was between 40,000 and 50,000 gold florins.

> “At that period the city,” writes Giovanni Cambi, “appeared to be richer than ever before. For whereas forty years earlier, fourteen hundred gold florins were given as a marriage portion <gloss>dowry</gloss> on both sides among citizens of the Greater Guilds, they now give as much as two thousand five hundred, and even three thousand gold florins!” ^3

<page-num>563</page-num>
<header>“FLORENCE WEALTHY THROUGH INDUSTRY!” <note>original: “FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA!”</note></header>

Machiavelli has a concise economic principle that accurately defines the true and healthy relationship between industrial and financial conditions when he writes the following about the Florentines—merchants and citizens—of his time. He says:

> “A people are wealthy when money does not leave their country, when they are content with what their own land produces, and when money is constantly brought in by those who desire the products of their industry, which they supply to foreign nations.” ¹

The wealth of the city during the first decade of the sixteenth century attracted princely usurpers and beggars from every land. To the King of France, the Republic paid 100,000 gold florins, and the same amount to the Emperor, while the King of Spain received fifty thousand.

In 1527, however, because of the many armed bands marching back and forth, the city was strongly fortified, and the freedom of the citizens was greatly restricted. No person was permitted to go more than sixteen miles beyond the city boundaries. Provisions for a fifteen-day period were not allowed to enter the city without paying a duty, except for wine and oil, on which the tax was reduced by fifty percent.²

The famous siege of Florence by Pope Clement VII and his mercenaries, under the Prince of Orange, in 1529–1530, found Michelangelo Buonarroti at the head of affairs as commander-in-chief of the forces and director-in-chief of the fortifications. The enemy approached the city shouting:

> “Prepare your gold brocades, Florence; we are coming to buy them with the length of our pikes!”

A very interesting remnant of the ancient commercial greatness of Florence is seen in the existence of the little "wicket-gates," or small shop doors, at the corners of noble palaces. Over them, one reads words such as “*Wine Cellar*” <note>original: “*Canova di Vino*”</note>, “*Wax Candle Shop*” <note>original: “*Canova di Torchi di Cera*”</note>, “*Oil Cellar*” <note>original: “*Canova dell’ Olio*”</note>, and so on, indicating that the products of the princely owners’ estates or workshops could be purchased—

...sell goods by retail on the premises. As a case in point, the Strozzi family still maintains a large candle factory and shop.

In the Buondelmonte Palace a few years ago, a pocket-sized writing tablet was discovered hidden away. The leaves of this memorandum book are made of wood and covered with a layer of wax. Upon this surface, the merchant to whom it belonged had used a stylus to make many entries and marks concerning his daily business. Unfortunately, the outer cover, which likely bore the owner's name, has disappeared; however, the date, 1300, remains quite legible.

Guido del' Antella left behind his <note>original: "Ricordanze"</note> *Memoirs*, which serve not only as his trade journal but also as a diary of domestic life. It is full of interesting details and reveals much about the private lives of Florentines in the fourteenth century. These *Memoirs* were continued by his sons and their descendants.

In 1375, the head of the family records that he hired a domestic servant named Caterina del' Passa at a wage of six gold florins a year, with a three-week annual holiday. For another maidservant—whom he calls a *schiava* <note>Italian for "slave."</note>—he arranged to pay only thirty *lire* <note>A unit of Italian currency.</note> a year. This honorable man seems to have been blessed with many <term>olive-branches</term> <note>A metaphorical reference to children, common in historical writing.</note>, as he notes the hiring of four or five nurses in succession, whose average wage was sixteen gold florins. Some of his children were sent out to be cared for by nurses on similarly favorable terms. ¹

This revelation of the domestic hearth of a typical Florentine home introduces a subject affecting the private life of the citizens that has hardly been touched upon by historians: the use of slaves.

Domestic service was repulsive to the freedom-loving and proud Florentines; both men and women avoided it, and there was constant difficulty in finding servants. The expansion of the city's trade and the initiative shown by merchant agents in foreign lands led to an external supply for this common need.

At first, returning merchants introduced young boys and girls one or two at a time, having been attracted to them in Eastern or—

The custom grew, fueled by the nomadic lives led in foreign lands by Florentine traders, until the slave trade became a feature of commerce in the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries. “Oriental slaves bought as live goods,” says Doctor <note>OCR originally read "Doltore," a misspelling of the Italian *Dottore*.</note> G. An ancestor of Baldovinetti—the painter—left drawings of three slaves in the margin of his *Zibaldone* <note>A commonplace book or journal used for various notes and sketches.</note>, whom he bought in 1377, 1380, and 1388:—“Dorothea, a Tartar from Russia, eighteen years or more of age; Domenica, of white skin, from Tartary; and Veronica, sixteen years old, whom I purchased almost naked from Bonaroti <note>Likely a member of the Buonarroti family, to which Michelangelo belonged.</note>, son of Simon de’ Bonaroti.” Such women entered the houses of wealthy citizens to perform humble tasks and to take care of the children.

Alessandra Macinghi, the mother of the Strozzi, wrote this to her son Filippo in 1469 while he was at Naples:—“Let me remind you of the need we have of a slave, for we have always had one. If you give orders to have one bought, ask for a Tartar, for they are the best for hard work and are simple in their ways.”

> “Slaves often enough obtained, through faithful labor, good behavior, and general aptitude, many a generous inheritance upon the death of their masters. Indeed, not infrequently the child of a female slave was looked upon as legitimate and took the master's name—thus Alessandro de’ Medici was the reputed son of Lorenzo, Duke of Urbino—though in all probability, Pope Clement VII was his father. His mother was a mixed-race slave, and he had dark skin, thick lips, and the curly hair of a Black man!

during the era of the Renaissance, and their treatment varied according to the character of their masters. Pistoia in 1205 led the way in freeing its slaves; Bergamo followed in 1237, Vercelli in 1243, Bologna in 1256, and Florence—in three stages—respectively in 1289, 1344, and 1415. The final date marked not only the absolute emancipation of all persons held in bondage, but also the proclamation that forbade citizens of the Republic from owning or buying slaves—whether old or young, male or female—under severe penalties for any who violated the law.

The character of the population and the great prosperity of Florence—beautiful and busy—proved the truth of the ancient couplet:

> ->"All people tremble and pay tribute;<-
> ->Both Lombards and Tuscans are terrified<-
> ->Of the Florentines!" <note>original: "Gens trepidat cuncta datque tributa, Ceu Longobardi, ceu Tuschi, sunt tremefacti Cum Florentibus!"</note><-

The old Mint of Florence was located behind the Church of Santa Croce. However, in 1252, when the currency was thoroughly overhauled and the financial transactions of its merchants and bankers had reached vast proportions, a new Mint was built at the Uffizi, where the present-day Post Office is situated.

Two officials called *Maestri della Zecca*—Masters of the Mint—presided over the manufacture and circulation of coinage. They were chosen by the Head of State: one was required to be a member of the "Calimala" Guild, and the other a member of the "Bankers and Money-changers" Guild. Their term of office was six months, the same as the Consuls.

In addition to these presidents, a goldsmith of proven honesty and intelligence was employed twice every year at the appointment of the new "Masters" to test and weigh a number of gold florins, both those in circulation and those newly minted. Any that failed his tests were rejected; of those approved, a number were enclosed in a small leather bag, which was firmly sealed and labeled as a guarantee or proof of quality—hence the name "*fiorino di suggello*" <note>sealed florin</note>.

<page-num>567</page-num>
<header># "FLORENCE IS WEALTHY THROUGH INDUSTRY!" <note>original: "FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA!"</note></header>

Gold and silver coins were generally struck without any alloy. The minters were well-accustomed to the mysteries of <term>cupellation</term> (a refining process where ores are heated to separate noble metals), for frequent mention is made in the archives of the <term>Mint</term> <note>original: "Zecca"</note> of "first water" <note>original: "acqua prima"</note> and "philosophical water of the first degree" <note>original: "acqua filosofica al primo grado"</note>. These were mixtures of saltpeter and acetic acid used for their property of separating gold and silver and for oxidizing metals, among other things.

Florentines in the thirteenth century understood the use of <term>touchstones</term> (dark stones used to test the purity of precious metals) when dealing with valuable metals. The family papers of Francesco Balducci Pegolotti and the records of the Peruzzi Company explain that the testing of Florentine currency was performed using <term>touchstones</term> <note>original: "paragoni"</note>. For example, the Company received four gold florins every year from the Mint for the rental of a touchstone, which they eventually sold outright in 1329 for twenty gold florins. The fee for testing coins with a touchstone was six <term>denari</term> (pennies). It appears likely that the money-changers kept a touchstone with them and charged their clients for its use on the spot.

The following is an extract from a manuscript:¹ "For four touchstones which we have in Florence, we are to receive on the <term>kalends of July</term> (the first day of the month) 1335, one hundred and sixty-four gold florins, to be paid to Giotto Peruzzi and our Company, as recorded in the 'Book of the Board' <note>original: "del Asse"</note> No. 5, page 14. One is in the gold Mint, for the rental of which we receive four florins a year; the other three are with Bartolo Uguccioni in his house at the shop."

In the Balducci Pegolotti manuscript, there is a treatise on the practice and method of treating and alloying gold and silver. The formula for refining gold through <term>cementation</term> required the composition of the 'cement'—brick-dust and salt—to be absolutely pure and free from earth and sand. The separation of gold and silver was performed using sulfur and lighted charcoal. Many other instructions follow, with the gold always being calculated by the carat and the alloy by the pound and ounce.

Balducci Pegolotti further says: "For the expenses of the Florence Mint, it may be calculated that the cost of melting..."

<meta>This page continues the technical and administrative history of the Florentine Mint, transitioning from the use of touchstones to the specific costs and yields of refining gold and silver through the cementation process, as documented by Balducci Pegolotti and in the Mint’s official registers.</meta>

Ten pounds of gold will be equivalent to one *denaro* <note>penny</note> of gold. In the process of refining gold—that is, separating the gold and silver from the <term>cement</term> <note>a mixture of chemicals, like salt and brick dust, used in an ancient refining process called cementation</note>—you will obtain five ounces of refined gold from every six ounces of raw gold. The cost of refining one pound of gold is 10 *soldi* (*piccioli* <note>small currency</note>) to cover the expenses of the chief refiner. The cost for one *fuoco*—or firing—in the mint, as established for the better protection of the Commune, is 4 *soldi* and 7 *denari* (*piccioli*) per pound; this covers the expenses of the <term>Rimettitori</term> <note>officials in charge of refining and delivering metals</note> of the said mint. Melting the cement and cleansing—a process performed on a mass of 90 pounds of cement—costs 35 *soldi* in "florins of account" (calculated at 29 *soldi* to the gold florin). The cost of separating the gold and silver taken from the cement is 2 *soldi* and 6 *denari* (*piccioli*) per pound. In Florence, the cost for a carat of gold separated from silver by cementation is 10 *soldi a fiorini* (at the rate of 29 *soldi* to the gold florin). The cost of the crude silver separated from the gold is 14 *soldi a fiorini* per ounce. Finally, the cost in Florence for the slag from the melted cement of each mass is 5 *soldi* (*piccioli*).

> "It may be calculated that for gold brought to the Florentine money-changers for sale, whether in leaf or in bars, the price will be—for 21-carat gold, 9 *soldi* and 7 *denari a fiorini*, and decreasing according to the carat. And the price is 8 *denari a fiorini* for each carat of silver."

Thus far wrote Balducci Pegolotti. The reader will notice that the pounds (*lire*), shillings (*soldi*), and pence (*denari*) are designated *a fiorini*, which refers to a "florin of account" and not a "market florin." This was a conventional or imaginary florin valued at 29 *soldi*, similar to the <term>scudo</term> and <term>pezza</term> <note>notional units of currency used in accounting rather than physical coins</note>.

The ancient Registers of the Florentine Mint, which have fortunately survived, provide details every six months regarding the administration of the mint and the striking of the currency. However, since no register was kept before 1303, the chronicler Giovanni Villani, who served as one of the Masters of the Mint in 1316, introduced an official book called the *Fiorinario*. This book, which is now kept in the Magliabecchiana Library, explained the stamps or symbols impressed upon the coins struck every six months. These symbols ceased to be recorded in 1373, as the Masters of the Mint, being members of the...

leading families, suppressed the official stamps, and minted money featuring the coats of arms of their own houses.

In 1327, the Duke of Calabria appointed two prominent merchants to serve as assayers <note>officials who test the purity of precious metals</note> of the gold and silver coinage for a period of six months. They were Giovanni Villani, of the “Calimala Guild” <note>the guild of cloth finishers and merchants in foreign cloth</note>, and Bartolommeo de’ Simonetti, of the “Guild of Bankers and Money Changers.”

Balducci Pegolotti also provides a description of corresponding foreign mints, their locations, and the metallic compositions used—that is, silver, gold, and alloys—according to the currency to be minted, along with their prices and the operating expenses of each mint. The mints mentioned by Pegolotti include the following: Tana <note>modern Azov</note> on the Black Sea, Torrisi <note>modern Tabriz</note> in Persia, Ajazza <note>modern Ayas</note>, Famagusta, Tunis, Chiarenza <note>modern Glarentza</note>, Castel di Castro <note>modern Cagliari</note>, Majorca, Messina, Naples, Ancona, Aquileia, and Venice. In Cambalu <note>modern Beijing</note>, the capital of the Chinese Empire, there was only a paper currency.¹

The reputation of the Florentines for their skill in minting was immense, and many foreign mints were actually managed by them. In 1269, the Tornaquinci Company managed the mint of Bologna. Under King Edward II, a member of the Frescobaldi family was appointed director of the London Mint to correct its deficiencies. In 1338, Angiolo Vernaccia and Francesco Benacquisti managed the mint of Aquileia; those of Rome, Naples, and Perugia were also governed by Florentines.

Paolino Pieri—in his “Chronicle” covering 1080 to 1305—and Targioni-Tozzetti, Vettori, and Borghini agree that several kinds of coins were minted and in circulation in Florence before the time of Frederick Barbarossa.

Nevertheless, Antonio Pucci reports that leather money was once in circulation, stamped with the Emperor’s head. He goes on to say that in 1240, Frederick II minted at his own expense a gold “Augustus” coin and placed a number of these coins into the hands of merchants and artisans. This favor was “highly valued by the people of Florence, who were very distressed by their situation of having only leather money, and they gladly exchanged it.”²

<page-num>570</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

While the coins of all the nations and cities with which Florentines conducted business were accepted and circulated in the city, and while each had its own market value and was subject to daily exchange rate fluctuations, Florence naturally had its own unique coinage system.

The currency was based on silver—the <term>lira</term> <note>the Italian pound</note> and the <term>fiorino</term> <note>florin</note>. The former represented the value of a pound weight of various silver coins. The earliest Florentine pound was likely issued during the reign of Charlemagne. It had a set value of twenty <term>soldi</term> <note>shillings</note>, of twelve <term>denari</term> <note>pence</note> each—which, as hardly needs to be mentioned, was the origin of our own British currency system.

The "florin," which also contained twelve *denari*, first appeared in 1150. Its name was, of course, derived from the name of the city. Originally, it was worth one-twentieth of a pound, and in 1181, it was equal in value to four English pence. Both the florin and the pound, or <term>pezza</term>, were silver coins.

Under another system of valuation, the *lira* was divided into twelve <term>crazie</term>, sixty <term>quattrini</term>, or two hundred and forty *denari*. The following table shows the value of the *lira* in grains of pure silver at various dates:

| | | |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1252—770 grains | 1350—225 $\frac{71}{118}$ grains | 1471—136 grains |
| 1305—391 $\frac{99}{171}$ grains | 1417—140 grains | 1531—100 $\frac{5}{6}$ grains |

The higher figures naturally point to periods of prosperity, while the lower figures indicate seasons of economic depression.

In 1252, "the <term>Signoria</term> <note>the governing body of the Florentine Republic</note> determined," says Peruzzi, "to mint a gold coin like the ancient <note>original: "nummo aures"</note> gold coins, which would be unrivaled in intrinsic value and artistic quality."¹ This coin, which was first given the name <term>Fiorino d'oro</term> <note>Gold Florin</note>, weighed seventy-two grains, or one-eighth of an ounce, and its standard purity was set at twenty-four carats. It bore on its face the image of St. John the Baptist, the city's patron saint, and on the reverse, the floral emblem—the lily, or iris. It was worth about ten English shillings.

¹ Peruzzi, "History of Commerce" <note>original: "Storia del Commercio"</note>, p. 125.

<page-num>571</page-num>
<header>"FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA!" <note>Florence is rich through industry!</note> 571</header>
<columns>2</columns>

In addition to its official name, the coin was known by several other titles based on variations in its shape and market value: the *fiorino di suggello* <note>mint-stamped florin</note>, the *fiorino di galea* <note>exchange florin</note>, and the *fiorino largo* <note>large florin or florin sterling</note>. Regardless of these names, every variety maintained a standard value.

<column-break/>

This magnificent coin was immediately accepted everywhere and served as the model for the gold currencies of England, France, and Spain. The <term>Zecca</term> <note>The Florentine Mint</note> was required to produce as many as four hundred thousand gold florins every year to satisfy the global demand.

As was the case with the silver florin, the face value of the gold florin fluctuated significantly. Initially, it was worth twenty <term>soldi</term> <note>shillings</note>, matching the silver coin, but as early as 1291 its value had risen to thirty *soldi*. In 1301, the Consuls of the Guilds met and established a fixed value of twenty-nine *soldi*. This rate was adopted by the Florentine banks and was recorded as a mandatory standard.¹

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Florentine currency, expanding on the different denominations, their specific uses in society, and the regulations established to prevent counterfeiting and ensure the stability of the exchange market.</meta>

<page-num>572</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

Gold florins from the 1291 valuation, however, remained in extensive circulation, and consequently much confusion followed. By a <term>Provvisione</term> <note>a legislative decree</note>, the new values were designated as "small florins," and their component parts were renamed *piccioli* in place of *soldi* and *denari*.¹

It was after the Fall of the Republic that the gold florin became known as a *ducato*, a *scudo*, or a *corona*.

The silver florin was used for daily market transactions and everyday shopping, whereas the gold florin was reserved for high-level financial business, international exchange, and transportation costs. The salaries of magistrates and officials were also paid in gold. According to the Statutes of 1415: "All merchants and artisans in the City and the <term>Contado</term> <note>the rural territory surrounding Florence</note> are required to use silver and copper coinage, and not the gold florin of commerce, in their dealings among themselves—except for members of the 'Calimala,' 'Wool,' 'Silk,' 'Bankers,' 'Doctors and Apothecaries,' and 'Furriers and Skinners'—the Seven Greater Guilds."²

During the fifteenth century, the smallest coins in circulation were made of bronze: the *piccioli* or *denari*. Four of these made a *quattrino nero* <note>black quattrino</note>—first coined in 1332—and five went to a *quattrino bianco* <note>white quattrino</note>.

*Moneta bianca* <note>white money</note> and *moneta nera* <note>black money</note> or *di rame* <note>made of copper</note>—referring to pure silver money and silver mixed with baser metals—were first distinguished in 1316.

The *quattrino* was the amount of the tax placed upon a barrel of wine at the City Gates. It was also called the "*Battezzone*" <note>Big Baptist</note> and featured the image of Saint John the Baptist on the front, just like the florins. Five *quattrini* made one *crazia*—the twelfth part of a *lira*. These *quattrini* were equal to seven *soldi*, which was also the value of a coin that was little used but whose value was often quoted: the *grosso* or *grossone*.

On March 21, 1307, ordinances were enacted against all those who possessed or passed counterfeit gold, silver, and copper coins, or those who clipped or debased genuine money. Every month, all coins in circulation were ordered to be returned to the Mint for examination and comparison with new, genuine issues. At the same time, all Bankers and Money-changers were directed to keep and prominently display tables of currency values. Such tables also were—

<page-num>573</page-num>
<header>->“FLORENCE RICH THROUGH INDUSTRY!” <note>original: “FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA!”</note><-</header>

...ordered to be posted in the Old Market <note>original: Mercato Vecchio</note>, the New Market <note>original: Mercato Nuovo</note>, at Or San Michele, on the Old Bridge <note>original: Ponte Vecchio</note>, and in other public places.¹

Debased coins were constantly issued by dishonest speculators; these were generally called “*Bargellini*,” a name given to the devalued coinage issued during the four-month term of the <term>Podestà</term> <note>the city's chief magistrate</note>, Lando da Gubbio.

The “*Presto*” <note>literally "Quick," here referring to a lending-office</note>, or Lending-office, had actually existed unofficially in Florence for a very long time before the Government of the Republic addressed the issue and established laws to regulate the borrowing and lending of money. To state the fact more clearly, we might say that every man who had a spare <term>florin</term> or two was, by that very fact <note>original: ipso facto</note>, a “*Presto*!”

In 1430, public attention was effectively directed toward an evil that had grown gradually until it was no longer solvable. The accumulation of money in the hands of bankers, merchants, and similar individuals had reached such vast proportions that the poorer citizens were being crushed under an unbearable yoke, having little or no chance of escaping their misery.

The borrowing of money had become a transparent excuse for demanding exorbitant, usurious interest. At last, the Magistracy took up the matter, and after much debate, they discovered a solution that—though it seems extraordinary to us—was effective. They decided to invite Jews to come and settle in Florence and bring their money with them!²

These cautious money-makers had, of course, made their influence felt all over Europe, but up to that date, they had never been permitted to set foot in Florence. An invitation was sent through the agents of the “*Calimala*” <note>the cloth-merchants' guild</note> and the other Guilds to all centers of Jewish population, extending a cordial welcome to any Jews who possessed wealth and offering them inducements to make Florence their home and their marketplace.

The invitation, it hardly needs to be said, was eagerly accepted, although it was accompanied by some strict and ungracious—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Florentine Republic invited Jewish settlers to the city to provide financial services and address the issue of exorbitant interest rates charged by local Christian lenders.</meta>

<page-num>574</page-num>
<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

restrictions. A Jewish settlement was formed in Oltrarno—which was immediately given the name *Street of the Jews* <note>original: Via dei Giudei</note>. The Jews were compelled by law to wear yellow badges to distinguish them from the citizens. They were forbidden to carry arms and to take part in any way in the government of the City and Republic. They were also forbidden to engage in any wholesale business, and they were denied admittance into the Craft Guilds. Their trading instincts were to be kept within reasonable bounds, and in no case were they allowed to charge interest on loans to citizens exceeding 20 percent.

Despite all these restrictions, the Jews prospered immensely in Florence. Their wealth and influence grew far beyond anything the bankers and merchants could achieve. They had not been in Florence fifty years when they had collectively made upwards of fifty million golden <term>florins</term>!

The discovery of this situation sparked the anger of the general public, who rose up as one and demanded the expulsion of every Jew from Florence. The voice of the people prevailed, as usual, and a decree was issued by the <term>Signoria</term> <note>the city's governing council</note> in 1495, expelling all Jewish inhabitants. However, only a few months passed before fickle public opinion shifted, and the decree was withdrawn.

The Jews, nevertheless, found themselves facing another and even more formidable enemy: the Church. The preaching friars—both Dominicans and Franciscans—spoke out not only against the Jewish moneylenders, but generally against the corrupt practice of charging exorbitant interest rates. Antonino—“the good Archbishop”—Bernardino da Feltre, and Girolamo Savonarola, in turn, denounced the wickedness of the money dealers. Being wise men, they did not just denounce a corrupt system without also proposing improvements. Their ideas were roughly as follows: either (1) loans should be made without any interest at all, or (2) money should be lent in exchange for a pledge <note>collateral</note>, with only a very low interest rate charged to cover the transaction costs.

--- Page 753 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the establishment of a state-run lending institution in Florence, following the advocacy of preaching friars like Bernardino da Feltre who campaigned against high-interest private moneylending.</meta>

<page-num>575</page-num>
<header>-> “FLORENCE RICH THROUGH INDUSTRY!” <note>original: “FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA !”</note> <-</header>

The <term>Signoria</term> <note>the city's governing council</note> were unanimously moved by the pleadings and reasoning of the good monks. They advocated for the adoption of the second suggested plan, aiming to protect the people from the high fees and overcharging of wealthy moneylenders. In fact, the solution reached gave Florence its first pawnshop, or “Presto”—established by state law and further confirmed by Church approval in decrees issued from the Vatican.

The “Presto” began its work in 1495 with a small capital of 2,890 <term>florins</term> <note>gold coins of Florence</note> (about £1,500) collected through private charity, interest-free loans, and deposits. In 1530, following the defeat of the rebels at Pisa, a grant was made to the “Presto” from confiscated property. Consequently, the reserve funds for operating the State Pawnshop increased to over £9,000.

The work of the “*Presto*” expanded quickly. To accommodate the public, three separate offices were opened in different parts of the city. Gradually, another development emerged: several branches of the main offices were authorized. These were managed by private individuals but remained subject to inspection by state officials. These private pawnshops, so to speak, were allowed to stay open when the main offices were closed. Here, people who could not wait for regular business hours could obtain money by leaving items as collateral. These items were transferred daily to the main offices, where only the owners could redeem them.

The pawnshops eventually became a danger to the public, because it became possible for anyone to pose as a branch of the “Presto.” Unsuspecting and trusting clients were often swindled with fees exceeding the legal rate and frequently lost their collateral when these fraudulent pawnbrokers sold their items prematurely.

From the middle of the sixteenth century, the Statutes of the Republic were filled with laws passed to regulate these dishonest practices. For example, no man or woman was allowed to work as a pawnbroker or “Vetturino” <term>vetturino</term> <note>literally a "carrier," here referring to a licensed agent who acted as a middleman for pawned goods</note> unless they held a license.

issued by the Administrator of the “Presto.”<note>1</note> The name “*Vetturino*” <note>Italian: carrier or driver</note> was due to the fact that a “*Vettura*,” <note>Italian: a carriage or vehicle</note> or vehicle, was necessary for the transport of the pledges to the head office day by day.

***

The era of the Medici was the “Golden Age of Florence.”

If the foundations of the <term>Commune</term> <note>the city-state government</note> and of her industry had been well and truly laid, and the superstructure of the Republic and of her commerce wisely and nobly reared, the brains and hands which planned and placed the capstone of the splendid edifice were none other than those of the great merchant-princes—the Medici.

The attitude of the early leaders of the family toward the industry and commerce of Florence was marked by admirable and consistent diligence, loyalty, and enthusiasm. If it is argued that they only sought to serve their own ends, it should be remembered that the pre-eminence, riches, and glory of the family were always the chief aims of all Florentines.

In this typical competition, the Medici did, through natural ability and the force of genius, outrun all competitors. They were entirely sympathetic toward popular aspirations and prejudices. They lived as citizens among citizens, keeping their private affairs unobtrusive and their public conduct unostentatious. Having risen from the middle class, they first entered the profession of medicine, but later took up the more influential occupation of banking.

Salvestro di Alamanno de’ Medici was the first member of the family who rose to eminence. A rich and ambitious *popolano*, <note>Italian: a member of the non-noble, commoner class</note> he

<page-num>577</page-num>
<header>### "FLORENCE RICH THROUGH INDUSTRY!" <note>original: "FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA !"</note></header>

Salvestro de' Medici was tactful enough to conceal his personal inclinations, but he acted upon the maxim he was never tired of quoting:—"Never show off in front of the public."

In 1376 he became *Capitano di Parte Guelfa* <note>Captain of the Guelph Party</note>, and, two years later, *Gonfaloniere di Giustizia* <note>Gonfalonier of Justice</note>—the nominal head of the State. His rivalry with Benedetto degli Alberti drove him to ally with the *Ciompi*—"the wooden shoes"—as the mass of wool industry workers were called. He and the popular leader, Michele Lando, controlled that chaotic uprising and steered the ship of State safely through those troubled waters.

The patriotic and statesmanlike course taken by Salvestro inspired the confidence of the common people, as well as the middle classes—both in himself and in his family. His death in 1388 marked the dawn of the Medici's rule.

Giovanni de' Medici, who was born in 1360, belonged to another branch of the family—that of Averardo de' Medici. He was a man of extraordinary strength of character—a natural ruler of men. He gained the goodwill of his fellow citizens through his unselfishness and generosity.

In 1421, Giovanni was elected *Gonfaloniere di Giustizia* <note>Gonfalonier of Justice</note> as the representative of the middle classes, in opposition to Rinaldo degli Albizzi and Niccolo da Uzzano. The Republic longed for peace and the <term>Crafts</term> <note>the trade guilds</note> for stability, but immense debts, incurred by many costly military campaigns, had to be paid. Giovanni proposed, in 1427, a tax that would not weigh too heavily upon any single group. Each citizen who possessed a capital of one hundred gold florins or more was required to pay the State half a gold florin—equivalent to five shillings. This tax, which was called "*Il Catasto*" <note>the hearth tax or property survey</note>, was unanimously accepted; it was said "it pleased the people greatly." Giovanni himself was taxed as highly as anyone, paying three hundred gold florins.

Giovanni allied himself with Agnolo Pandolfini, the leader of the Peace Party, who is remembered in the history of Florence as "The Peaceful Citizen." The principles of the party were: 1. Peace abroad, 2. Prosperity at home, and 3. Low taxation.

Giovanni was also instrumental in the founding of the *Studio Generale*—the University of Florence—from which such excellent results were gathered by craftsmen of all kinds. He died in 1429.

Cosimo de' Medici—Giovanni's eldest son—was perhaps the greatest member of all that noble family. Born in 1389, he showed mercantile talents early in life and was placed by his father, when he was a mere lad of seventeen, in charge of the foreign agencies and correspondence of the family's banking business. He used his opportunities so well that he quickly surpassed all the men of his house as a successful financier and merchant. He placed the fortunes of his family in such an unassailable position that their bankruptcy would have meant the total and irreversible insolvency of the State.

Cosimo was not unworthily acclaimed as "The Great Merchant." He could provide commercial advantages to all who asked. As the wealthiest citizen, he had absolute control of all markets. Bribes influenced his rivals, while gifts controlled the Church and the poor. He never interfered with the middle classes, but left them to their business and their pleasure. On the other hand, he did all he could to win over the lower classes, carrying on the democratic policy of Salvestro. Assuming the office of *Gonfaloniere di Giustizia* <note>Gonfalonier of Justice; the highest executive office in the Florentine Republic</note> in 1455, he made little or no effort to alter the form of government. His administration of public funds gave rise to the proverb: "Taxation must be used as a dagger!" The introduction in 1447 of the "*Scala*" or "Sliding Scale" <note>A progressive tax system where the tax rate increases as income increases</note> and its application gave this saying its point. For example, incomes of under fifty gold florins were taxed at eight percent, while those over fifteen hundred were taxed at fifty percent.

Cosimo dealt with the luxury and extravagance of his times in a very characteristic way. He persuaded rich merchants to undertake public office as a matter of pride and endowed those roles with increasing dignity and ceremony.

Certainly, perhaps as a counterweight to his own ambitions, he reduced some of the political power of the Guilds. By advancing
