By elevating families rising to wealth from the *Popolo Minuto* <note>The "small people"—the common people or lower classes</note> to association with the Greater Guilds, he checked the exclusive influence of the latter, while he also diminished the growing power of the Lesser Guilds. He used to say jokingly, "Two yards of scarlet cloth is enough to make a citizen!"

Cosimo spent enormous sums of money on charity and on beautifying the city. Every craft felt the impact of his generosity, for his heart and soul were dedicated to the prosperity of his city and its people. The five years of his exile served as a lesson to friend and foe alike—the absence of the Medici family meant ruin and decay.

One of Cosimo's famous sayings was, "One must always consult the will of the people," and "the People" responded by acclaiming him "*Padre della Patria*" <note>Father of the Country</note>. He died in 1464. He has been called "a great merchant and party leader—the first of Florentines by birth, and the first of Italians by culture." He will be remembered forever as a perfect example of the great Florentines of the fifteenth century.

Lorenzo de' Medici became the head of the family when the peak of its glory was at its greatest brilliance. Born in 1449, he entered into his inheritance—a structure of princely magnificence and financial security—as one fully suited for his position. The wealth of his house provided him with the means and the leisure he desired.

Unanimously elected *Capo della Repubblica* <note>Chief of the Republic</note> in 1470, following his grandfather, he emphatically enforced the principle that "the family is the unit of Florentine life." The authority of the *Podesta* <note>The chief magistrate of the city</note> and the judicial power of the *Tribunale della Mercanzia* <note>The Chamber of Commerce</note> were immediately diminished as Lorenzo assumed princely attributes for himself and his heirs.

The combined powers of the Consuls also required reform, and Lorenzo made an effort to reduce the number of the Guilds. This latter move was likely made to prevent the accumulation of capital rather than for political dominance. Regardless, it was

<header>THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE</header>

...aimed principally at the Greater Guilds. Indeed, matters went so far that the liquidation of the assets of the *Parte Guelfa* <note>The Guelph Party, a powerful political faction</note> and of the *Mercanzia* <note>The Court of Merchants</note> was carried out.

Lorenzo’s charities and his patronage of the arts and crafts gained him his title "*Il Magnifico*" <note>original: "The Magnificent"</note>—an acknowledgment of his claim to be addressed as "Your Magnificence." He was much more of a prince than a merchant, and the men who gathered around him thought more of display than of business. In truth, extravagant idleness began to take the place of frugal industry.

Nevertheless, he invited and patronized artisans and talented men from every land. Printing and engraving, embroidered tapestry, cameo engraving, painted porcelain, and many other useful and decorative handicrafts flourished in the Florentine home of their adoption. He himself was entirely lacking in interest or knowledge regarding commercial matters. Indeed, the principal foreign agents of his business house in Paris, Lyons, Bruges, Brussels, London, and elsewhere quickly sized him up and were not slow to profit from his unbusiness-like tendencies.

Lorenzo de’ Medici was by far the greatest of all the Medici in the breadth of his achievements. As a magistrate, orator, poet, artist, benefactor, and athlete, Lorenzo took top honors in the "University of Humanism" which he had so lavishly endowed. He is, so to speak, the epitome of the spirit and life of the Renaissance. His was the era of the Platonic Academy—his villa at Careggi was a second Areopagus <note>The high court of ancient Athens; used here to signify a gathering of great intellectual and moral authority</note>.

In short, there was nothing he could not do. One of his favorite sayings was: "Whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well." This was complemented by his boast: "I am a Florentine, and a Florentine is a citizen of the great world." With the death of Lorenzo de’ Medici in 1492—whom Benedetto Dei describes as: "The splendor not of Tuscany only, but of all Italy"—the most brilliant period of the Renaissance vanished.

Piero de’ Medici, son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, proved to be the

<page-num>581</page-num>
<header>"FLORENCE IS RICH THROUGH INDUSTRY!" <note>original: "FIRENZE RICCA PER INDUSTRIA!"</note></header>

The truth of the adage "Ability rarely runs in two consecutive generations" was proven here. He was just as feeble as his father was strong. Inheriting a unique legacy, he squandered it, and by his weakness of character brought ruin and disaster upon Florence and her commerce. He died miserably in 1503.

The decay of the merchant spirit among the Florentines began with his death. The later Medici, with few exceptions, did nothing to stop the decline of industry and commerce.

Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, during his temporary charge of the city's and the people's destinies in 1518, certainly restored some of her fading glory. He brought the public finances into order, checked the power of monopolies, lightened taxation, restored prestige to the Guilds, and entered into new commercial treaties.

Well-regarded by the common people due to his high position in the church, and by the wealthier citizens because of his name and family, he was wise enough to distance himself from all the political factions in the State. "It was," records Nardi the historian, "the universal opinion that never since the city had been under the rule of the Medici had it been governed with a greater appearance of civil liberty."¹ In 1523, Giulio became Pope, taking the name of Clement VII, and died in Rome in 1534.

---

Beginning in the middle of the sixteenth century, three conditions existed which made the position of Florence uncertain and even precarious:

1. The instability of political institutions.
2. The insecurity of property due to frequent commercial failures.
3. The competition of other markets and the discovery of America.

Regarding the latter, it is easy to understand how dreams of the New World distracted men's attention from the steady pursuit of their usual occupations. The dis-

World. Dante, in a mystic vision, had foretold this new terrestrial paradise with a prophetic voice as far back as 1306:
> “I turned to the right and focused my mind 
> Attentively on the other Pole, where I saw 
> Four stars never seen before except by the eyes 
> Of our first parents. Heaven seemed joyous 
> From their rays.” — “PURGATORIO,” canto i.

With the beginning of the sixteenth century, a new era dawned, brightening the sky of poetry and the arts as well as the river of literature and the crafts. The preliminary signs had made themselves felt in the growth of wealth, in the freedom from old prejudices, and in the release from primitive rules of living. Egotistical tendencies, which had been working very quietly but surely, prepared the way for the evolution of what we now call “Individualism.”

Here we have the limits and the markers of the Spirit of the Renaissance. Patriotism and family ties were weakened by a universal craving for pleasure and self-gratification. Idleness, sensuality, and skepticism—three harmful sisters—gained the upper hand and loosened the fabric of Florentine society.

The gradual disappearance of public spirit, the slow deterioration of general character, and the draining of personal energy are the dull tones that color the later pages of Florentine history with melancholy.

Bring down the curtain! The merchant and the artisan have taken off their everyday garments of leather, cloth, and fustian <term>A thick, durable twilled cloth, usually made of cotton and linen</term>! The ghosts of the Guildsmen pass silently along, stretching out their hands helplessly: their time has come and gone! But listen! Into the slumbers of the past, the softest, sweetest music steals, and many melodious Tuscan voices are singing in unison:
*“Florence—rich through industry!”* <note>original: "Firenze—ricca per industria!"</note>
*“Florence—Queen of the Arts!”* <note>original: "Firenze—Regina dell’ Arti!"</note>
*“Florence the Beautiful!”* <note>original: "Firenze la Bella!"</note>
*“Long live Florence the Beautiful!—the Beautiful!”* <note>original: "Evviva! Firenze la Bella!—la Bella!"</note>

<page-num>226</page-num>

### THE LIFE OF SIR THOMAS MORE.

Despite all his virtues and all his learning, he was not superior to the prejudices of his age; and, from a mistaken sense of religious duty, he became a persecutor.

While he was Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and the King's chief adviser, he had been most active in the persecution of the Lutherans <note>Followers of Martin Luther and the Protestant Reformation</note>; and, when he became Chancellor of England, his zeal against heresy was even more conspicuous. There were many cases in which, it is said, he directed the torture of those who were suspected of holding heretical opinions.

The next great event in the history of More is the publication of his *Utopia* <note>original: "Utopia" — More's famous work describing an ideal island society</note>. This was written in Latin and published at Basel <note>OCR: "Basle"</note> in 1516. It is one of the most remarkable books of that age.

Nothing shows the simplicity of More's character better than his conduct toward his father, Sir John More. The old man, who was a judge of the Court of King's Bench, used to sit in the court during the legal term; and whenever his son, the Lord Chancellor, passed through the court, he would stop to ask his father's blessing.

> ...King down the street of London, that these have put on their worldly garments and return in a state of gladness, even as though—along with their adversity—they may have and enjoy the substance of the joys that remain there, and many joys that they have enjoyed in lesser ways...

# CHRONOLOGY

## B.C.
200. Roman Camp of Florence <note>original: "Florentia"</note>
     The Flaminian Road assists early development and crosses the Arno River by
     the earliest <term>Old Bridge</term> <note>original: "Ponte Vecchio"</note>.

## A.D.
488. Baptistery of Saint John <note>original: "San Giovanni"</note> founded.
542. Totila, King of the Goths, besieges the settlement.
556. First Wall—<note>original: "Primo Cerchio"</note>—built.
625. Theodelinda, Queen of the Lombards, encourages industry.
724. Church of Saint Reparata <note>original: "Santa Reparata"</note> so named.
774. Church of Saint Minias on the Mountain <note>original: "San Miniato al Monte"</note> built.
786. Charlemagne, Emperor of the West, visits the town.
816. Pope Leo III encourages the crafts of Tuscany.
825. A <term>College of Arts</term> <note>original: "Collegium Artium"</note> founded under Emperor Lothair’s <term>Constitutions of Olona</term> <note>original: "Constitutiones Olonenses"</note>.
852. Wool trade flourishing in Florence.
934. Medical faculty in practice.
962. Otto I extends the <term>surrounding territory</term> <note>original: "Contado"</note> to a six-mile radius.
990. Benedictines settle and build the <term>Abbey</term> <note>original: "Badia"</note>.
1003. Florentine cloth merchants finish the Church of Saint Minias on the Mountain <note>original: "San Miniato al Monte"</note>.
1036. Boniface <note>original: "Bonifazio"</note> III, Marquis of Tuscany, a friend to Florence.
1038. Smithing and kindred trades flourishing.
,,   "Consuls" first named (Burello, Florenzetto, Broccada, and Servolo).
1062. Fulling mill first mentioned.
1063. Great Religious Revival.
1074-78. Second Wall—<note>original: "Secondo Cerchio"</note>—begun; the <term>district across the Arno</term> <note>original: "Oltrarno"</note> is incorporated.
1076. Countess Matilda of Tuscany greatly encourages crafts.
1079. <term>Old Market</term> <note>original: "Mercato Vecchio"</note> first so called.
1080. Old Roman bridge rebuilt in stone and called the <term>Old Bridge</term> <note>original: "Ponte Vecchio"</note>.
1096. First wool dyer named, Peter the Dyer <note>original: "Petrus-tentore"</note>.
1101. Consuls for the crafts first appointed by Matilda.
1107. Expansion of the city: Monte Orlandi and Prato incorporated.
1115. Death of Matilda; birth of the Commune—Florence declared independent
     of all external rule.
1138. City divided into six wards—<note>original: "Sestieri"</note>; <term>Good Men</term> <note>original: "Buonuomi"</note> are elected for each.
1150. Silver Florin first used.
,,   <term>Calimala Guild</term> <note>The Calimala was the guild of merchants who refined and dyed imported cloth</note> consuls take charge of the <term>Baptistery of Saint John</term> <note>original: "Battisterio di San Giovanni"</note>.
1154. First record of Florentine merchants trading with Great Britain—chiefly
     wool.
1165-1177. "Society of the Towers" for the <term>nobility</term> <note>original: "Grandi"</note>, and "Corporations" for
     the <term>common people</term> <note>original: "Popolani"</note> established.

<summary>This page provides a chronological timeline of Florence's history from 200 B.C. to 1177 A.D., highlighting key milestones in its architecture, governance, and the rise of its wool and craft guilds. It tracks the city's evolution from a Roman camp into an independent commune protected by two successive rings of walls.</summary>

--- Page 781 ---
<meta>This page continues the chronological history of Florence, moving from the 11th century into the late 12th and mid-13th centuries. It highlights the formalization of the guild system, the establishment of legal and financial institutions, and the beginning of the political conflict between the Guelphs and Ghibellines.</meta>

# CHRONOLOGY

1183. The Peace of Constance confirms self-government for Florence and other Tuscan <term>Communes</term> <note>Self-governing city-states</note>.
1187. College of Judges founded.
1190. First mention in documents of the "Calimala Guild" <note>The guild of merchants who refined and sold foreign cloth</note>.
1192. Frederick I <note>original: "Federigo I"</note> visits Florence and extends the <term>surrounding territory</term> <note>original: "Contado"</note> to a radius of ten miles.
" Consuls of the <term>Wool</term> <note>original: "Lana"</note>, <term>Refined Cloth</term> <note>original: "Calimala"</note>, and <term>Silk</term> <note>original: "Seta"</note> Guilds sign documents—the first of such records.
1193. The title "Rector" replaces that of Consul.
1194. First record of Florentine Bankers.
1197. Legal Tribunals fully established.
" First distinct mention of the Seven Greater Guilds—the Calimala Guild being entirely separated from that of the Wool Guild.
1198. The Tuscan League, under the leadership of Florence, is established by Pope Innocent III at <term>Saint Minias on the Mountain</term> <note>original: "San Miniato al Monte"</note>.
1199. First recorded mission of Florentine Bankers to London.
1200. Commercial Treaty with the Lords of the Mugello for the protection of trade routes.
" The silk industry is in a thriving condition. Early patterns for weaving were obtained from the pavement of the Baptistery.
1201. First mention of the Guild of Bankers.
1202. Florentines capture castles and protect various <term>Communes</term> <note>Self-governing towns</note>.
1204. The Rectors of the Guilds are styled "Priors."
" Ammirato's census of the population and occupations.
1206. The old title of Consul replaces that of Prior.
1207. The first <term>Chief Magistrate</term> <note>original: "Podesta"</note>—Gualfredotto Grasselli of Milan—is elected.
1208–1228. Wars with Pisa, Pistoia <note>original: "Pistoja"</note>, Semifonte, Siena, and other cities.
1215. A tragedy at the Buondelmonte-Amidei marriage originates the two great political parties—the Guelphs and Ghibellines.
1218. College of Doctors and Apothecaries in existence.
" The <term>Carraja Bridge</term> <note>original: "Ponte alla Carraja"</note> is built in stone.
" Inhabitants of the <term>surrounding territory</term> <note>original: "Contado"</note> are required to take an oath of allegiance to Florence.
1222. The first <term>Public Bank</term> <note>original: "Monte Comune"</note> or pawnshop opened.
1223. School of Medicine and Surgery founded.
1228. First State enactment affecting the Guilds is issued.
1233. The <term>Chief Magistrate</term> <note>original: "Podesta"</note>—Torcello da Strada—orders every adult male to register his name, age, and occupation.
1234. Mercantile companies affiliated with the various Guilds.
1236. First scheduled list of the Guilds—totaling twenty-one.
" Influential positions held by butchers and graziers.
" Streets of Florence paved with hard stone paving blocks.
1237. The <term>Bridge of Graces</term> <note>original: "Ponte alle Grazie"</note>—also known as Rubaconte—is built.
1238. The "Umiliati"—or Humble Fathers—arrive and settle <note>A religious order instrumental in the wool trade</note>.
1240. The "Misericordia" <note>A charitable brotherhood</note> founded.
1247–49. Party feuds and the encroachments of Frederick II <note>original: "Federigo II"</note> and of the Uberti family hinder trade and commerce.
1250. <term>Chief Magistrate</term> <note>original: "Podesta"</note> deposed—a <term>Captain of the People</term> <note>original: "Capitano del Popolo"</note> is appointed instead.
" Foreign <term>mercenary commanders</term> <note>original: "Condottieri"</note> first employed.

It documents key infrastructure projects like stone bridges and paved streets, alongside the creation of social institutions like the Misericordia.</summary>

-># THE GUILDS OF FLORENCE<-

1250. Thirty-six trade representatives are chosen—six for each <term>district</term> <note>original: "Sestiere"</note>—forming the first truly popular government of Florence.
1251. Uberto da Lucca is elected as the first <term>Captain of the People</term> <note>original: "Capitano del Popolo"</note>.
1252. The <term>Mint</term> <note>original: "Zecca"</note> is established. The Great Gold Florin is coined.
1252. The Holy Trinity Bridge <note>original: "Ponte alla Santa Trinita"</note> is built.
1254. Pisa grants free import rights for all Florentine goods.
1258. The <term>Bargello</term> <note>The headquarters of the Captain of the People and later a prison</note> is built.
1260. <term>Letters of Exchange</term> <note>original: "Lettere di Cambio"; early versions of bank checks or bills of exchange</note> are first issued by bankers.
1260. The Roman-era Old Bridge <note>original: "Ponte Vecchio"</note> is rebuilt.
1260. Battle of Montaperti.
1261. Count Guido Novello assumes supreme authority.
1261. The public prison—known as the <term>Stinche</term>—is opened.
1266. A second official list of the seven "Greater" and fourteen "Lesser" Guilds is issued.
1266. The Consuls of the seven Greater Guilds constitute the supreme governing body of the state.
1267. The <term>Guelph Party</term> <note>original: "Parte Guelfa"; the political faction supporting the Pope</note> is officially enrolled.
1267. First record of a Florentine commercial journey in Europe, undertaken by Guido del Antella.
1267. The Council of the <term>Heads of the Greater Guilds</term> <note>original: "Capitudini delle Arti Maggiori"</note> is established.
1267. Charles of Anjou, Lord of Florence, creates many new knights.
1269. Disastrous floods destroy bridges, factories, and other property.
1271–79. Serious family and political party feuds are prevalent. These do not hinder industry, but rather act as spurs to enterprise!
1278. Taddeo d'Alderotti is established as Professor of Medicine in Florence.
1280. The first <term>Lordship</term> <note>original: "Signoria"; the executive council of the Republic</note> assumes office.
1280. The first five Lesser Guilds are designated as <term>Intermediate Guilds</term> <note>original: "Arti Mediane"</note>, and their Consuls are admitted to the conferences of the Consuls of the seven Greater Guilds.
1282. Three "Priors of the Guilds" are elected; their powers are second only to those of the Chief Magistrate of the State.
1282. The Wool Guild <note>original: "Arte della Lana"</note> takes charge of the cathedral of <term>Saint Mary of the Flower</term> <note>original: "Santa Maria del Fiore"</note>.
1283. A third official list of the Guilds is issued, settling their order of precedence.
1284–85. The <term>Third Circle</term> <note>original: "Tertio Cerchio"</note> of city walls is built.
1284. Many new mercantile companies are added to the city's registers.
1285. The Hospital of <term>New Saint Mary</term> <note>original: "Santa Maria Nuova"</note> is founded.
1287. The square of Saint John <note>original: "Piazza di San Giovanni"</note> is enlarged for the festival of the patron saint.
1287. Feuds between the Cerchi and Donati families hinder public work.
1289. A great fire destroys many workshops and a large amount of merchandise.
1289. Battle of Campaldino.
1289. Slavery is abolished in Florence.
1291. Many miracles are reported at the Shrine of <term>Saint Michael in the Orchard</term> <note>original: "Or San Michele"</note>.
1291. Banners and coats of arms are granted to the nine lowest Guilds.
1292. Giano della Bella rises to power.
1293. The <term>Ordinances of Justice</term> <note>original: "Ordinamenti di Giustizia"</note> are promulgated <note>A set of laws designed to curb the power of the nobility and empower the guilds</note>.
1294. Construction begins on the Cathedral <note>original: "Duomo"</note>, the Old Palace <note>original: "Palazzo Vecchio"</note>, Santa Maria Novella, and Santa Croce.
1294–1310. Arnolfo di Cambio, the great builder and architect, reaches the height of his career.

<summary>This page provides a chronological timeline of Florence from 1250 to 1294, highlighting the creation of the Gold Florin, the rising political power of the trade guilds, and the commencement of major architectural landmarks like the Duomo and Palazzo Vecchio.</summary>

<page-num>603</page-num>

->### CHRONOLOGY<-

1296. "**The Statute**" <note>original: "Il Statuto"</note> was issued as a tentative General Code for the Guilds, coinciding approximately with the founding of the **Court of Commerce** <note>original: "Corte della Mercanzia"</note>.
1296. The Calimala Guild established many agencies in France.
1300. Many countries were represented at the Jubilee of Pope Boniface III <note>Historically Pope Boniface VIII; the text records III</note> by Florentines serving as ambassadors.
1300. A feud broke out between the "**Blacks**" and "**Whites**" <note>original: "Neri e Bianchi"</note> political factions.
1300. Dante Alighieri was elected Prior and was instrumental in expelling the leaders of both the **Blacks** and the **Whites**.
1301–1307. A full revision of the Statutes of all the Guilds was conducted. The New Code was first adopted by the "Calimala" Guild.
1305–1377. The Papal Schism occurred <note>The period of the Avignon Papacy</note>. This led to increased activities and privileges for Florentine Bankers.
1307. The Piazza della Signoria was laid out and paved.
1310. The city walls and moats were finished. This was a period of great scarcity and poor trade.
1312. A census and description of Florence were compiled by Dino Compagni.
1313. King Robert of Naples was named Lord of Florence.
1315. Many silk-workers from Lucca settled in Florence.
1315–1327. Francesco Balducci served as the agent of the Bardi family in Flanders and other locations.
1318. Troubles occurred among the wool workers.
1320. The **University of Florence** <note>original: "Studio di Firenze"</note> was founded.
1322. The constitution of the subordinate Guild of Goldsmiths was revised by officials of the "**Por Santa Maria**" <note>The Gate of Saint Mary Guild, which oversaw the silk trade and several smaller crafts</note>.
1324. The first official Register of Florentine merchants residing abroad was created.
1325. Charles, Duke of Calabria, was named Lord of Florence.
1326. The Scali Bank failed, losing 400,000 gold florins.
1328. A revision of the **Selection Process** <note>original: "Squittino"; the method of determining eligibility for public office</note> took place.
1328. The **Council of the People** <note>original: "Consiglio del Popolo"</note> and the **Council of the Commune** <note>original: "Consiglio del Comune"</note> were empanelled.
1329. The Statutes of the Society of Painters and the Society of Goldsmiths were passed.
1329. The **Public Platform** <note>original: "Ringhiera"</note> was fixed outside the Palazzo Vecchio.
1330. The factory doors of the **Humiliati** <note>original: "Umiliati"; a religious order famous for wool production</note> were closed by the General of the Order.
1335. "**The Old Statute**" <note>original: "Il Statuto Vecchio"</note> of the Silk Guild was promulgated.
1336. An alliance was formed between Florence and Venice.
1336. The Shrine of Or San Michele was decorated by the Guilds.
1336. A new Ponte Vecchio was built by Taddeo Gaddi.
1339. Florentine merchants were expelled from France.
1339. The Guild of Painters was incorporated.
1339. The first record appears of resident Florentine Consular Agents at foreign ports.
1339. The Bardi and Peruzzi Banks suffered disastrous failures.
1340. The Bell Tower <note>original: "Campanile"</note> was projected by Giotto.
1335–1410. Francesco Sacchetti, known as "The Echo of the Old Market!"
1342. The Duke of Athens, appointed Conservator of the Peace and Lord of Florence, favored the **Nobility** <note>original: "Grandi"</note> and the **Merchant Citizens** <note>original: "Popolani"</note> in turn.
1343. The Buonaccorsi Bank failed.
1343. An attack was made by the **Merchant Citizens** on the palaces of the **Nobility**.
1343. The **Lower Classes** <note>original: "Popolo Minuto"</note> rose to power.
1343. Niccolo Acciaiuoli founded the Carthusian Monastery <note>original: "Certosa"</note> at Montaguta for fifty apprentice youths.

<summary>This page outlines a timeline of 14th-century Florence, highlighting the codification of guild laws, the growth of the University, and the devastating bank failures of the Bardi and Peruzzi families. It also tracks the political instability involving the Duke of Athens and the shifting power between the nobility and the common people.</summary>
